a-coruna: A Coruña lies on a promontory in the Golfo Ártabro, a large gulf of the Atlantic. The oldest quarter, the Cidade Vella, is built on an ancient Celtic castro, supposedly inhabited by the Brigantes and Artabrians, and the city spread from the peninsula that later held the Tower of Hercules onto the mainland. The origin of the name is unclear; it seems to come from Crunia, first documented in the reign of Ferdinand II of León (1157–1188). English speakers once called the city The Groyne.

The Romans came to the region in the 2nd century BCE, and the town, then called Brigantium, grew in maritime trade. The Tower of Hercules was built during the 1st and 2nd centuries, but the town declined after the 4th century, and between the 7th and 8th centuries it was no more than a small village of labourers and sailors. In 1520 King Charles I of Spain met the courts at A Coruña and embarked from its harbour to be elected Holy Roman Emperor as Charles V. In 1589 María Pita was a heroine of the defence of the city against the English Armada.

On 30 November 1803 an expedition led by Francisco Javier Balmis left the port to spread the smallpox vaccine in America. In May 1808 the city rose against the French occupation, and on 16 January 1809 the Battle of Corunna was fought, in which General Sir John Moore was killed. During the first Carlist war the city, siding with the liberal cause, was never taken, and Queen Isabella II made it a provincial capital in 1849. In 1936 the army officers who backed the military coup took the city at once, and a bloody repression followed.

A Coruña is the capital of its province and the second-largest city of Galicia after Vigo, with a population of 251,277. It was the political capital of the Kingdom of Galicia from the 16th to the 19th centuries. The Tower of Hercules, a lighthouse in continuous operation since possibly the 2nd century CE, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the emblem of the city's flag. The University of A Coruña was established in 1989.
aachen: Aachen is the westernmost major city in Germany, about 61 km west of Cologne and Bonn, directly bordering Belgium and the Netherlands. It lies in the Meuse–Rhine Euroregion, at the northern foothills of the High Fens and the Eifel Mountains, on the Wurm River. Its name descends from Old High German ahha, meaning water or stream, which corresponds to the Latin Aquae and refers to the warm mineral springs that attracted settlers from the Neolithic era. The Latin name Aquae Granni meant the waters of Grannus, a Celtic god of healing worshipped at the springs.

Flint quarries used from about 3000 to 2500 BCE attest to the long occupation of the site. Roman settlers equipped the springs with several thermae around the 1st century. After the Roman troops withdrew, the settlement came under Frankish control around the 5th century, and later under Merovingian and Carolingian rule.

Pepin the Short had a castle residence built there, near the hot springs and between the Rhineland and northern France. Charlemagne first spent Christmas at Aachen in 768, the year of his coronation as king of the Franks. With the completion of the Carolingian Palace at the turn of the 9th century, the city became the main royal residence of the Frankish Empire, and it is sometimes called the cradle of Europe. After the Treaty of Verdun it lay in Middle Francia, and it became part of East Francia after the Treaty of Meerssen in 870.

From the early 16th century Aachen began to lose power and influence, and the coronations of emperors were moved to Frankfurt. The Peace of Lunéville of 9 February 1801 gave Aachen and the left bank of the Rhine to France, and in 1815 the Congress of Vienna passed it to the Kingdom of Prussia.

Aachen has around 264,000 inhabitants and is home to RWTH Aachen University, one of Germany's leading technological universities. Aachen Cathedral was begun about 796 on Charlemagne's orders and completed about 798. It was the largest cathedral north of the Alps, modelled on the Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna and built by Odo of Metz. Charlemagne was interred there on his death, and his remains can be seen there to this day.
aachen-cathedral: Charlemagne began the Palatine Chapel around 796 with the rest of the palace buildings, and the work is credited to Odo of Metz. A letter from Alcuin in 798 says it was nearing completion, and Pope Leo III consecrated it in 805. The octagon followed Byzantine models such as the Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna and the Little Hagia Sophia in Constantinople.

The design was a domed octagonal inner room, 14.46 metres across, enveloped by a sixteen-sided outer wall, with a high gallery called the Hochmünster. The high altar and imperial throne stood on the upper level. Its span and height were unsurpassed north of the Alps for over two hundred years.

Charlemagne died on 28 January 814 and was buried in the chapel, though the exact spot is unknown and he was probably laid in the Persephone sarcophagus. Otto III had the vault opened in the year 1000, and the Chronicle of Novalesia, written about 1026, reports that the emperor was found seated and crowned. Frederick Barbarossa reopened it in 1165 at Charlemagne's canonisation, and in 1215 Frederick II placed the remains in the gold and silver Karlsschrein, where they remain.

Between 936 and 1531 thirty-one German kings ascended the throne in the western gallery after their coronation at the altar of Mary. The Carolingian throne used material from the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. After Charlemagne's canonisation, an enormous flow of pilgrims led to the Gothic choir hall of 1355, and the relics in the Marienschrein of 1220–1239 have been shown every seven years since 1349.

The chapel was admired and imitated in the Middle Ages, in Essen Minster, the Old Tower at Mettlach and the abbey church at Ottmarsheim. It suffered a Viking raid in 881 and was restored in 983, lost its entire roof in the Fire of Aachen of 1656, and had its Baroque stucco removed in 1881. In the Second World War Allied bombing and ground fighting heavily damaged the city; the basic structure of the cathedral survived, but the 14th-century choir glazing, the Gothic Revival altar, much of the cloister and the Holiness Chapel were destroyed. Reconstruction took more than 30 years.
aarau: Aarau lies on the Swiss Plateau, in the valley of the Aare, on the river's right bank and at the southern foot of the Jura Mountains. It is 58 kilometres south of Basel and 65 kilometres northeast of Bern, and its municipality borders the canton of Solothurn to the west. The old city stands on a rocky outcrop at a narrowing of the valley, with newer districts to the south and east. The name goes back to Arowe, first recorded in 1248, and comes, like the name of the Aare, from the German word Au, meaning floodplain.

A few Neolithic artefacts have been found, and ruins of a Bronze Age settlement of about 1000 BCE were excavated near the present railway station. The Roman road between Salodurum (Solothurn) and Vindonissa passed through the area, and in 1976 divers found part of a seven-metre-wide wooden bridge of late Roman times in the Aare. The counts of Kyburg founded the town around 1240. It is first mentioned in 1248, and the first mention of a city-sized settlement dates to 1256.

The Kyburg line died out in 1273, and Agnes of Kyburg, who had no male relations, sold the family's lands to King Rudolf I von Habsburg, who granted Aarau its city rights in 1283. In the 14th century the town was extended in two stages and a second wall was built, with a deep ditch, now the street called Graben, separating it from its suburb. The buildings of the old town mostly come from the 16th century, when nearly all the medieval buildings were replaced or enlarged, and its growth within the walls ended in the 18th century. The Schlössli, founded shortly after 1200, is the oldest building, and the city hall was built around the Rore tower in 1515.

Aarau is the capital of the canton of Aargau and of the district of Aarau, and the largest town in the canton. It is German-speaking and predominantly Protestant, and the cantonal government is its largest employer. It is known for its painted gables, and its old town, the cantonal library, the state archive and the art museum are listed as heritage sites of national significance. The Kern & Co. firm, founded in 1819, made geodetic instruments there until it closed in 1991. Its population peaked at 17,045 in 1960, more than five times that of 1800.
aare: The Aare is the main tributary of the High Rhine; at their confluence its discharge even exceeds the Rhine's. From its source to the Rhine it is about 295 km long, descends 1,565 m and drains 17,779 square kilometres, almost entirely in Switzerland, close to half the country including all of Central Switzerland. It rises in the Aare Glaciers of the Bernese Alps, west of the Grimsel Pass, where the Finsteraargletscher and Lauteraargletscher join to form the Unteraargletscher, the main source of the Grimselsee. The river then flows northwest through the Haslital, forming the 46 m Handegg Waterfall.
The name goes back at least to the La Tène period; the river is attested as Nantaror, meaning Aare valley, on the Berne zinc tablet. Its Latin forms were Arula, Arola and Araris.

Past Innertkirchen the river carves through a limestone ridge in the Aare Gorge, where causeways attract thousands of visitors. It widens into Lake Brienz, crosses the plain of the Bödeli between Interlaken and Unterseen, and enters Lake Thun, the head of navigation. It then passes through Thun and Bern, where it flows beneath eighteen bridges and around the peninsula holding the Old City. It continues past Solothurn, Aarburg, Olten, Aarau and Wildegg, and below Brugg receives its major tributary the Reuss and then its second strongest, the Limmat. It turns north and joins the Rhine opposite Waldshut in Germany.

More than 40 hydroelectric plants stand along the Aare, among them the small Matte plant in Bern, fed by the Mattenschwelle weir. River swimming in the Aare is popular in Bern, and the water is sometimes full of bathers on summer days.
aargau: Aargau is one of the most northerly cantons of Switzerland and takes its name from the lower course of the Aare River, Aar-gau meaning 'Aare province'. It borders Germany to the north, with the Rhine forming the boundary, and the cantons of Basel-Landschaft, Solothurn and Bern to the west, Lucerne to the south, and Zürich and Zug to the east. Its area is 1,404 square kilometres. It forms part of the Swiss Plateau, north of the Alps and east of the Jura, and is one of the least mountainous cantons. The Aare, the Reuss and the Rhine are its large rivers, and it has hot sulphur springs at Baden and Schinznach-Bad and saline springs at Rheinfelden.

The area was controlled by the Helvetians, a tribe of Celts, as far back as 200 BCE. It was later occupied by the Romans, who built a major settlement, Vindonissa, near the present Brugg, and by the 6th century by the Franks. The Old High German name Argowe is first clearly attested, as Argue, in 795, and described a territory only loosely equivalent to the modern canton. It stretched between the Aare and the Reuss and took in parts of the present cantons of Bern, Solothurn, Basel-Landschaft, Lucerne, Obwalden and Nidwalden, but not the Baden district east of the Reuss, which belonged to Zürichgau.

Within the Frankish Empire the area was a disputed border region between the duchies of Alamannia and Burgundy. A line of the von Wetterau, the Conradines, held the countship of Aargau intermittently from 750 until about 1030. When the Holy Roman Empire formed in the later 10th century this became its sparsely settled outer border. By about 1200 most of the region was controlled by the ducal house of Zähringen and the comital houses of Habsburg and Kyburg. The canton's flag and arms date to 1803, an original design by Samuel Ringier-Seelmatter.

Aargau is one of the 26 cantons of the Swiss Confederation and has eleven districts. Its capital is Aarau, on its western border. It is one of the most densely populated regions of Switzerland and its population speaks mainly German. Its farmland is among the most fertile in the country, and three of Switzerland's five nuclear power plants and many hydroelectric plants stand in the canton, which is often called the energy canton. Near Brugg lie the ruined castle of Habsburg, the old convent of Königsfelden with its painted medieval glass, and the remains of Vindonissa at Windisch.
abacus: An abacus is a two-dimensional array of slidable beads or similar objects. In the earliest designs the beads lay loose on a flat surface or slid in grooves, and later they were made to slide on rods in a frame, which allowed faster handling. Each rod usually stands for one digit of a number in a positional system. Roman and East Asian abacuses resemble bi-quinary coded decimal, with a top deck of one or two beads for fives and a bottom deck of four or five beads for ones. One abacus supports several methods of addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and square and cube roots. The word is first recorded in Middle English in 1387, from Latin, which took it from Greek abax.

The earliest evidence for the Greek abacus dates to the fifth century BCE, and a table of wood or marble with small counters spread through Achaemenid Persia, the Etruscan world and Rome. Writing in the first century BCE, Horace refers to a wax abacus. A Roman example of the first century CE has eight long grooves with up to five beads each, marked from units up to millions, and eight shorter grooves for fives. The Roman system of counter casting was widely used in medieval Europe, and wealthy users had decorative minted counters called jetons.

The earliest written mention of the Chinese abacus, the suanpan, dates to the second century BCE. A painting of the Song dynasty, Along the River During the Qingming Festival, shows one beside an account book on an apothecary's counter. The soroban was brought to Japan from China in the fourteenth century, and the abacus reached Korea around 1400.

Pope Sylvester II reintroduced the abacus with beads on wires, so that it came into wide use again in eleventh-century Europe. It was widely used there as late as the seventeenth century, until decimal notation and written methods of calculation replaced it. The Russian abacus, the schoty, has a slanted deck with ten beads on each wire, one wire having four beads for quarter-rubles, and was used in shops and markets until the 1990s. The mathematician Jean-Victor Poncelet, who had been a prisoner of war in Russia, brought it to France around 1820 as a teaching aid.
abazins: The Abazins, also called Abazinians or Abaza, are an ethnic group of the Northwest Caucasus, closely related to the Abkhaz and Circassian peoples. They speak the Abaza language, a Northwest Caucasian language most closely related to Abkhaz and more distantly related to Ubykh and Circassian. Two dialects, Ashkharua and Tapanta, are spoken in Karachay-Cherkessia. The Tapanta, a branch of the Abaza, lived between the Besleney and Kabardian princedoms on the upper Kuban. Their culture and traditions are similar to those of the Circassians, and on many old maps Abazin territory is marked as part of Circassia.

Today the Abazins live mostly in Turkey, Syria, Jordan and Egypt, and in Karachay-Cherkessia and Stavropol Krai in the North Caucasus region of Russia. This scattering is attributed to atrocities committed by Imperial Russia during the Circassian genocide. The diaspora in Turkey, Egypt and the Middle East is largely descended from muhajirs, refugees from the Caucasian War with the Russian Empire.

Most of the Abazins in Turkey belong to the Ashkharua clan, which fought against the tsarist army and emigrated after losing the battle of Kbaada, at what is now Krasnaya Polyana in Sochi. The Tapanta clan fought on the Russian side. An estimated 150,000 Abaza live in Turkey, in the provinces of Eskişehir, Samsun, Yozgat, Adana, Kayseri and Sakarya and in İzmit and İstanbul. A large Egyptian clan, the Abaza family, is a prominent example in Egypt.

Historically the Abazins engaged in animal herding and some farming. They are predominantly Sunni Muslims. They first met Islam during their migrations to the region of Abazinia, through contact with the Nogais and other Muslim peoples, and adopted it under the influence of Muslim merchants and missionaries between the 16th and 19th centuries.
abbas-ibn-firnas: Abū al-Qāsim ʿAbbās ibn Firnās ibn Wardās al-Tākurunnī, who lived from about 809 or 810 to 887, was an Andalusi polymath: an inventor, astronomer, physician, chemist, engineer, musician and poet. Scholarly consensus holds that he was born in Ronda, in the province of Takurunna, lived in Córdoba and was an Umayyad mawlā, or client, of Berber descent. His lineage may have been linked to the early Muslim conquests of the Iberian Peninsula. Later accounts that stress Arabic contributions to science may describe him as a muladí.

Ibn Firnas devised a way of making colourless glass, made glass planispheres and corrective lenses known as reading stones, and built an apparatus with a chain of objects that simulated the motions of the planets and stars. He developed a process for cutting rock crystal, which allowed al-Andalus to stop exporting quartz to Egypt to be cut. He introduced the Sindhind to al-Andalus, with an influence on astronomy in Europe, and designed a water clock, the al-Maqata, and a prototype of a metronome.

He is also reported to have experimented with unpowered flight. The earliest known account is in a manuscript of the Cordoban court chronicle al-Muqtabis II, attributed to Ibn Hayyan, which says he covered himself in feathers fastened to silk, fitted two wings, rose into the air from near Rusafa, circled and landed far away, but injured his tailbone because he had not accounted for how birds land on their tails. The Algerian historian Ahmad al-Maqqari, writing some seven centuries later, gave a fuller version without naming his sources. Anderson reads the earlier account as describing a fixed-wing glide, while Richard Hallion thinks a medieval parachute drop with a cloak more likely.
A story that he watched a man called Armen Firman jump from a tower about twenty years earlier rests on limited secondary sources, and Armen Firman may be a Latinized form of his own name.

Ibn Firnas died in 887. In 1973 a statue of him by Badri al-Samarrai was installed at Baghdad International Airport, and in 1976 the International Astronomical Union named a lunar crater after him. The Abbas ibn Firnás Bridge in Córdoba, completed in 2011, bears his name.
abbas-ii-of-egypt: Abbas Hilmy was born in Alexandria on 14 July 1874, a great-great-grandson of Muhammad Ali. He was educated by British tutors in Cairo, including a governess who taught him English, and by European, Arab and Ottoman masters at a school his father set up near the Abdin Palace. He then attended school at Lausanne and Geneva, in preparation for the Theresianum in Vienna. Besides Arabic and Ottoman Turkish, he spoke English, French and German. He was still a student in Vienna when his father, Tewfik Pasha, died suddenly and he became Khedive on 8 January 1892, barely of age by Egyptian law.

Britain had occupied Egypt since 1882, and the young khedive resented the interference of the British Agent and Consul General, Sir Evelyn Baring, who became Lord Cromer in June 1892. Surrounded by European advisers who opposed the occupation, he tried to replace his prime minister with a nationalist, and the British Foreign Secretary wrote that he must consult the consul on cabinet appointments. In 1894 he disparaged Egyptian army units led by British officers, and the Sirdar, Sir Herbert Kitchener, threatened to resign until he apologised. By 1899 he had come to accept British counsel, and in 1900 he approved works such as the Aswan Low Dam and the Assiut Barrage.

Though he no longer opposed the British in public, he secretly supported the nationalist movement led by Mustafa Kamil Pasha and funded the newspaper Al-Mu'ayyad. In 1907 he formed the National Party, led by Kamil, against the moderate Ummah Party. Relations with Cromer's successor Sir Eldon Gorst were good, but they worsened after Kitchener replaced Gorst in 1912; Kitchener exiled or imprisoned National Party leaders and wanted to depose him.

On 25 July 1914 Abbas was in Constantinople, where he was wounded in an assassination attempt. When Britain declared war on the Ottoman Empire he was accused of deserting Egypt by not returning promptly, and the British believed he was plotting against their rule. On 18 December 1914 Britain declared a protectorate and deposed him, installing his uncle Hussein Kamel as sultan; the deposition ended the nearly four centuries of Ottoman Egypt that began in 1517. He formally abdicated on 12 May 1931, retired to Switzerland, where he wrote The Anglo-Egyptian Settlement (1930), and died in Geneva on 19 December 1944, aged 70.
abbas-ii-of-persia: Abbas II was born Soltan Mohammad Mirza on 30 August 1632 at Qazvin, the eldest son of Shah Safi and Anna Khanum, a Circassian concubine. Safi sought to have his sons blinded, but a eunuch who was to carry it out sympathised, and the prince kept his sight by feigning blindness until his father's death; this partly explains why he was still illiterate at ten. On 15 May 1642, aged nine and a half, he came to the throne and took the name Abbas. The grand vizier Saru Taqi, close to the queen mother, kept his post and governed as regent, while Abbas was educated as a king.

In 1645, aged thirteen, Abbas removed Saru Taqi from power, purged the bureaucracy and began his personal rule. His reign was largely peaceful: he avoided war with the Ottoman Empire and kept friendly relations with the Uzbeks. The exception was the war for Kandahar, which the Mughals had gained in 1638. After Shah Jahan failed to take Samarkand in 1648, court factions urged Abbas to act. He marched with 50,000 men and reached the city in January 1649, taking its strongholds after two months. His army was poorly equipped and underfed, and many deserted on the march; the success owed more to the weak position of the Mughals than to Safavid strength.

In the Caucasus, Rostom Khan of Kartli invaded Kakheti at Abbas's behest in 1648 and sent King Teimuraz I into exile. Abbas's army defeated the Russians who backed Teimuraz in a short conflict from 1651 to 1653, and he put down a Georgian rebellion in 1659 and 1660. From the middle years of his reign a financial decline set in that persisted until the end of the dynasty; Mohammad Beg, appointed in 1654, could not reverse it.

Abbas died aged thirty-four in 1666, in September or October according to differing accounts. Modern historians describe him as the last strong king of the Safavid dynasty, persistently concerned with affairs of state. Western observers portrayed him as tolerant and just, ruling a kingdom free of rebellion. Some historians criticise him for acts of cruelty and for forcing Iranian Jews to convert, while noting his tolerance of Christians. He drank heavily at court parties, and in 1653 a Shi'a scholar persuaded him to give up drinking, so that the sale of alcohol was banned for a short time.
abbasid-caliphate: The Abbasid Caliphate was the third Islamic caliphate. Its dynasty descended from Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib, an uncle of Muhammad of the Banu Hashim clan, and this kinship made the Abbasids appealing to those discontented with the Umayyads, who did not descend from the same family. The Abbasid Revolution (747 to 750) began in the eastern region of Khurasan, far from the Syrian centre of Umayyad influence. Al-Saffah reigned from 750 to 754, and in that time real power lay partly with a triumvirate of the revolutionary leader Abu Muslim, his brother Abu Ja'far, the future al-Mansur, and their uncle Abdallah ibn Ali.

The Abbasids first centred their government at Kufa, but in 762 the caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad and made it the capital. Its power and prestige are traditionally associated with the reign of Harun al-Rashid (786 to 809). After his death a civil war brought divisions, and the state created a professional army recruited mainly from Turkic slaves and built a new capital at Samarra in 836. From the 9th century provinces became autonomous under local dynasties such as the Aghlabids, Tahirids, Samanids, Saffarids and Tulunids. The seat returned to Baghdad in 892.

In the 10th century the caliphs were figureheads, while the Iranian Buyids and the Seljuq Turks held Baghdad from 945 and 1055. The Abbasids regained Iraq under al-Muqtafi (1136 to 1160) and extended their rule into Iran under al-Nasir (1180 to 1225). In 1252 Hulagu Khan was put in charge of a Mongol campaign in the Middle East, and in 1258 the Mongols sacked Baghdad and executed the caliph al-Musta'sim. The Mamluk sultans reinstated a surviving branch in Cairo in 1261, without political power, and the last Abbasid caliph, al-Mutawakkil III, lost even his symbolic authority with the Ottoman conquest of Egypt in 1517.

The period to 1258 is considered the Islamic Golden Age. Baghdad had the House of Wisdom, where Muslim and non-Muslim scholars translated and gathered works into Arabic, and many classics of antiquity survive because they were translated into Arabic and Persian and later into Turkish, Hebrew and Latin. Al-Kindi, al-Farabi and Avicenna combined Aristotelianism and Neoplatonism with Islamic ideas. The Abbasids adopted papermaking from China in the 8th century, and from them knowledge of gunpowder was transmitted from China. Samarra developed a standardised vocabulary of stucco decoration, and Abbasid potters developed lustreware. Under Abbasid rule the empire also became increasingly Arabized, particularly in Mesopotamia and the Levant.
abbeville: Abbeville lies on the river Somme in northern France, 20 km from the river's modern mouth in the English Channel, about 45 km northwest of Amiens and roughly 200 km from Paris. Most of the town stands on the east bank and on an island, at the head of the Abbeville Canal. In the medieval period it was the lowest crossing point on the Somme, and Edward III's army crossed nearby shortly before the Battle of Crécy in 1346. It is the historical capital of the County of Ponthieu.

The subsoil holds many remains of the Pleistocene, and their discovery helped found prehistory as a science. Jacques Boucher de Perthes found handaxes near Abbeville from 1838 and in 1846 published the first description pointing out that the stones had been chipped deliberately by early humans to form a tool. They were known as Abbevillian handaxes, though that term is becoming obsolete. The Romans occupied the place and named it Abbatis Villa, and the modern name means villa of the abbé, as it once depended on the Abbey of Saint-Riquier. Abbeville prided itself on never having been taken, was called Abbeville la pucelle, and received many privileges from the Capetian kings in reward for its loyalty.

In 1665 the Van Robais family founded the Manufacture Royale des Rames, making linens and tablecloths. The cloth trade declined after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes and the departure of Protestants, and the closing of the river port because of silt also hurt the economy. In the 18th century, according to Voltaire's account, the judges of Abbeville condemned the Chevalier de La Barre to torture and a slow death for impious songs and for passing a procession without removing his hat. The German army bombed the town almost to rubble in one night in the early days of the Second World War.

Abbeville is a commune in the Somme department of the Hauts-de-France region and a sub-prefecture of the department. Much of the town is modern and rebuilt. The Collegiate Church of Saint-Vulfran, begun in 1488 and continued in the 16th and 17th centuries, has a facade that is a masterpiece of flamboyant Gothic architecture, flanked by two towers, and was classified as a historical monument in 1840. The Boucher de Perthes Museum shows some of the stone tools, and the municipal library keeps 972 manuscripts, among them a Carolingian Gospel book dated 790–800.
abd-al-karim-qasim: Abd al-Karim Qasim was born on 21 November 1914 in Mahdiyya, a lower-income district of Baghdad, the youngest of three sons of a farmer who died during the First World War. He entered secondary school on a government scholarship, then the Military College, and graduated as a second lieutenant in 1934. He later graduated with honours from the Iraqi Staff College in December 1941. He served in the suppression of tribal uprisings in 1935, the Anglo-Iraqi War of 1941, the Barzani revolt of 1945 and the Arab-Israeli War of 1948–1949. His origins were disputed: official data claimed full Arab descent, while opponents alleged a Turkmen father and a Kurdish mother.

On 14 July 1958 Qasim used troop movements planned by the government to seize military control of Baghdad and overthrow the monarchy. King Faisal II had ordered the Royal Guard to offer no resistance, but the king, Crown Prince Abd al-Ilah and other members of the royal family were shot in the courtyard of the Rihab Palace, and the prime minister, Nuri as-Said, was among those executed. The coup had been planned by the Nationalist Officers' Organization, led by Qasim and Colonel Isma'il Arif, with Colonel Abdul Salam Arif as his closest collaborator.

As prime minister Qasim chose an Iraq First policy and refused to join Gamal Abdel Nasser's United Arab Republic, which split him from Abdul Salam Arif, who was removed from office on 30 September 1958 and sentenced to death in January 1959 before being pardoned. Qasim balanced the pan-Arabists in the army against the Iraqi Communist Party, whose ban he lifted. The Agrarian Reform Law of 30 September 1958 redistributed landholdings and capped ground rents. In March 1959 he withdrew Iraq from the Baghdad Pact, and the last British troops left the al-Habbaniyya base on 30 May 1959. A rally in Mosul on 6 March 1959 was followed by fighting between communists and nationalists that the army crushed.

In 1961 Kurdish separatists under Mustafa Barzani rose in revolt, and on 25 June Qasim announced that Kuwait was part of Iraq. British troops arrived on 1 July and were replaced by an Arab League force in September.

Qasim was overthrown by the Ba'athists in the Ramadan Revolution of 8 February 1963 and executed, the date given for his death being 9 February. Historians disagree about whether the United States Central Intelligence Agency helped plan the coup. Qasim was known as az-Zaʿīm, the Leader. His land reform weakened the landowners who had held power under the monarchy, and he provided low-cost housing for the inhabitants of Baghdad's slums. Even his harshest critics did not call him corrupt.
abd-al-malik-ibn-marwan: Abd al-Malik was born in Medina, in July or August 644 or in June or July 647, in the house of his father Marwan ibn al-Hakam. His parents belonged to the Banu Umayya, a strong and wealthy clan of the Quraysh. Traditional Muslim sources describe his upbringing as pious and rigorous. In 656 he witnessed the assassination of Caliph Uthman in Medina, which the historian A. A. Dixon says had a lasting effect on him. When a revolt against Caliph Yazid I broke out in Medina in 683, the Umayyads, Abd al-Malik among them, were expelled; it was part of the Second Fitna.

In 685 Marwan I appointed Abd al-Malik governor of Palestine and named him successor. Marwan died in April 685 and Yamani nobles managed the accession peacefully. Abd al-Malik held only Syria and Egypt, while most provinces still recognised the Mecca-based caliph Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr. After a failed invasion of Iraq in 686 he made an unfavourable truce with the Byzantine Empire in 689 and put down a coup attempt in Damascus by his kinsman al-Ashdaq in 690.

He then conquered Zubayrid Iraq and sent his general al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf to Mecca, where Ibn al-Zubayr was killed in late 692, reuniting the Caliphate. War with Byzantium resumed, bringing advances into Anatolia and Armenia, the destruction of Carthage and the recapture of Kairouan in 698. Al-Hajjaj, as viceroy, established the caliph's authority in Iraq and Khurasan. Abd al-Malik died on 9 October 705.

His most consequential reforms were a single Islamic currency in place of Byzantine and Sasanian coinage, and Arabic as the language of administration in place of Greek in Syria and Persian in Iraq. He also founded the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, the earliest archaeologically attested religious monument built by a Muslim ruler. He centralised rule over the provinces, using loyalist Arab troops from Syria to control them and forwarding tax surpluses to Damascus. His son al-Walid I succeeded him, and his centralised government became the prototype for later medieval Muslim states.
abd-al-rahman-i: Abd al-Rahman ibn Mu'awiya was born on 7 March 731 near Damascus, the son of the Umayyad prince Mu'awiya ibn Hisham and the grandson of the caliph Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik. Later Andalusi historians name his mother as a Berber woman called Rah, but no contemporary source attests her. He was twenty when the Abbasid Revolution of 748 to 750 overthrew the Umayyads. He fled with his brother Yahya, his young son Sulayman, some of his sisters and his Greek freedman Bedr, while Abbasid horsemen hunted the family. At the River Euphrates the horsemen called Yahya back with a promise of safety and killed him. Abd al-Rahman and Bedr escaped.

Abd al-Rahman became the first emir of the Emirate of Córdoba and ruled from 756 to 788. His rule in Iberia broke with the Abbasids, who had taken Damascus, and he founded an Umayyad line that lasted nearly three centuries, including the later Caliphate of Córdoba. He defeated a governor named Yusuf at Córdoba. He bought a standing army made up mainly of Berbers from North Africa and of slaves from other areas, since he could not always rely on the local population, and he built up a civil service.

Jews, Christians and other monotheists kept their faiths in exchange for the jizya, as was usual in the early years of Islamic expansion. Scholars disagree on how fast the population became Muslim: one view is that the bulk of it did early, another that about 80 per cent converted but not until near the 10th century. Abd al-Rahman also improved the infrastructure of al-Andalus and had the Great Mosque of Córdoba built in 785 to 787, which his successors enlarged until the 10th century.

Abd al-Rahman died in about 788 at Córdoba and was supposedly buried under the site of the Mezquita. He chose as his successor Hisham I, a son borne by a Spanish slave named Hulal. Another son, Sulayman, governor of Toledo, refused to accept Hisham's rule and was executed in 800 after challenging his nephew. Chroniclers report that the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur called Abd al-Rahman the Falcon of the Quraysh, as one who rose alone, by his own judgement, from flight to a realm of his own. He stood against Charlemagne, the Abbasids, the Berbers and other Muslim Spaniards, and his descendants ruled al-Andalus in the name of the house of Umayya, reaching their height under Abd al-Rahman III.
abd-al-rahman-ii: Abd al-Rahman II was born in Toledo in 792, the son of Emir al-Hakam I. In his youth he took part in the so-called massacre of the ditch, in which 72 nobles and hundreds of their attendants were massacred at a banquet by order of al-Hakam. He succeeded his father as Emir of Córdoba in 822. He was the fourth Umayyad emir of al-Andalus.

For twenty years Abd al-Rahman fought almost continuously against Alfonso II of Asturias, whose southward advance he halted. He built Murcia in 825 and settled it with Arab loyalists to ensure stability. He confronted rebellious citizens of Mérida in 835 by having a large internal fortress built, and in 837 he suppressed a revolt of Christians and Jews in Toledo with similar measures. He decreed that Christians were forbidden to seek martyrdom and had a Christian synod forbid it, and he was involved in the execution of the Martyrs of Córdoba.

In 839 or 840 he sent an embassy under al-Ghazal to Constantinople to sign a pact with the Byzantine Empire against the Abbasids. Another embassy may have gone to Ireland or Denmark, probably to encourage trade in fur and slaves. He also responded to requests for help from William of Septimania, who was in conflict with Charles the Bald over disputed lands.

In 844 Vikings landed at Cádiz, took Seville except for its citadel and attacked Córdoba itself, and Abd al-Rahman repulsed them. He then built a fleet and a naval arsenal at Seville to meet future raids.

Abd al-Rahman was known for a public building programme in Córdoba, including additions to the Mosque-Cathedral. He was a patron of the arts and of the great composer Ziryab. He died in Córdoba in 852.
abd-al-rahman-iii: Abd al-Rahman was born in Córdoba in December, around the year 890. He was a grandson of the emir Abdallah ibn Muhammad. His mother Muzna was a Christian concubine, and his paternal grandmother Onneca Fortúnez was a Christian princess of Pamplona, so that he was in part Arab and in part Hispano-Basque. His father Muhammad was imprisoned on a charge of plotting with the rebel Umar ibn Hafsun and was killed by his own brother al-Mutarrif. Abd al-Rahman grew up in his mother's household, where his father's sister was entrusted with his education. Abdallah passed over four living sons and named him heir, and he succeeded on 16 October 912 at about 21 or 22.

He inherited an emirate on the verge of dissolution, its power reaching little beyond Córdoba. Christian Asturias was advancing in the Douro valley, the Fatimids in Ifriqiya threatened to draw away the loyalty of Muslims, and Muwallad families, Muslims of Iberian origin, were in revolt. The most powerful, Umar ibn Hafsun, held much of eastern al-Andalus from his fortress of Bobastro. Within ten days of taking the throne Abd al-Rahman displayed a rebel leader's head in Córdoba, and he then led annual expeditions against the northern and southern tribes. To balance Arab and Berber subjects he brought into the court the saqalibah, slaves of East European origin.

In 929 he raised the emirate to the Caliphate of Córdoba and became its first caliph. He had earned the sobriquet al-Nasir li-Din Allah, the Defender of God's Faith, in his early twenties by supporting the Maghrawa Berbers in North Africa against Fatimid expansion. Northern Christian kingdoms fought him at Valdejunquera and Simancas, but by the end of his reign their rulers paid him homage. Envoys came from Otto I of Germany and the Byzantine emperor. In 949 he executed one of his sons for conspiring against him.

He was a patron of the arts, especially architecture. One third of his revenue met the ordinary costs of government, one third was hoarded and one third went to building. After declaring the caliphate he built the palace complex of Medina Azahara about seven kilometres west of Córdoba, modelled on the old Umayyad palace in Damascus as a tie to his ancestors. He also added to the Mosque of Córdoba, set up mints striking pure gold and silver coins, and expanded the city's library. His fleet became the most powerful in the Mediterranean of Europe. His reign of about half a century was known for religious tolerance toward Jews and Christians, and Córdoba became the leading intellectual centre of Western Europe.
abd-allah-ibn-al-zubayr: Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr was born in Medina in May 624, the eldest son of the Companion Zubayr ibn al-Awwam of the Banu Asad clan of the Quraysh. His mother Asma was a daughter of Abu Bakr and a sister of Aisha, and according to ninth-century historians he was the first child born to the Muhajirun, the earliest converts. As a young man he served in the conquest of Ifriqiya in 647, where he is said to have killed the Byzantine patrician Gregory, and in northern Iran in 650. He defended the house of the caliph Uthman during the siege of 656 and fought beside Aisha against Ali at the Battle of the Camel.

Ibn al-Zubayr did not oppose Mu'awiya I but in 676 refused to accept his nomination of Yazid I as successor, and rejected Yazid in 680. He escaped to Mecca, where Husayn joined him before Husayn's death at Karbala. By September 683 he controlled Mecca, calling himself the fugitive at the sanctuary. A Syrian army defeated his allies from Medina at al-Harra in the summer of 683 and besieged Mecca from 24 September, severely damaging the Kaaba. News of Yazid's death in November led the army to withdraw after Ibn al-Zubayr refused a recognition conditional on ruling from Syria.

He then declared himself commander of the faithful. After the death of Yazid's son Mu'awiya II, Umayyad authority collapsed and most provinces, including Egypt, Kufa and Yemen, offered allegiance, and coins were struck in his name in Fars and Kerman. His authority outside the Hejaz stayed largely nominal. Marwan I won at Marj Rahit in July 684 and took Egypt in March 685, and Kharijite gains in Arabia isolated Ibn al-Zubayr further.

In 691 Abd al-Malik defeated Mus'ab at Maskin and conquered Iraq. His commander al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf then besieged Mecca for six months. Most of Ibn al-Zubayr's followers, including his sons Khubayb and Hamza, surrendered on offers of pardon. On his mother's advice he went into battle and was killed in 692. Al-Hajjaj displayed the body on a gibbet until Abd al-Malik let his mother take it, and it was buried in Medina. His death ended the Second Fitna. He had argued that the caliph should be chosen by consultation among the Quraysh and not inherited by the Umayyads. Sources hostile to the Umayyads called him a model of piety, while others criticised him as jealous and harsh.
abd-el-krim: Abd el-Krim was born in 1882 in Ajdir, in the Rif, the son of a qadi, an Islamic judge and local leader, of the Ait Ouriaghel tribe. He and his brother M'Hammad received a Spanish education and spoke fluent Spanish and Riffian. In 1952 he defined himself as an ethnic Berber, while other accounts trace his family to Arab or sharifian ancestry; Riffian families kept no formal genealogies.

He worked in Melilla as a teacher, translator and secretary-interpreter for the Spanish native affairs office and wrote for the newspaper El Telegrama del Rif from 1906 to 1915. He was appointed chief qadi of Melilla in 1915. Noted as pro-German during the First World War, he was arrested after a complaint of involvement with the German consul, imprisoned in Chefchaouen from 1916 to 1918, escaped and regained his post as judge.

In 1920 he and his brother began a rebellion against Spanish incursions, aiming to unite the tribes of the Rif in an independent Republic of the Rif. In 1921 General Manuel Fernández Silvestre crossed the Ameqqran River with 60,000 men despite Abd el-Krim's warning that this would be an act of war. In June a Riffian force killed 179 of an estimated 250 Spanish troops at a post in the Abarran foothills. Silvestre committed suicide when defeat became clear, and in three weeks of battles 13,000 Spanish and colonial troops were killed. The defeat at Annual damaged the Restoration regime in Spain, and Miguel Primo de Rivera installed a dictatorship in September 1923.

After Abd el-Krim invaded French-occupied Morocco in April 1925 and reached as far as Fez, France sent a force under Marshal Henri Philippe Pétain which, with a Spanish army, made more than 250,000 soldiers backed by aircraft and artillery. After ten months of fighting, in which the French and Spanish used chemical bombs against the population, he surrendered to the French on 26 May 1926 at Targuist.

He was exiled to Réunion from 1926 to 1947. On the way to the south of France in 1947 he was freed by Moroccan nationalists and taken to Cairo, where he supported Arab nationalism, corresponded with Ho Chi Minh and backed the Algerian National Liberation Front. He refused Mohammed V's invitation to return after Moroccan independence in 1956 while French forces remained in North Africa, and died in 1963. His guerrilla methods, including the first use of tunnelling in modern warfare, are said to have influenced Ho Chi Minh, Mao Zedong and Che Guevara.
abdullah-ahmad-badawi: Abdullah bin Ahmad Badawi was born on 26 November 1939 in Kampung Perlis, Bayan Lepas, Penang, into a prominent religious family. His paternal grandfather, Syeikh Abdullah Badawi Fahim, was a religious scholar of Hadrami descent and a founding member of Hizbul Muslimin, which later evolved into the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party, and became the first Mufti of Penang after independence. His father, Ahmad Badawi, was a religious teacher and active member of UMNO. He graduated from the University of Malaya in 1964 with a degree in Islamic Studies and joined the Malaysian Administrative and Diplomatic Corps.

Abdullah resigned from the civil service in 1978 to become Member of Parliament for Kepala Batas, a seat his father had also held. He served as a deputy minister and, from 1981, as a minister without portfolio responsible for the Look East policy. He was later minister of defence and, from 1991, of foreign affairs under Mahathir Mohamad. In January 1999 he replaced Anwar Ibrahim as deputy prime minister and acting deputy president of UMNO after Anwar was removed from government, expelled from the party and arrested.

He became prime minister after Mahathir resigned in October 2003. He shelved several costly projects begun under Mahathir, created a royal commission on police corruption and required ministers to declare their assets. His Barisan Nasional won 198 of 219 seats in the 2004 election. He then introduced Islam Hadhari, a moderate interpretation of Islam calling for religious tolerance and modernity. Malaysia ended the ringgit's peg to the US dollar in 2005. A series of scandals and public protests damaged his standing, and in March 2008 the coalition lost its two-thirds majority and control of four state governments.

On 10 July 2008 Abdullah announced that he would step down, and on 3 April 2009 he was succeeded as prime minister by Najib Razak. The King conferred on him the title Tun. He was also known as a poet, and his poem I Seek Eternal Peace was translated into more than 80 languages. Abdullah died in Kuala Lumpur on 14 April 2025, aged 85, and was buried at the Heroes' Mausoleum.
abdullah-i-of-jordan: Abdullah was born in Mecca on 2 February 1882, the second of four sons of Hussein bin Ali, Sharif of Mecca. In 1910 he persuaded his father to stand for Grand Sharif of Mecca, and in the following year he became deputy for Mecca in the Ottoman parliament. In 1914 he made a clandestine visit to Cairo to meet Lord Kitchener, seeking British support for his father's ambitions. In 1915 he encouraged his father to correspond with Sir Henry McMahon about Arab independence, which led to the Arab Revolt.

During the Revolt of 1916 to 1918 Abdullah commanded the Arab Eastern Army. He began by attacking the Ottoman garrison at Ta'if on 10 June 1916, which he besieged, and then joined the siege of Medina. In early 1917 he ambushed an Ottoman convoy and captured £20,000 in gold coins meant to bribe the Bedouin.

After French forces took Damascus in July 1920, Abdullah moved his forces from the Hejaz into Transjordan intending to liberate it. Winston Churchill invited him to Cairo in 1921 and persuaded him not to attack Britain's French allies. Abdullah established the emirate on 11 April 1921. A legislative council set up in 1928 was only advisory, and he ruled as an autocrat. In the Second World War he was a faithful British ally.

The Hashemite Kingdom of Transjordan was proclaimed independent on 25 May 1946, and Abdullah was crowned king in Amman; it was renamed Jordan on 26 April 1949. He dreamed of a Greater Syria under a Hashemite throne, which made many Arab states distrust him. On 15 May 1948 he joined the all-Arab intervention, and the Arab Legion fought around Jerusalem. In 1950 Jordan annexed the West Bank, which angered Syria, Saudi Arabia and Egypt.

On 20 July 1951 Abdullah was shot dead at the entrance of the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem, during Friday prayers, by Mustafa Shukri Ashu, a Palestinian tailor's apprentice. His grandson Prince Hussein, beside him, survived when a medal deflected a bullet. The assassin was shot by the king's guards. Abdullah was succeeded by his eldest son Talal, and then by Talal's son Hussein.
abdur-rahman-khan: Abdur Rahman Khan, a Pashtun, was born in Kabul in the 1840s, the only son of Mohammad Afzal Khan and grandson of Dost Mohammad Khan, founder of the Barakzai dynasty. He spent most of his youth at Balkh. When Dost Mohammad died on 9 June 1863 after naming Sher Ali Khan his successor, Afzal Khan rose in revolt in the north, beginning a struggle among Dost Mohammad's sons that lasted nearly five years. Abdur Rahman fled across the Oxus into Bukhara after Sher Ali grew suspicious of him.

After Sher Ali's death he asked the Russians for leave to enter Afghanistan as a claimant, and was at first refused. They allowed it after Yaqub Khan's abdication and the British occupation of Kabul. He annexed Badakhshan and soon held all of Afghan Turkestan.

At a durbar on 22 July 1880 the British recognised him as Amir, promising arms and money and aid against unprovoked foreign aggression, provided he aligned his foreign policy with theirs. Ayub Khan, a son of Sher Ali, defeated his troops at Kandahar that July but was beaten there by General Frederick Roberts on 1 September 1880. Backed by British arms and money, Abdur Rahman consolidated his hold over the country, repeatedly facing revolts such as those of the Ghilzai. One source counts over 40 rebellions during his reign.

His government was a military despotism, resting on a well-appointed army, a widespread system of espionage and officials subservient to him. He also held open courts for petitioners. A British official called his rule a reign of terror, and up to 100,000 people are said to have been judicially executed in his 21 years. He moved troublesome Durrani and Ghilzai tribes to northern areas populated by Uzbek and Tajik communities. In 1895 and 1896 he directed the invasion of Kafiristan and the conversion of its people to Islam, and the region was renamed Nuristan.

In 1893 Mortimer Durand negotiated with him the agreement that fixed the frontier between Afghanistan and British India, the Durand Line. Habibullah Khan confirmed it in 1905 and Amanullah Khan in the Treaty of Rawalpindi in 1919.

Abdur Rahman died on 1 October 1901 in his summer palace, and his son Habibullah Khan succeeded him. He wrote an autobiography and treatises including one on jihad. Afghans hold mixed views of him. Many Pashtuns remember him as a ruler who began modernisation and kept the country from Russian occupation, though he depended on British arms and money to stay in power. His great-grandson Prince Abdul Ali Seraj said he united Afghanistan under one king and one flag.
abeche: Abéché lies in central-eastern Chad, surrounded by savanna. By road it is 749 kilometres northeast of the national capital, N'Djamena, 164 kilometres northwest of Adre on the border with Sudan, and roughly 90 kilometres southeast of Biltine. Its rainy season runs from June to September, and the hottest months are March to June. Its climate is hot and arid, and it is the hottest major city in Chad. The city stands on the trans-Saharan trade route, along which Islamic scholars and merchants travelled, and it is an important centre of cattle raising.

From the early 19th century Abéché was at the centre of the Islamic slave trade in Chad and an important city in the development of the religion in the region. It became the capital of the Wadai Sultanate in the 1890s, after the wells at Ouara, the former capital, had dried out.

In 1909 French troops invaded the kingdom and established a garrison in Abéché, forcing the sultan to renounce his throne. At that time Abéché was the largest city in Chad, with 28,000 people, but major epidemics reduced the population to 6,000 by 1919. In 1935 the French government ordered the sultanate restored, and Muhammed Ouarada, heir to the throne after his father became king, took up the title.

Abéché is the capital of the Ouaddaï Region and one of the largest cities in Chad. It contains the remnants of the old capital, including palaces, mosques and the tombs of former sultans. The Grand Mosque on the Place de l'Indépendance, built in the 19th century, is one of the oldest and most significant mosques in the country. The city's market is the principal one in Chad for camel exports and rugs, and camel-hair blankets are made in the area.
abellinum: Before the Roman conquest, the ancient Abellinum was a centre of the Samnite Hirpini on the Civita hill, about 4 km outside the current town of Avellino, in what is now Atripalda. It could correspond to the ancient Velecha, known from coins found in the area. The later Roman town lay on the left bank of the river Sabato.

The Romans conquered Abellinum in 293 BCE, and over the following centuries it changed name several times: Veneria, Livia, Augusta, Alexandriana and Abellinatium. A true Roman town, however, was built only after Lucius Cornelius Sulla's conquest in the civil wars in 89 BCE. He razed the old site and in 82 BCE founded the colony Veneria Abellinatium. The new city had massive walls and an orthogonal Hippodamian layout. In 7 CE Augustus renamed it Livia Augusta, for his wife Livia Drusilla, who owned the territory between Abellinum and Aeclanum. In the 3rd century Alexander Severus expanded the colony with a massive immigration of oriental settlers, which helped to spread Levantine cults such as Sol Invictus in the territory.

Economic crises in the 3rd and 4th centuries, violent earthquakes in 346 and disastrous volcanic eruptions in 472 followed. The town was Christianised around 500 and became an episcopal seat. The Goths invaded between 535 and 555, and after the Lombard conquest of southern Italy the ancient city was abandoned in 568, though historians dispute whether completely or partly. A new settlement grew on the Terra hill, where modern Avellino stands.

The ruins of Abellinum lie near the village of Atripalda, 4 km east of Avellino. They include the forum, faced by temples, baths, parts of the Serino aqueduct and a patrician domus, as well as an amphitheatre. Avellino itself is the capital of its province in Campania, with 51,819 inhabitants, about 47 km east of Naples.
abeokuta: Abeokuta lies on both banks of the Ogun River, in fertile wooded savanna broken by masses of grey granite, 77 kilometres north of Lagos by railway. The city stands below Olumo Rock, which has caves and shrines and carries spiritual significance. Its name already refers to several rock formations in the neighbourhood. Mud walls 29 kilometres long once surrounded it, and remnants still stand. Palm oil, timber, natural rubber, yams, rice, cassava, cotton and shea butter were the chief articles of trade, and the city exports cocoa, palm products and kola nuts. Rice and cotton were introduced by missionaries in the 1850s.

Accounts of the foundation differ in detail. All agree that Abeokuta was founded by Egba people around 1830 on and around Olumo Rock, at what had been a small farming village, as a refuge for displaced Yoruba during the collapse of the Oyo Empire and the wars that followed, and from slave hunters sent by Dahomey. One version says it replaced Orile Egba, a confederacy of towns said to date from about the 13th century. Another says the Egba withdrew from Ibadan after a chief named Lamodi shot an Ife chief named Ege, and took Sodeke as their leader. Other Egba and many Owu refugees soon joined them, but the groups did not fuse: Abeokuta was a federation of communities within a town wall.

Dahomey grew hostile because of the palm oil trade. In the Battle of Abeokuta in 1851 the Egba defeated King Gezo, and they beat back Dahomey again in 1864. In 1867 they expelled missionaries and traders after friction with the British at Lagos. In 1893, during the Yoruba Civil Wars, the alake of the Egba signed an alliance with the British governor, Sir Gilbert Carter, which formalised the Egba United Government. The Egba lands joined the colony of Nigeria in 1914 with Abeokuta as provincial capital. The Adubi War of 1918 resisted taxation and indirect rule, and the Abeokuta Women's Union led a revolt against unfair taxation in the 1940s.

Abeokuta has been the capital of Ogun State since 1976. The railway from Lagos, 77 kilometres long, was completed in 1899. Ake, the traditional residence of the alake, and Centenary Hall of 1930 stand in the Egba Alake's territory, and the Federal University of Agriculture, Abeokuta, was established in 1988. The census of 2006 counted 449,088 people in its two local government areas.
aberdeen: Aberdeen stands between two river mouths, and the city has little natural exposure of bedrock. It appears to sit on an inlier of Devonian Old Red sandstones and silts, while the outskirts spread onto older metamorphic and igneous rocks. The Rubislaw quarry supplied granite for much of the Victorian city. The name means mouth of the river Don: it is recorded as Aberdon in 1172, and its first element is the Pictish aber, 'river mouth'. The climate is oceanic, with winters milder than the northern latitude suggests, and very short days at the winter solstice, about 6 hours 41 minutes between sunrise and sunset.

The city began as two separate burghs: Old Aberdeen at the mouth of the Don, and New Aberdeen, a fishing and trading settlement where the Denburn waterway entered the Dee estuary. The earliest charter was granted by William the Lion in 1179 and confirmed rights granted by David I. During the Wars of Scottish Independence the city was under English rule, so Robert the Bruce besieged Aberdeen Castle and destroyed it in 1308. Edward III of England burned the city in 1336, but it was rebuilt.

5 per cent of the population. The city went bankrupt in 1817 after expensive infrastructure works but recovered with shipbuilding and fishing. By 1933 Aberdeen was Scotland's top fishing port. In the Second World War a raid on 21 April 1943 killed 98 civilians and 27 servicemen. Oil was discovered in the North Sea in 1969.

Aberdeen is the third most populous Scottish city, with 198,590 people in the main urban area in 2020. The University of Aberdeen, founded in 1495 as King's College, is the fifth oldest university in the English-speaking world and stands in Old Aberdeen. The harbour, established in 1136, is the largest in the north of Scotland and has been called the oldest business in Britain.

Local grey granite, which sparkles because of its high mica content, gives the city the nickname the Granite City. Its arms show three silver towers on red, a motif dating from at least the time of Robert the Bruce. The local dialect of Lowland Scots is known as Doric.
aberdeenshire: The Aberdeenshire council area covers 6,313 square kilometres, about 8 percent of Scotland. It borders Angus and Perth and Kinross to the south, Highland and Moray to the west and the city of Aberdeen to the east. It takes its name from the historic county, whose boundaries were substantially different. The council area includes the historic counties of Aberdeenshire and Kincardineshire, except the part forming Aberdeen City, together with part of Banffshire.

Many rivers and burns cross it, among them the Dee, the Don, the Ury and the Ythan. Lying in the rain shadow of the Grampians, it is generally dry for a maritime region, and coastal areas are subject to haar, a coastal fog. Since medieval times traditional paths such as the Causey Mounth and the Elsick Mounth have crossed the Mounth, a spur of mountainous land, from the Lowlands to the Highlands.

The area has many Neolithic and Bronze Age sites, including Longman Hill, Kempstone Hill and the Catto Long Barrow. The Beaker culture settled it, arriving from the south around 2000 to 1800 BCE, and stone circles and cairns were mostly built in that era. In the Iron Age hill forts were built. Around the 1st century CE the Taexali, who left little history, were believed to live along the coast. The Picts were the next documented inhabitants, and the Romans left signs at Kintore. There were Celtic monasteries at Old Deer and Monymusk.

Macbeth fell at Lumphanan in 1057. Edward I of England crossed the area twice with his army, in 1296 and 1303, and in 1307 Robert the Bruce was victorious near Inverurie. Other families, such as the House of Balliol, Clan Bruce and Clan Cumming, arrived with the Anglo-Norman penetration. Rivalry grew worse after the Protestant Reformation, the Gordon family adhering to Catholicism and the Forbes family to Protestantism. King's College in Old Aberdeen was founded in 1494 and Marischal College in 1593. The 17th century brought fighting under the Marquess of Montrose and in the Wars of the Three Kingdoms, but also trade with Germany, Poland and the Low Countries. The Rising of 1745 ended the ascendancy of Episcopalianism and the feudal power of landowners.

The historic county ceased to be used for local government in 1975; the present council area was created in 1996. Council headquarters are at Woodhill House in Aberdeen, which makes it the only Scottish council with its headquarters outside its jurisdiction. Fishing, farming and forestry have long been the traditional basis of the economy, joined by the oil and gas industry. The area has many castles, among them Balmoral, Dunnottar, Crathes, Drum, Huntly and Kildrummy, and part of the Cairngorms National Park.
aberystwyth: Aberystwyth is the largest town in Ceredigion, 16 miles from Aberaeron, the county's other administrative centre. The name means the mouth of the Ystwyth. It stands on Cardigan Bay on the west coast of Wales, near the confluence of the River Ystwyth and the Afon Rheidol. The seafront, with a pier, runs from Constitution Hill at the north end of the Promenade to the harbour at the south, and the castle divides the beach. The town lay in the historic county of Cardiganshire and forms a cultural link between North Wales and South Wales.

Flint was worked at Tan-y-Bwlch at the foot of Pen Dinas by Mesolithic hunter-gatherers, and the remains of a Celtic fortress on Pen Dinas show the site was inhabited before 700 BCE. South of the present town, across the Ystwyth, are the remains of a medieval ringfort believed to be the castle from which Princess Nest was abducted.

The fortified town was laid out from 1277 onwards and was administered from then as a borough. It was first called Llanbadarn Gaerog, meaning fortified Llanbadarn, and the name Aberystwyth is first recorded around 1400. It remained part of the ecclesiastical parish of Llanbadarn Fawr until the late 19th century. The Vale of Rheidol Railway, built between 1901 and 1902 to carry lead down from Devil's Bridge, opened for passengers in December 1902 and came to rely on tourism, as lead mining was in deep decline by its completion.

The town grew as a Victorian seaside resort and became more anglicised than the rest of the county. The 1891 census found 52.5 per cent of those answering the language question bilingual, 26.4 per cent Welsh monoglots and 21.1 per cent English monoglots.

Aberystwyth is a university and seaside town. University College Wales, now Aberystwyth University, was founded in 1872, when Wales had very limited degree-awarding capacity beyond St David's College, Lampeter, founded in 1822. Its Old College was built in 1865 as a hotel and sold to the university in 1867 after the owner's bankruptcy. The town also holds the National Library of Wales and the Aberystwyth Cliff Railway, which climbs Constitution Hill. Ysgol Gymraeg, opened in 1939, was the first designated Welsh medium school in Wales.
abgaal: The Abgaal belong to the Mudulood, one of the divisions of the Hiraab, with the Habar Gidir, Sheekhaal and Duduble. The clan is regarded as relatively young, its founder dating from the 1500s. A tradition recorded by the Italian scholar Enrico Cerulli makes the founder, Ali Isman, the son of Osman Darandolle of the Hiraab and of Faduma Sarjeele, a woman of the Gareen house that headed the Ajuran Sultanate.

According to the story, Faduma's father was warned that the boy's descendants would drive out his own and tried to poison him, but the mother drank the poison by mistake. The boy hid behind a camel and called the camels his grandfather, whence the name Abgaal, camel-grandfather. Cerulli read the story as a memory of fighting between Abgaal pastoral nomads coming from the north and the Ajuran.

Clan traditions say that the Abgaal Darandoolle began to arrive in the hinterland of Mogadishu in the sixteenth century, while the Muzaffar dynasty ruled the town, and manuscripts from Mogadishu record Abgaal nomads in the interior at about the same time. Towards the end of the seventeenth century an imam of Abgaal descent settled in the Shangaani quarter. His lineage, the Yaaquub, intermarried with merchant families of Yemeni origin and became known in the trade between the coast and the interior, and by the 1700s it ruled most of the town.

Traditions of the fall of the Ajuran speak of heavy taxes and of a quarrel over watering rights, after which the Darandoolle killed the Ajuran imam at a well called Ceel Cawl. According to oral tradition as reported by Lee Cassanelli, the Hiraab Imamate that followed was an alliance of related groups that ruled from the Shabelle valley to the arid lands of Mudug for at least two centuries. Mogadishu was its capital, and the port of Hobyo its commercial centre.

The Abgaal are divided into three main branches: the Harti, the eldest, the Wacbudhan and the Waceysle, the youngest. The imam of the Mudulood and of the Hiraab traditionally comes from the Abgaal, from the Owbakar sub-clan, while the ugaas of the Mudulood comes from the Reer Ugaas sub-clan. Mogadishu is regarded as Abgaal territory, and they form the majority of its population. Three presidents of Somalia, Ali Mahdi Muhammad, Sharif Sheikh Ahmed and Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, have been Abgaal, as was Daud Abdulle Hirsi, the first commander-in-chief of the Somali National Army.
abha: Abha stands high, well over two thousand metres up, in the Asir Mountains of south-western Saudi Arabia, on the western edge of Mount Al-Hijaz and near Jabal Sawda, the highest peak in the country. The high ground gives the city a mild climate for its latitude. It seldom sees temperatures above 35 °C and averages 278 millimetres of rain a year, most of it falling between February and April, with a smaller wet season in July and August. Snow falls occasionally on the higher ground, and the city harvests some of its irrigation water from rain. Saudis sometimes call it the Bride of the Mountain.

Abha was the capital of the Prince of Asir Ibn Ayde, who ruled under Ottoman authority until the First World War. In 1918 the prince Yahya bin Hasun Al Ayde, a grandson of Ibn Ayed, returned to the family throne at Abha with complete independence. In 1920 Asir was conquered by the Ikhwan tribesmen of Nejd, loyal to Ibn Saud, during the unification of Saudi Arabia. Many of the tribes of the surrounding region, among them Bani Shehr and Bal-Qarn, belong to the Azd, whose tribes are said to have migrated after the Marib Dam collapsed for the third time in the third century CE.

The city has four quarters, the largest of which contains a fortress, and hilltop forts are a characteristic feature. Shadda Palace, built in 1927, is now a museum of local handicrafts and household items. A coastal road linking Jeddah and Abha was completed in 1979, and the airport, designed by Dutch engineers, began flights in 1977.

Abha is the capital of Asir Province and a popular summer destination for Saudis, with a summer festival held there. King Khalid University, a public university, was founded in 1998 by merging two earlier institutions. The head office and main printing presses of the daily Al Watan are in the city.
abidjan: Abidjan lies on the south-east coast of Ivory Coast, on the Gulf of Guinea, around the Ébrié Lagoon, which divides it into a northern and a southern half. Le Plateau is the business district, and Port Bouët in the south holds the airport and main seaport. According to the oral tradition of the Tchaman, the name came from a misunderstanding: an old man cutting leaves, asked the name of the village by a European, fled shouting a phrase in Ebrié meaning 'I just cut the leaves'.

Abidjan was originally a small Atchan fishing village. In 1896, after deadly yellow fever epidemics, French colonists who had settled at Grand-Bassam decided to move to a safer place, and in 1898 they chose the site of Abidjan. It officially became a town in 1903, while nearby Bingerville served as capital of the colony from 1900 until 1934. The city grew quickly after a new wharf was built in 1931, and the Vridi Canal later made it an important sea port.

Abidjan became a municipality in 1956, with Félix Houphouët-Boigny as first mayor. At independence in 1960 it became the country's administrative and economic centre, and its population grew from 180,000 in 1960 to 1,269,000 in 1978. In 1983 Yamoussoukro was designated the official political capital, but many government institutions and all foreign embassies stayed in Abidjan.

Abidjan is the largest city of Ivory Coast and its economic capital, with 6,321,017 inhabitants in the Abidjan Autonomous District at the census of 14 December 2021. It is the most populous French-speaking city in West Africa; about sixty languages are spoken, the traditional language of the region is Ebrié, and Dioula has long been the trading lingua franca. Christians and followers of Islam make up nearly equal shares of the population. The African Development Bank is headquartered there.
abkhaz-people: Some scholars say the ancient Heniochi tribe were the progenitors of the Abkhaz. This warlike people came into contact with the Greeks through the Greek colonies of Dioskourias and Pitiuntas. In the Roman period the Abasgoi, or Abasgi, are mentioned as inhabiting the region, and Procopius described them as warlike worshippers of three deities.

The Abasgi lived within the Lazian Empire, also called Egrisi, a state in western Georgia. Their monarch was appointed by the Laz king with the approval of the Byzantine emperor. After Egrisi declined, the Abasgian prince Leon I acquired it with Byzantine support in the 7th century, and Abasgia became a kingdom with its capital at Kutaisi. It soon adopted Georgian in place of Greek, and in 978 Abkhazia united with the eastern Georgian kingdom through dynastic succession, forming the Kingdom of Georgia.

Christianity became the dominant religion of the Abkhaz in the 6th century, under the Byzantine emperor Justinian I, and was followed under the kings of Georgia in the High Middle Ages. The region came under the Ottoman Empire in the 16th century, which introduced Islam, and the population gradually became Muslim in the 16th and 17th centuries.

The Russian conquest, from the 1810s to the 1860s, was accompanied by a mass expulsion of Muslim Abkhaz to the Ottoman Empire; Christian Abkhaz were largely spared. A strong policy of Russification followed, and Russian replaced Georgian as the second language of the Abkhaz, which alienated them from Georgians despite their common heritage. As a result the Abkhaz diaspora is estimated at no less than twice the number living in Abkhazia. Some Abkhaz fought for Greece during the Greco-Turkish War of 1919 to 1922, and thousands then fled persecution to Greece. The war in Abkhazia of 1992 and 1993 left the Abkhaz an ethnic plurality of about 45 percent.

The Abkhaz language belongs to the Northwest Caucasian family, also called Abkhaz–Adyghe or Pontic, and the Abkhaz are closely related to Circassians and Abazins. There are three subgroups: the Bzyb, living by the Bzyb River; the Abzhui, living by the Kodori River, whose dialect is the basis of the literary language; and the Samurzakan in the southeast. The traditional economy rests on cattle breeding, beekeeping, viticulture and agriculture.

The Abkhaz are divided mainly between Orthodox Christian and Sunni Muslim of the Hanafi school, prevalent in Abkhazia and in Turkey respectively, though indigenous non-Abrahamic beliefs have always been strong. Many Abkhaz villages, some 250 Abkhaz-Abaza ones by one estimate, lie in Turkey, and the community there is believed to be larger than that in Abkhazia. In Egypt the Abaza family, which originated in Abkhazia, has contributed to political and literary life since the reign of Muhammad Ali Pasha.
abomey: Abomey, also called Agbome, was founded in the 17th century as the capital of the Kingdom of Dahomey, on the site of the former village of Kana. Traditional legends say the town was founded by Do-Aklin, a son of the king of Allada who ventured north to found his own kingdom. The name is thought to come from Danhomé, meaning belly of Dan, Dan being the original chief of the village.

Dahomey expanded rapidly in the 1700s, absorbing many surrounding kingdoms and growing rich from the slave trade. In the late 18th century a dry ditch alone surrounded Abomey, while the royal palaces had a mudbrick wall 20 feet high. By the 1840s it had an estimated population of 24,000. The French conquered the kingdom on 16 November 1892, and King Béhanzin torched the city and fled northward. The town then declined, as the French built a new administrative centre at Bohicon, to the east.

Abomey is the capital of the Zou Department of Benin and remains a centre for crafts. It houses the Royal Palaces of Abomey, earthen structures built by the Fon people between the mid-17th and late 19th centuries. UNESCO states that twelve kings ruled from 1625 to 1900, each building a palace within the same cob-wall area, except Akaba. Under Béhanzin the palaces covered some 44 hectares behind a wall 10 metres high and 4 kilometres long; only two of the twelve palaces survived the burning of 1892. The site became a World Heritage Site in 1985. Fifty of the 56 bas-reliefs of King Glèlè's palace have been replaced on the rebuilt structure.
aboriginal-australians: Archaeological evidence indicates that the ancestors of Aboriginal Australians first migrated to the continent 50,000 to 65,000 years ago. They reached it when it formed part of the Sahul continent, joined to New Guinea by a land bridge, though the journey still required crossing the sea at the Wallace Line. A 2021 modelling study suggests the first people may have landed in the Kimberley about 60,000 years ago and settled across the continent within 6,000 years.

Rising seas at the start of the Holocene, about 11,700 years ago, flooded large areas of the continental shelf where Aboriginal people had lived, separating Tasmania from the mainland. Aboriginal Australians and Papuans, who shared Sahul, became genetically distinct about 37,000 years ago. Aboriginal people may have one of the oldest continuous cultures on earth: in Arnhem Land the Yolngu have passed on oral histories through hundreds of generations.

Over the millennia Aboriginal people formed as many as 500 linguistic and territorial groups and developed trade networks, law and religion. At the time of European colonisation they spoke more than 250 languages. The population at first European settlement is estimated at no fewer than 314,500. After contact it declined until it reached a low in 1921, then recovered and passed the pre-contact figure by the end of the 20th century.

Before British colonisation there were perhaps five to sixteen languages in Tasmania, and the last speaker of a traditional Tasmanian language, Fanny Cochrane Smith, died in 1905. English-based creoles have arisen since contact, Kriol among them. In the 1970s and 1980s the outstation movement saw Aboriginal people move to small remote settlements on traditional land.

Languages and their groups are connected with stretches of territory known as Country, with which Aboriginal people have a profound spiritual connection. The anthropologist Harry Lourandos describes three main cultural areas, Northern, Southern and Central; the first two, richer in marine and woodland resources, were more densely populated. Group names include Koori in New South Wales and Victoria, Murri in Queensland and Noongar in southern Western Australia.

Traditional beliefs are passed on through dancing, stories, songlines and art, which together express the Dreaming, an account of ancient creation and daily life. Aboriginal identity has varied over time and place, with family lineage, self-identification and community acceptance of differing importance.
abraham-lincoln: Abraham Lincoln was born on 12 February 1809 in a one-room log cabin in Kentucky, the second child of Thomas Lincoln and Nancy Hanks Lincoln, and was raised on farms near Hodgenville. His father bought several farms but could not secure clear titles to any, and in 1816 the family moved to Indiana, where land titles were more reliable. His parents belonged to a Separate Baptist church whose members largely opposed slavery. His mother died of milk sickness on 5 October 1818, and his father married Sarah Bush Johnston the following year; Lincoln became close to his stepmother. He married Mary Todd on 4 November 1842.

Lincoln served four terms in the Illinois House of Representatives from 1834, as a Whig and supporter of Henry Clay, and championed the Illinois and Michigan Canal. He won election to the U.S. House of Representatives in 1846 and served from 1847 to 1849. The Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854, proposed by Senator Stephen A. Douglas, brought him back into political life. His Peoria Speech of October 1854 opposed slavery, and he became a leader of the new Republican Party. He reached a national audience in the 1858 Senate campaign debates with Douglas and won the 1860 presidential election.

Secession followed. South Carolina adopted an ordinance of secession on 20 December 1860, and six other states had followed by 1 February 1861, forming the Confederate States of America. Lincoln refused to recognise the Confederacy and declared secession illegal. He closely supervised the Union's strategy, including the choice of generals and a naval blockade of Southern ports. On 1 January 1863 he issued the Emancipation Proclamation, declaring slaves in states 'in rebellion' to be free. He delivered the Gettysburg Address on 19 November 1863, and he promoted the Thirteenth Amendment, which abolished chattel slavery in 1865.

On the evening of 14 April 1865, five days after the Confederate surrender at Appomattox, Lincoln attended the play Our American Cousin at Ford's Theatre in Washington. John Wilkes Booth, an actor and Confederate spy, entered his box at 10:15 pm and shot him in the back of the head. Lincoln was taken to the Petersen House across the street and died at 7:22 am on 15 April. He was the first U.S. president to be assassinated. His body lay in state in the White House and the Capitol, then travelled by funeral train to Springfield, Illinois, where crowds gathered along the route. The Lincoln Memorial on the National Mall was dedicated in 1922.
abruzzo: Abruzzo lies roughly in the middle of the Italian peninsula, from the heart of the Apennines to the Adriatic coast, with its western border with Lazio 80 km east of Rome.
