The west is mountainous and wild, with the Gran Sasso at 2,912 metres and Mount Majella at 2,793 metres, and the east is a coastal strip of sandy and pebbly beaches. The name probably comes from Aprutium, a popular form of (ad) Praetutium, the land of the Praetutii, an Italic people around present-day Teramo, a derivation first proposed by the Renaissance historian Flavio Biondo. Another suggestion links it to Latin abruptus, steep.

Flint tools show that archaic humans lived in the region about 700,000 years ago, and Neanderthal remains come from caves at Calascio. By the end of the Iron Age several tribes lived there, among them the Oscan-speaking Pentri, Carricini and Frentani and the Aequi, Praetutii, Vestini, Marrucini, Marsi and Paeligni. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire and the Gothic War, the Lombards arrived, and around 572 they divided the area between the Duchy of Benevento and the Duchy of Spoleto, whose first duke was Faroald I of Spoleto.

In 1302 the Peace of Caltabellotta left the southern peninsula, Abruzzo included, to the Capetian House of Anjou. The people rebelled against the French invasion of 1798 and 1799, and in 1806 Napoleon's client kingdom split Abruzzo Ultra in two at the Gran Sasso. The Bourbons returned after the Congress of Vienna and founded the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in 1816. Abruzzo joined the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1860 and the Kingdom of Italy in 1861, though some Bourbon supporters fought Garibaldi's volunteers and later joined in brigandage. In the Second World War the region lay on the Gustav Line, and the Battle of Ortona was among its most brutal fights.

Abruzzo is a region of Italy with a population of nearly 1.3 million, divided into four provinces named for L'Aquila, Teramo, Pescara and Chieti. L'Aquila is the regional capital and Pescara the largest city and major port. About half the territory is protected as national parks and nature reserves. The Museo Archeologico Nazionale d'Abruzzo in Chieti holds the Warrior of Capestrano, a statue from a necropolis of the 6th century BCE.
absalom: In the Hebrew Bible Absalom (Hebrew Avshalom, 'Father of Peace') is the third son of King David, born at Hebron to Maacah of Geshur. He is the only full sibling of Tamar, and both are described as exceptionally beautiful. He is also noted for his long hair. A verse in 2 Samuel records him saying that he had no son to keep his name in remembrance, and the text names a daughter, Tamar.

The narrative of 2 Samuel 13 begins when Tamar is raped by her paternal half-brother Amnon, David's eldest son. David is angered but at first does nothing, since Amnon is his heir. Absalom waits two years, then has his servants kill Amnon, who is drunk, at a feast to which all the king's sons were invited. He flees to his grandfather Talmai, king of Geshur, and is fully reinstated in David's favour only three years later.

Back in Jerusalem, Absalom built support by speaking to those who came to the king for justice, telling them their claims were good but that no one was deputed to hear them. He greeted petitioners with kisses and so, in the text's phrase, stole the hearts of the people of Israel. Some interpreters see in this a reflection of flaws in the judicial system of the united monarchy.

After four years he declared himself king and raised a revolt at Hebron, the former capital. All Israel and Judah are said to have flocked to him, leaving David with only the Cherethites and Pelethites and his bodyguard from Gath. The priests Zadok and Abiathar stayed in Jerusalem, their sons serving as David's spies. Absalom entered the capital, publicly took his father's ten concubines, and consulted the counsellor Ahitophel, who may, it has been suggested, have been moved by David's adultery with his granddaughter Bathsheba.

The revolt ended at the Battle of the Wood of Ephraim, where David's nephew and army commander Joab killed Absalom. Tamar is left, in the text's words, a desolate woman in her brother's house, guardian of his orphaned daughter. Rabbinic writers made his life a warning against false ambition and unfilial conduct, and held that his hair became his snare.

The story has been retold often. George Peele wrote a play on it, published in 1599, and John Dryden's satirical poem Absalom and Achitophel (1681) used it as an allegory for contemporary politics. Artists such as Guercino and Cabanel painted Tamar's story, and William Faulkner's novel Absalom, Absalom! takes its title from it.
absheron-peninsula: The Absheron Peninsula extends 60 kilometres eastward into the Caspian Sea and reaches a maximum width of 30 kilometres. Azerbaijan's outline is often compared to an eagle, with Absheron as its beak. The peninsula is technically the easternmost extension of the Caucasus Mountains, but its landscape is only mildly hilly, a gently undulating plain cut by ravines and dotted with salt lakes. It ends in a long spit of dunes called Shah Dili, the Shah Spit, the easternmost point of mainland Azerbaijan, now the Absheron National Park.

The climate is temperate and semi-arid, with warm, dry summers, cool and occasionally wet winters and strong winds throughout the year. Annual rainfall is about 200 millimetres or less, which makes it the driest part of Azerbaijan. The natural vegetation is dry steppe and semi-desert, and farming depends on irrigation. The ground consists of layers of clays, sandy clays, sands and limestones, and fresh groundwater is scarce because the thick clays hold highly mineralised water.

The name comes from the Persian ab shuran, meaning salty waters. Conrad Malte-Brun noted in 1810 that the peninsula also had the name Okoressa. Beginning in the 1870s Absheron was the site of some of the world's earliest petroleum production. The exploitation of its oil in the late 19th century drew large numbers of Iranian labourers to the Caucasus and Central Asia.

Absheron holds Baku, the most populous city of Azerbaijan, and the Baku metropolitan area with its satellite cities Sumqayit and Khyrdalan. It is divided into districts, two of them urban (Baku and Sumqayit) and others suburban, among them Absheron, Pirallahi and Khazar. Much of the landscape is still scarred with rusting oil derricks, and the petrochemical and refining industries have left their mark on the Caspian shore and the sea.
abu-al-abbas-al-saffah: Al-Saffah was born at al-Humayma, in present-day Jordan, in 721 or 722. He headed one branch of the Banu Hashim, a sub-clan of the Quraysh descended from Hashim, a great-grandfather of Muhammad, through al-Abbas, an uncle of the Prophet; hence the name Abbasid. This indirect link to Muhammad's clan was the basis of his claim to the caliphate.

Many believed, on the strength of hadith, that in the end times a leader or mahdi from Muhammad's family would deliver Islam from corrupt leadership. The Umayyad caliphs' half-hearted tolerance of non-Arab Muslims and Shi'as had failed to quell unrest, which produced a Shi'a revolt in Kufa under Zayd ibn Ali, put down in 740. The Abbasids chose to begin their rebellion in Khorasan, a remote but important military region.

In early October 749 al-Saffah's army entered Kufa. In February 750 it defeated the Umayyad caliph Marwan II at the Battle of the Zab, effectively ending a dynasty that had ruled since 661. Marwan fled and was killed in Egypt that August. Al-Saffah did not come forward to receive the people's pledge of allegiance until Marwan and many Umayyad princes were dead. He made Kufa his capital, ending the dominance of Damascus, and called himself al-Saffah, the Blood-Shedder, in his inaugural address in its Great Mosque.

Later tales say he invited the remaining Umayyads to a dinner and had them clubbed to death; the one survivor, Abd al-Rahman ibn Mu'awiya, reached al-Andalus, where Umayyad rule lasted three more centuries. Apart from his policy toward the Umayyads, historians widely regard him as a mild victor. Jews, Eastern Christians and Persians served in his government, and his army admitted non-Muslims and non-Arabs, whom the Umayyads had refused. In 751 Abbasid forces defeated the Tang army at the Battle of Talas, after the Karluk Turks changed sides; Muslim control of Transoxiana followed.

Al-Saffah died of smallpox on 8 June 754, on his way to Mecca. His own son was too young, so he named his brother Abu Ja'far as heir. His uncle Abd Allah ibn Ali, who had assembled an army for a campaign against the Byzantines, proclaimed himself caliph, claiming al-Saffah had promised him the succession. Abu Ja'far, who took the name al-Mansur, ruled until 775; he imprisoned his uncle in 754 and had him killed in 764.
abu-bakr-al-siddiq: Abu Bakr was born in Mecca into a rich family of the Banu Taym, part of the Quraysh tribal confederacy. His father was Abu Quhafa and his mother Umm al-Khayr, and through his father's line his ancestry meets that of Muhammad at Murrah ibn Ka'b. His love of camels earned him the nickname Abu Bakr, father of the camel's calf. He was a wholesale trader in cloth. According to Ibn Kathir he was the first free adult man to embrace Islam, and several leading companions, among them Uthman ibn Affan, converted through his preaching.

According to Islamic tradition Muhammad was commanded in 613 to call people to Islam openly, and Abu Bakr delivered the first public address inviting people to offer allegiance to Muhammad. Young men of the Quraysh beat him until he lost consciousness. In 622 he accompanied Muhammad to Medina, and they took refuge in a cave on Jabal Thawr while the Quraysh sent out search parties. Muhammad appointed him amir al-hajj to lead about 300 pilgrims from Medina to Mecca in 630 or 631, and in his last illness told him to lead the prayers.

After Muhammad's death in 632, the Ansar gathered at the Saqifa of the Banu Sa'ida clan, and Abu Bakr succeeded as the first caliph. Revolts by several Arab tribes, known as the Ridda Wars or Wars of Apostasy, followed. Some were led by men who claimed prophethood, among them Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid and Musaylima. In 633 small forces were sent into Iraq and Palestine and captured several towns. After the Battle of al-Yamama Umar saw that some five hundred Muslims who had memorised the Quran had died, and Abu Bakr, at first hesitant, appointed Zayd ibn Thabit to gather the verses in writing.

On 23 August 634 Abu Bakr fell sick with a high fever and did not recover. He named Umar as his successor after consulting some companions, the first caliph to nominate one. He is buried with Muhammad and Umar in the Green Dome of the Prophet's Mosque in Medina. Sunni tradition regards him as the legitimate successor to Muhammad and the first of the Rightly Guided Caliphs. Shi'a tradition holds that Muhammad had designated Ali at Ghadir Khumm and that Abu Bakr's appointment bypassed Ali's rightful claim.
abu-hanifa: Abu Hanifa came from Central Asia, though sources disagree on his birthplace, naming Kufa (the majority view), Kabul, Anbar, Nasa or Termez. They agree that he was born under the Umayyad Caliphate but differ on the year: 699 CE, held by the majority of classical scholarship, or 696, 689 or 680. His first name was Nu'man. He was born at least 60 years after the death of Muhammad, when some of the first generation of Muslims were still alive.

In his youth Abu Hanifa travelled to the Hejaz and studied in Mecca and Medina, and he later became established as a leading religious authority in Kufa. One of his main teachers there was Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman. He never held an official post as qadi. He kept an independent position toward political authority and was punished and imprisoned under both the Umayyads and the Abbasids because of his views and his refusal to accept the office of qadi in Kufa. He died in prison in Baghdad in 767 (AH 150).

The scholar Yusuf ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Mizzi listed 97 hadith scholars among his students, and Badr al-Din al-Ayni named another 260 who studied hadith and fiqh with him. His two best-known students were Abu Yusuf, who served as the first chief justice in the Muslim world, and Muhammad al-Shaybani, who taught the founder of the Shafi'i school, al-Shafi'i.

Abu Hanifa derived Islamic law, in order of preference, from the Qur'an, the authentic narrations of Muhammad known as hadith, the consensus of the Muslim community (ijma'), analogical reasoning (qiyas), juristic discretion (istihsan) and local custom ('urf). Modern scholarship regards him as the first to formally adopt analogical reasoning as part of Islamic law. Because Ali had moved the Islamic capital to Kufa and many first-generation Muslims settled there, the school came to be known as the Kufan or Iraqi school.

His school, the Hanafi, remains the most widely practised of the Sunni schools. Abu Hanifa received the honorific al-Imam al-A'zam, the highly venerated Imam. His tomb, surmounted by a dome erected by admirers in 1066, is still a shrine for pilgrims; the Ottoman ruler Suleiman restored it in 1535 after the Ottoman conquest of Baghdad.
abu-muslim: Sources differ on Abu Muslim's name and origin, and the suggestions that he descended from Persian heroes or from the Abbasids or Alids are all doubtful. He was most likely Persian, born in Merv or near Isfahan, in 718/9 or sometime between 723 and 727. He grew up in Kufa as a slave and saddler of the Banu Ijl clan, and there he met Shi'a Muslims.

Kufa was a centre of unrest against the Umayyad dynasty, whose policies favoured Arabs over non-Arab converts. In 737 he was accused of associating with ghulat sectarians and imprisoned. Abbasid missionaries freed him in 741/2, and Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Abdallah, head of the Abbasid clan, sent him in 745/6 to direct the missionary effort in Khurasan.

Khurasan, far from Syria and home to many Arab settlers and native converts who disliked the centralising tendencies of Damascus, offered fertile ground. When Abu Muslim arrived the province was in turmoil from the Third Fitna. In 747 he began the open revolt and took Merv in December 747 or January 748, defeating the governor Nasr ibn Sayyar and the Kharijite Shayban. He also defeated Bihafarid, leader of a syncretic Persian sect.

He then directed the Abbasid advance across the Iranian plateau into the Levant, which ended Umayyad authority and led to the proclamation of the Abbasid Caliphate. As governor of Khurasan he put down a Shi'a uprising in Bukhara in 750/1. His conciliatory policy toward Shia, Sunnis, Zoroastrians, Jews and Christians made him very popular.

The first caliph, Abu al-Abbas al-Saffah, trusted him in general but was wary of his power. His brother al-Mansur urged more than once that Abu Muslim be killed, and after becoming caliph he asked him to crush the rebellion of his uncle Abdullah ibn Ali, which he did. Relations then broke down over the spoils and over a transfer to Syria and Egypt, outside his power base. Reassured by al-Mansur's promise to keep him as governor of Khurasan, and by aides some of whom had been bribed, Abu Muslim went to meet him at al-Mada'in in 755. Al-Mansur listed his grievances, including a charge of heresy, and his guards killed him. His body was thrown into the Tigris.

His murder caused resentment and rebellion in Khurasan. Several leaders, including Ishaq al-Turk, the Zoroastrian cleric Sunpadh and al-Muqanna, revolted in his name, some claiming he had not died and would return. Legends and forms of veneration of him exist in Central Asia, Iran and Afghanistan, and at least three epic romances were written about him.
abu-simbel: Abu Simbel lies on the western bank of Lake Nasser in the Aswan Governorate of Upper Egypt, near the border with Sudan, about 230 km southwest of Aswan. The temples stand at the Second Nile Cataract, the border between Lower Nubia and Upper Nubia. Nubia was a major source of gold and other precious trade goods and was controlled by Egypt, so it mattered greatly to the Egyptians.

Ramesses II carried out an extensive building programme in Egypt and Nubia. He built several grand temples in Nubia in order to impress upon the Nubians Egypt's might and to Egyptianize the people of Nubia. Work at Abu Simbel began in the 13th century BCE and lasted for about 20 years. The complex was known as the Temple of Ramesses, Beloved by Amun. It has two temples: the Great Temple, dedicated to Ra-Horakhty, Ptah and Amun and to the deified Ramesses himself, and the Small Temple, dedicated to the goddess Hathor, personified by his chief wife Nefertari.

Over time the temples fell into disuse and a sand dune came to cover most of the Great Temple. By the 6th century BCE the sand already covered the statues of the main temple up to their knees. The site remained unknown to Europeans until March 1813, when the Swiss researcher Johann Ludwig Burckhardt found the small temple and the top frieze of the main temple.

The Great Temple is entered between four seated statues of Ramesses II, each 20 m high, with smaller figures of his family beside his legs. The facade behind them is 33 m high and 38 m wide. The complex was moved in 1968 to higher ground, under an artificial hill, to keep it from being submerged by Lake Nasser, within the International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia. Abu Simbel is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site known as the Nubian Monuments, and is open to visitors.
abu-tahir-al-jannabi: Abu Tahir Sulayman was an Arabized Persian, born in June or July 906 at Ganaveh on the coast of Fars. His father, Abu Sa'id, a tribal leader taught by Hamdan Qarmat of Kufa, had begun the militarization of the Qarmatians.

Most Arabic sources agree that Abu Sa'id named his eldest son, Abu'l-Qasim Sa'id, as heir and that Abu Tahir revolted against him and usurped power. Another tradition, reported by the Kufan anti-Isma'ili polemicist Ibn Rizam, holds that Sa'id was only a regent and handed over power in 917/918, when his brother was barely ten. It is likely that power was nominally shared among all the sons, with Abu Tahir dominant. Abu'l-Qasim was not executed and lived until 972.

In 926 he led his army as far north as Kufa and made the Abbasids pay large sums for him to leave. On his return he built palaces at Ahsa and declared it his permanent capital. In 928 Caliph al-Muqtadir sent against him the generals Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj, Mu'nis al-Muzaffar and Harun, who were beaten and driven back to Baghdad.

At Mecca in 930 he was at first refused entry, invoked the right of all Muslims to enter and swore that he came in peace. Once inside, his men rode into the Masjid al-Haram, massacred the pilgrims, set fire to the Kaaba and threw bodies into the Zamzam Well. The attack was believed to be meant to prompt the appearance of the Mahdi and followed millenarian excitement over the conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter in 928.

The Mahdi he recognised in 931, Abu'l-Fadl al-Isfahani, a prisoner who claimed descent from the Sasanian kings, restored the veneration of fire, burned religious books and had members of Bahrayn's notable families executed. In one account Abu Tahir's mother exposed him and his brother Sa'id killed him after eighty days; in others Abu Tahir denounced him as a false Mahdi and had him executed.

Abu Tahir took back control of the state and resumed his attacks on pilgrims crossing Arabia. He rejected the attempts of both the Abbasids and the Fatimids to persuade him to return the Black Stone. He died of smallpox in 944, aged about 38, and was succeeded by his three surviving sons and his nephews. According to the historian al-Juwayni the stone came back in 951, thrown in a sack into the Great Mosque of Kufa with a note: "By command we took it, and by command we have brought it back." Its removal had broken it into seven pieces.
abu-ubayda-ibn-al-jarrah: Abu Ubayda was born around 583 into the al-Harith ibn Fihr clan of the Quraysh, settled in the lower quarter of Mecca. His full name was Amir ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Jarrah. His father, Abd Allah, was among the Quraysh chiefs in the Fijar War against the Hawazin nomads. According to traditional accounts, he was the ninth person to accept Islam, embracing it with Uthman ibn Maz'un and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf before Muhammad began preaching from the house of al-Arqam. After the migration to Medina he was bound in brotherhood to Muhammad ibn Maslama.

Abu Ubayda fought at Badr in 624, where his father fought on the Quraysh side; commentators say Quran 58:22 was revealed about him after he killed his father there. At Uhud in 625 he stayed beside Muhammad when most of the army fled, and lost two front teeth drawing iron links of Muhammad's helmet or armour from his cheeks. He took part in all the major campaigns, led the Expedition of al-Khabt, and in 630 commanded the Muhajirun and Ansar in the Expedition of Dhat al-Salasil. Muhammad also sent him to instruct a Christian delegation from Najran, calling him trustworthy.

Traditions place him with Abu Bakr and Umar in the intervention that won the Ansar's allegiance to Abu Bakr at the Saqifa in 632. Al-Baladhuri denies that Abu Bakr sent him to Syria; modern historians date his dispatch to Umar's reign, around 636, as commander of reinforcements, with Khalid ibn al-Walid then holding supreme command. Khalil Athamina holds that Umar appointed him to the supreme command after the Muslim victory at the Yarmuk. He led the army that took Jerusalem in 636 and took Damascus, Homs, Antioch and Aleppo, then administered them.

During the drought of 638, Umar asked the governors for aid. Abu Ubayda sent caravans, and 4,000 camels loaded with food reached Medina first; Umar put him in charge of distribution and offered 4,000 dinars, which he refused. He died of the plague of Amwas in 639 and left no descendants. From the 13th century his tomb was traditionally held to be at Ammata in the Jordan Valley, which became known as Ghawr Abi Ubayda, though Tiberias and Beisan were also named. The Jarrahs, who claimed descent from him, kept the tomb and were exempt from taxes by the Ottoman authorities.
academie-francaise: The Académie grew from an informal literary group that came out of the salons held at the Hôtel de Rambouillet in the late 1620s and early 1630s. It met at the house of Valentin Conrart and then had nine members. Cardinal Richelieu made himself its protector, and new members were appointed in 1634. On 22 February 1635, at Richelieu's urging, King Louis XIII granted letters patent establishing it; those registered at the Parlement de Paris on 10 July 1637 charged it to give exact rules to the language and make it capable of treating the arts and sciences. Richelieu's model was the Accademia della Crusca, founded in Florence in 1582.

The National Convention suppressed all royal academies: in 1792 the election of replacements for dead members was prohibited, and in 1793 the academies were abolished. In 1795 a single body, the Institut de France, replaced them. Napoleon Bonaparte, as First Consul, restored the academies in 1803 only as divisions of the Institut. When Louis XVIII came to the throne in 1816 each class regained the title Académie, and since then its existence has been uninterrupted. The head of state has been the Académie's protector since Louis XIV took the role in 1672, after Richelieu and Pierre Séguier. It met at the Louvre from 1672 to 1805, and since 1805 at the Palais de l'Institut.

The forty seats are numbered, and candidates apply for a particular seat. A new member is elected by the Académie itself, and must deliver a speech that includes a eulogy of the predecessor. Members are called les immortels after the motto À l'immortalité on Richelieu's seal. They hold office for life but can be dismissed for grave misconduct; the first dismissal, in 1638, was for theft, and 20 members have been expelled in all, four of them at the end of the Second World War for association with the Vichy regime.

Marguerite Yourcenar was the first woman elected, in 1980. The Académie publishes the Dictionnaire de l'Académie française, whose first edition appeared in 1694, and awards more than sixty prizes, almost all created in the twentieth century.
acapulco: Acapulco lies on the Pacific coast of Mexico in the state of Guerrero, 380 km south of Mexico City, on a deep, semicircular bay. The municipality is 40 percent mountainous, 40 percent semi-flat and 20 percent flat, with elevations from sea level to 1,699 metres. The climate is tropical wet and dry, and Pacific hurricanes and tropical storms are a threat from May through November. The name comes from the Nahuatl Aca-pol-co, meaning where the reeds were destroyed or washed away, or at the big reeds, which inspired the city's seal, a glyph of two hands breaking reeds.

By the 8th century a small culture existed around the bay, first dominated by the Olmecs, who had two sites there, and then by others, including Teotihuacan and later Maya influence. In the 11th century Nahua migrants, ancestors of the Aztecs, came through. In the later 15th century, after four years of fighting, Acapulco became part of the Aztec Empire under Ahuizotl, but only transitorily: the Yopis, who controlled the territory, kept defending it until the Spanish arrived in the 1520s.

Europeans are said to have found the bay in one of two ways. Either explorers sent by Hernán Cortés subdued the area after 1523 and Captain Saavedra Cerón was authorised to found a settlement, or a small ship under Santiago Guevara found it on 13 December 1526.

Acapulco is a port of call for shipping and cruise lines running between Panama and San Francisco and the largest city of Guerrero. It rose to prominence between the 1940s and the 1960s as one of Mexico's oldest beach resorts. It was the eastern end of the trans-Pacific sailing route to Manila, then in a Spanish colony.
accra: Accra lies on the southern coast of Ghana, on the Gulf of Guinea. The name comes from the Akan word Nkran, meaning ants, a reference to the soldier ants and the anthills of the countryside around it. In the Ga language the town is called Ga, the same name as the Ga people. The historian Carl Christian Reindorf proposed a link between the martial qualities and migratory behaviour of the ants and those of the Ga. Anthills were sacred places, seen as points of contact between the known world and the world of the dead. The Danes spelled the name Akra.

By the 15th century the kingdom of Accra ruled the area from its capital at Ayawaso. Local inhabitants destroyed a Portuguese fort in 1576. In the 17th century the Dutch built Fort Crèvecœur, later called Ussher Fort, and the British built James Fort; Christiansborg also stood there. In 1677 the Akwamu ruler Ansa Sasraku sacked Ayawaso and beheaded the king, Okai Koi. The king's son Ofori retreated to Small Accra, the town beneath Fort Crèvecœur, and was driven into exile in Fetu in 1681.

Britain gradually acquired the other powers' interests, beginning in 1851 when Denmark sold Christiansborg; the Netherlands was the last to sell, in 1871. In 1877, at the end of the second Anglo-Asante War, Accra replaced Cape Coast as capital of the British Gold Coast, because its climate was drier. After a bubonic plague epidemic in 1908 the native-only neighbourhood of Adabraka was created to relieve crowding. A bridge over the Korle Lagoon in 1923 spurred settlement to the west, and cocoa became the largest export.

Accra is the capital and largest city of Ghana, and the Greater Accra Region has about 5.46 million people. Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana's first Prime Minister from 1957, drew up his own plan for the city. Its architecture ranges from 19th-century colonial buildings to modern towers. The Parliament, the Supreme Court and Black Star Square are there, and the city has an international airport and railway links to Tema, Sekondi-Takoradi and Kumasi.
aceh: The first evidence of human habitation in Aceh comes from a site near the Tamiang River, where shell middens and stone tools suggest occupation from around 10,000 BCE. Before Islam, Hindu-Buddhist culture existed in the area. Aceh is thought to have been one of the earliest centres of Islam in Southeast Asia: Marco Polo found Peureulak a Muslim town in 1292, and the gravestone of Sultan Malikussaleh, first Muslim ruler of Samudra, is dated 1297.

The Sultanate of Aceh was established by Sultan Ali Mughayat Syah in 1511, and in the early 17th century it was the wealthiest, most powerful and most cultivated state in the Strait of Malacca. The Dutch colonial government declared war on Aceh on 26 March 1873, citing pirates operating from Aceh. The campaign quickly drove out the sultan, but local leaders fought on in about four decades of guerrilla war marked by high levels of atrocities.

Aceh was incorporated into North Sumatra in 1950, which led to the Acehnese Rebellion of 1953–59. In 1976 Hasan Muhammad di Tiro proclaimed independence, and the Free Aceh Movement took up the struggle. On 26 December 2004 the Indian Ocean tsunami killed over 170,000 people in Aceh. It helped bring about the Helsinki Agreement of 15 August 2005, under which Aceh received special autonomy and the movement disarmed.

Aceh is a province of Indonesia on the northern end of Sumatra, with Banda Aceh as its capital and largest city. It is the only Indonesian province to officially integrate Islamic law. The Acehnese, the largest of ten indigenous groups, speak a language of the Aceh-Chamic group that was traditionally written in Arabic script. The 2020 census counted 5,274,871 people. Gunung Leuser National Park protects the Sumatran tiger, orangutan and Sumatran elephant.
achaea: Achaea lies in the northwestern part of the Peloponnese peninsula and forms a regional unit in the region of Western Greece. It is bordered by Elis to the west and southwest, Arcadia to the south and Corinthia to the east and southeast, with the Gulf of Corinth to the northeast and the Gulf of Patras to the northwest. The mountain Panachaiko, 1926 metres high, dominates the coast near Patras, and higher peaks lie in the south, among them Aroania at 2341 metres and Erymanthos at 2224 metres.

The Achaean League was a Hellenistic confederation of city states in Achaea, founded in 280/281 BCE. It grew to include most of the Peloponnese and much reduced Macedonian rule there. After Macedon's defeat by the Romans in the early 2nd century BCE, the League defeated a heavily weakened Sparta and took control of the whole peninsula. As Roman influence grew it revolted in the Achaean War, was defeated at the Battle of Corinth in 146 BCE, and was dissolved by the Romans. In 51/52 CE Lucius Junius Gallio Annaeanus was proconsul of Achaea; the Acts of the Apostles shows him presiding over the trial of Paul at Corinth.

Achaea remained a Byzantine province after the fall of the Western Roman Empire. Slavs reached the Peloponnese in the 6th and 7th centuries, but the coastal cities stayed largely Byzantine and a siege of Patras in 805/807 failed. After the Fourth Crusade the Principality of Achaea was founded in 1205, with the Barony of Patras, the Barony of Vostitsa, the Barony of Chalandritsa and the Barony of Kalavryta in the region. Patras, under its Latin Archbishop, became a semi-autonomous domain under the protection of Venice and the Holy See. The principality fell to the Byzantine Empire in 1430 and became part of the Despotate of the Morea, which fell to the Ottoman Empire in 1460. Venice held Achaea from 1687 to 1715.

In the Greek War of Independence Aigio was one of the first cities liberated, and all of Achaea was freed by the end of 1821. Tens of thousands of refugees from Asia Minor were settled around Patras after the Greco Turkish War of 1919-1922.

Achaea is one of the regional units of Greece, with its capital at Patras, the third largest city in the country. About two thirds of its people live near Patras, and the regional unit holds about one third of the population of the Peloponnese. Its five municipalities are Aigialeia, Erymanthos, Kalavryta, Patras and West Achaea. The Agia Lavra monastery lies a few kilometres west of Kalavryta.
achaemenid-empire: The empire takes its name from Achaemenes, credited as the progenitor of the dynasty, a minor seventh-century ruler of Anshan in south-western Iran and a vassal of Assyria. By the 7th century BCE the region of Persis had been settled by Persian people. From Persis Cyrus rose. He revolted against the Median Empire in 553 BCE and in 550 BCE defeated the Medes, captured Astyages and took the Median capital, Ecbatana. By inheriting Astyages' empire he also inherited its conflicts with Lydia and the Neo-Babylonian Empire, both of which he went on to defeat.

Cyrus's son Cambyses II used the army in Egypt against Psamtik III, while Cyrus himself died fighting a local Iranian insurgency. Darius I reinforced the empire, expanded Persepolis as a ceremonial capital and established the first Persian royal navy. The empire was repulsed from Scythia in 513 BCE and from Greece in 492–490 BCE and 480–479 BCE. The Ionian Revolt of 499 to 493 BCE began when Aristagoras, tyrant of Miletus, incited Ionia against Darius.

In 343 BCE Artaxerxes III invaded Egypt with 330,000 Persians and 14,000 Greeks. Artaxerxes IV Arses was poisoned by the eunuch Bagoas, who set Darius III on the throne. In 334 BCE Alexander the Great invaded Asia Minor, and in 330 BCE the empire was conquered in its entirety. Later Persian rulers in Fārs, the Frataraka, acted for the Seleucids and then became independent kings of Persis under the Parthians.

Cyrus founded the empire as a multi-state realm governed from four capitals: Pasargadae, Babylon, Susa and Ecbatana. It was divided into satrapies, between 20 and 30 at different times, each with a satrap, a general and a state secretary. Darius I introduced the daric, a gold coin, and the silver siglos, and a tax system tailored to each satrapy: Babylon was assessed at 1,000 silver talents, while Egypt supplied 120,000 measures of grain and 700 talents of silver.

The Immortals were a unit of 10,000 trained soldiers, and a postal system ran through relay stations. Elamite was the language of the chancellery while the court sat at Susa, and Aramaic gained in importance under Artaxerxes I. The Hebrew Bible reports that Cyrus released the Jewish people from the Babylonian captivity and helped rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem. Four kings are buried at Naqsh-e Rostam, and Cyrus's tomb at Pasargadae is a World Heritage Site.
achilles: In Greek myth Achilles was the son of Thetis, a Nereid, and Peleus, king of the Myrmidons. According to one account, Zeus and Poseidon had both courted Thetis until Prometheus warned Zeus of a prophecy that she would bear a son greater than his father, and the two gods had her wed Peleus. Achilles was raised in Phthia with his companion Patroclus and educated by the centaur Chiron.

The story that Thetis dipped him in the river Styx, leaving him vulnerable only at the heel, comes from the Achilleid of Statius, written in the first century CE. No source before Statius mentions general invulnerability: in the Iliad Achilles is wounded at the elbow.

According to the Iliad, Achilles came to Troy with 50 ships, each carrying 50 Myrmidons. On the way he wounded King Telephus of Mysia, a wound that would not heal until Achilles healed it, as an oracle had said. His most notable feat was the slaying of the Trojan prince Hector outside the gates of Troy.

The Iliad does not present his death, but other sources agree that Paris killed him near the end of the war with an arrow. His tomb in the Troad was venerated through antiquity by Thessalians, by Persian expeditionary forces, by Alexander the Great and by the emperor Caracalla. Dedications from Greek colonies on the Black Sea attest a heroic cult from the sixth century BCE, and in the third century CE stelae at Olbia name an Achilles Pontarches, invoked as protector of the city. Aeschylus wrote a trilogy about him, of which only fragments survive.
acropolis-of-athens: The Acropolis is a flat-topped rock that rises 150 metres above sea level in the city of Athens and has a surface of about 3 hectares. It is a klippe made of two rock units: the soft reddish Athens schist and the overlying Acropolis limestone, thrust over it by tectonic forces. The limestone is unstable and prone to rock slides. The marble of its buildings came from the quarries of Mount Pentelicus, northeast of the city. In ancient times the hill was also called Cecropia, after the first Athenian king Cecrops.

Habitation of the hill is evidenced as early as the 4th millennium BCE. A Mycenaean megaron palace probably stood there in the late Bronze Age, with a Cyclopean wall 760 metres long. Athena Polias had a temple, the Hekatompedon, built between 570 and 550 BCE. Around 500 BCE it was dismantled for a grander building, the Older Parthenon, which was still unfinished when the Persians sacked the city in 480 BCE. The Athenians built parts of it into the new northern wall, where they can still be seen.

Under Pericles, in the so-called Golden Age (460–430 BCE), the Parthenon and other temples were rebuilt, with the sculptor Phidias and the architects Ictinus and Callicrates responsible. Mnesicles began the Propylaea in 437 BCE, and the Erechtheion was built between 421 and 406 BCE. In the Byzantine period the Parthenon served as a church of the Virgin Mary. In 1687, during the Morean War, a Venetian bombardment hit the gunpowder the Ottomans kept in the Parthenon, and the explosion severely damaged it.

After Greek independence most Byzantine, Frankish and Ottoman additions were cleared from the site. The Parthenon mosque was demolished in 1843. The Acropolis Restoration Project, begun in 1975, reassembled original fragments with titanium dowels and used new Pentelic marble sparingly. The Acropolis Museum stands on the southern slope, 280 metres from the Parthenon.

In antiquity the Great Panathenaea, held every four years, ended with a procession to the Acropolis, where a new robe was placed on the statue of Athena. Since at least the mid-18th century the Acropolis has often been invoked as a symbol of the Greek legacy and of classical Greece.
acts-of-the-apostles: Acts is the second part of a two-volume work, Luke–Acts, whose first part is the Gospel of Luke. Together the two volumes make up 27.5 percent of the New Testament, the largest share attributed to a single author. The author is not named in the text. Church tradition from the 2nd century identifies him as Luke, a companion of Paul, and the first-person passages in Acts 16 to 27 have led many to read him as a participant in Paul's journeys. Critical opinion on the traditional attribution has been roughly evenly divided, and some scholars point to differences from Paul's own letters. The title was first used by Irenaeus in the late 2nd century and was not given by the author.

Most scholars date the work to 80 to 90 CE, because it uses the Gospel of Mark, looks back on the destruction of Jerusalem and shows no awareness of Paul's letters. Others allow an early 2nd-century date, while some argue against a late date because the book says nothing of the burning of Rome or of Paul's trial before Nero.

Acts has 28 chapters and moves from Jerusalem to Rome. It begins with the ascension of Jesus and the replacement of Judas Iscariot by Matthias. At Pentecost the Holy Spirit descends on the apostles, and the first believers share their property. After Stephen is stoned, persecution scatters the community, and the message reaches the Samaritans and the Gentiles. Saul of Tarsus, a persecutor, is converted by a vision. Peter preaches to the centurion Cornelius, and at Antioch the followers of Jesus are first called Christians.

The second half follows Paul. The Gentile mission, promoted from Antioch, is confirmed at a meeting in Jerusalem. Paul travels through western Asia Minor and the Aegean, founding churches. After a mob attacks him in Jerusalem he is imprisoned, claims his right as a Roman citizen to be tried in Rome and is sent there by sea. He spends two years under house arrest, proclaiming the Kingdom of God. The book ends without recording the outcome of his legal troubles.

Acts was read as a reliable history of the early church well into the post-Reformation era. The debate over its historicity was most vehement between 1895 and 1915, when Ferdinand Christian Baur argued that the author had rewritten history to present a united Peter and Paul. Most scholars now treat it as ancient historiography, with a theological purpose, and a middle range of scholars judge it relatively reliable by the standards of Hellenistic history writing. Its account agrees with Paul's letters on the outline of his career, though it differs on details.
acts-of-union-1707: England and Scotland shared a monarch from 1603, when James VI of Scotland inherited the English throne from Elizabeth I and became James VI and I. He announced an intention to unite the two realms, but the English Parliament feared an absolutist structure like Scotland's, and he withdrew his proposals while taking the title King of Great Britain. Union was tried again in 1606, 1667 and 1689. Religion kept the churches apart: the Church of Scotland was Calvinist, and attempts by James and Charles I to impose policy led to the Wars of the Three Kingdoms from 1639. Some Presbyterian leaders later saw union as a way to secure free trade and a Presbyterian kirk.

By the early eighteenth century the Scottish economy was weak: largely agrarian, with chronic deflation and tariff wars over linen. Colonial trade led to the failed Darien scheme. Queen Anne had favoured deeper integration since she came to the throne in 1702, and in 1705 both parliaments agreed to new negotiations.

Each country named 31 commissioners, led on the Scottish side by the Duke of Queensberry and the Earl of Seafield. Most Scots favoured union, while England's included many Whigs and only one Tory. They met at the Cockpit in London from 16 April to 22 July 1706. Within days England had a guarantee that the Hanoverian dynasty would succeed Anne to the Scottish crown, and Scotland had a guarantee of access to colonial markets.

In the Scottish Parliament the debate began on 3 October 1706. About 100 of its 227 members supported the Court Party, aided by some 25 of the Squadrone Volante. The opposing Country party included the Duke of Hamilton, Lord Belhaven and Andrew Fletcher of Saltoun. The Court party had significant funding from England, and included many in debt after the Darien Disaster. Article 1 passed by 116 votes to 83 on 4 November 1706, and the treaty as a whole was ratified on 16 January 1707 by 110 votes to 69. The Parliament of England then passed an equivalent act, and both took effect on 1 May 1707.

The Treaty of Union had 25 articles, 15 of them economic. It joined the two kingdoms in an incorporating union as Great Britain, with Queen Anne as sovereign and one parliament at Westminster, to which Scotland sent representative peers to the House of Lords. It created a customs and monetary union and restated the Act of Settlement 1701, barring Roman Catholics from the throne. The Church of Scotland remained the established church, the Court of Session stayed within Scotland and Scots law remained in force. A separate act secured the Presbyterian church, after which the church ended its open opposition. In 1708 English treason law was extended across Great Britain.
adam-smith: Adam Smith was born in Kirkcaldy, Fife, Scotland. His father, Adam Smith senior, was a Writer to the Signet who also served as comptroller of the customs in Kirkcaldy, and he died two months before the birth. His mother, Margaret Douglas, was the daughter of Robert Douglas of Strathendry. Smith was baptised on 5 June 1723, a date often treated as his birthday, but his actual date of birth is unknown. He attended the Burgh School of Kirkcaldy from 1729 to 1737, learning Latin, mathematics, history and writing.

At 14 he entered the University of Glasgow and studied moral philosophy under Francis Hutcheson. In 1740 he was the graduate scholar presented to study at Balliol College, Oxford, under the Snell Exhibition. He thought the teaching at Glasgow far better than that at Oxford, which he found intellectually stifling, and he is reported to have had a copy of David Hume's A Treatise of Human Nature confiscated there.

After his studies Smith delivered a successful series of public lectures at the University of Edinburgh, which led to a collaboration with David Hume during the Scottish Enlightenment. He then obtained a professorship at Glasgow, where he taught moral philosophy and wrote The Theory of Moral Sentiments. Later he took a tutoring position that allowed him to travel throughout Europe and meet intellectual figures of his era. He never married and lived with his mother after his return from France; she died six years before him. At his request his personal papers were destroyed after his death.

The Theory of Moral Sentiments was published in 1759 by the co-publishers Andrew Millar of London and Alexander Kincaid of Edinburgh. Smith kept revising it until his death and is believed to have considered it a better work than The Wealth of Nations.

An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations appeared in 1776 and is regarded as his magnum opus, marking the start of modern economic scholarship as a comprehensive system. In response to mercantilism, the policy of protecting national markets by reducing imports and increasing exports, he laid the foundations of classical free-market theory. He developed the concept of division of labour and argued that rational self-interest and competition can lead to economic prosperity. He explained the distribution of wealth and power by natural, political, social, economic, legal, environmental and technological factors rather than divine will. He was controversial in his day, and writers such as Horace Walpole satirised his approach and style. He died on 17 July 1790.
adana: Adana lies on the Seyhan River, 35 km inland from the northeastern shores of the Mediterranean Sea, on the 37th parallel north. It occupies the centre of the Cilician plain, called Çukurova in Turkish, a relatively large stretch of flat, fertile land south-east of the Taurus Mountains. Cilicia was important in the classical world because it lies by a pass in the Taurus Mountains, used for military campaigns and trade routes.

The name has been used for over four millennia. One theory derives it from an Indo-European expression a danu, meaning on the river. According to the Hittite inscription of Kava, Kizzuwatna, inhabited by Luwians and Hurrians, ruled Adana under Hittite protection by 1335 BCE. After the collapse of the Hittite Empire around 1191 to 1189 BCE the Denyen sea peoples took control until around 900 BCE. After the Greek migration into Cilicia in the 8th century BCE the region was unified under the Mopsos dynasty, with Adana as capital.

At the Battle of Sarus in April 625 Heraclius defeated the Sasanian forces of Shahrbaraz on the east bank of the river, after a charge across the bridge built by Emperor Justinian, now the Taşköprü. The Umayyad Caliph Abd al-Malik conquered Cilicia in 704. Suleiman ibn Qutulmish annexed Adana in 1084, and Armenian forces captured it in 1132. Under the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia it remained a centre of handicrafts and trade, and Venetian and Genoese merchants came for goods imported through the port of Ayas.

Ramazan Bey made Adana the capital of the Ramadanid Emirate, which was de facto independent through the 15th century until Selim I incorporated it into the Ottoman Empire in 1517. The Ramadanid beys held the administration of the Sanjak of Adana until 1608, when the Ottomans began direct rule. Under the Convention of Kütahya of 14 May 1833 Cilicia passed to Egypt, whose ruler's son Ibrahim Pasha demolished Adana Castle and the city walls in 1836, and the Convention of Alexandria of 27 November 1840 returned it to Ottoman rule. From the 19th century Adana was a major centre of cotton production.

Adana is a large city in southern Turkey and the administrative seat of Adana province, with a metropolitan population of 1,816,750 across its four districts: Seyhan, Yüreğir, Çukurova and Sarıçam. It remains a centre of regional trade. Among its landmarks are the Taşköprü, a 2nd-century Roman bridge, and the Ulu Cami, built in 1541 in the Ramadanid era. Adana kebabı, made from minced meat, is the city's best-known dish.
adda-river: The Adda, known in Latin as Abdua or Addua, is a tributary of the Po, 313 kilometres long. It rises in the Alpisella valley near the head of the Fraele glen, in the Rhaetian Alps near the border with Switzerland, and several smaller streams join it near Bormio. The highest point of its drainage basin is the summit of La Spedla, a subpeak of Piz Bernina, at 4,020 metres. It flows southwest and then west through the Valtellina, past Tirano, where the Poschiavino joins it from the right, and Sondrio, where the Mallero joins. This east to west run is unusual in northern Italy.

The river enters the northern end of Lake Como and contributes much of the lake's volume. It leaves by the lake's southeastern arm at Lecco, crosses the Lombardy Plain, receives the Brembo and the Serio from the left and joins the Po near Castelnuovo Bocca d'Adda, a few kilometres upstream of Cremona. Towns along it include Bormio, Tirano, Sondrio, Bellagio, Lecco, Brivio and Lodi.

The lower Adda historically marked the border between the Republic of Venice and the Duchy of Milan, as established by the Treaty of Lodi in 1454. Several battles were fought on its banks. In 1705 Prince Eugene of Savoy and the French fought at the bridgehead of Cassano d'Adda, where Alexander Suvorov led his forces across the river in 1799. At Lodi in 1796 Napoleon defeated Austrian forces. The Trezzo sull'Adda Bridge, built in 1377, had a single arch of 72 metres, the longest bridge arch built before metal was used in bridge construction.
addis-ababa: Addis Ababa lies in the Ethiopian Highlands, on the western edge of the Great Rift Valley, at an elevation of 2,355 metres, which makes it the highest capital in Africa. It stands at the foot of Mount Entoto and forms part of the watershed of the Awash. The high elevation moderates temperatures, and no month has a mean temperature above 22 degrees.

The name is Amharic for new flower; in Oromo the place is called Finfinnee, meaning fountain of hot mineral water. The city is surrounded by the Special Zone of Oromia, and the Constitution of Ethiopia says that the special interest of the State of Oromia in Addis Ababa, in social services and natural resources, is to be respected.

Menelik II, Negus of Shewa, founded the city in 1886, after finding Mount Entoto unpleasant two years earlier. It was then a resort town, and its many mineral springs drew nobles of the empire, who settled permanently, followed by artisans, merchants and foreign visitors. Menelik formed his imperial palace in 1887, and in 1889 Addis Ababa became the empire's capital, after which international embassies opened. Urban development began in the 20th century without prior planning. The Oromo left the area after Menelik's conquest and were physically removed from near the city under Haile Selassie and the Derg.

The city saw an economic boom in 1926 and 1927, with stone houses filled with imported European furniture, imported automobiles and expanded banks. During the Italian occupation a masterplan increased urbanisation and modernisation, in the hope that Addis Ababa would become a more colonial city. French and British consultants drew later master plans from the 1940s onwards.

Addis Ababa is the capital and largest city of Ethiopia and a federally chartered city. It is the headquarters of the African Union and the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa. Addis Ababa University is there. All Ethiopian ethnic groups are represented, the largest being the Amhara, Oromo and Gurage, and Amharic is the most common mother tongue.
adelaide: Adelaide lies on the Adelaide Plains, north of the Fleurieu Peninsula, between Gulf St Vincent in the west and the Mount Lofty Ranges in the east. The city stretches about 20 kilometres from the coast to the foothills. Its climate is a hot-summer Mediterranean one, with hot, dry summers and cool winters, and most rain falls in winter. The traditional owners of the region are the Kaurna, and in the Kaurna language the name Tarndanya refers to the city centre and the surrounding Park Lands. Aboriginal people have lived in the area for a very long time, and archaeological evidence of Aboriginal culture at Hallett Cove Conservation Park dates back 40,000 years.

Edward Gibbon Wakefield's ideas about colonial reform lay behind the project of a new colony, which Robert Gouger petitioned the British government to create. The South Australia Act 1834 followed. The first British colonisers arrived in February 1836, and colonial government began on 28 December 1836, when the governor made a proclamation near the Old Gum Tree in what is now Glenelg North. The date is still commemorated in South Australia as Proclamation Day. The city was named in honour of Adelaide of Saxe-Meiningen, wife of King William IV, and was founded as the planned capital of a freely settled British colony.

Colonel William Light, the first surveyor-general of South Australia, designed the city centre as a grid with five squares, ringed by parkland known as the Adelaide Parklands. His choice of site was at first unpopular with the early settlers and with the first governor, John Hindmarsh, because it lay far from the harbour at Port Adelaide and had little fresh water. The colony was founded on a vision of religious tolerance, which attracted many faiths and earned Adelaide the name City of Churches. Although it was English in culture, it drew German and other European nonconformists early on. The first German Lutherans arrived in 1838 and brought vine cuttings that founded the wineries of the Barossa Valley.

Adelaide was Australia's third largest city for most of the 20th century. Electric street lighting arrived in 1900 and electric trams in 1909, and 28,000 men were sent from the state to fight in the First World War.

Adelaide is the capital of South Australia and the seat of its government, with a bicameral Parliament made up of the House of Assembly and the Legislative Council. Its early buildings were often made of local bluestone. North Terrace, the cultural precinct, holds institutions built when the city was still Australia's third largest, among them the State Library of South Australia and the South Australian Museum. Light's plan of the Parklands survives, and the Parklands are now listed as national heritage.
aden: Aden lies on the north coast of the Gulf of Aden, near the eastern approach to the Red Sea and about 170 km east of the Strait of Bab al-Mandab, which makes it a gateway between the Red Sea and the Arabian Sea. The highlands of Jabal Shamsan rise in the south, with peaks above 500 metres, and like the rest of Yemen's highlands they are of volcanic origin. Aden encloses the eastern side of a vast natural harbour that forms the modern port.

The Greeks called Aden Arabia Emporion, the Arabian trading port, and in the 1st century BCE it was known as Eudaemon, a transshipping point for the Red Sea trade. According to the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, it fell on hard times in the 1st century CE when ships began to cross directly to India. The Book of Ezekiel names Aden among the merchants of Sheba.

The British Empire held the city from 1839 until independence in 1967. By 1920 it was a major commercial centre of the Arabian Peninsula and supplied coal and salt to passing ships. The oil refinery began operating in 1954, and British Petroleum ran it and the port until the South Yemeni government took them over in 1978. Aden was the capital of South Yemen from 1967 until the union with North Yemen in 1990.

Aden is the principal city of Aden Governorate, which has eight districts. Its airport and the main offices of Aden University are at Khormaksar, on the isthmus that links the peninsulas to the mainland.
adige: The Adige rises near the Reschen Pass, at 1,504 m, close to the borders with Austria and Switzerland, and flows through the artificial Lake Reschen. A church tower marks the site of the former village of Alt Graun, which was evacuated and flooded in 1953 after the dam was finished. Near Glurns the Rom joins it from the Swiss Val Müstair. It then runs eastward through the Vinschgau to Merano, where the Passer joins from the north. The section between Merano and Bolzano is called the Etschtal.

South of Bolzano the Eisack joins and the river turns south through a valley that has always been one of the major routes through the Alps, connecting the Reschen and Brenner passes; the Brenner, at 1,370 m, is considered the easiest of the main Alpine passes. Near Trento the Avisio, Noce and Fersina join. The river then crosses Trentino and Veneto, passing Rovereto, Verona and Rovigo, and reaches the Adriatic across the north-eastern Po Plain. In the delta the Adige and the Po run parallel without properly joining. The Mori–Torbole tunnel, an underground canal built for flood prevention, links the Adige with Lake Garda.

The origin of the name is unknown. Nineteenth-century theories, such as a derivation from Proto-Celtic meaning the water and a link with the River Tees, were never accepted by Celtic specialists and are now obsolete. The Chiusa di Salorno narrows the valley at Salorno and marks the southernmost part of the predominantly German-speaking province of South Tyrol. The Adige was named in the Lied der Deutschen of 1841 as the southern border of the German language area. Germany adopted the song as its national anthem in 1922, although Italy by then controlled the whole river. The marble trout, native to the river, is now far less common than before, partly because stocked brown trout interbreed with it.
adnan-menderes: Ali Adnan Menderes was born in 1899 in Koçarlı, Aydın, to a wealthy landowner of Crimean Tatar origin. He studied at the American College in İzmir and, in the Turkish War of Independence, fought the invading Greek army and received the Medal of Independence. In 1930 he organised a branch of the short-lived Liberal Republican Party in Aydın, and after it dissolved Atatürk himself invited him to join the Republican People's Party (CHP); he was elected deputy for Aydın in 1931.

Under İsmet İnönü he opposed statist policy. In June 1945 he joined Celâl Bayar, Fuat Köprülü and Refik Koraltan in the Motion with Four Signatures, which demanded more political freedom, and by September three of them had been stripped of CHP membership. The four founded the Democrat Party (DP) on 7 January 1946.

The DP won 52 percent of the vote in the first free elections in Turkish history, on 14 May 1950, and Menderes became prime minister. He won again in 1954 and 1957. Turkey fought in the Korean War and was admitted to NATO in 1952. With Marshall Plan aid, agriculture was mechanised and transport, energy and education advanced, though the economy slowed in the mid-1950s. He campaigned in 1950 on legalising the Arabic call to prayer, which had been banned.

His government instituted press censorship, had journalists arrested and tried to control the opposition parties and the universities. In September 1955, after a bomb exploded near the Turkish consulate in Thessaloniki, mobs in Istanbul destroyed thousands of shops, houses, churches and graves of the Greek minority, killing over a dozen people. Several sources link the government to the Istanbul pogrom, and Menderes later apologised and offered compensation.

A military coup on 27 May 1960 deposed the government. Menderes was tried on the island of Yassıada for violating the constitution, embezzlement and ordering the Istanbul pogrom, and was sentenced to death. He attempted suicide with sleeping pills, and appeals from Cemal Gürsel, İsmet İnönü and foreign leaders did not save him. He was hanged on İmralı on 17 September 1961, with the ministers Fatin Rüştü Zorlu and Hasan Polatkan. The Turkish Parliament pardoned all three on 17 September 1990, and his grave was moved to a mausoleum in Istanbul. Adnan Menderes University in Aydın and Adnan Menderes Airport in İzmir bear his name.
adolf-frederick-king-of-sweden: Adolf Frederick was born on 14 May 1710 at Gottorf Castle, near Schleswig, a member of a junior line of the House of Holstein-Gottorp. His father, Christian August, had been Protestant Prince-Bishop of Lübeck since 1705 and acted during the Great Northern War as administrator of Holstein-Gottorp for his underage nephew, Duke Charles Frederick. His mother, Albertina Frederica of Baden-Durlach, descended from earlier Swedish royalty.

From 1727 to 1750 he was prince-bishop of Lübeck, ruling a fief around Eutin. After Charles Frederick died in 1739 he became administrator of Holstein-Kiel for the duke's orphan son, Charles Peter Ulrich, who was soon invited to Russia by his aunt, Empress Elizabeth, and was later Peter III of Russia.

In 1743 the Hat faction elected Adolf Frederick heir to the throne of Sweden, wanting better conditions from Empress Elizabeth at the Treaty of Åbo. In 1744 he married Louisa Ulrika of Prussia, a sister of Frederick the Great. On the death of Frederick I on 25 March 1751 he became the first Swedish king from the House of Holstein-Gottorp, and he was crowned in Stockholm Cathedral on 26 November 1751.

Real power lay with the Riksdag of the Estates, often distracted by party strife. Twice he tried to free himself from its control. In 1756, urged on by Louisa Ulrika, he took part in a coup to abolish the rule of the Riksdag and restore absolute monarchy, and nearly lost his throne. In the December Crisis of 1768, guided by his eldest son Gustav, he overthrew the Cap senate but could make no use of the victory.

The reign saw a long period of internal peace, but finances stagnated under the mercantilist policies of the Hat administration. In the parliament of 1765–1766 the opposition took over the government and enacted reforms towards economic liberalism, as well as a Freedom of Press Act that ended censorship, keeping punishment only for libelling the monarch or the Church of Sweden.

Adolf Frederick died suddenly in Stockholm on 12 February 1771, with symptoms resembling heart failure or poisoning. Stories that he died of an enormous meal are considered propaganda by modern writers. His son Gustav III seized power in a military coup in 1772 and restored absolute rule. The king was regarded as dependent on others and lacking the talents of a statesman, but was reported to be a good husband and a gentle master. He had a talent for astronomy, music and military matters, and his favourite pastime was making snuffboxes. He and Louisa Ulrika had five children, among them Gustav III and Charles XIII.
adolf-hitler: Adolf Hitler was born on 20 April 1889 in Braunau am Inn, a town in Austria-Hungary close to the border with Germany. He was the fourth of six children of Alois Hitler and his third wife, Klara Pölzl, and three siblings died in infancy. Alois was the illegitimate child of Maria Schicklgruber and bore her surname until 1876, when he took the name Hitler. Adolf's refusal to accept school discipline led to conflict with his father, who beat him; his mother tried to protect him. He moved to Germany in 1913.

In July 1919 Hitler was sent by the army to infiltrate the German Workers' Party (DAP), which he joined as member 555, the party having begun its count at 500 to seem larger. The party became the Nazi Party, and in 1921 he was appointed its leader. A coup attempt at Munich in 1923 failed; he was sentenced to five years in prison, served just over a year, and dictated the first volume of Mein Kampf there.

The Great Depression gave the party its opening: it won 107 seats in 1930, and after the elections of November 1932 it held the most seats in the Reichstag without a majority. Franz von Papen and other conservatives persuaded President Paul von Hindenburg to appoint Hitler chancellor on 30 January 1933. The Enabling Act of 23 March began the change to Nazi Germany, and after Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934 Hitler became head of state. Unemployment fell from six million in 1932 to fewer than one million in 1936. He ruled by the Führerprinzip, giving contradictory orders to set subordinates against one another.

Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and Hitler ordered the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941. By January 1942 he had decided that the Jews, Slavs and other deportees considered undesirable should be killed.

On 29 April 1945 Hitler married Eva Braun in the Führerbunker in Berlin, and the next day they killed themselves to avoid capture by the Soviet Red Army. Few Germans mourned him. The historian Ian Kershaw calls him the embodiment of modern political evil.

According to R. J. Rummel, the Nazi regime was responsible for the killing of an estimated 19.3 million civilians and prisoners of war, in addition to about six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust. A further 28.7 million soldiers and civilians died from military action in the European theatre. Germany suffered wholesale destruction, described as Stunde Null, or Zero Hour.
adolfo-suarez: Adolfo Suárez González was born on 25 September 1932 in Cebreros, in the Province of Ávila, the eldest son of the lawyer Hipólito Suárez Guerra. Both his parents supported the Republicans during the Spanish Civil War. He studied law at the University of Salamanca, worked for the municipal government of Ávila from 1955, and joined Opus Dei. In 1958 he became personal secretary to the civil governor of Ávila, Fernando Herrero Tejedor, and rose with him through the Movimiento Nacional. He was programme director of the state broadcaster RTVE in 1965, sat in the Francoist Cortes from 1967 and, as its director general from 1969, became a close friend of Prince Juan Carlos.

After Franco's death Suárez became secretary-general of the Movimiento in December 1975. In July 1976 King Juan Carlos asked for the resignation of Carlos Arias Navarro and chose the relatively obscure Suárez as prime minister, at 43 the youngest of the 20th century. His Francoist ties won the trust of the right, while reformists were dismayed. The Political Reform Act, establishing universal suffrage and a bicameral parliament, passed the Francoist Cortes in November 1976 and a referendum in December. Between February and April 1977 the PSOE and the Communist Party were legalised, trade unions recognised and the Movimiento abolished. The legalisation of the Communist Party provoked fury in the military, and Suárez responded by sacking hardliners.

His Union of the Democratic Centre won the 1977 election. A new constitution making Spain a constitutional monarchy was approved by referendum in December 1978, and Suárez negotiated the creation of the autonomous communities. His coalition won again in 1979, but economic recession, violence by ETA, demands for regional autonomy and divisions in his own party eroded his power. He survived a no-confidence motion in May 1980 and announced his resignation in January 1981.

In February 1981, as parliament voted on his successor Leopoldo Calvo-Sotelo, Lieutenant-Colonel Antonio Tejero and about 200 Civil Guards stormed the chamber and held the deputies for some 22 hours. Suárez, with two others, stayed calmly seated. In 1981 the king made him Duke of Suárez, and he received the Prince of Asturias Concord Award in 1996. He founded the Democratic and Social Centre in 1982 and retired from politics in 1991. Alzheimer's disease ended his public life in 2003. He died on 23 March 2014 in Madrid, was given a state funeral, and is buried in the cloister of Ávila Cathedral.
adolphe-sax: Antoine-Joseph Sax was born on 6 November 1814 in Dinant, in what is now Belgium, the first of eleven children of Charles-Joseph Sax and Marie-Joseph Masson. He was called Adolphe from childhood. In 1815 the family moved to Brussels, where his father, a joiner and cabinet maker whose factory had closed, opened an instrument-making workshop and was later appointed instrument maker to the Dutch royal court. Adolphe studied flute, harmony and solfège at the Royal School of Music and clarinet privately with Valentin Bender, but chose his father's workshop over a career as a performer.

Sax's first important invention was an improved bass clarinet, patented when he was 24. He settled permanently in Paris in 1842 and began work on valved bugles. He did not invent the type, but his instruments, called saxhorns, were more successful than his rivals' and were made in seven sizes. Hector Berlioz arranged in February 1844 for one of his pieces to be played entirely on saxhorns. The family laid the ground for the modern euphonium, and the British brass band movement adopted it exclusively.

On 28 June 1846 he patented the saxophone, intended for orchestras and military bands. By then he had designed saxophones from sopranino to subcontrabass, though not all were built. It did not become a standard orchestral instrument, but its ability to play technical passages like a woodwind while projecting like a brass instrument led to its use in military bands in France and elsewhere. During the Crimean War he designed two machines that were never built, a locomotive-powered organ meant to be heard across Paris and a giant cannon, the Saxocannon.

Sax began teaching at the Paris Conservatory in 1857 and led its new saxophone course. Rival makers attacked his patents for more than twenty years, and he sued them for infringement. He went bankrupt three times, in 1852, 1873 and 1877. He was made a Chevalier of the Legion of Honour in 1849 and won the first Grand Prix de la Facture Instrumentale at the Paris International Exposition of 1867. He died of pneumonia in Paris on 7 February 1894, in poverty, and was buried in the Cimetière de Montmartre.
adolphe-thiers: Adolphe Thiers was born out of wedlock in Marseille on 15 April 1797, during the rule of the Directorate. His father, Pierre-Louis-Marie Thiers, a businessman and occasional government official under Napoleon, married his mother, Marie-Madeleine Amic, on 13 May 1797, which made Adolphe legitimate, but he soon disappeared. He contacted his son only in 1825, when Adolphe was becoming well known in Paris journalism, to ask for money. Thiers replied that his only loyalty was to his mother, who had raised him alone, though he later supported his father and half-brothers. On his mother's side he had Levantine ancestry: his maternal grandfather Claude Amic had worked in Constantinople and married a Greek-speaking woman there.

Thiers was a key figure in the July Revolution of 1830, which replaced Charles X with Louis Philippe, and in the Revolution of 1848, which ended the July Monarchy. He was prime minister in 1836 and 1840, dedicated the Arc de Triomphe, and arranged the return of Napoleon's remains from Saint Helena. He was first a supporter and then a vocal opponent of Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, and was arrested and briefly expelled from France when Napoleon III seized power.

Thiers opposed the Franco-Prussian War, but after France's defeat he was elected chief executive and negotiated its end. In March 1871 the Paris Commune seized power, and he gave the army the orders to suppress it. The National Assembly named him president of the Republic in August 1871, when he was seventy-four. His chief accomplishment was the departure of German soldiers from most of French territory two years ahead of schedule. Opposed by monarchists and by the republican left, he resigned on 24 May 1873 and was replaced by Patrice de MacMahon. He died on 3 September 1877, and Victor Hugo and Léon Gambetta led the procession at his funeral.

Thiers was also a popular historian. His ten-volume history of the French Revolution, published from 1823 to 1827, was the first large-scale history of it in French. It condemned the Terror and radical leaders such as Marat and Robespierre and praised moderates such as Mirabeau and Lafayette, and it did much to undermine support for the last Bourbon king. He followed it with a twenty-volume Histoire du Consulat et de l'Empire, helped by his access to Talleyrand and Napoleon's surviving generals. He was elected to the Académie Française in 1834.

He built the ring of fortifications around Paris known as the Thiers Wall, whose line now marks the city limits, and completed the column on the Place Vendôme. Judgements of him depended on the politics of those judging him: Karl Marx attacked him in 1871, while Gustave Flaubert wrote that no one had summed up France better.
adonis: The Greeks considered the cult of Adonis to be of Near Eastern origin. His name comes from the Canaanite word adon, meaning lord. Most modern scholars consider the story of Aphrodite and Adonis derived from a Levantine version of the earlier Mesopotamian myth of Inanna and Dumuzid. Ezekiel 8:14 mentions Adonis under his earlier East Semitic name Tammuz and describes women mourning his death near the north gate of the Temple in Jerusalem.

The earliest known Greek reference is a fragment of Sappho, in which a chorus of girls asks Aphrodite how to mourn Adonis, and she answers that they must beat their breasts and tear their tunics. When the cult entered Greek culture is disputed. In Cyprus the cult of Adonis gradually superseded that of Cinyras.

Later sources tell the myth. In Ovid's Metamorphoses Adonis is the son of Myrrha, who was cursed by Aphrodite with desire for her father, King Cinyras of Cyprus, and who was changed into a myrrh tree but still gave birth to him. Aphrodite took the baby to the underworld to be fostered by Persephone, who also fell in love with him. Zeus decreed that he would spend a third of the year with each goddess and a third with whomever he chose; he chose Aphrodite.
While hunting, Adonis was wounded by a boar and bled to death in Aphrodite's arms. Versions differ on who sent the boar: Ares, jealous, or Artemis, or Apollo. Anemones grew where his blood fell.

The festival of Adonia was held by Greek women every year in midsummer. It was already observed on Lesbos in Sappho's time and seems to have become popular in Athens in the mid-fifth century BCE. The women planted gardens of Adonis, quick-growing plants such as lettuce, fennel, wheat and barley in baskets or broken pottery, and set them on rooftops in the summer sun, where they sprouted and quickly withered. They then lamented loudly, tearing their clothes and beating their breasts, and carried a statuette of Adonis on a bier, with the withered plants, to the sea.
advance-australia-fair: Peter Dodds McCormick (1833–1916), a Scottish-born Australian composer, published the song in early December 1878 under the pen-name Amicus. It was first sung by Andrew Fairfax, with a concert band conducted by McCormick, at a function of the Highland Society of New South Wales in Sydney on 30 November 1878, Saint Andrew's Day. In a letter of 1 August 1913, McCormick said he had attended a concert at Sydney's Exhibition Building where various national anthems were played and felt aggravated that there was not one note for Australia. He wrote the first verse on the bus home and set it to music, and said the words and music came with ease.

The song grew in popularity, and an amended version was sung by a choir of around 10,000 at the inauguration of the Commonwealth of Australia on 1 January 1901. In 1907 the Australian Government awarded McCormick £100. The Australian Broadcasting Commission used it to announce its radio news bulletins from 1942 to 1952.

The original song had four verses. The second edition of 1879 begins Australia's sons let us rejoice, For we are young and free, and its second verse told of Cook raising Old England's flag, while its later verses spoke of Britannia and of rousing to arms against a foreign foe.

For the 1984 adoption the text was cut to two verses. The first was kept largely as the original, with the first line changed to Australians all let us rejoice, and the second is a modified form of the third verse sung at Federation in 1901, which begins Beneath our radiant Southern Cross. On 1 January 2021 the word young in the second line was replaced by one, in recognition of the legacy of Indigenous Australians.

The Whitlam government replaced God Save the Queen with Advance Australia Fair as the official national anthem in 1974, after an indicative opinion survey. The Fraser government restored God Save the Queen in January 1976 alongside three national songs: Advance Australia Fair, Waltzing Matilda and Song of Australia. A plebiscite in 1977 to choose the national song preferred Advance Australia Fair, and the Hawke government proclaimed it the national anthem in 1984. God Save the Queen became the royal anthem.

The song has drawn criticism for its archaic word girt and for a melody some call dull. It has also been criticised for failing to acknowledge Indigenous peoples; the line for we are young and free was said to ignore their long history. Versions in the Dharug language have been written, by Jacqueline Troy in 2003 and by Richard Green, performed in 2010. The version most often performed at official functions is a 1986 arrangement by Thomas Tycho.
adygea: Adygea lies in the foothills of the north-western Caucasus, with plains in the north and mountains in the south, the highest point being Chugush Mountain at 3,238 metres. Forests of European beech, oak and maple cover almost 40 per cent of its territory. The Kuban River, about 870 kilometres long and one of the major navigable rivers of the Caucasus region, forms part of its northern border, and the Bolshaya Laba River part of the eastern one. The Sukhoy Kurdzhips River flows near the archaeological site at Mezmaiskaya cave. The territory is rich in oil and natural gas and also holds gold, silver, tungsten and iron.

The Cherkess (Adyghe) Autonomous Oblast was established within the Russian SFSR on 27 July 1922, on territory of the Kuban-Black Sea Oblast settled mainly by the Adyghe, and was renamed Adyghe (Cherkess) Autonomous Oblast on 24 August 1922. Krasnodar was at first its administrative centre. In 1924 it was transferred to the newly created North Caucasus Krai, and in July 1928 it became the Adyghe Autonomous Oblast. In 1934 it passed to the new Azov-Black Sea Krai, and Maykop became its administrative centre in 1936. When Krasnodar Krai was established on 13 September 1937, the oblast became part of it.

On 3 July 1991 the oblast was raised to the status of a republic within the Russian Federation. Its first president, Aslan Dzharimov, was elected on 5 January 1992, and its constitution was adopted on 14 May 1995.

Adygea is a republic of Russia, entirely surrounded by Krasnodar Krai. Its capital and largest city is Maykop, which holds about a third of its population of roughly half a million. Russians are a majority, and the Adyghe, the indigenous Circassian people, form about a quarter, with smaller Armenian and Ukrainian communities. The official languages are Adyghe, a member of the Northwest Caucasian family, and Russian. The National Museum of the Republic of Adygea in Maykop is its largest museum.
aegukga: The first anthem of the Korean state came before the present song. After the Gabo Reform of 1894 and the founding of the Independence Club in 1896, about ten patriotic songs were written in the private sector, and their lyrics began to appear in the Independence Newspaper.
