A decree of Santa Anna ordered its separation but was never made official, and Aguascalientes continued to belong to Zacatecas for some years. It was later included as a state in a draft constitution passed by the 79 deputies present, which established the state.

The state has 11 municipalities, and most of its people live in the metropolitan area of its capital, also called Aguascalientes. It was once a major silver miner and a centre of railroad transport, thanks to its position between Mexico City, Guadalajara and Monterrey. Its San Marcos Fair is regarded as the national fair of Mexico.
agustin-de-iturbide: Agustín Cosme Damián de Iturbide y Arámburu was born in Valladolid, now Morelia, in Michoacán on 27 September 1783, the fifth child of his parents and the only male to survive. His father, Joaquín de Iturbide, came from a Basque family of gentry and migrated to New Spain as a younger son to make his fortune. The family were part of the landed class of Valladolid. In 1805 Iturbide entered the royal Spanish army and married Ana María Josefa Ramona de Huarte y Muñiz, whose dowry of 100,000 pesos bought the Hacienda of San José de Apeo.

When the War of Independence broke out in 1810, Miguel Hidalgo offered Iturbide the rank of lieutenant general in the insurgent forces, and he refused. He compiled a record of victories, often against far larger numbers, and earned the name El Dragón de Hierro, the Iron Dragon, but contemporaries of all factions also knew him for cruelty towards insurgents and their families. He was dismissed from command in 1816 over accusations of corruption and cruelty, and was reinstated in 1820 to defeat Vicente Guerrero.

The restoration of Spain's liberal Cadiz Constitution in 1820 made many in Mexico fear that the monarchy would be forced to abandon Spain. Iturbide allied with the insurgents under the Plan of Iguala of 1821, which aimed at an independent monarchy with Roman Catholicism as its official religion and the abolition of the caste system and slavery. The Treaty of Córdoba, signed with the Spanish official O'Donojú, offered the throne to Ferdinand VII or another European prince; when Spain refused, Iturbide entered Mexico City on 27 September 1821 and became president of the Regency.

He took the crown as emperor in 1822. Conflict with Congress, which claimed all the powers of the state, led him to dissolve it on 31 October 1822. A military revolt by Antonio López de Santa Anna, Guadalupe Victoria and Guerrero followed in December, and he abdicated on 19 March 1823.

Iturbide went into exile in Europe in May 1823. He returned to Mexico on 14 July 1824, landing at Soto la Marina, and was arrested by General Felipe de la Garza. He was executed by a local legislature on 19 July 1824. Early in the independence period the date of independence depended on politics: conservatives favoured 27 September, when Iturbide entered Mexico City, and liberals 16 September, Hidalgo's call to rebellion. Writing about him in modern Mexico is often hostile. The historian Eric Van Young calls him an opportunist who showed moments of political brilliance clouded by bad judgment.
ahab: Ahab was the seventh king of Israel, son and successor of Omri and husband of Jezebel, daughter of Ithobaal I of Tyre. According to 1 Kings he became king in the thirty-eighth year of Asa of Judah and reigned twenty-two years. Scholars date the reign differently: William F. Albright to 869-850 BCE, Edwin R. Thiele to 874-853 BCE and, most recently, Michael Coogan to 871-852 BCE. The Hebrew Bible says that under Jezebel's influence he abandoned Yahweh and set up the cults of Baal and Asherah. Edward Lipiński argues that his Baal was the Yahweh of Samaria, which Judean priests opposed as heresy, while others disagree on the evidence about Jezebel's upbringing.

Ahab continued Omri's policy toward Moab, a tributary of Israel; the Mesha Stele says Omri and Ahab oppressed Moab for many days. He allied himself with Jehoshaphat of Judah by marriage. He made peace with Aram-Damascus after its king promised to withdraw from conquered territory. In 853 BCE an Assyrian inscription, the Kurkh Monolith, records him among the allies defeated by Shalmaneser III at Qarqar, with 2,000 chariots and 10,000 men, though excavations of stables suggest the number of chariots was nearer the hundreds. Shalmaneser's later campaigns in 849 and 846 BCE imply that his victory had no lasting effect. Jezreel was Ahab's fortified chariot and cavalry base.

The Bible tells of four encounters with prophets, among them Elijah, who foretold a drought and condemned the execution of Naboth, and Micaiah, who warned that Ahab would die in battle. Ahab was mortally wounded by a stray arrow when he and Jehoshaphat tried to retake Ramoth-Gilead from the Arameans, and dogs licked his corpse, as Elijah had foretold.

Yahwist tradition judged his reign worse than those before it, since he institutionalised Baalism, and it faulted his oppressive policies. It also credits him with fortifying many Israelite cities and building an ivory palace. Rabbinic literature counts him among the wicked kings excluded from the world to come, though some teachers saw him as a model of repentance.
ahaggar-mountains: The Hoggar Mountains lie in the central Sahara in southern Algeria, along the Tropic of Cancer, and cover about 550,000 square kilometres, roughly 1,500 kilometres south of Algiers. The area is largely rocky desert with an average elevation above 900 metres. The mountains are mainly metamorphic rock about 2 billion years old, with younger rock where volcanic activity has laid down new material. Several of the more dramatic peaks, such as Ilamen, are extinct volcano domes worn away by erosion, which left the more resistant rock that plugged the cones. The highest peak, Mount Tahat, is 2,908 metres high.

Summers are hot and winters cold, with temperatures below freezing on winter nights, and rain is rare and sporadic. Because the climate is less extreme than in most of the Sahara, the range is a major location of biodiversity, including a number of relict species. The highlands are believed to be one of the main sources of the Tamanrasset River, an ancient river that flowed during the African humid period.

Rock paintings show that people settled here in prehistory, with dates as early as 6000 BCE. The massif is the land of the Kel Ahaggar Tuareg. The tomb of Tin Hinan, the woman believed to be the matriarch of the Tuareg, is at Abalessa, an oasis near Tamanrasset. In 1911 Charles de Foucauld built a hermitage at Assekrem, on the plateau at the top of the range, which a few Catholic monks still inhabit. France conducted underground atomic tests in the mountains in the 1960s.

Some wildlife has gone from the region. A population of African wild dogs just west of the range survived into the 20th century, and West African crocodiles persisted in the mountains until the early 20th century.

The mountains are home to the Ahaggar Cultural Park, called the Ahaggar National Park from 1987 to 2011, which covers about 450,000 square kilometres and holds Mount Tahat. Its vegetation includes Vachellia tortilis, myrtle and Tamarix aphylla. Barbary sheep and Dorcas gazelles live there, and BirdLife International has designated the park an Important Bird Area.
ahaz: Ahaz was the twelfth king of Judah and the son and successor of Jotham. His name is an abbreviation of Jehoahaz, meaning Yahweh has held. According to the Second Book of Kings he was 20 when he became king and reigned 16 years. The dates are disputed: Edwin R. Thiele placed a co-regency with Jotham from 736/735 BCE and a sole reign from 732/731 to 716/715 BCE, while William F. Albright dated his reign to 744 to 728 BCE.

At his accession Ahaz faced a coalition of Pekah of Israel and Rezin of Damascus, who wished to compel him to join them in opposing the Assyrians under Tiglath-Pileser III. The Book of Isaiah relates that the prophet counselled him to trust in God rather than foreign allies; Ahaz refused to ask for a sign, and Isaiah foretold the birth of a child to be called Immanuel. Ahaz instead called in the Assyrians. Tiglath-Pileser sacked Damascus and annexed Aram, and then took Galilee and other territory of Israel, deporting its people, as his own inscription also records. The campaign lasted two years, 734 to 732 BCE.

Judah was relieved of its neighbours, but its protector claimed suzerainty over it. In 732 Ahaz went to Damascus to swear homage to Tiglath-Pileser, and having admired an altar there he had a copy made in Jerusalem and made it a permanent part of Temple worship, with changes to the Temple's furniture. The biblical writers also say he offered his son by fire, or made him pass through fire; the words may describe a purification or a sacrifice. The Deuteronomistic historian judged his rule disastrous for the country's religion.

Ahaz died at the age of 36 and was succeeded by his son Hezekiah, whose reforms were largely aimed at undoing what Ahaz had done. According to 2 Chronicles, he was not laid in the tombs of the kings. Two inscribed objects name him. A clay seal impression reads Belonging to Ahaz, son of Yehotam, king of Judah, and most scholars think it authentic; a carnelian seal of the 8th century BCE, now at Yale University, belonged to Ushna, servant of Ahaz. The annals of Tiglath-Pileser III also record tribute from Ahaz of Judah.
ahmad-ibn-fadlan: Contemporary sources call Ahmad ibn Fadlan an Arab of Baghdad, but nothing is certain about his origin, ethnicity, education or the dates of his birth and death. From his own writing it appears that he was a faqih, an expert in Islamic jurisprudence, and that he had served for some time at the court of the Abbasid caliph al-Muqtadir before his mission.

In 921 Ibn Fadlan was sent from Baghdad as secretary to an ambassador of al-Muqtadir to Almış, the iltäbär or vassal king under the Khazars of Volga Bulgaria. The party, led by the eunuch Susan al-Rassi, left on 21 June 921. Its purpose was to explain Islamic law to the recently converted Bulgars and to answer the Bulgar king's request for help against the Khazars. Ibn Fadlan served as religious adviser and counsellor on doctrine and law.

The party travelled by caravan routes toward Bukhara, then turned north from what is now north-eastern Iran. Leaving Gurgan near the Caspian Sea, it crossed the lands of the Oghuz Turks, the Pechenegs on the Ural River and the Bashkirs, covering some 4,000 kilometres in all. It reached the Bulgar capital on 12 May 922. Ibn Fadlan read the caliph's letter to the Bulgar ruler and presented the gifts, but was criticised for not bringing the money promised to build a fortress against the enemies of the Bulgars.

His risāla, an account of the journey, long survived only in quotations in Yaqut's geographical dictionary, published in 1823 by Christian Martin Frähn. In 1923 Zeki Velidi Togan found a fuller 13th-century manuscript at Mashhad, which breaks off while describing the Khazars. Neither source seems to hold the complete report.

Ibn Fadlan judged the peoples he met largely by their practice of Islam, and he was angered by what he took to be unsound practice among the Bulgars. His longest passage concerns the Rūs, generally taken to be Volga Vikings trading by the river. He describes their appearance, their weapons and the ship funeral of a chieftain, which involved human sacrifice, and calls their hygiene shameless. He also gives early first-hand descriptions of the Oghuz Turks, who lived in felt tents, and of the Bashkirs. His text later inspired Michael Crichton's novel Eaters of the Dead.
ahmad-ibn-hanbal: Ahmad ibn Hanbal was born in November 780, a date his son Abdullah recorded. His family came originally from Basra and belonged to the Arab Banu Dhuhl tribe, and his father was an officer in the Abbasid army in Khorasan who later settled in Baghdad. Historians differ about his birthplace. Some say Merv, where his father and grandfather had worked, while the most accepted view is that his mother came pregnant from Merv and that he was born in Baghdad. His father died at about thirty, and his mother raised him with the help of his father's family.

He inherited a house in Baghdad and a property that yielded a small income. Ibn Kathir gives its amount as seventeen dirhams a month. Ahmad lived in poverty and worked as a baker. He did not marry until he was forty, which is said to be because he was busy seeking knowledge and travelled widely. Having studied jurisprudence and hadith under many teachers in his youth, he became widely known for his part in the Mihna, in which the caliph al-Ma'mun gave state support to the Mu'tazili doctrine that the Quran was created.

Ibn Hanbal's principal doctrine is called traditionalist thought, which accepts only the Quran and hadith as the foundations of orthodox belief, though he held that only a select few were authorised to interpret the texts. He affirmed the attributes of God that the Quran gives, such as hearing, sight and speech, and read the apparently anthropomorphic ones, such as God's hand and face, literally. He rejected the allegorical interpretation of the Jahmiyya and also the anthropomorphism of the Mushabbiha, and he upheld the formula bi-la kayfa, believing in them without asking how.

He compiled al-Musnad, the largest hadith collection, which influenced the methods later used in the collections of Bukhari and Muslim. Ibn al-Nadim's Fihrist lists works such as Kitab al-Zuhd, Kitab al-Iman and a book on the rites of the Hajj. Al-Tabari is reported to have counted him only an expert in prophetic tradition, but most scholars recognise him as a jurist, and al-Shafi'i called him an imam in eight fields. Al-Khallal and al-Khiraqi made the first written compilations of his legal views. His school, the Hanbali school, is dominant in Saudi Arabia and Qatar.
ahmad-shah-abdali: Ahmad Khan was born in the early 1720s into the Abdali tribe of Pashtuns. Sources differ on whether he was born at Herat or Multan; modern scholarship generally favours Multan, though Sajjad Nejatie argues that most contemporary sources, including the Tarikh-i Ahmad Shahi, say Herat. His father Zaman Khan, Sultan of Herat, died in 1721, and he was raised with his brother Zulfiqar Khan in Shindand and Farah. When Nader Shah defeated Zulfiqar Khan in 1731 to 1732, both brothers fled to Kandahar and were held as political prisoners by the Hotak king Hussain Hotak. Freed after Nader Shah conquered Kandahar, Ahmad accompanied him on his invasion of India in 1738 to 1739 and enlisted in the Afsharid army in 1742.

After Nader Shah's assassination in 1747 Ahmad Shah went to Kandahar with his regiments, made himself leader of the Durrani tribesmen and killed his uncle 'Abd al-Ghani Khan, the governor. On the way he seized a convoy carrying the annual tribute from Sindh, and his army grew to over 18,000. A legend that a jirga of tribal leaders chose him unanimously, placing wheat or barley on his turban, has no contemporary evidence. His tribe changed its name from Abdali to Durrani. In autumn 1747 he took Ghazni and then Kabul from Nasir Khan, who fled to Peshawar.

He began a series of invasions of India in 1748 that lasted 24 years. He annexed Punjab and Kashmir after his third invasion, sacked Delhi in 1757 in his fourth and destroyed the Maratha armies at the Third Battle of Panipat in his fifth, the largest battle of the 18th century. He fought over fifteen major campaigns, nine centred in India, three in Khorasan and three in Afghan Turkestan. Historians record that his campaigns left northern India in chaos, with massacres, pillaging and mass enslavement by Afghan soldiers. His government copied the Mughals and Safavids, and he exempted his own tribe from taxation.

Illness, perhaps a malignant wound on the nose or a facial cancer, left him unable to speak by summer 1772. He died at a palace at Maruf, east of Kandahar, on 16 or 23 October 1772, and was buried in Kandahar, where his son Timur Shah Durrani built a mausoleum in 1777. He had named Timur as heir over his eldest son Sulaiman Mirza, which led to a short civil war that Timur won without battle. Historians rank him among the foremost generals of eighteenth-century Asia, and he is often regarded as the founder of modern Afghanistan. Afghans call him Ahmad Shāh Bābā, Ahmad Shah the Father.
ahmad-shah-massoud: Massoud was born about 1953 in the village of Jangalak in the Panjshir Valley, into a Tajik family. He was named after Ahmad Shah Durrani and took Massoud as a nom de guerre in 1974. His father, Dost Mohammad Khan, was a colonel in the Royal Afghan Army. After primary school in Herat he attended the Franco-Afghan Lycée Esteqlal in Kabul, where he became proficient in French; later Islamist opponents mocked him as the Frenchman or the Parisian. He refused suggestions to seek a scholarship in France.

At Kabul University in the 1970s he joined the Muslim Youth, the student branch of the Jamiat-e Islami led by Burhanuddin Rabbani. In July 1975, with help from Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence, he led a rebellion in the Panjshir against President Daoud Khan. It briefly took the garrison at Rokha, but promised support from Kabul never came and it was suppressed. Afterwards the Islamist movement split between the moderates around Massoud and Rabbani and the radicals around Gulbuddin Hekmatyar, who founded the Hezb-i Islami.

After the communist coup of 27 April 1978, rural areas rose in revolt against the new government. In May 1979 Massoud walked into the Panjshir Valley with twenty-four companions and seized government outposts. An insurrection he began on 6 July 1979 initially failed, and he chose guerrilla war over conventional battle, then took full control of the Panjshir. He became the foremost mujahideen commander against Soviet forces in the Soviet–Afghan War of 1979 to 1989.

In April 1992 Massoud supported a broad coalition government of all resistance parties, while Hekmatyar sought sole rule and refused compromise. Massoud signed the Peshawar Accord and became Minister of Defense of the Islamic State of Afghanistan and its main military commander. Hekmatyar and other warlords attacked Kabul, beginning the Second Afghan Civil War of 1992 to 1996. After the Taliban rose in 1996 Massoud returned to armed opposition as military leader of the Northern Alliance, which by 2000 held only 5 to 10 per cent of the country.

On 9 September 2001, at Khwājah Bahā ud Dīn in Takhar Province, two al-Qaeda suicide attackers who had been granted an interview set off a bomb hidden in a camera. Massoud died in a helicopter on the way to a hospital in Tajikistan. The United Front officially announced his death on 16 September, and he was buried at Bazarak in the Panjshir, with hundreds of thousands attending. He had survived a number of attempts on his life over 26 years. Two days after his death came the September 11 attacks.
He is a folk hero among Afghans, especially Tajiks, and is called the Lion of Panjshir. In 2001 the interim government under Hamid Karzai gave him the title Hero of the Afghan Nation.
ahmad-shah-qajar: Ahmad Shah was born in Tabriz on 21 January 1898, the seventh and final ruling member of the Qajar dynasty. On 16 July 1909 rebels seeking to restore the 1906 Constitution overthrew his father, Mohammad Ali Shah, and a Grand Majles of 500 delegates placed the eleven-year-old Ahmad on the throne. His uncle, Ali Reza Khan Azod al-Molk, governed as regent until Ahmad reached his majority and was formally crowned on 21 July 1914. The Grand Majles abolished class representation and created five new seats for minorities, two for Armenians and one each for Jews, Zoroastrians and Assyrians. It also lowered the voting age from twenty-five to twenty.

Ahmad Shah tried to repair the damage of his father's rule by appointing the best ministers he could find, but he was an ineffective ruler facing internal unrest and intrusion by the British and Russian empires. The Second Majlis met in November 1910 and achieved little, since the central government was too weak to carry out what it proposed. During the First World War Russian and British troops fought Ottoman forces in Iran. In 1917 Britain used Iran as a springboard for an attack on Russia, and the new Soviet Union responded by annexing parts of northern Persia and pressing the government for concessions.

By 1920 the government had lost virtually all power outside the capital, and the Red Army, rebels and warlords controlled much of the countryside. The Anglo-Persian Agreement and new political parties further immobilised the country, and Iran had to borrow from the Imperial Bank of Persia. Under that agreement Iran received only a small fraction of the income of the Anglo-Persian Oil Company. On 21 February 1921 Colonel Reza Khan, Minister of War and commander of the Persian Cossack Brigade, carried out a nearly bloodless coup with three thousand men and eighteen machine guns and then became Prime Minister. He cancelled the Anglo-Persian Agreement and signed the Russo-Persian Treaty of Friendship.

In 1923 Ahmad Shah left Iran for Europe for reasons of health, and when the Majlis formally terminated the Qajar dynasty, proclaiming Reza Khan shah as Reza Shah Pahlavi in 1925, the tour became an exile. He died of influenza at the American Hospital of Paris in 1930 and was buried, under his will, in the family crypt at Karbala in Iraq. His brother, the former crown prince Mohammad Hassan Mirza, continued the dynasty through his descendants. Ahmad Shah had been married five times and had four children.
ahmadnagar: Ahmednagar lies in Maharashtra, in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats, and has a hot semi-arid climate. Monsoon rainfall averages less than a third of that received in Mumbai, so the city often suffers from drought. Its site was close to the village of Bhingar, and the town was founded on the ground of an older city of that name.

Ahmad Nizam Shah I founded the town in 1494 on a battlefield where he had defeated superior Bahmani forces, and named it after himself. As the Bahmani Sultanate broke up, he established a new sultanate there, known as the Nizam Shahi dynasty. Contemporary chroniclers describe the building. Sayyid Ali Tabataba'i notes that surveyors, architects and builders laid out the city with palaces, houses, squares, shops and surrounding gardens. Firishta wrote that in two years the new city rivalled Baghdad and Cairo in splendour, and his account suggests a design with gardens, palaces and pavilions inside and outside the walls that followed the conventions of a post-Timurid city.

The sultanate was one of the Deccan sultanates and lasted until the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan conquered it in 1636. Aurangzeb spent the later years of his reign, 1681–1707, in the Deccan and died at Ahmednagar in 1707; he is buried at Khuldabad, near Aurangabad. In 1759 the Peshwa of the Marathas took the place from the Nizam of Hyderabad, and in 1795 the Peshwa ceded it to the Maratha chief Daulat Rao Sindhia. A British force under Richard Wellesley besieged and captured it in 1803. It was restored to the Marathas but passed to the British again in 1817 under the Treaty of Poona.

In the 19th century American Christian missionaries opened the first modern schools in the town, among them girls' schools run by Cynthia Farrar around the 1850s. The reformer Jyotirao Phule visited them and was inspired to open a girls' school in Poona, and he enrolled his wife Savitribai Phule in Farrar's teacher-training programme. During the First World War a camp held German and Austrian civilian internees, captured crews of German ships and some Turkish soldiers taken in Mesopotamia.

Ahmednagar Fort, once thought almost impregnable, was used by the British to detain Jawaharlal Nehru and other nationalists, and Nehru wrote The Discovery of India there in 1944. The town has several dozen buildings and sites of the Nizam Shahi period, and the Tomb of Salabat Khan II, also called the Chand Bibi Palace, stands on a hilltop outside it. It is the home of the Indian Armoured Corps Centre and School and has a museum of armoured vehicles. Marathi is the main language of daily life. The city was officially renamed Ahilyanagar in 2024.
ahmadou-ahidjo: Ahmadou Ahidjo was born on 24 August 1924 at Garoua, a river port on the Benue in northern Cameroon, then a French mandate territory. His father was a Fulani village chief and his mother a Fulani of slave descent. She raised him as a Muslim and sent him to a Quranic school. He later studied at the Ecole Primaire Supérieur in Yaoundé for a career in the civil service and in 1942 joined the postal service as a radio operator. His postings in Douala, Ngaoundéré, Bertoua and Mokolo made him, according to his official biographer, the first civil servant from the north to work in the south.

Ahidjo entered territorial politics in 1946 and became prime minister in February 1958, aged thirty-four. He negotiated with France in Paris from June to October 1958, and the National Assembly set 1 January 1960 for independence. He faced opposition from the Union des Populations du Cameroun (UPC), a pro-communist party that rejected French influence; he defeated its rebellion by 1970 with French military help, using emergency powers.

After the plebiscite in the British Cameroons, the southern part voted to join the rest of Cameroon. Ahidjo and Premier John Foncha drafted a federal constitution at Foumban, and on 1 October 1961 the Federal Republic of Cameroon was formed with Ahidjo as president and Foncha as vice president. In 1962 a decree barred criticism of the government, and opposition leaders who opposed a single party were arrested and imprisoned. The Cameroon National Union became the sole party on 1 September 1966. On 20 May 1972 a referendum approved ending the federation, and the United Republic of Cameroon replaced it on 2 June 1972. Many Anglophones were displeased.

Ahidjo resigned, ostensibly for health reasons, on 4 November 1982, and Prime Minister Paul Biya succeeded him two days later. He remained head of the party, but a feud developed, and in July 1983 he went into exile in France. In February 1984 he was sentenced to death in absentia for a plot of June 1983, a sentence Biya commuted to life imprisonment; Ahidjo denied involvement.

He divided his last years between France and Senegal and died of a heart attack in Dakar on 30 November 1989. A law of December 1991 officially rehabilitated him. An agreement to return his remains was reached in June 2009, but he remained buried in Dakar. Oil revenue began to flow in 1977, and the system of patronage he built, in which jobs, licences and contracts came through the president in return for loyalty, is described by the sources as central to his rule.
ahmed-hassan-al-bakr: Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr was born on 1 July 1914 in Tikrit, in Ottoman Iraq, into the Abu Bakr clan of the al-Bejat branch of the Al-Bu Nasir tribe. After six years as a primary-school teacher he entered the Iraqi Military Academy in 1938. He took part in Rashid Ali al-Gaylani's failed revolt against the British in 1941 and was imprisoned and expelled from the army. Reinstated in 1956, he joined the Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party's Iraqi branch that year and was promoted to brigadier in 1957. He helped bring down the Hashemite monarchy in the 14 July Revolution, but in 1959 he was forced to retire again, accused of leading a rebellion at Mosul.

As chairman of the party's Military Bureau, al-Bakr recruited officers, often through personal attachments, and led the coup of February 1963, the Ramadan Revolution, which overthrew Abd al-Karim Qasim. He became prime minister and vice president under President Abdul Salam Arif, a moderate seeking a compromise between the party's radical and moderate factions. Arif ended the government in November 1963 and al-Bakr was jailed. He was later elected the Iraqi branch's Secretary General, and was jailed again after a failed attempt to oust the Arif government in 1964. His cousin Saddam Hussein became one of his closest associates and organised the party's security apparatus.

The coup of 17 July 1968 brought al-Bakr and the Ba'ath Party back to power. Saddam and Salah Omar al-Ali led it on the ground, while al-Bakr is said to have planned it; he phoned President Abdul Rahman Arif, who surrendered after a guarantee of his safety. Al-Bakr became president and chairman of the Revolutionary Command Council, then prime minister, and Saddam became vice president. Within weeks he removed the military officers Abd ar-Razzaq an-Naif and Ibrahim Daud, who had been made prime minister and minister of defence, and sent them into exile.

Under al-Bakr, Iraq signed a treaty of friendship with the Soviet Union on 9 April 1972, and the Iraq Petroleum Company was nationalised in June 1972; oil revenue rose from 219 million dinars in 1972 to 1.7 billion in 1974. A land reform of 1970 set limits on landholding and set up co-operatives. In 1974 heavy fighting broke out in northern Iraq with Kurdish nationalists under Mustafa Barzani, who had Iranian support. A decree of July 1978 made non-Ba'thist political activity illegal. In 1979 al-Bakr resigned all offices for health reasons, and Saddam succeeded him. He died in October 1982 of unreported causes and was buried in Baghdad's al-Karkh cemetery.
ahmed-sekou-toure: Sékou Touré was born on 9 January 1922 in Faranah, in French Guinea, one of seven children of Alpha Touré and Aminata Fadiga, who were subsistence farmers. He belonged to the Mandinka ethnic group and was the great-grandson of Samori Ture, the Muslim king who founded the Wassoulou Empire (1861–1890) and resisted French rule until his capture in 1898.

In 1936 he entered the Georges Poiret Technical College in Conakry but was expelled less than a year later, at the age of 15, for leading a student protest about the food. He quickly became involved in labour union activity and studied the works of Karl Marx and Vladimir Lenin.

In 1941 he became a postal clerk in Conakry. In 1945 he founded the Post and Telecommunications Workers' Union, the first trade union in French Guinea, and in 1946 he was a founding member of the African Democratic Rally. By 1948 he was general secretary of the territorial union of the Confédération Générale du Travail, and in 1952 he became leader of the Democratic Party of Guinea (PDG), the rally's Guinean section. In 1953 a general strike lasting 71 days, longer than in any other territory of French West Africa, forced the introduction of a new overseas labour code.

In 1960 he declared the PDG the only legal party, though the country had been effectively a one-party state since independence. He was elected president in 1961 as the only candidate and re-elected unopposed in 1968, 1974 and 1982. His policies were based on socialism, with nationalisation of foreign companies and centralised economic plans, and he received the Lenin Peace Prize in 1961. From 1965 to 1975 he broke off relations with France, supposedly because of French involvement in the creation of opposition groups.

Touré died on 26 March 1984 at the Cleveland Clinic in Ohio, where he had been taken for emergency heart surgery after falling ill in Saudi Arabia. Just hours before the PDG was due to name a successor on 3 April, the military seized power. The new rulers denounced the last years of his rule as a bloody and ruthless dictatorship, suspended the constitution, dissolved the National Assembly and abolished the PDG. Colonel Lansana Conté took the presidency on 5 April and the junta freed about 1,000 political prisoners.

Many people were killed under Touré's rule, most notably at Camp Boiro, and Amnesty International and other human rights organisations accused his government of oppression. His tomb is in the Camayanne Mausoleum, in the gardens of the Grand Mosque of Conakry.
ahmedabad: Ahmedabad lies in north-central Gujarat, on the banks of the Sabarmati River, and covers 505 km2. It is 25 km from Gandhinagar, the state capital, known as its twin city. The city is almost flat, and the Sabarmati frequently dried up in summer until water from the Narmada was diverted into it. Three lakes lie within the city limits: Kankaria, Vastrapur and Chandola. Kankaria was developed as an artificial lake by the Sultan of Gujarat, Qutb-ud-din, in 1451.

An early Bhil settlement called Ashaval is thought to have stood here. According to Merutunga, Karna, the Chaulukya ruler of Anhilwada, defeated Ashaval and founded a city nearby called Karnavati, whose exact location is not known. Chaulukya rule lasted until the 13th century, when Gujarat came under the Vaghela dynasty of Dholka, and in the 14th century under the Delhi Sultanate. In the early 15th century the governor Zafar Khan Muzaffar made himself independent as Muzaffar Shah I.

His grandson Sultan Ahmad Shah I moved the capital from Anhilvada in 1411 and laid the foundation of a walled city on the Sabarmati on 26 February 1411 at Manek Burj, named after the saint Maneknath. As was customary, the city was named after the sultan; other accounts say it was named after four Muslim saints called Ahmed. A British force under James Hartley captured it in 1780, during the First Anglo-Maratha War, and handed it back at the war's end. The East India Company took it over in 1818, and a railway link to Bombay opened in 1864. The city became the home of a growing textile industry and was nicknamed the Manchester of India.

Ahmedabad is the most populous city of Gujarat and the seat of the Gujarat High Court; the 2011 census counted 5,570,585 people. Under Ahmed Shah, builders fused Hindu craftsmanship with Persian architecture, and many mosques were built in this Indo-Saracenic style. A pol is the typical housing cluster of the old city, which was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in July 2017.
ahmose-i: Ahmose belonged to the Theban royal house of the Seventeenth Dynasty, a son of the pharaoh Seqenenre Tao and a brother of Kamose, the last pharaoh of that dynasty. His parents, Seqenenre Tao and Ahhotep I, were brother and sister, and the children of Senakhtenre Ahmose and Tetisheri. Thebes had rebelled against the Hyksos, the rulers of Lower Egypt, in the time of his father or grandfather. His father was killed when Ahmose was seven, and his mummy has many wounds, which suggests that he may have died in battle. Kamose died after a reign of only three years, apparently when Ahmose was about ten.

Ahmose took the throne as a boy of about ten and ruled about 25 years, dying at around 35. His mother Ahhotep acted as regent until he came of age, and descriptions of her roles, including the honorific carer for Egypt, suggest that she consolidated the Theban power base. The conflict with the Hyksos king Apepi had lasted almost thirty years in all. Ahmose began the conquest of Lower Egypt in about the eleventh year of the Hyksos ruler Khamudi's reign, although the order of events is not universally agreed. The main evidence is a short military diary on the back of the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus. He took the Hyksos capital Avaris and started raids into the Levant in pursuit.

He then reorganised the administration, reopened quarries, mines and trade routes, and began building on a scale not seen since the Middle Kingdom. His chief treasurer Neferperet reopened the quarries at el-Ma'asara in Ahmose's twenty-second year. The priest Manetho, writing in the third century BCE, thought the final expulsion of the Hyksos important enough to begin a new dynasty. Ahmose's chief wife was his sister Ahmose-Nefertari.

Ahmose's pyramid at Abydos was found in 1899 and identified as his in 1902. It was the last pyramid built by native Egyptian rulers, and its slope was about 60 degrees. Two temples built by Ahmose-Nefertari stand beside it. Along the same axis lay a pyramid dedicated to his grandmother Tetisheri, a rock-cut underground complex and a terraced temple against the cliffs. His eldest surviving son Amenhotep I succeeded him, as the heir Ahmose-ankh died before his father. His reign laid the foundations for the New Kingdom, in which Egyptian power reached its peak.
ahura-mazda: The name Ahura is most likely from Proto-Indo-European roots meaning to engender, and is cognate with Sanskrit ásura. Mazda reflects a Proto-Iranian word meaning intelligence or wisdom. Some scholars connect Ahura Mazda with the Vedic Varuna. Some Zoroastrian historians believe his worship existed before Zoroaster; R. C. Zaehner thought the earlier Ahura Mazda was associated with truth or universal order, and with water, light or the sun.

According to Zoroastrian tradition, Zoroaster received a revelation at the age of 30: he saw Vohu Manah, an Amesha Spenta, who led him into the presence of Ahura Mazda and taught him the principles of the Good Religion. Zoroaster taught that the destructive spirit Angra Mainyu was Ahura Mazda's inferior, not his equal.

Whether the Achaemenid kings were Zoroastrians is much debated, but they worshipped Ahura Mazda, and the Behistun Inscription of Darius the Great refers to him many times. In the early Achaemenid period he had no representation; from Cyrus to Darius III an empty chariot drawn by white horses was kept for him to accompany the army into battle. A winged figure once read as Ahura Mazda is now thought to represent the royal khvarenah, divine power and glory. Images began in the western satrapies in the late 5th century BCE.

Zoroastrian iconoclasm, traceable from the end of the Parthian period and the start of the Sasanian, ended images of him in worship, though he remained symbolised by a dignified male figure in investiture scenes. In the Sasanian period a divergent form, Zurvanism, made Ahura Mazda and Angra Mainyu twin sons of Zurvan. Five Sasanian kings took the name Hormizd.

Plutarch gives a Greek account of Oromazes, born from the purest light, at war with Areimanius, born from darkness; the scholar Mary Boyce judged it a fairly accurate knowledge of the basics of Zoroastrianism. In Manichaeism the name Ohrmazd Bay was used for the primal figure, the original man. In Sogdian Buddhism the name appears as Xwrmztʼ, and through the Uyghurs it reached the Mongols as Qormusta Tengri. The pre-Christian Armenians held Aramazd as an important deity.
ahvaz: Ahvaz stands on the banks of the Karun River in the Khuzestan plain, at an elevation of 12 m, near the border with Iraq. The Karun is the largest river in Iran by volume and flows through the centre of the city, which is known for the many large bridges that join its east and west parts. The older, residential part of the city lies on the left bank, the newer administrative and industrial district on the right. The climate is hot desert, with long, hot summers.

A settlement here is traced to the Achaemenid period under the name Taryana, on the Royal Road from Persepolis to Sardis. Under Ardashir I it was refounded on both sides of the river as Hormazd-Ardeshir, later shortened to Darawashir, and became capital of the province of Susiana. After the Muslim defeat of the Sasanian Empire in the 7th century CE, the western part, Horamshir, was destroyed and the Arabs rendered the market quarter's name as Sūq al-Ahvāz. The name Ahvaz is the Arabicized plural of Huzi, the old people of the region, from whom Khuzestan also takes its name.

In the 19th century Ahvaz was a small borough: 1,500 to 2,000 inhabitants according to Ainsworth in 1835, and 700 according to Curzon in 1890. In the 1880s the Karun was dredged and reopened to commerce, and a port, Bandar-e-Naseri, named for Naser al-Din Shah Qajar, grew beside the old village. Oil was found nearby in the early 20th century. The provincial government moved there from Shushtar in 1926, and the Trans-Iranian Railway reached the city in 1929. Iraq tried to annex Khuzestan in 1980, starting the Iran–Iraq War (1980–1988), and Ahvaz, close to the front lines, suffered severely.

Ahvaz is the capital of Khuzestan province, with more than 1.3 million people in its metropolitan area. Persian is the official language; Khuzestani Arabic, Bakhtiari and other languages are also spoken, and Neo-Mandaic is used among the Mandaeans. The city has been called the City of Bridges and the Oil Capital of Iran. Shahid Chamran University of Ahvaz, founded in 1955 as Gondishapur University, is the oldest institution of higher education in the city.
aichi-prefecture: Aichi lies near the centre of Honshu in the Chūbu region, facing Ise Bay and Mikawa Bay to the south. It borders Mie Prefecture to the west, Gifu and Nagano to the north and Shizuoka to the east. The prefecture measures 106 km from east to west and 94 km from south to north, covers 5,172.92 square kilometres and forms a major part of the Nōbi Plain. Its highest point is Chausuyama, at 1,415 m. Nagoya, the old capital of Owari, dominates the west.

The region was originally divided into the two provinces of Owari and Mikawa, which were united after the Meiji Restoration. In 1871, after the abolition of the han system, Owari, apart from the Chita Peninsula, became Nagoya Prefecture, while Mikawa joined the Chita Peninsula to form Nukata Prefecture. Nagoya Prefecture was renamed Aichi in April 1872, and on 27 November of that year it was united with Nukata Prefecture.

The name goes back to Ayuchi, which appears in a poem by Takechi Kurohito in the third volume of the Man'yōshū, about the cry of a crane over the Ayuchi tidal flats. The Fujimae tidal flat is all that remains of the older Ayuchi-gata, and it is now protected.

Aichi has a population of 7,461,111, and Nagoya, its capital and largest city, is the fourth-largest city in Japan. Other major cities include Toyota, Okazaki and Ichinomiya. The prefecture is home to the Toyota Motor Corporation. The Expo 2005 World Exposition was held at Seto and Nagakute. The Meiji Mura open-air architectural museum at Inuyama preserves buildings from the Meiji and Taishō periods, among them the reconstructed lobby of Frank Lloyd Wright's old Imperial Hotel, which stood in Tokyo from 1923 to 1967.
aime-cesaire: Aimé Césaire was born in 1913 at Basse-Pointe, Martinique, the son of a tax inspector and a dressmaker; his family belonged to the island's small black middle class. They moved to Fort-de-France so that he could attend the island's only secondary school, the Lycée Victor Schœlcher, where he found the town's racial and class prejudice upsetting. A scholarship took him to the Lycée Louis-le-Grand in Paris, where he met Léopold Sédar Senghor and, along with Léon Damas, shared an interest in French poetry. In 1935 he passed the entrance examination of the École Normale Supérieure and, with Senghor and Damas, created the review L'Étudiant noir, whose third number carried manifestos that began the Négritude movement.

Césaire began his long poem Notebook of a Return to the Native Land in 1934 in Šibenik, in Yugoslavia, and continued it after returning to Martinique in 1936. It first appeared in the Parisian periodical Volontés in 1939 after a publisher rejected it, and was issued as a book in 1947 with an introduction by André Breton. In 1941 he and his wife, Suzanne Roussi, founded the review Tropiques. He taught at the Lycée Schoelcher, where Frantz Fanon was a student. In 1950 he wrote Discourse on Colonialism, which argues that colonisation brutalises the colonisers and compares colonial violence with Nazism; later works include the play Toussaint Louverture (1960) and Une Tempête (1969), an adaptation of Shakespeare's The Tempest.

In 1945, with the support of the French Communist Party, Césaire was elected mayor of Fort-de-France and deputy for Martinique in the National Assembly. A law on departmentalisation was approved unanimously on 19 March 1946, though the new status brought few meaningful changes to the people of Martinique. After the Soviet suppression of the Hungarian Revolution in 1956 he resigned from the party in his Letter to Maurice Thorez. He founded the Parti Progressiste Martiniquais in 1958, presided over the Regional Council of Martinique from 1983 to 1988, declined to renew his Assembly mandate in 1993 after 47 years, and retired as mayor in 2001.

Césaire died in Fort-de-France on 17 April 2008, aged 94, and was given a state funeral at the Stade de Dillon. Martinique's airport at Le Lamentin was renamed after him in 2007, and a plaque in his name was inaugurated in the Panthéon in Paris in 2011. Fanon wrote of the liberating effect of Césaire's word and action. His works are described as significant contributions to postcolonial literature in France, its former colonies and the Caribbean.
ain: Ain is made up of four areas: Bresse, Dombes, Bugey and the Pays de Gex. In the north the plain of Bresse is bordered by the river Saône. In the south-east the Dombes has more than a thousand ponds and lakes, and in the east the southern Jura Mountains overlook the Bresse plain. The Gex region, which belongs geographically to the Lake Geneva basin, is separated from the rest by the last eastern chain of the Jura. In the alphabetical ordering of French departments Ain comes first and so has the number 01.

The first inhabitants settled about 15000 BCE, and the Calendar of Coligny, of the late 2nd century BCE, bears the oldest surviving Gaulish inscription. In 58 BCE Julius Caesar's action against the Helvetians, advancing over this territory, began the Gallic Wars. In the 6th century the diocese of Belley became the first bishopric in the region. The first large lordships emerged between 895 and 900 at Bâgé-le-Châtel, the nucleus of Bresse, and at Coligny.

In 1272 Sibylle de Bâgé married Amadeus V, Count of Savoy, and added Bresse to Savoy's domains. By the start of the 15th century almost the whole region was united under the house of Savoy. The Treaty of Lyon of 17 January 1601 ended the Franco-Savoyard War and Ain now belonged to Burgundy. The department was created in 1790, during the French Revolution.

The prefecture of Ain is Bourg-en-Bresse. The department lies on the Swiss border, adjoining the cantons of Geneva and Vaud. Its agriculture includes the poultry of Bresse, the carp of the Dombes and the wine of Bugey, and most of CERN's Large Hadron Collider lies in communes of the Arrondissement of Gex.
air-mountains: The Aïr is a triangular massif in northern Niger, within the Sahara, rising to more than 1,800 metres and extending over 84,000 square kilometres. It consists of nine almost circular massifs rising from a rocky plateau, bordered on the east by the dunes and plain of the Ténéré Desert. Its highest peak, Mont Idoukal-n-Taghès, at 2022 metres is the highest point in Niger. The granite intrusions appear dark, and the massif also has an extinct caldera, lava flows, volcanic cones and one of the largest ring dike systems in the world.

Though rainfall on the lower plateau is only 50 to 160 millimetres a year, the height gives the Aïr a Sahel climate, an island of green in the surrounding desert, especially after the rains of August and September. Dry valleys called koris hold rainwater in stone pools, creating oases that provide forage and some farming. More than 430 vascular plant species have been recorded.

The Aïr is known for rock art dating from about 6000 BCE to around 1000 CE. During the African humid period the region was pastoral, as images of cattle and large mammals show. Desertification began in the 3rd millennium BCE and Tuareg from further north migrated into the region. Later art shows war, with horses and chariots. The five-metre carvings of the Dabous Giraffes, discovered in 1999, are internationally known.

When Tuareg groups were pushed south by Arab invaders in the eighth and ninth centuries, Gobirwa Hausa lived in the southern Aïr. Successive Tuareg Kels have controlled the area since at least the twelfth century. Agadez was one of the farthest outposts of the Songhai Empire in the early 15th century, and in the sixteenth century the area came under the newly created Tuareg Sultanate of Agadez, which lasted until the French arrived at the end of the 19th century.

The French weakened the Tuareg Kels and provoked infighting and resistance. When Ag Mohammed Wau Teguidda Kaocen rose against them in 1917, many towns were destroyed on his way to the siege of Agadez, and a punitive expedition after the French retook it left formerly populous places abandoned.

The town of Agadez, in the heart of Tuareg country, is the capital of the Aïr. Much of the Tuareg population led a nomadic life until recently, depending on camels and goats, while the sedentary oasis communities of Timia, Aouderas and Tabelot traditionally exchanged produce for clothes and for salt brought by camel caravans from the Ténéré oases of Bilma and Fachi.
aircraft-carrier: The aircraft carrier followed the first flight of the Wright brothers at Kitty Hawk in 1903. On 14 November 1910 Eugene Burton Ely made the first experimental take-off of a Curtiss Pusher airplane from a United States Navy ship, the cruiser USS Birmingham. On 9 May 1912 Commander Charles Samson of the Royal Naval Air Service made the first take-off from a ship under way, flying from the battleship HMS Hibernia, the first practical demonstration of the carrier at sea.

Early in the First World War the Japanese ship Wakamiya conducted the first carrier-launched air raid, on 6 September 1914, lowering Farman seaplanes into the water by crane to attack ships off Qingdao. Neither target was hit. The first airstrike by aircraft flown off a carrier was the Tondern raid in July 1918, when seven Sopwith Camels launched from HMS Furious damaged a German airbase and destroyed two zeppelins.

An aircraft carrier is a warship with a full-length flight deck and hangar that make it a mobile airbase at sea. It lets a naval force project air power far from national territory without relying on local airfields. Since the Second World War the carrier has replaced the battleship as the flagship of a fleet, and it has largely changed naval battle from gunfire to air strikes beyond visual range.

Fleet carriers operate with the main fleet and are the largest and fastest. Escort carriers, smaller and slower, defended convoys and were often built on merchant hulls. Light carriers were fast enough for the main fleet but smaller. Aircraft are launched by catapult (CATOBAR), which suits heavy jets, or by short take-off and vertical landing (STOVL), which is cheaper to operate.

Only about 20 aircraft can be on the flight deck at once, and most are kept in a hangar several decks below and raised by elevator. Munitions are stored low, usually below the waterline so the area can be flooded in an emergency.

Carriers have been called the largest weapon system ever created. Admiral Sir Mark Stanhope of the Royal Navy said that countries that aspire to strategic international influence have aircraft carriers, and Henry Kissinger called one 100,000 tons of diplomacy. A few have been kept as museum ships, among them USS Yorktown, USS Intrepid and USS Midway.
aisha: Aisha was born in Mecca c. 614, the daughter of Abu Bakr and Umm Ruman, two of Muhammad's companions. The sources give little more about her childhood. After the death of Muhammad's first wife, Khadija bint Khuwaylid, his aunt Khawlah bint Hakim proposed that he marry Aisha, and her earlier engagement to Jubayr ibn Mut'im was annulled. The orientalist W. Montgomery Watt suggests that Muhammad hoped to strengthen his ties with Abu Bakr, as marriages in Arabian culture commonly did.

All extant hadiths agree that the marriage took place in Mecca but was not consummated until the month of Shawwal after the hijrah to Medina, in April 623. Classical sources give her age as six at marriage and nine at consummation, though Ibn Hisham's biography suggests she may have been ten. Her age later became a subject of modern debate.

In Sunni tradition Aisha ranks second only to Khadija among Muhammad's wives in his affection. Muhammad died in her apartment in Medina. She remained active in the Muslim community for 44 years afterwards and is credited with narrating over 2,000 hadiths, on ritual, inheritance, pilgrimage and other subjects. She issued legal opinions, and companions such as Urwah ibn al-Zubayr consulted her. She was known by the title al-Ṣiddīqa bint al-Ṣiddīq, "the truthful woman, daughter of the truthful man".

In 656 the third caliph, Uthman, was killed by rebels, which began the First Fitna. Aisha, with Talha ibn Ubayd Allah and al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, mobilised forces against the new caliph, Ali, demanding punishment for those responsible. The two sides met near Basra in the Battle of the Camel, named after the camel on which Aisha directed her troops from a howdah. Her forces were defeated and about 10,000 Muslims were killed, in what is considered the first major battle between Muslims.

Ali reproached Aisha but pardoned her and sent her back to Medina under an escort led by her brother, Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr. She withdrew from public politics and became a teacher, and in her last two years she spent much time telling stories of Muhammad. She died at her home in Medina on 17 Ramadan 58 AH (16 July 678). Abu Hurayra led her funeral prayer, and she was buried in the al-Baqi cemetery.
Sunni Islam reveres her as a leading scholar, hadith transmitter and teacher of several companions and of the tabi'in. Shia Muslims generally view her critically because of her opposition to Ali.
aix-en-provence: Aix-en-Provence lies in the south of France, about 30 km north of Marseille, in a plain overlooking the Arc river. The Montagne Sainte-Victoire can be seen to the east. The city has a Mediterranean climate, warm and sunny, though more extreme than Marseille's because of its inland position, and it is partly sheltered from the Mistral. Its old town, with narrow streets and mansions of the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, lies north of the Cours Mirabeau, a wide avenue that follows the line of the old city wall.

The city was founded in the late 2nd century BCE by the Roman consul Sextius Calvinus, who gave his name to its springs, after the nearby Gallic oppidum at Entremont had been destroyed. In 102 BCE the Romans under Gaius Marius defeated the Ambrones and Teutones in its vicinity. In the 4th century CE Aix became the metropolis of Narbonensis Secunda. The Visigoths occupied it in 477, the Franks and Lombards plundered it repeatedly in the following century, and it was occupied by the Saracens in 731 and by Charles Martel in 737.

In the Middle Ages Aix was the capital of Provence and reached its height after the 12th century, when under the houses of Barcelona and Aragon and then Anjou it became an artistic centre and seat of learning. Louis II of Anjou granted a royal charter for a university in 1409. Provence passed to the French crown in 1487, and in 1501 Louis XII established the parliament of Provence in Aix, which lasted until 1789. In the 17th and 18th centuries the town was the seat of the Intendance of Provence.

Aix-en-Provence is a subprefecture of the department of Bouches-du-Rhône, with about 148,000 inhabitants, and remains a university town. Its Cathedral of the Holy Saviour stands on the site of a Roman forum and combines styles from the 5th to the 17th century, with a Merovingian baptistery and a Romanesque cloister. The Festival d'Aix-en-Provence, an opera festival, was founded in 1948. The painter Paul Cézanne was born in the city, as was the composer Darius Milhaud. The older streets still carry names in both Provençal and French.
ajanta-caves: The caves were made in two phases. The first began around the 2nd century BCE and belongs to the 2nd century BCE to 1st century CE. Older accounts place the second phase between 400 and 650 CE, but later scholarship dates it to a brief period of 460 to 480. Walter Spink places the whole second phase in the 5th century. He holds that the earlier group, dated only approximately to between 100 BCE and 100 CE, was then abandoned for over three centuries. According to him the Vakataka emperor Harishena, who reigned from 460 until his death in 477, sponsored numerous new caves, and work stopped soon after his death, which left many caves unfinished.

The caves are carved from flood basalt of the Deccan Traps, layered horizontally and of variable quality. Excavation began with a narrow tunnel at roof level, which was widened downwards and outwards, as the unfinished Caves 21 to 24 and Cave 28 show. Flaws in the rock caused cracks and collapses, such as that of the portico of Cave 1.

The complex is carved into a 75-metre wall of rock and consists of monasteries (viharas) and worship halls (chaityas) of different Buddhist traditions. There are 36 identifiable foundations, and the numbering from 1 to 29 is a convenience that does not follow the order of construction. Cave 10 is a vast apsidal prayer hall of about the 1st century BCE, with 39 octagonal pillars and a stupa at the end with a path for walking round it. Textual records suggest that the caves served as a monsoon retreat for monks and as a resting place for merchants and pilgrims.

Most of the wall paintings come from the second phase and mainly narrate the Jataka tales, the legends of the Buddha's previous births as an animal or a human, including scenes from Aryasura's Jatakamala. Caves 1, 2, 16 and 17 hold the largest body of surviving ancient Indian wall painting. Spink holds that Cave 1, among the last excavated, was never dedicated for worship, and that its stress on royal imagery reflects Harishena's patronage. A fresco in Cave 2 shows children at a school.

Medieval Chinese Buddhist travellers mention the caves, which were later covered by jungle. They were brought to contemporary attention in 1819 when Colonel John Smith came upon them during a tiger-hunting expedition. The caves are in the northern wall of the U-shaped gorge of the Waghur river, in the Deccan Plateau, and form a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Ellora, about 100 kilometres away, has caves of a similar period, and the Ajanta style appears there and at other cave sites.
ajax-the-great: In Greek myth Ajax is the son of Telamon, himself a son of Aeacus and grandson of Zeus, and of Telamon's first wife Periboea. He is the elder half-brother of the archer Teucer and, through his uncle Peleus, a cousin of Achilles. The Iliad describes him as huge and the strongest of the Achaeans, trained by the centaur Chiron, and he carries a great shield of seven cowhides covered with bronze. His name is of uncertain origin. One folk etymology links it to a Greek verb meaning to lament, and Hesiod gave another, from the eagle that Zeus sent in answer to a prayer of Heracles. Athenians such as Cimon, Miltiades, Alcibiades and Thucydides traced their descent from him.

In the Iliad Ajax is chiefly a defensive warrior who covers the retreat of the Greeks and protects their ships, and he is not wounded in any of its battles. In Book 7 he is chosen by lot to duel with the Trojan Hector, and the fight lasts most of a day until heralds acting on the will of Zeus call a draw. The two exchange gifts, Ajax giving Hector a purple war-belt and Hector giving Ajax a silver-studded sword. Later, as Hector attacks the ships, Ajax leaps from ship to ship with an enormous spear and holds off the Trojans almost single-handed, though Hector burns one vessel. He often fights beside Teucer, who shoots from behind his shield.

In Book 9 Agamemnon sends Ajax, Odysseus and Phoenix to Achilles' tent, but Ajax cannot persuade Achilles to return to the fighting. After the death of Patroclus he and Menelaus fight off the Trojans and bring the body back, and after Achilles dies he recovers Achilles' body for burial while Odysseus holds the Trojans back.

When the council awarded Achilles' armour to Odysseus, with the help of Athena, Ajax killed himself with his sword. In the Little Iliad he first slaughters the cattle of the Greek army in a fit of rage. In Sophocles' play Ajax, Athena clouds his mind so that he slaughters sheep, imagining them the Greek leaders, and he kills himself rather than live in shame, with the sword Hector gave him. Homer says only that he lost the dispute, and in the underworld his shade refuses to speak to Odysseus.

Ajax was the guardian hero of Salamis, where a festival, the Aianteia, honoured him, and, after Salamis came under Athenian control, he became an Attic hero with a statue at Athens and a tribe named Aiantis. Since 2001 Yannis Lolos has excavated a Mycenaean palace at Kanakia on Salamis, which he suggests was the home of Ajax's dynasty.
ajmer: Ajmer lies in a valley of the Aravalli Range in the Indian state of Rajasthan, on the lower slopes of Taragarh Hill. Its name comes from Ajaya Meru, Sanskrit for invincible hill, given by a Chahamana ruler, either Ajayaraja I or Ajayaraja II, and referring to Taragarh Hill. To the northwest the Nagapathar Range protects it from the spread of the Thar Desert. Because of its central position in the state it is called the Heart of Rajasthan.

The sources disagree on the founding. A prashasti issued by Vigraharaja IV states that Ajayadeva, meaning Ajayaraja II, moved his residence to Ajmer, and the earliest mention of the city's name is in a text copied in 1113 CE, so Ajmer existed before then. A later text says an earlier king built the fort that became Taragarh, and a historian, R. B. Singh, finds this likely since inscriptions of the 8th century have been found there. Singh suggests that Ajayaraja II expanded the town, built palaces and moved the Chahamana capital there from Shakambhari. The Ghurids later annexed Ajmer, and it was later returned to Gaur Rajput rulers on condition of tribute. By the 15th century Mewar had captured it.

Akbar conquered Ajmer in 1556 and made it capital of the Ajmer Subah. The Mughals made frequent pilgrimages to the dargah of Moinuddin Chishti, and Jahanara Begum and Dara Shikoh, children of Shah Jahan, were born there in 1614 and 1615. Mughal patronage waned by the early 18th century. The Scindias conquered the city in 1752, and the British gained authority in 1818. Under British rule it was headquarters of the Ajmer-Merwara Province, and Mayo College was founded in 1875 for the sons of chiefs and nobles. After independence in 1947 Ajmer continued as a separate state until 1956, when it was merged into Rajasthan.

Ajmer is the administrative headquarters of its district and division, and had 542,321 inhabitants in the 2011 census. The Ajmer Sharif Dargah, the shrine of Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti at the foot of Taragarh Hill, has white marble buildings around two courtyards and draws many pilgrims. Other sights include Taragarh Fort, the mosque known as Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra, Akbar's fort, now a museum, and the Ana Sagar Lake. The temple town of Pushkar lies a few kilometres away.
akbar: Jalal ud-din Muhammad Akbar was born on 15 October 1542 at the Rajput fortress of Amarkot, in what is now Sindh, where his parents had been given refuge by the local Hindu ruler Rana Prasad. His father, Humayun, had been defeated by the forces of Sher Shah Suri at Chausa in 1539 and at Kannauj in 1540 and had fled westward. Akbar succeeded Humayun under a regent, Bairam Khan, who helped the young emperor expand and consolidate Mughal domains. In 1560, at the age of eighteen, Akbar dismissed Bairam Khan and ordered him to leave on the Hajj.

Mughal rule was still precarious when Akbar took the throne, as the Surs had reconquered Agra and Delhi. Having established Mughal rule over northern India, he turned to Rajputana, and from 1561 the Mughals engaged the Rajputs in warfare and diplomacy. Most Rajput states accepted his suzerainty, though Mewar and Marwar stayed outside it. He then conquered Gujarat and Bengal, and from 1593 he campaigned against the Deccan Sultans, taking Asirgarh Fort on 17 January 1601. At his death the empire stretched from the Bay of Bengal to Kandahar and Badakhshan.

Akbar organised his army and nobility through the mansabdari system, which assigned each officer a rank and a number of cavalry to supply, in 33 classes. In 1580 he replaced a system of annual assessment with the dahsala, which took one-third of the average produce of the previous ten years, paid in cash. He abolished the sectarian tax, appointed non-Muslims to high posts and married Rajput princesses, treating their families as equals, though some Rajputs saw marriage to Akbar as humiliation. Under him the economy of Mughal India tripled in size and wealth.

He built a new walled capital at Fatehpur Sikri from 1569, moved the capital to Lahore in 1585 and back to Agra in 1599. In 1575 he built the Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri, where discussions that began among Muslims were opened to people of all religions. Disillusioned with orthodox Islam, he promulgated Din-i Ilahi, a syncretic creed drawn mainly from Islam and Hinduism. His court historian Abul Fazl chronicled the reign in the Akbarnama.

Akbar fell ill with dysentery on 3 October 1605 and never recovered. He is buried in his mausoleum at Sikandra, Agra, next to the tomb of his favourite consort, Mariam-uz-Zamani. His son Prince Salim, later Jahangir, succeeded him. Akbar firmly entrenched the authority of the Mughal Empire after the Afghans had threatened it in his father's reign, and folk tales about him and his courtier Birbal remain popular in India.
akhaltsikhe: Akhaltsikhe lies in the Akhaltsikhe Basin at an elevation of about 1,000 metres, on both banks of the small river Potskhovi, a left tributary of the Kura, which divides the old city in the north from the new in the south. Its Georgian name means new fortress. Before the 12th century the settlement was called Lomsia, a name preserved into the medieval period by Armenians and Persians, and the change to Akhaltsikhe is associated with a new citadel built under the House of Jaqeli. Arabic sources give the name as Akhiskha, Persian ones as Akhesqeh and Turkish ones as Ahıska.

Human habitation in the area is attested from the Early Bronze Age. At Amiranis Gora, on the north-eastern outskirts, the earliest carbon date, 3790–3373 BCE, comes from a metallurgical workshop, and the site is one of the best with fixed stratigraphy for the Kura–Araxes culture. The town is mentioned among the places conquered by the general Habib ibn Maslama al-Fihri under the Umayyad caliph Mu'awiya I (661–680). During the Mongol domination of Georgia, the Jaqeli rulers of the principality of Samtskhe-Saatabago were given the title of atabeg and allowed autonomy.

The Ottomans took the town in 1579 during the Ottoman–Safavid War of 1578–1590 and spread Islam and Ottoman customs. In the early 17th century it became the centre of the Akhalzik Eyalet, known as Ahıska, with a resident pasha, and it became a leading hub of the Caucasian slave market. By the late 17th century it had 400 households of Turks, Armenians, Georgians, Greeks and Jews. Russian troops under General Ivan Paskevich captured it in 1828, and the Treaty of Adrianople of 1829 ceded it to the Russian Empire. Meskhetian Turks, who use the name Ahıska for their homeland, were deported by the Soviet authorities in November 1944.

Akhaltsikhe is the administrative centre of the Samtskhe–Javakheti region of southwestern Georgia. The 9th-century Akhaltsikhe Castle, called Rabati, stands in the old town and holds an Orthodox church, a mosque and a madrasa within a single walled enclosure. Jews have lived in the town since antiquity by local tradition; the community numbered over 3,500 at its largest in 1915, and most emigrated to Israel in the second half of the 20th century. Two historic synagogues remain.
akhenaten: Akhenaten was born Amenhotep IV, a younger son of the pharaoh Amenhotep III and his principal wife, Tiye. His elder brother, the crown prince Thutmose, was recognised as heir, but Thutmose's early death, perhaps around the 30th regnal year of Amenhotep III, left Amenhotep IV next in line. Little is known of his youth. Donald Redford dates his birth to c. 1363–1361 BCE, and the only certain servant of the prince is Parennefer, whose tomb mentions him.

He married Nefertiti, his Great Royal Wife, at a date that is not known. A secondary wife, Kiya, is also attested. He had seven attested daughters, six of them by Nefertiti, among them Meritaten and Ankhesenamun. Tutankhamun was his son-in-law and is considered likely to have been his son as well.

Amenhotep IV took the throne most likely in 1353 or 1351 BCE, at an age estimated anywhere from 10 to 23. Scholars disagree whether he shared power with his father for up to 12 years or not at all. Eric Cline, Nicholas Reeves and Peter Dorman argue for no coregency or one of at most two years, while Donald Redford and others reject any. In the fifth year of his reign he changed his name to Akhenaten, meaning 'Effective for the Aten'.

Worship of the sun had grown under the Eighteenth Dynasty, and Amenhotep III had given the Aten royal patronage, but he still devoted himself chiefly to Amun-Ra. Redford traced three stages in Atenism. In the first the disc still rested on the head of the falcon-headed Ra-Horakhty. In the second the Aten was raised above other gods and its name was placed in cartouches. In the last it was shown as a disc whose rays end in human hands. Egyptologists differ on whether the religion was monotheistic, monolatristic or henotheistic.

Amarna art, which flourished under Akhenaten and his immediate successors, is more naturalistic and shows more movement than traditional Egyptian art. Akhenaten himself is drawn with a sagging stomach, broad hips, thin legs and a long face. Some have argued that this reflects a medical condition, but Dominic Montserrat reports a broad consensus among Egyptologists that the forms are not to be read literally, and suggests they made the king a symbol of the androgyny of the Aten.

After his death his monuments were dismantled and hidden, his statues destroyed and his name left out of later lists of rulers, and traditional worship was gradually restored, notably under Tutankhamun. Later rulers called him 'the enemy' or 'that criminal'. He was almost lost to history until the late 19th-century discovery of Amarna, the city he built. A mummy found in tomb KV55 in 1907 may be his, although its identification has been questioned.
akhetaten: Amarna lies on the east bank of the Nile in the Egyptian province of Minya, about 58 kilometres south of al-Minya and 402 kilometres north of Luxor, the site of the previous capital, Thebes. The name Amarna comes from the Beni Amran, an Arab tribe that settled the area before the 18th century; the ancient name Akhetaten means the horizon of the Aten. The ruins are laid out north to south along a Royal Road. The royal residences lay mostly in the North City, the central city held the Great Temple of the Aten, the Great Royal Palace and the Bureau of Correspondence of Pharaoh, and the south held residential suburbs with the estates of nobles and the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose.

The city was built at the direction of the Pharaoh Akhenaten on a site that was effectively virgin, as a capital dedicated to the worship of the Aten. Construction began in or around Year 5 of his reign (1346 BCE) and was probably completed by Year 9, although it became the capital two years earlier. Most buildings were of whitewashed mudbrick, with the most important faced in local stone. Fourteen boundary stelae, thirteen of them known, ring the city and record Akhenaten's conditions for its foundation, including his wish to be buried there.

After Akhenaten's death in 1332 BCE the royal government of Tutankhamun left for Thebes, and the city was abandoned almost completely, though it seems to have remained active for a decade or so and a shrine to Horemheb shows partial occupation early in his reign. It stayed uninhabited until Roman settlement began along the Nile. Excavation has shown that gods such as Bes and Taweret were worshipped there despite the Aten cult. In 1887 a local woman digging for sebakh found over 300 cuneiform tablets, the Amarna Letters, mostly in Akkadian, the diplomatic language of the Late Bronze Age. The city's art broke with Egyptian convention, showing informal scenes of the royal family and more realistic figures.

Because the city was left almost intact, Amarna preserves great detail of its internal plan, though it is questionable how representative it is of ancient Egyptian cities. The French priest Claude Sicard first described it in 1714, and Napoleon's scholars made the first detailed map in 1798-1799. Flinders Petrie worked there in 1891-1892, and a German expedition under Ludwig Borchardt found the bust of Nefertiti in Thutmose's workshop in 1912; it is now in Berlin's Neues Museum. Excavation by the Amarna Project continues.
akim-oda: Akim Oda lies in the south of Ghana, surrounded by rain forest, in the basin of the Birim River, which flows through the town and is rich in gold and diamonds. The climate is semi-equatorial and wet. Rain falls heavily from April to June and again from September to November, and a dry season, with markedly lower temperatures, lasts from December to February. The town is the capital of the Birim Central Municipal District and had 60,604 residents as of 2013.

Cocoa is grown on formal and informal plantations, sometimes along the roads; the harvested beans are dried and kept in warehouses until they are shipped. North of the Birim there are palm oil plantations covering roughly 6,000 hectares, most of them small and independently owned, and bamboo is also cultivated. Local miners take gold and diamonds from the river bank by traditional methods, often with simple tools.

The forests near the town are cut for timber. Ghana's forest cover shrank from 8.2 million hectares in 1900 to 1.6 million in 2000, and forest plantations are being established near Akim Oda under the National Forest Plantation Development Program. Visitors are shown a tree described as the largest in West Africa, 12 metres in circumference and 66.5 metres high, and may see the mining from dug-out boats and ceremonies with Akan drumming.

The Akim Oda Government Hospital serves the Kotoku traditional area and takes referrals from nearby communities in the Akyem states; private hospitals in the town also serve Akyem Bosome and part of the Abuakwa traditional area. The public sector has more than fifteen primary and junior high schools and three senior high schools, and four radio stations broadcast from the town.
akita-prefecture: Akita Prefecture lies on the north-western side of Honshu, in the Tōhoku region, on the coast of the Sea of Japan. It borders Aomori Prefecture to the north, Iwate to the east, Miyagi to the southeast and Yamagata to the south. Its borders roughly form a rectangle 169 kilometres from north to south and 86 kilometres from west to east, covering 11,637 square kilometres. The Oga Peninsula is a prominent feature of the western edge, the Ōu Mountains, the longest range in Japan, mark the eastern border, and the higher Dewa Mountains run through the centre. Winters are cold, especially away from the sea.

The region was created from the ancient provinces of Dewa and Mutsu. Separated from the main centres of Japanese commerce, politics and population by several hundred kilometres and by mountain ranges, Akita remained largely isolated from Japanese society until after the year 600, and was a region of hunter-gatherers and principally nomadic tribes. The first historical record dates to 658, when Abe no Hirafu, governor of Koshi Province, conquered the native Ezo tribes at what are now the cities of Akita and Noshiro and built a fort on the Mogami River, which began Japanese settlement.

In 733 a new military settlement, later renamed Akita Castle, was built in what is now the Takashimizu area of Akita. The region served as a base from which the Japanese empire drove the Ezo people from northern Honshu. Under the Tokugawa shogunate it was given to the Satake clan, who ruled it for 260 years and developed the agriculture and mining that remain important. In 1871, during the Meiji Restoration, Dewa Province was reshaped and the old daimyō domains were abolished, which produced the modern borders of Akita.

The city of Akita is the capital and largest city, and Yokote, Daisen and Yurihonjō are other major cities. The economy has long rested on agriculture, fishing and forestry, and the prefecture is known for rice and sake. Population has declined since 1955. Kakunodate preserves many samurai houses, among them the former home of Odano Naotake, who illustrated Japan's first modern guide to human anatomy. The Namahage ritual in Oga on New Year's Eve and the Akita Kantō festival in August are among its best-known customs.
akkadian-empire: The Akkadian Empire takes its name from the city and region of Akkad, near the confluence of the Tigris and Euphrates. The city has not yet been identified on the ground, but it is known from textual sources, at least one of them older than Sargon's reign. The period is generally dated to 2334–2154 BCE by the middle chronology; the short-chronology dates of 2270–2083 BCE are now considered less likely. It followed the Early Dynastic Period and was succeeded by the Ur III Period, though both transitions are blurry.

Its founder, Sargon, was a usurper, and he is not known to have had a father or predecessor on the throne of Akkad, until then a marginal city. Later texts make it hard to separate legend from reality. Some historians, drawing on a late legend, suggest he rebelled against Ur-Zababa of Kish, but this is hypothetical. He then faced Lugal-zage-si of Uruk, the most powerful king in the south, and according to copies of his inscriptions defeated him around 2300 BCE. Lugal-zage-si was captured, made to wear a yoke and paraded at Nippur.

Sargon installed loyal governors in several Sumerian cities and so created a kingdom covering all of southern Mesopotamia, with Akkad as its capital. His influence is said to have stretched from the Mediterranean to Iran, and expeditions went as far as Dilmun and Magan. His sons Rimush and Manishtushu struggled to keep control, and both may have died violently. Sargon's grandson Naram-Sin called himself King of the Four Quarters and had himself called god of Akkad, with a cult in his honour, though whether he was considered a full deity is debated.

Naram-Sin's successors were weaker. The empire collapsed, probably through a combination of internal unrest, severe environmental and economic stress from a drought associated with the 4.2-kiloyear climate event, and threats from the Gutians, Amorites and Elamites.

The Akkadian language became the empire's lingua franca, while Sumerian stayed important in religion and literature. The kings had their exploits written in long inscriptions on stelae and statues, and their royal art, with a more naturalistic sculpture centred on the king, had a lasting influence on Mesopotamian art. Enheduanna, Sargon's daughter, served as high priestess and is often recognised as the first known named author in history. The kingdom of the Third Dynasty of Ur stood in the tradition of the first empire. Later, Sargon became the example to follow and Naram-Sin the example to avoid, and several rulers took the title King of Akkad.
akkadian-language: Akkadian is an East Semitic language attested in ancient Mesopotamia from the mid-third millennium BCE. It is the earliest documented Semitic language and is named after the city of Akkad, a major centre during the Akkadian Empire (c. 2334–2154 BCE).
