Akkadian names appear in Sumerian texts from the mid-3rd millennium BCE, and texts fully in Akkadian begin to appear from about the 24th century BCE.

It was written in cuneiform, adopted from the Sumerians. Sargon of Akkad's empire introduced Akkadian as a written language by adapting Sumerian cuneiform. In the Middle Bronze Age it virtually displaced Sumerian, assumed to have been extinct as a living language by the 18th century BCE. By the 20th century BCE two forms were in use, Assyrian and Babylonian.

Akkadian is a fusional language with grammatical case, and like other Semitic languages it builds words on consonantal roots, most of them of three consonants. It has three cases and three numbers, though the dual is vestigial. Unlike most Semitic languages it uses subject–object–verb word order. Sumerian influenced its phonology, vocabulary and syntax, and scholars describe the two languages as a sprachbund.

Cuneiform suited it poorly, since it could not represent the glottal stop, the pharyngeals and the emphatic consonants. Scribes used signs as Sumerian logograms, Sumerian syllables or Akkadian syllables. The sign AN, for example, can stand for ilum ('god'), for the god Anu or for the syllable -an-.

In its Assyrian and Babylonian forms Akkadian was the native language of the Mesopotamian empires through the later Bronze Age and became the lingua franca of much of the Ancient Near East by the time of the Bronze Age collapse c. 1150 BCE. It declined under the Neo-Assyrian Empire, by about the 8th century BCE, in favour of Old Aramaic. By the Hellenistic period only scholars and priests in the temples used it, and the last known Akkadian cuneiform document dates from the 1st century CE.

Hundreds of thousands of texts and fragments survive, including religious narrative, legal and scientific works and letters. Literary works include the Atrahasis Epic, the Enûma Elish, the Amarna letters and the Epic of Gilgamesh. The Chicago Assyrian Dictionary, in 21 volumes, was begun in 1921 and completed in 2011.
aksaray: Aksaray stands in the Central Anatolia region of Turkey, at an average elevation of 980 metres, with the Melendiz river running through it. Mount Hasan rises to 3,268 metres. The city was an important stopover on the Silk Road across Anatolia for centuries. Its name means white palace in Turkish. In antiquity the area was called Archelais Garsaura, which became Taksara under the Seljuks and then Aksaray.

Ancient Hittite texts first mention the place as Šinaḫuttum or Šinuhtu. The Aksaray Stela, written in Luwian hieroglyphs, was dedicated by a king named Kiyakiyas, who described his prosperity and the benevolence of the weather god Tarhunzas. He may be the king Kiyakki of Šinuḫtu who ruled before 718 BCE, when the Neo-Assyrian king Sargon II took the city and deported him.

The Hittite name Kurşaura became Garsaura, which Strabo mentions. Archelaus of Cappadocia, the last Cappadocian king, renamed the town Archelaïs, and in Roman times it was a colony and a bishopric. Its bishops attended councils from Nicaea in 325 to the Trullan Council of 692.

In Byzantine times, as Koloneia, it was an important military centre. Between 1081 and 1084 it formed part of the domain of Suleiman ibn Qutalmish, and later of the Sultanate of Rum, whose sultans left important landmarks in and around the town. Ibn Battuta, who visited in the 14th century, called it a beautiful city surrounded by waterways and gardens, with water brought to the houses, and noted its class of Muslim traders.

The Mongols raided it in 1277 and killed or enslaved 6,000 of its people. İshak Pasha incorporated it into the Ottoman Empire in 1470 after a long struggle against the Karamanids, and many inhabitants were moved to Constantinople, where a district also came to be named Aksaray. The nearby Lake Tuz, the main source of salt for Anatolia, helped the town to prosper.

Aksaray is the seat of Aksaray Province, with 247,147 inhabitants in 2021. The Red Minaret Mosque has a Seljuk minaret of 1236 from the reign of Aläettin Keykubat, and the Zincirye Medresesi, a Koranic school built by the bey of Karaman in 1345, now serves as the local library. The Aksaray Grand Mosque dates from 1408-09 and the Karamanoğlu dynasty, and the Hakiki Yusuf Baba complex holds the tombs of the 14th-century Somuncu Baba and the scholar Cemaleddin'i Aksaray.
aksumite-empire: Before Aksum, Eritrea and the Tigray Plateau were home to a kingdom known as Dʿmt, which archaeological evidence suggests was influenced by Sheba, now Yemen. Scholars once held that the Sabaeans founded Semitic civilisation in Ethiopia, but that view is now refuted and their influence is considered minor; it included the Ancient South Arabian script, which developed into the Geʽez script. Excavations at Betä Giyorgis show a settlement near Aksum dating to about the seventh to fourth centuries BCE. The Aksumite polity itself arose between 150 BCE and 150 CE, and its early centuries remain largely obscure.

Stuart Munro-Hay concludes that the early kingdom was probably a confederacy led by a district-level king who commanded the allegiance of lesser kings, so that its ruler was a king of kings. There is no evidence of a single royal lineage, and a new king of kings may have been chosen from among all the kings.

Mani, the founder of Manichaeism, counted Aksum among the four great powers of the 3rd century, with Persia, Rome and China. Under Gedara (c. 200 to 230) it took much of western Yemen, until a Himyarite and Sabean alliance pushed it out. Under Endybis (270 to 310) it began minting coins. Ezana (320s to c. 360) adopted Christianity as the state religion in the mid 4th century and conquered Meroë in 330 for a short time. After they adopted Christianity the Aksumites stopped building steles.

Aksum reached its height under Kaleb (514 to 542), who at the request of Byzantine emperor Justin I invaded the Himyarite Kingdom to end the persecution of Christians by its Jewish king Dhu Nuwas. With Himyar annexed, the kingdom spanned about 2,500,000 square kilometres, but it lost the territory in the Aksumite–Persian wars. Decline began by the 7th century, when currency ceased to be minted; Persian and later Muslim power in the Red Sea and the weakening of Rome, a major trade partner, damaged its economy. The final three centuries are considered a dark age, and the kingdom collapsed in uncertain circumstances around 960.

The Aksumites left their own alphabet, the Geʽez script, later modified to include vowels, and giant obelisks marking tombs, the best known of which is the Obelisk of Aksum. Greek was the official and literary language of the state, used in administration, diplomacy and trade, and Ezana made Geʽez an official language beside it. After the Muslim conquests isolated Aksum from the Greco-Roman world, Geʽez replaced Greek entirely. Texts were translated into Geʽez from the early Christian period, the best known being the Garima Gospels, dated between the 4th and 6th centuries. The Aksumite church gave rise to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.
al-andalus: Al-Andalus refers to the territories of the Iberian Peninsula under Muslim rule between 711 and 1492, a name first attested on dinars minted in 716 with inscriptions in Latin and Arabic. At its widest extent under Umayyad rule it covered most of the peninsula and Septimania in southern France. It was first divided into five administrative units, corresponding roughly to Andalusia, Castile and León, Navarre, Aragon and Catalonia, Portugal and Galicia, and Languedoc-Roussillon. Its boundaries then shrank in a series of conquests that Western historiography has traditionally called the Reconquista, until only the Emirate of Granada remained.

In 711 Tariq ibn-Ziyad led an army of 7,000 that landed at Gibraltar on 30 April, ostensibly to intervene in a Visigothic civil war. After a victory over King Roderic at the Battle of Guadalete on 19 July 711, he and Musa ibn Nusayr brought most of the Visigothic Kingdom under Muslim rule in seven years. Al-Andalus was first a province of the Umayyad Caliphate, with Córdoba as its capital. It became the Emirate of Córdoba (c. 750–929) and then the Caliphate of Córdoba (929–1031), under which Córdoba became a leading cultural and economic centre. Resistant Visigoths took refuge in the Cantabrian highlands and formed the Kingdom of Asturias.

After 1031 al-Andalus split into taifa states. The Christian capture of Toledo in 1085 brought in the Almoravid Empire, and then the Almohad Caliphate, both based in Marrakesh. In the 13th century most of the south fell to Portuguese, Castilian and Aragonese conquests. The Emirate of Granada (1238–1492), a tributary of the Crown of Castile, surrendered to the Catholic Monarchs in 1492.

Society in al-Andalus consisted of Muslims, Christians and Jews, with Arabs at the top, followed by Berbers, Muladies, Mozarabs and Jews. Non-Muslims had the status of ahl al-dhimma and paid a tax, and scholars still debate their treatment. Andalusi scholars advanced trigonometry (Jabir ibn Aflah), astronomy (al-Zarqali), surgery (al-Zahrawi), pharmacology (Ibn Zuhr) and agronomy. Alfonso X of Castile and other Christian monarchs had Andalusi libraries translated into Latin.

Many Muslims were forced to convert in the later Reconquista, particularly after the decrees of 1502 and 1526, and these converts, the Moriscos, were expelled in the early 17th century. Among the surviving monuments are the Cathedral of Córdoba, the Alhambra and the Giralda.
al-aqsa-mosque: The mosque stands on the southern part of the Temple Mount, or Haram al-Sharif, an enclosure that King Herod the Great expanded from 20 BCE during his rebuilding of the Second Jewish Temple. In the late Second Temple period the site held the Royal Stoa, a basilica along the southern wall, which was destroyed with the Temple during the Roman siege of Jerusalem in 70 CE. The Nea Church of Justinian, consecrated in 543, was once thought to have stood here, but remains identified as its were found in the Jewish Quarter in 1973.

According to Islamic tradition, Umar, the second caliph (r. 634–644), built a small prayer hall on the compound. In the reign of Mu'awiya I (r. 661–680) a quadrangular mosque for 3,000 worshippers is recorded. The present mosque was built by the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik (r. 685–705), his successor al-Walid I, or both, on the same axis as the Dome of the Rock.

An earthquake destroyed the mosque in 746, and the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur rebuilt it in 758. Al-Mahdi expanded it in 780 to fifteen aisles and a central dome. Another earthquake destroyed it in 1033, and the Fatimid caliph al-Zahir rebuilt it with seven aisles, preserving the outline that survives. The Fatimid caliph al-Mustansir Billah had its facade built in 1065.

After the Crusaders captured Jerusalem in 1099 the mosque served as a palace and as the headquarters of the Knights Templar. Saladin conquered the area in 1187 and restored its use as a mosque. The Ayyubids, Mamluks, Ottomans, the Supreme Muslim Council of British Palestine and the Jordanian administration all later renovated or enlarged it. The dome was destroyed by fire in 1969 and its painted interior was reconstructed using the trateggio technique.

The name al-Masjid al-Aqṣā, 'the furthest mosque', occurs in the Quran's Surah 17 and was first applied to the whole compound, since no buildings stood there then. The building discussed here is the silver-domed congregational mosque, called Jāmiʿ al-Aqṣā or the Qibli Mosque for its place at the southern end of the compound. Medieval writers such as al-Muqaddasi called it al-Mughattâ, 'the covered part'.

The mosque is 83 metres long and 56 metres wide and can hold up to 5,000 worshippers. It has seven aisles. Its facade has fourteen stone arches, mostly Romanesque, some made from sculpted material taken from Crusader buildings, and the porch was ordered by al-Mu'azzam Isa in 1217. It has 121 stained glass windows from the Abbasid and Fatimid eras. Unlike the Dome of the Rock, which reflects classical Byzantine architecture, it is characteristic of early Islamic architecture.
al-biruni: Al-Biruni's name comes from the Persian word bīrūn, meaning outskirts, since he was born in an outlying district of Kath, the capital of the Afrighid kingdom of Khwarazm. He spent his first twenty-five years in Khwarazm, studying Islamic jurisprudence, theology, grammar, mathematics, astronomy, medicine and philosophy. His mother tongue was Khwarezmian, an Eastern Iranian language. He was sympathetic to the Afrighids, who were overthrown by the rival Ma'munid dynasty in 995, and he then left for Bukhara, under the Samanid ruler Mansur II, where he corresponded with Avicenna.

In 998 he went to the court of the Ziyarid amir of Tabaristan, Qabus, and there wrote his first major work, al-Āthār al-bāqiya, on historical and scientific chronology, probably around 1000. He later made peace with the Ma'munids, whose court at Gurganj was gaining a reputation as a gathering place for scientists, and collaborated there with his former teacher Abu Nasr Mansur.

In July 1017 Mahmud of Ghazni invaded Khwarazm and took Kath. Al-Biruni and most other scholars left with him, possibly as prisoners, and were brought to Ghazni, where he spent much of the rest of his life. He was made court astrologer and from 1017 accompanied Mahmud on his campaigns in the Indian subcontinent, living there for several years. During those journeys he studied the Hindu faith and Indian culture, and wrote the Tārīkh al-Hind, which he finished around 1030. He died at Ghazni around 1050.

Of the 146 books attributed to him, 95 concern astronomy, mathematics and related subjects. In the Mas'ud Canon he observed, contrary to Ptolemy, that the Sun's apogee was mobile and not fixed. He wrote a treatise on the astrolabe, and a later work refuting astrology, which he distinguished from astronomy. He devised a method of finding the Earth's radius from the height of a mountain and the dip of the horizon, which he carried out at Nandana in present-day Pakistan. He also developed experimental methods for determining density with a hydrostatic balance, and classified gems by properties such as specific gravity and hardness rather than colour.

His Taḥqīq mā li-l-Hind explored nearly every aspect of Indian life, and he also translated the yoga sutras of Patanjali. He chose to record civilian and scholarly life rather than military and political history, and said he would set out the theories of the Hindus as they are, comparing them with similar Greek theories. He was conversant in Khwarezmian, Persian, Arabic and Sanskrit and also knew Greek, Hebrew and Syriac. He is widely considered an important Muslim authority on the history of religion, though he assumed the superiority of Islam. Some call him the first anthropologist, but others say he can hardly be considered one in the conventional sense.
al-farabi: Little is known of al-Farabi's life. The accounts of his origins vary and seem to rest on hearsay or guesses, and Arabic biographers of the 12th and 13th centuries had few facts and used invented stories. His full name was Abu Nasr Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Farabi, sometimes with the family name al-Tarkhani. His birthplace could have been any of several places in Central Asia, then called Khurasan, since farab is a Persian term for land irrigated by springs or a nearby river. Candidates include Farab (Otrar) on the Syr Darya, a village near Türkmenabat and Faryab in present-day Afghanistan.

From incidental accounts it is known that he spent most of his scholarly life in Baghdad with Syriac Christian scholars, among them Yuhanna ibn Haylan, Yahya ibn Adi and Abu Ishaq Ibrahim al-Baghdadi. He later spent time in Damascus and in Egypt before returning to Damascus, where he died around the middle of the 10th century. His religious affiliation is disputed, and some scholars place him as Sunni and others as Shia or influenced by Shia thought.

Al-Farabi is credited with over one hundred works, among them prolegomena to philosophy and commentaries on Aristotle, including the Nicomachean Ethics. His main influence was the Aristotelian tradition of Alexandria, with elements of Neoplatonism and of Ptolemy's planetary model. In logic he was mainly an Aristotelian but discussed future contingents, the relation of logic to grammar and Stoic forms of inference, and he introduced the concept of the poetic syllogism in a commentary on Aristotle's Poetics. He also wrote on alchemy, in The Necessity of the Art of the Elixir, and was a practical musician and music theorist.

In metaphysics he held that the subject was being as such, related to God only as a principle of absolute being, and Avicenna remarked that he understood Aristotle's Metaphysics only after reading al-Farabi's prolegomenon. His cosmology had the First Cause, by contemplating itself, give rise to a cascade of ten intellects, each bringing a celestial sphere into being, beneath which lies the material world. The process was necessary rather than willed, a view that al-Ghazzali later criticised.

Later writers called al-Farabi the Second Master, with Aristotle the first. He is credited as the first Muslim to present philosophy as a coherent system, and he is called the founder of Islamic political philosophy. Among those he influenced are Avicenna, Averroes, Maimonides and Albertus Magnus. He helped to pass on Aristotle's thought to the Christian West, and he is the only philosopher named in Maimonides's Treatise on Logic.

In Kazakhstan a large university, KazNU, bears his name, and monuments to him stand in Alma-Ata, Shymkent and Turkestan. An anniversary of his birth was marked in 1975, and the asteroid 7057 Al-Fārābī is named after him.
al-hoceima: Al Hoceima lies on the Mediterranean coast on the northern edge of the Rif Mountains, in the heart of the Central Rif, surrounded by the range's highest peaks, among them Mount Tidghin at 2,452 metres. It is the capital of Al Hoceima Province and remains a cultural centre for the Ayt Waryaghar tribe. Its name is an Arabised form of Alhucemas, the Spanish name of the nearby Spanish-owned Alhucemas Islands, meaning lavender islands, itself from the Andalusi Arabic al-Khuzāmā. Some, among them the author of the Spanish encyclopedia Espasa-Calpe, derive Alhucemas from al-Mazimma. The climate is a hot-summer Mediterranean one.

The Ait Ouriaghel Berber tribe, also called Beni Urriaguel, dominated the area. Abd el-Krim, whose father was a qadi of the Ait Youssef ou Ali clan, organised a guerrilla force against the Spanish during the Rif War and established the Republic of the Rif in 1921, which lasted until 1926. In September 1925 the Spanish general José Sanjurjo landed at Al Hoceima and claimed the territory for Spain. The Spanish developed the town and named it Villa Sanjurjo; its first mayor was Florian Gómez Aroca. The beach where Sanjurjo and his troops landed, Playa Quemado, is still one of its well-known beaches.

After Morocco became independent in 1956 the town grew quickly and the government gave it the name Al Hoceima, following the standard French spelling. The years from 1956 to 1959 were hard in the Rif. In October 1958 the Beni Urriaguel rebelled against the central administration, and two thirds of the Moroccan army, led by the crown prince, the future Hassan II, were sent to Al Hoceima; a significant number of people lost their lives in the Rif in this period.
Two earthquakes struck the city and its villages within ten years: one of magnitude 6.0 on 26 May 1994 and one of magnitude 6.4 on 24 February 2004, which killed more than 560 people.

Al Hoceima is a moderate-size city whose income comes from fishing and tourism, and it has the second-largest port of the Rif region after Nador. Many of its former inhabitants migrated to Europe between the 1960s and the 1980s, and large numbers of Moroccans in the Netherlands, France and Belgium come from the city; many return in summer. The first schools built by the Spanish, a college and an elementary school, and a Spanish Catholic church still exist. In the early 1950s and 1960s the small houses were mostly painted white and blue, colours that were regarded as the city's own, and in 2007 the mayor stated that new houses would be painted in them.
al-khwarizmi: Few details of al-Khwarizmi's life are known with certainty. Ibn al-Nadim gives his birthplace as Khwarazm, a region of Greater Iran now divided between Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, and he is generally thought to have come from there; his name means from Khwarazm. He was of Persian descent, probably Khwarezmian, but wrote his scientific works entirely in Arabic. The historian al-Tabari gives him the further epithets al-Majusi and al-Qutrubbulli. Roshdi Rashed holds that these belong to a second person, whereas David A. King affirms that he was born just outside Baghdad, at Qutrubbul. The epithet al-Majusi may point to Zoroastrian forebears, but the pious preface to his algebra shows that he was an orthodox Muslim.

Most of al-Khwarizmi's work was done between 813 and 833. Baghdad had become the centre of scientific studies and trade, and around 820 he was appointed astronomer and head of the library of the House of Wisdom, which the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun had established. He studied the sciences and mathematics, including the translation of Greek and Sanskrit scientific manuscripts. He is said to have assisted a project to determine the circumference of the Earth and to have overseen 70 geographers in making a world map for al-Ma'mun. During the reign of al-Wathiq he is said to have taken part in the first of two embassies to the Khazars.

His treatise on algebra, compiled between 813 and 833, presented the first systematic solution of linear and quadratic equations by reducing them to six standard forms using the operations al-jabr, restoration, and al-muqabala, balancing, and it gave algebra its name. It was written with the encouragement of al-Ma'mun and is full of examples from trade, surveying and legal inheritance. Robert of Chester translated it into Latin in 1145, and it was used until the 16th century as the principal mathematical textbook of European universities. His book on Hindu numerals, written about 825, spread the Hindu-Arabic numeral system, and its Latin translation in the 12th century introduced the term algorithm, from the Latinized form of his name, to the Western world.

His Zij as-Sindhind, based on Indian astronomical methods, held 116 tables for the Sun, Moon and five planets, and marked a turning point in Islamic astronomy. His Geography, finished in 833, reworked Ptolemy's and listed 2,402 coordinates; it corrected Ptolemy's overestimate of the length of the Mediterranean, 63 degrees of longitude, to nearly 50. He also wrote on the astrolabe, the sundial and the Hebrew calendar, and produced a book of annals that does not survive.
al-mamun: Abdallah, the future al-Ma'mun, was born in Baghdad on the night of 13 to 14 September 786 to Harun al-Rashid and a concubine, Marajil. That night, later called the night of the three caliphs, his uncle al-Hadi died and Harun became caliph. His mother died soon after, and Harun's wife Zubayda raised him. Though the eldest son, he was named second heir in 799, after his half-brother al-Amin, who was born to Zubayda, a woman of Abbasid descent. He was educated in Arabic, adab, music, poetry, law and hadith, and a modern scholar calls him the most intellectual caliph of his family.

Al-Ma'mun reigned from 813 and spent the early years in Merv, while Iraq was disturbed. In Mecca a claimant, Muhammad ibn Ja'far, proclaimed himself caliph in November 815 and soon abdicated. In Baghdad, neighbourhood watch groups led by preachers such as Sahl ibn Salama al-Ansari held authority until military chiefs crushed Sahl in 817 to 818. In 817 al-Ma'mun named Ali al-Rida, the eighth Shia Imam, as his heir. This may have been meant to reconcile the Alid and Abbasid branches of the family, but the Hashimites in Baghdad deposed him and elected Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi. Al-Rida died in 818, and Shia sources hold the caliph responsible for poisoning him.

With Byzantium, border raiding gave way to a larger contest after Michael II took power in 820. Crete fell to Andalusian invaders in 824, and Arabs from Tunis invaded Sicily in 827 and took Palermo in 831. In 830 al-Ma'mun invaded Anatolia and took forts, sparing those who surrendered. Theophilos took Tarsus in 831. Al-Ma'mun offered him the shahada, tribute or war, and died near Tarsus on 9 August 833, on the way to a campaign, after eating dates by a river. In 833 he also began the mihna, an inquiry that required acceptance that the Quran was created, which led to the imprisonment of Ahmad ibn Hanbal.

Al-Ma'mun gathered scholars of many religions at Baghdad. He sent an emissary to the Byzantine Empire to collect manuscripts and had them translated into Arabic. His peace treaty with the Byzantine emperor entitled him to a number of Greek manuscripts each year, among them Ptolemy's Almagest. He built the first observatory in the Round City of Baghdad and others elsewhere, with scholars from the House of Wisdom. Around 830 astronomers and geographers measured the arc between Tadmur and Raqqa, found it to be one degree of latitude, and calculated the circumference of the Earth at 40,007 kilometres, close to the modern value. His reign saw the publication of al-Khwarizmi's book on algebra. Almanon, a lunar crater, is named after him.
al-masudi: Little is known of al-Masudi apart from what he writes of himself. He was born in Baghdad and was descended from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, a companion of Muhammad. His travels occupied most of his life and took him to most of the Persian provinces, Armenia, Georgia, Azerbaijan and the Caspian region, where he recorded oil lands near Baku, as well as Arabia, Syria, Egypt, the Indus Valley and the western coast of India. He voyaged more than once to East Africa. How he funded these journeys is unknown, and it has been speculated that he traded.

He lived when books were cheap and Baghdad had large public libraries. He was a pupil or junior colleague of philologists such as al-Zajjaj and Ibn Duraid, read the philosophy of al-Kindi, al-Razi and al-Farabi, and knew Galen and Ptolemaic astronomy.

His major work, The Meadows of Gold (Murūj al-Dhahab), combines universal history with scientific geography, social commentary and biography. Only a draft survives, although he later wrote a revised edition. Shortly before his death he wrote the Kitāb al-Tanbīh wa'l-Ishrāf, an abridgement with new material on the Byzantines. Ahmad Shboul notes that he is distinguished among contemporaries by his coverage of non-Islamic lands: India, China, the Turkic peoples, the Khazars, Byzantium and even Britain. His account of the Rus is an important early source for Russian history; he describes them as a varied collection of peoples, pagan and without strong central authority.

He recounts that the Greeks called Constantinople simply the City, and from his writing the name Istanbul can be traced. Ernest Renan compared him to the Greek geographer Pausanias, and he is sometimes called the Herodotus of the Arabs. The Sunni scholar Ibn Hajar called his books imprecise because he was a Shi'a and a Mu'tazili.
al-mutasim: Muhammad, the future al-Mu'tasim, was born in the Khuld Palace in Baghdad in 796, according to al-Tabari. His father was the caliph Harun al-Rashid, and his mother, Marida bint Shabib, was a slave concubine whose family came from Soghdia. As one of Harun's younger sons he was at first of little consequence. From about 814 he began to form a corps of Turkish troops, first buying domestic slaves in Baghdad and then receiving Turkish slaves from Central Asia under an agreement with the Samanid rulers. The force numbered perhaps three to four thousand men at his accession, but it was highly trained and disciplined, and it made him a man of power in his own right.

Al-Ma'mun made no official provision for his succession. According to al-Tabari, on his deathbed he dictated a letter naming his brother rather than his son al-Abbas, and Abu Ishaq was acclaimed caliph on 9 August 833. It cannot be known whether the letter was genuine. Al-Mu'tasim relied almost exclusively on his Turks, and the historian Tayeb El-Hibri describes his regime as militaristic and centred on the Turkish corps. In 836 he established a new capital at Samarra, to set the regime apart from the restive populace of Baghdad, where the Turkish troops had come into conflict with residents.

He continued al-Ma'mun's support for Mu'tazilism and its inquisition, the miḥna, with the chief qadi Ahmad ibn Abi Duwad as a dominant influence at court. His armies suppressed the Khurramite uprising of Babak Khorramdin and a revolt by Mazyar of Tabaristan. In 838 al-Mu'tasim himself led a campaign against the Byzantine Empire, defeated Emperor Theophilos and sacked Amorium, a victory that became a cornerstone of caliphal propaganda. A plot against him in 838 led to a large-scale purge of the army, and about seventy commanders and soldiers were executed, according to the Kitab al-'Uyun.

Al-Mu'tasim fell ill on 21 October 841 and died on 5 January 842. He was buried in the Jawsaq al-Khaqani palace at Samarra, and his son al-Wathiq succeeded without opposition. The dominance of the Turkic military elite eventually led to the Anarchy at Samarra and the collapse of Abbasid power in the mid-10th century. Yet the system of slave soldiers, the ghulām system, that he inaugurated was widely adopted throughout the Muslim world.
al-qaeda: The name is a simplified transliteration of the Arabic al-qāʿidah, meaning the foundation or the base. The organisation was founded in a series of meetings held in Peshawar during 1988, attended by Abdullah Yusuf Azzam, Osama bin Laden, Mohammed Atef, Ayman Al-Zawahiri and other veterans of the Soviet–Afghan War. Building on the networks of Maktab Al-Khidamat, the founders decided to create a vanguard for jihad. The writings of the Egyptian Islamist ideologue Sayyid Qutb strongly inspired them. Qutb held that the Islamic world had reverted to the pre-Islamic ignorance known as jahiliyyah and that a vanguard of righteous Muslims was needed to restore Islam.

When Iraqi forces occupied Kuwait in 1990, bin Laden offered to support Saudi Arabia with his fighters. The Saudi government refused and sought the help of the United States instead. The stationing of American troops on the Arabian Peninsula led bin Laden to declare a jihad against the rulers of Saudi Arabia, whom he denounced as apostates, and against the United States. From 1992 the group had its headquarters in Sudan until it was expelled in 1996, and it then moved to Taliban-ruled Afghanistan. In 1996 and 1998 bin Laden issued two fatwas demanding the withdrawal of American troops from Saudi Arabia.

In 1998 the group carried out the bombings of the American embassies in Kenya and Tanzania, which killed 224 people. In 2001 it carried out the attacks of 11 September, which killed 2,996 people, including the 19 hijackers. Two airliners were flown into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center, a third into the Pentagon, and a fourth crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after passengers revolted. The United States launched the war on terror and invaded Afghanistan to remove the Taliban. In 2004 the group launched an Iraqi branch, which later became the Islamic State of Iraq and then separated from it. American forces killed bin Laden in Pakistan in May 2011.

Al-Qaeda controlled its day-to-day operations only indirectly: decision making on strategy was centralised, while execution was left to mid-level groups, which had to consult the leadership before large attacks. The top leadership included a shura council and committees for military operations, finance and information. Its financing came partly from bin Laden's personal wealth, the heroin trade and donations from supporters in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states. After the war on terror its leadership became isolated and the organisation regionalised into several groups, among them al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, in the Islamic Maghreb and in the Indian subcontinent, and al-Shabaab. Its long-term aim is a supra-national caliphate; its immediate objectives include the removal of American troops from the Arabian Peninsula.
al-shafii: Al-Shafi'i was born in Gaza, near Ashkelon, in the later eighth century. The oldest surviving biography, by Ibn Abi Hatim al-Razi, who died in 938 or 939, is a collection of anecdotes, some fantastical, and the first full biography is filled with what a modern eye calls pious legends. His father died while he was a child, and his mother took him to Mecca at about the age of two, where he grew up in poverty. He had memorised the Quran by seven and Malik ibn Anas's Muwatta by ten, and was authorised to issue rulings at fifteen.

He then went to Medina and studied for many years under Malik ibn Anas, whom he always called the Teacher, though he later differed from some of his views. At thirty he was appointed Abbasid governor of Najran in Yemen. In 803 he was accused of aiding the Alids in a revolt and was brought in chains to the caliph Harun al-Rashid at Raqqa. His defence persuaded the caliph to dismiss the charge, and the incident brought him into contact with the Hanafi jurist Muhammad al-Shaybani.

In Baghdad al-Shafi'i studied with al-Shaybani and developed his first school, influenced by both Abu Hanifah and Malik and later called his old school. He left for Mecca in 804, where he lectured at the Sacred Mosque and impressed students including Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and he returned to Baghdad in 810. In 814 he left for Egypt. There he lectured in the mosque of Amr, composed the surviving version of his al-Risala and dictated most of the texts collected in Kitab al-Umm to his disciples, who read them back for correction. His Egyptian teaching is called his new doctrine.

Al-Shafi'i gave attention to the methods by which the Quran and the sunna were applied in law. He framed rules for analogical reasoning (qiyas) and used it to chart a middle course between conservative traditionalism and legal innovation. His al-Risala was among the earliest works devoted to legal theory and gave it a systematic form.

Al-Shafi'i died in al-Fustat on 20 January 820. One authority says he died of injuries from an attack by supporters of a Maliki named Fityan, but Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani doubts the story, and the cause is not known. He was buried in the vault of the Banu Abd al-Hakam in the City of the Dead near Mokattam, and the Ayyubid sultan al-Kamil built the dome in 1212. His mausoleum remains an important site, and in Egypt his school came to compete with the Maliki school for supremacy.
al-walid-i: Al-Walid was born in Medina in about 674, the eldest son of Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, a member of the Umayyad family's Hejaz line. His mother, Wallada bint al-Abbas ibn al-Jaz, descended from a 6th-century chief of the Banu Abs. In 684 the Umayyads of the Hejaz were expelled by the rival claimant Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr and moved to Syria, where his grandfather Marwan I was recognised as caliph. As a prince, al-Walid led summer campaigns against the Byzantines in 696, 697, 698 and 699, and about 700 or 701 he patronised a fortified outpost, Qasr Burqu', on the desert route towards Mecca. He became heir apparent about 705, after the death of Abd al-Malik's brother Abd al-Aziz ibn Marwan.

Al-Walid acceded on 9 October 705 and continued his father's policies of centralisation and expansion. Unlike Abd al-Malik, he depended heavily on the viceroy al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, who ran the eastern half of the caliphate and influenced appointments and dismissals. In the east al-Hajjaj's lieutenant Qutayba ibn Muslim campaigned in Transoxiana between 705 and 715, winning the surrender of Bukhara, Khwarazm, Samarkand and Farghana, mostly through tributary alliances that left local rulers in place; after Qutayba's death in 716 local princes and the Turgesh nomads rolled back most of the gains. From 708 or 709 Muhammad ibn al-Qasim conquered Sind. In the west Musa ibn Nusayr conquered the Maghreb and Hispania, and the caliphate reached its largest territorial extent.

War spoils paid for building projects, among them the Great Mosque of Damascus, the al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem, the Prophet's Mosque in Medina and the city of Anjar. He is described as the first caliph to set up programmes of social welfare, aiding poor and disabled Arabs in Syria. His reign was marked by domestic peace and prosperity, and he kept a balance between the Qays and Yaman army factions. The cost of the wars, and his grants to Umayyad princes, burdened his successors.

Al-Walid died of an illness at Dayr Murran, an Umayyad winter estate outside Damascus, on 23 February 715, about a year after al-Hajjaj. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz led the funeral prayers. He had tried to nominate his son Abd al-Aziz in place of his brother Sulayman, whom his father had designated; Sulayman acceded and dismissed nearly all his governors, and expansion largely halted. Gerald Hawting calls the reigns of al-Walid and Abd al-Malik in some ways the high point of Umayyad power, and the historian Kennedy calls al-Walid's reign perhaps the zenith, though his own part in its successes is unclear. His Syrian contemporaries held him in high esteem.
al-walid-ii: Al-Walid ibn Yazid was the son of the Umayyad caliph Yazid II, who ruled until January 724, and of Zaynab bint Muhammad al-Thaqafi. Yazid had intended him to succeed at once but was persuaded by his brother Maslama to name his half-brother Hisham instead, with al-Walid second in the line of succession, a place he had been given at the age of eleven.

Hisham at first regarded his nephew with affection but grew disillusioned with his dissolute lifestyle, reduced his allowances and punished some of his associates. Al-Walid withdrew from the court to a remote desert residence, perhaps the ruined site now known as Qasr Tuba in the Jordanian desert. After the pilgrimage of 735 Hisham tried to persuade him to step down in favour of Hisham's own son Maslama, or to swear allegiance to Maslama as his successor, and al-Walid refused. Hisham secretly gathered support for Maslama, but the death of the general Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik in the late 730s was a major setback to the plan.

Al-Walid succeeded on the death of Hisham on 6 February 743. As heir he had been known for open-handedness, and as caliph he took special care of the crippled and blind, increasing their stipend. On 21 May 743 he named his two sons, al-Hakam and Uthman, to succeed him in that order. He ordered the arrest of Hisham's sons at Rusafa, but forbade any harm to Maslama and his household in memory of their old companionship. Al-Tabari quotes a number of his poems, and he was fond of versifying and of horse races.

His reputed drinking, singing and immorality aroused opposition, and he imprisoned Sulayman ibn Hisham. When Khalid ibn Abdallah al-Qasri, approached by plotters, declined to join and cautioned the caliph, al-Walid's anger was aroused; he imprisoned Khalid and handed him to Yusuf ibn Umar for fifty million dirhams, and Yusuf tortured and killed him, which intensely angered many of al-Walid's relatives. Yazid ibn al-Walid spoke against al-Walid's favour to the Qaysi Arabs over Yemenis and non-Arab Muslims, and drew support from the Qadariyyah and Murji'ah. Marwan ibn Muhammad wrote from Armenia urging prudence, but was disregarded.

Yazid slipped into Damascus and deposed the caliph in a coup, then distributed money from the treasury. Al-Walid was besieged in a castle outside the city. He fought well but in April 744, at Al-Aghdaf, in what is now Jordan, he was defeated and killed by the forces of Sulayman ibn Hisham. His cousin Yazid III succeeded him and imprisoned his two sons. According to Yazid's own account, al-Walid rejected an offer to set up a tribal assembly to decide the future of the realm and attacked.
al-zahrawi: Abu al-Qasim Khalaf ibn al-Abbas al-Zahrawi was born around 936 at Azahara, eight kilometres north-west of Córdoba, in the year the city was founded. His name's attribute al-Ansari suggests descent from the Ansar of Medina. He lived most of his life in Córdoba, where he studied, taught and practised medicine and surgery until shortly before his death about 1013, two years after the sacking of Azahara.

Few details of his life survive, since the destruction of the city in later conflicts. Ibn Hazm (993-1064) first lists him among the great physicians of Moorish Spain, and the first detailed biography, in al-Humaydi's Jadhwat al-Muqtabis, was completed some sixty years after his death. He served as court physician to the caliph al-Hakam II.

Al-Zahrawi specialised in curing disease by cauterisation, and he devised instruments to inspect the urethra and to examine, insert or remove foreign bodies in the throat, the ear and other organs. He described treating a slave girl who had cut her own throat, suturing the wound so that she recovered with only some hoarseness, and concluded that an incision in the larynx is not dangerous. He is also recorded as describing the drainage of fluid in children with hydrocephalus.

He wrote that before practising surgery a physician must know anatomy and the function of the organs, and he recalled a man who cut into a swelling of the neck thought to be an abscess, when it was an aneurysm, and the patient died on the spot. He stressed treating patients regardless of social status and spoke affectionately of his students as his children.

His Kitab al-Tasrif, a thirty-volume encyclopedia of medicine completed in the year 1000, draws on a career of almost fifty years. The first volume treats general principles, the second pathology, and most of the rest pharmacology; one chapter covers cosmetics. The last volume, On Surgery and Instruments, is the first illustrated surgical guide. He put surgery last because he held it the highest form of medicine, to be practised only after the other branches are mastered. It describes more than 200 instruments, the use of catgut for internal stitching, lithotrity with an instrument he called michaab, and dental work such as ligating loose teeth with gold or silver wire.

Gerard of Cremona translated the surgical volume into Latin in the 12th century, and it became a standard text at universities such as Salerno and Montpellier and the main surgical source in Europe for about five hundred years. Guy de Chauliac quoted the work over 200 times in the 14th century, and Pietro Argallata called its author the chief of all surgeons. The street where he lived in Córdoba is named Calle Albucasis.
alabama: Alabama covers 135,760 square kilometres and is bordered by Tennessee to the north, Georgia to the east, Florida to the south and Mississippi to the west, with a short coastline on the Gulf of Mexico. About three-fifths of the land belongs to the Gulf Coastal Plain, which slopes gently towards the Mississippi River and the Gulf. The north is mostly mountainous, with the Tennessee River cutting a large valley. The land rises from sea level at Mobile Bay to Mount Cheaha at 735 metres, and two thirds of it is forest.

The state takes its name from the Alabama people, a Muskogean-speaking tribe who lived just below the meeting of the Coosa and Tallapoosa rivers. The name first appears in accounts of Hernando de Soto's expedition of 1540. Its meaning is disputed: some scholars derive it from Choctaw words meaning 'clearers of the thicket' or 'herb gatherers', while the popular 'Here We Rest' has no support from experts in Muskogean languages.

Indigenous peoples lived in the area for thousands of years. The agrarian Mississippian culture covered most of the state from about 1000 to 1600 CE, and one of its major polities was centred on Moundville, the second-largest complex of the classic Middle Mississippian era after Cahokia. Finds there were the basis for scholars' definition of the Southeastern Ceremonial Complex. At the time of European contact the peoples of the region included the Cherokee and the Muskogean-speaking Alabama, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek and Koasati.

The Spanish expedition of Hernando de Soto passed through Mabila and other parts of the state in 1540. The French founded the first European settlement, Old Mobile, in 1702 and moved it to the present site of Mobile in 1711, claiming the region as part of Louisiana until 1763. The British held it from 1763 until the American Revolutionary War, and Spain held Mobile as part of Spanish West Florida until 1813.

Alabama was recognized as a state in December 1819. In the antebellum period it was a major cotton producer and made wide use of enslaved African American labour. In 1861 it seceded to join the Confederate States of America, with Montgomery as the first capital, and it rejoined the Union in 1868. Decades of economic hardship followed. The establishment of NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center at Huntsville in 1960 helped build a local aerospace industry.

Montgomery is the capital, Huntsville the largest city, and Mobile the oldest. The 2020 census counted about 5 million people. Moundville Archaeological Site preserves the Mississippian past, and the National Park Service administers the Tuskegee Airmen National Historic Site, the Selma to Montgomery National Historic Trail and the Trail of Tears National Historic Trail within the state.
alan-garcia: Alan Gabriel Ludwig García Pérez was born on 23 May 1949 in the Barranco District of Lima into a middle-class family. He first met his father at the age of five, because the father was imprisoned at El Sexto Prison for membership of the Peruvian Aprista Party. His mother founded the party's base in the Camaná Province of the Arequipa Region. He went to party meetings with his father from a very young age, and at fourteen gave a speech in honour of the party's founder Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre. Mentored by Haya de la Torre, he served in the Constituent Assembly of 1978 to 1979, was elected to Congress in 1980 and became General Secretary of the APRA in 1982.

García won the presidential election of 14 April 1985 with 45 per cent of the votes. His opponent Alfonso Barrantes of the United Left withdrew from the runoff, and García took office on 28 July. It was the first time the APRA had come to power in its 60-year history, and at 36 he was the youngest president in Latin America. His economic policy rested on APRA's early anti-imperialist values and distanced Peru from international markets. Hyperinflation reached 7,649 per cent in 1990, and foreign debt rose to 19 billion dollars by 1989. The currency, the inti, was replaced in 1991 by the nuevo sol.

After Alberto Fujimori's self-coup of 5 April 1992, García, who had been suspended as senator for life and was accused of illicit enrichment, went into exile for nine years in Colombia and France. He returned on 27 January 2001 and lost the second round of that year's election to Alejandro Toledo. In 2006 he defeated Ollanta Humala in a run-off on 4 June with about 53 per cent of the vote, and he governed from 28 July 2006 to 2011. During this term Peru signed free trade agreements with the United States and China, and poverty fell from 48 to 28 per cent. He placed fifth in the 2016 election.

On 17 April 2019 García shot himself while police were presenting him with an arrest warrant in a corruption investigation linked to the Odebrecht company, and died later that day. President Martín Vizcarra declared three days of mourning. Opinion on his career is divided: he was known as an immensely charismatic orator, and is considered one of Peru's most controversial politicians.
alan-turing: Alan Mathison Turing was born in Maida Vale, London, on 23 June 1912, while his father, Julius Mathison Turing, was on leave from the Indian Civil Service. His mother was Ethel Sara Turing, née Stoney, of an Anglo-Irish family. At Sherborne School in Dorset, which he entered in 1926, he formed a close friendship with Christopher Morcom, who has been described as his first love; Morcom died of complications of bovine tuberculosis in February 1930, shortly before graduation.

Turing sat the King's College, Cambridge scholarship examination in mathematics in 1930 and graduated from King's. He earned a doctorate from Princeton University in 1938. On returning to Cambridge he attended the 1939 lectures of Ludwig Wittgenstein on the foundations of mathematics, where the two disagreed, Turing defending formalism and Wittgenstein holding that mathematics invents its truths rather than discovering absolute ones.

From September 1938 Turing worked part-time with the Government Code and Cypher School and, with Dilly Knox, studied the Enigma cipher machine of Nazi Germany. At Bletchley Park he specified an electromechanical machine, the bombe, which could break Enigma more effectively than the Polish bomba kryptologiczna from which its name derived; with an enhancement by Gordon Welchman it became a main tool against Enigma messages. He took on the German naval Enigma as head of Hut 8, solving the essential part of its indicator system in December 1939 and devising Banburismus, a sequential statistical technique. In July 1942 he devised Turingery against the Lorenz cipher.

After the war he joined the National Physical Laboratory, and on 19 February 1946 presented the first detailed design of a stored-program computer, the Automatic Computing Engine. In 1948 he joined Max Newman's Computing Machine Laboratory at the University of Manchester. In 1951 he turned to mathematical biology and published The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis in January 1952, proposing that chemicals reacting and diffusing together, a reaction-diffusion system, could account for the main phenomena of morphogenesis.

In 1952, after acknowledging a sexual relationship with another man, Turing was prosecuted for gross indecency. He received probation conditional on chemical castration and lost his security clearance. He died on 7 June 1954, aged 41, of cyanide poisoning, and the inquest ruled the death a suicide; his family and biographers have variously accepted, questioned or disputed that verdict.

His wartime work, covered by the Official Secrets Act, went unrecognised in his lifetime. Following a 2009 campaign, Prime Minister Gordon Brown apologised for the appalling way he was treated, and Queen Elizabeth II granted him a pardon in 2013. The Alan Turing law, part of a 2017 law, retroactively pardoned men cautioned or convicted under the criminalisation of homosexual acts.
alanya: Alanya lies on the southern coast of Turkey, in Antalya Province, 133 km east of the city of Antalya. It occupies a small peninsula on the Gulf of Antalya, in Pamphylia, between the Taurus Mountains to the north and the Mediterranean, along about 70 km of coastline. This natural strategic position made it a local stronghold for many Mediterranean-based empires, including the Ptolemaic, Seleucid, Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman empires.

Finds in the nearby Karain Cave indicate occupation as far back as the Paleolithic, and evidence shows a port at Syedra, south of the modern city, in the Bronze Age. The city appears in the 4th-century BCE periplus of Pseudo-Scylax, and the castle rock was probably inhabited under the Hittites and the Achaemenid Empire. After Alexander the Great's conquest it was first fortified in the Hellenistic period. Under Ptolemaic rule the port became a popular refuge for Mediterranean pirates. It resisted Antiochus III in 199 BCE but was loyal to the pirate Diodotus Tryphon, who seized the Seleucid crown from 142 to 138 BCE, and Antiochus VII Sidetes completed a new castle and port in 137 BCE.

Its names show its history. It was Korakesion in Greek, from a Luwian word for a protruding city, and Kalonoros under the Byzantine Empire. Its main political importance came in the Middle Ages under the Seljuk Sultanate of Rûm and Alaeddin Kayqubad I, from whom the city takes its name; it became Alaiye. His building campaign produced Alanya Castle, dating from 1226, the Kızıl Kule (Red Tower) and the Tersane (shipyard). In the 13th and 14th centuries Italian traders called the city Candelore or Cardelloro. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk finalised the form Alanya during a visit in 1935. It became a municipality in 1872. After the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923 many of its Christians were resettled in Nea Ionia in Greece.

Alanya is a district and resort city of Antalya Province, with a district population of 364,180 in 2022. Tourism has been the dominant industry since 1958. On the peninsula stands Alanya Castle, a Seljuk citadel built over earlier fortifications, with the Süleymaniye mosque and caravanserai built by the Ottoman ruler Suleiman inside it. Old walls surround much of the eastern peninsula, and within them stand historic villas, most built in the early 19th century. Akşebe Sultan, the castle's first commander under Kayqubad I, is buried in a mausoleum within the walls.
alaric-i: According to Jordanes, a 6th-century Roman writer of Gothic origin, Alaric was born on Peuce Island in the Danube Delta and belonged to the noble Balti dynasty of the Thervingian Goths, but this cannot be verified. The historian Douglas Boin says only that he came from the Thervingi or the Greuthung. Alaric was probably a child when the Goths, pressed by the Huns, crossed the Danube and fought a war with Rome.

He grew up along Rome's frontier among veterans of the Battle of Adrianople of 378, in which the Goths killed Emperor Valens. A treaty of 382 required the Goths to supply troops to the Roman army in exchange for peace and land. Alaric began his career under the Gothic soldier Gainas and later joined the Roman army.

In 391 Alaric led a mixed band of Goths and allies into Thrace and was stopped by the Roman general Stilicho. By 392 he was in Roman service, and in 394 he led a Gothic force that helped Emperor Theodosius defeat the usurper Eugenius and his general Arbogast at the Battle of Frigidus. About 10,000 of his men died there.

He expected promotion to magister militum and command of regular Roman units, was refused, and mutinied. Theodosius died on 17 January 395, and modern writers regard Alaric as king of the Visigoths from that year. Jordanes records that he persuaded his people to seek a kingdom by their own exertions rather than serve others in idleness.

With the Empire divided between Theodosius's sons Arcadius and Honorius, Alaric exploited the rivalry between East and West, though he needed Roman authority to be supplied by Roman cities. In 396 he marched through Thermopylae and sacked Athens, and archaeology shows widespread damage there. Stilicho drove him into Epirus. Alaric invaded Italy in late 401 or 402. Stilicho met him at Pollentia on Easter Sunday, where he took Alaric's wife and children prisoner, and again at Verona, and each time allowed him to withdraw. Between 404 and 405 Alaric stayed in a Pannonian province, where he could play East against West.

Alaric marched into Italy again and died there, and his Goths sacked Rome in 410. His brother-in-law Ataulf succeeded him and married Honorius's sister Galla Placidia. According to Michael Kulikowski, Alaric had given his people a sense of community that outlived him. The Goths stayed together inside the empire and settled in Aquitaine, which Honorius granted them in 418 or 419, where they created the first autonomous barbarian kingdom inside the Roman frontiers.
alaric-ii: Alaric II succeeded his father Euric as king of the Visigoths on 28 December 484. He was the great-grandson of Alaric I, who sacked Rome in 410. His dominions included most of Hispania, Gallia Aquitania and the greater part of Gallia Narbonensis. His reign is poorly documented: the historian Herwig Wolfram notes that it gets no full treatment in the sources and is overshadowed by his death at Vouillé, and Isidore of Seville gives it a single paragraph, mostly about that battle.

The earliest recorded event concerns Syagrius, former ruler of the Domain of Soissons, who had been defeated by Clovis I of the Franks and took refuge with Alaric. According to Gregory of Tours, Clovis intimidated Alaric into surrendering him, and Clovis later had him executed. In 490 Alaric sent an army to raise Odoacer's siege of Pavia, where his fellow Gothic king Theodoric the Great was trapped. About 495 Visigothic rule in Hispania proved not deeply established, and Alaric took part in repressing the uprising of Burdunellus, which ended at Caesaraugusta in 496. By 502 he and Clovis had met near Amboise and made a peace treaty.

Alaric was an Arian, like the early Visigothic nobles, but he eased his father's persecution of Catholics and permitted them to hold the council of Agde in 506. He exiled Caesarius, bishop of Arles, to Bordeaux for a year on suspicion of conspiring with the Burgundians. He also appointed a commission under the referendary Anianus to prepare an abstract of Roman laws and imperial decrees as the authoritative code for his Roman subjects, known as the Breviary of Alaric.

Clovis broke the peace of 502 and invaded Visigothic territory, despite the diplomatic intervention of Theodoric, Alaric's father-in-law. Forced by his magnates to fight, Alaric met him at the Battle of Vouillé near Poitiers in 507. The Goths were defeated and, according to Gregory of Tours, Clovis himself killed Alaric. Clovis took the royal treasury at Toulouse, though with Ostrogothic help much of the Gallic territory was later recovered.

The gravest result was disarray in the kingdom. Alaric left an illegitimate elder son, Gesalec, and a legitimate younger son, Amalaric, still a child. Gesalec proved incompetent, and in 511 Theodoric took the throne ostensibly on Amalaric's behalf. The Montagne d'Alaric near Carcassonne is named after him, and local tradition says he buried a vast treasure there.
alasehir: Alaşehir lies in the valley of the Kuzuçay, called Cogamus in antiquity, at the foot of the Bozdağ Mountain, ancient Mount Tmolus. The town stands on high ground commanding the fertile plain of the Gediz River, the ancient Hermus. In antiquity it lay in Lydia, on the road between Sardis and Laodicea, and it was well known for its vulnerability to earthquakes. The Turkish name, meaning multicoloured town, is first attested in the memoir of the 13th-century historian Ibn Bibi.

The city was founded by the Attalid kings of Pergamon in the 2nd century BCE and named Philadelphia, meaning the city of him who loves his brother, for Attalus II Philadelphus. When the last Attalid king, Attalus III, died in 133 BCE, he bequeathed his kingdom to Rome. In 17 CE the city suffered badly in an earthquake, and Emperor Tiberius relieved it of taxes. Philadelphia is generally agreed to be the sixth of the seven churches addressed in the Book of Revelation, whose letter describes a community with little power and gives it no rebuke. Ignatius of Antioch wrote an epistle to its Christians in the early 2nd century.

In the 6th century Philadelphia was called little Athens for its festivals and temples. The Seljuk Turks took the city in 1074 and 1093-1094, and the Byzantine emperor Alexios I recovered it in 1098. In the 14th century the patriarch of Constantinople made it the metropolis of Lydia, because it had not capitulated to the Ottomans. It prospered in the 13th and 14th centuries, with a Genoese trading colony and a trade in leather goods and red-dyed silk.

Surrounded by Ottoman emirates but nominally loyal to the Byzantine emperor, it was the last Byzantine Greek stronghold in Asia Minor until Bayezid I took it in 1390. Timur captured it twelve years later. After the Greco-Turkish War much of the town was destroyed by fire, and refugees from it settled in the Athens suburb of Nea Filadelfia after the population exchange of 1923.

Alaşehir is a municipality and district of Manisa Province in Turkey, connected to İzmir by a 105-kilometre railway. Its name is associated with Sultana raisins. Remains of ancient Philadelphia include a theatre, a stadium, a temple, a necropolis, stretches of Byzantine wall and the Basilica of St John, built about 600.
alaska: Alaska lies at the northwest corner of North America, very near to Asia. It borders Canada's Yukon and British Columbia to the east, with the Pacific Ocean to the south, the Bering Sea, Bering Strait and Chukchi Sea to the west and the Arctic Ocean to the north. About 500 miles of Canadian territory separate it from Washington. In the Bering Strait the Russian Big Diomede Island and the Alaskan Little Diomede Island are only 3 miles apart. Its coastline is longer than that of all the other U.S. states combined. The name derives from an Aleut idiom, alaxsxaq, meaning 'the mainland'.

Indigenous peoples occupied Alaska for thousands of years before European contact, and linguistic and DNA studies support the settlement of North America by way of the Bering land bridge. At the Upward Sun River site the remains of a six-week-old infant belonged to a population genetically separate from other Native groups, which the archaeologist Ben Potter named Ancient Beringian. The Tlingit and Haida lived in the southeast, and all three of these peoples and others of the Pacific Northwest Coast suffered smallpox outbreaks from the late 18th century, the worst in the 1830s and 1860s.

The Russian Empire began to colonise the area in the 18th century, establishing Russian America. The expense and difficulty of holding it led to its sale to the United States in 1867 for US$7.2 million. Alaska became a territory on 11 May 1912 and the 49th state on 3 January 1959.

Alaska is a state of the United States, with Juneau as its capital and Anchorage as its most populous city. Juneau is on the mainland but has no road connection to the rest of the North American highway system. More than half the state is federally owned, in national forests, national parks and wildlife refuges. The Alaska Native Heritage Center celebrates the state's 11 cultural groups.
alatri: Alatri is a town and comune of the province of Frosinone in the region of Lazio, Italy. Its Latin name was Aletrium. The area of the modern town was settled as early as the 2nd millennium BCE, and the ancient town was a city of the Hernici. A hill in the centre of the city was adopted as its citadel.

Aletrium was a town of the Hernici which, together with Veroli, Anagni and Ferentino, formed a defensive league against the Volsci and the Samnites around 550 BCE. In 530 BCE the Hernici allied with the Rome of Tarquinius Superbus, which confirms the Etruscan influence in the area that archaeology also shows. Its relations with Rome in the 4th century BCE are told differently by different sources. In the time of Cicero it was a municipium and remained one throughout the imperial period.

After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the city decayed, and the Christian bishop was the only respected authority. In 543, during the Gothic Wars, Totila's troops sacked and destroyed Alatri. In the 12th century it became an important stronghold of the popes when Rome was unsafe for them. The following century it became a free commune under the authority of the bishops and the pope, governed by consuls until 1241, when a podestà was introduced. In the 15th century it began to lose its freedom, and after the short rule of Filippo Maria Visconti in 1434 it had to accept papal suzerainty. Spanish soldiers occupied it in 1556, and it became part of Italy in 1870.

Alatri has about 30,000 inhabitants and is known for its megalithic acropolis. Well-preserved polygonal fortifications of local limestone, probably up to about 9 m high, survive around the city, and on the citadel hill huge terrace walls over 15 m high enclose an area of 220 by 100 m. The Cathedral of San Paolo is documented since 930, and the Collegiata of Santa Maria Maggiore was largely rebuilt in the 13th century.
alawites: The Alawites trace their faith to Muhammad ibn Nusayr, an Iraqi teacher of the ninth century who was a disciple of the Twelver imams Ali al-Hadi and Hasan al-Askari. After al-Askari died, a dispute over his succession arose in the Shia community, and Ibn Nusayr claimed to be the Bab (Door) and Ism (Name) of the dead imam and to have received his secret teachings. His teaching appears to be one of several early mystical ghulat movements.

The community was organised under Hamdanid rule in northern Syria (947–1008) by al-Khaṣībī, a follower of Ibn Nusayr who died in Aleppo about 969. His grandson and pupil Abu Sa'id Maymun al-Tabarani moved in 1032 to Latakia, then held by the Byzantine Empire, and died in 1034. The historian Stefan Winter calls him the last definitive scholar of Alawism, who founded its calendar and gave its teachings their final form.

Alawites have faced periods of subjugation or persecution under Muslim empires including the Abbasids, Mamluks and Ottomans. Until the 1920s the community usually called itself Nusayri, after Ibn Nusayr. Intellectuals within it then promoted the name Alawi, to stress a link with mainstream Islam and especially Shia Islam, and a name the French authorities also used.

The French Mandate of Syria, established in 1920, was a turning point. The French recruited many minority members into their armed forces and created areas reserved for minorities, among them the Alawite State. That state was later dismantled, but Alawites kept an important role in the Syrian army and later in the Ba'ath Party. After Hafez al-Assad took power in the 1970 coup, the state promoted a national ideology among Alawites to replace their traditional identity.

Alawite doctrine is secretive: some teachings are revealed only to a chosen few, and the community has practised taqiya, the concealment of belief, to avoid persecution. Its central belief is a divine Trinity of Ma'na (meaning), Ism (Name) and Bab (Door), which Alawites hold to have been incarnated seven times in human form. The seventh incarnation consists of Ali ibn Abi Talib, Muhammad and Salman al-Farisi. Alawites also believe in reincarnation, and the faith has been described as syncretic, drawing on Gnosticism, neo-Platonism and Christian practices such as a Mass with bread and wine.

Alawites have traditionally lived in the coastal mountains of western Syria, with Latakia and Tartus the main cities, and on the plains around Hama and Homs. They make up about 9 to 12 percent of Syria's population.
alba-iulia: Alba Iulia is the seat of Alba County in west-central Romania, on the river Mureș in the historical region of Transylvania. Its names reflect its layers of history. In Roman times the settlement was called Apulum, from the Dacian Apoulon mentioned by Ptolemy. From the 9th to the 11th centuries it bore the Slavic name Bălgrad, white castle. The Hungarian name Gyulafehérvár refers to Gyula II, a mid-10th-century Hungarian warlord baptised in Constantinople. The Saxons later called it Karlsburg, in honour of Charles VI.

Nearby stood the Dacian centre of Apulon. After Dacia became a Roman province the capital of Dacia Apulensis was established here, and Apulum, the largest urban centre in Roman Dacia, was the seat of the XIII Gemina Legion; its castrum, at 37.5 hectares, is the largest in Romania. According to the Gesta Hungarorum a regent named Jula or Geula, grandfather of Stephen I of Hungary, built his capital here in the 10th century and about 950 built the first church of Transylvania. After Stephen adopted Catholicism a Catholic bishopric was established, and the present cathedral dates from the 12th or 13th century. John Hunyadi used the citadel in 1442 to prepare against the Ottoman Turks and was entombed in the cathedral.

After the partition of the Kingdom of Hungary the city became in 1542 the capital of the autonomous Principality of Transylvania, until 1690. On 29 November 1599 Michael the Brave of Wallachia entered it and became Voivode of Transylvania, uniting Wallachia, Moldavia and Transylvania under his rule until he was murdered in 1601. Prince Gábor Bethlen founded an academy there. The city passed to the Habsburgs in 1690, and between 1716 and 1735 a seven-bastion baroque fortress, Alba Carolina, was built for Charles VI. On 1 December 1918 the National Assembly of Romanians of Transylvania and Hungary gathered there to proclaim the union of Transylvania with Romania, and in 1922 Ferdinand I was crowned king in the Orthodox cathedral.

The Upper Town, with the fortress, contains the Roman Catholic and Orthodox cathedrals, the Princely Palace, the Union Hall and the Batthyaneum Library, founded in 1780, which holds half of the 9th-century Codex Aureus of Lorsch. The Orthodox cathedral was built between 1921 and 1923. The city is historically important for Romanians, Hungarians and Transylvanian Saxons.
alban-berg: Alban Berg was born in Vienna on 9 February 1885, the third of four children of Johanna and Konrad Berg, whose father ran a successful export business. The family's finances declined after Konrad died in 1900. Berg cared more for literature than music as a child and several times considered becoming a writer. He began to compose at fifteen, teaching himself. In October 1904 he started to study counterpoint, theory and harmony with Arnold Schoenberg, and from 1907 composition, working with him for six years until 1911. He married the singer Helene Nahowski on 3 May 1911. The Piano Sonata, Op. 1, published in 1910, grew from his student sketches.

From Schoenberg Berg took the idea of developing variation, that every aspect of a work should grow from a single basic idea, and later the twelve-tone technique. His circle in Vienna included Alexander von Zemlinsky, Gustav Klimt, Karl Kraus and Adolf Loos. In 1913 two of his Altenberg songs, with a very large orchestra, were performed under Schoenberg at the Skandalkonzert, which caused a riot and had to be halted. Berg served in the Austro-Hungarian Army from 1915 to 1918 and worked on his first opera, Wozzeck, during leave in 1917. He completed it in 1922, and three excerpts performed in 1924 brought his first public success. The first performance was in Berlin on 14 December 1925.

Other works include the Chamber Concerto of 1923 to 1925 and the Lyric Suite of 1926, which was later shown to use elaborate cyphers to record a secret love affair. He began his second opera, Lulu, in 1928. In the 1930s the Nazis cancelled performances of his music in Germany and eventually proscribed it as degenerate, and Berlin rejected Lulu in the spring of 1934. He interrupted its orchestration to write a Violin Concerto, commissioned by Louis Krasner, in 1935.

Berg died in Vienna on Christmas Eve 1935, aged 50, of blood poisoning from a furuncle on his back, apparently caused by an insect sting in November, and was buried at Hietzing Cemetery. He had orchestrated only two of the three acts of Lulu, which were first performed in Zürich in 1937. His widow Helene banned any completion of the third act, and Friedrich Cerha's orchestration, made in secret, was first performed in Paris under Pierre Boulez in 1979. The Violin Concerto was dedicated to the memory of Manon Gropius, and it too was performed after his death. Berg is regarded as one of the most important composers of the 20th century and the most widely performed opera composer of the Second Viennese School.
albanians: Albanians speak Albanian, an Indo-European language and the only surviving representative of the Albanoid branch of the Paleo-Balkan group. Most scholars hold that they descend at least partly from the Illyrians, but which other Paleo-Balkan groups contributed to their ethnogenesis is still debated. The name Albanoi first appears in the 2nd century CE in Ptolemy, who describes an Illyrian tribe around present-day central Albania. The first certain reference to Albanians as an ethnic group is by the 11th-century chronicler Michael Attaleiates, who places them in the theme of Dyrrhachium.

The Komani-Kruja culture, attested from late antiquity to the Middle Ages in central and northern Albania, is significant for the study of the transition from the classical population to the medieval Albanians. Their own name for themselves, Shqiptarë, is the most common native ethnonym, while Arnaut and Arbanasi are among the names used by neighbours.

Christianity in Albania was under the Bishop of Rome until the 8th century, when its dioceses passed to the patriarchate of Constantinople. After the schism of 1054 the north became identified with Roman Catholicism and the south with Eastern Orthodoxy. In 1190 Albanians established the Principality of Arbanon, with its capital at Krujë. When the Ottoman Empire overpowered the Balkans in the 15th century, the League of Lezhë, a union of Albanian principalities led by Gjergj Kastrioti Skanderbeg, resisted successfully.

By the 17th and 18th centuries many Albanians had converted to Islam, which offered equal opportunities in the Ottoman Empire. More than 40 Grand Viziers were of Albanian origin. The Albanian wālī Muhammad Ali founded a dynasty that ruled Egypt and Sudan until the middle of the 20th century. Albanians declared independence in 1912 during the Balkan Wars, and the borders set after the Treaty of Bucharest left about half the ethnic Albanian population outside them. Albania was governed by a communist government under Enver Hoxha from after the Second World War until 1991.

Albanian society was traditionally organised in tribes, the fiset, each a kin community usually tracing descent through the male line to one forebear. Tribal life depended on the Kanun, a code of oral customary law, and had chiefs, councils and blood feuds. It remained largely intact in the north until the communists took power in 1944, and is regarded as the only European tribal system of this kind to survive to the mid-20th century.

Albanians are traditionally both Christians and Muslims: Catholics, Orthodox, Sunnis and Bektashis. Albanian communities also settled outside the Balkans, such as the Arbëreshë in southern Italy and the Arvanites in southern Greece. Around five million Albanians live across the Balkan Peninsula, and a large diaspora lives in Europe and beyond.
albany-new-york: Albany lies on the west bank of the Hudson River, about ten miles (16 km) south of the river's confluence with the Mohawk River, and about 135 miles (217 km) north of New York City. It sits toward the north end of the navigable Hudson. The city is the economic and cultural core of New York State's Capital District, a metropolitan area that includes Schenectady, Saratoga Springs and Troy.

The Hudson River area was first inhabited by Algonquian-speaking Mohicans, who called it Pempotowwuthut-Muhhcanneuw, meaning the fireplace of the Mohican nation. The Iroquoian-speaking Mohawk, based to the west along the Mohawk River, called it skahnéhtati, through the pine woods, after the path they took there.

When the English captured New Netherland in 1664 the name Beverwijck was changed to Albany, in honour of Prince James, Duke of Albany, later King James VII and II. Duke of Albany was a Scottish title, given since 1398 generally to a younger son of the King of Scots. The Dutch briefly regained the town in August 1673 and called it Willemstadt; the English took permanent possession in 1674 under the Treaty of Westminster. Governor Thomas Dongan chartered Albany as a municipality on 22 July 1686, as a strip of land one mile wide and sixteen miles long, with about 500 people.

Albany was a centre of transportation for much of its history. By 1815 it was the turnpike centre of the state, and with canals and railroads it became the hub for pioneers travelling to Buffalo and the Michigan Territory. It was the original eastern terminus of the Erie Canal and was home to some of the earliest railroads in the world. Democratic Party politics dominated the city from the 1920s, when Daniel O'Connell's machine overcame the Republican one built in the 1890s by William Barnes Jr. Erastus Corning 2nd was mayor from 1942 until his death in 1983.

Albany is the capital of New York and the seat of Albany County. Its population was 99,224 at the 2020 census. It is governed by a mayor and a Common Council under the Dongan Charter of 1686, revised by referendum in 1998, which gives it the oldest active city charter in the United States.

The Empire State Plaza, built between 1965 and 1978 under Governor Nelson A. Rockefeller and the architect Wallace Harrison, dominates the view of the city. Beside it stands the 19th-century New York State Capitol, which houses the State Legislature and the governor's office. The New York State Museum, the New York State Library and the New York State Archives are in the Cultural Education Center at the south end of the plaza. The First Church in Albany, established in 1642, is the second-oldest Reformed Church in America.
albarracin: Albarracín lies in a meander of the Guadalaviar River, in the province of Teruel in Aragon, with the Sierra de Albarracín rising to the south and west. It is the capital of the mountainous comarca of that name. The town is surrounded by stony hills, red sandstone boulders and cliffs, which draw rock climbers, particularly boulderers. It stands near the ancient Roman city of Lobetum. In the Visigothic period it was called Santa María de Oriente, and the Arabs called the area Alcartam, probably from the earlier name Ercávida. Its present name is thought to come from the Banu Razin, so that it means the place of the sons of Razin; its official name until the 19th century was Ciudad de Santa María de Albarracín.

The Hawwara Berber dynasty of the Banu Razin made Albarracín its capital from the early 11th century until the Almoravids took it in 1104. From the later 12th century until 1300 it was an independent lordship, the Sinyoría d'Albarrazín, established after the partition of the Taifa of Albarracín under Pedro Ruiz de Azagra. Peter III of Aragon conquered it in 1284 and deposed the ruling House of Azagra. The last man to hold the title of Señor de Albarracín was Juan Núñez I de Lara; his son Juan Núñez II de Lara remained pretender until 1300, when the city and its lands were formally incorporated into the Kingdom of Aragon.

A Jewish community lived in the town from before the 12th century, according to the earliest written records. It suffered antisemitic incidents until the expulsion of the Jews in 1492. In the Spanish Civil War control of the town shifted several times between Republican and Nationalist forces. A Republican offensive in July 1937 took it on 8 July, except the town hall and cathedral, where soldiers and civilians were besieged; Nationalist reinforcements retook it on 13 July.

Albarracín has been a National Monument since 1961 and received the Gold Medal for Merit in the Fine Arts in 1996. It has been proposed to UNESCO for World Heritage status, and it has belonged to the association of the Most Beautiful Villages of Spain since its founding. The 2007 census recorded 1,075 inhabitants.
albert-camus: Albert Camus was born on 7 November 1913 in Mondovi, now Dréan, in French Algeria, into a working-class family. His mother, Catherine Hélène Camus, was of Balearic Spanish ancestry, deaf and illiterate. He never knew his father, Lucien Camus, a poor agricultural worker killed in action with a Zouave regiment in October 1914. Camus grew up in the Belcourt district of Algiers, without many material possessions.
