As a second-generation French inhabitant of Algeria he was a pied-noir, a French citizen with more rights than Arab and Berber Algerians under the indigénat.

His teacher Louis Germain gave him free lessons to prepare for a scholarship competition, and in 1924 Camus won a place at a lyceum near Algiers, although his grandmother had planned for him to become a manual worker. He later studied philosophy at the University of Algiers, and dedicated his Nobel Prize speech to Germain.

Camus was in Paris when the Germans invaded France in 1940. He tried to flee but finally joined the French Resistance, writing for and editing the outlawed newspaper Combat. He was a lifelong opponent of capital punishment. On the left he opposed Joseph Stalin and the Soviet Union as totalitarian, which brought him into conflict with others there, above all with Jean-Paul Sartre. During the Algerian War (1954–1962) he kept a neutral stance, advocating a multicultural and pluralistic Algeria, a position most parties rejected. In 1957 he received the Nobel Prize in Literature at the age of 44, the second-youngest recipient in history and the first laureate in literature born in Africa.

Camus wrote novels, plays, essays and short stories. His best-known works include The Stranger (1942), The Plague (1947), The Fall (1956), the essays The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) and The Rebel (1951), and the play Caligula, written in 1938 and performed in 1945. His thought is associated with absurdism: life is void of meaning, or man cannot know its meaning if it exists, and man should embrace this. In The Myth of Sisyphus he wrote that there is only one really serious philosophical question, and that is suicide.

Some count him an existentialist, but he rejected the term repeatedly. He said his philosophical origins lay in ancient Greek philosophy, Nietzsche and the 17th-century moralists, and his critique was aimed chiefly at the existentialism of Sartre. He is remembered for his sceptical humanism and his support for political tolerance, dialogue and civil rights. He died on 4 January 1960.
albert-einstein: Einstein was born in Ulm on 14 March 1879, a subject of the Kingdom of Württemberg in the German Empire. His parents, Hermann Einstein and Pauline Koch, were secular Ashkenazi Jews. The family moved to Munich in 1880, where his father and uncle Jakob founded a company making electrical equipment. His parents worried that he had a learning disability because he was slow to talk, and a compass his father gave him when he was five began a lifelong fascination with electromagnetism. He found the rote learning of the Luitpold Gymnasium harmful to creativity and left it to join his family in Italy.

He renounced his German citizenship on 28 January 1896, avoiding conscription, and enrolled that year at the Swiss federal polytechnic school in Zurich, graduating in 1900. He gained Swiss citizenship a year later and secured a permanent position at the Swiss Patent Office in Bern.

His first paper, on capillary attraction, appeared in 1901. In 1905, sometimes called his annus mirabilis, he published papers on the photoelectric effect, on Brownian motion, which showed that the movement could be taken as firm evidence that molecules exist, and on special relativity, and demonstrated that mass and energy are equivalent. The paper on the electrodynamics of moving bodies was received on 30 June 1905 and reconciled Maxwell's equations with Newtonian mechanics.

In 1915 he proposed a general theory of relativity that extended his mechanics to gravitation, and a paper of the following year introduced the cosmological constant and is regarded as the first step in modern theoretical cosmology. In 1917 he introduced spontaneous and stimulated emission, the latter the core mechanism behind the laser. In his last years he objected to the randomness of quantum theory and tried unsuccessfully to devise a unified field theory, which left him increasingly isolated from mainstream physics.

In 1914 Einstein moved to Berlin, and in 1917 he became director of the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics. He was visiting the United States in 1933 when Adolf Hitler came to power; horrified by the Nazi persecution of Jews, he stayed, and became an American citizen in 1940. He died on 18 April 1955.

The Nobel committee found that no nomination in 1921 met Alfred Nobel's criteria, so the prize in physics was carried forward and awarded to Einstein for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect. The element einsteinium was named after him in 1955, and Time named him Person of the Century in 1999.
albert-i-of-belgium: Albert was born in Brussels on 8 April 1875, the fifth child and second son of Prince Philippe, Count of Flanders, and Princess Marie of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen. He grew up in the Palace of the Count of Flanders, at first third in line to the throne. When his older brother Baudouin, who had been prepared for the crown, died young, he unexpectedly became second in line at the age of 16. Retiring and studious, he prepared strenuously for kingship, and in his youth he travelled incognito round working-class districts to observe living conditions.

On 2 October 1900 he married Elisabeth of Bavaria in Munich. They had three children: Leopold, later Leopold III, Charles, and Marie-José, last Queen of Italy. The couple cultivated friendships with scientists, artists and musicians and made their court at Laeken a kind of cultural salon.

Albert succeeded his uncle Leopold II on 23 December 1909 and took the accession oath in Dutch as well as French, an innovation. He and Elisabeth were popular for a simple lifestyle that contrasted with Leopold II's aloof, autocratic manner. Shortly before accession he had toured the Belgian Congo, annexed in 1908, found it in poor condition and recommended reforms to protect the native population.

During the First World War most of Belgium was under harsh German occupation. Albert worked through secret diplomatic channels for a negotiated peace without victors or vanquished, but neither Germany nor the Entente favoured it. At the end of the war he commanded Army Group Flanders of Belgian, British and French divisions in the final offensive that liberated Belgium. At the Paris Peace Conference in April 1919 he sought reparations and security, and advised against a harsh treaty with Germany, but his advice played a small role. In 1918 he formed a Government of National Union of Catholics, Liberals and Socialists and helped bring about universal male suffrage. In 1920 he changed the family name from Saxe-Coburg-Gotha to House of Belgium.

A passionate alpinist, Albert died on 17 February 1934 climbing alone on the Roche du Vieux Bon Dieu at Marche-les-Dames, near Namur. Official investigations gave two possible explanations: a boulder he leaned on came loose, or the pinnacle holding his rope broke, so that he fell about 18 metres. Rumours of murder were dismissed by most historians, and DNA testing of bloodstained leaves in 2016 concluded he had died at that spot. He was buried in the Royal Crypt at the Church of Our Lady of Laeken and succeeded by Leopold III. In 1925, influenced by Carl E. Akeley, he founded Africa's first national park, now Virunga National Park. Belgians call him the Knight King or Soldier King.
albert-ii-of-germany: Albert was born in Vienna on 10 August 1397, the son of Duke Albert IV of Austria and Joanna Sophia of Bavaria. He succeeded to the duchy at the age of seven on his father's death in 1404. His uncle Duke William of Inner Austria, of the rival Leopoldinian line, acted as regent, followed in 1406 by William's brothers Leopold IV and Ernest the Iron. Their quarrels and attempts to control the Albertinian territories produced near civil-war conditions. Albert, who had received a good education, took up the government of Austria proper in 1411, after Leopold's death, and with the help of his advisers cleared the duchy of the evils that had arisen during his minority.

In 1422 he married Elisabeth of Luxemburg, daughter and heiress of King Sigismund of Hungary, who later became Holy Roman Emperor and king of Bohemia. The marriage brought Albert claims to many realms of Central and Eastern Europe. He assisted Sigismund against the Hussites, which drew the Austrian duchy into the Hussite Wars; Sigismund designated him his successor and made him Margrave of Moravia in 1423. The Austrian lands were devastated several times, and Albert took part in the Battle of Domažlice in 1431, where the imperial troops were defeated.

When Sigismund died in 1437, Albert was crowned king of Hungary on 1 January 1438 and moved his court there. He was crowned king of Bohemia six months later but could not take possession of the country, and he was fighting the Bohemians and their Polish allies when he was elected King of the Romans at Frankfurt on 17 March 1438. He was never crowned emperor. His wars against heretics went with persecution of Jews in Austria. Taxes were laid on Jewish communities to fund his campaigns, and after Hussite raids Austrian Jews were accused of collaboration and arms trading. A charge of host desecration at Enns in 1420 gave him a pretext to destroy the community.

According to the chronicler Thomas Ebendorfer, on 23 May 1420 Albert ordered the Jews imprisoned and forcibly converted; those who would not convert were sent off in boats down the Danube, and wealthy Jews were held, some tortured and stripped of property. Pope Martin V intervened to stop the forced baptism of children. On 12 March 1421 Albert sentenced the remaining Jews to death, and ninety-two men and 120 women were burned at the stake outside Vienna's walls. He died at Neszmély on 27 October 1439 while defending Hungary against the Turks, and was buried at Székesfehérvár. His children included Ladislas V Posthumus, who was born after his death.
albert-luthuli: Albert John Luthuli was born in about 1898 at the Solusi Mission Station, a Seventh-day Adventist mission near Bulawayo in Rhodesia, to John and Mtonya Luthuli. His father died when he was about six months old, and his mother, who had spent her childhood in the royal household of King Cetshwayo, raised him. In 1908 he moved to Groutville in Natal, where his family had lived, to attend school under the care of his uncle. After finishing his studies at Adams College in 1922 he stayed there as a teacher, one of its first African staff. His grandfather Ntaba had been elected chief in 1860 by the Christian community of the Umvoti Mission Station, and several relatives followed him in the office.

Luthuli became secretary of the Natal Native Teachers' Association in 1928 and its president in 1933. In the same year he was asked to succeed his uncle Martin as chief of the Umvoti River Reserve. He took two years to decide, since the post paid less than one-fifth of his teacher's salary. He was elected at the end of 1935 and held the chieftainship from January 1936. He joined the African National Congress in 1944. In 1946 he entered the Natives Representative Council, which adjourned that August in protest at the use of force against a mineworkers' strike.

He became president of the Natal branch of the ANC in 1951. In 1952 the government removed him as chief because he would not choose between the chieftainship and the ANC, and in December of that year he was elected President-General, with Nelson Mandela as his deputy. He received four banning orders, the first on 30 May 1953. After the Sharpeville massacre, in which sixty-nine Africans were killed, Mandela and others argued for armed resistance. Luthuli at first opposed violence and later gradually accepted it for the movement, while remaining committed to nonviolence himself.

Luthuli received the 1960 Nobel Peace Prize in 1961. Under his fourth ban, issued by the Minister of Justice John Vorster and effective from 31 May 1964, he was kept from travelling even to Stanger. United States Senator Robert F. Kennedy flew by helicopter to Groutville in 1966 to visit him. On 21 July 1967 Luthuli walked from his house toward his store and field near Gledhow station and died on the way back. The official account at the time was that a goods train struck him, but another account holds that he was murdered. The Luthuli Museum opened on 21 August 2004, and the ANC's headquarters in Johannesburg, Luthuli House, bears his name.
albert-schweitzer: Ludwig Philipp Albert Schweitzer was born on 14 January 1875 in Kaysersberg, in Alsace, which had less than four years earlier become part of the German Empire. He later became a French citizen after the First World War. He grew up in Gunsbach, where his father was the Lutheran pastor and taught him to play music. The medieval parish church there was shared by two congregations, who prayed in different areas at different times on Sundays. Growing up in this setting, Schweitzer developed the belief that true Christianity should always work towards a unity of faith and purpose.

Schweitzer rapidly gained prominence as a musical scholar and organist. His study J. S. Bach: Le Musicien-Poète appeared in 1905, and he rewrote it in German in two volumes in 1908. He became a deacon at the church of Saint Nicholas in Strasbourg in 1899 and was ordained in 1900. In 1905, aged thirty, he answered a call from the Society of the Evangelist Missions of Paris, which sought a physician, though its committee considered his Lutheran theology incorrect. Despite protests from friends and family he resigned his post and began a three-year course in medicine. He planned to spread the Gospel by the example of healing rather than preaching, and founded the hospital at Lambaréné in French Equatorial Africa, now Gabon.

His Geschichte der Leben-Jesu-Forschung of 1906, published in English in 1910 as The Quest of the Historical Jesus, established his reputation. It criticised the liberal view of Jesus and maintained that his life must be read in the light of his own convictions, which reflected late Jewish eschatology. The keynote of his philosophy, which he considered his chief contribution to mankind, was Reverence for Life. He thought Western civilisation was decaying because it had abandoned affirmation of life as its ethical foundation. He was one of colonialism's harshest critics, yet was sometimes accused of paternalism, and he received the 1952 Nobel Peace Prize.
albert-speer: Albert Speer was born in Mannheim on 19 March 1905 into an upper-middle-class family, the second of three sons. He followed his father and grandfather into architecture, beginning at the University of Karlsruhe because the hyperinflation of 1923 limited his parents' income, then moving to Munich in 1924 and to the Technische Hochschule Berlin-Charlottenburg in 1925. There he studied under Heinrich Tessenow, whom he greatly admired, and after passing his exams in 1927 he became Tessenow's assistant at 22. He married Margarete Weber on 28 August 1928, and they had six children.

Speer applied for Nazi Party membership in January 1931. In 1932 Karl Hanke recommended him to Joseph Goebbels, and he renovated the Party's Berlin headquarters. The organisers of the 1933 Nuremberg Rally asked him for designs, which brought him into contact with Hitler for the first time and won him a national post for the presentation of Party rallies. Hitler had him manage the building site for Paul Troost's renovation of the chancellery, and Speer joined his inner circle. In 1937 he was appointed General Building Inspector for Berlin, and in that capacity was responsible for the Central Department for Resettlement, which evicted Jewish tenants from their homes.

On 8 February 1942 Fritz Todt, Reich Minister of Armaments and Munitions, died in a plane crash at Rastenburg, and Hitler appointed Speer in his place. Speer cancelled a seat on the plane the night before. He took over Todt's other posts and, by April 1942, had persuaded Hermann Göring to create a Central Planning Board that gave him authority over raw materials and production. Using misleading statistics, he promoted an armaments miracle that was widely credited with keeping Germany in the war. In 1944 a task force he set up to increase fighter production became instrumental in exploiting slave labour.

At the Nuremberg trial Speer was found guilty of war crimes and crimes against humanity, principally for the use of slave and forced labour, and was acquitted on the other two counts. On 1 October 1946 he was sentenced to 20 years. Three of eight judges favoured death, and the sentence was a compromise. He served the term in Spandau Prison and was released in 1966. He died of a stroke on 1 September 1981.

His memoirs, Inside the Third Reich and Spandau: The Secret Diaries, presented him as an apolitical technocrat who regretted not having discovered the regime's crimes. Historians call this image the Speer myth. It began to fall apart in the 1980s, and Adam Tooze later called the idea of an apolitical technocrat absurd. Martin Kitchen argues that much of the rise in arms production owed to systems set up by Todt and that Speer knew of the Final Solution.
alberta: Alberta is bordered by British Columbia to the west, Saskatchewan to the east, the Northwest Territories to the north and the U.S. state of Montana to the south. Its southern border is the 49th parallel north and its northern border the 60th parallel, and its western boundary follows the Continental Divide in the Rocky Mountains. The eastern part of the province lies on the Great Plains, and the Rocky Mountains cast a rain shadow over much of it.

The province was named after Princess Louise Caroline Alberta (1848–1939), the fourth daughter of Queen Victoria and wife of John Campbell, Marquess of Lorne, Governor General of Canada (1878–83). Alberta has a rich diversity of Late Cretaceous dinosaur fossils, with at least 38 dinosaur type specimens collected there.

Paleo-Indians arrived in what is now Alberta at least 10,000 years ago, toward the end of the last ice age. Over time they differentiated into various First Nations. The Plains peoples of the south, such as those of the Blackfoot Confederacy and the Plains Cree, generally lived by hunting buffalo, while northerly peoples such as the Woodland Cree and Chipewyan hunted and trapped other animals and fished. The territory was also used by fur traders of the rival Hudson's Bay Company and North West Company.

The Dominion of Canada bought the lands that would become Alberta in 1870. From the late 1800s to the early 1900s many immigrants arrived, in an effort to prevent the prairies from being annexed by the United States, and growing wheat and cattle ranching became very profitable. The Alberta Act of 1905 created the province.

Until the 1930s politics was shared between the Liberals and the agrarian United Farmers of Alberta, and the Social Credit Party then held office continually from 1935 to 1971. Massive oil reserves were discovered in 1947, and the exploitation of the oil sands began in 1967. In 1950 Alberta became the second province, after Saskatchewan, to adopt a publicly funded health programme, a precursor of the modern medicare system.

Alberta is a province of Canada with Edmonton as its capital and Calgary as its largest city, and English is its official language. It is governed as a parliamentary democracy with a unicameral Legislative Assembly. Six UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie within it: the Canadian Rocky Mountain Parks, Dinosaur Provincial Park, Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump, Waterton-Glacier International Peace Park, Wood Buffalo National Park and Writing-on-Stone Provincial Park.
albertus-magnus: Albertus Magnus was probably born before 1200, since well-attested evidence shows he was over 80 when he died in 1280. Two later sources give his age as about 87, which led to 1193 being commonly given as his birth year, but that information cannot be confirmed. He was probably born in Lauingen, in what is now Bavaria, since he called himself Albert of Lauingen. He was probably educated chiefly at the University of Padua, where he was taught Aristotle's writings. In 1223 (or 1229) he joined the Dominican Order and studied theology at Bologna and elsewhere.

Albert taught for several years as lecturer at the Dominican house in Cologne, and also in Regensburg, Freiburg, Strasbourg and Hildesheim. In 1245 he became master of theology under Guerric of Saint-Quentin, the first German Dominican to do so, and taught at the University of Paris, where Thomas Aquinas began to study under him. He was the first to comment on virtually all of Aristotle's writings, which led him to the teachings of Avicenna and Averroes. In 1254 he became provincial of the Dominican Order. At the General Chapter at Valenciennes in 1259 he helped set up a program of studies that made philosophy part of Dominican training.

In 1260 Pope Alexander IV made him bishop of Regensburg, an office he resigned within a few years. Pope Urban IV then relieved him of his duties as bishop and asked him to preach the Eighth Crusade in German-speaking countries. He then became known as a mediator, and in 1258 his verdict, the Große Schied, ended a conflict between the citizens of Cologne and the archbishop.

Albert's writings, collected in 1899, filled thirty-eight volumes, on topics from logic and theology to botany, astronomy, mineralogy and zoology. He believed that Aristotle's approach to natural philosophy posed no obstacle to a Christian view of the natural order. His books on botany, zoology and minerals drew on ancient sources and on his own empirical investigations. In embryology it has been claimed that little of value was written after Aristotle until Albert, who identified organs within eggs. Many alchemical works were later falsely attributed to him, and there is scant evidence that he performed alchemical experiments himself.

Albert died on 15 November 1280 in the Dominican convent in Cologne. His relics are in a Roman sarcophagus in the crypt of St. Andrew's Church there. He was beatified in 1622, canonized and proclaimed a Doctor of the Church on 16 December 1931 by Pope Pius XI, and named patron saint of natural scientists in 1941. His feast day is 15 November.
albi: The first settlement at Albi dates to the Bronze Age. After the Roman conquest of Gaul in 51 BCE the town became the Civitas Albigensium, the territory of the Albigeois. Excavations have found no traces of Roman buildings, which suggests a modest settlement. In 584 Gregory of Tours reported that most of the townsfolk died of plague. In 1040 the town expanded and built the Pont Vieux, or Old Bridge, and its new quarters show considerable urban growth. It grew rich from trade and from the tolls charged to travellers on the bridge.

Early in the 13th century the Pope and the French king joined forces against the Cathars, who held their own version of ascetic Christian dualism, which the Catholic Church considered a dangerous heresy. Repression was severe, many Cathars were burnt at the stake, and the area, until then virtually independent, was afterwards annexed by the French Crown. Late in the 13th century the bishop Bernard de Castanet completed the Palais de la Berbie, a fortress-like episcopal palace, and ordered the building of Sainte-Cécile cathedral from 1282. Trade in woad then made the town prosperous, and the fine Renaissance houses show the fortunes of its woad merchants. A small medieval Jewish community was annihilated in the 1320s during the Shepherds' Crusade.

Albi is the prefecture of the Tarn department, on the river Tarn 85 km northeast of Toulouse, and the seat of an archbishop. Along with Toulouse and Montauban it is one of the main cities built in Languedoc red brick. Its episcopal city was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2010.

Sainte-Cécile is a masterpiece of Southern Gothic, built between the 13th and 15th centuries, with an austere defensive exterior and a rich interior. Its rood screen is carved in the Flamboyant Gothic style and carries over 200 polychrome statues. The Pont Vieux, 151 metres long on eight arches, is still in use after almost a millennium. The Toulouse-Lautrec Museum in the Palais de la Berbie holds more than 1,000 works by the painter Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, who was born in Albi in 1864.
albigensian-crusade: The Cathars held a dualist theology, in which the physical world was evil and created by a demiurge, Rex Mundi, while God was pure spirit. They rejected the Catholic priesthood, the real presence in the Eucharist and Purgatory, and replaced baptism with the consolamentum, given by the laying on of hands. Between 1022 and 1163 eight local church councils condemned them, and the Third Lateran Council repeated the condemnation in 1179. Many adherents lived around Albi, which gave the Albigensians their name.

They were most successful in the Languedoc, where political control was divided among many local lords. Its people spoke Occitan, not French, and did not consider themselves French. The County of Toulouse was a fief of the Angevin Empire, and the Crown of Aragon was in places more influential than the French king. After the murder of his legate Pierre de Castelnau in 1208, which he suspected Raymond VI, Count of Toulouse, of ordering, Pope Innocent III declared a crusade and offered the lands of the heretics to any French nobleman who would take up arms.

By mid-1209 some 20,000 to 30,000 Crusaders gathered, many staying only 40 days. The papal legate Arnaud Amalric, Abbot of Cîteaux, took command. On 18 June 1209 Raymond VI declared himself repentant, was scourged by the new legate Milo and took the Cross, so that his lands could not be attacked. The Crusaders turned instead to the lands of his nephew Raymond Roger Trencavel, viscount of Béziers and Carcassonne, who was not himself a Cathar but tolerated them. His request for peace was refused, and the Crusaders marched first on Béziers.

From 1209 to 1215 the Crusaders captured Cathar lands and crushed the movement. From 1215 to 1225 a series of revolts returned much of the land to the counts of Toulouse, but a renewed crusade retook it and by 1244 had driven Catharism underground. On 16 March 1244, after a siege of Montségur, over 200 Cathar perfects were burned there.

The crusade realigned the County of Toulouse with the French crown and diminished the distinct culture of Languedoc. The Inquisition was established under Pope Gregory IX in 1234 and, with the Dominicans preaching against heresy, had crushed Catharism as a popular movement by the 14th century; most penances were light and the majority of the accused escaped death. Historians differ on its character: Raphael Lemkin called it one of the most conclusive cases of genocide in religious history, while Robert E. Lerner argued that it was proclaimed against unbelievers, not a people. The troubadour tradition declined as the Occitan courts that supported it were destroyed.
alborz: The Alborz stretches from the border of Azerbaijan along the western and entire southern coast of the Caspian Sea, then runs north-east and merges into the smaller Aladagh Mountains, bordering the parallel ridge of the Kopet Dag in the northern parts of Khorasan. It is divided into the Western, Central and Eastern Alborz. The Western range, usually called the Talysh, runs south-south-eastward almost along the Caspian's western coast, while the Central Alborz, the range in the strictest sense, runs west to east along the whole southern shore.

The range forms a barrier between the south Caspian and the Iranian plateau and is only 60 to 130 km wide. Its rocks are mostly sedimentary, chiefly Jurassic limestone over a granite core. The mountains were folded mainly during the Miocene, as the Arabian plate collided with the Iranian plate and the Eurasian plate pressed from the other side. Mount Damavand, in the Central Alborz, is the highest mountain in Iran at 5,610 m.

The name comes from Harā Barazaitī, a mountain named in the Avesta, the main text of Zoroastrianism; the Proto-Iranian form means Mountain Rampart. In Middle Persian it became Harborz. Many high peaks were given the name, including Mount Elbrus in the Caucasus, and the Persian poet Ferdowsi in the Shahnameh speaks of the mountains as though they lay in India. Zoroastrians seem to identify the range with the dwelling place of the Peshyotan, and the Ilm-e-Kshnoom sect identifies Damavand as the home of the Saheb-e-Dilan, the Masters of the Heart.

Archaeological evidence shows people in the region since at least the late Lower Paleolithic. Darband Cave in Gilan Province has evidence from that period, though its many bear bones and few stone artefacts suggest mainly a bear den. Neanderthals were probably present in the Middle Paleolithic, since their fossils were found at Azykh Cave in the north-west, and stone tools come from Buzeir Cave and Kiaram Cave. A riverside site at Garm Roud in Mazandaran Province dates to about 30,000 years ago and gives evidence for modern humans.

The southern slopes are usually semi-arid or arid, while the northern slopes are humid and covered by the lush Caspian Hyrcanian mixed forests, in zones of Hyrcanian forest, beech and oak. Animals include the Persian leopard, the Syrian brown bear and the bezoar ibex; the Caspian tiger, now extinct, also lived there. Because of its snowy winters the range has several ski resorts, among them Dizin, and its attractions include Alam Kuh, Tochal and Ovan lake.
albrecht-durer: Dürer was born on 21 May 1471, the third child and second son of Albrecht Dürer the Elder, a successful goldsmith who had moved to Nuremberg from Ajtós in Hungary by 1455, and Barbara Holper. Of the couple's eighteen children only three survived. After his apprenticeship Dürer took the customary Wanderjahre, about four years away from 1490. He may have hoped to work under the engraver Martin Schongauer, who died shortly before Dürer reached Colmar in 1492, and he stayed with Schongauer's brothers there and in Basel. In 1493 he went to Strasbourg, where he painted his first self-portrait, probably to send to his fiancée in Nuremberg.

Within three months of his marriage Dürer left alone for Italy, perhaps because of plague in Nuremberg, and studied in Venice, where he admired Giovanni Bellini and copied Andrea Mantegna. On his return in 1495 he opened his own workshop. His early woodcuts were larger, more finely cut and more complex in composition than most German woodcuts before them. It is now thought unlikely that he cut the blocks himself, a task for specialist craftsmen. On a second Italian journey, from 1505 to 1507, he returned to painting and made the altarpiece known as the Feast of the Rosary for the German community in Venice.

Back in Nuremberg from mid-1507 he painted Adam and Eve (1507) and the Assumption of the Virgin (1509) and completed the Great Passion and the Life of the Virgin woodcut series, both published in 1511. In July 1520, after the death of Emperor Maximilian I, he travelled to the Netherlands to renew the imperial pension and to win the favour of Charles V. His diary records to whom he gave, exchanged or sold prints, and shows that the trip was not profitable.

In his last years Dürer produced comparatively little as an artist, partly through declining health and partly because he was preparing treatises. His Four Books on Measurement dealt with geometry, from lines and regular polygons to architecture, typography and polyhedra. The Four Books on Human Proportion, of 1528, expressed the body's parts as fractions of its height, based in part on observation of two to three hundred living persons in his own words. In 1527 he published a book on the fortification of cities. He wrote in German, using craftsmen's language, rather than in Latin. His prints were the medium through which most contemporaries knew his art, and they influenced Raphael, Titian and Parmigianino to promote their own work through printmakers.
albrecht-von-wallenstein: Albrecht von Wallenstein was born on 24 September 1583 at Heřmanice in Bohemia, into a poor Protestant branch of the old Czech House of Waldstein. His parents were Lutheran and Utraquist Hussite, and after their deaths he lived for two years with his uncle Heinrich Slavata, a member of the Unity of the Brethren, whose faith he adopted. He studied at the Protestant Latin school at Goldberg and then at the University of Altdorf, where brawls and sword fights landed him in the town prison. He later studied at Bologna and Padua and became fluent in German, Czech, Latin and Italian.

He served in the Long Turkish War from 1604 to 1606, converted to Catholicism in 1606, and in 1609 married a wealthy widow whose estates came to him when she died in 1614. Three years later he began a career as a mercenary by raising forces for the Emperor in the Uskok War against Venice.

In the Bohemian Revolt of 1618 he took the Catholic side, marching his regiment to Vienna with the Moravian treasury. After the Battle of White Mountain on 8 November 1620 he secured confiscated Protestant lands and formed them into the Duchy of Friedland in northern Bohemia. He became an imperial count palatine in 1622, a prince in 1623 and Duke of Friedland in 1625. That year he raised an army of 50,000 men, and a year later he defeated the Protestants at Dessau Bridge.

He became imperial generalissimo and, from April 1628, Admiral of the Baltic Sea. In 1630 Emperor Ferdinand II, wary of his ambition, released him from service. Protestant victories led Ferdinand to recall him, and he defeated the Swedish king Gustavus Adolphus at Alte Veste; Gustavus was later killed at Lützen. He relied on astrologers, among them Johannes Kepler, who drew a horoscope for him, and he suffered from painful joint illness from 1620.

In the summer of 1633 Wallenstein arranged armistices to negotiate peace, believing the war could last decades. Plotters accused him of treachery, and a secret court found him guilty. On 24 January 1634 the Emperor signed a secret patent removing him from command, and an open patent of 18 February charged him with high treason. Losing the support of his army, he travelled from Plzeň to Cheb on 23 February hoping to meet the Swedes.

On the night of 25 February Scottish and Irish officers in his force killed his loyal officers at a feast and then Wallenstein himself in his lodgings. The Emperor rewarded the assassins. Plays, poems and pamphlets about him appeared soon afterwards, and Schiller made his last period the subject of a play trilogy completed in 1788.
alcaeus: Alcaeus was born into the aristocratic warrior class of Mytilene, the strongest city-state on Lesbos and by the end of the 7th century BCE the most influential of the North Aegean Greek cities, with a strong navy and colonies guarding its trade routes in the Hellespont. The Penthilid clan had long ruled it as kings, but in his lifetime they were a spent force and rival aristocratic factions fought for supreme power. Alcaeus and his older brothers took passionate part in the struggle with little success. Melanchrus was overthrown between 612 and 609 BCE by a faction that included his brothers and Pittacus, but Alcaeus was then too young to take part.

Later verses show that the poet, his brothers and Pittacus plotted against the tyrant Myrsilus and that Pittacus betrayed them, after which Alcaeus and his brothers went into exile. Pittacus was voted supreme power by the assembly of Mytilene and governed from 590 to 580 BCE, apparently well, even allowing Alcaeus and his faction to return. Before 600 BCE Mytilene fought Athens for Sigeion, and according to Herodotus Alcaeus threw away his shield to escape and then marked it in a poem to his friend Melanippus. He probably travelled widely in exile, including at least once to Egypt.

Alexandrian scholars, Aristophanes of Byzantium and Aristarchus of Samothrace, collected his poems into ten books in the 3rd century BCE and counted him among the canonical nine lyric poets. His work survives only in fragments, in quotations by ancient scholars and in papyri from Oxyrhynchus and elsewhere in Egypt. Like Sappho and Anacreon he is counted a monodist, a solo singer, who wrote in his native Aeolic dialect, for friends, in short, metrically simple stanzas, among them the Alcaic stanza named after him.

Conventionally his works are grouped as political songs, drinking songs, hymns, love songs and miscellaneous pieces. His political songs treat the power struggles on Lesbos as a partisan, cursing opponents and rejoicing in their deaths. Dionysius of Halicarnassus said that without the metre they would be political rhetoric. He used few metaphors but liked the allegory of the storm-tossed ship of state. Almost all his love poetry is lost. The Roman poet Horace modelled odes on his forms and imagined meeting Alcaeus and Sappho in Hades, and Quintilian praised his attacks on tyrants while regretting his turn to love.

He and Sappho were contemporaries and countrymen who may have exchanged poems, and later Greek critics assumed they were lovers. The first modern printing of his verses was in Michael Neander's edition of the nine lyric poets, published at Basle in 1556.
alchemy: Alchemy comprises a plurality of traditions extending across about four millennia and three continents. Three major strands appear mostly independent, at least in their earlier stages: Chinese alchemy, closely connected to Taoism; Indian alchemy, called Rasayana, tied to the Dharmic faiths; and Western alchemy around the Mediterranean, whose centre shifted from Greco-Roman Egypt to the Muslim world and finally to medieval Europe. Whether they share a common origin is still an open question. The word comes from the Arabic al-kīmiyā, itself borrowed from Late Greek khēmeía.

Western alchemy began in Hellenistic Egypt, where Alexandria was a centre, from the Egyptian goldsmith's art, Greek philosophy and various religious traditions. Its texts are pseudepigraphic. The earliest historically attested author is Zosimos of Panopolis, writing around 300, who drew on older authors such as Mary the Jewess and Pseudo-Democritus, whose Four Books were probably written in the first century.

Alchemists tried to purify, mature and perfect materials. Common aims were chrysopoeia, the transmutation of base metals such as lead into noble metals, particularly gold; an elixir of immortality; and panaceas that could cure any disease. The philosopher's stone was variously linked with all of these, and the perfection of body and soul was thought to follow from the Great Work. Islamic and European alchemists developed laboratory techniques, theories and terms, some still in use, kept to the Greek idea of four elements, and guarded their work in secrecy with cyphers and symbolism. Mary the Jewess is credited with improvements to equipment, including the water-bath known as the bain-marie.

After the fall of the Roman Empire alchemy's centre moved to the Islamic world, and the works attributed to Jābir ibn Hayyān, known in Latin as Geber, introduced a new approach in the late ninth and early tenth centuries. Alchemy entered Latin Europe on 11 February 1144 with Robert of Chester's translation of the Liber de compositione alchemiae, and translation flourished in 12th-century Toledo.

Alcohol, elixir and athanor entered European vocabulary this way. The tradition flourished for some two hundred years after the 17th century and perhaps peaked in the 18th, until the rise of quantitative experiment ended it. Robert Boyle (1627–1691) pioneered the scientific method in chemistry, which led to the modern chemistry of Lavoisier and John Dalton.
alcibiades: Alcibiades was born in Athens. The family of his father, Cleinias, had old connections with the Spartan aristocracy, and the name Alcibiades was of Spartan origin. His mother, Deinomache, was the daughter of Megacles, head of the powerful Alcmaeonid family, so that Pericles and his brother Ariphron were her cousins. After Cleinias died at the Battle of Coronea in 447 BCE, Pericles and Ariphron became the boy's guardians.

According to Plutarch, Alcibiades had several teachers, Socrates among them, and was well trained in rhetoric, though ancient writers often mention his unruly behaviour. He fought at the Battle of Potidaea in 432 BCE, where Socrates was said to have saved his life, and returned the favour by rescuing Socrates at the Battle of Delium in 424 BCE.

Alcibiades first rose to prominence by urging aggressive Athenian action after the Peace of Nicias, the uneasy truce with Sparta. After the charges of sacrilege he vanished at Thurii and contacted the Spartans, who gave him sanctuary. Athens condemned him to death in absentia and confiscated his property. At Sparta he warned the ephors that the Athenians hoped to conquer Sicily, Italy and even Carthage; Donald Kagan thinks he knowingly exaggerated.

Having made powerful enemies in Sparta as well, he went to the Persian satrap Tissaphernes, whom he advised to delay bringing in the Persian fleet, so that Athens and Sparta would wear each other out. Thucydides says his real aim was restoration to Athens. He finally returned to Athens in the spring of 407 BCE, sailing into Piraeus to a hero's welcome.

In antiquity he divided opinion. Thucydides holds that his habits gave offence to everyone and led the Athenians to commit affairs to other hands, to the city's ruin, while Plutarch calls him the least scrupulous of men. Diodorus describes him as brilliant in spirit and intent on great enterprises. Scholars have argued that the Sicilian expedition, had it been under his command rather than that of Nicias, might have avoided disaster.
alcide-de-gasperi: De Gasperi was born on 3 April 1881 in Pieve Tesino in Tyrol, then part of Austria-Hungary, the son of a local police officer of limited means. He was active in the Social Christian movement from 1896 and studied literature and philosophy in Vienna from 1900, inspired by Pope Leo XIII's encyclical Rerum novarum. In 1904 he was imprisoned briefly with other students after protesting for an Italian-language university. From 1906 he edited the newspaper Il Trentino, which defended Italian culture in Trentino against Germanisation; at that time he did not seek unification with Italy. He sat in the Austrian Reichsrat from 1911 for six years, and in the First World War he sided with Italy.

In 1919 he helped found the Italian People's Party with Luigi Sturzo and served in the Italian Parliament from 1921 to 1924. He first backed the party's participation in Benito Mussolini's government but diverged from the Fascists over the Acerbo Law and violence against the constitutional parties, culminating in the murder of Giacomo Matteotti. The party was dissolved in November 1926. He was arrested in March 1927 and sentenced to four years in prison; the Vatican negotiated his release. From 1929 until July 1943 he worked as a cataloguer in the Vatican Library. In 1943 he published Ideas for Reconstruction, a programme for the Christian Democracy party, of which he became general secretary in 1944.

He became prime minister in December 1945, leading eight successive governments until 1953, at first with the Communists and Socialists. He was provisional head of state from 12 June to 28 June 1946, after a referendum in which 54 per cent voted for a republic. Italy signed the peace treaty of 1947, which lost its eastern border area to Yugoslavia, and joined NATO in 1949 and the European Coal and Steel Community. The Gruber–De Gasperi Agreement of September 1946 made South Tyrol an autonomous region. In May 1947 he formed a government without the Communists and Socialists, and in April 1948 the Christian Democrats won 48.5 per cent.

The 1953 election followed a change in the electoral law that its opponents called the Scam Law; the governing coalition won 49.9 per cent, just short of the supermajority bonus, and De Gasperi was forced to resign on 2 August. He gave up the party leadership in June 1954 and died on 19 August 1954 at Sella di Valsugana in Trentino. He is buried in the Basilica di San Lorenzo fuori le Mura in Rome, and the process for his beatification was opened in 1993. His former secretary Giulio Andreotti said that he taught his followers to search for compromise and to mediate.
alcmaeon-of-croton: Alcmaeon was born in Croton in Magna Graecia and was the son of Peirithous. Some say he was a pupil of Pythagoras, though there are reasons to doubt that he was a Pythagorean at all: his name seems to have crept into the lists of Pythagoreans given by later writers, and since 1950 the scholarly consensus holds him to be a figure independent of them. Although he wrote mainly on medical topics, there is some suggestion that he was a philosopher of science rather than a physician. Nothing more is known of the events of his life.

Alcmaeon was considered by many an early advocate of anatomical dissection and was said to be the first to identify the Eustachian tubes. Whether he dissected animals or human bodies is disputed, since Calcidius, the authority for the claim, says only that he first dared to undertake exsectio, and some modern scholars doubt Calcidius altogether. He was the first to dwell on the internal causes of illness, suggesting that health is a state of equilibrium between opposing powers and that illness arises from problems of environment, nutrition and lifestyle.

Theophrastus's De Sensu summarises his study of the senses. Where Empedocles held that sensation arises from like acting on like and placed the mind in the heart, Alcmaeon held that it arises from unlike and placed the seat of the mind in the head. He distinguished sensation from thought, which separated animals from man. He also held that sleep occurs when blood withdraws from the surface of the body to the larger vessels, and that death follows if it withdraws entirely.

A book titled On Nature is attributed to him, but only titles and a few fragments of his writings survive, preserved by Stobaeus, Plutarch and Galen. He taught that the soul is immortal because, like the heavenly bodies, it contains a principle of motion. The extent to which he can be counted as a Presocratic cosmologist is controversial, since the evidence is slight.
alcoy: The first traces of human presence near Alcoy date to about 60,000 years ago, when Neanderthal hunters settled at a site now called El Salt. Rock paintings near la Sarga date to about 10,000 to 6,500 years ago. From about the middle of the third millennium BCE people moved from the caves to the plain, where cereals were grown, and mountain fortifications were built at places such as Mola Alta de Serelles and El Puig. After the Roman conquest of the Iberians, rural villas and a necropolis appeared in the area.

The town was established in 1256 by James I of Aragon, who built a castle over the Serpis river to secure the southern frontier of the Kingdom of Valencia during the Reconquista. In 1291 James II of Aragon gave it to the Sicilian admiral Roger of Lauria, and it returned to royal possession only in 1430. In the War of the Spanish Succession Alcoy backed Archduke Charles, was besieged and lost many privileges, which began a period of decline.

Alcoy, or Alcoi in Valencian, is a city in the province of Alicante and has industries in textiles, paper, food and metal. In 1821 about 1,200 peasants destroyed 17 newly introduced wool carding and spinning machines that threatened their livelihoods, the first large-scale Luddite action in Spain, and in 1873 its workers rose in the Petroleum Revolution. The city has several Art Nouveau buildings built between 1904 and 1911, including the Casa d'Escaló and the Cercle Industrial, and a cemetery on the European Cemeteries Route. Its Art Deco Pont de Sant Jordi is the most popular image of the city. The Moors and Christians festival in April is its main tourist celebration.
alcuin-of-york: Alcuin was born in Northumbria, presumably in the 730s, and nothing is known for certain of his parents or family. The Vita Alcuini calls him of noble English stock, which scholars have usually accepted. His own writings name relatives such as Wilgils of Ripon, the father of the missionary Willibrord, and Beornrad, abbot of Echternach. Donald A. Bullough suggests that the family was of free but subordinate status, and that Alcuin and his kin rose through connections with the aristocracy.

He came as a young man to the cathedral church of York in the time of Archbishop Ecgbert and his brother, the Northumbrian king Eadberht. Ecgbert, a disciple of Bede, oversaw a reform of the English church that stressed the clergy and the tradition of learning that Bede had begun, and he was devoted to Alcuin. The York school was a centre of the liberal arts, literature, science and religious learning. Alcuin became a teacher in the 750s and head of the school after Æthelbert became archbishop in 767. He became a deacon but was never ordained a priest.

At Charlemagne's invitation Alcuin became a leading scholar and teacher at the Carolingian court, where he was a figure in the 780s and 790s. Einhard's Life of Charlemagne calls him the most learned man anywhere to be found. He is considered one of the chief intellectual architects of the Carolingian Renaissance, and many dominant intellectuals of the era were his pupils. He drew on the York school as a model, reviving the trivium and quadrivium. In 796 he was made abbot of Marmoutier Abbey, at Tours, where he worked on perfecting the Carolingian minuscule script, and he stayed there until his death.

His output included theological and dogmatic treatises, a few grammatical works and a number of poems. His nine scriptural commentaries consist mostly of sentences taken from the Church Fathers, and he engaged in textual criticism of the Vulgate; four Bibles were prepared by him or under his direction at Tours, probably in 799–801. He also wrote lives of saints, among them Willibrord, and opposed the Spanish Adoptionism of bishops Felix of Urgell and Elipandus of Toledo. A collection of about 53 mathematical word problems, the Propositiones ad acuendos juvenes, is sometimes attributed to him, and more than 310 of his letters survive.

Alcuin died on 19 May 804. The Church of England and the Episcopal Church honour him on 20 May, and he is traditionally venerated as a Blessed in the Catholic Church. Alcuin College at the University of York is named after him.
aldus-manutius: Aldus Manutius was born at Bassiano, near Rome, between 1449 and 1452, into a wealthy family, and was sent to Rome to become a humanist scholar. He studied Latin there under Gaspare da Verona and attended lectures by Domizio Calderini in the early 1470s. From 1475 to 1478 he studied Greek at Ferrara under Battista Guarino. In 1482 he went to Mirandola with his friend Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, who recommended him as tutor to his nephews Alberto and Leonello Pio, princes of Carpi. The families of Pico and Alberto Pio paid the first costs of his press and gave him lands in Carpi. He decided that Venice was the best place for his work and settled there in 1490.

In Venice he met the printer Andrea Torresano, who became his lifelong partner and printed his Latin grammar, the Institutiones grammaticae, on 9 March 1493. The Aldine Press, established in 1494, issued its first book in March 1495, Constantine Lascaris's Erotemata. Its first great achievement was a five-volume folio Aristotle, begun in 1495 and completed in 1497 and 1498, and it printed nine comedies of Aristophanes in 1498. Manutius wanted to give readers Greek works in their original form. He commissioned Greek and Latin types resembling humanist handwriting, the first known precursor of italic type, and introduced small portable books, the enchiridia, a predecessor of the paperback.

Erasmus asked him to publish his Latin translations of Hecuba and Iphigenia in Aulis; Iphigenia in Aulis appeared in December 1507. Erasmus then went to Venice, spent ten months at the press and lived in the house of Manutius and Torresano, and there expanded his collection of proverbs from 819 to 3,260 entries, published as the Adagiorum Chiliades in 1508. Wars interrupted the press, but in 1513 Manutius issued a Plato dedicated to Pope Leo X. In 1505 he married Maria, Torresano's daughter, which combined the partners' shares.

Manutius wrote his will on 16 January 1515 and died on 6 February. Torresano and his two sons carried on the business, and Manutius's son Paulus, born in 1512, later took it over, leading it from 1539 with his brothers under the imprint Sons of Aldus until his death in 1574. A Greek Septuagint he had begun appeared in 1518, the first printed. Paul F. Grendler wrote that Manutius ensured the survival of a large number of ancient texts and greatly eased the spread of Italian Renaissance humanism to the rest of Europe.
aleksandr-solzhenitsyn: Aleksandr Isayevich Solzhenitsyn was born in Kislovodsk on 11 December 1918. His father, Isaakiy Semyonovich Solzhenitsyn, was of Russian descent, and his mother, Taisiya Zakharovna, of Ukrainian descent. The family defied the Soviet anti-religious campaign of the 1920s and remained devout members of the Russian Orthodox Church, but at a young age he became an atheist and embraced Marxism–Leninism. In the Second World War he commanded a sound-ranging battery in the Red Army, was involved in major action at the front, and was twice decorated; he received the Order of the Red Star on 8 July 1944.

In February 1945, while serving in East Prussia, he was arrested by SMERSH over nineteen months of correspondence with a friend, Nikolai Vitkevich, in which they criticised Joseph Stalin and the conduct of the war.

After the Gulag and internal exile, Solzhenitsyn was freed and exonerated following Nikita Khrushchev's Secret Speech of 1956. He taught at a secondary school by day and wrote in secret by night. In his Nobel lecture he recalled that until 1961 he was convinced he would never see a line of his work in print. His first novel, One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich, appeared in 1962 with Khrushchev's approval, and Matryona's Place in 1963 was his last work published in the Soviet Union.

After Khrushchev's removal in 1964 publication stopped and he became a non-person; by 1965 the KGB had seized some of his papers, including the manuscript of In the First Circle. Cancer Ward appeared abroad in 1966, In the First Circle in 1968 and August 1914 in 1971.

He kept working in secret on The Gulag Archipelago, published in 1973. On 12 February 1974 he was arrested and deported the next day to Frankfurt, West Germany, and stripped of his Soviet citizenship; the KGB had found the manuscript of its first part. His citizenship was restored in 1990, and in 1994 he returned to Russia, living in a dacha at Troitse-Lykovo in west Moscow.

Solzhenitsyn was awarded the 1970 Nobel Prize in Literature for the ethical force with which he pursued the indispensable traditions of Russian literature. The Gulag Archipelago amounted to a head-on challenge to the Soviet state and sold tens of millions of copies. In later political writings such as Rebuilding Russia he opposed any nostalgia for Soviet communism and called for a strong presidential republic balanced by local self-government. He died of heart failure near Moscow on 3 August 2008, aged 89, and was buried at the Donskoy Monastery in a spot he had chosen. A bronze statue of him stands on the seafront in Vladivostok.
aleppo: Aleppo lies about 120 km inland from the Mediterranean on a plateau 380 metres above sea level, with farmland to the north and west and the dry Syrian Desert to the east. It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, and its long history is attributed to its position as a trading centre between the Mediterranean and Mesopotamia, at one end of the Silk Road. The modern city occupies the ancient site, so archaeologists have scarcely touched it. The Amorites called the city Ḥalab in the second millennium BCE, and the Hittites Ḥalpa or Ḥalpu.

The first record of Aleppo comes from the third millennium BCE, in the Ebla tablets, where it is written Ha-lam. Excavations at Tell as-Sawda and Tell al-Ansari show that Amorites occupied the area by the late third millennium, and tablets from Ebla and Mesopotamia speak of it as part of the Amorite state of Yamhad. The main temple of the storm god Hadad stood on the citadel hill. Alexander the Great took the city in 333 BCE, and between 301 and 286 BCE Seleucus Nicator founded a Hellenic settlement there, calling it Beroea after the Macedonian city. Bishops of Beroea attended the councils of the 4th and 5th centuries.

The Sasanian king Khosrow I pillaged and burned the city in 540, and Rashidun forces under Abu Ubaidah ibn al-Jarrah took it in 637. In 944 it became the seat of an independent emirate under the Hamdanid prince Sayf al-Dawla, and was then home to the poet al-Mutanabbi and the philosopher al-Farabi. The Byzantine general Nikephoros Phokas sacked it in 962, the Fatimids took it in 1017, and the Mirdasid dynasty ruled it from 1024 to 1080, apart from two short intervals.

The Ottoman sultan Selim I took Aleppo in 1516, when it had about 50,000 inhabitants. For centuries it was the largest city of the Syrian region and the Ottoman Empire's third largest after Constantinople and Cairo. The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 diverted much trade to the sea, and Aleppo began a slow decline. After the First World War it lost its northern hinterland and the Baghdad Railway to Turkey, and in 1939 its main access to the sea.

Aleppo is the capital of the Aleppo Governorate in northern Syria. Its covered souq, about 13 km long, is the largest in the world, and its architecture shows the work of Romans, Byzantines, Umayyads, Seljuks, Ayyubids, Mamluks and Ottomans. UNESCO declared the Old City a World Heritage Site in 1986.
alessandro-manzoni: Alessandro Manzoni was born in Milan on 7 March 1785. His maternal grandfather was the philosopher Cesare Beccaria, and his biological father was probably Giovanni Verri rather than Pietro Manzoni. His parents separated in 1792, and from the age of six he was schooled in religious boarding schools run by the Somaschi and Barnabite fathers. He was drawn early to poetry and to ideals of liberty and reason, and his poem The Triumph of Liberty (1801) praised the French Revolution.

After his father's death in 1807 he joined his mother's household at Auteuil and met the Idéologues, including Claude Charles Fauriel. In 1808 he married Henriette Blondel, a Calvinist banker's daughter who became a Roman Catholic in 1810. That year Manzoni passed through a religious crisis that took him from agnosticism to an austere Catholicism. His Sacred Hymns appeared in 1815.

Manzoni began Fermo e Lucia on 24 April 1821, after reading the novels of Walter Scott in French translation, and finished the first manuscript in September 1823. The reshaped novel, The Betrothed (I promessi sposi), was published a volume a year in 1825–1827. It follows two ordinary fiancés, Renzo Tramaglino and Lucia Mondella, through famine, war and plague and through corruption in Church and State in 17th-century Lombardy under Spanish rule. Real figures appear, among them Cardinal Federico Borromeo and the outlaw called the Unnamed, historically identified with Francesco Bernardino Visconti.

The novel went through 68 editions and sold over 60,000 copies in fourteen years. Manzoni's tragedy Adelchi (1822), on Charlemagne's overthrow of the Lombard domination in Italy, carried veiled allusions to Austrian rule. Later he wrote mainly essays, above all on language. In 1868 he reported to the minister Emilio Broglio, proposing that Florentine be taught in schools. He supported Italian unification and became a senator in February 1860.

Manzoni outlived his first wife, who died on 25 December 1833, his second wife, Teresa Borri, six of his children and his closest friends. His eldest son, Pier Luigi, died on 28 April 1873. Manzoni had fallen on 6 January while leaving the San Fedele church, and he died of cerebral meningitis, a complication of the blow to his head, on 22 May 1873. His funeral was held in Milan Cathedral with almost royal pomp, and he was buried in the Monumental Cemetery of Milan.

He is counted with Ugo Foscolo and Giacomo Leopardi as one of the three crowns of Italian Romanticism. The Betrothed is a symbol of the Risorgimento for its patriotic message, and it was a milestone in the development of the modern and unified Italian language.
aleut: Archaeological evidence indicates that the Aleuts first occupied the Aleutian Islands about 9,000 years ago, beginning with the eastern islands, where sites on Unalaska and Anagula date to that period. They then spread westward, and the oldest sites on the western islands begin to appear about 2,500 years ago. Their technologies centred on food and resources from the sea and coast: fishing, gathering marine invertebrates and hunting sea mammals. Tools were made from local obsidian and chert, bird bones for needles and awls, and mammal bones for wedges, spoons and harpoon points. Before sustained European contact about 25,000 Aleuts lived in the archipelago.

In the 18th century Russian traders, the promyshlenniki, set up settlements on the islands, driven by demand for the furs the Aleuts hunted. They took Aleut women and children hostage to force the men to hunt foxes and sea otters, and often enslaved Aleut men as well. The Aleuts also suffered heavy deaths in the 19th and early 20th centuries from Eurasian infectious diseases to which they had no immunity, and their customary ways of life were disrupted. Russian Orthodox missionaries reached Kodiak in 1794 and many Aleuts became Christian; Saint Peter the Aleut is counted among the earliest Christian martyrs in North America.

In the 1820s the Russian-American Company, which administered much of the North Pacific, moved many Aleut families to the Commander Islands and to the Pribilof Islands, which still have majority-Aleut communities. The islands are now divided politically between Alaska and Russia's Kamchatka Krai.

The Aleuts call themselves Unangan in the eastern dialect and Unangas in the western, terms translated as 'original people'. Their language, Unangam Tunuu, belongs to the Eskaleut family and was written in Cyrillic from 1829 and in Latin script from 1870. An estimated 150 people in the United States and five in Russia speak it, and there are revitalisation efforts.

Aleuts traditionally lived in barabaras, partly underground houses roofed with driftwood, grass and earth, which sheltered several families from wind, rain and cold. They fish for salmon, cod, crabs and shellfish and hunt seals, walrus and whales, drying, smoking or roasting the catch, and many still eat locally sourced foods. The 2000 census counted 11,941 people who identified as Aleut and 17,000 more with partial Aleut ancestry.
aleutian-islands: The Aleutian Islands are a chain of 14 main volcanic islands and 55 smaller ones. They extend westward roughly 1,200 miles (1,900 km) from the Alaska Peninsula towards Kamchatka and separate the Bering Sea to the north from the Pacific Ocean to the south. The 57 volcanoes of the islands form the northernmost part of the Pacific Ring of Fire. Before 1867 the islands were known as the Catherine Archipelago. The climate is oceanic, with heavy rainfall and almost constant fog, and the vast majority of the chain has no native trees.

The first occupants probably arrived following Beringian migrations. The earliest archaeological sites, on Unalaska, date to about 9,000 years ago, those on Adak to about 6,000 years ago, and the western islands were settled last, about 2,500 years ago. The native people call themselves Unangan and are generally known as Aleut. They developed a culture tied to marine resources, with boat building, tools for fishing and sea-mammal hunting, and noted basketry and weaving.

In 1741 Vitus Bering and Aleksei Chirikov sailed from Russia on a voyage of discovery, and after a storm separated them Chirikov found several eastern islands and Bering several western ones. Bering was shipwrecked and died on the Commander Islands, and his survivors reported that the islands were rich in fur-bearing animals. Siberian fur hunters moved eastward across the chain, and the islands belonged to Russia until the Alaska Purchase of 1867. Grigory Shelikhov founded a company in the 1780s based on the systematic exploitation of the indigenous peoples, with sporadic conflict such as the Awa'uq Massacre. The first Orthodox missionaries arrived in 1793.

On 3 June 1942 Japanese forces invaded Attu and Kiska, the only invasions of the United States during the war. The United States moved over 800 civilians to camps in the Alaska Panhandle, and more than 90 Americans were taken to Japan as prisoners. American forces landed on Attu in May 1943 and on Kiska later that year, where 313 Allied men died from accidents. The United States tested nuclear weapons underground on Amchitka from 1965 to 1971.

Most of the islands belong to the U.S. state of Alaska, while the Commander Islands, farther west, belong to Kamchatka Krai in Russia. The 2020 census recorded 7,152 people on the islands, 4,254 of them in Unalaska, the main settlement. Fishing is the main economic activity, and nearly all the islands are protected within the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge. Large seabird colonies breed there, and sea otters help keep kelp forests along the coasts.
alexander-dubcek: Alexander Dubček was born in Uhrovec, Czechoslovakia, on 27 November 1921. When he was three his family moved to the Soviet Union in search of work and a better life, and he spent most of his childhood in Interhelpo, an Esperantist industrial cooperative in Kyrgyzstan. In 1933 the family moved to Gorky. In 1938 they chose to return to Czechoslovakia rather than renounce their citizenship. At 17 he joined the then-illegal Communist Party of Slovakia. He fought against the wartime pro-German Slovak state of Jozef Tiso and, in August 1944, joined the Jan Žižka partisan brigade during the Slovak National Uprising, in which his brother died.

After the Communist Party took power in 1948, Dubček rose through party posts in Trenčín, Bratislava and Banská Bystrica. He studied in the Soviet Union from 1955 to 1958 and was transferred to Prague in 1960. There he worked on the commissions that rehabilitated victims of repression in 1962–1963, and learning of the mechanisms of repression, he later said, was a watershed that dedicated him to reform. The Czechoslovak economy had begun to plateau in the early 1960s, and reformers concluded that the country had fallen behind the rest of the world.

Dubček was First Secretary of the party from January 1968 to April 1969 and became best known for the slogan Socialism with a human face. His reforms accelerated cultural and economic liberalisation, and culture changed most quickly. On the night of 20–21 August 1968 Soviet-led Warsaw Pact forces, reportedly about half a million troops, invaded Czechoslovakia. Albania, Romania and East Germany did not take part.

The invasion was meant to enable a coup by conservatives, but it could not succeed because of the lack of a viable pro-Soviet leadership and the popularity of Dubček. He was forced to resign in April 1969 and succeeded by Gustáv Husák, and was expelled from the party in 1970.

Dubček then lived as a nonperson whose very mention was banned, in Bratislava. In November 1989, during the Velvet Revolution, he spoke to a crowd at the trial of the Bratislava Five on 14 November, was briefly arrested on 17 November at the students' march in Prague, and appeared on 23 November in Bratislava.

He became Chairman of the federal parliament from 1989 to 1992, and the European Parliament awarded him the Sakharov Prize in 1989. He died on 7 November 1992 of injuries from a car crash on 1 September on the D1 motorway near Humpolec. A later investigation ruled the cause aquaplaning at excessive speed, though his son Pavol remained sceptical. Andrei Sakharov wrote that the breath of freedom under Dubček was a prologue to the peaceful revolutions in eastern Europe.
alexander-graham-bell: Alexander Bell was born in Edinburgh on 3 March 1847, the son of the phonetician Alexander Melville Bell and Eliza Grace Bell. For his eleventh birthday his father allowed him to adopt the middle name Graham. He left the Royal High School in Edinburgh at fifteen, having completed only four forms, and his interests lay in the sciences. His father, grandfather and brother were all associated with work on elocution and speech, and both his mother and his wife were deaf. With his brother Melville he built an automaton head that could say a few words. In 1870 Bell travelled with his parents to Ontario, where the family bought a farm near Brantford.

In April 1871 Bell went to Boston to train teachers of the deaf in his father's Visible Speech system. In 1872 he became professor of Vocal Physiology and Elocution at the Boston University School of Oratory, and in autumn 1873 he decided to concentrate on experiments in sound. His work on a harmonic telegraph, which would send several messages through one wire at different pitches, led towards the telephone.

On 14 February 1876 Bell's lawyer filed his application at the US Patent Office on the same day that Elisha Gray filed a caveat for a telephone design, and there is considerable debate about who arrived first. Bell received the first US patent for the telephone on 7 March 1876, and on 10 March he called his assistant Thomas Watson in another room. Over 18 years the Bell Telephone Company faced 587 court challenges, and none established priority over Bell's patent. He married Mabel Hubbard on 11 July 1877 and co-founded the American Telephone and Telegraph Company in 1885.

Bell held 18 patents in his own name and shared 12 more. With Charles Sumner Tainter he invented the photophone, which sent speech on a beam of light. He also built an early metal detector after the shooting of President James A. Garfield in 1881, and he began experiments on powered flight in 1891. He took an interest in heredity and bred sheep on his estate in Nova Scotia for more than 30 years. He served as the second president of the National Geographic Society from 1898 to 1903. Bell died at his estate in Cape Breton on 2 August 1922, aged 75.
alexander-hamilton: Hamilton was born on 11 January 1755 or 1757 in Charlestown, the capital of Nevis in the British Leeward Islands. He and his older brother, James Jr., were born out of wedlock to Rachel Lavien, a married woman of half-British and half-Huguenot descent, and James A. Hamilton, a Scotsman. He was orphaned as a child, taken in by a merchant, and given a scholarship to King's College (now Columbia University) in New York City.

In 1775, after the fighting at Lexington and Concord, he joined a New York volunteer company and was elected an officer. In 1776 he raised the New York Provincial Company of Artillery and was appointed captain. He served for four years as aide-de-camp to George Washington and fought at the Siege of Yorktown.

Hamilton resigned his commission in March 1782 and was appointed to the Congress of the Confederation, whose want of power he had criticised. He founded the Bank of New York, led the Annapolis Convention of 1786 and was a delegate to the Philadelphia Convention, which drafted the Constitution. He wrote 51 of the 85 installments of The Federalist Papers.

Washington appointed him first secretary of the treasury, and he was sworn in on 11 September 1789. He argued that the Constitution's implied powers allowed the First Bank of the United States, funded by a tariff on imports and a whiskey tax, to take on the states' war debts. His views became the basis of the Federalist Party, opposed by the Democratic-Republican Party under Thomas Jefferson. He resigned in 1795 and resumed his law practice.

Hamilton opposed Aaron Burr's candidacy for governor of New York in 1804. Letters published in the Albany Register alleged that he had expressed a despicable opinion of Burr, and Burr demanded an apology. Hamilton refused because he could not recall such an insult, and a duel was arranged. It took place at Weehawken, New Jersey, on 11 July 1804. Hamilton was mortally wounded and died the next day.

His interpretations in The Federalist Papers remain highly influential and are cited in scholarly studies and court decisions. His dispute with Jefferson over a national bank was addressed in McCulloch v. Maryland, which largely adopted Hamilton's view.
alexander-i-of-russia: Alexander was born in Saint Petersburg on 23 December 1777, the eldest son of Paul I of Russia, and he and his younger brother Constantine were raised by their grandmother, Catherine the Great. He took in the ideas of Jean-Jacques Rousseau from the free-thinking atmosphere of her court and from his Swiss tutor, Frédéric-César de La Harpe, and learned the traditions of Russian autocracy from his military governor, Nikolay Saltykov. He disliked his father as emperor even more than his grandmother, writing that Russia had become a plaything for the insane.

Alexander became emperor on 23 March 1801, when his father was assassinated, and was crowned in the Kremlin on 15 September. Historians still debate his role in the murder. The most common theory is that he knew of the conspiracy but insisted that his father should not be killed. He appointed a Private Committee of young friends to plan reforms leading to a constitutional monarchy. In practice he continued absolutist policies, though he introduced major educational reforms in 1803 and 1804, including more universities. Plans for a parliament and a constitution were never carried out.

In foreign policy he changed Russia's position towards France four times between 1804 and 1812. After defeats at Austerlitz and Friedland he formed an alliance with Napoleon in the Treaty of Tilsit in 1807, and in 1809 he took Finland from Sweden. The alliance collapsed by 1810, above all over Poland. Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812 was a catastrophe for the French. After the defeat of Napoleon at Leipzig in 1813, Alexander, as supreme commander of the coalition forces in Germany, ordered them to cross the Rhine, and allied forces occupied Paris in 1814. He formed the Holy Alliance to suppress revolutionary movements in Europe.

From the end of 1818 his liberal views began to change, and Metternich gained influence over him. In the second half of his reign he became increasingly arbitrary and fearful of plots, ended many earlier reforms and purged schools of foreign teachers. Speransky was replaced as adviser by Aleksey Arakcheyev, who oversaw the creation of military settlements.

In the autumn of 1825 Alexander travelled to the south of Russia because his wife was ill. He caught typhus and died at Taganrog on 19 November 1825 by the Old Style calendar. He left no legitimate children, since his two daughters had died in childhood, and neither of his brothers wished to become emperor. After a period of confusion his younger brother Nicholas I of Russia succeeded him. A popular legend holds that he faked his death and lived as a hermit under the name Feodor Kuzmich. Historians regard him as a complex and often contradictory ruler whose achievements in foreign policy were not matched by equally far-reaching domestic reforms.
alexander-ii-of-russia: Alexander Nikolayevich was born in Moscow, the eldest son of Nicholas I of Russia and Charlotte of Prussia. He became Tsesarevich in 1825, when his father took the throne. Under Nicholas the intellectual atmosphere of Saint Petersburg suppressed freedom of thought. The poet Vasily Zhukovsky supervised his education. In 1837 he toured twenty provinces of Russia and was the first Romanov heir to visit Siberia.
He met Princess Marie of Hesse in Darmstadt on a tour of Europe, and they married in Saint Petersburg on 16 April 1841. The marriage produced six sons and two daughters.

Alexander became emperor on 2 March 1855. On 15 January 1856 he took Russia out of the Crimean War on the unfavourable terms of the Treaty of Paris, which cost the Black Sea Fleet. This gave him room for domestic reform: the Edict of Emancipation of 1861, which abolished serfdom, and changes to the courts, local self-government, censorship, schools and the army. Many reforms met intense backlash and were cut back, and after an assassination attempt in 1866 he moved towards a more conservative stance.

In 1863 a Polish uprising led him to strip Poland of its separate constitution and incorporate the kingdom directly into the Russian Empire. In 1867 he sold Alaska to the United States. The Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878 brought independence to Bulgaria, Montenegro, Romania and Serbia. He also approved military plans in the Caucasus that culminated in the Circassian genocide.

After a last attempt on his life in February 1880, Count Loris-Melikov was given extraordinary powers against the revolutionaries, and his proposals called for a form of parliamentary body. On 13 March 1881 (1 March in the old-style calendar) Alexander was assassinated in Saint Petersburg. A bomb thrown by Nikolai Rysakov of the Narodnaya Volya damaged his carriage but left him unhurt, and a second member, Ignacy Hryniewiecki, then threw something at his feet.

Alexander had approved Loris-Melikov's plans as the first step towards a constitution. His successor, Alexander III, on the advice of Konstantin Pobedonostsev, abandoned them. The assassination brought suppression of civil liberties, use of the Okhrana secret police, and anti-Jewish pogroms and the May Laws.
alexander-iii-of-scotland: Alexander was born at Roxburgh on 4 September 1241, the only son of Alexander II and his second wife, Marie de Coucy, and became king at the age of seven on his father's death on 6 July 1249. His minority was marked by a bitter struggle between two parties, one led by Walter Comyn, Earl of Menteith, the other by Alan Durward, Justiciar of Scotia. When he married Margaret of England, daughter of Henry III, on 26 December 1251, Henry demanded homage for the Scottish kingdom, but Alexander did not comply. Two years after the meeting at Kelso in 1255, Menteith's party seized the king and forced the creation of a regency representing both sides.

On reaching his majority in 1262 Alexander laid a formal claim to the Western Isles before King Haakon IV of Norway, who rejected it and in 1263 invaded. Alexander prolonged negotiations off the Isle of Arran until the autumn storms, which damaged Haakon's ships. The Battle of Largs on 2 October 1263 was indecisive, but Haakon turned for home and died in Orkney on 15 December. In 1266 his son Magnus the Lawmender concluded the Treaty of Perth, ceding the Isle of Man and the Western Isles to Scotland in return for payments. Norway kept Orkney and Shetland until 1469.

Queen Margaret died in 1275, and all three of their children were dead by 1284, so that year Alexander had the Estates recognise his granddaughter Margaret, Maid of Norway, as heir presumptive. He married Yolande of Dreux on 1 November 1285. On 19 March 1286, after an evening at Edinburgh Castle, he rode through the dark and a storm to visit the Queen at Kinghorn, ignoring warnings at Inverkeithing, and was found dead with a broken neck near the shore the next morning. He was buried in Dunfermline Abbey.

The Maid of Norway died uncrowned in 1290, and six years of government by the Guardians of Scotland ended with the inauguration of John Balliol on 30 November 1292.
