A Scots poem recorded by Andrew of Wyntoun mourns the plenty lost with Alexander's death, though Richard Oram points out that the climate was already worsening at the time. A monument was raised near the spot of his death in 1886.
alexander-iv-of-macedon: Alexander IV was the younger son of Alexander the Great and Roxana of Bactria, a Sogdian. An older full brother had died in infancy in 326 BCE. Alexander the Great also had a son named Heracles, born of an informal relationship with Barsine, and Heracles's illegitimacy made the younger boy the primary successor.

When Alexander the Great died on 11 June 323 BCE, Roxana was between six and eight months pregnant and the child's sex was unknown. The infantry supported Philip III, the dead king's half-brother, who had a cognitive disability. The chiliarch Perdiccas, commander of the Companion cavalry, persuaded them to wait. The factions compromised: Perdiccas would rule as regent, Philip would reign only as a figurehead, and a male child would also be king. Alexander IV was born in the second half of 323 BCE.

Perdiccas was assassinated by his officers in 321 or 320 BCE, and at the Partition of Triparadisus Antipater became regent. He took Roxana and the two kings to Macedon. When he died in 319 BCE he left Polyperchon as successor, passing over his own son Cassander, who allied himself with Ptolemy Soter, Antigonus and Philip's wife Eurydice and declared war on the regency.

Cassander took full control of Macedon after Antigonus destroyed Polyperchon's fleet in 318 BCE, and Roxana and the boy fled with Polyperchon to Epirus. Olympias, with Aeacides of Epirus, then invaded; Eurydice's army refused to fight the mother of Alexander the Great and defected. Philip and Eurydice were executed on 25 December 317 BCE, leaving Alexander IV king under Olympias as regent. Cassander returned in 316 BCE, executed Olympias and held the king and his mother in the citadel of Amphipolis under Glaucias.

The peace of 311 BCE that ended the Third Diadoch War recognised Alexander IV's rights and stated that he would succeed Cassander when of age. Supporters of the Argead dynasty then began to argue that, as a teenager, he should rule himself. Cassander then ordered Glaucias to kill the boy and his mother secretly, and according to Pausanias they were poisoned.

The year of death is disputed, within a range from 311 to 304 BCE. Hammond and Walbank place it soon after the death of Heracles, though Peter Green argues Heracles died later. Alexander IV was recognised as king in Egypt and Babylonia until 304 BCE, which some take as posthumous dating and Harry Tolley as a sign he lived that long. A tomb found by Manolis Andronikos at Vergina in 1977/8 is believed to be his, and the skeleton appears to be of a youth in his mid-to-late teens, which would support the later date.
alexander-kerensky: Alexander Kerensky was born in Simbirsk, now Ulyanovsk, on 4 May 1881, the eldest son of Fyodor Mikhailovich Kerensky, a teacher and director of the local gymnasium. His father had taught Vladimir Ulyanov, later known as Lenin, and the two families were friends. In 1889 the family moved to Tashkent. Kerensky studied history and philology and then law at St Petersburg University, and took his law degree in 1904.

He became known as a defence lawyer in political trials of revolutionaries and in 1912 published material on the Lena massacre, after visiting the goldfields on the Lena River. That year he was elected to the Fourth Duma for the Trudoviks, a non-Marxist socialist labour party, and joined a Freemason society of anti-monarchy forces. In November 1916 he used the opening of the Duma to denounce the imperial ministers as guided by Grigori Rasputin.

After the February Revolution of 1917 Kerensky became vice-chairman of the Petrograd Soviet and a member of the Provisional Government, the only man in both. He became Minister of War after the crisis over Pavel Milyukov's note of May and urged soldiers at the front to do their duty. Under Allied pressure he launched the Kerensky Offensive on 1 July 1917. It was at first successful but was driven back by a German counter-attack, and the army showed that it was no longer willing to attack. Officers, angry that he had handed control to soldier committees, called him the persuader-in-chief.

After the July Days and the suppression of the Bolsheviks, Kerensky succeeded Georgy Lvov as prime minister on 21 July 1917. Following the Kornilov Affair at the end of August he made himself Supreme Commander-in-Chief, and on 15 September proclaimed Russia a republic. He continued the war, which was unpopular, while Lenin promised peace, land and bread, and an estimated two million men had unofficially left the army by autumn. On 7 November 1917 the Bolsheviks seized government buildings and the Winter Palace. Kerensky fled to Pskov, tried to retake Petrograd, was beaten at Pulkovo and eventually reached France.

During the Russian Civil War he supported neither the Bolsheviks nor the White Movement. He lived mostly in Paris and New York City and worked for the Hoover Institution at Stanford University. He died in New York on 11 June 1970 at the age of 89. The Russian and Serbian Orthodox churches refused his body, because of his Freemasonry and because they saw him as largely responsible for the Bolshevik seizure of power, and he was buried in the non-sectarian Putney Vale Cemetery in London.
alexander-kolchak: Kolchak was born in Saint Petersburg on 4 November 1874 (16 November in the modern calendar). His family was of Moldavian origin and both parents came from Odessa. His father, a former major-general of the marine artillery and a veteran of the 1854 siege of Sevastopol, worked as an engineer at an ordnance works near the capital. Kolchak entered the Naval Cadet Corps in 1888, graduated with honours in 1894 and served in the Baltic and Pacific between 1895 and 1899, publishing articles on hydrology.

As a lieutenant he joined Baron Eduard von Toll's Russian Polar expedition on the ship Zarya as hydrologist and cartographer. In the winter of 1901 he and Toll rode dog sleds for 500 km to survey the Taymyr Peninsula, and in spring they studied the New Siberian Islands. Kolchak returned in December 1902; Toll and three other explorers went further north and were lost. Kolchak took part in two Arctic expeditions to look for them, without finding them. He became a recognised expert on naval mines and the author of 16 articles on Arctic research.

Hearing of the war with Japan in December 1903, Kolchak summoned his fiancée Sophia Omirova to Siberia for a hurried wedding and went to Port Arthur. He served on the cruiser Askold and later commanded the destroyer Serdity, laying mines by night; one sank the Japanese cruiser Takasago. He was wounded and captured at the siege, and on his return lobbied the State Duma for submarines and aircraft. He became the youngest vice admiral in the Imperial Navy and was Baltic Fleet Chief of Operations when the First World War began.

Early in the Civil War he served briefly as Minister of War and Navy in the Provisional All-Russian Government until a November 1918 coup installed him as Supreme Ruler, heading a military dictatorship from Omsk. He opposed democracy, which he tied to pacifism, internationalism and socialism. After initial successes in early 1919 his forces lost ground for lack of local support and failure to unite the anti-Bolshevik leaders.

Omsk fell to the Red Army in November 1919 during the Great Siberian Ice March, and Kolchak moved his headquarters to Irkutsk. He was betrayed and detained by the Allied mission's chief, Maurice Janin, and the Czechoslovak Legion, which gave him to local Socialist-Revolutionaries in January 1920. The Bolsheviks shot him on 7 February 1920. His government won diplomatic recognition from no country, and he alienated the Czechoslovak Legion; the American commander Graves refused him military aid.
alexander-nevsky: Alexander was born in Pereslavl-Zalessky on 13 May 1221, although an older tradition placed his birth on 30 May 1220. He was the second son of Yaroslav Vsevolodovich, who held Pereslavl-Zalessky and the throne of Novgorod during the Mongol conquest of 1237 to 1238 and inherited the Grand Principality of Vladimir in 1238 after the death of his elder brother Yury. There is no consensus on the identity of Alexander's mother, whom his vita names as Feodosiya.

Alexander is first mentioned directly in 1228, when his father left him and his elder brother to rule Novgorod. Fyodor died in the summer of 1233, aged 14, leaving Alexander the eldest surviving son. In 1239 he married Aleksandra, a daughter of the prince of Polotsk, Bryacheslav Vasilkovich, and they had five children, among them Dmitry of Pereslavl, Andrey of Gorodets and Daniel of Moscow.

In 1236 the Novgorod Republic appointed Alexander prince of Novgorod. His father chose him and the veche approved, since it needed his armies. He ruled there in 1236 to 1240, 1241 to 1256 and 1258 to 1259. Alexander continued his family's anti-Western views, which made him unpopular with the veche. After the Mongols won the Battle of the Sit River in 1238 and Yuri II of Vladimir was killed, Yaroslav received the khan's permission to become prince.

In 1240 the Swedes, led by Birger Jarl, launched what is called the Second Swedish Crusade. According to Russian sources, their army landed at the confluence of the Izhora and Neva, and Alexander attacked it on 15 July 1240 and won the Battle of the Neva. The title Nevsky is attested from the 15th century. He also fought German crusaders in the Battle on the Ice in 1242. He agreed to pay tribute to the Golden Horde, which allowed him to preserve the Eastern Orthodox Church, and from 1252 to 1263 he was Grand Prince of Vladimir.

In 1263 Alexander visited Berke of the Golden Horde on a diplomatic mission. He fell ill on the way back and died at Gorodets on 14 November 1263, and was buried in Vladimir on 23 November. Veneration began almost at once. His remains were found incorrupt in 1380 and Macarius, Metropolitan of Moscow, canonized him in 1547. Peter the Great had the relics moved to Saint Petersburg in 1724, and Catherine I founded the imperial Order of Saint Alexander Nevsky in 1725.

His image as defender of Russia was used later, in Sergei Eisenstein's 1938 film and by Soviet authorities during the Second World War, who introduced a Soviet Order of Alexander Nevsky in 1942. Critics argue that the size and importance of his victories were exaggerated for political purposes and that he helped ensure the Golden Horde's dominance over Russia.
alexander-obrenovic: Alexander was born on 14 August 1876 to King Milan and Queen Natalie of Serbia, and belonged to the Obrenović dynasty. In 1889 Milan unexpectedly abdicated and withdrew to private life, proclaiming his son king. As Alexander was only thirteen, three regents were appointed, with Jovan Ristich at their head, and his mother also became a regent. On 13 April 1893 Alexander ordered the regents arrested, declared himself of age and dissolved the national assembly. On 21 May he abolished his father's liberal constitution of 1889 and restored the earlier one.

In 1894 the young king brought Milan back to Serbia, and in 1898 he made him commander-in-chief of the army; Milan was regarded as the real ruler of the country in these years. In 1898 penalties fell on the Radical and Russophil parties, which the court sought to tie to an attempted assassination of the former king. In the summer of 1900 Alexander suddenly announced his engagement to Draga Mašin, a widow who had served as maid of honour to his mother. She was nine years older than the king and unpopular in Belgrade society, and many believed she could not bear children.

His father had been arranging a match with a German princess, and both Milan and the prime minister, Vladan Đorđević, resigned. Alexander's mother also opposed the marriage and was banished from the kingdom. Nicholas II of Russia agreed to act as principal witness, and the wedding took place in August 1900, but the marriage weakened the king's position with the army and the wider country.

In 1901 Alexander issued a moderately liberal constitution of his own initiative, which introduced for the first time in Serbia a parliament of two chambers, the skupština and a senate, and granted an amnesty to the persecuted Radicals. It reconciled the parties but not the army, which was alarmed by rumours that one of Draga's brothers would be named heir presumptive. The country's growing dependence on Austria-Hungary was also resented. In March 1903 the king suspended the constitution for half an hour, long enough to publish decrees replacing the senators and councillors of state.

In 1902 Peter Karađorđević had been proclaimed king by followers at Šabac, and conspiracies formed. A group of officers led by Captain Dragutin Dimitrijević, known as Apis, invaded the palace in Belgrade. They found the royal couple, murdered them in the early morning of 11 June 1903 and threw their bodies from a window. Both were buried in the crypt of St. Mark's Church, Belgrade.
alexander-of-greece: Alexander was born on 1 August 1893 at Tatoi Palace near Athens, the second son of Crown Prince Constantine and Princess Sophia of Prussia. He was related to royalty across Europe: his mother was a daughter of Frederick III, German Emperor, and Wilhelm II was his uncle. He was mischievous and extroverted, unlike his serious elder brother George. Educated in Greece at the Hellenic Military Academy, he was known more for his mechanical skills than for intellect, and was among the first Greeks to own an automobile.

He distinguished himself in the Balkan Wars of 1912-13, serving on his father's staff during the capture of Thessaloniki. In 1915 he fell in love with Aspasia Manos, the daughter of his father's Master of the Horse, and the couple became secretly engaged.

Alexander swore the constitutional oath on 11 June 1917, after the Entente Powers and the followers of Eleftherios Venizelos forced Constantine into exile. Russia's provisional government protested and wanted him called only regent, but was brushed aside. Only the Archbishop of Athens, his father, his brother and the prime minister Alexandros Zaimis attended, and he was in tears.

His father told him to consider himself a regent. The family left for exile, though Alexander stayed, and the royal household was gradually replaced by enemies of his father. His new ministers openly called him the son of a traitor, and Venizelos ruled as prime minister with Entente support. In 1919 Alexander married Aspasia Manos, though his father had asked him to wait until the war ended.

Both Venizelists and royalists opposed a marriage to a commoner, and the scandal forced the couple to leave Greece for several months. Under his reign Greek territory grew considerably, following the Entente's victory and the early stages of the Greco-Turkish War of 1919-1922.

On 2 October 1920 Alexander tried to part his dog from a pet Barbary macaque in the Tatoi grounds and was bitten deeply on the leg and torso by another monkey. The wounds were dressed but not cauterised, and sepsis set in. The government refused to let his mother return from exile, and he died on 25 October 1920 at the age of 27, twelve hours before his grandmother, Queen Olga, arrived. His descendants were excluded from the succession because of the marriage.

His death raised questions about the monarchy. Prince Paul refused the throne while his father and brother lived. In elections on 14 November 1920 the monarchists won, Venizelos left Greece, and a referendum restored Constantine I. Greece then lost the Greco-Turkish War, and the gains on the Turkish mainland were lost. Winston Churchill wrote that perhaps a quarter of a million people died of this monkey's bite.
alexander-pushkin: Alexander Pushkin was born in Moscow on 6 June 1799 (26 May in the Old Style calendar). His father, Sergei Lvovich Pushkin, came from a noble family that traced its ancestry to the 12th century. His mother, Nadezhda Ossipovna Gannibal, was a granddaughter of Abram Petrovich Gannibal, an African page taken to Constantinople as a gift for the Ottoman Sultan and later sent to Peter the Great.

Entrusted to nursemaids and French tutors, Pushkin spoke mostly French until the age of ten and learned Russian from household serfs and his serf nanny, Arina Rodionovna. His first poem appeared in 1814, when he was 15, and in 1817 in the first graduating class of the Imperial Lyceum at Tsarskoye Selo, where he absorbed the thought of the French Enlightenment.

In 1820 Pushkin published his first long poem, Ruslan and Ludmila, to much controversy. His commitment to social reform angered the government, which transferred him from the capital in May 1820. In Chișinău, in Bessarabia, he wrote The Prisoner of the Caucasus and The Fountain of Bakhchisaray. After a further clash with the authorities in Odessa he was exiled to his mother's estate of Mikhailovskoye, near Pskov, from 1824 to 1826.

At Mikhailovskoye he worked on the verse novel Eugene Onegin, which was serialized between 1825 and 1832, and in 1825 wrote the drama Boris Godunov. He could not get permission to publish the play until five years later, and its uncensored original was not staged until 2007. His poem Ode to Liberty was found among the belongings of the Decembrist rebels of 1825, and he was summoned to Moscow; many of the Decembrists were his friends.

By the autumn of 1836 Pushkin was deeper in debt and faced rumours that his wife, Natalia Goncharova, was having an affair. On 4 November he challenged Georges d'Anthès to a duel, but the challenge was withdrawn after friends intervened. D'Anthès then married her sister Ekaterina, yet continued to pursue Natalia in public. After Pushkin sent him a highly insulting letter in late January 1837, a duel could not be avoided. He was fatally wounded and died on 10 February 1837 (29 January in the Old Style).

Pushkin's works supplied material for composers: Mikhail Glinka's Ruslan and Lyudmila, and Pyotr Tchaikovsky's Eugene Onegin (1879) and The Queen of Spades (1890). His short drama Mozart and Salieri became the libretto of an opera by Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov. In 1937 the town of Tsarskoye Selo was renamed Pushkin in his honour.
alexander-suvorov: Alexander Suvorov was born in Moscow, in a mansion on the Arbat given as a dowry by his maternal grandfather, Fedosey Manukov. His family was a noble one originating from Novgorod. His father, Vasily Ivanovich Suvorov, was a general-in-chief and a senator, and is credited with translating the works of Vauban into Russian. Suvorov entered the army in 1745 and served nine years in the Semyonovsky Lifeguard Regiment while attending classes at the Cadet Corps of Land Forces. He spent most of his time in the barracks, where the troops loved him and others thought him eccentric.

He was among the best-educated Russians of his time. He knew mathematics, history and geography, spoke German, French, Italian, Polish, Turkish, Arabic and Finnish, and had studied military works from Plutarch to his contemporaries. His first battle experience came in the Seven Years' War, where he took part in the victory over Frederick the Great at the Battle of Kunersdorf in 1759.

In the War of the Bar Confederation Suvorov captured Kraków in 1768 and won victories at Orzechowo and Opatów. Stormings of the fortified positions at Lanckorona and near Tyniec Abbey failed in 1771, which were among the few tactical setbacks of his career. In the Russo-Turkish War of 1768 to 1774 he captured Turtukaya twice and won at Kozludzha. From 1777 he built more than 30 fortifications on the Kuban with about 12,000 men, after which attacks from across the river ceased.

In the Russo-Turkish War of 1787 to 1792 he fought at Kinburn and Focșani and won the Battle of Rymnik, followed by the storming of Izmail. In 1794 he put down the Polish uprising and defeated the Poles at Praga. He quarrelled with Catherine the Great's heir Paul I, who after becoming emperor in 1796 often disagreed with him. In February 1799, with France winning in Europe, Paul reinstated him as field marshal. Given command of the Austro-Russian army, he won at the Trebbia and captured Milan and Turin. He then led his exhausted, outnumbered army out of the Swiss Alps after being cut off by André Masséna, and was promoted generalissimo.

Suvorov died of illness in Saint Petersburg on 18 May 1800 (6 May Old Style) and was buried in the Alexander Nevsky Lavra, where his gravestone reads simply: Here lies Suvorov. After Paul I was murdered within a year, his son and successor Alexander I erected a statue to his memory in the Field of Mars. Suvorov wrote military works, the best known being The Science of Victory and the Suzdal Regulations, and he is remembered for sayings such as: Perish yourself but rescue your comrade. Poets including Gavrila Derzhavin, Alexander Pushkin and Mikhail Lermontov mentioned him, and he appears in Leo Tolstoy's War and Peace.
alexander-the-great: Alexander was born in Pella, the capital of Macedon, probably on 20 July 356 BCE, the son of Philip II and his fourth wife, Olympias, daughter of King Neoptolemus I of Epirus. According to the biographer Plutarch, Olympias dreamed that a thunderbolt struck her womb, and Plutarch suggested that Zeus was Alexander's father. Alexander claimed descent from Heracles and Perseus through his father and from Achilles through his mother. Aristotle tutored him until he was 16, after which he governed as regent while Philip fought the Thracians.

Philip was assassinated by his chief bodyguard Pausanias, probably on 25 October 336 BCE, and the army proclaimed the 20-year-old Alexander king. He executed his cousin Amyntas IV and two Macedonian princes, destroyed the city of Thebes and took over the League of Corinth. In 334 BCE he launched a pan-Hellenic invasion of the Achaemenid Persian Empire. After conquering Asia Minor he won decisive battles at Issus and Gaugamela, overthrew Darius III and took the whole empire.

In 326 BCE he invaded India and defeated the king Porus at the Battle of the Hydaspes, but facing a mutiny he turned back at the Beas River. According to Curtius, he slaughtered the entire population of Massaga. At Opis his troops mutinied again, resenting his adoption of Persian customs and his promotion of Persian officers.

Alexander died in Babylon on 10 or 11 June 323 BCE, at age 32. Plutarch describes a fever that worsened until he could not speak, while Diodorus tells of pain after a large bowl of unmixed wine. Civil wars then broke out and the Diadochi broke up the empire, beginning the Hellenistic period. He founded more than twenty cities, the most prominent being Alexandria in Egypt. The works of those who knew him, including Ptolemy and Nearchus, are lost, and Arrian, who drew on Ptolemy and Aristobulus, is generally considered the most reliable of the later writers.
alexander-von-humboldt: Friedrich Wilhelm Heinrich Alexander von Humboldt was born in Berlin on 14 September 1769 and baptised a Lutheran. He was the younger brother of the Prussian minister and linguist Wilhelm von Humboldt. He graduated from the Freiberg School of Mines in 1792 and became an inspector in the Prussian Department of Mines in Bayreuth and the Fichtel Mountains. His gold ore output in his first year exceeded that of the previous eight years combined. He also opened, at his own expense, a free school for miners and tried to set up an emergency relief fund for them.

In Madrid Humboldt obtained authorisation from the Spanish crown to travel in its American realms, after a planned French voyage was postponed. With the botanist Aimé Bonpland he sailed from La Coruña on 5 June 1799, climbed the volcano Teide on Tenerife, and landed at Cumaná, Venezuela, on 16 July.

Between 1799 and 1804 they travelled through Venezuela, Cuba, the Andes and New Spain. In Bogotá, José Celestino Mutis gave Humboldt access to his great pictorial record of plants. Humboldt identified the source of the Orinoco River, and in 1802 he climbed in Ecuador to 19,286 feet, a world record altitude for a Westerner at the time. In 1804 he made an unplanned visit to the United States at the invitation of President Thomas Jefferson.

Humboldt spent his personal fortune publishing the results, in nearly thirty volumes with Bonpland as co-author. The Political Essay on the Kingdom of New Spain and the Personal Narrative of Travels were widely read. He was elected to the Prussian Academy of Sciences in 1805 and, in his sixtieth year, made an expedition to Russia.

His quantitative work on botanical geography laid the foundation of biogeography, and his advocacy of long-term, systematic geophysical measurement pioneered modern geomagnetic and meteorological monitoring. His multivolume Kosmos, which took shape in lectures at the University of Berlin in 1827–1828, sought to unify diverse branches of scientific knowledge and presented the universe as one interacting whole. In 1800 and again in 1831 he described local effects of development on climate. He died on 6 May 1859. Scholars argue over whether his writing carries an imperial bias; Pratt contends that he portrayed the South American natural world as free of people.
alexandra-feodorovna-alix-of-hesse: Alix was born on 6 June 1872 at the New Palace in Darmstadt, the sixth child and fourth daughter of Louis IV, Grand Duke of Hesse, and Princess Alice of the United Kingdom, the second daughter of Queen Victoria. Her older brother Prince Friedrich, who had haemophilia, died after a fall in May 1873, when she was about a year old.

Queen Victoria wanted her to marry into the British royal house and in 1889 invited her to Balmoral to meet Prince Albert Victor, known as Eddy. He proposed, and in May 1890 Alix refused him, writing that she saw him only as a cousin. Her heart lay elsewhere. She had met the Russian heir, Nicholas, in 1884 at the wedding of her sister Elisabeth to Grand Duke Sergei Alexandrovich in Saint Petersburg, and her sister and brother-in-law favoured a match with him.

Nicholas proposed in April 1894 at Coburg. Alix at first declined, because marriage to the Russian heir required her to leave Lutheranism for Russian Orthodoxy, but she later accepted. After Alexander III died on 1 November 1894, she was received into the Orthodox Church the next day as Grand Duchess Alexandra Feodorovna. She and Nicholas married on 26 November 1894 in the Grand Church of the Winter Palace. They were crowned in the Dormition Cathedral in the Kremlin on 26 May 1896.

The couple had four daughters, Olga, Tatiana, Maria and Anastasia, and a son, Alexei, who had haemophilia. His illness shaped her relations with religious advisers and healers, among them Grigori Rasputin, whom she came to believe could help the boy. She supported the preservation of the autocracy and opposed some proposed reforms. Historians still debate how far she influenced Nicholas II and how far she was responsible for the decisions of his government.

Nicholas abdicated on 15 March 1917 (2 March in the old-style calendar). The family was held under house arrest at the Alexander Palace at Tsarskoye Selo and later moved to Yekaterinburg. On 17 July 1918 Alexandra, Nicholas and their five children were murdered by Bolshevik forces at the Ipatiev House, together with several members of their household.

The Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia recognised the family as martyrs in 1981. Alexandra was reinterred with Nicholas and three of their children in the Peter and Paul Cathedral in Saint Petersburg in 1998, and the Russian Orthodox Church canonised her as a passion bearer in 2000.
alexandria: Alexandria lies at the western edge of the Nile Delta and extends about 40 km along Egypt's northern coast. In ancient times the very large Lake Mariout lay directly south of it. Just to the east, where Abu Qir Bay is now, there were marshland and several islands, and port cities such as Canopus and Heracleion existed there from the 7th century BCE; Heracleion has been rediscovered underwater. A small Egyptian fishing village, Rhakotis, had existed nearby since the 13th century BCE, and it grew into the Egyptian quarter of the new city.

Greek Alexandria was divided into regions: Rhakotis, occupied chiefly by Egyptians, Brucheum, the royal or Greek quarter, and a Jewish quarter in the northeast. The city was laid out as a grid of parallel streets, each with a subterranean canal. As capital of the Ptolemaic Kingdom it became the foremost commercial, intellectual and cultural centre of much of the Hellenistic age and late antiquity, and at one time was the most populous city in the ancient world. It was also a major centre of early Christianity and the seat of the Patriarchate of Alexandria.

The Royal Library is generally thought to have been founded at the beginning of the 3rd century BCE under Ptolemy II, after his father had built the temple of the Muses, the Museion, from which the word museum derives.

In 619 the city fell to the Sassanid Persians. The Byzantine emperor Heraclius recovered it in 629, and in 641 the Arabs under 'Amr ibn al-'As took it after a siege of fourteen months. Egypt's capital then moved to Fustat, now part of Cairo. The Mamluk Sultan Qa'it Bay built the Citadel of Qaitbay in 1477 on the site of the Lighthouse of Alexandria. From the late 18th century the city was one of the most important trading centres in the world, thanks to the overland link between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea and the trade in Egyptian cotton, and its rebirth in the early 19th century began under Muhammad Ali.

Alexandria is Egypt's principal seaport, its second city after Cairo and the largest city on the Mediterranean coast. Surviving monuments include Pompey's Pillar, a Roman triumphal column about 30 m high, and the Catacombs of Kom El Shoqafa, a multi-level labyrinth forgotten until it was found by accident in 1900.
alexandru-ioan-cuza: Alexandru Ioan Cuza was born at Bârlad on 20 March 1820 into the boyar class of Moldavia, the son of Ioan Cuza, a landowner in Fălciu County, and Sultana, of the Phanariote and Genovese Cozadini family. He was educated at Iași, Pavia, Bologna and Athens and, after a brief military service, in Paris from 1837 to 1840. In the revolutions of 1848 he played a part prominent enough to establish his liberal credentials, and was shipped to Vienna as a prisoner, from where he escaped with British support. In 1858 he became Moldavia's minister of war and a speaker in the ad hoc Divan at Iași, where he strongly advocated union with Wallachia.

The pro-unionist Partida Națională nominated Cuza in both principalities, using an ambiguity in the Treaty of Paris. He was elected Prince of Moldavia on 5 January 1859 (Julian calendar) and, after street pressure changed the vote in Bucharest, Prince of Wallachia on 24 January. The Ottoman sultan did not recognise his authority until 23 December 1861, and then only for the length of Cuza's rule. On 5 February 1862 the union was formally declared, under the name Romania, with Bucharest as its capital, one assembly and one government.

With his councilor Mihail Kogălniceanu, Cuza nationalised monastic estates in 1863; probably more than a quarter of the farmland was held by untaxed dedicated monasteries,. After conservatives defeated his land bill, he held a plebiscite that approved wider suffrage and rule by decree. The Agrarian Law gave peasants title to the land they worked, with landlords keeping one third. Further measures included a Criminal Code and a Civil Code based on the Napoleonic Code and tuition-free compulsory primary education in 1864.

Cuza's land reform and his reliance on a shrinking group of appointed officials drew growing opposition, and financial distress and a scandal over his mistress added to it. A coalition of Conservatives and Liberals, called the monstrous coalition, ended his rule: military conspirators broke into the palace one morning in February 1866 and made him sign his abdication, and the next day led him across the border. Prince Karl of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen was proclaimed Domnitor as Carol I on 20 April 1866. Cuza lived in exile, chiefly in Paris, Vienna and Wiesbaden, and died at Heidelberg on 15 May 1873. He is often counted among the founders of the modern Romanian state.
alexei-brusilov: Aleksei Alekseyevich Brusilov was born on 31 August 1853 in Tiflis, into a family in which three generations had served as officers in the Imperial Russian Army. His father, a lieutenant general, died of tuberculosis in 1856, and his Polish mother died soon after; he was raised by relatives in Kutaisi. He entered the Imperial Corps of Pages in Saint Petersburg in 1867 and in 1872 was posted as an ensign to the 15th (Tver) Dragoon Regiment, stationed near Kutaisi. He served in the Russo-Turkish War of 1877-78 and was decorated for the assault on the fortress of Ardagan and for attacks around Kars.

From 1881 Brusilov was at the Cavalry Officer School in Saint Petersburg, which he commanded from 1902 and made a recognised centre for training cavalry staff officers. He then commanded the 14th Army Corps in the Warsaw Military District from 1908 and the 12th Army Corps in Kiev from 1913. In July 1914 he took command of the 8th Army in Galicia, which crushed the Austro-Hungarian Third Army and advanced nearly 150 kilometres before retreating with the rest of the front. In the Great Retreat of 1915 the 8th Army withdrew 180 kilometres.

On 29 March 1916 he was given the Southwest Front. Earlier Russian offensives had struck ever narrower sections of the line. Brusilov instead attacked along the whole front, using fire on command posts and roads rather than saturation bombardment. Over three months the front advanced an average of more than 30 kilometres along more than 400 kilometres and took 450,000 Austro-Hungarian prisoners, but the supporting attack from the West Front was not delivered and Germany moved 17 divisions from France and Belgium to halt it.

He was one of eight Russian commanders awarded the Sword of Saint George with Diamonds. After asking for the Tsar's abdication in 1917 under pressure from General Mikhail Alekseyev, he became Commander in Chief on 4 June 1917 and was replaced by Lavr Kornilov after the failure of the Kerensky Offensive.

Brusilov sided with the Bolsheviks in the Russian Civil War. In May 1920 he published an appeal in Pravda to former officers to join the Red Army, and he served on a commission on its size and structure before becoming Inspector of Cavalry. He retired in 1924 and died in Moscow on 17 March 1926 of congestive heart failure; he was buried in the Novodevichy Convent. His memoirs appeared in English in 1930 as A Soldier's Notebook, 1914-1918. Many pro-tsarist historians avoided praising him because of his service in the Red Army, and Anton Denikin portrayed him as having suffered a psychological breakdown during the 1916 offensive. Bernard Montgomery counted him among seven outstanding fighting commanders of the First World War.
alexios-i-komnenos: Alexios was the son of John Komnenos and Anna Dalassene and the nephew of Isaac I Komnenos, emperor from 1057 to 1059. His father had declined the throne when Isaac abdicated, and died a monk in 1067. Alexios and his elder brother Manuel served with distinction against the Seljuk Turks under Romanos IV Diogenes. In 1074 western mercenaries under Roussel de Bailleul rebelled in Asia Minor, and Alexios subdued them by 1076.

In 1078 Nikephoros III made him commander of the field army in the West, and he defeated the rebellions of Nikephoros Bryennios the Elder at the Battle of Kalavrye and of Nikephoros Basilakes. While troops were assembling against the expected Norman invasion under Robert Guiscard, the Doukas faction convinced him to join a conspiracy against Nikephoros III. His mother Anna Dalassene and the empress Maria of Alania played prominent roles in the coup of 1081.

As emperor from 1081, Alexios faced a Norman invasion of the western Balkans under Robert Guiscard and his son Bohemond. After initial defeats he allied with the Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV and had recovered most of the losses by 1085. In 1091 he won a decisive victory over the Pechenegs at the Battle of Levounion in Thrace with help from Cuman allies. In the later 1090s he turned to Asia Minor, most of which had fallen to the Seljuk Turks. His envoys appealed to Pope Urban II at the Council of Piacenza in 1095, and Urban called the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont. It concluded with much of western Anatolia restored to Byzantine rule.

He faced more rebellions than any other Byzantine emperor, from pretenders such as the monk Raictor, the Seljuq Turkic emir Tzachas, who took the title of emperor in 1092, and an impostor claiming to be Leo Diogenes. In 1092 he replaced the debased gold solidus with a gold coin of higher fineness, the hyperpyron. In his last twenty years he lost popularity, persecuted followers of the Paulician and Bogomil heresies, and burned the Bogomil leader Basil at the stake.

Alexios died on 15 August 1118 and was succeeded by his son John II Komnenos, whom he had crowned co-emperor at five in 1092. His daughter Anna Komnene later wrote the Alexiad on his reign. By allying with powerful noble families, he co-opted most of the nobility into his extended family and government, which gave continuity: every later emperor was related to him by descent or marriage. This undermined bureaucratic effectiveness by placing family connections over merit.
alexios-iii-angelos: Alexios was the second son of Andronikos Angelos Doukas and Euphrosyne Kastamonitissa; his paternal grandmother was Theodora Komnene, a daughter of Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, so he belonged to the extended imperial family. Around 1183 he conspired with his father and brothers against Emperor Andronikos I Komnenos and spent several years in exile at Muslim courts, including Saladin's. In 1185 Andronikos ordered his younger brother Isaac II executed; Isaac killed the leader of the agents, took refuge in Hagia Sophia and roused the populace, and the riot that followed deposed Andronikos and made Isaac emperor. By 1190 Alexios had returned to court and received the title sebastokratōr.

In March 1195, while Isaac II was hunting in Thrace, the troops acclaimed Alexios emperor, with the covert support of his wife Euphrosyne Doukaina Kamatera. He captured Isaac at Stagira, blinded him and kept him a close prisoner. To secure his position he scattered money so freely that the treasury emptied, and he gave army officers such licence that the empire was left practically defenceless. In 1196 Emperor Henry VI demanded a tribute of gold, which Alexios raised by plundering imperial tombs. The Seljuk Turks overran the east, and the Kingdom of Hungary, the Bulgarians and the Vlachs raided the Balkan provinces. In 1197 Dobromir Chrysos made himself master of Vardar Macedonia.

In 1202 Alexios IV Angelos, Isaac's son, appealed to the Fourth Crusade assembled at Venice. The crusaders reached Constantinople in June 1203. Alexios III took no effective measures, and his son-in-law Theodore Laskaris was defeated at Scutari. In July the crusaders took part of the walls and set fires that left 20,000 homeless. On 17 July Alexios led out an army that outnumbered them but turned back without fighting, and that night he fled by boat with his daughter Irene and about 1,000 pounds of gold.

From Adrianople and Mosynopolis Alexios tried to rally support, and in 1204 he received Alexios V Doukas, who married his daughter Eudokia and was later blinded and deserted by him. He eventually surrendered to Boniface of Montferrat, escaped in 1205, was recaptured and was ransomed about 1209 by Michael I of Epirus, who sent him to Asia Minor. There he plotted against Theodore Laskaris, now emperor of Nicaea, with the support of Sultan Kaykhusraw I. The sultan was defeated and killed at the Battle of Antioch on the Meander in 1211, and Alexios was captured and confined to a monastery at Nicaea, where he died later that year.
alexis-de-tocqueville: Tocqueville came from an old Norman aristocratic family and was the great-grandson of the statesman Malesherbes, who was guillotined in 1793. He took a law degree at the University of Paris in 1826. In 1831 the July Monarchy gave him a mission to examine prisons in the United States, and he travelled there with his friend Gustave de Beaumont as far as Michigan and New Orleans. He returned within nine months and published a report, The Penitentiary System in the United States.

He sat in the lower house for the Manche department from 1839 to 1851, on the centre-left, and was regarded as parliament's foremost expert on Algeria, which France had invaded in 1830. In the Second Republic he joined the commission drafting the constitution and sided with the Party of Order against the socialists. He opposed Louis Napoléon Bonaparte's coup of 2 December 1851, was detained at Vincennes and released, and withdrew from politics.

Democracy in America, published in 1835 with a second volume in 1840, set out to help the French understand their position between a fading aristocratic order and an emerging democratic one. Tocqueville saw democracy as balancing liberty and equality. He believed that Americans overcame selfish individualism by associating for common purposes, and warned that radical equality could lead to materialism and to new forms of tyranny, a despotism more dangerous than that of the Roman emperors. The book is considered an early work of sociology and political science.
In The Old Regime and the Revolution, begun after he left politics, he argued that the Revolution continued the modernising and centralising of the French state begun under Louis XIV.

Tocqueville suffered from tuberculosis and died of it on 16 April 1859. He was buried in the Tocqueville cemetery in Normandy and survived by his English wife, Mary Mottley, whom he had married in 1836; they had no children. His liberalism has been read in contrasting ways across the political spectrum.
alexis-of-russia: Alexis was born in Moscow on 19 March 1629, the son of Tsar Michael and Eudoxia Streshneva. He came to the throne at sixteen, after his father died on 12 July 1645, and was crowned on 28 September in the Dormition Cathedral. He was placed in the care of his tutor Boris Morozov, a boyar open to Western ideas, who pursued a peaceful foreign policy and in January 1648 arranged the tsar's marriage to Maria Miloslavskaya, marrying her sister Anna himself ten days later.

Morozov's demand for two years of tax arrears, tripling the burden, and his reputation as corrupt led Muscovites to rise against his faction in the Salt Riot of May 1648. The young tsar had to dismiss them and exile Morozov to a monastery. The unrest was partly responsible for the new legal code, the Sobornoye Ulozheniye, issued in 1649.

From 1648 Alexis reformed the army, creating New Order Regiments of reiters, soldiers, dragoons and hussars, with European military specialists made available by the end of the Thirty Years' War. Rebellions followed in Pskov and Novgorod in 1650. By the 1660s the wars with Poland and Sweden strained public finances; copper coins minted from 1654 devalued the ruble and brought the violently suppressed Copper Riot of 1662. In 1669 the Don Cossacks rose under Stenka Razin, who seized towns along the Volga until his failed siege of Simbirsk in October 1670; he was captured in April 1671 and drawn and quartered in Moscow.

In 1653 Alexis took advantage of Poland's disorder after the Khmelnytsky Uprising to attempt to annex parts of White and Little Russia. The 1654 campaign took Smolensk, and the Treaty of Pereyaslav brought Russian dominance over the Cossack Hetmanate in left-bank Ukraine. A war with Sweden from 1656 achieved little, and the Peace of Kardis of 2 July 1661 returned Russia's conquests. The Truce of Andrusovo of 11 February 1667 left Smolensk, Kiev and the eastern bank of the Dnieper with Russia. In 1649 he had broken off relations with England after the execution of Charles I.

In 1653 Patriarch Nikon began reforms to bring Russian Orthodox practice into line with the Greek church, among them making the sign of the cross with three fingers instead of two. Alexis supported him until Nikon abandoned his post in 1658. The Great Moscow Synod of 1666 deposed Nikon and excommunicated those who opposed the reforms, who broke away as the Old Believers and were harshly persecuted. The siege of the Solovetsky Monastery, where some had fled, ended on 22 January 1676. Alexis died on 8 February 1676 and was remembered as Tishayshy, the most quiet. Peter I was his son by his second wife, Natalya Naryshkina.
alfonso-vi-of-castile: Alfonso was the second son of Ferdinand I, King of León and Count of Castile, and Queen Sancha, and so would not normally have inherited the throne. At the end of 1063, probably on 22 December, Ferdinand summoned a Curia Regia at León and announced how his lands would be divided. Alfonso received the Kingdom of León, with Asturias, Astorga, El Bierzo and Zamora, together with the tribute payments (parias) of the taifa of Toledo. His elder brother Sancho received the new Kingdom of Castile and the parias of Zaragoza, and his younger brother García received Galicia, raised to a kingdom, with the parias of Badajoz and Seville.

Alfonso was crowned at León in January 1066. After the death of their mother on 7 November 1067, he faced the ambitions of Sancho II, who considered himself the sole rightful heir, and seven years of war among the three brothers followed. At Llantada the brothers agreed to a trial by ordeal in which the winner would take the loser's kingdom; Sancho won, but Alfonso did not comply. Later the two joined forces to divide García's Galicia between themselves. Alfonso took the title king of Galicia in 1071 and of Castile in 1072.

The conquest of Toledo in 1085 led him to style himself most victorious king of Toledo, of Spain and of Galicia. It also provoked an Almoravid invasion that he spent the rest of his reign resisting. His armies suffered decisive defeats at Sagrajas in 1086, Consuegra in 1097 and Uclés in 1108. At Uclés his only son and heir, Sancho Alfónsez, the child of his concubine Zaida, was killed. Valencia was abandoned, but Toledo remained part of the expanded realm.

Alfonso had five wives and two concubines according to Bishop Pelagius of Oviedo. His daughter Urraca, by Constance of Burgundy, succeeded him. His illegitimate daughter Teresa married Count Henry of Portugal, and their son Afonso Henriques became the first king of Portugal. In May 1107 Alfonso had imposed recognition of Sancho Alfónsez as heir, and after Sancho's death the succession passed to Urraca.

Alfonso died in Toledo on 1 July 1109, where he had come to try to defend the city from an imminent Almoravid attack. He was buried at the Royal Monastery of San Benito in Sahagún. He encouraged the Cluniac reforms in the monasteries of Galicia, León and Castile, made the first grant of a Leonese monastery to Cluny in 1073, and replaced the Mozarabic rite with the Roman one.
alfonso-viii: Alfonso was born at Soria on 11 November 1155, the son of Sancho III of Castile and Blanche, and was named after his grandfather Alfonso VII of León and Castile, who had divided his kingdoms between his sons. His father died in 1158, and the two-year-old king was regarded as nominal by nobles to whom a minority was convenient. The houses of Lara and Castro both claimed the regency, as did his uncle Ferdinand II of León. The regency fell to Manrique Pérez de Lara, and at barely fifteen Alfonso began restoring order, recovering Toledo by surprise from the Laras.

His uncle Sancho VI of Navarre had seized border lands, including much of La Rioja. In 1170 Alfonso sent an embassy to Bordeaux to seek the hand of Eleanor, daughter of Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine, which gave him a powerful ally. In 1188 the Treaty of Seligenstadt made his eldest child Berengaria heiress of Castile after any sons, and at Carrión de los Condes that year Alfonso knighted Alfonso IX of León, who accepted the Castilian king as overlord. Berengaria's marriage to Alfonso IX in 1197 brought a lasting peace, though the pope annulled it.

He took Cuenca on 21 September 1177. The Treaty of Cazola of 1179 defined the zones of expansion of the Christian kingdoms against the Almohads. In 1195 he was roundly defeated at Alarcos by the caliph Abu Yusuf Yaqub al-Mansur, and for seventeen years the frontier stood in the hill country outside Toledo. In 1212, through the mediation of Pope Innocent III, a crusade was called. Aragonese under Peter II, Navarrese under Sancho VII and Franks joined the Castilians. On 16 July they routed the caliph Muhammad al-Nasir at Las Navas de Tolosa.

Alfonso died on 5 October 1214 and was succeeded by his surviving son, Henry I. He founded a studium generale at Palencia, the first Spanish university, though it did not survive him, and with Eleanor he was the first to make the Alcázar of Segovia a residence. Through his daughters Berengaria and Blanche he was the grandfather of two monarchs who became saints.
alfonso-x-of-castile: Alfonso was born on 23 November 1221 in Toledo, the eldest son of Ferdinand III and Elizabeth (Beatrice) of Swabia. His mother was a cousin of Emperor Frederick II, to whom he is often compared. For his first nine years he was heir only to Castile; then his father united the kingdoms of Castile and León. He began as a soldier under his father at sixteen, and in the 1240s he helped conquer Muslim strongholds in Al-Andalus, among them Murcia, Alicante and Cádiz. In 1249 he married Violante, daughter of King James I of Aragon.

Alfonso succeeded his father in 1252. He invaded Portugal in 1253 and took the Algarve, which he returned in 1263. In 1254 he allied with Henry III of England and renounced Castile's claim to Gascony when his half-sister Eleanor married Henry's son Edward. In 1256 his descent from the Hohenstaufen gave him a claim to the German crown, and a dissident faction elected him king of Germany in 1257. He never went to Germany, while his rival Richard of Cornwall was crowned at Aachen. To raise money he debased the coinage, then set an arbitrary tariff to hold prices down, which ruined what trade there was. His nobles rebelled in 1272, and in 1275 the Pope won his oral renunciation of the imperial claim.

His eldest son Ferdinand died in 1275 at the Battle of Écija, leaving two infant sons. Alfonso's second son Sancho claimed to be heir, with the nobles' support, and a civil war led Alfonso in 1282 to accept Sancho. Only Seville, Murcia and Badajoz stayed loyal to the king. He died at Seville in 1284, leaving a will that tried to exclude Sancho and a legacy of civil war. In 1273 he created the Mesta, an association of sheep owners, which later grew powerful.

Alfonso's court employed Jewish, Christian and Muslim scholars who translated works from Arabic and Hebrew into Latin and Castilian under his supervision, and Castilian came to replace Latin in the royal chancery. Their main work was in astronomy and astrology, including the Alfonsine tables based on the calculations of al-Zarqali. He sponsored the Crónica general, finished in 1264, and the General Estoria, a world history left incomplete at the birth of Christ. He began the Siete Partidas, one of the most comprehensive law codes of medieval Europe, though it was promulgated only by his great-grandson. His Cantigas de Santa Maria, in Galician–Portuguese, comprise 420 poems with musical notation, mostly on miracles attributed to the Virgin Mary.
alfonso-xii: Alfonso was born in Madrid on 28 November 1857, the eldest son of Queen Isabella II. His official father, her husband Francisco de Asís, was generally viewed as effeminate, impotent or homosexual, which led writers to question Alfonso's paternity. When the Revolution of 1868 forced Isabella to leave Spain, he went with her to Paris and was sent to study at the Theresianum in Vienna. On 25 June 1870 his mother abdicated in his favour in Paris.

The Cortes chose Prince Amadeo of Savoy as king in November 1870, but he abdicated in early 1873 after attacks on his life and the outbreak of the Third Carlist War. The First Spanish Republic followed, facing war in Cuba, uprisings in Spanish Morocco and the Carlist rising. Antonio Cánovas del Castillo led a group favouring a Bourbon Restoration and took charge of Alfonso's education, sending him to the Royal Military College, Sandhurst.

On 1 December 1874 Alfonso issued the Sandhurst Manifesto, which set out the ideological basis of the Restoration and proclaimed him the sole representative of the Spanish monarchy. At the end of 1874 Brigadier Martínez Campos led battalions to Sagunto, rallied the troops sent against him and entered Valencia in the king's name. The republic's president resigned and power passed to Cánovas. Alfonso was proclaimed king on 29 December 1874. In 1876 a campaign against the Carlists, in which he took part, ended with the defeat of Don Carlos.

Cánovas was the real architect of the Restoration, which proved a civilian regime lasting until Primo de Rivera's coup in 1923. The Constitution of 1876 and the Pact of El Pardo of 1885 endorsed turnismo, the alternation of conservative and liberal prime ministers. In 1881 Alfonso refused to sanction a law fixing ministers' terms at 18 months, and when Cánovas resigned he called the Liberal leader Práxedes Mateo Sagasta to form a government.

Alfonso died on 25 November 1885, aged 27, at the Royal Palace of El Pardo near Madrid. He had tuberculosis, but the immediate cause of death was a recurrence of dysentery. His widow, pregnant, became regent, and their son Alfonso XIII was born in 1886. Alfonso had won popular affection by visiting districts struck by cholera and by the Andalusian earthquake of 1884. His reign is credited with ending the political instability of the previous decades, and a monument to him by José Grases Riera was completed in the Parque del Buen Retiro in Madrid in 1922.
alfonso-xiii: Alfonso XIII was born at the Royal Palace of Madrid on 17 May 1886, the posthumous son of Alfonso XII, who had died in November 1885, and so he became king at birth. His mother, Maria Christina of Austria, served as regent until his sixteenth birthday in 1902. During the regency, in 1898, Spain lost Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines to the United States in the Spanish–American War.

He received largely a military education, which gave him a Spanish nationalism strengthened by a military vocation, and he often presented himself as a soldier-king. He took his oath to the constitution before the Cortes on 17 May 1902. In 1906 he married Princess Victoria Eugenie of Battenberg, and their wedding was marred by an attempt on the king's life, from which he emerged unharmed.

Like other European monarchs of his time Alfonso played a political role, which involved a controversial use of his constitutional powers. He helped to keep Spain neutral in the First World War, using his links with other royal families, and was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize in 1917 for his work with the European War Office.

Several factors weakened his constitutional legitimacy: the breakdown of the turno system, the crisis of the Restoration system in the 1910s, a trio of crises in 1917, and the violence in Morocco. The dictatorship of Miguel Primo de Rivera was installed in 1923 through a military coup, and the king acquiesced.

When the dictatorship failed, Alfonso withdrew his support, Primo de Rivera resigned in 1930, and the king tried to return to the position before 1923, but he had lost most of his political capital. On 12 April 1931 a republican coalition won a sweeping majority in the major cities in the municipal elections, which were seen as a plebiscite on the monarchy. The Civil Guard's José Sanjurjo reportedly told ministers that the armed forces could not be relied on to sustain the monarchy. Alfonso left Spain, and the Second Spanish Republic was peacefully proclaimed on 14 April 1931.

In November 1931 the Constituent Cortes debated his responsibility as king, citing interference in state institutions, his use of the army, and his part in the operation that ended in the disaster at Annual. It passed an act declaring him guilty of high treason.

On 15 January 1941 Alfonso renounced his rights to the Spanish throne in favour of his son Juan, and he died in Rome on 28 February 1941 of angina pectoris. His remains were moved to El Escorial in January 1980. He promoted tourism, including state-run lodges called Paradores, and patronised football clubs that took the title Real, the first being Deportivo de La Coruña in 1907.
alfred-deakin: Alfred Deakin was born on 3 August 1856 in Fitzroy, Melbourne, the younger of two children of William and Sarah Deakin, who were of English and Welsh descent. They had emigrated from Britain in 1850 during an economic depression and moved from Adelaide to Melbourne because of the Victorian gold rush. His father worked in the carrying and coaching trade and later for Cobb and Co, earning enough to keep the family comfortably middle class. Deakin worked as a barrister and journalist and in February 1879, aged 23, stood for West Bourke in the Victorian Legislative Assembly, winning in a general election in July 1880 after a first result was voided.

Deakin held Victorian ministerial office from 1883 and in the 1890s became a leading figure in the federation of the Australian colonies. He was a delegate to the federal conventions, served on the committees that drafted the constitution, campaigned at the referendums and lobbied the British government for its adoption. After Federation in 1901 he was the first attorney-general under his friend Edmund Barton, and he became prime minister on 24 September 1903 when Barton left for the High Court.

He served three terms, 1903 to 1904, 1905 to 1908 and 1909 to 1910, leading a Liberal Protectionist party that held the middle ground between Free Traders and the Australian Labor Party. His second term, the longest, saw laws such as the Copyright Act 1905 and the Quarantine Act 1908 and the founding of the Commonwealth Bureau of Census and Statistics and Bureau of Meteorology. In 1909 he joined the Free Traders and Joseph Cook in the Fusion, forming Australia's first majority government; some, including Sir William Lyne, called it a betrayal. Labor won both houses in 1910, and Deakin led the opposition, campaigning against constitutional amendments in 1911, until he retired in 1913.

In 1914 he chaired a royal commission on wartime food supply and in 1915 led the Australian delegation to the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco. A degenerative neurological condition led to his death on 7 October 1919, aged 63. Contemporaries called him Affable Alfred. He is regarded as the principal architect of the Australian settlement, which combined the White Australia policy, compulsory arbitration, protectionism, state paternalism and support for the British Empire. He refused a knighthood, appointment to the Privy Council and most honorary degrees.
alfred-dreyfus: Alfred Dreyfus was born in Mulhouse, Alsace, on 9 October 1859, the youngest of nine children of Raphaël and Jeannette Dreyfus. His family belonged to a long established Alsatian Jewish family, and his father became a prosperous industrialist who started a cotton mill. After the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 and the German annexation of Alsace-Lorraine, the family moved to Basel and later to Paris. Seeing his family uprooted by the war prompted him to choose a military career.

He entered the École Polytechnique in October 1877 and was commissioned a sub-lieutenant in 1880. He became a captain in 1889, married Lucie Eugénie Hadamard in 1891, and graduated ninth in his class from the École Supérieure de Guerre, afterwards joining the General Staff as its only Jewish officer.

A torn-up note, the bordereau, was found in a wastebasket at the German Embassy and passed to French intelligence. It showed that information on artillery was reaching the German military attaché Maximilian von Schwartzkoppen. Suspicion fell on Dreyfus, who was arrested for treason on 15 October 1894. A closed court martial convicted him on 22 December 1894 and sentenced him to life imprisonment on Devil's Island. On 5 January 1895 he was formally degraded in the courtyard of the École Militaire, crying out: I swear that I am innocent.

In August 1896 Lieutenant Colonel Georges Picquart found evidence that the traitor was Major Ferdinand Walsin Esterhazy, and was transferred to Tunisia. Esterhazy was acquitted by a secret court martial. Émile Zola's J'Accuse...! of 1898 brought new momentum to the campaign. A second trial in 1899 again found Dreyfus guilty, but President Émile Loubet pardoned him that year. A military commission exonerated him on 12 July 1906, and he was reinstated as a major.

Dreyfus returned as a reserve artillery major when the First World War began, was promoted to lieutenant colonel, and served mostly behind the lines, though in 1917 he was at Verdun and the Chemin des Dames. He died in Paris on 12 July 1935, aged 75, and was buried in the Montparnasse Cemetery. A statue of Dreyfus holding his broken sword stands on Boulevard Raspail, and his family gave over three thousand documents to the Museum of Jewish Art and History in Paris.
alfred-nobel: Alfred Nobel was born in Stockholm on 21 October 1833, the third son of the inventor and engineer Immanuel Nobel and Andriette Nobel. The family was impoverished, and only Alfred and his three brothers survived childhood. After business failures Immanuel went bankrupt and moved to Saint Petersburg, where he grew successful as a manufacturer of machine tools and explosives. In 1842 the family joined him. Private tutors taught the boy, who excelled in chemistry and languages and became proficient in Swedish, French, Russian, English, German and Italian. His only schooling was eighteen months at the Jacobs Apologistic School in Stockholm, and he never attended university.

Nobel studied with the chemist Nikolai Zinin, and in 1850 he went to Paris, where he met Ascanio Sobrero, who had synthesized nitroglycerin three years before. Sobrero opposed its use because it was unpredictable, but Nobel set out to find a way to control it as a commercial explosive. He filed his first patent, for a gas meter, in 1857, and invented a detonator in 1863 and the blasting cap in 1865. On 3 September 1864 a shed used for preparing nitroglycerin exploded at the factory in Heleneborg, killing five people, including his younger brother Emil; he lost his licence to produce explosives and founded Nitroglycerin AB in Vinterviken, in a more isolated area.

In 1867 he patented dynamite, nitroglycerin absorbed in kieselguhr, which was safer to handle, and first demonstrated it at a quarry in Redhill, Surrey. He took the name from the Greek word for power. Gelignite followed in the 1870s and ballistite in 1887. His brothers Ludvig and Robert founded the oil company Branobel, which operated mainly in Baku, and Nobel invested in it. During his life he was issued 355 patents, and by his death his business had established more than 90 explosives and armament factories.

On 27 November 1895, at the Swedish-Norwegian Club in Paris, Nobel signed his last will, setting aside 94 per cent of his assets, 31,225,000 Swedish kronor, to establish the five Nobel Prizes, to be awarded without distinction of nationality. A well-known story that a premature French obituary, calling him the merchant of death, moved him to this has not been verified, and some historians dismiss it as a myth. He had developed angina pectoris by 1895, and he died on 10 December 1896 after a stroke, aged 63. He never married. In 1968 Sveriges Riksbank gave the Nobel Foundation funds for a prize in economics in his honour, which has been disputed as a true Nobel Prize.
alfred-the-great: Alfred was the youngest son of King Æthelwulf of Wessex and his first wife Osburh. His grandfather Ecgberht became king of Wessex in 802. Asser, writing in 893, says Alfred was born at Wantage in Berkshire, though the West Saxon genealogical lists imply a slightly earlier date, and historians differ over the exact year. His public life began in 865, at 16, when Æthelred came to the throne, and Asser gave him the title secundarius, perhaps marking him as a recognised successor.

Æthelred died in April 871, leaving two under-age sons, and Alfred became king in accordance with an agreement the brothers had made earlier that year at Swinbeorg. After his victory at Edington in 878 he made an agreement with the Vikings dividing England between Anglo-Saxon territory and the Danelaw, and oversaw the conversion of the Viking leader Guthrum to Christianity. In 886 he began styling himself King of the Anglo-Saxons after reoccupying London.

In the late 880s or early 890s he issued a law code, a domboc, combining his own laws with those of Ine of Wessex in 120 chapters. He said he kept the laws that pleased him and rejected others on the advice of his councillors. He also began a revival of learning, perhaps inspired by Charlemagne, recruiting scholars from Mercia, Wales and abroad and having Latin works the king thought most necessary for all men to know translated into English. A chronicle of the rise of his house gave the West Saxon kings a genealogy back to Adam.

Alfred married Ealhswith, daughter of a Mercian nobleman, in 868. Their children included Edward the Elder, who succeeded him, and Æthelflæd, who became lady of the Mercians. He died on 26 October 899 at 50 or 51; how he died is unknown, though Asser's description of a lifelong painful illness has led modern doctors to suggest Crohn's disease or haemorrhoids. His will is the oldest to survive of any English king. He has been called the Great since at least the 13th century, though the epithet was popularised only from the 16th, and he is the only native-born English monarch given it.
alfredo-stroessner: Alfredo Stroessner Matiauda was born in Encarnación on 3 November 1912. His father, Hugo Stroessner, was an accountant from Hof in Bavaria who had emigrated to Paraguay in the late 1890s; his mother, Heriberta Matiauda, was of Guaraní and Spanish criollo descent. He joined the Paraguayan army at the age of 16 and, after attending military school in Asunción, fought in the Chaco War against Bolivia, reaching the rank of first lieutenant by its end.

In the 1947 Paraguayan Civil War he supported the Colorado Party and played an important role in its victory. Opposition parties had been banned from 1947. In 1951 he became commander-in-chief of the army.

Stroessner objected to President Federico Chaves's plan to arm the national police and removed him in a coup on 4 May 1954. The National Assembly appointed Tomás Romero Pereira president, and he called special elections. Stroessner was the Colorado Party's nominee and won on 11 July 1954 as the only candidate. He took office on 15 August 1954 and was re-elected seven times, in 1958, 1963, 1968, 1973, 1978, 1983 and 1988, nearly always by margins above 80 percent. The constitution of 1967 permitted his re-election, and changes in 1977 effectively allowed indefinite rule.

Soon after taking office he placed the country under a state of siege, which allowed indefinite detention without trial and banned public meetings. It was renewed every 90 days until 1987, apart from a brief period in 1959, and in practice it applied to Asunción only after 1970. He was a committed anti-communist who brought Paraguay into the World Anti-Communist League and justified repression as a defence of the country. He gave a free hand to the military and to the Minister of the Interior, Edgar Ynsfrán, and relied on Colorado Party militias to crush dissent.

Lieutenant General Andrés Rodríguez Pedotti, his confidant, seized power in a coup on 2 and 3 February 1989, and Stroessner went into exile in Brazil on 5 February. He died in Brasília on 16 August 2006, aged 93. Puerto Presidente Stroessner, named for him, became Ciudad del Este in 1989. In 1992 the so-called Archives of Terror were found, documents showing that his government took part in Operation Condor, the anti-communist agreement for persecuting exiles.

His government exiled 20,814 Paraguayans. Around 425 to 500 people were forcibly disappeared, and an estimated 18,000 to 20,000 were tortured or otherwise abused. His 35 years in office were the longest of any South American ruler. His supporters, known as Stronistas, still hold that his was a time of security and stability.
algarve: The Algarve lies in the southernmost area of continental Portugal and the southwesternmost area of mainland Europe, covering 4,997 km2. It borders the Alentejo region to the north and the Atlantic Ocean to the south and west, while the Guadiana River marks the border with Spain on the east. The highest point is Pico da Fóia, 902 m, in the Monchique mountains. The Ria Formosa Lagoon, a nature reserve of over 170 km2, is a stopping place for hundreds of bird species. The western part of the region is called Barlavento and the east Sotavento.

Human presence in southern Portugal dates back to the Paleolithic and Neolithic periods, attested by megalithic stones at Vila do Bispo, Lagos and Alcoutim. Around 1000 BCE the Phoenicians founded Cádiz and, subsequently, ports along the Algarve coast. By the sixth century BCE the Cynetes, called Conii in Latin, were established in the region, then called Cyneticum; their ethnic and linguistic origins remain widely disputed.

The region came under Roman control after Fabius Maximus Servilianus defeated the Lusitanians and the Turduli, and remained under Roman influence for around 600 years, from 200 BCE to 410 CE. The name Algarve comes from the Arabic al-ġarb, meaning the west, that is, Western Al-Andalus; the Portuguese used it for the lands to their south under Muslim control, and it narrowed to the southwesternmost region.

After victories over the Wattasids in 1471 won Asilah and Tangier, the Portuguese called their North African possessions the Algarve-Beyond-the-Sea. Portuguese monarchs held the title of King or Queen of the Algarves until the Portuguese Republic was established.

The Algarve is the southernmost NUTS II region of continental Portugal, with 16 municipalities and its administrative centre at Faro, where the University of Algarve is also located. Surviving traces of the past include the Roman ruins of Milreu at Estói, the Megalithic Monuments of Alcalar, the Ribat of Arrifana, and Vila Real de Santo António, an example of the Marquis of Pombal's urban planning after the 1755 earthquake.
algebra: Algebra began in attempts to solve problems involving arithmetic calculations and unknown quantities, in Babylonia, Egypt, Greece, China and India. One of the earliest documents is the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus from Egypt, written around 1650 BCE, which solves linear equations. Babylonian clay tablets of about the same time explain methods for linear and quadratic equations, including completing the square. The Greeks used algebraic methods to solve geometric problems, and in the 3rd century CE Diophantus treated equations in his Arithmetica and was the first to experiment with symbolic notation for polynomials.

Whether these early works are algebra or only precursors is disputed, since they treated specific cases. In 825 CE Muḥammad ibn Mūsā al-Khwārizmī published The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing. He classified equations into six standard forms and gave systematic step-by-step procedures, abstracted from particular geometric figures, which made algebra a self-contained discipline distinct from geometry. Thābit ibn Qurra in the 9th century and Omar Khayyam in the 11th and 12th also contributed.

The word comes from the Arabic al-jabr, which originally referred to the surgical treatment of bonesetting. Al-Khwārizmī used it in the 9th century to name a method of transforming equations, and his treatise was translated into Latin as Liber Algebrae et Almucabola. The word entered English in the 16th century and at first meant only the theory of equations. Equations were described in words and abbreviations until the 16th and 17th centuries, when a rigorous symbolic formalism developed.

In the mid-19th century the scope widened to cover many kinds of algebraic operations and structures and the laws, called axioms, that they follow. Elementary algebra, taught in schools, generalises arithmetic by using variables for unknown quantities; linear algebra studies systems of linear equations; abstract algebra studies structures such as groups, rings and fields. Its methods also serve geometry, topology, number theory, calculus and logic.
algeciras: Algeciras stands on the western shore of the Bay of Gibraltar, opposite the Rock of Gibraltar and near the Strait of Gibraltar, the narrowest crossing between Europe and Africa. The Arabic name al-Jazira al-Khadra means green island or green peninsula. The traditional explanation derives it from the small island of Isla Verde, but this has been questioned, since Arab sources called that island Umm Hakim. The site was also that of the Roman port of Portus Albus and of the town of Iulia Traducta, and the earliest remains are Neanderthal.

In 859 Viking ships under Hastein and Björn Ironside besieged the city for three days, laid waste to much of it and burnt its two main mosques, but the inhabitants regrouped and drove them out. In 914 the Cordobese emir Abd al-Rahman III took the city, which had supported rebels, and had shipbuilding docks built for the Umayyad navy. It was an independent taifa from 1035 to 1058. In 1274 Nasrid Granada ceded it to the Marinids, and after 1282 Abu Yusuf built a walled precinct, al-Bunayya, across the Río de la Miel. Alfonso X of Castile besieged the city in 1278 without success.

Ferdinand IV of Castile laid the first siege in 1309. Alfonso XI began a second in 1342, and the city surrendered in March 1344. He made it the seat of a diocese, whose bishops of Cadiz held the title Aliezira until 1851, and Genoese and Catalan traders settled there. The Nasrids of Granada seized the town in 1369 with a Marinid fleet and Muhammed V of Granada ordered it destroyed; some date this scorched-earth policy to 1375. Refugees from Gibraltar refounded it after the Anglo-Dutch capture of that town in 1704. In 1705 it was described as a heap of stones, and in 1760 Charles III rebuilt it on its present rectangular plan.

The Algeciras campaign between the French and Spanish navies and the Royal Navy took place off the city in July 1801. In 1906 the town hall hosted the Algeciras Conference on the future of Morocco, which confirmed Morocco's independence against German threats and gave France control of banking and police interests.

Algeciras is a municipality of the province of Cádiz in Andalusia, with a registered population of 123,078 in 2020, the largest in the Campo de Gibraltar. Its port is the main crossing point between Spain and Tangier and other ports in Morocco, the Canary Islands, Ceuta and Melilla. The city is also a fishing and industrial centre.
algeria: Algeria is the largest country in Africa and the Mediterranean basin, covering 2,381,741 square kilometres. The Sahara covers most of it. In the north, the Tell Atlas and the Saharan Atlas form two parallel sets of reliefs, and the area from the coast to the Tell Atlas is fertile; south of it lies steppe, then the desert. The highest point is Mount Tahat, at 3,003 metres, in the Hoggar Mountains of the central Sahara. About 90% of Algerians live in the northern coastal area, and Algiers, Oran, Constantine and Annaba are the main cities.

Early finds show that hominins lived on the Mediterranean fringe of northern Africa earlier than previously thought. Neolithic life, richly depicted in the Tassili n'Ajjer paintings, predominated until the classical period. The Carthaginians established settlements on the coast, and by 600 BCE a Phoenician presence existed at places such as Icosium, now Algiers, and Hippo Regius.

They avoided conquering the strong Berber tribes of the interior, collected tribute and traded, and the Berbers supplied them with goods, slaves and skilled cavalry. Amazigh societies, among them the Numidians, whose kingdom became one of the earliest major states in the region, were also shaped by Roman, Vandal and Byzantine influences.

From the 7th century the spread of Islam and the arrival of Arab tribes gradually transformed the region, and from the 8th to the 15th centuries local Islamic dynasties ruled. The Regency of Algiers, established in 1516, became a largely autonomous state owing nominal allegiance to the Ottoman Empire. France invaded in 1830 and formally annexed Algeria in 1848, though it was not fully conquered until 1903. French rule brought mass European settlement that displaced the local population, and by the mid-1870s indigenous Algerians had declined by up to a third through warfare, disease and starvation.

Resistance to French colonisation ran from the campaigns of Emir Abdelkader and the Mokrani Revolt to the nationalist movements of the 20th century. The Sétif and Guelma massacre in 1945 catalysed the resistance that led to the outbreak of the Algerian War in 1954, and Algeria gained independence in 1962. A civil war lasted from 1992 to 2002. The country is a semi-presidential republic with a population of about 47 million. Its official languages are Arabic and Amazigh, most people speak Algerian Arabic, and Sunni Islam is the official religion.
algerian-war: France captured Algiers in June 1830, on the pretext of a slight to its consul, after Charles X and his ministers decided in January of that year on an invasion. The conquest spread inland under Marshal Bugeaud, the first Governor-General, and was violent, marked by a scorched earth policy. Between 500,000 and 1,000,000 of about 3 million Algerians are estimated to have been killed in the first three decades. Algeria was declared an integral part of France by the Constitution of 1848, in three departments, and French and other Europeans settled there; they later became known as the pieds-noirs.

The war effectively began on 1 November 1954, the Toussaint Rouge, when guerrillas of the National Liberation Front (FLN) attacked military and civilian targets across Algeria. The FLN was weak at first, and its armed wing had only some 3,000 badly equipped men. According to the historian Natalya Vince, its leaders knew they could not win militarily and used guerrilla warfare and urban terrorism to erode France's political will and expose French repression.

They also worked to internationalise the conflict, which became entangled with the Cold War. French forces used torture, indiscriminate shootings and bombing of villages, destroyed over 8,000 villages and moved over 2 million Algerians into regroupment camps. More than 12,000 Algerians died in FLN purges. Reports of torture reaching France in 1956 and 1957 made it known there as la sale guerre, the dirty war.

The war brought down the Fourth Republic in 1958, replaced by the Fifth with a stronger presidency. Charles de Gaulle opened negotiations with the FLN, which ended in the Évian Accords of March 1962.
