At first it was the general assembly of the Icelandic Commonwealth, where the most powerful leaders, the goðar, met to decide legislation and dispense justice. All free men could attend, and it was usually the main social event of the year. The centre was the Lögberg, or Law Rock, where the Lawspeaker presided and recited the laws in effect.

The Gulathing Law was adopted at the first Althing in 930, introduced by Úlfljótr, who had spent three years in Norway studying its laws. According to Njáls saga, the Althing declared Christianity the official religion in 1000, after Thorgeir Ljosvetningagodi, a pagan chieftain, proposed one law and one religion for the whole of Iceland.

The legislative section, the Lögrétta, was the most powerful institution. It comprised the 39 district chieftains, nine additional members and the Lawspeaker. After the country was divided into four quarters around 965 a court of 36 judges was set up for each at the Althing. When the Icelanders submitted to the Norwegian king under the Old Covenant of 1262, the Commonwealth ended and the goðar ceased to rule. The Lögrétta, now of 36 members, shared legislative power with the king. When Denmark introduced absolute monarchy, Icelanders gave up the right to initiate and consent to legislation, and the Althing served almost only as a court.

A royal decree disbanded it in 1800, and a High Court in Reykjavík took over its functions. A decree of 1843 provided for a new Althing, which met in Reykjavík on 1 July 1845 as a consultative assembly of 26 members, elected by only about 5 percent of the population. The Constitution of 1874 gave it joint legislative power with the Crown, and it met from 1881 in the newly built Parliament House. A constitutional amendment confirmed on 3 October 1903 granted home rule. The Act of Union took effect on 1 December 1918, and the Althing declared the republic at a session at Þingvellir on 17 June 1944.

The Althing claims to be the longest-running parliament in the world. Its two chambers were merged into one in 1991. The unicameral parliament now has 63 members, elected every four years by party-list proportional representation, and sits in the Alþingishús, built of hewn Icelandic stone in 1881.
alvar-aalto: Hugo Alvar Henrik Aalto was born on 3 February 1898 in Kuortane, Finland. His father, Johan Henrik Aalto, was a Finnish-speaking land surveyor, and his mother, Selma Matilda Hackstedt, was a Swedish-speaking postmistress. The family moved to Alajärvi and then to Jyväskylä. In 1916 he began to study architecture at the Helsinki University of Technology, interrupted by the Finnish Civil War, in which he fought on the White side. He graduated in 1921, opened an office in Jyväskylä in 1923 and on 6 October 1924 married the architect Aino Marsio.

His career ran from the 1920s to the 1970s. His style moved from the Nordic Classicism of his early houses and first public buildings, such as the Jyväskylä Workers' Club of 1925, to a rational International Style modernism in the 1930s and then to a more organic modernism from the 1940s. His first completed church, at Muurame, shows the transition to Functionalism. In 1949 Sigfried Giedion's Space, Time and Architecture gave him more attention than any other modernist architect, including Le Corbusier. He received the Royal Gold Medal of the Royal Institute of British Architects in 1957.

Aalto saw architecture as a total work of art, and with Aino he designed the building together with its interior surfaces, furniture, lamps and glassware. He regarded painting and sculpture as branches of the tree whose trunk is architecture. He invented a form of laminated bent-plywood furniture in 1932, patented in 1933, and was the first furniture designer to use the cantilever principle in wooden chairs. The ceiling of the Vyborg Library is an undulating wave of red-hearted pine, and the stairway at Villa Mairea evokes a forest with beech columns bound with withes.

His standing has been questioned. The historians Manfredo Tafuri and Francesco Dal Co argued that his historical significance had perhaps been exaggerated and that his architecture was unsuited to urban types, while in his last decade fellow Finnish architects found his work unfashionably individualistic beside rationalism and constructivism.
alvaro-obregon: Álvaro Obregón was born on 19 February 1880 at Siquisiva, near Navojoa in Sonora, the eighteenth child of Francisco Obregón and Cenobia Salido. His father had once owned a large estate, but the Liberal government confiscated it in 1867 because his business partner had supported Emperor Maximilian, and he died in the year of Álvaro's birth. The boy grew up in straitened circumstances with his mother and sisters, a poor relation of a locally prominent family. Sonora's economy was tied closely to the United States, and Obregón made a living as a young man by farming garbanzos; in 1909 he invented a garbanzo harvester and founded a company to manufacture it.

Obregón took no part in Francisco Madero's rising of 1910. He volunteered in April 1912 to oppose Pascual Orozco's revolt, winning battles by traps and surprise assaults, and rose to colonel. After the coup of February 1913 that brought Victoriano Huerta to power he joined the Revolution under Venustiano Carranza and became the Constitutionalist Army's most prominent general along with Pancho Villa. In 1915 he defeated Villa, though he lost his right arm. Carranza made him Minister of War, and he founded a staff college, a school of military medicine and a department of aviation. In 1920 he, Plutarco Elías Calles and Adolfo de la Huerta ousted Carranza under the Plan of Agua Prieta.

As president from 1920 to 1924 he named José Vasconcelos Secretary of Public Education; about 1,000 rural schools and 2,000 public libraries were built, and Mexican muralism began. In August 1923 he signed the Bucareli Treaty on rights of U.S. oil interests, which brought U.S. diplomatic recognition. When he chose Calles as his successor, de la Huerta rebelled; Obregón took the field and defeated him with U.S. arms and aircraft.

After Calles took office in 1924 Obregón farmed in the Yaqui Valley, introducing modern irrigation. In October 1926 Congress repealed term limits, and he won the 1928 election, after two old allies who opposed his re-election, Francisco Serrano and Arnulfo R. Gómez, were killed. On 17 July 1928, before he could take office, José de León Toral, a Roman Catholic opposed to the government's anti-Catholic policies, shot him at La Bombilla Café in Mexico City, during the Cristero War. Toral was tried and executed by firing squad.

The assassination caused a political crisis, resolved when Calles founded the National Revolutionary Party, later the Institutional Revolutionary Party. The historian Linda B. Hall called Obregón the organiser, peacemaker and unifier. He is generally seen as one of the revolution's ultimate victors, but has no posthumous cult like those of Villa and Emiliano Zapata.
alzey: Alzey lies in Rhenish Hesse, on the western edge of the northern Upper Rhine Plain, about 30 kilometres south-west of Mainz and 22 kilometres north-west of Worms. It is surrounded by the northern part of the Alzey Hills. The river Selz, a tributary of the Rhine, flows through the town, in places underground. The climate is oceanic, with low annual rainfall of about 535 millimetres. The town is also called Volkerstadt, because it is one of the Nibelungenstädte: the character Volker von Alzey appears in the Nibelungenlied.

Settlement in the area goes back to the Neolithic. Alzey was founded as a Roman vicus in the province of Germania Superior, and its name first appears on an altar stone dedicated to the nymphs on 22 November 223 by the Vicani Altiaienses, the villagers of Alzey. The village was destroyed about 350, and the fort Castra Alteium was built over it about 390. The Burgundians settled here as Roman confederates after 406 and 407, and their kingdom was destroyed in 436 by the Roman general Flavius Aëtius with Hunnish help, events worked into the Nibelungenlied. Alzey later passed to the Alamanni and the Franks, and in 897 it is first mentioned as an imperial fief.

By 1156 Alzey belonged to the Palatinate, and Konrad von Staufen became count palatine in the imperial castle, which was completed in 1118. Rudolf von Habsburg gave it the rank of town in 1277. Spanish forces under Ambrogio Spinola took it in 1620 in the Thirty Years' War, and in 1689 French troops burned the town and castle in the Nine Years' War. France annexed it in 1798, and it passed to the Grand Duchy of Hesse in 1816. A winemaking school founded in 1909 had Georg Scheu as its first head, and the Scheurebe grape is named after him.

Alzey is the fifth-largest town in Rhenish Hesse and the seat of the Alzey-Worms district. Since 1947 it has belonged to Rhineland-Palatinate. It is a centre of wine growing, with a well-kept old town of timber-frame houses within the ruins of the medieval town wall, and a winemakers' festival each September. The town has a history museum.

A Jewish community is recorded from the 14th century. Its members were murdered in 1349 during the Black Death, and it was renewed some years later. The synagogue built in 1791 was destroyed on 9 November 1938, and 76 Jews were deported from the town.
amadeo-i-of-spain: Amadeo was born in Turin on 30 May 1845, the second son of Victor Emmanuel II, later the first king of a unified Italy, and of Archduchess Adelaide of Austria. He bore the title Duke of Aosta from birth. He entered the Royal Sardinian Army as a captain in 1859 and fought in the Third Italian War of Independence in 1866 with the rank of major-general, leading his brigade at the Battle of Custoza and being wounded at Monte Croce. On 30 May 1867 he married Donna Maria Vittoria dal Pozzo, a Piedmontese noblewoman and sole heir to her father's large fortune. Victor Emmanuel had at first opposed the match.

After the Glorious Revolution deposed Isabella II in September 1868, the new Cortes looked for a liberal candidate from a new dynasty. The Duke of Aosta, descended on both sides from Spanish kings, was elected king on 16 November 1870. While he travelled to Spain, General Juan Prim, his chief supporter, was assassinated, and Amadeo swore to uphold the 1869 Constitution in Madrid on 2 January 1871 in the presence of Prim's corpse. The progressive faction later split between Prim's two successors, Práxedes Mateo Sagasta and Manuel Ruiz Zorrilla.

General Serrano headed the first government and organised the first elections under Amadeo, which returned a majority of 235 seats for the governing coalition. The opposition nonetheless included 52 Republicans, 51 Carlists and 18 Moderates, and the coalition was fragile. The reign met growing republicanism, Carlist rebellions in the north and the Cuban independence movement. After about three years Amadeo abdicated and returned to Italy in 1873, and the First Spanish Republic was declared.

Back in Italy, Amadeo resumed the title Duke of Aosta. The Republic lasted less than two years, and in November 1874 Alfonso XII, the son of Isabella II, was proclaimed king. Maria Vittoria died in 1876, leaving three sons, and in 1888 Amadeo married his niece Princess Maria Letizia Bonaparte. He remained in Turin until his death on 18 January 1890, and his friend Puccini composed the elegy Crisantemi for string quartet in his memory. The Philippine municipality of Amadeo in Cavite, established in 1872, and Lake Amadeus in central Australia, named by the explorer Ernest Giles, are named after him.
amadeus-viii-duke-of-savoy: Amadeus was born in Chambéry on 4 September 1383, the son of Amadeus VII, Count of Savoy, and Bonne of Berry. He became count in 1391, when his father died on 2 November, a death attributed to poisoning or at least bad treatment by his physicians. His father's testament had named his own mother Bonne of Bourbon as regent rather than his wife, which set off a struggle at court between grandmother and mother that drew in the dukes of Berry, Bourbon and Orléans and King Charles VI of France. The grandmother acted as regent until 1397.

His early rule saw the centralisation of power and the territorial expansion of Savoy. In 1416 Sigismund, King of the Romans, raised him to Duke of Savoy, the first to hold the ducal title. In 1418 his cousin and brother-in-law Louis of Piedmont, the last male of the elder branch of the House of Savoy, died, leaving Amadeus as his heir-general and uniting the male lines of the house. From 1401 to 1422 he campaigned to recover the area around Geneva and Annecy, and he encouraged attempts to negotiate an end to the Hundred Years' War.

After his wife Mary of Burgundy died in 1428, he founded the Order of Saint Maurice with six other knights in 1434. They lived in a quasi-monastic state at the castle of Ripaille near Geneva, under a rule he drew up himself, while his son Louis acted as regent of the duchy. Amadeus was sympathetic to conciliarism, the movement to have the Church governed by councils, and had close relations with the Council of Basel. On 25 June 1439 the council deposed Pope Eugene IV, and on 5 November it elected Amadeus pope, with 26 votes in the ballot. He accepted on 5 February 1440 and took the name Felix V, naming his son Louis Duke of Savoy.

Felix V left Basel for Lausanne in 1442, and the council later moved its sessions to Lausanne. After Eugene IV died in 1447, both sides favoured a settlement. On 7 April 1449 Felix V accepted the authority of Pope Nicholas V and resigned; he was named a cardinal and Bishop of Sabina and papal legate in the territories of Savoy. He is the last historical antipope recognised by a significant part of the Catholic clergy. He died in Geneva on 7 January 1451 and was buried at Ripaille.
amalasuntha: Amalasuintha was probably born in Ravenna in 495, the only child of Theodoric and his wife Audofleda, the sister of Clovis, King of the Franks. The marriage, made about 493, was political: Theodoric had defeated the various Gothic kingdoms and sought an alliance with the Franks. On her father's side she belonged to the Amali dynasty. She was married to Eutharic, an Amali prince, to ensure a legitimate heir, and they had two children, Athalaric and Matasuntha. Eutharic died in 522, which alarmed Theodoric, since his kingdom lacked an adult male heir.

Athalaric was ten years old when Theodoric died, and Amalasuintha took control of the kingdom as regent, although Cassiodorus and Procopius call Athalaric king. According to Procopius, the Gothic aristocracy wanted him raised in the Gothic manner, while she wanted him to resemble the Roman princes. She had close ties to the Byzantine emperor Justinian I, which made her adherence to Roman learning and customs the more objectionable to the Goths. Cassiodorus and Procopius both praised her wisdom and her command of Greek, Gothic and Latin.

Conscious of her unpopularity, she banished, and afterwards put to death, three Gothic nobles whom she suspected of plotting against her. Amory, Heather and Heydemann have suggested that one of them was Tuluin, a powerful Gothic noble and general. She also opened negotiations with Justinian, with the aim of removing herself and the Gothic treasure to Constantinople. Athalaric died in 534, most likely from heavy drinking combined with a disease, probably diabetes. She then ruled as queen and made her older cousin Theodahad co-ruler, hoping to win over her harshest critics, since he led the military aristocracy that opposed her pro-Roman stance.

Instead, Theodahad fostered the discontent of the Goths and had Amalasuintha imprisoned on the island of Martana in Lake Bolsena. There she was murdered while bathing, on 30 April 535 according to Agnellus, though Massimiliano Vitiello has suggested May. Procopius reports that she was considering handing Italy to Justinian around the time of her death. Some evidence suggests that the Byzantine empress Theodora arranged the killing through Justinian's ambassador Peter the Illyrian; modern scholarship holds that she acted on Justinian's behalf, since the murder gave him a clear justification to attack. He used it as a reason for the Gothic War. In 536 Witigis deposed Theodahad and had him put to death. Carlo Goldoni wrote a tragedy on her life, presented at Milan in 1733.
amalfi-coast: The Amalfi Coast is a stretch of coastline overlooking the Tyrrhenian Sea and the Gulf of Salerno, in the Province of Salerno in the Campania region. It lies south of the Sorrentine Peninsula and north of the Cilentan Coast, and takes its name from the town of Amalfi, which has historically been its main geographical and political hub. The climate is Mediterranean, with warm summers and mild winters. The relatively steep southern shore of the Sorrentine Peninsula leaves little room for rural and agricultural development, and the only land route is the 40-kilometre Amalfi Drive, which runs along the coast from Vietri sul Mare in the east to Positano in the west.

During the 10th and 11th centuries the Duchy of Amalfi existed on the territory of the coast, centred on the town of Amalfi. The coast was afterwards controlled by the Principality of Salerno, until Amalfi was sacked by the Republic of Pisa in 1137.

Thirteen municipalities lie on the coast, many centred on tourism, and it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997. Terraced gardens along the whole coastline grow a lemon called the sfusato amalfitano, used for limoncello liqueur. Another local liqueur, concerto, a dark rosolio with spicy notes, is made in Tramonti. Amalfi is known for a hand-made thick paper called bambagina, historically used for private writings, legal acts and revenue stamps, and other products include anchovies from Cetara and the colourful handmade ceramics of Vietri. The Rulers of Amalfi are the central figures of John Webster's Jacobean tragedy The Duchess of Malfi, and the Dutch artist M. C. Escher made a number of artworks of the coast.
amanullah-khan: Amanullah Khan was born on 1 June 1892 at Paghman near Kabul, the third son of Emir Habibullah Khan by his second wife. He became governor of Kabul and held command of the army and the treasury. On 20 February 1919 Habibullah, on a hunting trip in Laghman Province, was shot in the head in his tent by an unknown assassin.

Habibullah's brother Nasrullah Khan was declared Emir at Jalalabad the next day. Amanullah, who had stayed in Kabul, seized the treasury and the central government. He proclaimed himself Emir within days and, despite an oath on the Quran that Nasrullah would come to no harm, had him arrested on 3 March. A court held on 13 April executed a colonel for the murder and, on manufactured evidence, judged Nasrullah complicit. Nasrullah received a life sentence and was killed in jail about a year later.

On 3 May 1919 Amanullah launched a surprise attack on British India, beginning the Third Anglo-Afghan War. After early successes the fighting settled into a stalemate, since Britain was still bearing the costs of the First World War. An armistice at the end of 1919 freed Afghanistan of British control over its foreign affairs.

With his father-in-law and foreign minister Mahmud Tarzi he drafted the country's first constitution, ratified on 11 April 1922 by 872 tribal elders and officials at a Loya Jirga in Jalalabad. More than 320 schools were founded, primary education was made compulsory, and strict dress codes for women were overturned, a policy in which his wife Queen Soraya Tarzi took part. A rebellion at Khost against these changes was put down in 1925. From late 1927 to 1928 he toured Europe, Turkey and other countries, where he met rulers including King George V and Mustafa Kemal Atatürk.

After his return, measures such as abolishing the veil, moving the weekly day of rest from Friday to Thursday and ordering Western clothes stirred conservative opposition. Habibullah Kalakani attacked Kabul on 14 December 1928 and took it on 7 January 1929. Amanullah abdicated on 14 January in favour of his half-brother Inayatullah Khan, who surrendered four days later. An attempt to retake the capital failed in April, and on 23 May 1929 he fled to India, never to return.

Mohammad Nadir Shah replaced Kalakani on 13 October 1929 and reversed most of the reforms, though his successor King Zahir later introduced a more gradual programme. Amanullah settled in Rome, where loyalists several times tried unsuccessfully to restore him. He died in Zürich on 26 April 1960 and was buried at Jalalabad near his father's tomb.
amapa: Amapá lies in the far north of Brazil and borders French Guiana for 730 kilometres, the Atlantic Ocean for 578 kilometres, Pará, and Suriname for 63 kilometres. Its capital and largest city is Macapá. About 90 per cent of its area is Amazon rainforest, and the mouth of the River Oiapoque marks the northern end of Brazil's coastline. Tumucumaque Mountains National Park, established in 2002, is the largest tropical forest national park in the world.

In the colonial period the region was called Portuguese Guiana and was part of Portugal's State of Brazil. From 1637 to 1654 it was merged into the Captaincy of Pará as the Captaincy of Cabo de Norte. It exported lumber, resins, annatto, vegetable oils and salted fish to Europe, and the French established sugarcane plantations. The discovery of mineral deposits drew British and Dutch invaders, whom the Portuguese repelled. The Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 set the boundary between Brazil and French Guiana, but the French did not respect it. A fort was built at São José de Macapá as a base of Portuguese power, and in the 18th century France retook control of the area.

The dispute with France continued until 1900. Gold and rubber raised the Portuguese population in the 19th century and brought it to a head, though French settlers had founded the Republic of Independent Guyana, which lasted from 1886 to 1891. Brazil took the claim to international arbitration at Geneva, which found for Brazil on 1 December 1900. The area was then incorporated into Pará as Araguari, and in 1943 became the federal territory of Amapá.

The discovery of rich manganese deposits at Serra do Navio in 1945 changed the local economy, and manganese remained its largest source of revenue. The decision to make Amapá a state was made on 5 October 1988, when Brazil's new constitution was promulgated, and the first state legislators took office on 1 January 1991. The state has 733,759 people at the 2022 census, most of them living in Macapá and Santana. Indigenous peoples such as the Galibi do Oiapoque, Karipuna, Palikur and Wayampi live in demarcated territories, and French is taught in schools because of the nearness of French Guiana.
amar-sonar-bangla: The Partition of Bengal took effect on 16 October 1905, after the Viceroy of India, Lord Curzon, announced it on 20 July. It split the Bengal Presidency into two parts along communal lines, East Bengal and Assam having a Muslim majority and West Bengal a Hindu one, a division claimed to have been politically motivated. Songs such as this one were meant to rekindle the unified spirit of Bengal and to raise public consciousness against it. Some sources claim the song was written in that context, but the original manuscript was never found, so the date of composition cannot be established with certainty.

Prashanta Kumar Paul, in his biography of Tagore, claimed that it was first sung on 25 August 1905 at an essay conference in Kolkata. Its lyrics appeared in September 1905 in the journals Bongodorshon and Baul, and the music in notation in the journal Shongeet Biggnan Praveshika. Tagore's niece Indira Devi wrote down the notation as she heard it from Tagore himself.

The words are an ode to Mother Bengal. Amar means my, and sonar, from sona, gold, is used as a term of endearment, so that Sonar Bangla can express both beloved and precious. The melody derives from Ami Kothay Pabo Tare, a song of the Baul singer Gagan Harkara, set to the rhythm cycle Dadra tala.

In Syed Ali Ahsan's English translation, the poem speaks of the air like a flute, the scent of mango orchards in Falgun, paddy fields in Ogrohayon, banyan trees along the riverbanks, and a childhood spent in the mother's playhouse with her soil smeared on the body. It closes with the speaker offering his head beneath her feet. Only the first ten lines are sung as the national anthem.

The Provisional Government of Bangladesh adopted the song in 1971, during the Bangladesh Liberation War, and Samar Das composed the orchestral version. When the Constitution of Bangladesh was drafted in 1972, two songs were proposed, this one and Dwijendra Lal Roy's Dhana Dhanya Pushpa Bhara, and Amar Sonar Bangla was selected.

According to Ziauddin Ahmed, the choice has drawn criticism since at least 1975. Some opponents point out that Bengali Muslims of East Bengal had welcomed the partition the song was written against. Others object that the word mother refers to a Hindu goddess. After the coup of 15 August 1975 a committee recommended replacements, including Kazi Nazrul Islam's Notuner Gaan, but the process halted when the president was removed. In 1979 Prime Minister Shah Azizur Rahman proposed Shahnaz Rahmatullah's Prothom Bangladesh instead, as Tagore was not Bangladeshi.
amarna-letters: The Amarna letters, cited as EA for el-Amarna, are an archive on clay tablets, mainly diplomatic correspondence between the Egyptian administration and its representatives in Canaan and Amurru, or the leaders of neighbouring kingdoms. They span no more than 30 years in the middle of the 14th century BCE and were found at el-Amarna, the modern name of Akhetaten, the capital founded by Akhenaten. They are written in cuneiform, the writing system of ancient Mesopotamia, and not in Egyptian. Most are in a variety of Akkadian sometimes called Canaanite-Akkadian.

The known tablets total 382 with fragments, of which 350 are letters and the rest literary and school texts. Jørgen Knudtzon published 358 in Die El-Amarna-Tafeln (1907 and 1915), still the standard edition; the other 24 were excavated later.

The archive covers the reign of Akhenaten and that of his predecessor Amenhotep III. It sheds light on Egypt's relations with Babylonia, Assyria, Syria, Canaan and Alashiya, and with Mitanni and the Hittites. Letters of the Babylonian king Kadashman-Enlil I anchor Akhenaten's reign in the mid-14th century BCE. The letters contain the first mention of a group called the Habiru, whose possible connection with the Hebrews remains debated. Tushratta of Mitanni complains that Akhenaten sent him plated statues instead of solid gold ones. Rib-Hadda of Byblos pleads for Egyptian military help in more than 58 letters. Abdi-Heba of Jerusalem asks for archers against the Habiru and writes, in EA 287, that the king has placed his name in Jerusalem forever and cannot abandon it.

Local Egyptians digging in the ruins of Amarna found most of the tablets around 1887 and sold them on the antiquities market. Flinders Petrie recovered 21 fragments in 1891 and 1892, and only 26 tablets and fragments were found in their archaeological context. The first group is now scattered among museums, with 202 or 203 tablets in Berlin, 99 in the British Museum and 49 or 50 in Cairo. William L. Moran notes that the chronology presents problems that still elude definitive solution, and that the archive spans at most about thirty years, perhaps only fifteen. It closed when the city was deserted, commonly believed to be in the second year of Tutankhamun, about 1332 BCE.
amasya: Amasya lies in the Black Sea Region of northern Turkey, in a narrow cleft of the Yeşilırmak (Iris) river. Almost vertical cliffs and the high peaks of the Canik and Pontus mountains bound the valley, and the town takes the shape of a letter V as it follows a sharp bend in the river. Although it is near the Black Sea, the valley is set apart from the coast and has an inland climate, well suited to apples.

Archaeological research shows that the site was settled in turn by Hittites, Phrygians, Cimmerians, Lydians, Greeks, Persians and Armenians. A Pontic kingdom under the Persian Mithridatic dynasty arose at the end of the 4th century BCE, and Amaseia was its capital until 26 BCE. In 70 BCE a Roman force under Lucullus took the city from Armenia, and Pompey made it a free city and administrative centre of the province of Bithynia and Pontus. Strabo described it as it was between 60 BCE and 19 CE. Around 112 Trajan made it part of Cappadocia.

Amaseia was the seat of a Christian metropolitan bishop from the 3rd century. Turkic migrations reduced the Christian population from the 12th century, and in 1317 the metropolitan Callistus could not enter his see during a violent Turkoman attack, so with the permission of Patriarch John XIII the metropolitanate was moved to Limnia in the Empire of Trebizond. The Ottoman sultans Murad II and Selim I were born in Amasya, and young princes were sent there to govern.

Before the First World War the town had 30,000 inhabitants, among them 13,788 Armenians. They were deported during the Armenian genocide, and afterwards the Armenian quarter, the bazaar, the Armenian church and the Greek church were burnt. In 1922 the Orthodox metropolis counted 40,000 Greek Orthodox Christians, half of them Greek, and all Greeks were forcibly removed in the population exchange of 1923.

Amasya is the seat of Amasya Province, with a population of 114,921 in 2021. Wooden Ottoman houses along the Yeşilırmak have been restored and now serve as cafes, restaurants and hotels, and the rock tombs of the Pontic kings are carved into the cliffs above them. Local folklore places the tale of Ferhat and Shirin here: for love of the princess Shirin, Ferhat tunnelled through a mountain, and the story has been retold as a play, a novel and an opera.
amazons: The Amazons were portrayed as female warriors and hunters, known for strength, archery and riding. Their society was closed to men and they raised only their daughters, returning their sons to their fathers, with whom they socialised briefly in order to reproduce. According to Apollonius of Rhodes they were the offspring of Ares and the nymph Harmonia. The origin of the word is uncertain. It may derive from an Iranian word for warriors, and the Greeks folk-etymologised it as breastless, which led to a tradition that they removed the right breast. Ancient art always shows them with both breasts, and the false etymology may have produced the myth.

Greek authors placed their homeland at the edge of the known world. Most often it was Pontus on the southern shore of the Black Sea, where the queen ruled from Themiscyra on the Thermodon river. In the Iliad they appear in the Trojan War, and in the lost Aethiopis the queen Penthesilea, of Thracian birth, brought an Amazon force to Troy after Hector's death. She was killed in single combat by Achilles. The hero Bellerophon fought them in Lycia, and Diodorus Siculus lists twelve Amazons who died fighting Heracles in his quest for the girdle of Hippolyta.

Herodotus wrote in the 5th century BCE that the Sauromatae, predecessors of the Sarmatians, arose from a union of Scythians and Amazons. He also saw the Lycians, who traced descent through the mother, as descendants of the Amazons. Many classical scholars regard the Amazons as wholly fictional, invented by Greek men as anti-women or to stand for Persians. Later authors, among them Stephanus of Byzantium and Jordanes, who made the Goths' women Amazons under Marpesia, gave them lists of names and further exploits.

From about 550 BCE Amazons appeared on vases as fighters and riders, and after the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE the Amazonomachy became a popular subject on pottery, in sculpture and on buildings such as the Parthenon. The motif remained popular into Late Antiquity.

Archaeology has offered a possible historical basis. About 20 per cent of the warrior graves on the lower Don and lower Volga held women dressed for battle, and armed women make up as much as a quarter of Sarmatian military burials. Over a thousand nomad graves between the Black Sea and Mongolia show that women warriors existed in the steppe cultures, though it is not known for certain that these people inspired the Greek myth. Amazons also appear in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream and in Heinrich von Kleist's drama Penthesilea of 1808.
amberg: The town was first mentioned in 1034 as Ammenberg and became an important trading centre in the Middle Ages, exporting mainly iron ore and iron products. In 1269 it passed to the Wittelsbach dynasty that ruled Bavaria, and in 1329 the town and the whole region fell to the Palatinate branch of the family, which gave the region the name Upper Palatinate. It was no longer politically part of the duchy of Bavaria. In the 16th century its rulers turned to Protestantism and the town to Lutheranism; later attempts to introduce the more radical Calvinism failed because citizens were reluctant. In 1628 Amberg and the Upper Palatinate became part of the electorate of Bavaria.

On 24 August 1796, in the French Revolutionary Wars, the Battle of Amberg was fought in and around the city: 35,000 French under Jean Baptiste Jourdan faced 40,000 Austrians under Archduke Charles, and the French lost significantly more men in an Austrian victory. Amberg was the regional capital of the Upper Palatinate until 1810, when power passed to the larger city of Regensburg.

Jews had settled in Amberg before 1294, when the first documentation appears. In 1298 thirteen of the town's Jews died in the Rindfleisch massacres. In 1347 six families received permission to settle, and in 1367 a yeshiva opened. The community was expelled in 1403 and the synagogue was annexed to the nearby church. Twelve Jews remained in the town in 1942. A displaced persons camp near the town housed mostly Jewish refugees and survivors after 1945.

Amberg lies in the Upper Palatinate, about halfway between Regensburg and Bayreuth. After World War II, when Bavaria fell into the American sector, it was home to a United States Army post, Pond Barracks, which closed in 1992 and was turned over to the local community, mostly for social housing.
ambon-island: Ambon Island has an area of 743 square kilometres and lies off the south-west coast of Seram, on the north side of the Banda Sea. It is 51 kilometres long and almost divided in two by Ambon Bay. The smaller south-eastern part, Leitimur, is joined by a narrow neck to the larger northern part, Leihitu, also called Hitoe. The highest mountains, Wawani and Salahutu, are volcanoes with hot springs. The island belongs to Wallacea, which deep water has always separated from the Asian and Australian continents, so it has few native mammals but many birds and insects. It gave its name to Amboyna, a prized figured wood first exported from it.

The Portuguese were the first Europeans to land, in 1512, and made Ambon a centre of their activity in Maluku. They set up a factory in 1521 but did not hold it peacefully until 1580, and were regularly attacked by the Muslims of Hitu on the north coast. The Dutch took the fort in 1605 under Steven van der Hagen without a shot. Ambon was the headquarters of the Dutch East India Company from 1610 to 1619, until Batavia was founded. An English settlement at Cambello, begun about 1615, was destroyed by the Dutch in 1623, with tortures of its inhabitants that became known as the Ambon Massacre.

The Company imposed a clove monopoly centred on Ambon, and until the nineteenth century the Dutch forbade clove trees on their other islands. Hitu resisted. Its leader Kakiali was murdered by a traitor in 1643, and Telukibesi's last stand at the fortress of Kapahaha ended in July 1646. A further revolt, the Great Ambon War, began in 1651 and was crushed by Arnold Vlaming van Oudshoorn in 1656 with great loss of life. The British held Ambon in 1796 to 1802 and in 1810 to 1814. Imperial Japanese forces captured the Dutch military base in 1942, and more than 300 Allied prisoners of war were then shot in the Laha massacre.

The island consists of the city of Ambon, the capital of Maluku province, in the south, and three districts of the Central Maluku Regency in the north. About 482,800 people lived there in mid 2023. The Ambonese are of mixed Malay and Papuan origin and are mostly Christians or Muslims. Ambonese Malay, which developed as the trade language of central Maluku, is the main language, and many families still carry Portuguese names such as Muskita and De Fretes. Cassava and sago are the chief crops, and cloves and nutmeg, once the main exports, are now grown in limited quantities.
ambrogio-lorenzetti: Ambrogio Lorenzetti was born about 1290 and was active as a painter from about 1317 to 1348. His elder brother was the painter Pietro Lorenzetti. He was influenced by both Italo-Byzantine art and classical art forms, and his work shows the influence of Simone Martini while being more naturalistic. His earliest dated work is a Madonna and Child of 1319, now in the Museo Diocesano at San Casciano. He is documented in Florence until 1321 and returned there after spending a number of years again in his native Siena. He experimented with perspective and physiognomy and studied classical antiquity, interests often thought to have begun later in the Renaissance.

In his Madonna and Child the debt to Byzantine art is clear, especially in the frontality of the Virgin, but he conveys the monumentality of the figures without chiaroscuro, using colour and patterns. His Maestà, completed in 1335, adds an intense scene of maternal bonding that was unusual in Sienese art, and it contains allegorical elements that refer to Dante. Ghiberti mentions his interest in an antique statue found in an excavation at Siena, attributed to Lysippus.

His best-known work is the Allegory of Good and Bad Government, three fresco panels painted between February 1338 and May 1339 in the Sala dei Nove, the council hall of the nine executive magistrates of the Republic of Siena, in the Palazzo Pubblico. The Effects of Good Government on Town and Country is a pictorial encyclopedia of incidents in a peaceful medieval town and countryside. The landscape in the series is the first to appear as a subject in Western art after the Classical period. One of the frescoes, the Allegory of Bad Government and its Effects, holds the first evidence of the hourglass. His last work, the Annunciation of 1344, contains one of the first uses of clear linear perspective.

Both Ambrogio and Pietro are believed to have died of bubonic plague in 1348. Ambrogio's will is dated 9 August 1348. Giorgio Vasari included a biography of him in his Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, describing his manners as more those of a gentleman and philosopher than those of an artist.
ambrose: Ambrose was born in 339 into a Roman Christian family of Greek descent, at Augusta Treverorum, modern Trier, then the capital of the province of Gallia Belgica. Scholars disagree on who his father was: some identify him with the praetorian prefect of Gaul Aurelius Ambrosius, others with an official named Uranius. A legend says that bees settled on his face in his cradle and left a drop of honey, taken as a sign of future eloquence. Trained in rhetoric and law, he served as Roman civil governor of Aemilia-Liguria at Milan before the people unexpectedly chose him as bishop by acclamation in 374.

As bishop Ambrose defended Nicene Christianity against Arianism, tried to mediate between the emperors Theodosius I and Magnus Maximus, and opposed the execution of Priscillianist heretics. After a massacre he excommunicated Theodosius, maintaining that an emperor is within the church, not over it. He advocated monasticism and asceticism, and his writing helped transmit Eastern Christian theology to the Latin West.

Despite heavy administrative duties he preached and presided at the Eucharist several times a week and dealt directly with the poor, widows, orphans and his clergy. He respected local customs, and advised Augustine of Hippo to follow the custom of the church where he found himself, since at Rome Ambrose fasted on a Saturday and at Milan did not. This gave rise to the saying When in Rome, do as the Romans do.

Ambrose wrote works of advocacy for Nicene Christianity, among them De Virginibus (377), the Exameron (386-390) and De officiis ministrorum (377-391), a practical guide for his clergy. De sacramentis contains the earliest witness to the present Roman Canon of the Mass, though its authorship is less certain than that of De mysteriis.

He was an important innovator in Christian hymnody. Hilary of Poitiers had written Latin hymns earlier, but only fragments survive, so Ambrose's are the earliest extant complete Latin hymns. Four, including Veni redemptor gentium, are universally accepted as his, each with eight four-line stanzas in iambic tetrameter. Ambrosian chant bears his name, but no melody in it can be attributed to him. With Augustine, Jerome and Gregory the Great he is one of the four Latin Doctors of the Church, formally declared in 1298.
amelia-umbria: Amelia is a town and comune in the province of Terni, in central Italy, not far from the border with Lazio. It stands on the slope of a hill at about 406 metres above sea level, between the valley of the Tiber and that of the Nera, close to the point where the two rivers meet. It lies 24 kilometres from Terni and 13 kilometres from Narni.

According to Cato, the city was founded 964 years before the Third Macedonian War, which corresponds to 1135 BCE. The date cannot be given certain historical value, but it shows the great age attributed to the place. Another tradition, associated with Pliny the Younger, gives 1136 BCE and names either Amisio, said to be a king of the Aborigines, or a supposed princess of Veii as founder. The city later came under Etruscan influence. The opening of the Via Amerina in 240 BCE linked Rome and Umbria, and the town then began to take on an urban form.

Troops from Amelia fought against Hannibal's advance, and the town became a prosperous Roman municipium. Cicero described it as a flourishing municipality whose fertile land reached to the Tiber. Under Augustus its lands were divided among veterans, though it did not become a colony. Amelia is recorded as a bishop's seat from the 4th century, and the Goths later destroyed the city. In 731 the Lombard king Liutprand seized it, and in 1240 the troops of Frederick II sacked it. It remained tied to the Papal States until Piedmontese troops entered it on 21 September 1860.

Amelia is almost entirely encircled by polygonal walls of the 6th to 4th centuries BCE, among the most complete of their type. Their limestone blocks, sometimes more than 2 metres long, are fitted without mortar, and eighteenth-century travellers attributed them to the Pelasgians. The town also keeps Roman cisterns of the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE, ten barrel-vaulted chambers cut in the rock, and a bronze statue of Germanicus found outside the Porta Romana in 1963. Amelia is known for its dried figs, a product recorded since antiquity.
amenemhat-i: Amenemhat I was not of royal lineage. His parents were Senusret and Nefert, possibly related to the nomarchial family of Elephantine. Texts from the period place her in the Upper Egyptian nome of Ta-Seti, and many scholars in recent years have argued that she was of Nubian origin. He was probably the same man as the vizier Amenemhat who led an expedition to Wadi Hammamat under his predecessor Mentuhotep IV, and he possibly overthrew him. Scholars differ on whether he killed Mentuhotep IV, but there is no independent evidence of it, and there may even have been a period of co-regency between the two.

Amenemhat I was the first king of the Twelfth Dynasty of the Middle Kingdom. The relationship to his predecessors remains unclear. The inscriptions of a local governor, Nehri, suggest that his early reign was beset by political turmoil. He moved the capital from Thebes to Itjtawy. His Horus name, Wehemmesu, means 'renaissance' or 'rebirth' and alludes to the Old Kingdom, whose pyramid tombs and artistic motifs the kings of the Twelfth Dynasty emulated after the First Intermediate Period.

The composition of literary works such as the Prophecy of Neferti and the Instructions of Amenemhat, and the return to pyramid complexes like those of the 6th dynasty, are often seen as attempts to legitimise his rule. He built his pyramid at Lisht, with a core of roughly hewn limestone that contained relief blocks taken from Old Kingdom monuments, and it is now a ruined mound some 20 metres tall. A stele dated to year 30 of Amenemhat and year 10 of Senusret I shows that Senusret I became co-regent in year 20, the first known co-regency of a king and his son.

Both the Instructions of Amenemhat and the Story of Sinuhe suggest that Amenemhat was assassinated before he could celebrate his first Sed festival. In the Instructions the dead king tells his son how his own bodyguard attacked him at night. This was apparently while Senusret I was leading a campaign against the Libyans. Senusret hurried back to the palace without alerting his army, and a civil war broke out shortly afterwards, which he had to suppress. How he secured the throne is unknown.
amenemhat-iii: Amenemhat III, also written Amenemhet III, was the sixth king of the Twelfth Dynasty and the son of Senusret III. No text states the relationship outright, but it is inferred from their coregency. His mother is unknown. Two of his wives, Aat and Khenemetneferhedjet III, were buried in his pyramid at Dahshur, and his one confirmed daughter, Neferuptah, appears to have been groomed as his successor, since her name is written in a cartouche. She seems to have died before him.

The regnal dates roll over from Year 19 of Senusret III, its highest dated attestation, to Year 1 of Amenemhat III, and the two are believed to have shared the throne for about twenty years, with Amenemhat III as the active king, though not all scholars accept a coregency.

The campaigns and domestic policy of Senusret III left Amenemhat III a stable Egypt, and there is little evidence of military expeditions in his reign: a small mission in Year 9 near the fortress of Kumma in Nubia is recorded in a rock inscription whose author says that nobody died on the return. A few expeditions went to Punt.

Mining of turquoise and copper in the Sinai reached its peak, with more than fifty texts at Serabit el-Khadim, Wadi Maghara and Wadi Nasb, and near-permanent settlements grew up round the workings. Quarries at Wadi Hammamat, Wadi el-Hudi, Tura, Hatnub and Aswan were also worked.

These resources paid for a large building programme, above all in the Faiyum, where he dedicated a temple to Sobek and a chapel to Renenutet, set up two colossal statues of himself at Biahmu and contributed to the excavation of Lake Moeris. He built at Bubastis and enlarged the temples of Hathor at Serabit el-Khadim and of Ptah at Memphis. In his Year 30 he held his Sed festival, the jubilee that renews royal authority.

He built two pyramids, at Dahshur and Hawara, the first king since Sneferu to build more than one, and was buried in the second, at Hawara, in his Year 46. Flinders Petrie found only burned fragments of bone and wood in the burial chamber, which suggests that robbers burned the coffins and mummy.

Late in his reign he made Amenemhat IV a junior coregent, and Sobekneferu later succeeded Amenemhat IV as the last ruler of the dynasty. Scholars link the lack of a recorded male heir to the decline of the Twelfth Dynasty. Amenemhat III was deified and worshipped in the Faiyum for centuries. His statues of his later years show heavy eyelids, sunken cheeks and deep lines, a departure from the idealised youth of earlier kings, according to the art historian Gay Robins.
amenhotep-iii: Amenhotep III was the son of Thutmose IV and a minor wife, Mutemwiya, and was born about 1401 BCE. He probably became pharaoh at between 6 and 12 years of age. A regent would likely have ruled until he came of age, but none is attested in the surviving records. In his second regnal year he married Tiye, daughter of Yuya and Thuya, who remained Great Royal Wife throughout his reign. They had at least two sons, Thutmose and the future Amenhotep IV, and at least four daughters. He also married daughters of the rulers of Mitanni, Babylon and Arzawa, and, in his last decade, at least two of his own daughters, Sitamun and Iset.

The only military campaign in which he is known to have taken part was against a rebellion in Kush in his fifth year, commemorated on stelae near Aswan and Saï. His court is known mainly from officials' tombs at Thebes, among them the viziers Ramose and Ptahmose and the Viceroy of Kush, Merimose. He built the palace of Malkata, begun about his eleventh year, and moved there permanently around year 29. He held three Sed festivals, in years 30, 34 and 37, jubilees that affirmed the king's fitness to rule and his transition to divinity.

Diplomatic letters from Assyria, Mitanni, Babylon, Hatti and other states survive among the Amarna Letters, often asking for gold. In one, the Babylonian king Kadashman-Enlil I quotes the pharaoh refusing him an Egyptian princess: no daughter of the king of Egypt is given to anyone. Amenhotep did take foreign princesses as wives. In his thirty-sixth year the Mitannian king Tushratta sent the statue of Ishtar of Nineveh to Egypt, most likely to bless the pharaoh's marriage to Tadukhipa. Historians disagree whether he shared a coregency with Amenhotep IV; most now argue for none, or at most two years.

His latest attested date is year 38, and he may have died early in year 39. Reliefs show him weak, and scientists believe he suffered from arthritis and obesity, with painful, worn teeth. He was buried in tomb WV22 in the Western Valley, though his mummy was later moved to the cache in KV35, where Victor Loret found it in 1898. He left more surviving statues than any other pharaoh, over 250, and built at Karnak, Luxor and across Nubia. His mortuary temple fell into ruin within two hundred years, leaving the Colossi of Memnon, each 18 m high. His son Amenhotep IV, later Akhenaten, succeeded him and moved the capital from Thebes to Amarna.
american-civil-war: The war grew from the desire of the Southern states to preserve slavery. Historians in the 21st century overwhelmingly agree on the centrality of slavery in the conflict, at least for the Southern states, though they disagree on the Union's reasons for refusing to let the South secede. Abraham Lincoln, a Republican who opposed slavery's expansion, won the presidential election of 1860, and Southern leaders feared he would put slavery on a course toward extinction.

South Carolina's convention voted unanimously to secede on 20 December 1860. Six more Deep South states followed in January and February 1861 and seized federal forts and arsenals. The war began on 12 April 1861, when Confederate forces opened fire on Fort Sumter in Charleston harbour. Four more states seceded afterwards, so that the Confederacy, led by President Jefferson Davis, comprised eleven states.

In the western theatre the Union captured New Orleans and, under Ulysses S. Grant, won at Fort Henry and Fort Donelson in February 1862, gaining control of the Tennessee and Cumberland rivers. On 1 January 1863 Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation, which made abolition a Union war goal. The Union siege of Vicksburg split the Confederacy at the Mississippi, and General Robert E. Lee's incursion north failed at the Battle of Gettysburg. A naval blockade of Southern ports, announced in April 1861, cut the South's trade.

In 1864 Lincoln made Grant commander of all Union armies. General William Tecumseh Sherman took Atlanta on 2 September 1864 and marched to Savannah, seizing provisions and destroying railroads. Richmond fell on 2 and 3 April 1865, and Lee surrendered to Grant at Appomattox Court House on 9 April. Lincoln was shot on 14 April and died the next day.

The war left an estimated 700,000 soldiers dead, along with an undetermined number of civilians, and it remains the deadliest in United States history. About 190,000 African Americans served in the Union Army after the Emancipation Proclamation. The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery, freeing four million people. The war destroyed much of the South's wealth, including the value held in enslaved people.

Reconstruction, which lasted until 1877, rested on three amendments to the Constitution: the thirteenth outlawing slavery, the fourteenth guaranteeing birthright citizenship and equal protection, and the fifteenth prohibiting the denial of voting rights on account of race. The white South developed the myth of the Lost Cause, which the historian Alan T. Nolan calls a rationalisation to vindicate those in rebellion.
american-revolution: After the Glorious Revolution in England, Britain followed a trade policy of salutary neglect, and the Thirteen Colonies were largely left to govern themselves. Discontent began shortly after the French and Indian War ended in 1763. Parliament imposed new taxes on the colonists, ostensibly to compensate for the cost of the war, and in 1765 delegates from several colonies met at the Stamp Act Congress in New York City and argued that taxation without representation violated their rights as Englishmen.

Tension rose again after the Townshend Acts, and British troops sent to Massachusetts were involved in the Boston Massacre of 1770. In December 1773 a faction of the Sons of Liberty dumped chests of tea owned by the British East India Company into Boston Harbor. Parliament answered with the Intolerable Acts, meant to end self-government in Massachusetts, which instead increased American support for revolution.

The Battles of Lexington and Concord on 19 April 1775, fought when the British tried to seize the rebels' weapons, began the war. The Second Continental Congress created the Continental Army and appointed George Washington its commander-in-chief. The army besieged Boston and forced the British to withdraw by sea in March 1776. Congress passed the Lee Resolution for independence on 2 July 1776 and unanimously adopted the Declaration of Independence on 4 July.

The British returned in July, landed in New York and defeated Washington in August at the Battle of Brooklyn, the largest battle of the war. France and Spain later entered the war. On 28 September 1781 Washington commanded the capture of a British army under General Cornwallis at the Siege of Yorktown, after which opinion in Parliament shifted towards ending the war on American terms.

On 3 September 1783 the British signed the Treaty of Paris, recognising American independence and ceding nearly all the territory east of the Mississippi River and south of the Great Lakes. The British largely abandoned their Indigenous allies, who were not party to the treaty, and kept forts in American territory until the Jay Treaty of 1795.

The national government under the Articles of Confederation could not tax, and the Philadelphia Convention of 1787 produced a Constitution, ratified in 1788. The new government under President George Washington took office in March 1789, and the Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791. The first successful revolution against a European empire also gave other colonial peoples a model of self-government.
american-revolutionary-war: After the British victory over France in the Seven Years' War, which ended with the Peace of Paris of 1763, tensions grew between Britain and its Thirteen Colonies. The war's debt and demands from British taxpayers for cuts in spending meant that Parliament expected the colonies to pay for their own defence. The Sugar Act and Stamp Act brought new taxes, and the Rockingham ministry repealed the Stamp Act in 1765 but asserted Parliament's authority in the Declaratory Act. After the Boston Massacre of 5 March 1770 and the Intolerable Acts of 1774, twelve colonies sent delegates to the First Continental Congress, which passed the Continental Association in October 1774, a boycott of British goods.

The war began on 19 April 1775 with the Battles of Lexington and Concord, after which British troops lost around 300 men on their withdrawal to Boston. In June 1775 the Second Continental Congress created the Continental Army and unanimously appointed George Washington its commander. It adopted the Declaration of Independence on 4 July 1776, the text written almost exclusively by Thomas Jefferson. The British captured New York City in November 1776, but Washington crossed the Delaware on the night of 25 to 26 December and overwhelmed the Hessians at Trenton, taking 900 prisoners.

In October 1777 a British force under John Burgoyne surrendered at Saratoga, which convinced France and Spain that American independence was viable. France signed a Treaty of Alliance in February 1778, and Spain allied with France against Britain in 1779. The British then turned to the southern colonies, where they had wrongly assumed strong Loyalist support. In 1779 the Sullivan Expedition ravaged the lands of the Haudenosaunee allied with Britain. A Franco-American army besieged General Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia, in September and October 1781, and the French navy cut off his escape, so that he surrendered.

Fighting largely ceased in North America after Yorktown, though the British wars with France and Spain went on for two more years. In the Treaty of Paris, signed on 3 September 1783, Britain recognised the sovereignty and independence of the United States. The Treaties of Versailles settled its conflicts with France and Spain, and Britain gave Tobago, Senegal and small territories in India to France, and Menorca, West Florida and East Florida to Spain. Historian Terry M. Mays describes the war as three kinds of conflict: a colonial dispute over trade regulation as well as taxation, a civil war between Patriots, Loyalists and the neutral, and a wider war with France and Spain.
americas: The Americas are a landmass made up of North America and South America. Together with their islands they cover 8% of Earth's surface and 28.4% of its land area, and they make up most of the land in the Western Hemisphere. The mainland extends about 14,000 km from north to south, and its climate ranges from arctic tundra in northern Canada, Greenland and Alaska to tropical rainforest in Central America and South America. A long chain of mountains, the American Cordillera, runs along the west coast, while the flatter east is dominated by river basins such as the Amazon and the Mississippi. The two continents were joined by the Isthmus of Panama by about three million years ago.

Humans first settled the Americas from Asia between 20,000 and 16,000 years ago, though the dates and routes are subject to research. The pre-Columbian era saw urban settlement, agriculture and monumental architecture in Mesoamerica, among the Olmec, Zapotec, Aztec and Maya, and among the Andean civilizations. Norse settlements in Greenland, and perhaps on the mainland, were later abandoned.

The voyages of Christopher Columbus from 1492 to 1504 brought permanent contact with Europe and began a period of exploration, conquest and colonisation. Large numbers of Indigenous people were enslaved, and diseases from Europe and West Africa devastated them. Decolonisation began with the American Revolution in the 1770s and largely ended with the Spanish–American War in the late 1890s. The name America was first recorded in 1507, on a world map by Martin Waldseemüller, and is generally thought to derive from Amerigo Vespucci.

The Americas have more than a billion inhabitants and 35 sovereign states, together with dependent territories of Denmark, France, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and the United States. The legacy of European settlement is a set of shared cultural traits, most notably Christianity and the use of West European languages, chiefly Spanish, English, Portuguese and French. The population descends from Indigenous peoples and from people of European, African and Asian ancestry, along with people of mixed ancestry.
amharic: Amharic belongs to the Ethio-Semitic group, a subdivision of the Semitic branch of the Afroasiatic languages. Linguistic analysis suggests that Semitic languages were present in Ethiopia as early as 2000 BCE, and archaeology places Semitic speakers there before 500 BCE. One theory brings them from South Arabia; Messay Kebede and Daniel E. Alemu argue that movement across the Red Sea was a matter of reciprocal exchange, if it happened at all, and that Ethio-Semitic speakers were not foreign invaders.

Amharic has been the language of courts, trade and the military since the late 12th century. By one account Amhara nobles supported the Zagwe prince Lalibela, who made Amharic Lisane Negus, the tongue of the king; the title and the language's use at court are otherwise traced to the emperor Yekuno Amlak. The oldest surviving written Amharic dates from the reign of Amda Seyon I in the 14th century, whose poems known as Soldier songs praised him and his troops.

Amharic is written from left to right in an extended form of the Ge'ez script, called fidäl. It is an abugida: each character stands for a consonant plus a vowel. There are 34 basic characters, each in seven forms, and 49 further letters for sounds involving w, some 288 in all. Some consonants have more than one series of letters, because the letters once stood for distinct sounds that merged. Gemination, the lengthening of a consonant, distinguishes words, as in alä, he said, and allä, there is, but the script does not mark it. The dialects are mutually intelligible, and the Beta Israel speak Jewish Amharic, which replaced many Christian phrases with Jewish ones.

Amharic is the first language of the Amhara and a lingua franca among other peoples in Ethiopia's towns. It is the official working language of the federal government and of several regions, and until 2020 it was the sole official language of Ethiopia. The Bible was first translated into it by Abu Rumi in the early 19th century, and Haddis Alemayehu's novel Love to the Grave is regarded as the best known in the language.

The word Rastafari comes from Ras Täfäri, the title and name of Haile Selassie before his reign, and Rastafari treats Amharic as a holy language. After the emperor visited Jamaica in 1966, study circles in Amharic were organised there, and reggae artists of the 1970s such as Ras Michael and the Abyssinians sang in it.
amhran-na-bhfiann: Peadar Kearney wrote much of the text in the Swiss Café at the corner of O'Connell Street and North Earl Street in Dublin. Kearney and Patrick Heeney had collaborated on songs since 1903. Kearney's first draft, handwritten on copybook paper, sold at auction in Dublin in 2006 for 760,000 euros. After the magazine The United Irishman rejected the text, Irish Freedom published it in 1912. The Irish Volunteers used it as a marching song, and rebels sang it in the General Post Office during the Easter Rising of 1916. It grew more popular among rebels held in the Frongoch internment camp after the Rising.

The Free State adopted no official anthem at first, since the aftermath of the Civil War made the government wary of controversy, and former unionists still regarded God Save the King as the anthem. W. T. Cosgrave avoided naming the song the national anthem for fear of antagonising unionists in Northern Ireland, yet did not want to leave a potent symbol to republican opponents. Radio Éireann played it at closedown from 1926. In 1934 the Department of Finance bought the copyright for 1,200 pounds, and bought it again in 1965 for 2,500 pounds after copyright law changed. The 1937 Constitution created the office of President of Ireland, for whom the Presidential Salute, the first four bars followed by the last five, is played.

Liam Ó Rinn, later Chief Translator of the Oireachtas, wrote the Irish translation, which was published in An tÓglach on 3 November 1923. Several other translations existed by 1923, and Ó Rinn criticised them as unreadable, since they were in literary Classical Irish rather than the spoken language of the Gaeltacht. From the 1930s the Gaelic Athletic Association encouraged singing the anthem in Irish at its matches. The English version has been almost totally eclipsed, and many are unaware that the Irish words are a translation. Only the chorus is the anthem, though the song has three verses. Colm Ó Lochlainn said the tune sounded to him something between a Sousa march and a German regimental song.
amiens: The first known settlement on the site was Samarobriva, meaning Somme bridge, the central settlement of the Ambiani, one of the principal tribes of Gaul. The Romans named the town Ambianum, the settlement of the Ambiani. In the 4th century the name of the people replaced the old name of Samarobriva, and Amiens became an episcopal seat. It was part of Francia from the 5th century, and the Normans sacked the city in 859 and again in 882.

The town was fought over in both World Wars, was repeatedly occupied by both sides and suffered heavy damage. The Battle of Amiens in 1918 was the opening phase of the Hundred Days Offensive, which led directly to the Armistice with Germany. The Royal Air Force bombed the town heavily in the Second World War, and afterwards it was rebuilt to the plans of Pierre Dufau with wider streets, in brick, concrete and white stone with slate roofs. Auguste Perret designed the railway station and the nearby Tour Perret.

Amiens lies on the Somme, 120 km north of Paris and 100 km southwest of Lille, and is the prefecture of the Somme department in the Hauts-de-France region. It has 136,449 inhabitants (2023). Its landmark is Notre-Dame d'Amiens, the largest Gothic cathedral in France.

The writer Jules Verne lived in the city from 1871 until his death in 1905 and served on the city council for 15 years. The Musée de Picardie, opened in 1867 after a visit by Napoleon III, was the first building in France built to serve as a museum and was nicknamed the Little Louvre of the Province. The commune has 60 listed monuments, and local specialities include almond macarons and duck pâté in pastry.
amilcar-cabral: Amílcar Lopes Cabral was born on 12 September 1924 in Bafatá, Portuguese Guinea, to Cape Verdean parents from Santiago. He was educated at the Gil Eanes secondary school in Mindelo, Cape Verde, and then at the Instituto Superior de Agronomia in Lisbon. There he founded the Centro do Estudos Africanos, which used cultural activities as cover for dissident politics under the Estado Novo, which banned unions and associations.

From 1953 Cabral conducted an agricultural census in Portuguese Guinea, travelling more than 60,000 kilometres, which gave him close knowledge of the land and its people. In 1956 he founded the PAIGC, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde, and in the same year was among the founders of the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola, together with Agostinho Neto.

From 1963 he led the PAIGC's guerrilla war against the Portuguese government, which became one of the most successful wars of independence in modern African history. He set up training camps in Ghana with the permission of Kwame Nkrumah. As an agronomist he had his soldiers teach farmers better methods and till the fields beside them, and the PAIGC ran a travelling bazaar selling staple goods below colonial prices, and a roving hospital supplied from the USSR and Sweden.

In his writings Cabral argued that the peasantry of Guinea was a great physical force but not by itself a revolutionary one. He held that the petty bourgeoisie would inherit state power and should commit suicide as a class by identifying with workers and peasants. He also held that liberation could not be complete without the full participation of women.

On 20 January 1973 Cabral was shot dead at a roadblock in Conakry by Inocêncio Kani, a former PAIGC rival, and another party member. Theories of Portuguese or Guinean involvement remain unproven, and about one hundred PAIGC officers and soldiers accused of the conspiracy were summarily executed. His half-brother Luís Cabral became leader of the Guinea-Bissau branch of the party and later President of Guinea-Bissau. Cabral died before the independence of Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde. Cape Verde's main international airport at Sal and a university in Bissau bear his name.
amir-khusrau: Khusrau was born in 1253 at Patiyali, in what is now Uttar Pradesh, the son of Amir Saif ud-Din Mahmud, a Turkic officer, and Bibi Daulat Naz, a native Indian. His father belonged to the Turkic Hazara-yi Lachin clan of Transoxiana and came to India after the invasion of Central Asia by Genghis Khan, finding refuge at the court of Sultan Shams ud-Din Iltutmish of Delhi. His father died in 1260, when Khusrau was eight. He began to write poetry at nine, and his first divan, Tuhfat us-Sighr, was compiled in 1271.

Khusrau joined the army of Malik Chajju, a nephew of Sultan Ghiyas ud-Din Balban, and his poetry came to the notice of the royal court. He then served Balban's sons as patrons, including Khan Muhammad at Multan.Jalal ud-Din Firuz Khalji, who took the throne in 1290, gave him the title Amir. Under Ala ud-Din Khalji he wrote the Khaza'in ul-Futuh on the sultan's buildings, wars and administration, and by 1298 had completed his Khamsa, five masnavis modelled on the quintet of the earlier Persian poet Nizami Ganjavi. In 1310 he became a disciple of the Chishti Sufi Nizamuddin Auliya, and he died in October 1325, six months after his master, and was buried beside him in Delhi.

Khusrau wrote chiefly in Persian, but also in Hindavi and Punjabi, in verse forms such as the ghazal, masnavi, qata, rubai and do-baiti. He is regarded as the father of qawwali, which he is credited with creating by fusing Persian, Arabic, Turkic and Indian singing traditions, and with introducing the ghazal into India. Musicians credit him with six styles, among them qaul, qalbana and khyal, but the evidence for this is insufficient. Many Hindustani verses are attributed to him, although there is no evidence that they were composed before the 18th century. His riddles remain a popular form of Hindavi poetry.
amman: Amman lies on the East Bank Plateau, an upland crossed by three major wadis, at an elevation of 700 to 1,100 metres. The city was originally built on seven hills and now spans more than 19. Its areas take their names from the hills (jabal) or valleys (wadi) they occupy, as in Jabal al-Luweibdeh and Wadi Abdoun.

Settlement in the area dates to at least the 8th millennium BCE at 'Ain Ghazal, now on the city's outskirts. Around 7000 BCE this aceramic Neolithic village covered 15 hectares and had about 3,000 inhabitants, four to five times the population of contemporary Jericho. The site was found in 1974 by workers building a road.

The ancient city was the capital of the Ammonites, who called it Rabat ʿAmmān. After Alexander the Great conquered the Near East in 332 BCE, the region east of the Jordan became a disputed frontier between the Ptolemies and the Seleucids. Ptolemy II, who reigned from 283 to 246 BCE, founded a military colony on the site that grew into a Greek-type city, and renamed it Philadelphia after his own epithet. The Rashidun Caliphate conquered the region from the Byzantines in the 630s and restored the old name as Amman. The Umayyads built a large palace on the Citadel hill, but earthquakes, including a severe one in 749, later devastated the town.

Amman was resettled in 1878, when several hundred Muslim Circassians, expelled from the North Caucasus by the Russian Empire, were directed there by the Ottoman authorities. Their first houses were built with stones from the Roman theatre. A city council was established in 1909, and the town became a hub on the Hejaz Railway by 1914. Its population grew from roughly 1,000 in 1890 to around 1,000,000 in 1990, mainly through immigration, including Palestinians in 1948 and 1967 and Iraqis in 1990.

Amman is the capital and largest city of Jordan, which it became the capital of as Transjordan in 1921. It had about four million inhabitants in 2015, some 42 per cent of the country's population, and is governed as the Greater Amman Municipality. The Jordan Museum holds the Neolithic limestone statues of 'Ain Ghazal, and the Roman theatre and the Umayyad Palace remain among its monuments.
ammianus-marcellinus: Ammianus was born around 330 in the Roman Levant, possibly in Syria or Phoenicia, into a noble family of Greek origin. He called himself a former soldier and a Greek, and Greek was his native language, though he also knew Latin. His enrolment among the elite protectores domestici, the household guards, indicates a middle-class or higher birth. He entered the army young, under Constantius II, and was sent to serve under Ursicinus, governor of Nisibis in Mesopotamia and magister militum, with whom he campaigned twice in the East.

Ammianus travelled with Ursicinus to Italy against Silvanus, an officer who had proclaimed himself emperor in Gaul. Ursicinus had Silvanus assassinated and stayed to help install Julian as Caesar of Gaul, Spain and Britain. In 359 Constantius sent Ursicinus back east to meet a Persian invasion led by King Shapur II. Ammianus served again as a staff officer and was at Amida when the Persians besieged and sacked it; he barely escaped with his life.

After Constantius dismissed Ursicinus, Ammianus seems to have retired, though some modern scholars think he continued to serve. He accompanied Julian, whom he admired, against the Alamanni and the Sassanids, and went with the new emperor Jovian as far as Antioch. He was living at Antioch in 372, when he claims to have witnessed how Theodorus and others, suspected of divining Valens's successor, were tortured and punished. He later settled in Rome. The year of his death is unknown, but scholars place it between 392 and 400 at the latest.

In Rome in the 380s Ammianus wrote the Res gestae in Latin, a history from the accession of Nerva in 96 to the death of Valens at Adrianople in 378, in effect a continuation of Tacitus. It praises the Serapeum of Alexandria as the glory of the empire, so it was presumably finished before the building's destruction in 391. Of its thirty-one books the first thirteen are lost. The eighteen that survive, covering 353 to 378, are the foundation of modern understanding of the fourth-century empire. Its report of the earthquake and tsunami of 21 July 365 at Alexandria accurately describes the sequence of quake, retreating sea and sudden wave.

Scholars generally describe him as a pagan tolerant of Christians. He remarked that no wild beasts are so hostile to men as Christian sects are to one another, and he condemned Julian for his attachment to sacrifice and for his edict barring Christians from teaching posts. Edward Gibbon judged him an accurate and faithful guide, while Kimberly Kagan argues that his battle accounts stress the soldiers' experience at the cost of the larger picture. Almost every manuscript derives from a ninth-century text, Vatican lat. 1873, made at Fulda.
amol: Amol is a city in the Central District of Amol County, Mazandaran province, Iran, and the capital of both the county and the district. It stands on the Haraz River, less than 20 kilometres south of the Caspian Sea and less than 10 kilometres north of the Alborz mountains, at an altitude of 76 metres. It lies 124 kilometres northeast of Tehran by one measure and 60 kilometres west of the provincial capital, Sari. Mount Damavand, the highest peak in Iran and the Middle East, rises to the south. The Haraz route is one of the oldest roads joining the north of Iran to the central plateau. Most Amoli people speak the Mazandarani language as their mother tongue, and Persian is the lingua franca.

Amol is one of the oldest cities in Iran. Its foundation goes back to the Amardi tribe, who inhabited the region in the Iron Age and are mentioned by the Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus. A number of historians and geographers believe it was established in the 1st millennium BCE, and some attribute its birth to the reign of the mythological king Tahmuras. Excavation at Qaleh Kesh has found ancient jewellery dated to the 1st millennium BCE or the Bronze Age.

In the era of the Alid dynasties and the Marashi dynasty, Amol was the capital of northern Iran, and it was also the capital of the Bavand and Ziyarid dynasties. Its inhabitants embraced Islam during the reign of the Abbasid caliph Mahdi (775 to 785), after initially resisting the Arabs. In the ninth century it was one of the largest cities in Iran. During the Umayyad period Sa'id ibn al-As led an army of 4,000 against Tabaristan in the reign of Muawiyah I, and his war with Farrukhan the Great lasted two years. The city has suffered earthquake and flood damage several times and recovered each time. The historian Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari, who lived from 839 to 923, came from Amol.

Amol is known as a centre of rice cultivation. The Rice Research Institute of Iran was established there in 1963. The old bazaar, whose origins date to before Islam, forms the core of the old city. Among its historic sites are the Mausoleum of Mir Bozorg, the Jameh Mosque and Malek Bahman Castle. The 2016 census counted 237,528 people.
amorbach: Amorbach lies on the small river Mud in the north-eastern part of the Odenwald, in the Miltenberg district of Lower Franconia, Bavaria. It has around 4,000 inhabitants. The town began as a Benedictine monastery, which bit by bit grew into a settlement.

Amorbach was raised to the status of a town in 1253. It belonged to the Bishopric of Würzburg until 1656, when it passed to the Archbishopric of Mainz. After the German Mediatisation of 1803 secularised the archbishopric, Amorbach became the residence town of the short-lived Principality of Leiningen. It became part of the Kingdom of Bavaria only in 1816.

Several members of the princely house were born or died there, among them Carl Friedrich Wilhelm, 1st Prince of Leiningen, who died in 1807, and Emich Carl, 2nd Prince, who was the first husband of Princess Victoria of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld, mother of Queen Victoria, and the father of Queen Victoria's elder half-siblings, Carl and Feodora. The printer Johann Amerbach, who lived from about 1440 to 1513, was a son of the town.

Amorbach is the family seat of the princely Haus zu Leiningen and was recognised as a climatic spa in 1965. Its Baroque buildings draw visitors. The Stumm organ of 1782 in the former abbey church, with 5,116 pipes, is played daily at 12:00 and 15:00. The late-Baroque parish church of St Gangolf, built in 1751–3 by the brothers Johann Franz Wolfgang Damian von Ostein and Johann Friedrich Karl von Ostein, Archbishop of Mainz, was inspired by St Peter's Church at Mainz and has ceiling frescoes by Johannes Zick. The tithe barn of 1488, built to store produce paid as tithes to the prince, now serves as a cabaret theatre. In 1992 the town received the Europa Nostra Medal.
amorgos: Amorgos is the easternmost island of the Cyclades and the nearest to the Dodecanese. With 16 neighbouring islets, the largest of which is Nikouria, it forms a municipality of 126 square kilometres. Its position near the ancient Ionian towns of Miletus, Halicarnassus and Ephesus made it one of the first places through which the Ionians passed to the Cycladic islands and on to the Greek mainland.
