It has also been known as Yperia, Platagy, Pagali, Psichia and Karkisia.

Burial tombs and other finds show an intense presence on Amorgos in the first period of Cycladic civilisation, from 3200 to 2000 BCE, with almost a dozen inhabited centres. The island is the origin of many Cycladic figurines. The Kapsala figurines, from about 2700 BCE, are the earliest of the canonical types, a reclining female with folded arms, and the Dokathismata type, of 2400 to 2100 BCE, has a more slender and sometimes angular outline than the common Spedos type.

In the Archaic period three independent city-states stood on the island, probably with their own constitutions but one currency: Arkesini, Minoa and Aigiali. Because one was called Minoa, it has been suspected that Cretans settled there early, but no archaeological evidence supports this. About 630 BCE the poet Semonides led a Samian colony to the island. Amorgos belonged to the Delian League and the Second Athenian League. The walls of Arkesini and the towers scattered across the island are remains of this age. In 322 BCE Athens and Macedonia fought the naval Battle of Amorgos.

After the Fourth Crusade the island became a dependency of the duchy of Naxos, later disputed by other Venetians. In 1312 a Hospitaller fleet defeated a fleet of Menteshe there. Under Ottoman rule, from 1537 to 1829, it was called Yamurgi, and it became part of Greece on independence in 1830. An earthquake on 9 July 1956 with its epicentre about 30 km south of the island, of magnitude 7.7, caused a local tsunami of up to 30 m, which killed 53 people.

The monastery of Panagia Hozoviotissa stands on a cliff north-east of Chora. It was built early in the second millennium to protect an icon dated to 812, which is displayed inside. A group of windmills stands on a hill above Chora. The island is reached only by boat, and its geography prevents mass tourism. The film The Big Blue of 1988 by Luc Besson, with its views of the island's marine life, brought it international attention.
amorites: The Amorites were a Northwest Semitic-speaking Bronze Age people who originated in western Mesopotamia and first appear in Sumerian records around 2500 BCE. The most common view places their homeland in central Syria, identified with Jebel Bishri or the Syrian steppe. In Sumerian and Akkadian texts the term Amurru, written mar.tu, refers to the Amorites, their principal deity and their kingdom. Tablets from Ebla show them as a rural group on the middle and upper Euphrates, and for the Akkadian emperors mar.tu was one of the four quarters around Akkad. Naram-Sin of Akkad records defeating a coalition of Sumerian cities and Amorites near Jebel Bishri around 2240 BCE.

By the last days of the Third Dynasty of Ur, immigrating Amorites were such a force that Shu-Sin built a wall of 270 kilometres from the Tigris to the Euphrates to hold them off. Mesopotamian texts describe them as nomadic tribes under chiefs, often with contempt. After Ur declined, Amorite rulers gained power in several city-states, a rise that peaked in the Old Babylonian period. Shamshi-Adad I of Ekallatum conquered Assur, and Babylon became the major power under Sumu-la-El and his successors, among them Hammurabi, who destroyed the Amorite kingdom of Mari.

An Amorite presence in Egypt is thought to date from the 19th century BCE; the Fourteenth Dynasty had rulers with names such as Yakbim, and the Hyksos seem to have included Amorites. The Amorite era in Mesopotamia ended in the 16th century BCE with the fall of Babylon, which the Kassites occupied around 1595 BCE. Syrian Amorites then came under the Hittites and the Middle Assyrian Empire, and from about 1200 BCE they disappear from the record, displaced or absorbed by other West Semitic peoples, among whom the Arameans rose to prominence.

The Amorite language is known only from personal names and loanwords in other languages' texts, and was closely related to Canaanite and Aramaic. Their chief god was Amurru, with a consort Ašratum, whose name is cognate with Asherah. Dagan was supreme in many cities of the Euphrates region. The Hebrew Bible uses the name for highlanders of Canaan, descendants of Canaan in Genesis, and for the kings Sihon and Og east of the Jordan.
amos-prophet: According to the Bible, Amos was a shepherd and a sycamore fig farmer from Teqoaʿ, and an older contemporary of Hosea and Isaiah. He was active about 760 to 755 BCE, in the reigns of Jeroboam II of Israel and Uzziah of Judah. His own words, I am not a prophet nor a son of a prophet (7:14), mark him as outside the schools of prophets, and later prophets also begin by telling the story of their calling. The book dates his prophecies to two years before an earthquake.

Jeroboam II, who ruled about 781 to 741 BCE, had conquered Syria, Moab and Ammon and extended his lands from the source of the Orontes River to the Dead Sea. The northern kingdom enjoyed a long peace and a revival of art and commerce, but social corruption and the oppression of the poor were widespread, and some mixed the worship of the Lord with that of pagan deities.

Amos felt called to preach at Bethel, where there was a royal sanctuary, and to announce the fall of the reigning dynasty and of the northern kingdom. The head priest Amaziah denounced him to Jeroboam II and advised him to leave. Many scholars see no reason to doubt that he was forced out and returned home. Prevented from delivering his message, he is held to have written it down.

Amos is widely recognised as the first prophet to write down all the messages he received, and no earlier literary prophet is known; most later prophets followed his example. Isaiah certainly knew his book and imitated it in his early speeches. What is known of Amos derives solely from the book, and in recent years scholars have grown more sceptical of its account of his life. The apocryphal Lives of the Prophets says Amos was killed by the son of Amaziah and buried in his homeland.

The Book of Amos is attributed to him and is counted among the Twelve Minor Prophets. Its central teaching is that God is ethical, so that religion consists not in ritual but in righteousness. Prayers and sacrifices do not make up for bad deeds, and behaving justly matters more than ceremony, as in Amos 5:21–24, which ends with the call to let justice roll on like a river. Amos held that economic justice was necessary to preserve the nation, and he is described as an uncompromising monotheist.

He presents the relationship between God and Israel as a moral contract: if the people fall below God's moral requirements, the relationship will be dissolved. Amos is commemorated with the other minor prophets in several churches, with a feast day on 15 June in the Eastern Orthodox calendar.
amphora: An amphora has two expansive handles joining the shoulder of the body to a long, narrow neck. Most were made with a pointed base, so that they could be stood upright by embedding them in soft ground such as sand. Two principal forms existed: the neck amphora, in which neck and body meet at a sharp angle, and the one-piece amphora, in which they form a continuous curve. Neck amphorae were common in early Greece and were gradually replaced by the one-piece type from around the 7th century BCE.

An amphora holds less than half a ton, typically under 50 kilograms, whereas the larger storage jar called the pithos holds between half a ton and two and a half tons. Most amphorae stood around 45 centimetres high, and the wine amphora held a standard measure of about 39 litres.

Amphorae carried wine, olive oil and garum, and also olives, grain, fish and other agricultural products. The pointed base suited shipping: the jars were packed upright or on their sides in as many as five staggered layers, with ropes through the handles and heather or reeds as packing. They were produced on an industrial scale until approximately the 7th century CE.

Stamps and painted inscriptions recorded the workshop, the weight and the contents, and historians use them to reconstruct ancient trade networks. Because amphorae were too cheap to return to their origin, empty ones were broken up at their destination. At Rome the fragments formed Monte Testaccio, a hill 45 metres high. In Greece, painted amphorae were made for ceremonial purposes: Panathenaic amphorae, filled with olive oil from a sacred grove, were prizes at the Panathenaic Festivals.

Amphorae are of great use to maritime archaeologists, since they often indicate the age of a shipwreck and the origin of its cargo. The largest known wreck of an amphora cargo ship, carrying 6,000 jars, was found off Kefalonia. The German scholar Heinrich Dressel made the first systematic classification of Roman types, and the Dressel table is still used for many of the about 66 distinct types identified.
amr-ibn-al-as: Amr ibn al-As was the son of al-As ibn Wa'il, a wealthy landowner of the Banu Sahm clan of the Quraysh of Mecca, and inherited from him an estate and vineyards near Ta'if. Reports conflict about when he became a Muslim; the most credible version places it in 629 or 630, not long before Muhammad conquered Mecca. In 633 the first caliph, Abu Bakr, sent him as one of four commanders to conquer Syria and appointed him governor of Palestine, where he won the Battle of Dathin on 4 February 634.

From southern Palestine Amr launched the conquest of Byzantine Egypt; most Muslim sources say with Caliph Umar's reluctant approval, though some accounts say he acted without authorisation. With about 4,000 cavalry and no siege engines he took Pelusium and Bilbeis after month-long sieges and halted before Babylon, at the head of the Nile Delta. In July 640 he defeated the Byzantines at Heliopolis, and Babylon yielded on 9 April 641. Alexandria surrendered in 641 or 642, and Amr then advanced west as far as Cyrenaica and Tripoli.

He guaranteed the security of Egypt's people in a treaty with the Byzantine governor Cyrus and imposed a poll tax on non-Muslim adult men. He kept the Coptic-dominated bureaucracy and founded Fustat, beside Babylon, as the garrison town, because Umar rejected Alexandria as the capital. Amr ruled with relative independence and amassed great wealth, and Caliph Uthman dismissed him in 646 after he and Abd Allah ibn Sa'd accused each other of incompetence.

Amr then criticised Uthman openly. In the First Fitna he sided with Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan against Caliph Ali, in return for the promise of Egypt, and in July or August 658 he defeated Ali's troops at al-Musannah and took Fustat. Mu'awiya, once caliph, confirmed him in Egypt.

Amr died of natural causes, most credibly in 43 AH (663–664 CE), and was buried at the foot of the Muqattam hills east of Fustat; the grave is not identified. He left seventy sacks of gold dinars, which his sons refused to inherit and Mu'awiya confiscated.
amritsar: Amritsar lies in the Majha region of Punjab, 28 kilometres from the India-Pakistan border and 47 kilometres north-east of Lahore. It takes its name from Amṛta Sarovara, Sanskrit for Pool of Nectar, the pool that surrounds the Golden Temple, and it was formerly also called Rāmdāspur. Tradition links the area to the Ramayana: the Bhagwan Valmiki Tirath Sthal is believed to be the ashram of Maharishi Valmiki, where Sita gave birth to Lava and Kusha.

In the Sikh tradition Guru Ram Das, the fourth guru, founded the city in 1574. One account says that the land was bought with Sikh donations from the owners of the village of Tung, another that Guru Amar Das chose the site. Ram Das first completed the pool, built his centre next to it and invited merchants and artisans from other parts of India to settle. The town grew under Guru Arjan Dev, financed by donations and built by volunteers, and in 1604 he installed the scripture of Sikhism in the new Harmandir Sahib. Ahmad Shah of the Durrani Empire besieged Amritsar in 1762 and again in 1766 and 1767, massacred its people and destroyed the city.

Under the Sikh Empire Maharaja Ranjit Singh fortified the city in 1822, and Sher Singh later completed the walls with twelve gates. The British annexed Punjab in 1849 and built a thirteenth gate in 1866. They supported a textile industry, and Khalsa College made the city a centre of colonial education. On 13 April 1919, the day of Vaisakhi, Colonel Reginald Dyer ordered troops to fire into a crowd of thousands in the Jallianwala Bagh without warning, for about ten minutes. A British government inquiry put the death toll at 379, and the Indian National Congress estimated about 1,000.

After the partition of India many Hindu and Sikh refugees from the Lahore and Sialkot districts settled in Amritsar. In June 1984 the Indian army carried out Operation Blue Star to remove militants from the Golden Temple, an action that remains controversial. Official reports gave 83 army deaths and 493 civilians killed, while independent estimates run to more than 5,000. The city is the holiest in Sikhism and the Golden Temple its most-visited gurdwara. In 2011 the municipality had 1,159,227 inhabitants, with Hindus and Sikhs the two main communities, and the city is known for wooden chessboards and chess pieces.
amsterdam: Amsterdam lies in the province of North Holland, in the western Netherlands, at an elevation of about 2 metres below sea level. The river Amstel ends in the city centre and connects to a large number of canals that eventually terminate in the IJ. The surrounding land is flat and formed of large polders, and the city is connected to the North Sea by the North Sea Canal. More than 100 kilometres of canals run through it, most of them navigable. The three main ones are the Prinsengracht, the Herengracht and the Keizersgracht.

Farmers settled around the area of the later city about three millennia ago, along the prehistoric IJ and upstream on its tributary the Amstel. A permanent settlement was not possible until water issues were controlled, because the river mouth and banks were too wet. Amsterdam was founded at the mouth of the Amstel, which was dammed to control flooding, and it began as a small fishing village in the 12th century. Its population was around 1,000 in 1300. It grew in the 15th and 16th centuries, mainly through the Baltic grain trade after the Burgundian victory in the Dutch–Hanseatic War in 1441.

The population then rose sharply during the Dutch Revolt. Many people from the Southern Netherlands fled north, especially after Antwerp fell to Spanish forces in 1585, and Jews from Spain, Portugal and Eastern Europe, Germans and Scandinavians also settled there. The population more than doubled between 1585 and 1610, stood at about 50,000 in 1600 and reached 200,000 in the 1660s. It then stabilised around 240,000 for most of the 18th century. The Amsterdam Stock Exchange was founded in 1602. In the 19th and 20th centuries the city expanded, and new neighbourhoods and suburbs were built.

Amsterdam is the capital and largest city of the Netherlands, though it is not the seat of government, which is in The Hague. Its 17th-century canal belt, the grachten, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and preserves narrow canal houses with gabled façades. The Rijksmuseum, opened in 1885, holds Dutch Golden Age art, and the Stedelijk Museum opened in 1895. The city has two universities, the University of Amsterdam and the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, and hosted the Summer Olympics in 1928.
amur-river: The Amur, called the Heilong River in Chinese, rises where its two main headstreams, the Shilka and the Argun, meet in the hills of north-eastern China. It flows east along the border between the Russian Far East and Northeast China, then turns north-east beyond Khabarovsk, where it is joined by the Ussuri and ceases to form the border.

Its largest tributary is the Songhua. Measured with the Argun, it is 4,444 km long and drains a basin of desert, steppe, tundra and taiga. Its mouth faces the northern end of Sakhalin, and the island's name derives from a Tungusic word for black, as in the Manchu name for the river, Sahaliyan Ula.

For many centuries the valley was home to Tungusic peoples such as the Evenki, Nanai and Ulch, to the Daur, to some Ainu and, near the mouth, to the Nivkhs. Fishing in the river and its tributaries was the main livelihood of many of them. The Chinese called them collectively the Wild Jurchens, and used a term meaning Fish-skin Tatars for the Nanai and related groups because of their clothes of fish skin.

The Mongols of the Yuan dynasty kept a tenuous military presence on the lower Amur in the 13th and 14th centuries. Under the Yongle and Xuande Emperors the Ming dynasty reached the river: expeditions led by the eunuch Yishiha reached Tyr several times between 1411 and the early 1430s and obtained at least the nominal allegiance of the lower Amur's peoples, but the Ming presence soon faded.

Russian Cossacks led by Vassili Poyarkov and Yerofey Khabarov explored the Amur in 1643-44 and 1649-51 and collected tribute from local peoples, building the fort of Albazin on the upper river. The Qing turned north once their conquest of China was secure, founded Aigun about 1683-84 and took Albazin in 1685. The Treaty of Nerchinsk of 1689 left the whole valley from the meeting of the Shilka and the Argun downstream in Chinese hands. The region then remained a backwater of the Qing Empire for about a century and a half.

Russians returned to the river in the mid-19th century, and the Manchus yielded all lands north of the river to the Russian Empire by the Treaty of Aigun in 1858. Lands east of the Ussuri and along the lower Amur passed to Russia by the Convention of Peking in 1860.

The river gives its name to China's province of Heilongjiang and to Russia's Amur Oblast. The Khabarovsk Bridge, finished in 1916, let Trans-Siberian trains cross the river all year without ferries or tracks on the ice. The basin shelters the Amur tiger and leopard, and the kaluga, a sturgeon that can reach 5.6 m.
anabaptism: Anabaptism traces its origins to the Radical Reformation of the 16th century. Historians classify medieval groups with a similar approach to the Bible as forerunners, among them the Waldensians, the Hussites and the Brethren of the Common Life, and the 15th-century Bohemian reformer Petr Chelčický taught most of the beliefs now held integral to it. In Switzerland it began as an offshoot of the reforms of Ulrich Zwingli. Some of his young followers thought he moved too slowly, and the division became plain at a disputation in Zürich in October 1523, when Conrad Grebel asked what should be done about the mass.

Scholars disagree about its roots. One theory holds that the movement began in Zürich and spread from there, another that it developed from several independent movements. Research has also been coloured by enemies who slandered the Anabaptists and by supporters who defended them. It was long popular to class all Anabaptists with the radicals of Münster, and those who sought to correct this error tended to over-correct and deny any link between the larger movement and its most radical elements.

Anabaptists hold that baptism is valid only when candidates freely confess their faith in Christ and ask for it, so they reject the baptism of infants. The name is an exonym meaning one who baptizes again; early members refused it, saying infant baptism was not in scripture and their baptism of believers was their first true one. Early Anabaptists set out their beliefs in the Schleitheim Confession of 1527, written by Michael Sattler, who was arrested and executed soon afterwards.

Most adhere to a literal reading of the Sermon on the Mount, which they take to teach against hatred, violence, oaths, military action and participation in civil government. They see themselves primarily as citizens of the kingdom of God. Practices often include the love feast with feet washing, the holy kiss, and sharing possessions.

Roman Catholics and Protestants alike persecuted Anabaptists with torture and execution. Under Zwingli's Protestants, Manz became the first Anabaptist martyr in 1527, and King Ferdinand declared drowning, called the third baptism, the best antidote to Anabaptism. Anabaptism was never established by any state. Many found refuge in Moravia, which was more tolerant and became a centre of the movement.

The Amish, Hutterites and Mennonites descend directly from the early movement. According to the figures given, there were over 2.03 million baptized Anabaptists in 87 countries in 2025, mostly in Africa and North America. Voluntary church membership, freedom of conscience and the priesthood of all believers are among the 16th-century ideas that have influenced Western society.
anacreon: Anacreon came from Teos on the coast of Ionia, a tradition attested as early as Herodotus. The year of his birth is not known. When Persia conquered Teos in the 540s BCE the Teians moved to Abdera in Thrace, and Anacreon was probably already an adult. He then spent time on Samos. According to Himerius he was invited there to educate Polycrates, the future tyrant, whom Strabo reports to have been one of the main subjects of his poetry. Herodotus places him still on Samos in 522 BCE, when Polycrates was murdered.

From Samos he went to Athens on the invitation of Hipparchus, presumably after Hipparchus came to power in 528/7 BCE. Ancient sources do not say whether or when he left. He may have gone after the assassination of Hipparchus in 514 BCE or the expulsion of Hippias in 510 BCE, though some evidence places him in the city later.

Anacreon wrote in the Ionic dialect, in metrical verse composed to be sung or recited to the lyre, mostly as monody rather than for a chorus. His themes were love, infatuation, disappointment, revelry, parties and festivals, and everyday life. Two short hymns, to Artemis and to Dionysus, of eight and eleven lines, stand first among his few undisputed remains. The Suda and Athenaeus mention five books of his lyrics, but only fragments survive, gathered from citations by later writers.

A collection of poems by anonymous imitators, the Anacreontea, was long believed to be his own work. It survives in a 10th-century manuscript, and its poems were composed between the 1st century BCE and the 6th century CE, not in his Ionic dialect.

Anacreon probably died at the beginning of the fifth century BCE; Gregory Hutchinson says around 500, Hans Bernsdorff suggests 495 and David Campbell says 485. Valerius Maximus reports that he choked on a grape seed, a story generally regarded as apocryphal. An epigram in the Greek Anthology places his tomb on Teos.

He was depicted on Athenian red-figure vases while still alive, and later Greeks included him among the Nine Lyric Poets. By the Hellenistic period a caricature of him as drunken and lustful was established, though Plato portrayed him as a wise man. He was an important influence on Horace. The edition of the Anacreontea by Henricus Stephanus in 1554 began a fashion for short, playful Anacreontic verse that peaked in the eighteenth century.
anagni: Anagni is a hill town of about 424 metres above sea level in the province of Frosinone, in Lazio, east-southeast of Rome. It keeps the look of a small medieval town, with twisting streets and steep lanes inside Roman boundary walls. The first people known by name in the area were the Hernici, said to have come from the Aniene valley, and Anagni was an important city and spiritual centre of theirs, built on an acropolis and partly defended by walls of almost squared stone.

In 307 BCE the Hernici, except for Alatri, Veroli and Ferentino, declared war on Rome and, after setbacks, surrendered. In 306 BCE Anagni and the other states that had borne arms were admitted to citizenship without the vote, forbidden councils and intermarriage, and left only magistrates in charge of religious rites. Several emperors later spent their summers there, among them Marcus Aurelius, Septimius Severus, Commodus and Caracalla.

Anagni has been a bishop's seat since the 5th century. From the 10th and 11th centuries the popes regarded it as a safer and healthier place than Rome, and it became one of their favourite residences. In 1160 Pope Alexander III excommunicated Emperor Frederick Barbarossa in the cathedral, and on 29 September 1227 Pope Gregory IX excommunicated Emperor Frederick II there. The town produced four popes in a century, three of them of the Conti family, among them Innocent III.

In 1303 Guillaume de Nogaret, adviser to Philip IV of France, and Sciarra Colonna led about two thousand mercenaries against the palaces of Pope Boniface VIII. The pope was held for three days without food or drink until the townspeople rose and freed him. This is called the Outrage of Anagni, and a later legend says Colonna slapped the pope with his gauntlet. Boniface died in Rome on 11 October 1303. The move of the papal court to Avignon began a long decline, and Duke Werner von Urslingen sacked the town in 1348.

The Romanesque cathedral of Saint Mary, built in 1071–1105 with Gothic additions in the mid-13th century, has frescoes among the best preserved examples of Romanesque and Byzantine art in Italy, and an unrestored Cosmati floor. The Communal Palace was built in 1163 by the Brescian architect Jacopo da Iseo. Excavations since 2006 at the imperial Villa Magna, south of the town, have revealed a large, richly decorated building devoted to wine production.
analects: According to Ban Gu, writing in the Book of Han, the Analects began as individual records kept by Confucius's disciples of their conversations with him, which they collected and jointly edited after his death in 479 BCE. During the Han dynasty the work was titled Lunyu, which may mean edited conversations or selected speeches. Scholars agree that large portions were composed in the Warring States period and that the work reached its final form in the mid-Han dynasty.

Liu Xiang records that two versions existed at the beginning of the Han: the Lu version of twenty chapters and the Qi version of twenty-two. A third Old Text version, written in characters not used since the Warring States period, was found hidden in a wall of a house believed to be Confucius's. The received text is mostly based on the Lu version.

The chapters are grouped by theme but do not form a continuous argument, and adjacent chapters are often unrelated. Confucius describes himself as a transmitter of the traditions of the early Zhou, not an originator. The central idea is ren, an all-encompassing state of virtue that, in the text, no living person had completely attained. Asked to define it, Confucius responds indirectly, with examples, and the basic step towards it is filial piety.

In politics the text holds that a good ruler is self-disciplined and governs by education and example rather than by punishment. Confucius blames social chaos on rulers who claim titles they do not deserve. Education is a fundamental theme, and he is traditionally credited with teaching three thousand students, seventy of whom mastered what he taught. The Analects is arguably the most reliable source for his biography.

During most of the Han period the Analects was not a principal text of Confucianism. Under Emperor Wu only the Five Classics were canonical, and the Analects was treated as a collection of Confucius's commentary on them. By the Eastern Han it was widely read by schoolchildren. In the late Song dynasty Zhu Xi promoted it as one of the Four Books, and it came to be regarded as more insightful than the older Five Classics.

He Yan's Collected Explanations, written in 248 CE, is the oldest complete commentary still extant and remained the standard guide for nearly a thousand years. The Analects has been among the most widely read books in China for more than two thousand years, and its ideas continue to influence East Asian thought and values.
anambra-state: Anambra State is named after the Omambala River, which flows through it and is a tributary of the Niger; Anambra is the anglicised form of Omambala. The state is bordered by Delta and Edo States to the west across the Niger, by Imo and Rivers to the south, Abia to the southeast, Enugu to the east and Kogi to the north. Its climate is tropical wet and dry.

Archaeological excavations at Igbo-Ukwu and Ezira show that the area's history stretches to the 9th century, with great works of art in iron, bronze, copper and pottery. These revealed a sophisticated system of divine kingship that held sway in the area from about 948 until 1911. The area has been the site of numerous civilizations, including the ancient Kingdom of Nri, whose capital was the town of Igbo-Ukwu. Awka was the craft industrial centre of the Nri hegemony, and Onitsha developed as a river port and commercial city on the Niger in the pre-colonial era.

Britain recognised some traditional kings and leaders under indirect rule in the Protectorate of South Nigeria, and from the 19th century appointed some leaders as Warrant Chiefs, authorising them to collect taxes. The old Anambra State was formed in 1976 from the former East Central State. During the Nigerian Civil War of 1967 to 1970 the area was part of the secessionist Republic of Biafra, and it was severely affected by the war.

Anambra is a state in southeastern Nigeria, with Awka as its capital and Onitsha as its most populous city. Nnewi is the second largest commercial and industrial city. The population is primarily Igbo, and the Igbo language is a lingua franca throughout the state. It consists of 21 local government areas, and most people are Christian, chiefly Catholic, Anglican and Pentecostal. The Onitsha Ofala Festival, marking the climax of the New Yam, is held each October.
ananda-mahidol: Ananda Mahidol was born on 20 September 1925 in Heidelberg, where his parents Prince Mahidol Adulyadej of Songkla and Mom Sangwan were studying. He was the first Thai king born outside the country. The family returned to Thailand in 1928, and Prince Mahidol died in 1929. After the revolution of 1932 ended the absolute monarchy, his mother took her children to Lausanne in 1933, officially for their health and education. When King Prajadhipok abdicated in 1935, the cabinet had to decide on the succession because Prince Chula Chakrabongse, whose father had married a foreigner, was also a candidate. Pridi Banomyong persuaded the cabinet to exclude him, and the National Assembly elected Ananda Mahidol on 2 March 1935, when he was nine.

The king stayed in Switzerland to study while regents acted for him. In 1938 he visited Siam for the first time as monarch, and Field Marshal Plaek Phibunsongkhram was prime minister during most of his reign. Japan invaded Thailand on 8 December 1941, and from 24 January 1942 Thailand was a formal ally of Japan. The regent Pridi Banomyong refused to sign the declaration of war on the Allies, so it was legally invalid. After Japan surrendered on 15 August 1945 the king returned in December 1945 with a law degree. He won the affection of the Thai people, and visited Sampheng Lane in Bangkok's Chinatown to ease post-war tensions.

On 9 June 1946 the king was found shot dead in his bedroom in the Boromphiman Throne Hall, four days before he was to return to Switzerland. An initial radio announcement spoke of an accident, but a commission of inquiry reported in October 1946 that the death could not have been accidental, and that neither suicide nor murder had been satisfactorily proved.

After Plaek Phibunsongkhram's coup of November 1947, the king's secretary Chaliao Pathumrot and two pages, But and Chit, were tried for conspiracy to murder. After a trial that ended in 1951 and two appeals, the Supreme Court convicted all three, who were executed on 17 February 1955. Theories have since pointed to an accident, suicide or murder. The pathologist Keith Simpson considered suicide highly unlikely, and Rayne Kruger concluded that it was most probably an accidental suicide. His brother Bhumibol Adulyadej succeeded him. Ananda Mahidol was cremated at Sanam Luang on 29 March 1950.
anapa: The area was settled in antiquity as a major seaport, Sinda, and the capital of Sindica. In the 6th century BCE Pontic Greeks built the colony of Gorgippia there, naming it after a king of the Cimmerian Bosporus. In the 2nd and 3rd centuries BCE it flourished within the Bosporan Kingdom, and its guild of shipowners controlled maritime trade in the eastern Black Sea. It was inhabited until the 3rd century CE, when neighbouring tribes of Circassian or Adyghe origin, the Natkhuay, overran it and gave Anapa its modern name. The Genoese renamed the settlement Mapa at the turn of the 14th century and held it until an Ottoman fleet arrived in 1475.

In 1781 French engineers built a fortress at Anapa for the Ottomans, in the reign of Abdul Hamid I. Russia attacked it repeatedly, and it was all but destroyed in the last siege, in 1829. The town passed to Russia under the Treaty of Adrianople and was granted town status in 1846. Ottoman forces occupied it again from 1853 to 1856, during the Crimean War. Elizabeth Pilenko, later named a saint in the Eastern Orthodox Church, was its mayor during the Russian Revolution. Nazi Germany, helped by Romanian troops, occupied the town from 30 August 1942 to 22 September 1943 and demolished it entirely.

Anapa lies on the northern coast of the Black Sea in Krasnodar Krai, near the Sea of Azov. It is a resort town with a number of sanatoria and hotels, and the 2021 census recorded 81,863 inhabitants. Its sights include a museum of the ancient city of Gorgippia, the gates of the Turkish fortress, the Church of St Onuphrius and a lighthouse.
anarchism: The word comes from the Ancient Greek anarkhia, meaning without a ruler, and appears in English from 1642, when it stressed disorder. Factions in the French Revolution called their opponents anarchists, although few of those accused shared much with later anarchists. The first political philosopher to call himself an anarchist and give the word a positive meaning was Pierre-Joseph Proudhon.

Precursors are found in the ancient world: the Taoist philosophers Zhuang Zhou and Laozi in China, and in Greece the Cynics, the Stoics and tragedians who used the myth of Antigone to show the conflict between state law and personal autonomy. Modern anarchism emerged from the Enlightenment. By the late 1870s several schools were well defined, and the movement spread across the world from 1880 to 1914.

Anarchism seeks to abolish institutions that perpetuate authority, coercion or hierarchy, above all the state and capitalism, and to replace them with stateless societies of voluntary associations based on free association and reciprocity. It is counted as part of the libertarian wing of the socialist movement.

Its schools are grouped into two traditions. Individualist anarchism stresses freedom from restraint on the individual, while social anarchism seeks the free potential of society through equality and social ownership. Mutualism, developed by Proudhon, aims at reciprocity, federation and a bank of the people; in What Is Property? (1840) he described a third form of society, the synthesis of communism and property. Collectivist anarchism, associated with Mikhail Bakunin, advocates collective ownership of the means of production, to be won by violent revolution. The communist and syndicalist currents followed.

Anarchists took part in revolutions, notably the Paris Commune, the Russian Civil War and the Spanish Civil War, whose end marked the close of the classical era. In that era some anarchists used assassination as propaganda of the deed, mostly in the late 1870s, 1880s and 1890s, while Emma Goldman and Errico Malatesta defended limited violence as a necessary reaction to state violence. Others took the path of nonviolence. Francisco Ferrer founded the Escuela Moderna in Barcelona in 1901, a secular school that the state harassed until it closed. In the last decades of the 20th century and the 21st the movement has revived within anti-capitalist, anti-war and anti-globalisation movements.
anastasio-somoza-debayle: Anastasio Somoza Debayle, nicknamed Tachito, was born on 5 December 1925, the third child of Anastasio Somoza García and Salvadora Debayle. From the age of ten he was educated in the United States, with his elder brother Luis, and he graduated from the United States Military Academy at West Point on 6 June 1946. His father, who was president of Nicaragua from 1937 to 1947 and again from 1950, made him chief of staff of the National Guard on his return, which made him head of the armed forces. After their father's assassination on 21 September 1956 Luis became president, and Anastasio helped ensure that presidents loyal to the family held office until 1967.

Elected president on 5 February 1967, Somoza took office on 1 May. Luis had ruled more gently than their father, but Anastasio shared his father's intolerance of dissent, and his rule soon resembled it, with harsh repression. Barred from immediate re-election, he arranged for a three-man junta to hold office from 1972 while he kept command of the National Guard and so stayed the de facto ruler. A Managua earthquake on 23 December 1972 killed about 5,000 people and virtually destroyed the city. Martial law was declared and Somoza took formal control as head of the National Emergency Committee. He reportedly embezzled much of the money sent from abroad to rebuild the city.

He was re-elected in 1974, by which time the Catholic Church had begun to speak out against his government. In 1975 he began a campaign against the Sandinista National Liberation Front, targeting people suspected of supporting it, and human rights groups condemned his record by the late 1970s. Support for the Sandinistas grew, especially after the earthquake and after the United States under President Jimmy Carter withdrew its support, partly over the murder of the American journalist Bill Stewart by government soldiers. The newspaper publisher Pedro Chamorro, an opponent of the Somozas, was assassinated on 10 January 1978.

On 17 July 1979 Somoza resigned and fled to Miami, taking with him, it is claimed, much of the national treasure; the Sandinistas found less than two million dollars in the treasury, and the country's foreign debt stood at 1.6 billion dollars. Refused asylum in the United States, he took refuge in Paraguay and bought a house in Asunción. A Sandinista commando team ambushed his car there on 17 September 1980 with machine guns and an RPG-7 rocket, and killed him and two others. He was buried in Miami. A Brazilian newspaper estimated in 1979 that the Somoza family's fortune stood between 2 and 4 billion dollars. His memoirs, Nicaragua Betrayed, blamed the Carter administration for his downfall.
anastasius-i-dicorus: Anastasius was born at Dyrrachium into an Illyro-Roman family, probably no later than 431. He had one black eye and one blue eye, which gave him the nickname Dicorus, meaning two-pupiled. Before becoming emperor he was a silentiary, a palace official. His brother Paulus was consul in 496, and his extensive family included many relatives who held office, among them his nephews Hypatius and Pompeius. After his coronation he proclaimed that his family had a noble Roman lineage descended from Pompey the Great, an attempt, according to the historian Anthony Kaldellis, to prove his Romanness.

After the death of Zeno in 491, crowds in the Hippodrome of Constantinople demanded an Orthodox and Roman emperor. Zeno's widow Ariadne chose Anastasius over Zeno's brother Longinus, which upset the Isaurians. The patriarch of Constantinople required him to pledge not to repudiate the Council of Chalcedon, since Anastasius sympathised with the Monophysites. Ariadne married him on 20 May 491. He abolished the hated tax on receipts and in 498 the chrysargyron tax on merchants and traders. He also had taxes paid in cash rather than goods, paid soldiers in money, and in 498 revived the monetary system with the solidus and the follis.

His reign saw two wars. The Isaurian War of 492 to 497 followed Longinus's supporters' revolt, which was broken at the Battle of Cotyaeum, and many Isaurians were relocated to Thrace. In the Anastasian War of 502 to 505 against Sassanid Persia, the Persians took Theodosiopolis and Amida, the Romans recovered Amida for gold, and peace followed in 506. Anastasius built the fortress of Daras and the Anastasian Wall to protect Constantinople from Bulgar raids. His moderate Monophysite policy broke down in 512, when he deposed the Metropolitan of Chalcedon and provoked riots. The following year the general Vitalian rebelled and marched on Constantinople.

Anastasius died childless in Constantinople on 9 July 518. According to a probably fictional account in the Anonymous Valesianus, he left his succession to chance, and the first person to enter his room the next morning was Justin, commander of the Excubitors, who became emperor. Victor of Tunnuna gives his age at death as 88, a figure most modern historians accept. He left the treasury with 23,000,000 solidi, or 320,000 pounds of gold, and the stable government and sound finances he created allowed his successors, most notably Justinian I, to pursue more ambitious policies. His coinage remained in circulation long after his reign, and four of his solidi have been found as far away as China.
anatolia: Anatolia, also called Asia Minor, is a peninsula in West Asia that makes up the majority of the land area of Turkey. It is bounded by the Mediterranean to the south, the Aegean to the west, the Sea of Marmara to the northwest and the Black Sea to the north. The name comes from the Greek Anatolē, meaning the East, the direction of the rising sun. The oldest known name for a region within it is the Land of Hatti, later used for the whole territory of the Hittites.

Anatolia was an early centre of farming. About 9,000 years ago a major migration of Anatolian Neolithic farmers into Europe began, and Çatalhöyük, dated to about 7,000 BCE, is considered the most advanced of its Neolithic settlements. Written records begin with clay tablets of about 2000 BCE from Kültepe, which belonged to an Assyrian trade colony. The earliest attested peoples were the Hattians in the centre and the Hurrians in the east, followed by Indo-European speakers of Hittite, Luwian and Lydian. Minted coinage first appeared in Lydia in the 7th century BCE. In the 6th century BCE the Persian Achaemenid Empire conquered all of Anatolia.

Greek came to dominate the peninsula's languages in the Hellenistic and Roman periods, and by the 4th century CE western and central Anatolia were overwhelmingly Christian and Greek-speaking. In the ten years after the Battle of Manzikert in 1071, Seljuk Turks migrated over large areas, beginning the slow change to a Muslim, Turkish-speaking land. Control was divided between the Byzantine Empire and the Seljuk Sultanate of Rûm. The Mongols swept through the east and centre in 1255 and stayed until 1335. The Ottomans, under Osman I and his son Orhan, absorbed the Anatolian beyliks in the 15th century and completed the conquest in 1517.

Between 1894 and 1924, millions of Christians and other non-Turkic peoples, among them about two million Greeks and an estimated 1.5 million Armenians, were killed or expelled by Ottoman Turkish authorities from most of the area of modern Turkey.
anaxagoras: Anaxagoras was born in Clazomenae in the early 5th century BCE, when Asia Minor was under the control of the Persian Empire, and he may have been born into an aristocratic family. He came to Athens and there became close to the statesman Pericles. According to Diogenes Laërtius and Plutarch, in later life he was charged with impiety, and the charges may have been political, owing to his association with Pericles. Laërtius says that Pericles spoke in his defence.

Anaxagoras was nevertheless forced to retire to Lampsacus, where he died of starvation around 428 BCE. The citizens of Lampsacus raised an altar to Mind and Truth in his memory and founded an annual celebration, the Anaxagoreia. The inscription over his grave read: Here Anaxagoras, who in his quest of truth scaled heaven itself, is laid to rest.

Responding to the claim that change is impossible, Anaxagoras described the world as a mixture of primary imperishable ingredients, a thing differing from others by the preponderance of some ingredients over the rest. He introduced nous, cosmic Mind, as an ordering force that moved and separated the original mixture, and whose first and only described manifestation is motion.

He was the first to explain eclipses correctly, and his theories may have rested on observation of the eclipse of 463 BCE. He described the Sun as a fiery mass larger than the Peloponnese, held the Moon to be earthy with mountains, and was among the first to assert that the Moon reflects sunlight. He thought the stars were fiery stones too far away to give heat, and he put forward the notion of panspermia. According to Plutarch, he was the first Greek to attempt squaring the circle, a problem he worked on in prison.

Only fragments of his book of philosophy survive, through the work of Simplicius of Cilicia in the 6th century CE. The book was reportedly on sale for a drachma in the Athenian marketplace and was known to Sophocles, Euripides and Aristophanes. In Plato's Phaedo, Socrates says that as a young man he eagerly read the books of Anaxagoras, though he describes his later disillusionment. Dante places him in the First Circle of Hell, and in 1935 a lunar crater was named after him.
anaximander: Anaximander, son of Praxiades, lived in Miletus, a city of Ionia. The ancient chronologist Apollodorus of Athens gave his birth in the third year of the 42nd Olympiad, 610 BCE, and said he was sixty-four in the second year of the 58th Olympiad (547 to 546 BCE) and died shortly afterwards. He belonged to the Milesian school and was influenced by Thales, though it is debatable whether Thales was actually his teacher. Themistius called him the first of the known Greeks to publish a written document on nature, so his text was among the earliest in prose. Only one fragment of it survives. By the time of Plato his philosophy was almost forgotten, and what remains comes from Aristotle, Theophrastus and a few later reporters.

Aelian depicts Anaximander as leader of the Milesian colony to Apollonia on the Black Sea coast, from which some infer that he was a prominent citizen, perhaps sent as a legislator. Strabo and Agathemerus, citing Eratosthenes, say he was the first to publish a map of the world. Others had drawn maps, but his innovation was to represent the entire inhabited land known to the Greeks, and the map probably inspired Hecataeus of Miletus to draw a more accurate one.

The Suda associates him with the introduction of the gnomon in Greece and says he took part in building or adjusting sundials at Lacedaemon to show the solstices and equinoxes. The gnomon itself, and the division of the day into twelve parts, came from the Babylonians according to Herodotus. Cicero reports that he warned the people of Lacedaemon to leave their city, because an earthquake was near, and the city collapsed when the top of Taygetus split.

Ancient writers credit him with the first use of the word apeiron, 'infinite' or 'limitless', for the original principle of things. In his model the Earth floats at the centre of the infinite, supported by nothing and staying in place because of its indifference, a view Aristotle thought ingenious. It is shaped like a cylinder whose height is a third of its diameter, and its flat top is the inhabited world.

He described the heavens as hollow concentric wheels of fire pierced with holes, through which the Sun, Moon and stars are seen. The diameter of the solar wheel was twenty-seven times that of the Earth, or twenty-eight according to other sources. According to Simplicius he also speculated on a plurality of worlds that appeared and disappeared. He attributed thunder and lightning to the action of elements, not of gods. He held that the sea is a remnant of the moisture that once surrounded the Earth, and that animals first arose from warmed water and earth, humans taking shape inside fishlike creatures until puberty.
ancient-olympic-games: The Greeks gave the games a mythological origin, attributing them to the gods, and competing legends survived about who was responsible. Aristotle reckoned the first Olympics to date from 776 BCE, and most later ancient historians accepted this, though the date cannot be verified. It is generally accepted that the games began some time in the eighth century BCE, and major games at Olympia probably arose around 700 BCE. The victor lists show that victors' names and details were unreliable until the sixth century BCE.

During the Olympic truce, announced by three runners called spondophoroi sent from Elis, armies were forbidden to enter Olympia, and legal disputes and the death penalty were suspended. The truce mainly allowed athletes and visitors to travel safely and did not stop all wars in Greece. Thucydides records that the Spartans were barred from the games and that violators of the truce were fined 2,000 minae for an assault on Lepreum.

After the Roman conquest the games continued but declined in popularity. In 86 BCE the Roman general Sulla robbed Olympia to finance a war. Under Augustus the games revived: Marcus Agrippa restored the damaged temple of Zeus, and in 12 BCE Augustus asked King Herod of Judea to subsidise the games. A bronze plaque found in 1994 proves that an international games continued until at least 385 CE. The last recorded games were held under Theodosius I in 393, though archaeological evidence indicates that some were held afterwards.

The program began with a single foot race, the stade of just over 192 metres, the only event at the first thirteen games. It grew to twenty-three contests, though no more than twenty featured at any one Olympiad. The diaulos was added in 724 BCE, wrestling and the pentathlon in 708 BCE, boxing in 688 BCE and the four-horse chariot race in 680 BCE. Most events were limited to male athletes, though women could take part by entering horses in the equestrian events.

The games were also a religious festival in honour of Zeus, with 100 oxen sacrificed to him on the middle day. The temple of Zeus, built by the architect Libon, held a gold and ivory statue by the sculptor Pheidias, about 13 metres tall, which was counted among the seven wonders of the ancient world.
andalusia: Andalusia occupies the south of the Iberian Peninsula, with the Atlantic and the Gulf of Cádiz to the west, the Mediterranean to the east and south, and the Strait of Gibraltar separating it from Morocco. In the north the Sierra Morena separates it from the plains of the Meseta Central. The valley of the Guadalquivir, the longest river in Andalusia at 657 km, forms the Baetic Depression, and to the south lie the Baetic mountains, which include Mulhacén in the Sierra Nevada, the highest point of the Iberian Peninsula. The interior is the hottest part of Europe in summer.

The position of Andalusia at the southern tip of Europe, between Africa and Europe and between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean, has made it a meeting place of civilisations since the Metal Ages. Its minerals and fertile land drew settlers from the Phoenicians to the Greeks, who influenced early cultures such as Los Millares, El Argar and Tartessos. The region's history and culture have also been shaped by Iberians, Carthaginians, Romans, Vandals, Visigoths, Byzantines, Berbers, Arabs, Jews, Romanis and Castilians.

The name comes from Arabic al-Andalus, which is first attested on dinars minted in 716 by the new Muslim government of Iberia, inscribed in Latin and Arabic. Its own origin is disputed. It was traditionally derived from the Vandals; later proposals include a Gothic term, put forward by Halm in 1989, and a pre-Roman source, suggested by Bossong in 2002.

During the Islamic Golden Age Córdoba surpassed Constantinople to become the biggest city in Europe, the capital of al-Andalus and a centre of learning that produced many philosophers and scientists. The Crown of Castile settled the Guadalquivir Valley in the 13th century, and the mountainous east, the Emirate of Granada, was subdued in the late 15th century. Atlantic harbours then prospered on trade with the New World. An unequal distribution of land in large estates caused recurring unrest in the countryside in the 19th and 20th centuries.

Andalusia is an autonomous community of Spain, divided into eight provinces: Almería, Cádiz, Córdoba, Granada, Huelva, Jaén, Málaga and Sevilla. These were set by Javier de Burgos in the territorial division of 1833. Seville is the capital, and the High Court of Justice sits in Granada. Many things regarded internationally as Spanish, among them flamenco, are Andalusian in origin. Authors of the region wrote in Arabic and Hebrew as well as Spanish, including Ibn Hazm, Ibn Tufail, Ibn Zamrak and Solomon ibn Gabirol.
andaman-and-nicobar-islands: The territory consists of 836 islands and islets, of which only 31 are inhabited. They form two clusters, the Andaman Islands in the north and the Nicobar Islands in the south, separated by the Ten Degree Channel, which is 150 kilometres wide. The islands lie between the Bay of Bengal to the west and the Andaman Sea to the east. Indira Point, on Great Nicobar, is the southernmost point of India, and Barren Island is the only active volcano in India.

Genetic and cultural studies suggest that the indigenous Andamanese may have been isolated from other populations for more than 30,000 years. The Nicobar islands lay on a major trade route between India and South East Asia. In the 11th century Rajendra Chola I used them as an intermediate naval base for expeditions in South East Asia, and Chola inscriptions of 1050 name them Ma-Nakkavaram, meaning great open or naked land in Tamil.

Settlers of the Danish East India Company reached the Nicobar Islands on 12 December 1755, but repeated outbreaks of malaria killed the colonists. In 1858 the British founded a penal colony on Ross Island, near Port Blair, mainly for prisoners of the Indian rebellion of 1857. Clearing forests led to frequent conflict with the Andamanese, and many prisoners died of conflict, disease and starvation. The Danish sold their rights to the Nicobar islands to the British on 16 October 1868. The Cellular Jail, built from 1896 to 1906, held political prisoners and independence activists.

Japan captured Port Blair on 23 March 1942. On 29 December 1943 it gave provisional control of the islands to the Azad Hind organisation of Subhas Chandra Bose, though real control stayed with the Japanese. Looting and killings were reported during the occupation, among them the Homfreyganj massacre of 30 January 1944, in which 44 civilians were shot on suspicion of spying. The Japanese surrendered on 15 August 1945. In 1956 the islands became a separate union territory.

The territory is a union territory of India, with Port Blair as its capital and largest city. Hindi is the official language and English an additional one. The islands include North Sentinel Island, home to the Sentinelese, an uncontacted people.
andernach: Andernach has about 30,000 inhabitants and lies in the district of Mayen-Koblenz, 21 kilometres north of Koblenz, on the left bank of the Rhine near the end of the Neuwied basin. A few hundred metres downstream the Rhine valley narrows, forming the northern part of the Middle Rhine stretch. In Roman times this narrow passage was called the Porta Antunnacensis, or Andernachian Gate, formed by two hills, the Krahnenberg and the Engwetter.

The Romans founded Antunnacum in 12 BCE on the site of an old Celtic settlement, probably called Antunnuac. Both names mean village or farm of Antunnos, a man not yet identified. The town held its bimillenary feast in 1988. From the 12th to the 19th century it was the southernmost outpost of the Electorate of Cologne. Its arms, known since 1344, pair a black cross, for Cologne, with keys of St Peter, for the Archbishopric of Trier, of which Andernach also formed part. The oldest town seal, made before 1200, shows St Mary as patron of its citizens. In the 19th century the town was noted for millstones, bricks and clay for tobacco pipes.

Benjamin of Tudela in the 12th century named Andernach among 13 Rhine towns with important Jewish communities. The community was periodically persecuted from the 13th to the 15th century, notably in 1348 and 1349 during the Black Death. A new community was founded in 1860. On Kristallnacht in 1938 the synagogue was set on fire; at least 11 Jews from Andernach were murdered in the Holocaust, and none lived there after 1945. Between 1941 and 1944 about 1,560 patients were sent from a transit hospital in the town to the Hadamar Euthanasia Centre, where they were murdered.

The medieval fortifications survive in part: the Round Tower, 56 metres tall and finished in 1453, the ruins of the archiepiscopal castle with its keep, and stretches of wall with two gates. The Old Crane, a stone treadwheel crane of the 16th century, worked from 1561 to 1911 loading millstones, tuff blocks and wine casks, and is one of only a few of its kind in Europe to survive. The Church of Our Lady is the town's oldest historical attraction, parts of it going back to the 11th century, and a cold-water geyser in the Namedyer Werth nature reserve rises to as much as 64 m. The writer Charles Bukowski was born in Andernach, and Honoré de Balzac set his story L'Auberge rouge there.
anders-celsius: Anders Celsius was born in Uppsala on 27 November 1701. His family came from Ovanåker in the province of Hälsingland, and their family estate was at Doma, also known as Höjen or Högen; the name Celsius comes from the estate's name by way of the Latin celsus, meaning mound. He was the son of the astronomy professor Nils Celsius, the nephew of the botanist Olof Celsius and the grandson of the mathematician Magnus Celsius and the astronomer Anders Spole. A talented mathematician from an early age, he studied at Uppsala University, where his father taught, and became a professor of astronomy there in 1730.

In 1730 Celsius published the Nova Methodus distantiam solis a terra determinandi. He studied the aurora with his assistant Olof Hiorter and was the first to suggest a connection between the aurora borealis and changes in the Earth's magnetic field, having observed that larger deflections of a compass needle matched stronger auroral activity. At Nuremberg in 1733 he published 316 observations of the aurora made by himself and others between 1716 and 1732. In the early 1730s he travelled to Germany, Italy and France and visited most of the major European observatories. In Paris he advocated measuring an arc of the meridian in Lapland.

In 1736 he joined the expedition organised by the French Academy of Sciences and led by Pierre Louis Maupertuis to measure a degree of latitude near the pole and compare it with a similar expedition to Peru. The expeditions confirmed Isaac Newton's belief that the Earth is an ellipsoid flattened at the poles. His part in it brought him respect in Sweden and helped win resources for a modern observatory at Uppsala, which he founded in 1741 with instruments bought on his travels. He also published catalogues of magnitudes for some 300 stars, and noted that much of Scandinavia is slowly rising above sea level, though he wrongly thought the water was evaporating.

In 1742 he proposed his temperature scale in a paper to the Royal Society of Sciences in Uppsala. His thermometer was calibrated with 0 for the boiling point of water and 100 for the freezing point, and in 1745 Carl Linnaeus reversed it to make measurement more practical.

Celsius became secretary of the Royal Society of Sciences in Uppsala in 1725 and held the post until he died of tuberculosis on 25 April 1744. He supported the foundation of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm in 1739 by Linnaeus and five others, was elected a member at its first meeting, and proposed its name. The temperature scale was later renamed Celsius in his honour.
andhra-mahabharatam: Nannaya began the translation from Sanskrit at the request of the king, and his part marks the earliest known beginning of a written literary tradition in Telugu. It is composed in the Champu style and is so polished that several scholars think it probable that literary works existed in Telugu before him. No such writings have been found, apart from references to songs and poems and some verses in inscriptions, and Telugu tradition honours him as the Adi Kavi, the first poet.

Tikkana, who lived from 1205 to 1288, was born into a Niyogi Brahmin family and was a minister of the Nellore Chola ruler Manumasiddhi II. Errana, also called Yerrapragada, was a poet at the court of King Prolaya Vema Reddy, who reigned from 1325 to 1353 and founded the Reddy dynasty; he bore the titles Prabandha-parameshvara and Shambhudasudu, servant of Shiva.

The work is not a stanza-by-stanza translation but a Telugu rendering that keeps the core narrative of the Mahabharata. Nannaya wrote the Adi Parvam, the Sabha Parvam and part of the Aranya Parvam, the Book of the Forest. Tikkana wrote the fifteen books from the Virata Parvam to the Svargarohana Parvam but did not touch the half-finished third book, because it was considered inauspicious to take up what Nannaya had left incomplete. It remained unfinished for more than a century until Errana completed it. He began his portion in the style of Nannaya and ended it in the style of Tikkana, as a bridge between the two.

The Sanskrit epic is reckoned at 100 parvas and 100,000 verses. In Telugu Nannaya arranged it in eighteen parvas, divided into chapters called ashvasas, without the subdivision into upaparvas, and left out the Harivamsa; Tikkana followed his arrangement, and Errana wrote the Harivamsa as a separate work.

The three poets are revered by later Telugu poets as the Kavitrayam, the trinity of poets, and became models for all who followed. Though written by three hands over about two and a half centuries, the work is read as a single book, as if one poet had composed it in one period. Errana went on to translate the Ramayana from Sanskrit and to write an independent work, the Nrusimhapuranamu.
andhra-pradesh: Andhra Pradesh lies on the east coast of southern India, bounded on the east by the Bay of Bengal, with a coastline of 974 km, the second longest of any Indian state. The Eastern Ghats separate the coastal plains from the Deccan Plateau, and the Godavari, Krishna, Tungabhadra and Penna rivers flow east to the sea. The state has two regions, Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema. Its name comes from the Andhras, a people mentioned in the Aitareya Brahmana, whom scholars see as both a tribal and a territorial name.

Stone tools from Hanumanthunipadu have been dated to about 247,000 years ago. Megasthenes reported in his Indica, around 310 BCE, that the Andhras lived in the Godavari and Krishna deltas and ranked second only to the Mauryans in military strength. After Ashoka's death in 232 BCE smaller kingdoms replaced Maurya rule, and the Satavahana dynasty ruled most of the Deccan from the 1st to the 3rd century CE. Later rulers included the Vishnukundinas, the Telugu Cholas, who ruled the south intermittently from the 6th to the 13th centuries, and the Eastern Chalukyas, who ruled the Vengi region from the 7th century to the early 12th. The oldest Telugu inscription, the Kalamalla sasanam, dates to 575.

After the Vijayanagara Empire was defeated at the Battle of Talikota in 1565, the Sultanate of Golconda controlled parts of Andhra, and most of the region came under the Mughal Empire in the 17th century. The British controlled much of it as part of the Madras Presidency for two centuries. Potti Sreeramulu fasted to death at Madras in 1952, demanding a state for Telugu speakers. Andhra State was split from Madras State on 1 October 1953, with Kurnool as its capital, and on 1 November 1956 it became Andhra Pradesh, with Hyderabad as capital, when states were redrawn on linguistic lines. Telangana was separated from it in 2014.

Telugu, one of the classical languages of India, is the official language and the mother tongue of 89.21% of the population at the 2011 census. Amaravati is the capital and Visakhapatnam the largest city. Kuchipudi, an Indian classical dance, originated in the village of Kuchipudi in Krishna district, and the state is the birthplace of the Amaravati school of art, which influenced South and Southeast Asian art. Its pilgrimage centres include the Venkateswara temple at Tirumala.
andijan: Andijan lies 450 metres above sea level on the south-eastern edge of the Fergana Valley, near the border between Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan, surrounded by the foothills of the Pamir and Tian Shan mountains. The climate is cold semi-arid, with cold winters and hot summers. The long frost-free season of about 210 days favours cotton, mulberry and citrus crops around the city.

Andijan is more than 2,500 years old and is regarded as the oldest city in Uzbekistan. Archaeologists have found items from the 7th and 8th centuries BCE, and it was an important place on the Silk Road. It was the birthplace of Babur, who laid the basis of the Mughal dynasty. After the Khanate of Kokand was formed in the 18th century, the capital moved from Andijan to Kokand, and Russia conquered the khanate and the city in 1876. In 1898 followers of the Sufi leader Madali Ishan attacked the Russian barracks, killing 22. On 16 December 1902 an earthquake levelled much of the city, killing as many as 4,500 residents.

After Soviet rule began in 1917 Andijan became an important industrial city of the Uzbek SSR, and the Soviet division of Central Asia separated it from its historical hinterland in the Fergana Valley. On 13 May 2005 Uzbek troops opened fire on a crowd protesting against poor living conditions and corrupt government. Estimates of the dead range from 187, the government's count, to several hundred. The government blamed the Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan, which critics dispute, and later acknowledged that poor economic conditions and popular resentment played a part.

Andijan is the administrative, economic and cultural centre of Andijan Region in Uzbekistan. It remains an industrial city, producing chemicals, appliances, furniture and pumps. Its sights include the Jame Mosque Complex, built from 1883 to 1890, and the Devonaboy Jome Masjid of 1899, which reopened in 1944 after Soviet closure.
andong: Andong is the capital of North Gyeongsang Province in South Korea and the largest city in the northern part of the province. The Nakdong River flows through it, and it is a market centre for the surrounding agricultural areas. It is known as a centre of culture and folk traditions, among them the Andong masks and the mask dance festival held each year.

Around 1 BCE the town was founded by the Jinhan people and called Gochang. During the Three Kingdoms period the area was controlled by the kingdom of Silla. In 930 the Battle of Gochang was fought there between Hubaekje forces and the Goryeo army led by Wanggeon, who won control of the city and renamed it Andong.

Under the Joseon dynasty Andong became a centre of Confucianism and was extremely conservative for a long time, producing many leading Confucian scholars. Yi Hwang (1501–1570), one of the most prominent of all Korean scholars, came from Andong; he retired there late in life and began the Confucian academy Dosan Seowon, which was finished after his death. Its principal families, among them the Andong Kim, Andong Jang and Andong Kwon clans, were influential in Korean politics.

After the 16th century Andong became less influential until the early 19th century, when a marriage of the local Kim family brought strong influence over the royal family. The city was almost destroyed in intense fighting during the Korean War in the early 1950s, but was quickly rebuilt.

Hahoe Folk Village, perhaps the most notable folk village in South Korea, was listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage site together with Yangdong Folk Village in 2010. Other seowon, or Confucian academies, include Byeongsan Seowon, which honours Yu Sŏngnyong, and Imcheon Seowon, for Kim Sŏngil. Andong's local foods include heotjesabap, a variety of bibimbap, Andong jjimdak, a chicken dish, and Andong soju, a rice spirit made by traditional methods.
andre-massena: André Masséna was born Andrea Massena on 6 May 1758 in Nice, then part of the Kingdom of Sardinia, the son of Jules César Masséna, a wine merchant, and Catherine Fabre. His father's family came originally from Piedmont and had lived for at least three centuries in the Vésubie valley. His father died of tuberculosis in 1764, and his mother, who quickly remarried, entrusted the children to relatives of her first husband. André was the eldest of three sons and was six years old. He began as an enlisted soldier under the old regime and rose without a formal military education.

In the Revolutionary Wars Masséna served in the Army of the Var in the occupation of the County of Nice in 1792, and helped suppress the barbet movement that resisted it. Under Napoleon Bonaparte in Italy in 1796 he commanded a division; he and the other divisional commanders were at first sceptical of the younger general but were soon won over. Napoleon later wrote that Masséna was extraordinarily courageous and firm and ready to fight again after a defeat.

In 1799 he commanded the Army of Helvetia against Austrian and Russian forces. He was driven from Zurich by Archduke Charles on 4 to 6 June, entrenched behind the Limmat, and on 25 September defeated the Austro-Russians under Korsakov at the Second Battle of Zurich, a victory with considerable strategic effect for France. He opposed some of Bonaparte's political choices, but received the baton of Marshal of the Empire on 19 May 1804. In 1809 he commanded IV Corps, mostly conscripts, against Austria, and Napoleon rewarded him with the titles Duke of Rivoli and Prince of Essling.

On 17 April 1810 Napoleon gave Masséna the Army of Portugal for a third French invasion of that country, after the failed attempts of Junot and Soult. He had told the Emperor he had little enthusiasm for the task. Short of supplies, with unstable communications and subordinates who did not cooperate, he could muster only about 60,000 men to face Wellington. The failure earned him the Emperor's disgrace, and he received no further major command in the Empire.

He lived at Rueil writing his memoirs, which were in fact written by General Jean-Baptiste-Frédéric Koch. In 1813 he commanded the 8th military division at Toulon. He rallied to the Bourbon Restoration and died in Paris on 4 April 1817. His reputation for greed and plunder earned him the nickname the rotten child of victory, set against Napoleon's the dear child of victory, and most French marshals of the time served under his command at some point.
andrea-mantegna: Mantegna was born at Isola di Carturo, near Padua, in the Venetian Republic, the second son of a carpenter named Biagio. At 11 he was apprenticed to the Paduan painter Francesco Squarcione, who collected antique statues, reliefs and vases for others to study, and who taught him Latin and set him to study fragments of Roman sculpture. At 17 Mantegna left the workshop, later claiming that Squarcione had profited from his work without paying him enough.

In 1448 he was called to the team painting the Ovetari Chapel in the church of the Eremitani and finished most of it alone. Almost all of the cycle was lost in the Allied bombing of Padua in 1944. In 1453 Jacopo Bellini consented to the marriage of his daughter Nicolosia to Mantegna.

Mantegna left Padua young and never returned. Between 1457 and 1459 he painted the San Zeno Altarpiece in Verona. In 1460 Marquis Ludovico III Gonzaga appointed him court artist at Mantua, on a salary of 75 lire a month, and from December 1466 he lived there. The Camera degli Sposi in the ducal palace, presumably finished in 1474, has portraits of the Gonzaga family, and its spatial construction, especially the ceiling oculus, had a profound effect on Correggio.

In 1488 Pope Innocent VIII called him to paint frescoes in a Vatican chapel, later destroyed under Pius VI in 1780. Back in Mantua in 1490, he worked for Isabella d'Este and finished around 1492 the nine tempera Triumphs of Caesar, sold in 1628 to King Charles I of England. He and his workshop also led the production of prints in Venice before 1500.

Mantegna died at Mantua on 13 September 1506, in financial difficulty and forced to sell an antique bust of Faustina. His sons set up a monument to him in the church of Sant'Andrea in 1516. His figures are sculptural and his landscapes stony, and his main legacy is considered to be spatial illusionism, a tradition of ceiling decoration followed for almost three centuries. Giovanni Bellini followed him in his early works, Albrecht Dürer reproduced several of his engravings, and Correggio built on his perspective research in the dome of Parma Cathedral.
andrea-palladio: Palladio was born at Padua on 30 November 1508 and named Andrea di Pietro della Gondola. His father, Pietro, was a miller. At thirteen he was apprenticed for six years to the stonecutter Bartolomeo Cavazza da Sossano, whose working conditions are said to have been particularly hard. In 1524 he settled in Vicenza, where he joined the guild of stonemasons and bricklayers and made monuments and decorative sculpture. Very little is known of his private life. He received a dowry from the family of his wife, Allegradonna, in 1534, and they had four sons and a daughter.

His earliest villa is generally held to be the Villa Godi, begun in 1537. The Basilica Palladiana in Vicenza, begun in 1546, brought him to the first rank of the architects of northern Italy; he added two-storey loggias to a city hall finished in 1459, and it was not completed until 1617. In 1550 he gained the support of the Venetian aristocrat Daniele Barbaro, through whom he became known to the Cornaro, Foscari and Pisani families. The villas that followed included the Villa Cornaro at Piombino Dese and the Villa Barbaro at Maser.

Barbaro and his brother Marcantonio introduced him to Venice, where he worked on the monastery of San Giorgio Maggiore between 1560 and 1562. His style was severe compared with the lavishness of Venetian Renaissance architecture. In 1570 he succeeded Jacopo Sansovino as Proto della Serenissima, chief architect of the Republic of Venice.

Palladio died on 19 August 1580, at either Vicenza or Maser, not long after work began on his last building, the Teatro Olimpico in Vicenza. Vincenzo Scamozzi completed it, and it was inaugurated in 1584. His buildings stand in a small corner of Italy, yet they influenced neoclassical architects in Britain and the United States in the 18th and 19th centuries. Inigo Jones brought Palladian ideas to England, and Thomas Jefferson's Monticello drew on his villas. More than 330 of his original drawings survive in the collections of the Royal Institute of British Architects. Vicenza, with 23 of his buildings, and his 24 villas in the Veneto are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
andreas-papandreou: Andreas Papandreou was born on 5 February 1919 on the island of Chios, the son of Zofia Mineyko and the liberal politician Georgios Papandreou, who later became prime minister. He studied at Athens College and then at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens. During the dictatorship of Ioannis Metaxas he was arrested for alleged Trotskyism, and in 1938 he left for the United States. He received a doctorate in economics from Harvard University in 1943, served in the United States Navy, and taught at the University of Minnesota, Northwestern University and the University of California, Berkeley, where he became chair of the economics department.

Papandreou returned to Greece in 1959, after years of resisting his father's wish that he prepare to succeed him. He led an economic research programme at the invitation of Prime Minister Konstantinos Karamanlis and later the Athens Economic Research Center. After he joined the Centre Union in 1963, his rapid rise and radical rhetoric added to the political instability that preceded the coup of April 1967. The colonels' regime arrested him and charged him with treason. Under American pressure it released him on Christmas Day 1967 on condition that he leave the country, and he taught in Stockholm and then in Toronto until 1974.

After the junta fell he founded PASOK in 1974, and the party won the elections of 1981. His governments expanded access to education and healthcare, strengthened workers' rights and passed a new family law. In 1982 he secured official recognition of all the wartime resistance groups, including EAM-ELAS, and the return of Greek communist refugees of the Civil War. His second term was marked by financial scandals, above all the Koskotas affair, and by a deteriorating economy. PASOK's vote fell to 38 percent in June 1989, and he was indicted over the Koskotas scandal. He won office again in 1993 and continued the austerity policies of his predecessor Konstantinos Mitsotakis.

Papandreou resigned as prime minister in January 1996 because of ill health and died on 23 June 1996. His son George Papandreou later led PASOK from February 2004 and was prime minister from 2009 to 2011. Assessments of his record differ. Admirers point to the social reforms of his first administration, which Greeks remember favourably, and to the shift of political power from the long-dominant conservatives to a centre-left and more populist politics. Critics point to patronage, corruption scandals, foreign borrowing and a confrontational foreign policy that left Greece diplomatically isolated.
andreas-vesalius: Vesalius was born Andries van Wesel on 31 December 1514 in Brussels, into a family of physicians. His grandfather Everard van Wesel was royal physician to Emperor Maximilian, and his father Anders van Wesel was Maximilian's apothecary and later valet de chambre to Charles V. He entered the University of Leuven in 1528 and moved in 1533 to Paris, where he studied Galen under Jacques Dubois and Jean Fernel and examined excavated bones in the charnel houses of the Cemetery of the Innocents. He left Paris in 1536 when war broke out between the Holy Roman Empire and France, and graduated at Leuven the following year.

On the day of his graduation he was offered the chair of surgery and anatomy at Padua. Anatomy had been taught mainly from Galen's texts, with an animal dissection done by a barber-surgeon under the lecturer's direction. Vesalius did the dissection himself and urged his students to do it, treating direct observation as the only reliable source. From 1539 a judge at the Padua criminal court supplied him with the bodies of executed criminals. In 1543, at Basel, he publicly dissected the felon Jakob Karrer von Gebweiler and gave the assembled skeleton to the university, where it survives as the oldest anatomical preparation in the world.

Soon after the Fabrica appeared he became imperial physician to Charles V, and other physicians mocked him as a mere barber-surgeon. In 1551 the emperor ordered an inquiry at Salamanca into the religious implications of his methods, which cleared his work. In 1555 he became physician to Philip II. In 1564 he went on a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, probably as a pretext to leave the Spanish court.
