He was shipwrecked on Zakynthos on the return and died there, aged 49, in such debt that a benefactor paid for his funeral.

Vesalius found that Galen had worked on animals, since Roman custom did not allow human dissection, and had dissected Barbary macaques. Galen's account of the heart required openings in the wall between the ventricles, and for 1400 years anatomists claimed to find them, until Vesalius admitted he could not. He showed that the human sternum has three parts and that humans lack the rete mirabile found in sheep. His former professor Jacobus Sylvius answered that the human body itself had changed since Galen's time. Vesalius encouraged students to check even his own findings.
andrei-rublev: Little information survives about Rublev's life, and even his birthplace is unknown. He probably lived in the Trinity Lavra of St. Sergius, near Moscow, under Nikon of Radonezh, who became hegumen after the death of Sergius of Radonezh in 1392. The first mention of him is in 1405, when he decorated icons and frescoes for the Cathedral of the Annunciation in the Moscow Kremlin together with Theophanes the Greek and Prokhor of Gorodets. His name came last in the list of masters, as the junior in rank and age. Theophanes, an important Byzantine master who had moved to Russia, is considered to have trained him.

Chronicles record that with Daniel Chorny he painted the Dormition Cathedral in Vladimir in 1408 and the Trinity Cathedral in the Trinity Lavra of St. Sergius between 1425 and 1427. After Daniel's death he went to Moscow's Andronikov Monastery, where he painted his last work, the frescoes of the Saviour Cathedral. He is also believed to have painted at least one miniature in the Khitrovo Gospels.

The only work authenticated as entirely his is the icon of the Trinity, of about 1410. It is based on an earlier icon, the Hospitality of Abraham, which illustrates Genesis 18. Rublev removed the figures of Abraham and Sarah and, through composition and symbolism, turned the subject to the mystery of the Trinity. His art is said to combine two traditions, the highest asceticism and the classical harmony of Byzantine style, and his figures are peaceful and calm.

Rublev died at the Andronikov Monastery between 1427 and 1430. His work influenced many artists, among them Dionisy, and the Stoglavi Sobor of 1551 promulgated his icon style as a model for church painting. The Andrei Rublev Museum at the Andronikov Monastery has displayed his work and related art since 1959. The Russian Orthodox Church canonised him in 1988, and his feast day is 29 January. In 1966 Andrei Tarkovsky made the film Andrei Rublev, loosely based on his life. The historian Serge Aleksandrovich Zenkovsky counted him among the names that signify the Russian spiritual and cultural revival of the late 14th and early 15th centuries.
andrew-ii-of-hungary: Andrew was the younger son of King Béla III of Hungary and Agnes of Antioch. The year of his birth is not known, but historians place it around 1177. In 1188 his father invaded the Principality of Galicia and granted it to him. His rule there was unpopular, since Hungarian soldiers insulted local women and did not respect Orthodox churches, and the boyars expelled him in August 1189 or 1190. In December 1197 he allied with Duke Leopold VI of Austria and defeated the royal army of his brother King Emeric at Mački. Emeric then gave him Croatia and Dalmatia, which he governed almost as an independent ruler.

After Emeric's death on 30 November 1204, Andrew acted as regent for his nephew Ladislaus III, who died in Vienna on 7 May 1205. Andrew was crowned at Székesfehérvár on 29 May. He gave away royal castles and estates as inheritable grants, a policy he called the new institutions. The historian László Kontler holds that the turmoil of his reign began to break up the social order that had arisen under Stephen I. Andrew also took the title King of Galicia and Lodomeria and fought at least a dozen wars for the two principalities, but local boyars and neighbouring princes repelled him.

In July 1217 he set out on the Fifth Crusade and reached Acre in October, but the crusade failed. He returned to a kingdom he called destroyed and deprived of its revenues. The royal servants, the servientes regis, rose up, and in 1222 he issued the Golden Bull, confirming their privileges. His Diploma Andreanum of 1224 confirmed the privileges of the Transylvanian Saxons.

Andrew died on 21 September 1235 and was buried in Egres Abbey. His first wife, Gertrude of Merania, was murdered in 1213, and their daughter Elizabeth was canonised during his lifetime. Their son Béla IV succeeded him. His third wife, Beatrice d'Este, bore a son, Stephen, after his death, and Béla and his brother Coloman did not accept the child as legitimate. Andrew's grandson, also named Andrew, became the last monarch of the House of Árpád.
andrew-jackson: Andrew Jackson was born on 15 March 1767 in the Waxhaws region of the Carolinas to Scots-Irish Presbyterian parents who had emigrated from Ulster in 1765. During the American Revolutionary War he and his older brothers served on the Patriot side. After the war he worked as a saddler and a teacher, studied law in Salisbury, North Carolina, and was admitted to the bar in September 1787, then was appointed a prosecuting attorney in the Western District of North Carolina, the later Tennessee.

Jackson was elected Tennessee's first U.S. representative in 1796, was a senator in 1797 and served as a Tennessee Superior Court justice from 1798 to 1804. He bought the plantation called the Hermitage near Nashville, which grew to 1,000 acres and was one of the largest cotton-growing plantations in the state. As commander of the Tennessee militia he led troops in the Creek War of 1813–1814, and the Treaty of Fort Jackson forced the Creek to cede large areas of what are now Alabama and Georgia. His victory over the British at the Battle of New Orleans in 1815 made him a national hero. He later commanded American forces in the First Seminole War, which helped lead Spain to negotiate the cession of Florida.

In 1824 Jackson won a plurality of the vote, but the House of Representatives elected John Quincy Adams. His supporters alleged a corrupt bargain and formed a coalition that became the Democratic Party. Jackson defeated Adams in a landslide in 1828 and was inaugurated on 4 March 1829.

In 1830 he signed the Indian Removal Act, which displaced tens of thousands of Native Americans from east of the Mississippi River and caused thousands of deaths in what became known as the Trail of Tears. In 1832 he vetoed the renewal of the Second Bank of the United States, which he saw as a fourth branch of government run by an elite.

Jackson's presidency ended on 4 March 1837, and he retired to the Hermitage, where he remained influential in national and state politics. He died on 8 June 1845. His legacy is controversial: supporters call him a defender of democracy and the Constitution, while critics describe an autocratic demagogue and condemn his policies toward Native Americans and his enslavement of hundreds of people at the Hermitage.
andrew-the-apostle: The name Andrew, from the Greek andreía, meaning manhood or valour, appears to have been common among Jews and other Hellenised people since the second or third century BCE, and no Hebrew or Aramaic name is recorded for him. He was born to a Jewish family in Bethsaida, in Galilee, possibly between 5 and 10 CE. The New Testament says he was the brother of Simon Peter and, like him, a son of Jonah. His Greek name has been read as pointing to a cultural openness in his family, in a Galilee where Greek language and culture were quite present.

Andrew and Peter were fishermen by trade, which is why tradition says Jesus called them to be fishers of men. According to Mark 1:29 they shared a house at Capernaum. In Matthew and Mark, Jesus sees the two brothers fishing on the Sea of Galilee and calls them together. In the Gospel of John, Andrew is first a disciple of John the Baptist; he follows Jesus, recognises him as the Messiah and introduces Peter, which is the source of the title First-Called used by the Eastern Orthodox Church.

The apocryphal Acts of Andrew, mentioned by Eusebius and Epiphanius of Salamis, shows signs of a mid-2nd-century origin. It describes his supposed travels, his miracles and his martyrdom. Eusebius dismissed it as the work of a heretic and absurd, and it appears among rejected books in the Decretum Gelasianum. Georgian church tradition regards Andrew as the first preacher of Christianity in Georgia. It derives from Byzantine sources, notably Niketas David Paphlagon, who died about 890 and wrote that Andrew preached to the Iberians, Sauromatians, Taurians and Scythians. Georgian ecclesiastics of the 10th and 11th centuries used the story to give their church an apostolic origin.

Relics said to be Andrew's were kept at Patras, and according to one account Constantius II had most of them moved to Constantinople around 357. In 1208, after the sack of Constantinople, Cardinal Peter of Capua took relics of Andrew to Amalfi, where most remain in the cathedral crypt. In 1461 Thomas Palaiologos fled Patras before the Ottomans with what was said to be Andrew's skull and gave it to Pope Pius II. A legend says the monk Regulus carried some bones to Fife in Scotland, though the relics probably reached Britain in 597 and Fife in 732, with Bishop Acca of Hexham.

Andrew is the patron saint of Scotland, Romania, Russia, Ukraine and Patras, among other places, and his saltire cross appears on the flag of Scotland. His feast is on 30 November in the Eastern and Western churches.
andromeda-galaxy: The Andromeda Galaxy is a barred spiral galaxy, also catalogued as Messier 31, M31 and NGC 224, and originally called the Andromeda Nebula. Its name comes from the constellation of Andromeda, named after the princess who was the wife of Perseus in Greek mythology. 56 kiloparsecs (152,000 light-years), which makes it the largest member of the Local Group in extent. Estimates of its total mass lie between about 8 and 11 hundred billion solar masses, of the same order as the Milky Way, and the relative masses of the two have been revised several times.

A merger with another galaxy 2 to 3 billion years ago is thought to have formed much of its halo. At its centre lies a dense star cluster and a supermassive black hole, and some 460 globular clusters are associated with the galaxy.

Around 964 the Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi described it in his Book of Fixed Stars as a nebulous smear or small cloud, the first historical reference to it and the earliest known reference to a galaxy other than the Milky Way. In 1612 the German astronomer Simon Marius described it from telescopic observations. Pierre Louis Maupertuis conjectured in 1745 that the blurry spot was an island universe.

Charles Messier catalogued it as M31 in 1764 and wrongly credited Marius as its discoverer, although it is visible to the naked eye. In 1785 William Herschel took it for the nearest of the great nebulae, and guessed its distance at no more than 2,000 times that of Sirius. In 1850 William Parsons, 3rd Earl of Rosse, drew its spiral structure.

Immanuel Kant had proposed in 1755 that the Milky Way is only one of many galaxies, and had argued that elliptical nebulae such as Andromeda were galaxies like it. In 1917 Heber Curtis observed a nova in Andromeda and found 11 more in the photographic record. They were on average 10 magnitudes fainter than novae elsewhere in the sky, which gave him a distance estimate of 500,000 light-years, the first within a factor of ten of the modern value. Curtis became a proponent of the island universes hypothesis. The estimated distance was doubled in 1953, when a second, dimmer type of Cepheid variable star was discovered.

The galaxy lies about 2.5 million light-years from Earth. It is visible to the naked eye in dark skies, and best seen from the Northern Hemisphere on autumn nights, when it passes high overhead. It is approaching the Milky Way at about 110 kilometres per second. Earlier calculations predicted a collision in about 4 billion years, but later ones, using a higher sideways velocity measured by the Gaia spacecraft, found a much lower probability of a merger.
andronikos-ii-palaiologos: Andronikos was born on 25 March 1259 at Nicaea, the eldest surviving son of Michael VIII Palaiologos. He was acclaimed co-emperor after his father recovered Constantinople from the Latin Empire in 1261 but was not crowned until 8 November 1272. He was compelled to support his father's unpopular Church union with the Papacy, and when Michael's death in 1282 made him sole emperor he at once repudiated it. He could not resolve the related schism among the Orthodox clergy until 1310.

Andronikos faced an empty treasury and was forced in 1285 to dismantle the imperial fleet, which left the empire dependent on Genoa. He devalued the hyperpyron and raised taxes. His campaigns brought little: an attack on Thessaly in 1283 ended when an epidemic killed its commander, an expedition to Epirus in 1292 failed, and a war with Venice from 1296 to 1302 changed almost nothing. By diplomacy he married Yolanda of Montferrat, ending the Montferrat claim to the Kingdom of Thessalonica, and in 1298 married his five-year-old daughter Simonis to King Stefan Milutin of Serbia.

The Anatolian frontier was his chief concern. Alexios Philanthropenos won victories there in 1294 and 1295 but then rebelled, and was blinded and captured by his own Cretan soldiers. After the disastrous Battle of Bapheus in 1302 the government hired the Catalan Company under Roger de Flor. After Roger's murder in 1305 the Catalans turned on their employers and devastated Thrace, Macedonia and Thessaly before conquering the Duchy of Athens. Meanwhile the Turkish beyliks advanced: the Aydinids took Smyrna in 1310, and Prusa fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1326.

Andronikos disowned his grandson Andronikos III Palaiologos after the death of his son Michael IX in 1320, and the First Palaiologan Civil War followed, lasting with interruptions until 1328. In 1328 Andronikos III entered Constantinople and the old emperor was forced to abdicate. He died as a monk in Constantinople in 1332 and was buried in the Lips Monastery. His reign marked the beginning of the restored empire's final decline.
andronikos-iii-palaiologos: Andronikos was born in Constantinople on 25 March 1297, the son of the co-emperor Michael IX Palaiologos and Rita of Armenia. In 1320 he accidentally caused the death of his brother Manuel, and his father died in grief soon afterwards. His behaviour and that of his circle of young aristocrats opened a rift with his grandfather, Andronikos II Palaiologos, who disowned him. Andronikos fled, rallied supporters in Thrace and began to reign as a rival emperor in 1321. Intermittent civil war followed until 1328, when he became sole emperor on 24 May and his grandfather retired to a monastery.

His reign saw the last failed attempts to hold back the Ottoman Turks in Bithynia. Sultan Orhan defeated a relief attempt for besieged Nicaea at the Battle of Pelekanon in June 1329, took Nicaea in 1331 and Nicomedia in 1337, and only Philadelphia and a few ports remained Byzantine in Anatolia. In the Balkans Tsar Ivan Alexander of Bulgaria defeated the Byzantines at Rusokastro on 18 July 1332, and Serbia gained Ohrid, Prilep and Strumitsa by the peace of 26 August 1334.

There were also successes. A fleet deposed the Genoese ruler Martino Zaccaria and regained Chios in 1329, Phocaea returned in 1334, and Byzantine control was extended over Thessaly and, from 1337, Epirus. John Kantakouzenos, as megas domestikos, held effective administrative authority, while the emperor enjoyed hunting and war. Andronikos also created a panel of four judges, the Universal Justices of the Romans.

Andronikos III died at Constantinople on 15 June 1341, aged 44, possibly of chronic malaria. His son John V Palaiologos was only nine and needed a regent. Within months a dispute over the regency and the position of John Kantakouzenos led to a destructive civil war, which left the empire unable to prevent the rise of the Serbian Empire or the Ottoman entry into Europe. Historians generally do not blame his leadership for the later decline, and hold that under him the empire came closest to regaining power in the Balkans after the Fourth Crusade.
andujar: Andújar is a municipality in the province of Jaén, in Andalusia, divided by the Guadalquivir River. The northern part holds the Natural Park of the Sierra de Andújar, and to the south lie agricultural fields. The city itself stands on the right bank of the river, on the Madrid-Córdoba railway. It was long known for its porous earthenware jars, the alcarrazas or botijos, which keep water cool in the hottest weather and were made from a whitish clay found nearby.

The first known inhabitants were the Oretani, an Iberian people, who founded the town of Isturgi on the site now occupied by the hamlet of Los Villares de Andújar. In Roman times the Municipium Isturgi Triumphale flourished through its production of terra sigillata and its position on the Guadalquivir, and after the empire it survived as the Visigothic town of Sturgi. When the Moors invaded in the 8th century the population moved to the present site. After the Battle of Guadalete in 711 the region became part of Al-Andalus, and the town was first called Anduyar under Muhammad I of Córdoba, in 853. The Almohads fortified it in the 12th century.

In 1225 the Muslim king of Baeza handed the castles of Jaén, Andújar and Martos to Ferdinand III of Castile, though some scholars believe the transfer happened at another time. Troops of the military orders of Santiago and Calatrava occupied the area, and Andújar became a rendezvous for the Christian armies fighting south of the Sierra Morena. Its Muslim inhabitants left at the end of 1226, and the first Christian settlers arrived in 1227 or 1228. Henry IV of Castile granted it the title of city in 1467.

In 1808 French troops occupied the city, and General Pierre Dupont de l'Étang made it his headquarters; after he lost the battle at Bailén, the capitulations were signed at Andújar in the Palace of Gracia Real. In 1835 the first Junta of Central Sovereignty of Andalusia met there, regarded as a pioneer of the autonomist movement in Andalusia. During the Spanish Civil War Republican forces besieged a Nationalist force sheltering in the sanctuary of Our Lady of the Cabeza for eight months.

The municipality has 35,619 people (2024). Its best-known festival is the Pilgrimage of the Virgen de la Cabeza, held on the last Sunday of April. According to local legend, on the night of 12 August 1227 a shepherd named Juan Alonso de Rivas found the image of the Virgen de la Cabeza on a hill after seeing strange lights and hearing a bell.
angers: Angers lies about 300 km south-west of Paris and is the prefecture of the Maine-et-Loire department. It stands just south of the confluence of the Loir, the Mayenne and the Sarthe, which together form the short, wide river Maine, and the Maine runs south through the city to the Loire a few kilometres away. The meeting of three rivers and the nearness of the Loire make a natural crossroads, which favoured the founding of the ancient Juliomagus. The oldest streets and buildings stand on the promontory where the castle rises, and their structure dates from the 13th, 14th and 15th centuries.

The first sign of human presence dates to around 400,000 BCE, and burials of about 4500 to 3500 BCE were found on the castle grounds. In the 5th century BCE the Andecavi, a Celtic people, settled north of the Loire, and by the end of the Iron Age Angers was a fairly densely populated hillfort. Ptolemy mentions it around 150 CE as Juliomagus, a name that joins Julius, probably Julius Caesar, to the Celtic magos, meaning market. The Roman town had villas, baths, an amphitheatre and a Mithraeum.

Angers received its first bishop in 372, at the election of Martin of Tours. The abbey of Saint-Aubin was built in the 7th century to house the sarcophagus of Saint Albinius, and Saint-Serge Abbey was founded a century later by the Merovingian kings Clovis II and Theuderic III. The castle was built between 1230 and 1240 by Louis IX of France, with walls about a kilometre long and 17 towers.

After the Black Death and the Hundred Years War had weakened the city, King René of Anjou revived it, making Angers a cultural and political centre. The city received its communal charter from Louis XI in February 1475. In 1619 Louis XIII gave the governance of Anjou to his mother, Marie de' Medici, who settled in Angers with her chaplain, Cardinal Richelieu. The French Revolution abolished Anjou as a political entity in 1790, and in March 1793 the royalist army of the War of Vendée had to attack Angers to cross the Loire again.

Angers has 157,555 inhabitants within its 42.70 square kilometres. It remains the prefecture of Maine-et-Loire. The Château d'Angers houses the Apocalypse Tapestry, the largest ensemble of medieval tapestry in the world. The city lies at the edge of the Val de Loire World Heritage Site.
angkor: The ruins of Angkor lie among forests and farmland north of the Great Lake, Tonlé Sap, and south of the Kulen Hills, near the modern city of Siem Reap. The name comes from the Khmer nokor, meaning kingdom, itself derived from the Sanskrit nagara, city. In Angkorian times non-religious buildings, including the king's residence, were built of perishable materials such as wood, because only the gods had a right to residences of stone, so the surviving monuments are almost all religious. A 2007 study using satellite photographs concluded that Angkor was the largest pre-industrial city in the world by area, with a water network of canals and reservoirs that offset the unpredictable monsoon.

The Angkorian period began shortly after 800, when Jayavarman II declared the independence of Kambujadesa from Java and took the title devaraja, god-king. King Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat between 1113 and 1150. In 1177 the Cham launched a water-borne invasion, sacked the capital Yasodharapura and killed the king. A Khmer prince rallied his people, defeated them, and in 1181 took the throne as Jayavarman VII. He built the walled city of Angkor Thom with the Bayon at its centre, and the temples of Ta Prohm and Preah Khan, and made Mahayana Buddhism the state religion. His successor Jayavarman VIII, a Shaivite iconoclast, began a Hindu restoration around 1243.

In 1296 the Chinese diplomat Zhou Daguan spent a year at Angkor under King Indravarman III, and his account The Customs of Cambodia describes religion, kingship, agriculture, slavery and commerce. Angkor fell under Ayutthayan suzerainty in 1351. The end of the Angkorian period is generally placed around 1431, when Ayutthaya sacked it, though the main cause of its decline is unknown. Through the 15th century nearly all of it was abandoned except Angkor Wat, which remained a Buddhist shrine.

Angkor, in Siem Reap Province, contains over a thousand temples, among them Angkor Wat, the Bayon and Ta Prohm, and was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992. The Portuguese friar António da Madalena is the first recorded European visitor to Angkor Wat, in 1586. From 1907 to 1970 the École française d'Extrême-Orient cleared the forest, repaired foundations and installed drains, and scholars of the school, among them George Coedès, laid the foundations of present understanding of the site.
angkor-thom: Angkor Thom, from the Khmer for Great City, was the last and most enduring capital of the Khmer Empire. King Jayavarman VII established it as the centre of his massive building programme, and one inscription found in the city calls the king the groom and the city his bride. It was not the first Khmer capital on the site. Yasodharapura, dating from about three centuries earlier, lay slightly further northwest, and Angkor Thom overlapped parts of it. The Baphuon, a former state temple, and Phimeanakas, which was incorporated into the Royal Palace, stand within its walls. The name Angkor Thom came into use from the 16th century.

The city covers 9 square kilometres on the west bank of the Siem Reap River. Its laterite walls, 8 metres high and flanked by a moat, are each 3 kilometres long. A gate stands at each cardinal point, with roads leading to the Bayon, Jayavarman's state temple, at the centre. Archaeologists interpret the walls and moat as the mountains and oceans around the Bayon's Mount Meru.

The gate towers, 23 metres high, carry faces like those of the Bayon, which may represent the king, the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, guardians of the cardinal points, or some combination. Each causeway across the moat has devas on one side and asuras on the other, holding a naga in a tug-of-war that appears to refer to the Churning of the Sea of Milk. Most of the enclosed land held secular buildings, of which nothing remains.

The last temple known to have been built there, Mangalartha, was dedicated in 1295. The city is believed to have supported 80,000 to 150,000 people. The Ayutthaya Kingdom sacked it, and the Khmers under Ponhea Yat moved their capital southeast to Phnom Penh. Angkor Thom was abandoned before 1609, when an early western visitor described an uninhabited city. The Poem of Angkor Wat, composed in Khmer verse in 1622, describes its beauty.
angkor-wat: Angkor Wat was commissioned by the Khmer king Suryavarman II in Yaśodharapura, the capital of the Khmer Empire, as his state temple, and is generally considered to have been intended as his mausoleum. No contemporary inscription naming the temple has been found, so its original name is unknown; it may have been Vrah Viṣṇuloka. Work stopped after the king's death, leaving some bas-reliefs unfinished. In 1178 the Chams sacked Angkor. The Khmer empire was then restored by Jayavarman VII, who founded a new capital at Angkor Thom, with the Bayon as its state temple, and Angkor Wat was gradually converted into a Buddhist site.

The temple stands on a site of 162.6 hectares. It combines the temple mountain with the later plan of concentric galleries. The outer wall measures 1,024 m by 802 m, and a moat 190 m wide surrounds it. The layout is generally read as a representation of Mount Meru: the central quincunx of towers stands for its five peaks, and the walls and moat for the surrounding ranges and ocean. Lay people were admitted only to the lowest level. Unlike most Angkorian temples it faces west.

Most of the visible blocks are Kulen sandstone, quarried about 40 km to the northeast, with laterite for the outer wall. The monument contains five to ten million blocks, none heavier than 1.5 tons. At the equinoxes the rising sun aligns with the central tower when seen from the western causeway, an alignment generally regarded as intentional.

Portuguese traders and missionaries in the 16th century found a stone city in the forests that had seemed abandoned for over 150 years, and the Capuchin friar António da Madalena explored the ruins in 1586. In 1860 the French naturalist Henri Mouhot brought the temple to wider notice in the West. The École française d'Extrême-Orient founded the Conservation d'Angkor in 1908, and major restoration followed in the 1960s. The work was abandoned under the Khmer Rouge. The Angkor area became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992. Angkor Wat has remained a Buddhist monastery and appears on the Cambodian national flag.
anglesey: Anglesey lies off the north-west coast of Wales. At 676 square kilometres it is the largest island in Wales and the Irish Sea and the seventh largest in Britain. The Menai Strait, about 250 metres wide at its narrowest, separates it from the mainland. It is low-lying, with low hills across the north, of which Holyhead Mountain, at 220 metres, is the highest. Holy Island lies to its west and belongs to the same county. Large parts of the coast are an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, and cliffs such as South Stack hold seabird colonies.

Settlement began in the Mesolithic period. One of the first villages in Wales was built at Llanfaethlu from about 4000 BCE, and the burial chamber of Bryn Celli Ddu began as a henge enclosure around 3000 BCE. Anglesey has long been associated with the druids. In 60 CE the Roman general Gaius Suetonius Paulinus, determined to break their power, attacked the island with an amphibious Batavian vanguard and destroyed the shrine and the sacred groves, but news of Boudica's revolt made him withdraw before he had consolidated the conquest. Gnaeus Julius Agricola finally brought the island into the Roman Empire, and in the Roman period it was notable for copper mining.

The medieval House of Aberffraw, which ruled the Kingdom of Gwynedd until 1283, originated on Anglesey and kept courts at Aberffraw and Rhosyr. After Edward I conquered Wales, Beaumaris Castle was built at the island's south-eastern corner. In the nineteenth century the Menai Strait was bridged by Thomas Telford's Menai Suspension Bridge of 1826 and by the Britannia Bridge, originally designed by Robert Stephenson in 1850.

Holyhead, on Holy Island, is the largest town and a ferry port for Dublin, and Llangefni is the administrative centre. Anglesey is regarded as a heartland of the Welsh language. Beaumaris Castle is part of the Castles and Town Walls of King Edward in Gwynedd World Heritage Site. The English name may derive from the Old Norse Ǫngullsey, Hook Island, or Ǫnglisey, Ǫngli's Island; the reading Island of the Angles has no merit.
anglicanism: Anglicanism declared its independence from the Holy See through the Act of Supremacy in 1534, a separation consolidated by the Elizabethan Settlement of 1559. The Church of England kept the apostolic succession of its bishops, while its formularies of the mid-sixteenth century correspond closely to those of historical Protestantism. The Settlement joined the radical 1552 prayer book to the conservative 1549 one in the Book of Common Prayer of 1559. In the first half of the seventeenth century some Anglican divines presented the church as a middle way, a via media, between Lutheranism and Calvinism.

After the American Revolution, Anglican congregations in the United States and British North America became autonomous churches with their own bishops. Through the British Empire and Christian missions this model was adopted for many new churches, especially in Africa, Australasia and the Asia-Pacific. The term Anglicanism was coined in the late nineteenth century for the tradition common to these churches and the Scottish Episcopal Church.

Anglicans base their faith on the Bible, the traditions of the apostolic church, the Church Fathers and, historically, the Thirty-nine Articles. Doctrine is not set by a central authority or a founder, and high-church Anglicans look to the prayer books as its main expression, by the principle lex orandi, lex credendi, "the law of prayer is the law of belief". The Book of Common Prayer, first issued in 1549, replaced the various Latin rites with one volume in English. Its 1662 version was mandatory in England and Wales and in standard use until the mid-twentieth century.

The ministry is threefold: deacons, priests and bishops. The Anglican Communion has no international juridical body. Its provinces have historically been in full communion with the see of Canterbury, whose archbishop is first among equals with no direct authority outside England. He invites the bishops to the Lambeth Conference, first convened in 1867 by Archbishop Charles Longley.

The Oxford Movement of the mid-nineteenth century revived practices close to Roman Catholicism, and the Tractarians, especially John Henry Newman, saw the English church as a via media between Protestant and Catholic traditions; Newman later rejected the theory. Anglicans have been active in social causes: William Wilberforce against slavery, Lord Shaftesbury for factory and mine reform, Frederick Denison Maurice in Christian socialism, and Desmond Tutu and Ted Scott against apartheid. By 2020 the centre of Anglicanism had shifted to the Global South, with 63,556,000 adherents in Africa and 24,400,000 in Europe.
anglo-dutch-wars: The English and the Dutch both sought profits overseas as the Age of Exploration began, and by the middle of the 17th century the Dutch had one of Europe's largest merchant fleets, with more merchant ships than all other nations combined. After the execution of King Charles I in 1649, Oliver Cromwell united Great Britain in the Commonwealth of England and expanded the navy, promoting officers on merit. In 1651 Parliament passed the first of the Navigation Acts, which required that goods imported into England be carried by English ships or ships of the exporting countries, which excluded Dutch middlemen.

The first war began after a skirmish off Dover on 29 May 1652, when Maarten Tromp refused to lower his colours to an English fleet under Robert Blake. England declared war on 10 July. After defeating the Dutch at the Kentish Knock, the English were routed at Dungeness in December, but later used the line of battle to drive the Dutch from the Channel and the North Sea. Tromp was killed at Scheveningen in August 1653, and the Treaty of Westminster ended the war on 5 April 1654.

The second war (1665–1667) followed a renewed deterioration in relations after the Restoration. The English took New Netherland and New Amsterdam, and the Dutch captured the Royal Navy flagship Prince Royal in the Four Days' Battle in June 1666. In June 1667 the Dutch raid on the Medway, led by Michiel de Ruyter, burned warships and towed away the Royal Charles.

In the third war (1672–1674) Charles II, bound by the secret Treaty of Dover, was obliged to help Louis XIV attack the Dutch Republic. De Ruyter won a series of victories over the Anglo-French fleet and prevented an invasion, and Parliament forced Charles to make peace. The fourth war, fought from 1780 to 1784, followed Dutch support for the American rebels and was a British victory.

England was successful in the first war and the Dutch in the second and third. In 1688 William of Orange invaded England and became king, which ended further Anglo-Dutch conflict for a time. In the following century the Royal Navy became the most powerful maritime force in the world, while the Dutch States Navy fell to fourth place, and the fourth war was a profound humiliation for the Dutch. In the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars Britain captured most of the Dutch colonial empire.
anglo-irish-treaty: The Irish War of Independence ended in a truce in July 1921, and Éamon de Valera met David Lloyd George in London four times in the week from 14 July. De Valera argued that Britain was negotiating with a sovereign state, which Lloyd George continually denied, and in August he became President of the Republic mainly so that he could accredit plenipotentiaries. The Irish team, led by Arthur Griffith and Michael Collins, went to London with draft treaties and instructions to refer the full text of any draft back to the cabinet before signing. De Valera himself did not attend. Both sides knew that failure would end the truce and bring a war neither wanted.

Formal sessions began in October, with the Irish delegation based at 22 Hans Place in Knightsbridge, and informal talks followed in which only Griffith and Collins and two British negotiators took part. It was clear that a 32-county Irish Republic was not on offer, and the main outstanding point was the form of an oath to the monarch. Collins and Griffith won concessions on the oath and on defence and trade, together with a boundary commission and a clause upholding Irish unity. The treaty was signed soon after two in the morning on 6 December 1921. Collins later said that Lloyd George had threatened immediate and terrible war if it was not signed at once, and no message was sent to Dublin beforehand.

Crown forces were to withdraw from most of Ireland, which became a self-governing dominion of the British Empire, like Canada and Australia, with the King as head of state, represented by a Governor General. Members of the new parliament were to swear an oath of allegiance to the Irish Free State and to be faithful to King George V in virtue of common citizenship. Northern Ireland could withdraw within a month, in which case a Boundary Commission would draw the border. Britain kept control of the Treaty Ports for the Royal Navy, and the Free State was to take a share of the United Kingdom's debt.

De Valera came out against the treaty on 8 December, but the cabinet voted four to three to recommend it to the Dáil. The British Commons approved it on 16 December by 401 to 58 and the Lords by 166 to 47. The Dáil approved it on 7 January 1922 by 64 to 57, and the meeting the treaty required confirmed it on 14 January. The main dispute was dominion status as against an independent republic, and partition was a significant matter of dissent. The split led to the Irish Civil War, which the pro-treaty side won. The Irish Free State came into being on 6 December 1922.
anglo-saxon-chronicle: The first version of the Chronicle is lost. Known as the Common Stock, it was created in the late ninth century, probably in Wessex, in the reign of King Alfred the Great (r. 871–899), and dates to around 893, since it covers the return of the Vikings from the Continent in that year and a version was available to Bishop Asser for his Life of King Alfred of 893. It drew on annals relating to Kent, the South Saxons, Mercia and, above all, Wessex, and on sources now otherwise lost, some as early as the seventh century. Its earliest annal, for 60 BCE, records Julius Caesar's invasions of Britain.

The Common Stock was intended chiefly to legitimise the House of Wessex and the reign of Alfred. Copies were made and sent to monasteries across England, where they were updated, partly independently.

Almost all the material is in annals, year by year. Nine manuscripts survive in whole or in part, labelled A to I; none is the original. The oldest, the Winchester or Parker Chronicle, was begun at Old Minster, Winchester, towards the end of Alfred's reign and carries entries in the hands of several scribes through the tenth century. The Peterborough Chronicle was copied after a fire at that monastery in 1116 and continued to 1131, and in one manuscript the annals were still being added in 1154.

The manuscripts reflect the places and aims of their compilers. One includes the Mercian Register, covering 902 to 924 with a focus on Æthelflæd. Most copies include a poem on the Battle of Brunanburh in 937. The annal for 829 says the Northumbrians offered Egbert submission and peace, whereas the Northumbrian chronicles used by Roger of Wendover say he laid waste the province and made King Eanred pay tribute. Copying also introduced errors: the whole Common Stock is out by two years for the period 756 to 845.

Much of what the Chronicle records appears nowhere else, and it provides a relatively clear chronological framework, so it is among the most influential sources for England between the end of Roman authority and the decades after the Norman Conquest. Nicholas Howe called it and Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English People the two great Anglo-Saxon works of history. Its annals from 1131 onwards in the Peterborough text give key evidence for the change from Old English to early Middle English.

John of Worcester, William of Malmesbury and Henry of Huntingdon each had a copy and adapted it. Benjamin Thorpe's edition of 1861 gave the manuscripts the letters used today, and the standard modern English translations are by Dorothy Whitelock, David Douglas and Susie Tucker, and by Michael Swanton.
anglo-saxons: The Anglo-Saxon period in Britain is considered to have begun by about 450 and ended in 1066. Although the settlers came from continental Europe, their culture developed in Britain, and by the 8th century an identity called Englisc had grown out of their interaction with Romano-British culture.

Bede gave the earliest detailed account of their origins in the early 8th century: he believed the first settlers came from several tribes of northern Europe, among them the people of Old Saxony, the Jutes of Jutland and the Angles, whose homeland he placed between the two. Roman writers describe the earliest Saxons as North Sea raiders, and the Romans placed a commander over a chain of coastal forts, the Saxon shore. The compound term Anglo-Saxon first appears in the mid-8th century.

At the end of the 6th century the missionary Augustine landed on the Isle of Thanet and went to King Æthelberht's town of Canterbury, sent by Pope Gregory the Great to Christianise Kent. From the conversions the first well-attested English kings and kingdoms appear in the written record. The period of competing kingdoms is traditionally called the Heptarchy, a term scholars have not used since the early 20th century because there were more than seven kingdoms. By 660 smaller territories had coalesced into kingdoms, and larger ones dominated the smaller.

After the Norman Conquest many nobles were exiled or joined the peasantry, and it has been estimated that only about 8% of the land was under Anglo-Saxon control by 1087. Some nobles went to Scotland, Ireland and Scandinavia, and others to the Byzantine Empire, where Anglo-Saxons became the predominant element in the Varangian Guard. For most of the population little changed at once, except that a Norman lord replaced an Anglo-Saxon one.

Royal dynasties often claimed descent from Woden, but the true basis of kingly power was war-leadership. Kings were buried as warriors, and war helmets rather than crowns were used in coronations until the 10th century. Warriors fought for the king in return for food, shelter and gifts such as weapons, and loyalty was owed to the person of a lord, so a kingdom was only as strong as its king.

Kings issued written law codes, one of the earliest attributed to Æthelberht of Kent. Women enjoyed considerable independence, as abbesses of double monasteries, as landholders and as legal principals. Buildings were mainly timber with thatch roofs, and Old English was spoken until the mid-12th century, when it had evolved into Middle English.
anglo-zanzibar-war: Britain recognised Zanzibar's sovereignty in 1886, and Britain and Germany competed for trade rights and territory in East Africa. The agreement of 14 June 1890 made Zanzibar a British protectorate and required any candidate for the sultanate to obtain the permission of the British consul. Sultan Hamad bin Thuwaini, who came to the throne in 1893, kept close ties with Britain, though his subjects disliked the growing British control and the abolition of the valuable slave trade.

Hamad died suddenly on 25 August 1896, and some suspected his nephew Khalid bin Barghash of having killed him. Khalid moved into the palace without British approval, though they preferred Hamoud bin Mohammed. He ignored warnings from the consul Basil Cave and General Lloyd Mathews and mustered about 2,800 men, mostly civilians but including 700 askaris, with artillery and machine guns aimed at the British ships in the harbour.

On 26 August the government of Lord Salisbury authorised Cave and Rear-Admiral Harry Rawson to use whatever means they thought necessary, and Rawson sent an ultimatum requiring Khalid to haul down his flag and leave the palace by 09:00 on 27 August. Khalid replied that he did not believe the British would open fire. At 09:02 the ships Racoon, Thrush and Sparrow began a bombardment, and the wooden palace caught fire.

In a small naval action the old royal yacht Glasgow fired on St George and sank in the shallow harbour. The shelling ceased at around 09:40, with the sultan's artillery silenced and his flag shot down. Sources give the length of the war as 38, 40 or 45 minutes, depending on where its start and end are placed, and 38 minutes is the most often quoted.

About 500 Zanzibaris were killed or wounded, most of the dead from the fire, and the only British casualty was a petty officer who recovered. Khalid took refuge in the German consulate, whose consul refused extradition because the treaty excluded political prisoners, and on 2 October a German ship took him to Dar es Salaam. British forces captured him in 1916, and he died at Mombasa in 1927.

Hamoud was installed as sultan with much reduced powers, at the head of an essentially British-run government. The war ended Zanzibar's sovereignty and began a period of heavy British influence, and there were no further rebellions during the 67 years of the protectorate. Several months later Hamoud, prompted by the British, abolished slavery in all its forms.
angola: Angola covers 1,246,700 square kilometres on the western coast of Southern Africa, making it the seventh-largest country in Africa. It borders Namibia, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and its province of Cabinda is an exclave on the Atlantic coast. Luanda, the capital, lies on the coast in the north-west. Angola has four natural harbours: Luanda, Lobito, Moçâmedes and Tômbua. Like the rest of tropical Africa it has alternating rainy and dry seasons, and the dry season is known as the cacimbo.

Before the Bantu migrations the region was populated by nomadic Khoi and San hunter-gatherers. In the first millennium BCE Bantu peoples arriving from the north displaced them and introduced bananas, taro and large cattle herds. States were formed by the 13th century, and the Kingdom of Kongo achieved hegemony from the 14th century. To its south lay Ndongo and Matamba, and the title ngola, held by the kings of Ndongo and Matamba, gave the Portuguese the name Angola. The Portuguese established relations with Kongo in 1483, and Diogo Cão reached the area in 1484.

Paulo Dias de Novais founded São Paulo de Loanda in 1575 with a hundred families of settlers and four hundred soldiers, and Benguela was fortified in 1587. Kongo fought three wars against the Portuguese, ending in the Portuguese conquest of Ndongo. The colony did not reach its present borders until the early 20th century, and met strong resistance from groups such as the Cuamato, the Kwanyama and the Mbunda.

After an anti-colonial struggle from 1961 to 1974, Angola became independent in 1975 as a one-party republic and at once fell into a civil war. The ruling MPLA, backed by the Soviet Union and Cuba, fought the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, supported by the United States and South Africa, and the National Liberation Front of Angola, backed by Zaire. The civil war ended in 2002, and the peace allowed the resettlement of 4 million displaced persons.

The 2010 constitution made the leader of the winning party in parliamentary elections president, so that there are no separate presidential elections. Oil and diamonds have been the most important resources since independence. Angola had 36,604,681 inhabitants at the 2024 census. Portuguese is the official language and is spoken natively by 45.5 per cent, and Umbundu, Kimbundu and Kikongo are the most widely spoken indigenous languages.
angouleme: Angoulême stands on a plateau overlooking a meander of the river Charente, and is nicknamed the balcony of the southwest. The old city is built on a rocky outcrop at an altitude of 102 m, above a cliff 80 m high. Ramparts have surrounded the plateau since Roman times and were repeatedly destroyed and rebuilt until reconstruction stopped in the 19th century. The city's position at the crossroads of key routes exposed it to many sieges.

Little is known of the city before the Roman period, except that the plateau held an oppidum called Iculisma. Held by the Visigoths, who followed the Arian form of Christianity, the city was first besieged by Clovis in 507 and taken in 508, miraculously according to Gregory of Tours. On 18 May 1204 King John of England signed a charter creating the commune of Angoulême. Under the Treaty of Brétigny the city passed in 1360 to the English, and John Chandos took possession of it for Edward III in October 1361.

Angoulême was the seat of the County of Angoumois, which came to a branch of the Valois family from which came François I, born in Cognac in 1494. In 1524 the navigator Giovanni da Verrazzano told François I that he had discovered a new territory, which he named New Angoulême in the king's honour; the area later became New Amsterdam and then New York. In the Revolution the city was called Mountagne-Charente. German troops arrived on 24 June 1940 and neutralised between 10 and 20 thousand French soldiers.

Angoulême is the prefecture of the department of Charente, with a population a little under 42,000. Papermaking and printing have been connected with the town since the 14th century, helped by the steady temperature and volume of the water of the river Touvre. The cathedral of Saint-Pierre, a Romanesque church of the 12th century, was partly rebuilt in the later 19th century by Paul Abadie. The town hall, also by Abadie, keeps two 13th-century towers, Lusignan and Valois, from the castle of the counts. Since 1983 the city has had a school of fine arts with France's first cartoon section.
anguilla: Anguilla lies east of Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands and directly north of Saint Martin, from which it is separated by the Anguilla Channel. The main island is about 16 miles (26 km) long and no more than about 3 miles (5 km) wide at its widest point, and the territory also includes smaller islands and cays with no permanent population, among them Dog Island, Scrub Island and Sombrero. It is flat and low-lying, built of coral and limestone, with thin, poor soil. The Italian word anguilla, meaning eel, gave the island its name, in reference to its shape. The Indigenous Arawakan name was Malliouhana.

Indigenous peoples who migrated from South America first settled Anguilla, and the earliest artefacts found there date from around 1300 BCE. Settlement remains date from 600 CE, and the rock ledges of Big Spring hold more than 100 petroglyphs from between 600 and 1200 CE. It is uncertain when Europeans first saw the island. The Dutch West India Company built a fort in 1631, which the Spanish destroyed in 1633.

According to traditional accounts, English settlers from Saint Kitts colonised the island from 1650, planting tobacco and some cotton. The French took it temporarily in 1666 and returned it the next year under the Treaty of Breda. Enslaved Africans were probably brought by the early settlers, and archival evidence shows at least 100 enslaved people there by 1683. They worked on sugar plantations, and in time they and their descendants vastly outnumbered the white settlers. The British Empire ended the slave trade in 1807 and outlawed slavery in 1834.

Anguilla was placed under the administrative control of Saint Kitts in 1825 and federated with Saint Kitts and Nevis in 1882, against the wishes of many Anguillans. Full adult suffrage came in 1952. In 1967 the associated state of Saint Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla gained internal autonomy, and on 30 May 1967 Anguillans forcibly ejected the Saint Kitts police and declared independence from Saint Kitts. The revolution, led by Atlin Harrigan and Ronald Webster among others, aimed at separation and a return to British colonial status. Britain sent 300 troops in March 1969, and the Anguilla Act 1971 confirmed British authority. Anguilla formally seceded from Saint Kitts and Nevis in 1980.

Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory with The Valley as its capital. It is internally self-governing, with a governor appointed by the British government. Its people are mostly descended from enslaved Africans. English is the main language, alongside an English-lexifier Creole called Anguillian. Boat racing is the national sport.
ani: Ani stands on a triangular, naturally defensive site about 1,340 metres above sea level, protected on the east by the ravine of the Akhurian River and on the west by the Bostanlar valley. It lies in the Turkish province of Kars, about 400 metres from the border with Armenia. The city stood on various trade routes, and its buildings are of local volcanic basalt, a tufa that is easily carved and comes in colours from creamy yellow to rose-red and black. Walls encircled the city, with a double line on the northern side, the only part not guarded by rivers or ravines; chroniclers credit King Smbat (977–989) with building them.

Armenian chroniclers first mention Ani in the 5th century as a hilltop fortress of the Kamsarakan dynasty. By the early 9th century it had passed to the Bagratuni dynasty, and between 961 and 1045 it was the capital of their kingdom. Byzantium held it from 1045. In 1064 a Seljuk army under Alp Arslan took it after a siege of 25 days and, according to an eyewitness quoted by Sibt ibn al-Jawzi, massacred its people and took some 50,000 prisoners.

In 1199 Queen Tamar of Georgia captured the city and in 1201 gave its governorship to the generals Zakare and Ivane, whose Zakarian dynasty regarded itself as successor to the Bagratunis. Prosperity returned: defences were strengthened and many churches built. The Mongols besieged Ani unsuccessfully in 1226 but captured and sacked it in 1236, massacring many of its people. A devastating earthquake in 1319 and the shifting of regional trade routes completed its decline.

The Cathedral, begun in 989 under Smbat II and finished in 1001 to the design of the architect Trdat, has pointed arches and clustered piers that give it the look of Gothic architecture, which it predates by several centuries; its dome collapsed in 1319. The Church of St Gregory of Tigran Honents, finished in 1215, is the best preserved monument and holds an extensive fresco cycle. The minaret of the Mosque of Manuchihr, named for the first of the Shaddadids, also survives.

The city was called the City of 1,001 Churches, though the real number was far smaller: archaeologists have excavated 50 churches, 33 cave chapels and 20 chapels. Its population is put at perhaps 100,000, though some historians doubt this. The archaeological site was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2016.
ankara: Ankara lies on the central Anatolian plateau between the Kızılırmak and Sakarya rivers, in one of the driest regions of Turkey, surrounded mostly by steppe. Its historical centre is a rocky hill rising 150 metres over the left bank of the Ankara River, a tributary of the Sakarya, and the hill is still crowned by the ruins of Ankara Castle. The Galatians laid the castle's foundations on a lava outcrop and the Romans completed it; the Byzantines and Seljuks later restored it.

In antiquity the city was Ánkyra in Greek and Ancyra in Latin, from a Greek word meaning 'anchor'; it has been linked with the Hittite cult centre Ankuwaš, though this is debated. After the Seljuk Turks annexed it in 1073 it became known in many European languages as Angora, a form preserved in the names of the Angora goat, rabbit and cat, whose hair and wool were exported for centuries.

The oldest settlements around the city centre belonged to the Bronze Age Hattic civilization, which the Indo-European Hittites gradually absorbed between about 2000 and 1700 BCE. The city grew greatly under the Phrygians from around 1000 BCE, helped by a mass migration from Gordion after an earthquake damaged that capital. Phrygian tradition venerated King Midas as founder of Ancyra, but Pausanias noted that the city was far older, which agrees with archaeology. Lydians, Persians and Greeks followed. Ancyra was the capital of the Celtic state of Galatia from 280 to 64 BCE and then of the Roman province of Galatia, from 25 BCE to the 7th century CE.

The Ottomans made the city capital of the Anatolia Eyalet from 1393 to the late 15th century, of the Angora Eyalet from 1827 to 1864 and of the Angora Vilayet from 1867 to 1922. On 23 April 1920 the Grand National Assembly of Turkey was established there, and Ankara became the headquarters of the national movement in the Turkish War of Independence. It became the capital of the Republic on 29 October 1923, succeeding Istanbul. Planned for 500,000 inhabitants, it had about 75,000 in 1927. From the 1950s it grew faster than planned as people migrated from the countryside, building many unplanned houses called gecekondu.

Ankara is the capital of Turkey and the centre of its road and railway networks, with 5,782,285 people in the province in 2022. The citadel and the remains of a Roman theatre survive in the oldest quarter, and the Roman statues found at the theatre are shown in the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations. The region is also known for its pears, honey and Muscat grapes.
anklam: Anklam, formerly known as Tanglim and Wendenburg, lies on the banks of the Peene river, 8 kilometres from its mouth in the Kleines Haff, the western part of the Szczecin Lagoon. It is the head of navigation on the Peene. It was the capital of the former district of Ostvorpommern and, since September 2011, belongs to the district of Vorpommern-Greifswald. It had 12,177 inhabitants in 2021.

In the early Middle Ages an important Scandinavian and Wendish settlement stood nearby, at the place now called Altes Lager Menzlin, and Anklam began as an associated Wendish fortress. Part of the Duchy of Pomerania, the abandoned fortress became a settlement named Tanglim after its new founder during the German expansion eastwards. It received town status in 1244 and joined the Hanseatic League, a membership that brought it a measure of wealth, though it stayed small.

Because of its military importance Anklam suffered greatly in the Thirty Years' War, when Swedish and Imperial troops fought over it for twenty years; Imperial forces held it from 1627 to 1630 and Swedish forces afterwards. It became part of Swedish Pomerania in 1648 and was captured by Frederick William of Brandenburg in 1676. In 1713 Russian soldiers looted it; the town was not burned, as Peter the Great had ordered, largely through the resistance of Christian Thomesen Carl. The Treaty of Stockholm in 1720 gave the southern parts of Swedish Pomerania to Prussia. In the 19th century railways joined it to Berlin and Stettin, and linen, leather, beer and soap were made there.

Several bombing raids by the U.S. Air Force in 1943 and 1944, and the burning and levelling of most of the town by the advancing Soviets in the last days of the war, nearly destroyed it. In February 1945 a death march of Allied prisoners of war from Stalag XX-B passed through. After the war it was rebuilt in a rather uniform socialist style and, from 1952 to 1990, formed part of Bezirk Neubrandenburg.

Among its remaining buildings is the church of St Mary, of the 12th century, rebuilt in the 15th century, given a modern spire in the 19th and repaired in 1947. The Otto-Lilienthal-Museum commemorates the aviation pioneer, born there in 1848, and the Museum im Steintor covers local history. Others born in Anklam include the architect Gustav Lilienthal, the diplomat Ulrich von Hassell and the opera singer Johanna Gadski.
anna-komnene: Anna was born on 1 December 1083 to Alexios I Komnenos and Irene Doukaina, the eldest of seven children. Alexios had become emperor in 1081 by usurping Nikephoros Botaneiates. She was born in the Porphyra Chamber of the imperial palace, which made her a porphyrogenita. At birth she was betrothed to Constantine Doukas, son of Emperor Michael VII, probably as a political match to support the legitimacy of her father, and from about 1090 she was raised in the household of his mother, Maria of Alania.

Her education covered Greek literature, philosophy, theology, mathematics and medicine. Georgios Tornikes said in a funeral oration that she read the Odyssey in secret from her parents. She gained expertise in medicine, helped treat her father in his last illness and administered a large hospital in Constantinople.

Anna and Constantine were heirs until her brother John II Komnenos was designated emperor in 1092. Constantine died around 1094, and about 1097 she married Nikephoros Bryennios, a soldier and historian whose family had held the throne before her father. When Alexios died in 1118, John was acclaimed emperor in Hagia Sophia.

Niketas Choniates, writing after 1204, says Anna was driven by ambition and revenge to plot against John, that Bryennios refused to join her, and that she forfeited her estates. Leonora Neville argues she was probably not involved, since only Choniates portrays her as a rebel. After her husband's death she entered the Kecharitomene convent, founded by her mother, and stayed there for the rest of her life.

In the convent Anna studied philosophy and history and held scholarly gatherings, including those on Aristotelian studies. She wrote the Alexiad in the mid-1140s or the 1150s, citing her husband's unfinished history as a reason. She drew on old soldiers, accounts from her father and uncles, and the imperial archives. It is written in Attic Greek modelled on Thucydides, Polybius and Xenophon.

The Alexiad describes weapons, tactics and battles and relations between Alexios and the West. She wrote of events of her childhood, and wrote to praise her father and denigrate his successors. Still, it is the only Byzantine eyewitness account of the First Crusade, giving the alarm felt in Constantinople at the western armies, whom she calls Celts.
anna-of-kiev: Anne was a daughter of Yaroslav the Wise, Grand Prince of Kiev, and his second wife Ingegerd Olofsdotter of Sweden. Her birth date is unknown: Philippe Delorme has suggested 1027, and Andrew Gregorovich 1032. She was almost certainly the youngest daughter. A Cyrillic signature on a document of 1061 suggests that she could write her name. Yaroslav had married several of his children to Western rulers in an attempt to avoid Byzantine influence.

Negotiations for her marriage to King Henry I of France began in the late 1040s, after the death of his first wife and their only child. Henry needed an heir, and the Church increasingly disapproved of marriages between relatives, so he sought an unrelated bride. He sent Bishop Gauthier of Meaux and others to Yaroslav's court, and no record of the dowry survives. Anne travelled to Reims in 1050.

Anne married Henry, who was nearly twenty years older, on 19 May 1051, and was crowned immediately afterwards, the first French queen to celebrate her coronation at Reims Cathedral. They had three sons, Philip, Robert, who died young, and Hugh. Anne is often credited with introducing the Greek name Philip into the royal houses of Western Europe. Few records show her taking part in the royal council, but a charter of 1058 grants a privilege with her approval and that of her children.

Henry died on 4 August 1060 and Philip succeeded him. Count Baldwin V of Flanders became his guardian, but Anne's name appears in four times as many charters as Baldwin's. Her only surviving signature, in Cyrillic, probably reading Ana Reina, dates from this time.

Evidence of Anne's role in government disappears in 1061, around the time she married Count Ralph IV of Valois. The marriage was controversial because Ralph was Henry's cousin and was still technically married to his second wife, and he was excommunicated. Ralph died in 1074. In 1062 Anne paid for the restoration of a chapel at Senlis, which became the Abbey of St. Vincent. The date of her death is unknown: Delorme believes it was 5 September 1075, and others propose 1080.
anna-of-russia: Anna was born in Moscow on 7 February 1693, the daughter of Tsar Ivan V and Praskovia Saltykova. Ivan V, who was co-ruler with his younger half-brother Peter the Great but was mentally disabled, died in 1696, and Peter ruled alone. Her widowed mother raised Anna and her two sisters strictly. In 1708 Peter brought the family to St Petersburg, and Anna greatly enjoyed the splendour of the court. To increase his influence in Courland, Peter arranged her marriage to Frederick William, Duke of Courland, on 11 November 1710. The duke died on 21 January 1711, and Anna then ruled the duchy from Mitau for almost twenty years.

When Peter II died childless in 1730 the male line of the Romanov dynasty was extinct. The Supreme Privy Council chose Anna, a childless widow with some experience of government, in preference to her elder sister Catherine. It hoped she would be a figurehead, and made her sign Conditions under which she could not declare war, impose taxes or spend state revenue without its consent. On 7 March 1730 a faction opposed to the Dolgorouki and Galitzin families petitioned her, and she repudiated the Conditions. Some of their framers were hanged and many exiled to Siberia, and she ruled as an absolute monarch.

Her reign is often called the Age of Biron, after her favourite Ernst Johann von Biron, a Baltic German. Baltic Germans were favoured with offices, though the historian Walter Moss cautions that the picture of total German domination is exaggerated. Her Secret Office of Investigation punished political crimes, and Russian authorities listed around 20,000 victims. Russia fought a war with the Ottoman Empire from 1735 to 1739, which gained only Azov and its environs. The first ballet school in Russia was founded in 1738.

As her health failed Anna named her grandnephew Ivan VI as successor and Biron as regent. She died on 28 October 1740, aged 47, of a kidney stone. Ivan VI was a baby of two months, and Elizabeth Petrovna, Peter's daughter, soon won the favour of the people, imprisoned Ivan and exiled his mother. In the West Anna's reign was traditionally seen as a continuation of the transition from old Muscovy to the European court Peter had envisioned, while in Russia it is often called a dark era.
annaba: Annaba lies in the north-eastern corner of Algeria, close to the Tunisian border and near the small Seybouse River. The present city grew up on the site of Aphrodisium, the seaport of the Roman city of Hippo Regius, and has since spread south over Hippo's ruins. Its former names Bône and Bona derive from Ubbo, a local form of Hippo. The Arabic name means "place of the jujubes", after the abundance of that fruit in the region.

Hippo Regius entered the record at the end of the 3rd century BCE as a possession of Massinissa's Numidian kingdom. Augustine of Hippo was its bishop from 396 until his death in 430. The Vandals destroyed the city in the 5th century and ruled it for about a century; in 534 their king Gelimer surrendered at Bône to Belisarius, general of the emperor Justinian I. After the Muslim conquest of the Maghreb in 699 Abbasids, Aghlabids, Fatimids and Zirids ruled it in turn. Flooding and the ravages of the Banu Hilal in 1033 led to its relocation to its present site.
The Kingdom of Sicily conquered it in 1153 and the Almohads took it in 1160. Hafsid rule began in 1250, and Ottoman rule in 1533, apart from Spanish rule from 1535 to 1540.

Under French rule from 1832, as Bône, it was a main French settlement with a sizeable pied-noir minority. A sheltered port of 80 hectares was built between 1856 and 1869 for iron ore from the Mokta el Hadid mine, and the railway from the mine, opened in 1864, was the first in Algeria. The mine produced 22,000 tonnes in 1865 and 255,000 in 1869. Bône had 10,000 inhabitants before the mine and 41,000 by 1924. In 1943 it was a crucial road and sea base for the Allied invasion of Tunisia in Operation Torch. It remained part of French Algeria until independence in 1962.

Annaba is a leading industrial centre of Algeria, with a large steel complex at El Hadjar south of the city. The Basilica of Saint Augustine recalls the ancient diocese of Hippo. The Bône War Cemetery, 5 kilometres from the city, holds 868 Commonwealth burials of the Second World War.
annaberg-buchholz: Annaberg-Buchholz lies in the Ore Mountains of Saxony, beside the Pöhlberg, which rises to 832 metres above sea level, and is the capital of the district of Erzgebirgskreis. The upper Ore Mountains were heavily forested until Franconian farmers settled them in the 12th and 13th centuries. Frohnau, Geyersdorf and Kleinrückerswalde, now part of the town, have been attested since 1397.

Silver deposits were discovered in the area in 1491, and Annaberg developed under the patronage of George, Duke of Saxony, and Barbara Jagiellon. They founded St. Anne's Church and a Franciscan monastery, dissolved in 1539, and Barbara gave the church a relic of Saint Anne, which made it a regional pilgrimage destination. The church, built between 1499 and 1525, is the largest of its kind in Saxony. The mines produced silver, tin and cobalt until before the First World War.

Barbara Uthmann introduced braid and lace-making in 1561, and Belgian refugees fleeing the Duke of Alba developed the craft in the 1590s. Annaberg and Buchholz were joined by rail to Chemnitz in the 19th century and each had a school for lace-making. In 1945 the two towns merged. From 1952 to 1990 the town was part of the Bezirk Karl-Marx-Stadt of East Germany.

The old town and market square are well known, and the Ore Mountains are called the Land of Christmas for their markets and carved figures. Annaberg's Christmas market ends with a miners' parade, the Bergparade. The town has monuments to Luther, to the mathematician Adam Ries and to Barbara Uthmann, and an Adam Ries Museum. After reunification in 1990 some old mines were restored for visitors. The Frohnauer Hammer, a working hammer mill at Frohnau, was declared a technical monument in 1907 and is open to the public.
annapolis-maryland: Annapolis lies on Chesapeake Bay at the mouth of the Severn River, 25 miles south of Baltimore and about 30 miles east of Washington, D.C. The city is part of the Atlantic Coastal Plain and is relatively flat, its highest point only 50 feet above sea level. It is the closest state capital to the national capital and, in land area, the smallest of the capital cities of the United States. It has a strong maritime culture and is known as America's Sailing Capital.

In 1649 Puritan exiles from Virginia, led by the third proprietary governor of Maryland, William Stone, founded a settlement called Providence on the north shore of the Severn. The settlers later moved to a better-protected harbour on the south shore. The settlement there was known from 1683 as the Town at Proctor's, then as the Town at the Severn, and in 1694 it received the name Anne Arundel's Towne. In 1696 St. John's College was founded in the city.

In 1783–1784 Annapolis was the seat of the Confederation Congress, the former Second Continental Congress, and the temporary national capital. On 23 December 1783 General George Washington resigned his commission as commander of the Continental Army before the Congress in the new Maryland State House. The Congress ratified the Treaty of Paris, which ended the American Revolutionary War, there on 14 January 1784, so that Annapolis became the first peacetime capital of the United States. It was also the site of the 1786 Annapolis Convention, which called on the states to send delegates to the Constitutional Convention held at Philadelphia the next year.

The Maryland State House, begun in 1772, with the legislature first meeting there in 1779, is the oldest in continuous legislative use in the United States. It is topped by the largest wooden dome built without nails in the country. In 1861 the midshipmen of the Naval Academy, established in 1845, were moved to Newport, Rhode Island, until 1865, and Camp Parole, a camp for paroled soldiers, was set up on the grounds of St. John's College; the Annapolis National Cemetery holds those who died. In July 1940 Grand Duchess Charlotte of Luxembourg arrived in Annapolis in exile.

Annapolis is the capital of Maryland and the county seat of Anne Arundel County, with a population of 40,812 at the 2020 census. The state legislature, the governor's office and the appellate courts are located there. The United States Naval Academy stands adjacent to the city limits, and the city hosts each year the largest in-water sailboat show in the world.
anne-frank: Annelies Marie Frank was born on 12 June 1929 in Frankfurt, the younger daughter of Edith Frank, née Holländer, and Otto Heinrich Frank. Her sister was Margot. The family were Reform Jews who lived among a mixed community of Jewish and non-Jewish citizens, and her parents, who encouraged reading, kept an extensive library. In 1934, after Adolf Hitler had been appointed to govern Germany, the family moved to Amsterdam, among about 300,000 Jews who left Germany between 1933 and 1939. Anne joined the 6th Montessori School there. German occupation trapped the family in May 1940, and in 1941 she lost her German citizenship and became stateless.

For her thirteenth birthday on 12 June 1942 Anne received an autograph book with a small lock, which she decided to use as a diary and named Kitty. On 6 July 1942, as persecution of Jews increased, the Franks moved into a hiding place, the Achterhuis or Secret Annex, a three-storey space entered from a landing above the Opekta offices on the Prinsengracht, where Otto Frank's trusted employees acted as their helpers. A bookcase later covered the door. In the diary she wrote about the restrictions on Dutch Jews and about the strongly differing personalities of the people sharing the annex, and about her relationships with her family. She grew closer to Margot as she matured, and was closest emotionally to her father.

On 4 August 1944 German police led by SS-Oberscharführer Karl Silberbauer raided the annex. How it was found is uncertain: a biography of 2015 suggested a betrayal, and research published by the Anne Frank House in 2016 pointed to an investigation of ration-card fraud as a possible cause, without ruling out betrayal. The Franks were taken to Westerbork and, on the last transport from there, to Auschwitz on 3 September 1944. On 1 November 1944 Anne and Margot were moved to Bergen-Belsen, where they died, probably of typhus, in February or March 1945.

Otto Frank was the only member of the family to survive. Miep Gies and Bep Voskuijl had saved Anne's notebooks, and in July 1945 Gies gave them to him. He published the diary in 1947, and it appeared in English in 1952 as The Diary of a Young Girl. It has been translated into more than 70 languages and is the basis of several plays and films. Later editions restored passages cut from the first, including pages removed by Otto Frank himself. The Anne Frank House, opened on 3 May 1960, preserves the Prinsengracht building.
anne-of-brittany: Anne was born on 25 or 26 January 1477 in the Castle of the Dukes of Brittany in Nantes, the eldest child of Duke Francis II of Brittany and his second wife Margaret of Foix. She was raised by a governess, Françoise de Dinan, and probably learned to read and write in French and perhaps a little Latin. Because Francis II had no son, the Estates of Brittany recognised her as his heiress on 10 February 1486, and he promised her in marriage to various princes to obtain aid against the King of France.

Francis II died on 9 September 1488, after being defeated at Saint-Aubin-du-Cormier, and Anne became Duchess of Brittany at eleven. On his deathbed he made her promise never to consent to the subjugation of the duchy to France. She married Charles VIII of France in 1491 and was crowned queen at St. Denis on 8 February 1492, although the king forbade her to use the title of duchess. None of their children survived early childhood.

When Charles VIII died on 4 April 1498 she took charge of the administration of Brittany. She agreed to marry the new king, Louis XII, if he obtained an annulment from his wife Joan, and they married at Nantes on 7 January 1499. The contract recognised her right to the title Duchess of Brittany and made the couple's second child her heir, though this clause was not respected. She was crowned again on 18 November 1504, and was a patron of poets, musicians and artists.

Anne died of a kidney-stone attack at the Château de Blois on 9 January 1514. Her will left Brittany to her second daughter Renée, but Louis XII ignored it, confirmed the elder daughter Claude as duchess and married her to Francis, son of Louise of Savoy, who became King Francis I in 1515. This marriage later led to the formal union of France and Brittany.

Royal propaganda presented Anne as a perfect queen, a symbol of union between France and Brittany, and Breton regionalists chose her as a figure of patriotism in the mid-19th century. Historians disagree about her character: Georges Minois called her limited, petty and vindictive, while Philippe Tourault described a favourable personality attached to her country. With her husbands she built at the châteaux of Blois and Amboise.
anne-of-cleves: Anne was born in Düsseldorf in 1515, on either 22 September or 28 June, the second daughter of John III, Duke of Cleves, and Maria, Duchess of Jülich-Berg. She grew up in Schloss Burg near Solingen. Her father was influenced by Erasmus and followed a moderate course in the Reformation, siding with the Schmalkaldic League against Emperor Charles V. In 1527 she was betrothed to Francis, son of Antoine, Duke of Lorraine, but the betrothal was cancelled in 1535. Her brother William became Duke of Jülich-Cleves-Berg after their father's death in 1538. She had received no formal education and could read and write only in German.

Thomas Cromwell urged the match on Henry VIII, who sought an alliance with the German Protestants against France and the Holy Roman Empire. Hans Holbein the Younger painted Anne and her sister Amalia at Düren, and the king, finding the portrait flattering, agreed to the marriage. The treaty was signed on 4 October 1539. Henry first met Anne privately at Rochester on New Year's Day 1540, disguised, and was disappointed; he is reported to have said she was nothing so fair as she had been reported. The wedding took place on 6 January 1540 at Greenwich, performed by Archbishop Thomas Cranmer.

The marriage was never consummated. Anne was told to leave court on 24 June, and she consented to an annulment, granted on 12 July 1540 on grounds of non-consummation and her earlier pre-contract to Francis of Lorraine. Cromwell, the moving force behind the match, was attainted for treason. Anne received a generous settlement, including Richmond Palace and Hever Castle, and became known as the King's Beloved Sister, with precedence over all women in England except the king's wife and daughters.

Anne stayed in England for the rest of her life and never returned to Germany. She changed religion with the monarch, conforming to Catholic worship in 1540 and again under Mary I, whose coronation procession she joined in 1553. She lost royal favour in 1554 after Wyatt's rebellion, when the imperial ambassador Simon Renard suspected her of involvement in a plot linked to Elizabeth. She dictated her will in July 1557 at Chelsea Old Manor, where she died on 16 July, probably of cancer. She was buried in Westminster Abbey on 3 August, and she was the last of Henry VIII's wives to die.
anne-robert-jacques-turgot: Turgot was born in Paris on 10 May 1727, the youngest son of Michel-Étienne Turgot, provost of the merchants of Paris, from an old Norman family. He was educated for the Church and admitted to the Sorbonne in 1749, but in 1750 decided not to take holy orders, saying that he could not bear to wear a mask all his life. That year he wrote a work on the Idea of Progress, which covers the whole of culture, including institutions, legal codes and economy.
