He met the physiocrats Quesnay and Vincent de Gournay and wrote articles for the Encyclopédie.

In August 1761 Turgot became intendant of the generalité of Limoges, among the poorest and most over-taxed parts of France, and remained thirteen years. He surveyed the land to assess the taille more justly and replaced the corvée with a money tax, which let him leave a good system of highways.

Louis XVI made him minister of the navy in July 1774 and Controller-General of Finances on 24 August. His principles were no bankruptcy, no increase of taxation and no borrowing. His edict of 13 September 1774 freed the grain trade, and after the poor harvest of 1774 he firmly repressed the bread riots known as the guerre des farines. In January 1776 he presented the Six Edicts, of which the two most opposed suppressed the corvées and the craft guilds' privileges. He had nearly everyone against him, the queen included, and on 12 May 1776 he was ordered to resign. He spent his last years in scientific and literary study and died on 18 March 1781.

His best-known work, Reflections on the Formation and Distribution of Wealth, was written in 1766 and published separately in 1776. It divides society into three classes, develops Quesnay's theory that land is the only source of wealth, proposes a single tax on the land's net product and demands complete freedom of commerce and industry. He is thought to have been the first political economist to postulate something like the law of diminishing marginal returns in agriculture.
anschluss: The idea of an Anschluss, a union of Austria and Germany in a Greater Germany, arose after the unification of Germany in 1871 excluded Austria, and gained support after the Austro-Hungarian Empire fell in 1918. The Treaty of Versailles and the 1919 treaty of Saint Germain forbade the union. Support was strong in the 1920s, particularly on the Austrian left and centre, because many believed Austria, stripped of its imperial lands, was not viable economically. After Adolf Hitler became German chancellor on 30 January 1933 the aim was identified with the Nazi regime. Austrian Nazis assassinated the Austrian chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss during an attempted coup in July 1934.

On 12 February 1938, at Berchtesgaden, under threat of invasion, Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg accepted an ultimatum to appoint the Austrian Nazi Arthur Seyss-Inquart as minister of the interior. On 9 March he announced a referendum on independence for 13 March. On 11 March Hitler demanded its cancellation and Schuschnigg's resignation, and President Wilhelm Miklas reluctantly appointed Seyss-Inquart in his place. Seyss-Inquart invited the German army to cross the border to restore order.

The 8th Army crossed on the morning of 12 March, and the Austrian army had been ordered not to resist. Many Austrians cheered the troops, though one anti-Nazi German observer suspected the welcome was staged. Within days 70,000 people had been arrested. A referendum on 10 April officially recorded 99.7 per cent approval. Historians agree the votes were accurately counted, but the vote was neither free nor secret, and about 360,000 people, 8 per cent of the eligible voters, had lost the right to vote.

The campaign against Austria's Jews began at once. They were driven through the streets of Vienna and their homes and shops were plundered, and over 6,000 Jews were arrested during the Kristallnacht pogrom of 9 and 10 November. The Anschluss was among the first steps towards the Greater German Reich, followed by the Munich Agreement of September 1938 and the dismantling of Czechoslovakia in March 1939. The Moscow Declaration of 1943 declared the annexation null and void, and a provisional government did the same on 27 April 1945. Austria stayed under Allied control until the Austrian State Treaty of 1955 restored its sovereignty.
anselm-of-canterbury: Anselm was born in or around Aosta between April 1033 and April 1034. At fifteen he wished to enter a monastery but could not obtain his father's consent. At 23 he left home and wandered for three years through Burgundy and France, and in 1059 he reached the Benedictine abbey of Bec in Normandy, where his countryman Lanfranc of Pavia was prior. On the advice of Maurilius, Archbishop of Rouen, he entered Bec as a novice at 27, was elected prior in 1063 and, after the death of the founder Herluin, abbot in 1078.

Anselm became Archbishop of Canterbury in 1093. He asserted the primacy of Canterbury over York and the Welsh bishops, and historians have traditionally seen his term as the English part of the Investiture Controversy. His resistance to royal control of the Church led to exile twice, from 1097 to 1100 and from 1105 to 1107, and in exile he took part in the Council of Bari.

The Monologion, written in 1075 and 1076, gives reasons for belief in God without appeal to scripture, at the request of his fellow monks. The Proslogion, of 1077 and 1078, seeks a single argument that proves God's existence: the being than which none greater can be conceived must exist, since one lacking existence could be surpassed. The monk Gaunilo answered with a parody about a perfect island, and Anselm replied that he had misunderstood. Kant's treatment gave it the name ontological argument.

Cur Deus Homo, written from 1095 to 1098 as a dialogue with his student Boso, argues that humanity's offence against God could be repaid only by one both divine and human, whose death has infinite worth. It largely replaced the earlier theory centred on Satan's power over fallen man, though critics have found its argument legalist.

Anselm died on 21 April 1109, now his feast day. His chaplain Eadmer wrote a biography soon after, and his students included Gilbert Crispin and Anselm of Laon. His works influenced Thomas Aquinas, Duns Scotus and William of Ockham, and he is often called the father of scholasticism. Thomas Becket asked for his canonization in 1163, and he was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church in 1720. Modern scholars remain divided: Southern upholds Eadmer's picture of a reluctant churchman, while Vaughn sees a skilled political operator.
antananarivo: Antananarivo stands about 1,280 metres above sea level in the Central Highlands of Madagascar, 160 kilometres from the east coast and 330 kilometres from the west coast. The city occupies the summit and slopes of a long, narrow, rocky ridge about 4 kilometres in length, rising some 200 metres above the rice fields to the west. It was originally a town called Analamanga, "Blue Forest", established by the Vazimba, considered the island's first occupants.

According to oral history, the Merina King Andrianjaka, who had migrated from the south-east coast, took the site with a garrison of 1,000 soldiers, and the city later took its name, Antananarivo, "City of the Thousand", from them under King Andriamasinavalona. Andrianjaka built a rova, a fortified royal compound, that grew to enclose the royal palaces and the tombs of Merina royalty. Accounts date the founding to around 1610 or 1625. Early Merina kings used statute labour to build a system of irrigated paddy fields and dikes around the city, of which the largest, the Betsimitatatra, still produces rice.

By 1810, when Radama I came to the throne, Antananarivo was the largest and most economically important city on the island, with over 80,000 inhabitants. Radama admitted the first European settlers, artisan missionaries of the London Missionary Society, who arrived in 1820 and opened the city's first public schools. His conquests brought nearly two-thirds of the island under his control, and the Merina sovereigns declared Antananarivo the capital of the whole island. Between 1829 and 1842, through war, forced labour, disease and harsh justice, the population of Imerina fell from 750,000 to 130,000. In the last years of the kingdom, most of the city's 50,000 to 75,000 people were slaves, largely captured in provincial campaigns.

The French military invaded Antananarivo in September 1894, and the queen surrendered after a cannon shell blasted a hole through a building at the Rova. The French made it the capital of their colony, writing the name as Tananarive. They built the Governor General's Residency at Antaninarenina, later the presidential offices, cut tunnels through two of the largest hills, and brought in water from the Ikopa River, sewers and electricity.

Antananarivo is the capital and largest city of Madagascar, with 1,274,225 inhabitants at the 2018 census and an urban area of almost 2.3 million. It is home to the Presidency, National Assembly, Senate and Supreme Court. The royal compound's largest building, the Manjakamiadana palace, stands at the summit of the hills; a fire in 1995 left only its stone casing, which was restored by 2009. Before the mid-19th century houses were built of wood, grasses and reeds, and only family tombs were of stone, a material thought fitting for the dead.
antanas-smetona: Antanas Smetona was born on 10 August 1874 in the village of Užulėnis in the Kovno Governorate of the Russian Empire, the eighth of nine children of a farming family of former serfs. His father died when he was eleven. He attended the Palanga Progymnasium, where Lithuanian books banned by the Tsarist authorities were easier to obtain, and the Jelgava Gymnasium, and in 1897 entered the law faculty of the University of Saint Petersburg. He joined Lithuanian student societies, rejected the socialist ideas he met, and was briefly imprisoned and deported to Vilnius for taking part in the student protests of February 1899. He graduated in 1902.

Smetona moved to Vilnius, worked at the Vilnius Land Bank until 1915 and devoted much of his time to the Lithuanian press, editing papers and founding the newspaper Viltis in 1907. In September 1917 he was elected chairman of the Council of Lithuania, and on 16 February 1918 he signed the Act of Independence. On 4 April 1919 the State Council elected him the first president of the Republic of Lithuania, and on 19 April 1920 the Constituent Assembly elected Aleksandras Stulginskis in his place.

Smetona led the coup of December 1926 that deposed President Kazys Grinius, and he became president again on 19 December. He dissolved parliament a year later and on 15 May 1928 promulgated a constitution with wider presidential powers. In 1929 he removed his prime minister Augustinas Voldemaras and took dictatorial powers. He was re-elected in 1931 and 1938 as the only candidate, and a third constitution of 1938 kept the authoritarian character of the second. His regime repeatedly arrested members of the banned Communist Party. It also put Nazis in the Memel region on trial in 1934–1935, and Memel was surrendered to Hitler in 1939. According to the account followed here, no anti-Jewish law was passed under his rule.

After the Soviet ultimatum of June 1940 Smetona proposed armed resistance, but the government and army commanders thought it hopeless. On 15 June he handed his duties to Prime Minister Antanas Merkys and crossed into Germany, then went on through Switzerland, Lisbon and Brazil to the United States, arriving in March 1941. He settled in Cleveland, where he worked on a history of Lithuania and his memoirs. He died on 9 January 1944 in a fire at his son's house; the official record blamed an overheated furnace, and a Soviet cause is considered doubtful. Lithuania has held since 1990 that Merkys's takeover of the presidency was illegal, since Smetona never formally resigned. Historians still debate his legacy.
ante-pavelic: Ante Pavelić was born on 14 July 1889 in the village of Bradina in Herzegovina, then Ottoman territory occupied by the Austro-Hungarian Empire. His parents had moved there from Lika to work on the Sarajevo-Metković railway line. He grew up near Jajce and in Travnik, where he became an adherent of the nationalist ideas of Ante Starčević and Josip Frank. A lawyer, he joined the Croatian Party of Rights, entered its leadership in 1918, and was elected to the Zagreb city assembly in 1921.

After King Alexander declared his 6 January Dictatorship in 1929, Pavelić left Yugoslavia. The Ustaša movement, founded on principles of racialism and intolerance, has 7 January 1929 as its official foundation date. In March 1929 it began a campaign of terror within Yugoslavia, and on 29 April Pavelić and Ivan Mihailov of the Internal Macedonian Revolutionary Organization signed the Sofia Declaration to separate Croatia and Macedonia from Yugoslavia. He was sentenced to death in absentia that August. Benito Mussolini allowed him to live in Rome and train paramilitaries, and in 1934 the Ustaše carried out the assassination of King Alexander in Marseille.

Slavko Kvaternik declared the Independent State of Croatia on 10 April 1941 in Pavelić's name, and Pavelić, calling himself the Poglavnik, took control of the puppet government. The Ustaše imposed anti-Serbian, antisemitic and anti-Roma policies that resulted in the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Serbs and tens of thousands of Jews and Roma, many in concentration and extermination camps run by the Ustaše. Hundreds of thousands of Orthodox Christians were forcibly converted to Catholicism or expelled to German-occupied Serbia. By November 1943 his regime controlled little of the state's territory.

Pavelić left Croatia on 6 May 1945 and fled to Austria. He reached Rome in 1946 disguised as a priest and arrived in Buenos Aires on 6 November 1948, where he served as a security adviser to Juan Perón. He was shot in an assassination attempt on 10 April 1957 and then went to Madrid, where Spain granted him asylum. He died there on 28 December 1959, aged 70, of his wounds, and was buried in San Isidro Cemetery. The mass killings and persecutions of the Independent State of Croatia have been described as the single most disastrous episode in Yugoslav history.
antequera: Antequera lies at 575 metres above sea level, at the foot of the mountain ranges of El Torcal and the Sierra de la Chimenea, in a fertile valley bounded to the north by the Guadalhorce River. It is called the heart of Andalusia because of its central position among Málaga, Granada, Córdoba and Seville. The surrounding vega has long produced cereals, olive oil and vegetables.

Two Bronze Age burial mounds on the northern outskirts, the dolmens of Menga and Viera, date from the third millennium BCE and are the largest such structures in Europe. Menga was built with thirty-two megaliths, the largest weighing about 180 tonnes. The Romans knew the city as Anticaria, part of Hispania Baetica, and it was known for its olive oil. The present street plan largely follows that of the Roman town.

Anticaria was conquered around 716 and became Medina Antaquira under the Umayyad Caliphate. After the Christian victory at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 it became an important border town of the Nasrid Emirate of Granada and was attacked repeatedly for about two hundred years. On 16 September 1410, after a siege of nearly four months, it capitulated to a Castilian army led by the infante Ferdinand of Trastámara. The Muslim population was forced to leave for Archidona and Granada; 895 men, 770 women and 863 children departed.

The city grew after the conquest of Málaga in 1487 and became a centre of grain production and commerce in the sixteenth century. A humanist university, the Real Colegiata de Santa María la Mayor, was founded in 1504, and a school of poets arose, including Pedro Espinosa. Antequera was the site of the drafting of the Federal Constitution of Antequera in 1883 and of the Pact of Antequera in 1978, which led to autonomy for Andalusia.

Antequera is a city and municipality in the province of Málaga, in the autonomous community of Andalusia, and the largest municipality in the province by area. The Antequera Dolmens Site, which includes Menga, Viera, El Romeral, the Peña de los Enamorados and El Torcal, was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2016. There are 32 churches and convents in the city.
anthony-eden: Robert Anthony Eden was born on 12 June 1897 at Windlestone Hall, County Durham, the third of four sons of Sir William Eden and Sybil Frances Grey, into a conservative family of landed gentry. He attended Sandroyd School in Surrey and, from January 1911, Eton College. His elder brother John was killed in action on 17 October 1914, aged 26. After the First World War Eden studied Oriental Languages, with Persian as his main language and Arabic as his second, at Christ Church, Oxford, from October 1919. He learned French and German on continental holidays, and in February 1934 conversed with Adolf Hitler in German.

Eden contested Spennymoor as a Conservative in 1922 without success and later sat for Warwick. In August 1931 he held his first ministerial office as Under-Secretary for Foreign Affairs. He became Foreign Secretary at 38, after Samuel Hoare resigned over the collapse of the Hoare-Laval Pact, and supported non-interference in the Spanish Civil War, but he resigned over Neville Chamberlain's policy of appeasement towards Benito Mussolini's Italy. In 1939 he returned to government as Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs, and Winston Churchill, on becoming prime minister in 1940, appointed him Secretary of State for War. He again served as Foreign Secretary from 1951, having been regarded as Churchill's crown prince since 1942.

Eden succeeded Churchill as prime minister in April 1955. In July 1956 Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal after Anglo-American funding for the Aswan Dam was withdrawn. Eden believed this violated the Anglo-Egyptian treaty of October 1954 and feared that Nasser meant to form an Arab alliance able to cut Europe's oil supplies; with France he decided Nasser should be removed from power. The United States refused to support the Anglo-French military response. Two months after ordering an end to the operation Eden resigned, on grounds of ill health and because he was widely suspected of having misled the House of Commons about collusion with France and Israel.

Eden left the Commons after 33 years and entered the House of Lords as the Earl of Avon in 1961. He died of metastatic prostate cancer at Alvediston Manor, Wiltshire, on 14 January 1977, aged 79. He was twice married; his son Simon was killed in action with the RAF in Burma in 1945.

He is generally considered among the least successful British prime ministers of the 20th century, though two broadly sympathetic biographies have shifted opinion somewhat, and most historians argue that he made a series of blunders at Suez, especially in not realising the depth of American opposition. Contemporaries judged him differently: Dick Crossman called him the idealist without conviction, while Nikita Khrushchev said that until Suez Eden had been in the top world class.
anthony-the-great: Most of what is known about Anthony comes from the Life of Anthony, written in Greek about 360 by Athanasius of Alexandria, which presents him as an illiterate holy man. He was born in Koma in Lower Egypt to wealthy landowning parents. When he was about 20 his parents died and left him responsible for his unmarried sister. Soon after, he took to heart the words of Matthew 19:21, gave away part of the family land to his neighbours, sold the rest and gave the money to the poor. He placed his sister with a group of Christian virgins and began an ascetic life. He probably spoke only Coptic, and seven letters dictated in that language survive.

For about fifteen years Anthony stayed near his village, first as the disciple of another local hermit. Ascetics already existed before him, but he went out into the desert proper, to the Nitrian Desert about 95 kilometres west of Alexandria, where he stayed 13 years. He ate only bread, salt and water, and at most once a day. According to Athanasius the devil attacked him with boredom, laziness and the phantoms of women. Around the age of 35 he withdrew to an abandoned Roman fort at Pispir, where he stayed some 20 years while food was thrown over the wall. Disciples settled in caves around the mountain, and about 305 he emerged to guide them.

He later withdrew to Mount Colzim, between the Nile and the Red Sea, where the monastery of Deir Mar Antonios still stands. About 311, during the Diocletianic persecutions, he went to Alexandria to visit the imprisoned, and in 338 he went there again to help refute the teachings of Arius. The emperor Constantine wrote to ask for his prayers.

Anthony died on about 17 January 356 and was buried in a secret grave on the mountain. His remains were reportedly discovered in 361 and moved to Alexandria, later to Constantinople, and in the 11th century were given to the French Count Jocelin. A church to house them, Saint-Antoine-l'Abbaye, was completed in 1297. Skin diseases such as ergotism were called Saint Anthony's fire. His temptations were depicted by Hieronymus Bosch and Matthias Grünewald, among many artists, and retold by Gustave Flaubert. He is called the Father of All Monks, though he was not the first monk and did not himself create a monastery.
antibes: Antibes lies on the French Riviera in the Alpes-Maritimes, between Cannes and Nice. Its cape, the Cap d'Antibes, is one of the area's two major landforms, with Cap Ferrat to the northeast. The resort of Juan-les-Pins is within the commune, and the Sophia Antipolis technology park lies northwest of it. There are 48 beaches along 25 km of coastline around Antibes and Juan-les-Pins. Port Vauban, with more than 2,000 moorings, is the largest yachting harbour in Europe, and its old port was the heart of the ancient Greek city.

Traces of early Iron Age occupation have been found in the area of the castle and cathedral. An indigenous community had ties with Mediterranean peoples, including the Etruscans, as the underwater amphorae and wrecks off Antibes show, though most trade was with the Greek world through the Phocaeans of Marseille. Antibes was founded as a Greek colony by Phocaeans from Massalia, probably in the 4th century BCE, and named Antipolis, Opposite-City, from its position across the Var estuary from Nice.

The Bishopric of Antibes was established c. 450 by Pope Leo I. In the 10th century raiders from Muslim Spain menaced the coast until Count William I of Provence captured their stronghold at Fraxinetum in 975. He gave the liberated lands to his knights, and one of them, Rodoald, became Lord of Antibes.

Saracen pirates burned the cathedral in 1124 and kept preying on the town, and in 1244 the bishops moved to Grasse, where they stayed for five centuries. In 1383 Marie de Blois confiscated the lordship from the bishops of Grasse and awarded it two years later to the Genoese brothers Marc and Luc Grimaldi, who built the Château Grimaldi. Provence passed to King Louis XI and to France in 1481, which made Antibes a border town facing the County of Nice, then part of the Savoyard state. Andrea Doria sacked it in 1536, and Henry II ordered the building of Fort Carré in 1550, later reinforced by Vauban.

From December 1746 an Austro-Savoyard army under Maximilian Ulysses Browne besieged Antibes. It lifted the siege on 1 February 1747, but its guns had levelled 350 houses and destroyed the cathedral again, which Louis XV later rebuilt. On 1 March 1815 Napoléon Bonaparte landed at Golfe-Juan, 5 km to the southwest, on his return from Elba. He hoped for a warm welcome at Antibes, but the townspeople closed their gates to him. Antibes was transferred from Var to Alpes-Maritimes in 1860. In 1926 the municipality bought the Château Grimaldi, where Pablo Picasso lived for six months in 1946; it now houses the Musée Picasso.
antigonid-dynasty: The Antigonid dynasty was a Macedonian Greek royal house of the Hellenistic period, founded by Antigonus I Monophthalmus, a general and successor of Alexander the Great who first came to power in the wars of the Diadochi. It was one of four dynasties established by Alexander's successors, the others being the Seleucid, Ptolemaic and Antipatrid dynasties. The Argead dynasty of Macedon had become extinct when Cassander ordered the assassination, in 310 or 309 BCE, of the 14-year-old Alexander IV, son of Alexander the Great, and his mother Roxane, and the Antigonid and Antipatrid dynasties, the latter led by Cassander, son of Antipater, sought to fill the vacuum.

In 307 BCE Demetrius, son of Antigonus, ousted Cassander's governor of Athens, Demetrius of Phalerum, and after defeating Ptolemy I at the Battle of Salamis in 306 BCE he conquered Cyprus. Antigonus then took the title basileus, king, from the assembled armies, and ruled territory from the Aegean to the Middle East, sometimes called the Antigonid Empire. A revived coalition of Cassander, Ptolemy I Soter, Seleucus I Nicator and Lysimachus decisively defeated the Antigonids at the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE, where Antigonus was killed.

Demetrius, who is known as Poliorcetes, survived, took Athens and in 294 BCE made himself king of Macedon. In 288 BCE Pyrrhus and Lysimachus drove him out, and he died a prisoner of Seleucus I Nicator. After a long period of instability his son Antigonus II Gonatas established the family's control over Macedon and over most of the Greek city-states by 276 BCE, despite the loss of the Asian territory. Antigonus III Doson extended Macedonian influence in southern Greece and re-established the Hellenic Alliance with himself as leader. Under Philip V, Macedon first came into conflict with Rome, already a decisive power in the Mediterranean.

The last Antigonid king, Perseus, who reigned from 179 to 168 BCE, became known as the champion of Greek resistance to Rome, but he could not stop the Roman legions. His defeat at the Battle of Pydna in 168 BCE, in the Third Macedonian War, ended the dynasty, and Macedon came under the control of the Roman Republic. A rebel against Rome, Andriscus, claimed to be a son of Perseus.
antigonus-i-monophthalmus: Antigonus was born in Macedonia around 382 BCE to a nobleman named Philip. Ancient sources disagree about his family, some calling it peasant stock and others linking it to the royal house, but the family was in all probability socially prominent. When he first appears in the sources he commands a large part of Alexander's army, including about 7,000 allied Greek infantry. Plutarch records that an Antigonus lost an eye to a catapult bolt at the Siege of Perinthus in 340 BCE. He was an exceptionally large man, made more formidable by the missing eye.

In 334 BCE he commanded the allied Greek infantry in Alexander's invasion of Persia, and when Alexander marched east he appointed him satrap of Phrygia. He took a garrison of mercenaries into his own service and sent 1,500 of his mercenaries to reinforce Alexander before Issus.

After Alexander's death in 323 BCE the Partition of Babylon confirmed Antigonus in Phrygia, Lycaonia, Pamphylia, Lycia and western Pisidia. He incurred the enmity of the regent Perdiccas by refusing to help Eumenes take Cappadocia, and fled to Greece with his son Demetrius. After Perdiccas was murdered in 321 BCE, Antigonus became Strategos of Asia at Triparadisus and defeated the remnants of the Perdiccan faction at Orkynia and Cretopolis. After Antipater's death in 319 BCE he defeated Eumenes, entered Babylon and seized the treasury at Susa. Seleucus fled to Ptolemy, and Ptolemy, Cassander and Lysimachus joined a league against Antigonus.

In the Third Diadochi War he took Tyre after a year's siege. Seleucus regained Babylonia, and a peace followed in 309 BCE in which Antigonus held Greece, Asia Minor, Syria, Phoenicia and northern Mesopotamia, the height of his power. After his son Demetrius defeated Ptolemy at sea at Salamis in 306 BCE and conquered Cyprus, Antigonus took the title of king, which the other dynasts soon did as well. His invasion of Egypt failed, and Demetrius's siege of Rhodes in 305 and 304 BCE ended in a treaty.

Cassander, Seleucus, Ptolemy and Lysimachus allied against Antigonus, and the forces of Seleucus, Lysimachus and Cassander's general Prepelaos defeated him and Demetrius at the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE. He died there, struck by a javelin, in his eighty-first year; he had never lost a battle before. With his death plans to reunite Alexander's empire ended, and his kingdom was divided mostly between Lysimachus and Seleucus. Demetrius took control of Macedonia in 294 BCE, and Antigonus's descendants, the Antigonid dynasty, held it until the Roman conquest after the Battle of Pydna in 168 BCE.
antigua-guatemala: Antigua Guatemala lies in the Panchoy Valley of the central highlands, and three large volcanoes dominate its horizon. The Volcán de Agua, about 3,766 metres high, rises to the south; it took its Spanish name after a lahar from it buried the second site of the capital in 1541. To the west are Acatenango and the Volcán de Fuego, which is almost constantly active at a low level.

The first capital was founded on 25 July 1524 at the Kaqchikel Maya city of Iximche and named Ciudad de Santiago de los Caballeros de Guatemala. After Kaqchikel uprisings it was moved in 1527 to the Valley of Almolonga, where a lahar destroyed it on 11 September 1541. The authorities moved the capital eight kilometres north, and on 10 March 1543 Spanish conquistadors founded the present city, again named Santiago de los Caballeros. For 230 years it was the seat of the Captaincy General of Guatemala, which covered the present Guatemala, Belize, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica and the state of Chiapas in Mexico. It was laid out in a grid around a central square.

Franciscans, Jesuits and the Brothers of San Juan de Dios founded convents, schools and hospitals, and the Royal University of San Carlos Borromeo began classes on 7 January 1681. Earthquakes damaged the city repeatedly, notably in 1717 and 1751. After the Santa Marta earthquakes of 1773 the Crown ordered the capital moved in 1776 to the Valley of the Shrine, the site of the present Guatemala City. The abandoned city was called la Antigua Guatemala. Its population, at a peak of about 65,000 in the 1770s, fell as most residents left.

Antigua is the capital of Sacatepéquez Department. It was declared a National Monument on 30 March 1944 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979, for its Spanish Baroque-influenced architecture, layout, churches and ruins. The Arco de Santa Catalina and the Palace of the Captaincy General, which houses the National Museum of Guatemalan Art, survive among the ruins. The city is known for its Holy Week processions over carpets of dyed sawdust and flowers.
antikythera-mechanism: The device is believed to have been made by Hellenistic scientists. Proposed dates range from 205 BCE through 150 to 100 BCE to about 87 BCE. It must predate the shipwreck that carried it, dated by several lines of evidence to about 70 to 60 BCE. Researchers in 2022 proposed 23 December 178 BCE as its initial calibration date, while others favour 204 BCE. Machines of similar complexity did not appear again until the 14th century in western Europe.

How it came to be on a Roman cargo ship is unknown. Its design drew on the astronomy of the 2nd century BCE, and Hipparchus of Rhodes, who studied the Moon's irregular motion, may have been consulted. Researchers in 2008 traced the calendar on the Metonic Spiral to Corinth or one of its colonies.

The mechanism was housed in a wooden case of about 34 by 18 by 9 centimetres. The front dial has a fixed ring of the twelve zodiac signs and, outside it, a movable ring. Scans in 2005 suggested 35 meshing bronze gears, 30 still visible, which followed the Sun and Moon through the zodiac, predicted eclipses and modelled the Moon's changing speed. The largest gear is about 13 centimetres across and had 223 teeth.

Inscriptions on the back door act as a manual and name the 76-year Callippic cycle, the 19-year Metonic cycle and the Saros cycle of 223. Whether it also showed the five classical planets is debated, since no planetary gearing survives. Freeth and Jones found that a simulation with planetary pointers is inaccurate, with the Mars pointer up to 38 degrees wrong at times, because of limits in Greek planetary theory rather than in the gearing.

Sponge divers from Symi under Captain Dimitrios Kontos found the wreck off Point Glyphadia on Antikythera in early 1900, at a depth of 45 metres. The mechanism was recovered in 1901 and went unnoticed for two years among statues and other finds. In 1902 the politician Spyridon Stais saw a gear in it, and the museum director Valerios Stais made the first study. The lump is now 82 fragments in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. In 2005 a Cardiff University team led by Mike Edmunds used X-ray tomography to read faint inscriptions. Cicero describes two machines of Archimedes brought to Rome by Marcus Claudius Marcellus, suggesting the device was not unique.
antioch: Antioch stood in northern Syria at the site of modern Antakya, in Hatay Province, Turkey. It lay in the southwest of the Amuq plain, a fertile lowland watered by three rivers. The Orontes skirted the plain's southern edge and cut westward through the mountains to the Mediterranean. Wheat, barley, olives and wine were grown there, and cypress wood and building stone were abundant. The plain had been inhabited for thousands of years, with Bronze Age powers at Tell Atchana and Tell Tayinat, and it stayed under Achaemenid rule until Alexander the Great invaded in 333 BCE.

After Seleucus I Nicator won the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE he ordered four settlements to secure northern Syria: Seleucia Pieria and Laodicea on the coast, and Antioch and Apamea inland. Antioch was founded in 300 BCE on a grid plan modelled on Alexandria, with the citadel on Mount Silpius. Later rulers added walled quarters, and it became known as Tetrapolis. It was the Seleucid capital from 240 BCE until the Romans took control in 63 BCE, then capital of Roman Syria, and may have had more than 500,000 inhabitants at its peak, the third largest city of the empire.

Antioch was a chief centre of early Christianity, and the New Testament asserts that the name Christian first arose there. When the emperor Julian visited in 362 he ordered the bones of the martyred bishop Babylas moved from the temple of Apollo at Daphne, which provoked a large Christian procession. A tax sedition in 387 cost the city its metropolitan status. Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah took it for the Rashidun Caliphate in 637.

The Crusaders captured Antioch in June 1098 after a siege of eight months, and it became the centre of the Principality of Antioch. On 18 May 1268 Baibars took the city; he promised to spare its people but broke his promise and razed it, killing or enslaving nearly the whole population. By 1432 only about 300 houses within its walls were inhabited.

Little of the Roman city is visible beyond the fortification walls climbing the mountains east of Antakya, several aqueducts and the Church of St Peter. Most of it lies beneath alluvial deposits of the Orontes. Excavations between 1932 and 1939 did not find Constantine's Great Octagonal Church or the imperial palace, but recovered Roman mosaics from villas and baths. The Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Antioch still bears the city's name.
antiochus-iii-the-great: Antiochus III was the son of Seleucus II Callinicus and Laodice II, born about 242 BCE near Susa in Persia. He succeeded his brother Seleucus III Ceraunus, who was murdered in Anatolia, while he himself was in Babylon. He was about eighteen and inherited a disorganised state. Asia Minor had become detached, and Bactria and Parthia had broken away. Soon after his accession Media and Persis revolted under their governors, the brothers Molon and Alexander. An attack on Ptolemaic Syria, made under the influence of his minister Hermeias, ended in failure. Only in 221 BCE, advised by Zeuxis, did Antiochus go east in person, and the rebellion collapsed.

After his defeat by Ptolemy IV at the Battle of Raphia in 217 BCE, Antiochus turned to Asia Minor and by 214 BCE had driven his cousin Achaeus, who had taken the royal title, into Sardis. He had Achaeus executed. In 209 BCE he invaded Parthia, and in Bactria defeated Euthydemus I at the Battle of the Arius; after the Siege of Bactra he allowed Euthydemus to keep his royal title. He crossed into the Kabul valley and renewed his friendship with the Indian king Sophagasenus, receiving elephants, and returned by Seistan and Kerman in 206 or 205 BCE. These campaigns earned him the name the Great, and he took the title Basileus Megas, Great King.

Returning west, he renewed the war against the Ptolemies, and his victory over Scopas at the Battle of Panium in 198 BCE marked the end of Ptolemaic rule in Judea. His expansion in Asia Minor and Thrace earned the antagonism of Rome. In 192 BCE he invaded Greece with 10,000 men, advised by the exiled Hannibal and elected commander of the Aetolian League. The Romans under Manius Acilius Glabrio routed him at Thermopylae in 191 BCE, and Scipio Asiaticus defeated him at Magnesia ad Sipylum in 190 BCE. By the Treaty of Apamea in 188 BCE he gave up all lands north and west of the Taurus Mountains, which Rome gave mostly to Rhodes and Eumenes II of Pergamon.

The outlying provinces he had recovered reasserted their independence after Apamea. Antiochus mounted a new expedition to the east and was killed in 187 BCE while pillaging a temple of Bel at Elymaïs. His son Seleucus IV Philopator succeeded him, and later another son became Antiochus IV Epiphanes. Josephus portrays Antiochus III as friendly to the Jews of Jerusalem: he lowered taxes, granted subventions to the Temple and let the Jews live by the law of their forefathers, and he resettled 2,000 Jewish families from Babylonia in Lydia and Phrygia. The First Book of Maccabees recalls his defeat by the Romans.
antiochus-iv-epiphanes: Antiochus was a son of the Seleucid king Antiochus III the Great. Under the Treaty of Apamea of 188 BCE he became a political hostage of the Roman Republic, and when his elder brother Seleucus IV Philopator took the throne in 187 BCE he was exchanged for Seleucus's son Demetrius. He then lived in Athens, where he was when Seleucus was assassinated in 175 BCE by the minister Heliodorus. With the help of Eumenes II of Pergamum he reached Syria by November 175 BCE and took the throne as co-regent with Seleucus's infant son, who died in 170 BCE, possibly murdered by Antiochus.

Antiochus cultivated a reputation for extravagance. He scattered money in the streets of Antioch and held a great parade at Daphne, and his unexpected behaviour, such as appearing in the public baths, led detractors to call him Epimanes, the Mad, a play on his title Epiphanes, God Manifest. In 170 BCE the guardians of Ptolemy VI Philometor declared war to recover Coele-Syria. Antiochus defeated the Egyptian army, advanced into Egypt and captured Ptolemy. In 168 BCE he attacked again, but before he reached Alexandria the Roman envoy Gaius Popillius Laenas delivered a Senate order to withdraw, drew a circle in the sand round him, and demanded an answer before he left it. Antiochus withdrew.

In 171 BCE Antiochus had replaced the High Priest Jason with Menelaus, who offered a bribe. In 168 BCE a rumour that the king had died led Jason to attack Jerusalem, and Antiochus, returning, restored Menelaus and killed many Jews. According to 1 Maccabees he then outlawed Jewish rites, made the Temple a cult that included the worship of Zeus, and built a Greek citadel, the Acra. The Maccabean Revolt followed. Traditionally it is seen as resistance to foreign oppression, but some modern scholars see Antiochus as intervening in a civil war between traditionalist and Hellenized Jews.

Antiochus led the main army east against the Parthians, retook Armenia, but was driven from Persepolis, and died at Isfahan in 164 BCE. Polybius and the books of the Maccabees judge him harshly, but some historians doubt Polybius, who was a friend of Antiochus's rival Demetrius I. Jewish tradition remembers him as the persecutor of the story of Hanukkah.
antioquia-department: Antioquia covers 63,612 square kilometres in the central north-west of Colombia, with a narrow section on the Caribbean Sea in the Urabá region. About 80 per cent of its territory is mountainous, crossed by the Cordillera Central and the Cordillera Occidental of the Andes. The Cordillera Central divides to form the Aburrá valley, where the capital, Medellín, lies. The basis for the name is uncertain. A common explanation is that it was named after the Hellenistic city of Antioch on the Orontes.

Before Spanish colonisation the region was populated mainly by the Kalina, or Mainland Caribs, whose best-known groups in central Antioquia were the Catía, Nutabe and Tahamí, while the Quimbaya lived in the south. The Spaniards dominated or exterminated the Carib, and many Indigenous people died in epidemics of diseases from Europe and Asia. Rodrigo de Bastidas was the first known Spaniard in the area, in 1500. The first military incursion was an expedition under Francisco César in 1537, which reached the Cauca River; the warriors of the chief Nutibara harassed it until it returned to Urabá.

In 1541 the conquistador Jorge Robledo led an expedition north along the Cauca and founded Santa Fe de Antioquia. In 1813 it was declared the capital of the sovereign state of Antioquia, and it remained the seat of government until 1826, when Medellín became the capital. Antioquia kept a sovereign government until the Colombian Constitution of 1886. Its mountains left it isolated and short of farmland, so it depended on trade, especially in gold, after reforms that followed a visit in 1785 by the Crown inspector Juan Antonio Mon y Velarde.

Antioquia is one of the 32 departments of Colombia, and more than half of its population lives in the metropolitan area of Medellín, the second-largest city in the country. Other important towns are Rionegro, Apartadó, Puerto Berrío and Santa Fe de Antioquia, the old capital. The department is divided into nine subregions and 125 municipalities.
antofagasta: Antofagasta lies about 1,100 kilometres north of Santiago on a coastal plain, south of the Mejillones Peninsula and north of Cerro Coloso, at an average elevation of 40 metres. The urban area begins abruptly, breaking the monotony of the desert. The Tropic of Capricorn passes north of the city, near the Cerro Moreno International Airport, and a monument opened on 21 December 2000 marks it and works as a solar calendar. The name is presumed to derive from that of Antofagasta de la Sierra in Catamarca Province, Argentina.

In the 18th century the territory appeared on maps of the Captaincy General of Chile, depending on Copiapó, and it was disputed between Chile and Bolivia until the Boundary Treaty of 1866. On 18 September 1866 José Santos Ossa and Francisco Puelma obtained a Bolivian concession over nitrate lands after finding rich saltpeter deposits at the Salar del Carmen, and formed the Sociedad Exploradora del Desierto de Atacama. On 8 May 1872 the Bolivian government designated Antofagasta a Puerto Mayor, opening it to world trade.

In 1873 Bolivia signed a secret defensive alliance with Peru, and a contract with a Chilean company, the Compañía de Salitres y Ferrocarril de Antofagasta, which Bolivia's congress never ratified. In 1874 Chile and Bolivia signed a border treaty that barred new taxes on Chilean capital for 25 years. In the Bolivian version of events, congress imposed a tax of 10 cents because the contract was not in force; when Bolivia reactivated the tax after a Chilean note, it cancelled the company's concession. Chile occupied Antofagasta on 14 February 1879, which triggered the War of the Pacific (1879–83). The Treaty of Peace and Friendship, signed on 20 October 1904 and promulgated on 21 March 1905, fixed the border permanently.

A British community erected a clock tower in 1912 that replicates Big Ben, in the Plaza Colón. A mudslide on 18 June 1991 killed 92 people, left 16 missing and about 20,000 homeless, and destroyed 493 buildings; an earthquake of magnitude 7.3 struck on 30 July 1995.

Antofagasta is the capital of Antofagasta Province and Antofagasta Region, with a population of 401,096 at the 2024 census. It is a port and the chief service hub of one of Chile's major mining areas, where silver and saltpeter were historically important and copper has been by far the most important mineral since the mid-19th century. It is also a university city, home to the Catholic University of the North and the University of Antofagasta.
antoine-watteau: Jean-Antoine Watteau was born in October 1684 in Valenciennes, once an important town of the County of Hainaut that passed to France after the Franco-Dutch War. He was the second of four sons of Jean-Philippe Watteau, a roofer, and Michelle Lardenois. He left for Paris in 1702 and, after working as a scene-painter, found employment copying Flemish and Dutch genre paintings, where he developed his sketchlike technique. By 1705 he was assistant to Claude Gillot, in whose studio he came to know the characters of the commedia dell'arte, a lifelong passion. He then moved to the workshop of Claude Audran III, curator of the Palais du Luxembourg, where he saw the canvases of Peter Paul Rubens for Marie de Medici, a major influence.

Watteau failed to win the Prix de Rome in 1709 and 1712. He was accepted as an associate member of the Academy in 1712 and a full member in 1717, taking five years to deliver his reception piece, the Pilgrimage to Cythera. He then lived with the collector Pierre Crozat, whose collection let him study Rubens and the Venetian masters. He lacked aristocratic patrons, and his buyers were bourgeois, bankers and dealers.

His best-known works include Pierrot, long identified as Gilles, and Fêtes venitiennes. His last major work, the Shop-sign of Gersaint, was painted for the Paris dealer Edme François Gersaint in eight days, working only in the mornings, and has been compared with Las Meninas as a meditation on art and illusion. Sickly from childhood, he went to London in 1720 to consult Dr. Richard Mead, then returned to France and died in 1721, perhaps of tuberculous laryngitis, aged 36.

Watteau was little known in his lifetime beyond a small circle. His fêtes galantes are tinged with wistfulness at the transience of love, in contrast to the whimsy of Boucher and Fragonard later. Jean de Jullienne published etchings after his drawings in 1726 and 1728 and engravings after his paintings in 1735, which spread his influence across Europe. The Watteau dress, with loose pleats hanging from the shoulder at the back, is named after him. J. M. W. Turner was among his admirers in England, and Edmond de Goncourt published a catalogue raisonné in 1875.
anton-bruckner: Bruckner was born in Ansfelden on 4 September 1824, the eldest of the five children who survived of eleven born to the village schoolmaster Anton Bruckner Sr. His father was his first music teacher, and he learned the organ as a child, sometimes practising twelve hours a day. After his father died in 1837 he became a choirboy at the Augustinian monastery of Sankt Florian. He worked as an assistant teacher at Windhaag, where pay was appalling and his superior constantly humiliated him, and a belief in his own inferiority stayed with him all his life. From 1845 he spent ten years at Sankt Florian as teacher and organist, and in 1855 he was accepted as a pupil by the Vienna theorist Simon Sechter.

In 1868 he hesitantly took over Sechter's post at the Vienna Conservatory and concentrated on symphonies, which were poorly received and at times called wild and nonsensical. He was unhappy in Vienna, where the critic Eduard Hanslick dominated musical life; by aligning himself with Wagner in the feud between the followers of Wagner and of Johannes Brahms, he made an unintentional enemy of him. Supporters such as the conductors Arthur Nikisch and Franz Schalk brought his music to the public.

Bruckner composed eleven symphonies, from the Study Symphony in F minor of 1863 to the unfinished Symphony No. 9 in D minor, written between 1887 and 1896. Only the Fourth, the Romantic, had a subtitle from the composer. By the mid-twentieth century musicologists recognised that his orchestration followed the sound of the pipe organ, alternating between groups of instruments as an organist changes manual. His sacred music includes a Te Deum, a Magnificat, about forty motets and at least seven Masses. Helgoland of 1893 was his last completed composition, and his String Quintet in F major dates from 1879.

Bruckner died on 11 October 1896 and is buried at Sankt Florian. His admirers included Gustav Mahler. The leaders of Nazi Germany approved of his music, and Adolf Hitler consecrated a bust of him at the Walhalla in Regensburg in 1937. The Brucknerhaus in Linz, which opened in 1974, is named after him.
anton-denikin: Anton Denikin was born on 4 December 1872 in Włocławek in the Russian Empire. His father, Ivan, was born a serf and served 25 years in the army, retiring as a major, and his mother Elżbieta was a Polish Catholic. The family lived in poverty and Anton was raised in the Orthodox faith. He entered the army in 1889 and the Academy of the General Staff in 1895, and in the Russo-Japanese War a hill was named Denikin's sopka in his honour.

In the First World War Denikin commanded the 4th Rifle Brigade, the Iron Brigade, one of the most decorated units in the army, and was promoted to lieutenant general in 1915. After the February Revolution he became chief of staff to the Supreme Commander and criticised the Provisional Government's army reforms, and in August 1917 he was arrested for supporting General Lavr Kornilov. After the October Revolution he reached Novocherkassk, helped found the Volunteer Army and took command in April 1918, after Kornilov was killed.

In January 1919 he became Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of South Russia. His Moscow Directive of 20 June 1919 began an offensive that took Kharkov, Kiev and Orel and came within 350 kilometres of Moscow. His supply lines were overstretched and peasant uprisings troubled his rear. His advance in Ukraine was accompanied by antisemitic pogroms, mostly by Cossack units, which killed tens of thousands; he forbade them, but his orders were not enforced. A Red Army counter-offensive defeated the Whites at Orel and Voronezh in late October. Denikin resigned in favour of General Pyotr Wrangel on 4 April 1920.

In exile Denikin wrote a five-volume history of the Civil War, The Russian Turmoil. When Germany invaded the Soviet Union in 1941 he urged émigrés to support the Red Army. He moved to the United States in December 1945 and died of a heart attack on 7 August 1947. His remains were reburied at the Donskoy Monastery in Moscow in 2005.

His reputation is disputed: Soviet writers portrayed him as an enemy of the people, while admirers saw a patriot. Historian Peter Kenez judged him a decent man but an ineffective leader, whose government failed to carry out an effective land reform and whose slogan of a great, united and indivisible Russia alienated the Cossacks and national minorities.
anton-webern: Anton Webern was born on 3 December 1883 in Vienna, the only surviving son of Carl von Webern, a civil servant and mining engineer. He grew up mainly in Graz and Klagenfurt. His mother Amalie was a trained pianist and singer, and he learned piano, cello and probably counterpoint from the local musician Edwin Komauer. He studied the Franco-Flemish School under Guido Adler, and Arnold Schoenberg taught him to compose from the music of Bach, the First Viennese School and Brahms. In 1911 he married his cousin Wilhelmine Mörtl, and the Catholic Church solemnised their union in 1915, after three children had been born.

Early in his career Webern was an unhappily peripatetic conductor, often assigned light music or operetta. From 1918 to 1921 he worked with Schoenberg, Alban Berg and Erwin Stein at the Society for Private Musical Performances in Vienna. He rose as a choirmaster and conductor and championed the music of Gustav Mahler. After the Austrofascists crushed the Social Democrats in the 1934 Austrian Civil War, his long association with them cost him a promising domestic conducting career, and he relied on teaching and editing for income.

He was marginalised as a cultural Bolshevist in Austria and Nazi Germany, and little of his mature music was performed in the Reich. He opposed fascist cultural positions but espoused pan-Germanism, and his hope for stable governance of Austria within Nazi Germany proved misplaced. He helped Jewish friends emigrate and hide while repeatedly considering emigrating himself. A soldier accidentally killed him after the end of the Second World War, on 15 September 1945.

Webern's music was concise, organic and sparing, built on very small motifs and palindromes. After his Op. 2 his music and Schoenberg's was freely atonal, and he later adopted twelve-tone technique. His earliest works were mostly Lieder, and the German Romantic Lied left a lasting influence on his lyricism and intimacy, even as his music became more abstract. About 1913 to 1926 he worked on almost sixty songs. His String Trio, Op. 20 (1926 to 1927) was his first large-scale non-vocal work in more than a decade.

His music was long considered difficult by performers and inaccessible by listeners. After the Second World War composers including René Leibowitz and Pierre Boulez championed it, and it became central to the postwar avant-garde at the Darmstädter Ferienkurse and to the tradition known as post-Webernism. Igor Stravinsky assimilated it, and choreographers have set it to dance. Scholars have contested his legacy in the serial wars.
antonie-van-leeuwenhoek: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was born in Delft on 24 October 1632. His father, a basket maker, died when Antonie was five, and his mother came from a well-to-do brewer's family. At sixteen he became a bookkeeper's apprentice at a linen-draper's shop in Amsterdam. In July 1654 he married Barbara de Mey in Delft and opened a draper's shop. In 1660 he became chamberlain for the sheriffs in the city hall, a post he held for almost 40 years, and in 1669 he was appointed land surveyor by the court of Holland. He knew the painter Johannes Vermeer, whose will he executed in 1675. He was Dutch Reformed and Calvinist, and believed his discoveries were further proof of the wonder of creation.

Wanting to see the thread of his cloth better than the magnifying lenses of the time allowed, Van Leeuwenhoek took up lensmaking. A small glass rod pulled apart in a flame yields two whiskers of glass, and putting the end of one back in the flame forms a very small, high-quality lens. He kept his methods secret. He made more than 500 lenses and at least 25 single-lens microscopes, of which nine survive and magnify up to 275 times.

His friend, the physician Reinier de Graaf, introduced his work to the Royal Society in London, which in 1673 published a letter from him on mold, bees and lice. In 1674 he concluded that the moving objects under his microscope were little animals. His report of single-celled organisms, dated 9 October 1676, was met with scepticism until observers sent by the Royal Society confirmed his observations in 1677. He was elected to the Society in February 1680 but never attended a meeting, and he wrote only in colloquial Dutch. Visitors included Leibniz, John Locke and Peter the Great, though he refused to show them his best microscopes.

He was the first to recognize that the structures Marcello Malpighi and Jan Swammerdam had seen in blood were red blood cells. His records include protists in 1674, spermatozoa in 1677, the banded pattern of muscle fibres in 1682 and bacteria in 1683. He also experimented on himself, examining blood drawn from his finger and his own skin. He died on 26 August 1723, aged 90, and was buried in the Oude Kerk in Delft.
antonin-dvorak: Dvořák was born on 8 September 1841 in Nelahozeves, near Prague, then in the Austrian Empire. He was the eldest of 14 children, eight of whom survived infancy. His father František worked as an innkeeper, a professional zither player and a butcher. In 1847 he entered primary school and learned the violin from his teacher Joseph Spitz, playing in a village band and in church. In 1873 he married Anna Čermáková, the sister of Josefína Čermáková, with whom he had first fallen in love. They had nine children, several of whom died in infancy.

After public successes in Prague in 1872 and 1873, he won the Austrian State Competition in 1874, and again in 1877, when the critic Eduard Hanslick and Johannes Brahms were on the jury. Their offer of help led to his publication by Simrock. A London performance of the Stabat Mater at the Royal Albert Hall on 10 March 1883 began a run of performances in England and the United States, and he visited Britain at least eight times. His Seventh Symphony was written for the London Philharmonic Society and premiered on 22 April 1885.

From 1892 to 1895 Dvořák directed the National Conservatory of Music in New York, whose president, Jeannette Thurber, offered him $15,000 a year, twenty-five times his Prague pay, and admitted women and black students. On holiday in Spillville, Iowa, in 1893 he wrote the String Quartet in F major, Op. 96, known as the American. He returned to Bohemia on 27 April 1895 and died on 1 May 1904.

Dvořák drew on Slavic folk dance forms, among them the Bohemian furiant and sousedská, the Polish polonaise and mazurka and the Ukrainian dumka, which gave its name to his Dumky Trio. His nine symphonies generally follow classical models, and the Symphony From the New World has been numbered in turn the 5th, 8th and 9th, because four symphonies were only published after his death. In 1896–1897 he wrote five symphonic poems, four of them based on ballads from the collection Kytice by the folklorist Karel Jaromír Erben.

The Stabat Mater, the longest extant setting of that text, was inspired by the death of his daughter Josefa. His opus numbers do not always follow the order of writing: publishers gave early works high numbers to make a composer seem established, and Dvořák sometimes gave a work a lower number so that he could sell it outside his contract.
antonine-wall: Construction began around 142 on the orders of Emperor Antoninus Pius, who never visited Britain. Quintus Lollius Urbicus, governor of Roman Britain at the time, first supervised the work. Estimates of how long it took vary widely, with six and twelve years most commonly proposed. Pressure from the Caledonians probably led Antoninus to send the empire's troops farther north. The wall was meant to extend Roman territory and replace Hadrian's Wall, 160 km to the south, as the frontier of Britannia, but the Romans never conquered the Caledonians and the wall suffered many attacks.

The wall ran for about 63 km from Old Kilpatrick on the Firth of Clyde to Carriden, near Bo'ness, on the Firth of Forth. It was a bank about 3 metres high and 5 metres wide, of layered turves on a stone foundation, with a wide ditch on the north side and a military road to the south. It is thought a wooden palisade stood on top. Unlike Hadrian's Wall it had no ditch system behind it. The stone foundations and wing walls of the first forts show that a stone wall like Hadrian's was planned at first, but this was quickly changed.

The Romans first planned forts every 10 km, then revised this to every 3.3 km, with at least nine smaller fortlets between them, and a road called the Military Way linked all the sites. Rough Castle Fort is the best preserved, and Kinneil is the most visible fortlet. Coastal forts such as Inveresk served as outposts or supply bases, and forts further north, among them Ardoch and Strageath, were brought back into service. The soldiers who built the wall set up decorated distance slabs naming the length each legion built, and twenty survive. Research at Glasgow University has shown that they were once brightly painted.

The wall was abandoned within two decades of its completion, when the legions withdrew to Hadrian's Wall in 162. When Septimius Severus campaigned in Scotland in 208 to 210, there is no evidence that he paid any attention to it. Writing in 730, Bede, following Gildas, mistakenly ascribed it to the Britons. Medieval chronicles called it Gryme's dyke, which became Graham's dyke, a name still found at Bo'ness.

William Roy mapped it systematically in 1764, and where later development has destroyed it his drawings are the only reliable record. Sir George Macdonald published his survey in 1911. In the 16th century George Keith, 5th Earl Marischal, set a stone from the wall in the walls of Dunnotar Castle. The Antonine Wall was listed on 7 July 2008 as an extension to the World Heritage Site Frontiers of the Roman Empire, and several sites along it are in the care of Historic Environment Scotland.
antoninus-pius: Antoninus was born Titus Aurelius Fulvus Boionius Antoninus in 86, near Lanuvium, the son of Titus Aurelius Fulvus, consul in 89, and Arria Fadilla. His family was a relatively new senatorial house from Gallia Narbonensis, supported by the Flavians. After his father's early death he was raised by his maternal grandfather Gnaeus Arrius Antoninus, a friend of Pliny the Younger.

Between 110 and 115 he married Annia Galeria Faustina the Elder. He became consul in 120, administered part of Italy as one of four proconsuls, and was proconsul of Asia, probably in 134 and 135. On 25 February 138 Hadrian adopted him, on condition that he adopt Marcus Annius Verus and Lucius, son of Lucius Aelius, later the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus.

Antoninus made few changes at first, and his ruling team centred on a group of conservative senatorial families. He persuaded the Senate to grant divine honours to Hadrian, which is the most likely reason for the title Pius. J. J. Wilkes notes that he probably never commanded a Roman army and was never within five hundred miles of a legion in his twenty-three years. In Britain the governor Quintus Lollius Urbicus invaded southern Scotland and built the Antonine Wall from the Firth of Forth to the Firth of Clyde; it was decommissioned from the mid-150s and abandoned in the early 160s, for reasons that remain unclear.

He left a treasury of about 2.7 billion sesterces, suspended taxes in cities hit by fire and earthquake, and gave grants to rebuild Greek cities after earthquakes in about 140 and in 152. He is also credited with dividing imperial property into the patrimonium and the res privata.

Marcus Aurelius, consul with Antoninus in 140, took on more duties as the emperor aged. Antoninus died in 161, probably on 7 March, shortly after Marcus and Lucius were designated joint consuls. The Antonine Plague, brought back by soldiers after the Parthian victory, soon depleted the treasury. The only complete ancient account of his life, the Historia Augusta, is unreliable and largely fabricated, though it is the sole source to mention the Antonine Wall. Edward Gibbon and others praised him as an ideal landed gentleman, while some historians take a less favourable view. Only one of his four children reached adulthood, but he was ancestor of four generations of prominent Romans, including the emperor Commodus.
antonio-da-correggio: Antonio Allegri was born in the small town of Correggio, near Reggio Emilia, around 1489. His father was a merchant, and little else is known of his youth. It is often assumed that his first artistic education came from his father's brother, the painter Lorenzo Allegri. In 1503–1505 he was apprenticed to Francesco Bianchi Ferrara in Modena, where he probably became familiar with the classicism of Lorenzo Costa and Francesco Francia. After a trip to Mantua in 1506 he stayed in Correggio until 1510, and by 1514 he was an independent and increasingly well-known artist there.

By 1516 Correggio was in Parma, where he spent most of the rest of his career. His first major commission, in 1519, was the ceiling of a private chamber of the abbess Giovanna Piacenza in the convent of St Paul, painted as an arbour pierced by oculi with playful cherubs. He then painted the Vision of St John on Patmos in the dome of San Giovanni Evangelista, and about three years later an Assumption of the Virgin in the dome of Parma Cathedral, crowded with layers of figures seen from below (sotto in su). Their illusionistic treatment of the dome influenced later fresco painters, from Pordenone to the Baroque artists Lanfranco and Baciccio.

He also painted a series of the loves of Jupiter from Ovid's Metamorphoses, commissioned by Federico II Gonzaga of Mantua and given to the visiting Holy Roman Emperor Charles V. It includes Leda and the Swan, Danaë, Ganymede Abducted by the Eagle and Jupiter and Io. Among his religious works are the Lamentation and the Martyrdom of Four Saints, both in the Galleria Nazionale of Parma.

Correggio died suddenly in his home town on 5 March 1534 and was buried the next day in San Francesco, near his early Madonna of St Francis, now in Dresden. Contemporaries remembered him as a shadowy, melancholic and introverted man. He left few direct followers outside Parma, but Vasari knew his work half a century later, and visitors' diaries of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries led to a reassessment of him in the Romantic period. His illusionistic experiments, in which imagined space replaces the natural, seem to prefigure Mannerist, Baroque and Rococo approaches.
antonio-de-oliveira-salazar: Salazar was born on 28 April 1889 in Vimieiro, near Santa Comba Dão, to a family of modest income. His father, a small landowner, had begun as an agricultural labourer and become manager for the Perestrelos, a wealthy landowning family. At eleven Salazar won a free place at the seminary in Viseu, where he studied from 1900 to 1908; he considered the priesthood but decided against it after receiving holy orders.

He studied law at the University of Coimbra from 1910, graduated in 1914 with 19 points out of 20, and specialised in finance. He took the chairs of economic policy and finance in 1917 and received his doctorate the next year. His politics grew from Catholic views aroused by the First Republic's anti-clerical stance.

After the coup of 28 May 1926 Salazar entered government as finance minister with the support of President Óscar Carmona and balanced the budget within a year. He became Prime Minister in 1932 and recast the Ditadura Nacional as the corporatist Estado Novo, whose constitution of 1933 was co-written by Marcelo Caetano. Its stated basis was Catholic social doctrine, but in practice its stability rested on suppressing dissent.

A secret police, founded in 1933 and reorganised in 1945 as the PIDE, monitored the population, applied censorship and suppressed opponents. Humberto Delgado, who challenged the regime in the 1958 presidential election, was assassinated by the PIDE in 1965. Salazar supported Francisco Franco in the Spanish Civil War and kept Portugal neutral in the Second World War. Portugal was a founding member of NATO in 1949 and joined the United Nations in 1955. Colonial war broke out in 1961, the year India annexed Goa.

In August 1968 Salazar suffered a cerebral haemorrhage, which most sources attribute to a fall from a chair. On 25 September President Américo Tomás dismissed him and appointed Marcelo Caetano. Those around him did not tell him he had been removed, and he died on 27 July 1970. He never married and had no known descendants.

The Estado Novo outlived him by four years and fell to a military coup in 1974, leading to a liberal-democratic constitution in 1976. Historians find a detached judgement difficult: his rule brought more stability and prosperity than most Portuguese then living had known, but at the expense of democracy and civil liberties.
antonio-gramsci: Gramsci was born in Ales, in the province of Oristano, the fourth of seven sons of Francesco Gramsci and Giuseppina Marcias. His father was a low-level official of Arbëreshë (Italo-Albanian) descent, and the family moved through several Sardinian villages before settling in Ghilarza. In 1898 Francesco was convicted of embezzlement and imprisoned, which left the family destitute. The young Gramsci had to leave school and take casual jobs until his father's release in 1904.

In 1911 he won a scholarship to the University of Turin, sitting the examination at the same time as Palmiro Togliatti. He studied literature and linguistics under Matteo Bartoli and joined the Italian Socialist Party in late 1913. Poor health, money problems and political commitment led him to give up his studies in early 1915.

The failure of the workers' councils to grow into a national movement convinced Gramsci that a Communist party in the Leninist sense was needed. The group around L'Ordine Nuovo allied with Bordiga's far larger abstentionist faction, and on 21 January 1921 the Communist Party of Italy was founded at Livorno. Gramsci was a leader from the start but subordinate to Bordiga until 1924. In 1922 he went to Russia as the party's representative, where he met the violinist Julia Schucht; they married in 1923.

On 9 November 1926 the Fascist government passed emergency laws after an alleged attempt on Mussolini's life, and police arrested Gramsci despite his parliamentary immunity. His prosecutor said: "For twenty years we must stop this brain from functioning." He was sentenced to five years on the island of Ustica and then, the following year, to twenty years in Turi. His health failed in prison, and a campaign organised by Piero Sraffa at Cambridge demanded his release. He was moved to a clinic at Formia in 1933 and to one in Rome two years later, and was too ill to travel when his sentence ended in April 1937.

Gramsci filled more than 30 notebooks in prison, covering Italian history, fascism, Taylorism and Fordism, the state, religion and popular culture. His best-known concept, cultural hegemony, holds that the capitalist class maintains power not only by force but by spreading its own values until they pass for common sense. He divided the state into political society, which rules by force, and civil society, where leadership rests on consent. He also rejected economic determinism and the idea that revolution follows automatically from historical laws, and argued that each class produces its own organic intellectuals. Critics charge that his approach treats ideas as a struggle for power.
antonio-jose-de-sucre: Antonio José de Sucre y Alcalá was born on 3 February 1795 in Cumaná into an aristocratic family that traced its roots to Flanders. In 1814 he joined the struggle for South American independence from Spain and quickly became a capable military leader. He became known as the Gran Mariscal de Ayacucho, the Grand Marshal of Ayacucho.

On 24 May 1822 Sucre led a Patriot army against a Royalist army under Field Marshal Melchor Aymerich on the slopes of the Pichincha volcano near Quito. The Royalist defeat brought the liberation of Quito and secured the independence of the provinces of the Real Audiencia de Quito, from which Ecuador would emerge. On 9 December 1824, as Simón Bolívar's lieutenant, he led the Patriot forces to victory over Viceroy José de la Serna at Ayacucho, at Pampa de La Quinua. Afterwards José de Canterac signed the capitulation of the Royalist army. The Peruvian Congress promoted Sucre to Marshal and the Colombian legislature to General in Chief.

On Bolívar's orders Sucre entered Upper Peru on 25 February 1825. Most Royalist troops there refused to fight on, and Pedro Antonio Olañeta died at the Battle of Tumusla on 2 April. Sucre reconvened the Constituent Assembly in Chuquisaca, which declared independence on 6 August 1825 and named the new state after Bolívar. Bolívar declined the presidency and passed it to Sucre, who became the first president of Bolivia and gave it its first Constitution in 1828.

A strong movement arose against Bolívar, his followers and the Bolivian constitution, and Sucre resigned in 1828. On 27 February 1829, heavily outnumbered, he defeated a Peruvian invasion force led by José de La Mar at the Battle of Tarqui.

Sucre was killed on 4 June 1830 in an ambush at Berruecos while travelling to Quito. The plot is attributed to José María Obando and carried out by men who later confessed, among them Apolinar Morillo and Juan Gregorio Sarria, and the identity of the conspirators remains a subject of historical speculation. Some have argued that his death left Bolívar with no clear successor. Sucre is buried in the Cathedral of Quito, as he had wished, where his wife Mariana Carcelén came from. Sucre, the capital of Bolivia, and Sucre State in Venezuela are named after him.
antonio-lopez-de-santa-anna: Santa Anna was born in Xalapa, Veracruz, on 21 February 1794 into a respected criollo family. His father was a lawyer, and his mother supported his wish for a military career against his father's wish that he be a shopkeeper. Through her friendship with the intendant of Veracruz he received a military appointment on 6 July 1810, though under age. He fought for the Spanish crown against the insurgency for over a decade, switching to the insurgents in 1821. His origins on the coast gave him immunity to yellow fever, an advantage over officers from elsewhere.

Agustín de Iturbide, ruler of the new Mexican Empire, gave him command of Veracruz and then removed him; in December 1822 Santa Anna rebelled with Guadalupe Victoria and Guerrero, and the Plan of Casa Mata of 1 February 1823 called for a republic. At Tampico he forced the Spanish general Isidro Barradas to surrender on 11 September 1829, ending Spain's last attempt to retake Mexico, and styled himself the Victor of Tampico.

He was elected president on 1 April 1833 but left government to Vice President Valentín Gómez Farías, whose anticlerical reforms he ended by dissolving Congress on 12 June 1834. In 1835 he repealed the liberal Constitution of 1824; Texas declared independence on 2 March 1836, and his expedition to recover it ended in disaster.

He lost part of a leg in the Pastry War of 1838 and used this to re-enter politics. In the Mexican–American War he took the presidency in 1846 and fought on to the end; one historian says that more than any other single person it was Santa Anna who denied Polk's dream of a short war. Invited back by conservatives, he was elected president on 17 March 1853 and declared himself dictator for life as His Most Serene Highness. He ceded territory to the United States in the Gadsden Purchase in 1854, and the Plan of Ayutla removed him in 1855.

From 1855 to 1874 Santa Anna lived in exile in Cuba, the United States, Colombia and Saint Thomas. In New York he tried unsuccessfully to sell chicle for carriage wheels, though he introduced chewing gum to the United States. President Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada allowed him to return to Mexico in 1874, and he died in Mexico City on 21 June 1876. Historians call the thirty years after independence the Age of Santa Anna and have called him an uncrowned monarch. He is often remembered in Mexico as a vendepatria, a traitor to the fatherland, because of the territory lost to the United States during his rule.
antonio-pigafetta: Pigafetta was born to a prominent noble family in Vicenza in north-eastern Italy. Archival research indicates that his father was Giovanni Pigafetta and his mother a noblewoman named Lucia, daughter of Marco Muzan. They married in March 1492, so Antonio was born after that date. Details of his education are unknown, though he later boasted of having read many books. A tradition says he sailed the Mediterranean with the Knights of Rhodes as a youth, but there is no record of it. He entered the service of the papal ambassador Francesco Chiericati, also from Vicenza, whom Pope Leo X sent to the Spanish court in 1518, and he travelled with the ambassador's retinue to Zaragoza and Barcelona.

In Spain Pigafetta heard of Ferdinand Magellan's plan to find a western route to the Spice Islands and persuaded Chiericati that taking part would benefit the Vatican. Provided with letters of introduction, he set out for Seville in May 1519. Magellan hired him for 1,000 maravedís a month, enrolled under the name Antonio Lombardo as one of the servants of the captain and supernumeraries.

When the fleet sailed in August 1519 he was assigned to the flagship Trinidad, served Magellan and became his great admirer. He had no set duty except to keep a daily record, which he did diligently, noting geography, climate, natural history and above all the appearance, customs and languages of the peoples met. His own observations were accurate, but he tended to accept the most outrageous tales told to him. He was wounded on Mactan in April 1521, where Magellan was killed, recovered, and was one of the 18 men who returned on the Victoria under Juan Sebastián Elcano, reaching Sanlúcar de Barrameda in September 1522 out of about 240 who set out.

Pigafetta wrote his Relazione del primo viaggio intorno al mondo in Vicenza between late 1523 and January 1524. It is a collection of descriptions, events, translations, thoughts and illustrations, and it includes the first known use of the name Pacific Ocean on a map. His record of Cebuano is the first recorded document concerning that language. He presented lavish manuscripts to Charles V, John III of Portugal, Francis I of France and the Grand Master of the Knights Hospitaller, but all those copies are lost. Having returned with little wealth, he could not pay his share of the printing costs, and the work was not printed in his lifetime; Giovanni Battista Ramusio first published it in 1550.

Only four manuscripts survive, three in French and one in Italian, the last in the Biblioteca Ambrosiana in Milan. Carlo Amoretti published it there in 1800, though he altered many words. After the voyage Pigafetta also gained membership of the Knights of Rhodes.
antonio-vivaldi: Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was born on 4 March 1678 in Venice, the son of Giovanni Battista Vivaldi and Camilla Calicchio. He suffered from tightness of the chest, interpreted as a form of asthma, which kept him from playing wind instruments. His father, a barber before he became a professional violinist, taught him the violin. In 1693 he began studying for the priesthood and was ordained in 1703, and he was soon nicknamed il Prete Rosso, the Red Priest, after the colour of his hair.

In September 1703 Vivaldi became maestro di violino at the Ospedale della Pietà, an orphanage in Venice that gave the most talented girls a musical education and a place in its orchestra and choir. He composed most of his major works there over the next thirty years, including concertos, cantatas and more than sixty sacred works. His first opera, Ottone in villa, was performed in Vicenza in 1713, and he then became impresario of the Teatro San Angelo in Venice. His oratorio Juditha triumphans, composed in 1716 to celebrate the Republic of Venice's victory over the Turks, was sung entirely by the girls of the Pietà.

In 1717 or 1718 he was offered the post of Maestro di Cappella at the court of Prince Philip of Hesse-Darmstadt in Mantua, and he spent three years there. The Four Seasons, four violin concertos giving musical expression to the seasons, was published in Amsterdam in 1725 as the first four of the twelve concertos of Il cimento dell'armonia e dell'inventione. In 1728 he met the Emperor Charles VI at Trieste, who gave him the title of knight, a gold medal and an invitation to Vienna.
