Vivaldi composed more than 500 concertos, over 50 operas and a large body of sacred choral music.

Vivaldi went to Vienna, probably to stage operas, but Charles VI died soon after his arrival and left him without patronage or steady income. He became impoverished and died during the night of 27 to 28 July 1741, aged 63, of an internal infection. He was buried in a simple grave in the Bürgerspital-Gottesacker cemetery.

After almost two centuries of decline, his reputation revived in the early 20th century. In 1926 researchers found fifteen bound volumes of his music in a monastery in Piedmont, containing 300 concertos, 19 operas and over 100 vocal-instrumental works. Johann Sebastian Bach was deeply influenced by his concertos and arias, and transcribed six of them for solo keyboard and three for organ.
antsiranana: Antsiranana, named Diego-Suarez before 1975, is a city in the far north of Madagascar and the capital of Diana Region. It stands on Antsiranana Bay, one of the largest deep-water harbours in the Indian Ocean, though its remote location long made it unimportant for freight traffic. The first European to sight the island, the Portuguese captain Diogo Dias, did so on 10 August 1500 and named it the Isle of Saint Lawrence. The place took its name Diego Suarez from the first name of Dias, in Portuguese Diogo, and the surname of Admiral Fernão Soares, who recognised it in February 1506.

In the 1880s France coveted the bay as a coaling station for steamships. After the first Franco-Hova War, Queen Ranavalona III signed a treaty on 17 December 1885 granting France a protectorate over the bay and its surroundings. The French set up the French Establishment of Diego-Suarez under Frigate Captain Caillet, regarded as the founder of the city. The first inhabitants were Creoles from Réunion and Mauritius and from other French possessions, with runaway slaves, Antankarana and Sakalava making up much of the rest. The colony had 2,500 people in 1886, a civil governor from 1887 and a Decauville railway from 1900. In 1905 the Second Pacific Squadron of Imperial Russia anchored there and was resupplied on its way to the Battle of Tsushima.

In 1942 Diego-Suarez was the primary objective of Operation Ironclad, the start of the Allied invasion of Madagascar. The Allies feared that Japan would pressure Vichy France into granting use of the island, as it had with French Indo-China the year before. Japanese midget submarines attacked the British ships in the harbour, damaging the battleship HMS Ramillies and sinking the tanker British Loyalty. France kept a military base in the city after Malagasy independence in 1960 and withdrew its forces between 1973 and 1975.

The city had an estimated population of 115,015 in 2013. It has a cruise port that receives periodic visits, and Arrachart Airport links it mainly with other parts of Madagascar. The University of Antsiranana was founded in 1976. Its churches include the Roman Catholic Cathedral of St. Matthew, and there are also mosques.
antwerp: Antwerp lies on the river Scheldt, which links it to the North Sea through the Westerschelde estuary, about 40 kilometres north of Brussels and 15 kilometres south of the Dutch border. The city allegedly began as a Gallo-Roman vicus, and excavations near the Scheldt in 1952 to 1961 found pottery and glass from the mid-2nd to the end of the 3rd century. It was first named in the 4th century, when it was settled by the Germanic Franks.

After the silting-up of the Zwin and the decline of Bruges, Antwerp, then part of the Duchy of Brabant, grew in importance, and its population doubled between 1500 and 1569. At the end of the 15th century the foreign trading houses were moved from Bruges to Antwerp. The old Mediterranean trade routes were losing importance, and the new sea routes round Africa to Asia and across the Atlantic to America helped to push the city into prominence. Its stock exchange, first built in 1531, was the first purpose-built commodity exchange in the world.

The Treaty of Münster of 1648, which recognised the independence of the United Provinces, stipulated that the Scheldt be closed to navigation, which destroyed Antwerp's trade. The closure lasted until 1863, though it was relaxed under French rule from 1795 to 1814. By 1800 the population had fallen below 40,000. Napoleon funded a new dock, still named the Bonaparte Dock, and the deepening of the Scheldt, hoping to counter the Port of London, but he was defeated at Waterloo before the plan was complete. Belgian insurgents captured the city in 1830, while a Dutch garrison under General David Hendrik Chassé held the citadel, until he surrendered to a French army in December 1832.

Antwerp is the capital of Antwerp Province and the most populous municipality in Belgium, with 565,039 inhabitants. Its port is one of the largest in Europe, and the city is a centre of the diamond trade. It hosted the Summer Olympics in 1920. In the 17th century it had a school of painting that included Rubens, Van Dyck and Jordaens, and Rubens's former home and studio is now a museum.
anuradhapura: Anuradhapura lies in the north central plain of Sri Lanka, on the banks of the Malwathu Oya, 205 kilometres north of Colombo. According to the Mahāvaṃsa, a minister of Prince Vijaya named Anuradha founded a village, Anuradhagama, near the river, then called the Kadamba. In 377 BCE, in the reign of King Pandukabhaya, the village was formally established as the capital of the Sinhalese kingdom.

The Mahāvaṃsa places the city's founding in 437 BCE, but excavation of the citadel area puts human settlement as far back as the 10th century BCE. The protohistoric Iron Age there, from 900 to 600 BCE, shows iron technology, pottery, the horse, domestic cattle and paddy cultivation, and by 700 to 600 BCE the settlement covered at least 50 hectares. In the 2nd century CE Ptolemy named a place, Anourogrammoi, that scholars read as Anuradhapura.

The chronicles say King Pandukabhaya planned the city with gates and quarters for traders, and that it covered a square kilometre, one of the largest cities in Asia. It was the first capital of the Sinhala kingdom of Rajarata and the longest-serving ancient capital of Sri Lanka. It was a centre of Theravada Buddhism and a pilgrimage site, with temples and monasteries that cover over 100 square kilometres. Under King Dhatusena (455 to 473) the Theravada canon was redacted and 18 new viharas were built. The Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi is regarded as the oldest documented planted tree in the world, believed to descend from the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya.

The city was largely deserted after invasions by the Chola king Rajaraja I in 993 and by his son Rajendra I in 1014. The Culavamsa says the Chola army destroyed it utterly. Several later Sinhalese kings tried to return the capital to Anuradhapura, but the political centre had shifted to Polonnaruwa. Anuradhapura remained a pilgrimage site. In 1821 John Davy described it as a small mean village in the midst of a desert, with a large tank, stone pillars and mounds as its remains. British colonial authorities began surveys and restoration in the late 19th century.

Much of the modern city was moved in the mid-20th century, under the Anuradhapura Preservation Plan of 1949, to a planned New Town to the east so as to preserve the ancient capital. The ancient city was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982. Among its monuments are the Ruwanwelisaya, Thuparamaya, Abhayagiri Dagaba and Jetavanarama.
anwar-sadat: Sadat was born on 25 December 1918 in Mit Abu El Kom, in Monufia Governorate, to a poor family with 14 children. His Upper Egyptian father was a medical officer who had met his mother while posted in Sudan. He graduated from the Royal Military Academy in Cairo in 1938, joined the Signal Corps and was posted to Sudan, where he met Gamal Abdel Nasser. Together with other junior officers they formed the Free Officers, a group committed to ending British rule and state corruption.

During the Second World War Sadat belonged to the Young Egypt Party and collaborated with Nazi Germany in Egypt. He was arrested and imprisoned for much of the war, and was jailed again after the assassination of the finance minister Amin Osman in January 1946. He took part in the coup of 23 July 1952 that overthrew King Farouk I and read the revolution's first statement over the radio.

Under Nasser, Sadat was minister of State from 1954, edited the daily Al Gomhuria, presided over the National Assembly from 1960 to 1968 and was vice president from 1964. Nasser's supporters expected his successor to be short-lived and easy to manipulate. On 15 May 1971 Sadat announced a Corrective Revolution, dismissing and imprisoning Vice President Ali Sabri and Interior Minister Sharawi Gomaa and purging committed Nasserists.

After the October War, which began on 6 October 1973 with a crossing of the Suez Canal, a ceasefire followed under United Nations Security Council Resolution 338. Disengagement agreements with Israel were signed on 18 January 1974 and 4 September 1975. In 1977 Sadat visited Jerusalem and spoke before the Knesset. The peace treaty with Menachem Begin was signed in Washington on 26 March 1979 after the Camp David talks mediated by Jimmy Carter. It provided for mutual recognition and Israeli withdrawal from Sinai. Most Arab states rejected it, and the Arab League suspended Egypt from 1979 to 1989.

In September 1981 Sadat ordered the arrest of more than 1,500 people, among them Islamist militants, Coptic clergy and intellectuals. On 6 October 1981, at the annual parade in Cairo, Lieutenant Khalid Al-Islambuli and others fired on the grandstand. Sadat and eleven others died. Vice President Hosni Mubarak succeeded him. Five men, including Al-Islambuli, were executed on 15 April 1982, and Israel completed its withdrawal from Sinai, except Taba, by 25 April 1982.
anyang: Settlement near Anyang is very old. At Xiaonanhai, on the western edge of the present city, more than 7,000 artefacts, including stone tools and fossil animal bones, have been unearthed from the Stone Age occupation, which has been called the Xiaonanhai culture. Later tradition places the capitals of the sage-kings Zhuanxu and Emperor Ku in the area around 2000 BCE, and their mausoleums are shown today in Sanyang village, south of Neihuang County.

At the beginning of the 14th century BCE King Pangeng of the Shang dynasty established his capital about 2 kilometres north of the modern city, on the banks of the Huan River. This city, Yin, was the first stable capital in Chinese history, and the dynasty founded there also came to be called the Yin dynasty. The capital served 12 kings in 8 generations, among them Wu Ding, under whom the dynasty reached the height of its power. It ended when King Wu of the Zhou destroyed the dynasty in 1046 BCE.

Anyang itself became the seat of Anyang County around 607 CE and has remained so since. Its Tangyin County contains Yue Village, the birthplace of the Song dynasty general Yue Fei. Until 1912 the town was called Zhangde; it received its present name after the founding of the Republic of China. In 1949 the prefecture was briefly detached from Henan and placed in the experimental province of Pingyuan, and it returned to Henan in November 1953.

Anyang is a prefecture-level city and the northernmost city of Henan, bordering Hebei and Shanxi. Its population was 5,477,614 at the 2020 census, and the great majority are Han Chinese. The ground rises in the west into the foothills of the Taihang Mountains and falls in the east to the North China Plain. Industry, notably iron and steel and coal coking, is its main economic base.

Among its monuments are the Wenfeng Pagoda, believed to have been built in 925 and rebuilt under the Ming, which is the symbol of the city, and the Tianning Temple, founded under the Tang dynasty. The Yin ruins, with the tomb of Fu Hao, lie about 2 kilometres north-west of the city; the Yinxu museum opened there in 2005, and UNESCO named the site a World Heritage Site in 2006.
anzus: After the fall of Singapore and the decline of British power in Asia, Australia sought other partners for its security. Australia and New Zealand also feared a resurgent Japan and the spread of communism to their north. In 1950 Percy Spender, Australia's minister for external affairs, sought a broad Pacific security agreement and said it would be meaningless without the United States. The outbreak of the Korean War in mid-1950 changed American views. The treaty eased antipodean fears that Japan might again become a threat, though the United States was at first reluctant and the president offered an informal guarantee instead.

The treaty was concluded at San Francisco on 1 September 1951 and entered into force on 29 April 1952. It recommits the parties to the purposes of the United Nations, and each declares that an armed attack on any of them would be dangerous to its own peace and safety and that it would act to meet the common danger in accordance with its constitutional processes. Unlike NATO, it has no automatic commitment to armed assistance, since Spender expected the United States Senate to wish to keep the power to declare war. It also has no integrated defence structure or dedicated forces.

New Zealand took part in the Vietnam War directly as an ANZUS member. After the Labour Party won the New Zealand election in 1984, Prime Minister David Lange barred nuclear-powered and nuclear-armed ships from New Zealand ports. In February 1985 New Zealand refused a visit by the destroyer USS Buchanan, because the United States would neither confirm nor deny whether its ships carried nuclear weapons.

After talks broke down, the United States announced in 1986 that it was suspending its obligations to New Zealand, calling it a friend but not an ally. Lange did not withdraw from the treaty, and New Zealand's policy became law in 1987. Australia did not support the ban and continued to allow American ship visits. The treaty remains in force between Australia and the United States, whose officials meet annually in the AUSMIN talks.
aomori-prefecture: Aomori is the northernmost prefecture of the Tōhoku region, on the northern end of Honshu. The Pacific Ocean flanks it to the east and the Sea of Japan to the west, with the Tsugaru Strait linking the two to the north, across which lies Hokkaido. The Shimokita and Tsugaru Peninsulas enclose Mutsu Bay, and between them lies the smaller Natsudomari Peninsula. The highest point is Mount Iwaki, an active stratovolcano of almost 1,625 m.

The name Aomori means green forest. It was first given to a port settlement established by the Hirosaki Domain in 1624, and most likely comes from a small forest on a hill nearby that fishermen used as a landmark.

Humans have lived in the prefecture for at least 15,000 years. The oldest evidence of pottery in Japan was found at the Ōdai Yamamoto I Site, and suggests that the Jōmon period began about 15,000 years ago. By 7,000 BCE fishing cultures had developed along the shores. Settlement at the Sannai-Maruyama Site, in the present-day city of Aomori, began around 3,900 BCE and shows wide interaction with people across Jōmon Japan, including Hokkaido and Kyushu. It ended around 2,300 BCE for unknown reasons, likely because its subsistence economy could not sustain growth during a neoglaciation. At the Kamegaoka site the Jōmon period continued up to 300 BCE, and small statuettes called Shakōkidogū have been found.

After centuries of rule by the Nanbu and Tsugaru clans, the prefecture was formed out of the northern part of Mutsu Province during the Meiji Restoration. Its population grew until the late 20th century, peaked at 1.52 million in 1985 and has declined since.

Aomori's economy is dominated by farming, forestry and fishing, especially apple orchards. Tsugaru-jamisen, a style of music played on the shamisen, was born in the Tsugaru region. The embroidery styles kogin-zashi and Nanbu hishizashi began in the Edo period, when peasant women used them to make linen clothing sturdier and warmer in the winters, since cotton was unavailable to the lower class. The Jōmon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan and Shirakami-Sanchi are World Heritage Sites, and the most noted festival is the Aomori Nebuta Matsuri.
aosta: Aosta is in the Alps, 110 km north-northwest of Turin, at the confluence of the Buthier and the Dora Baltea. It stands at the junction of the Great and Little St Bernard Pass routes, and near the Italian entrance of the Mont Blanc Tunnel and the Great St Bernard Tunnel. This position gave the city considerable military importance in antiquity. Its location in the rain shadow of the Mont Blanc massif leaves it with cool to very cold winters, hot summers and relatively dry conditions throughout the year.

Aosta was settled in proto-historic times and became a centre of the Salassi, many of whom the Romans killed or sold into slavery in 25 BCE. The campaign was led by Terentius Varro, who founded the Roman colony of Augusta Praetoria Salassorum, housing 3,000 retired veterans. After 11 BCE Aosta became the capital of the province of Alpes Graies. Its layout was that of a Roman military camp.

After the fall of the Western Empire the city was conquered in turn by the Burgundians, the Ostrogoths and the Byzantines. The Lombards, who had annexed it to their Italian kingdom, were expelled by the Frankish Empire under Pepin the Short. Under Charlemagne it gained importance as a post on the Via Francigena, which led from Aachen to Italy.

In the 10th century Aosta became part of the Kingdom of Burgundy, and after its fall in 1032 it passed to the lands of Count Humbert I of Savoy. The inhabitants were granted the privilege of holding an assembly of the states-general in 1189, and an executive council was nominated from it in 1536, which lasted until 1802. After the Congress of Vienna restored Savoy rule, the council was reconstituted and recognized by Charles Albert of Sardinia, at the birth of his grandson Prince Amedeo, who was created duke of Aosta.

Aosta is the capital of the bilingual Aosta Valley. The Roman town walls are preserved almost in their entirety, enclosing a rectangle of 724 by 572 metres, with twenty towers in all. The Porta Praetoria, the eastern gate dating to the 1st century, keeps its original form apart from the marble covering. The Roman theatre, built in the late reign of Augustus, held up to 4,000 spectators and its southern façade, 22 metres tall, remains. Outside the walls stands the Arch of Augustus, built to celebrate the victory over the Salassi. Anselm of Aosta, Archbishop of Canterbury from 1093 to 1109, was born in the city.
aosta-valley: The Aosta Valley is an Alpine valley which, with its tributary valleys, includes the Italian slopes of Mont Blanc, Monte Rosa, Gran Paradiso and the Matterhorn. Mont Blanc, at 4,810 m, makes it the highest region of Italy by its highest point. It is bordered by Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes in France, by Valais in Switzerland and by Piedmont. The region covers 3,260.90 km2 and is the smallest, least populous and least densely populated region of Italy.

The early inhabitants were Celts and Ligures. Rome conquered the region from the Salassi around 25 BCE and founded Augusta Prætoria Salassorum, now Aosta, to secure the mountain passes. In 1031–1032 Humbert I of Savoy received the title Count of Aosta from Emperor Conrad II and built a fortification at Bard. Saint Anselm of Canterbury was born in Aosta in 1033 or 1034. In 1191 Thomas I of Savoy granted the communes a charter of liberties, whose rights were defended until 1770. In the mid-13th century Emperor Frederick II made the county a duchy.

The region stayed in Savoy lands apart from French occupations in 1539–1563, 1691 and 1704–1706, and rule by the First French Empire from 1800 to 1814. As part of the Kingdom of Sardinia it joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1861. The Fascist government established a province of Aosta in 1927; it ceased to exist in 1945, and the region gained special autonomous status in 1948.

The Aosta Valley is the Autonomous Region of Aosta Valley, with Aosta as its capital. Italian and French are the official languages, and the Valdôtain dialect of Franco-Provençal is also recognised. It was the first government authority to adopt modern French as its sole official language, in 1536, three years before France itself. Its medieval castles include Fénis, Issogne, Sarre and Bard Fort.
apache: The Apache are several Southern Athabaskan-speaking peoples of the Southwest, the Southern Plains and northern Mexico, linguistically related to the Navajo. The six major groups are the Chiricahua, Jicarilla, Lipan, Mescalero, Plains and Western Apache. Anthropological evidence suggests that the Apache and Navajo lived in the north, where other Athabaskan speakers still live, before migrating to the Southwest sometime between 1200 and 1500 CE. Their homelands, known collectively as Apacheria, include high mountains, canyons, deserts and the southern Great Plains. The word Apache is Spanish; the first known written record is by Juan de Oñate in 1598, and the most widely accepted theory is that it comes from the Zuni word meaning Navajos.

The Apache fought the invading Spanish and Mexican peoples for centuries, though Spanish colonists and Apache bands also traded with each other; a band might be friendly with one village and raid another. The first Apache raids on Sonora seem to date from the late 17th century. As tensions grew, the Mexican government passed laws offering cash rewards for Apache scalps. In the 19th-century American Indian Wars the United States Army found the Apache to be fierce warriors and skilful strategists.

In 1875 the United States military forced the removal of about 1,500 Yavapai and Tonto Apache from the Rio Verde reserve to San Carlos, 180 miles away, on a march through flooded rivers and mountain passes that killed several hundred people. They were interned there for 25 years while settlers took their land. Most United States accounts place the final defeat of an Apache band on 4 September 1886, when 5,000 troops forced Geronimo's group of 30 to 50 men, women and children to surrender at Skeleton Canyon, Arizona. The army sent them and the Chiricahua scouts who had tracked them to confinement in Florida and then Fort Sill, Oklahoma.

Before the reservations Apache lived in extended family units, usually of a couple, their unmarried children, their married daughters and those daughters' husbands and children, living near one another. Housing varied: tipis on the plains, wickiups of wood and brush in the highlands, and earthen hogans in northern Mexico. Food came from hunting, gathering, trade, raiding and, among some groups, cultivation. The Apache distinguished raiding, done by small parties for a specific economic purpose, from war, waged by large parties usually for retribution.

Each Apache tribe is today politically autonomous, with tribes and reservations in Arizona, New Mexico, Texas and Oklahoma, and Apache settled in Sonora, Chihuahua and Coahuila in Mexico. Their languages are endangered, and Lipan is reported extinct.
apartheid: The Afrikaans word apartheid means separateness, and its first recorded use was in 1929. The policy grew out of the racism of colonial factions and out of South Africa's industrialisation, in which segregation was developed to nurture early industry such as mining and cheap labour was taken from groups the state classed as peasants and migrants. By 1948 black political organisations and leaders, among them Alfred Xuma, James Mpanza, the African National Congress and the Council of Non-European Trade Unions, were demanding political rights, land reform and the right to unionise.

Apartheid is commonly divided into petty apartheid, the segregation of public facilities and social life, and grand apartheid, which separated housing and employment by race. The first apartheid law was the Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act of 1949, followed by the Immorality Amendment Act of 1950. The Population Registration Act of 1950 classified all South Africans as Black, White, Coloured or Indian according to appearance, known ancestry, socioeconomic status and cultural lifestyle. The Reservation of Separate Amenities Act of 1953 enforced segregation of public premises and services, and the Bantu Education Act of 1953 created a separate school system designed to prepare black people for lives as a labouring class.

Where people lived followed their classification. Between 1960 and 1983, 3.5 million Black Africans were removed from their homes and forced into segregated areas, most of them to restrict the black population to ten designated homelands, or bantustans. Four of these, Transkei, Bophutatswana, Venda and Ciskei, were declared independent, but they had little economic infrastructure and were in practice controlled by South Africa. In the 1950s about 60,000 people were moved from Johannesburg to the new township of Soweto.

Apartheid met domestic and international opposition. The Sharpeville massacre of 1960 brought more condemnation abroad, and the United Nations and others imposed arms embargoes and economic sanctions. Resistance inside the country grew more militant in the 1970s and 1980s, and from 1985 to 1989 serious political violence centred on the Black townships under states of emergency. Reforms under P. W. Botha, including a tricameral parliament, failed to satisfy most activists.

F. W. de Klerk announced on 2 February 1990 that he would repeal discriminatory laws and lift the 30-year ban on the leading anti-apartheid groups. The apartheid laws were abolished in 1991, and the first election with universal suffrage was held on 27 April 1994, with the African National Congress winning 62.65 per cent of the vote. The legacy of apartheid persists in social and economic inequality, and the 1976 International Convention on the Suppression and Punishment of the Crime of Apartheid and the 2002 Rome Statute made apartheid a crime in international law.
apelles: Much of what is known of Apelles comes from Pliny the Elder, who rated him superior to earlier and later painters and dated him to the 112th Olympiad (332–329 BCE), possibly because he painted a portrait of Alexander the Great. Apelles first studied under Ephorus of Ephesus and, after gaining some celebrity, under Pamphilus at Sicyon, so that he is said to have combined Dorian thoroughness with Ionic grace. He was drawn to the court of Philip II, painted him and the young Alexander, and became the recognised court painter of Macedon. His picture of Alexander holding a thunderbolt was ranked by many beside the sculptor Lysippus's Alexander with the spear. Plutarch, centuries later, found it unconvincing for making Alexander's complexion too dark.

None of his paintings survives. Those recorded include Aphrodite Anadyomene, Aphrodite rising from the sea, for which tradition says Alexander's former mistress Campaspe was the model; a portrait of Antigonus I Monophthalmus on horseback, shown in three-quarter view so as to hide the king's blind eye; and an allegory of Calumny, described by Lucian, in which an innocent youth is falsely accused by Ignorance, Envy, Treachery and Deceit. Pliny says the Calumny arose from a rival's false accusation that Apelles had joined a conspiracy against Ptolemy IV Philopator, which almost cost him his life. Some pictures were taken to Rome and displayed in public; the Emperor Claudius had Alexander's face in two of them replaced with that of Augustus.

Pliny attaches several sayings to him, perhaps from a lost treatise. Among them are his judgement that Protogenes knew when to take his hand from the picture, that a shoemaker should venture no further than the shoe, and Nulla dies sine linea, not a day without a line. Another story tells of a contest of ever finer lines drawn between Apelles and Protogenes on a panel at Rhodes. Pliny also says Apelles had a secret black varnish, which preserved paintings and softened their colour, and which was lost with his death.

Apelles is said to have been at work on an Aphrodite of Kos when he died, and the picture was left unfinished, since no one had the skill to complete it. His fame lasted: Italian Renaissance painters repeated his subjects. Sandro Botticelli based his Calumny of Apelles on Lucian's description and also his Birth of Venus on the painter's works, and Raphael may have portrayed himself as Apelles in The School of Athens. The 15th-century mathematician Luca Pacioli wrote that even Apelles must now give way to Leonardo da Vinci.
apennines: The Apennines are a mountain range made up of parallel smaller chains that extend c. 1,200 km along peninsular Italy. In the northwest they join the Ligurian Alps at Altare, and in the southwest they end at Reggio di Calabria. Since 2000 the Italian Environment Ministry has defined the Apennines System to include the mountains of north Sicily, a total distance of 1,500 km. The range has three sectors, northern, central and southern. The eastern slopes down to the Adriatic Sea are steep, whereas the western slopes form foothills on which most of the towns of peninsular Italy stand. The range has about 21 peaks over 1,900 m, most of them in the central Apennines.

The Apennines rose from the sea beginning in the early Neogene, about 20 million years ago, and the process continues. They are much younger than the Alps, which were millions of years old by then, and do not share their origin. Compression raised a fold and thrust belt on the Adriatic side, while the crust under the Tyrrhenian Sea spread and produced fault-block mountains on the west.

The name is most often derived from the Celtic penn, mountain or summit, which would have been assigned in the 4th century BCE or earlier during the Celtic domination of northern Italy, and it first applied to the north Apennines. Historical linguists have never found a derivation they all agree on, and none is accepted unquestionably.

The Apennine culture, named for the range, is a technology complex of central and southern Italy from the Middle Bronze Age, the 15th and 14th centuries BCE. Its pottery was a burnished ware incised with spirals, meanders and geometrical zones filled with dots or dashes. Its people were cattle herdsmen who grazed their animals on the mountain meadows of central Italy and lived in small hamlets in defensible places. On the move between summer pastures they built temporary camps or lived in caves and rock shelters. Their pottery has been found on the Capitoline Hill in Rome, and on Ischia and Lipari.

In the north, the Bocchetta di Altare, at 436 m, is the border between the Ligurian Alps and the Ligurian Apennines. It is the main and only feasible overland route between the coastal plain of Liguria and the north Italian plain, and defenders of north Italy have had to control it since ancient times, as its fortifications show.

The Apennines preserve some relatively intact ecosystems, among them some of the best-preserved forests and montane grasslands in Europe, now protected by national parks. They are among the few places in Europe where large predators such as the Italian wolf and the Marsican brown bear still exist. The highest peak, Corno Grande, carries the Calderone glacier, the only glacier in the Apennines.
aphra-behn: Little is known of Behn's early life, perhaps partly because she obscured it herself. She was baptised on 14 December 1640. Accounts of her parentage differ. One version says her father was a barber named John Amis, and The Histories and Novels of the Late Ingenious Mrs. Behn of 1696 names Bartholomew Johnson, a barber, and Elizabeth Denham, a wet-nurse. Colonel Thomas Colepeper, the only person who claimed to have known her as a child, wrote that she was born at Sturry or Canterbury. Shortly after a supposed return to England from Surinam in 1664, she may have married Johan Behn, a merchant of possibly German or Dutch origin. He died or the couple separated soon after, and she kept the name Mrs Behn professionally.

Behn came to the notice of Charles II, who employed her as a spy in Antwerp. After her return to London and a probable brief stay in debtors' prison, she began writing for the stage. She belonged to a circle of poets and libertines that included John Wilmot, Lord Rochester, and wrote under the pastoral pseudonym Astrea. Her plays include The Rover of 1677 and The Emperor of the Moon of 1687, one of her longest-running. She was a monarchist and a Tory supporter. During the Exclusion Crisis an epilogue and a prologue she wrote brought her legal trouble, and she afterwards devoted most of her writing to prose and translations.
She published five prose works under her own name, among them Oroonoko in 1688, the story of the enslaved Oroonoko and his love Imoinda, possibly based on her travel to Surinam twenty years earlier.

Behn declined an invitation from Bishop Burnet to write a welcoming poem to King William III, and she died shortly after, on 16 April 1689. She is buried in the East Cloister of Westminster Abbey, not in Poets' Corner. Later women dramatists, among them Delarivier Manley, Mary Pix, Susanna Centlivre and Catherine Trotter, acknowledged her as their most vital predecessor. Until the mid-20th century she was repeatedly dismissed as a morally depraved minor writer. Oroonoko is regarded as one of the first abolitionist and humanitarian novels in English. Virginia Woolf wrote that all women together ought to let flowers fall upon her tomb, for it was she who earned them the right to speak their minds.
apia: Apia stands on a natural harbour at the mouth of the Vaisigano River, on the central north coast of Upolu, the second-largest island of Samoa. It lies on a narrow coastal plain, with Mount Vaea, 472 metres high and the burial place of the writer Robert Louis Stevenson, directly to the south. The climate is tropical rainforest, with an average temperature of 26 °C and roughly 3,000 millimetres of rain a year, the wettest months being December to March.

Apia was originally a small village, with a population of 304 in 1800, from which the later capital took its name. The village still exists inside the modern urban area, with its own matai (leaders) and fa'alupega (genealogy and customary greetings). The modern city was founded in the 1850s, and the high chief Seumanutafa Pogai held his title there until his death in 1898.

On 15 March 1889 seven warships from Germany, the United States and Britain refused to leave the harbour as a typhoon approached, each unwilling to be the first to move. All were sunk or damaged beyond repair except the British cruiser Calliope, which steamed out at about a mile an hour and rode out the storm. Nearly 200 American and German sailors died.

Germany ruled the western islands as German Samoa from 1900 to 1914, with Apia as capital. New Zealand occupied them in August 1914 and governed them from 1920 until independence in 1962, first under a League of Nations mandate and then, after 1945, as a United Nations trust territory. The Mau movement organised non-violent protests in Apia's streets; on 28 December 1929, called Black Saturday, the New Zealand constabulary killed the paramount chief Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III during a peaceful Mau gathering. From 1941 to 1944 the United States Navy ran Naval Base Upolu.

Apia is the capital and largest city of Samoa and has been its official capital since 1959. The urban area had 35,974 people at the 2021 census and consists of about 45 traditional and freehold villages, with no single city administration. Mulinuʻu, the old ceremonial capital at its western end, holds the Parliament House. Stevenson's home at Vailima is now a museum. The Bahá’í House of Worship for the Pacific, opened in 1984, stands in the city, and Apia Harbour is the country's busiest port.
apollo: Apollo was regarded by the Greeks as among the most characteristically Greek of the gods. His name is generally not found in the Linear B tablets, with only a doubtful possible attestation. Scholars have traced elements of his cult to several sources. The Homeric Hymn to Apollo depicts him as an intruder from the north, and the Doric form of his name, Apellon, is linked to the festival apellai of the Dorians. Some connect him with the Minoan deity Paiawon, and Apollo Delphinios was a sea god worshipped especially in Crete and the islands. His mother Leto was associated with earlier deities of Asia Minor.

In myth Apollo was the son of Zeus and Leto and the twin brother of Artemis. Hera pursued Leto, who found refuge on Delos, where the twins were born. Apollo was the god of healing, prophecy, music, poetry and archery, and was represented as the ideal of the kouros, a beardless athletic youth. He could deliver people from epidemics and bring plague with his arrows, and was called Alexikakos, the averter of evil. As god of music he led the Muses, and the lyre was his common attribute. His chief epithet was Phoebus, meaning bright.

He also encouraged the founding of towns and the establishment of civil constitutions, and his oracles were often consulted before laws were set in a city. In the 5th century BCE his worship was imported to Rome, and he was often identified with Helios, the Sun. In Celtic lands he was seen as a healing and sun god, as Apollo Belenus in parts of Gaul, northern Italy and Noricum.

Apollo had two widely influential cult sites, Delos and Delphi, and Delian and Pythian Apollo were so distinct that both might have shrines in one place. His cult was fully established when written sources began about 650 BCE. In the archaic period he became extremely important as an oracular god, and names such as Apollodorus and cities called Apollonia testify to his popularity. His oracle at Abae in Phocis was consulted by Croesus, and other notable oracles stood at Claros and Didyma. The oldest temple probably to Apollo Ismenius at Thebes was built in the 9th century BCE.
apollonius-of-perga: Very little biographical information survives. The 6th-century commentator Eutocius of Ascalon says that Apollonius came from Perga in Pamphylia in the times of Ptolemy III Euergetes, who reigned from 246 to 222 or 221 BCE, so he was probably born after 246 BCE. Specific birth and death years given by modern scholars are only speculative. The remaining autobiographical material suggests that he lived, studied and wrote in Alexandria. The prefaces to the books of the Conics are letters to friends, the first two to Eudemus of Pergamon, and they say that a geometer named Naucrates, a house guest at Alexandria, first requested the work.

Apollonius wrote many geometrical works, but only the Conics survives in quantity. Its first four books are preserved in the original Greek, and books five to seven only in an Arabic translation by Thabit ibn Qurra, commissioned by the Banu Musa. Book eight is lost, and Edmond Halley's Latin reconstruction of it cannot be tested against the original. Books one to seven present 387 propositions, and book one gives the basic definitions of cones and conic sections. His definitions of ellipse, parabola and hyperbola are the ones in use today.

Other works are known only from commentators, chiefly Pappus of Alexandria, who describes Cutting off an Area, Determinate Section, Tangencies, Neusis and Plane Loci. Apollonius's explanation of planetary motion by eccentric orbits, commonly believed until the Middle Ages, is credited to him. Eutocius wrote a commentary on books one to four in the 6th century, and these books were first printed in Latin in 1566. Thomas Heath's English translation appeared in 1896.
apollonius-of-tyana: Apollonius came from Tyana in Cappadocia and was born into a respected and wealthy Greek household. The dates of his life are uncertain, because his main biographer, Philostratus the Elder, and the historian Cassius Dio give accounts that cannot be reconciled, and modern scholars therefore differ on when he was born. Apart from the Adana Inscription of the 3rd or 4th century, little about him can be learned from sources other than Philostratus. As a Pythagorean he opposed animal sacrifice and lived on a frugal vegetarian diet, in keeping with that tradition.

According to James Francis, the most that can be said is that Apollonius appears to have been a wandering ascetic, philosopher and wonderworker of a type common in the eastern part of the early empire. A minimalist view holds that he spent his life in the cities of Asia Minor and northern Syria, including Tyana, Ephesus, Aegae and Antioch, though his letters suggest wider travels and he probably visited Rome. Philostratus gives two and a half of the eight books of his Life to a journey to India, on which Apollonius met Damis at Hierapolis Bambyce in Syria, who became his lifelong companion. Many modern scholars dismiss the journey as fanciful, though not all rule it out.

He was tried for allegedly using magic to conspire against the emperor and was sentenced to death, and his followers believed he ascended to heaven. Philostratus and Cassius Dio both report that he saw the murder of Domitian at Ephesus at midday on the day it happened in Rome, in the year 96. Most modern scholars agree that he existed.

Several writings and many letters are ascribed to him, but some are lost and others survive in fragments of disputed authenticity. Of a treatise On sacrifices only a short, probably authentic fragment survives, and a biography of Pythagoras that Porphyry and Iamblichus mention is lost. Some of the letters may be forgeries or literary exercises. Lucian of Samosata attacked his school as fraud, and Philostratus wrote to answer him, stressing that Apollonius was a serious philosopher and not a magician.

According to the Historia Augusta, Emperor Aurelian spared Tyana in 272 after a vision of Apollonius. Talismans attributed to him stood in several cities of the Eastern Roman Empire, and some Byzantine writers condemned them as sorcery. In the Middle Ages works of magic and alchemy were falsely attributed to him, and the Arabic tradition knew him as Balinus, master of talismans. Pagan writers such as Hierocles and Porphyry set his miracles against those of Jesus, a comparison that later deists and others took up, and until the Enlightenment he was usually treated in Europe as a magician who served the devil.
apostolic-palace: In the 5th century Pope Symmachus built a papal palace close to Old St. Peter's Basilica, which served as an alternative residence to the Lateran Palace. A second, fortified palace was sponsored by Pope Eugene III and extensively modified under Pope Innocent III in the twelfth century. The Lateran Palace suffered destructive fires in 1307 and 1361, and the Vatican Palace fell into disrepair during the Avignon Papacy. In 1447 Pope Nicholas V razed Eugene III's fortified palace to build a new building, the present Apostolic Palace.

Construction took place mainly between 1471 and 1605. The present form of the palace is largely the work of Pope Sixtus V, in whose honour the Vatican calls it the Palace of Sixtus V. Work on the current version began on 30 April 1589, and later popes, among them Urban VII, Clement VIII and Innocent XI, completed its parts. In the 20th century Pope Pius XI added an art gallery and museum entrance.

The palace covers 162,000 square metres and is more accurately a series of self-contained buildings arranged around the Courtyard of Sixtus V, northeast of St Peter's Basilica. It holds the papal apartments, offices of the Catholic Church and the Holy See, chapels, the Vatican Museums and the Vatican Library.

The Sistine Chapel, named for Sixtus IV, was frescoed by Renaissance artists including Michelangelo, Sandro Botticelli, Pietro Perugino, Pinturicchio and Domenico Ghirlandaio. The Raphael Rooms were commissioned by Pope Julius II in 1508 or 1509 from the young Raphael, and after Raphael's death in 1520 his assistants finished the frescoes in the Sala di Costantino. The Borgia Apartments were decorated for Pope Alexander VI by Pinturicchio between 1492 and 1494. The loggias, designed by Donato Bramante, were decorated by Raphael with frescoes of 52 biblical events.

The Sistine Chapel is the venue where the College of Cardinals elects each new pope in a conclave, held behind closed doors. Since the 17th century the papal apartments on the top floor have been the official residence of the pope. In the 15th century the palace was placed under the authority of a prefect, a post that lasted until the 1800s, and in 1884 Pope Leo XIII created a committee to administer the palace.
appalachian-mountains: The Appalachians extend from central Alabama to Newfoundland along a southwest-northeast axis. The highest peak is Mount Mitchell, 2,037 metres, in the Black Mountains of North Carolina, part of the Blue Ridge Mountains. Saint Pierre and Miquelon, an overseas collectivity of France, is part of the range, so it technically spans three countries. The range is geologically related to the Scottish Highlands, the Atlas Mountains, the Scandinavian Mountains and the Ouachitas, which all once belonged to the Central Pangean Mountains.

Their formation began about 1.1 billion years ago with the creation of the supercontinent Rodinia, when the Grenville orogeny built mountains whose rocks remain in the Blue Ridge and the Adirondacks. Rodinia later broke up and the Iapetus Ocean formed, precursor of the Atlantic, where the rocks of the Valley and Ridge province were laid down. The modern Appalachians arose from three orogenies beginning about 480 million years ago, making them one of the oldest surviving mountain ranges. They once reached elevations similar to the Alps and Rockies before 240 million years of erosion wore them down to the lower, rugged peaks of today.

The name comes from the village the Narváez expedition, including Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, found near present-day Tallahassee in 1528 and transcribed as Apalchen. The Spanish altered it to Apalachee and used it for the tribe and the region spreading inland to the north; it is the fourth-oldest surviving European place-name in the United States. After Hernando de Soto's expedition of 1540 Spanish cartographers began to apply the name to the mountains; the first use for the range is on Jacques le Moyne de Morgues's map of 1565. The name was not commonly used for the whole range until the late 19th century, and Allegheny Mountains was often more popular.

The ridges and valleys run against most east-west highways and railroads, so the range was a barrier to east-west travel that was extremely important in shaping the expansion of the United States in the colonial era. Much of its economy was historically based on logging and coal mining, which attracted many migrants who contributed to a new cultural region. Many communities have since moved into manufacturing and services.

The range holds a wide variety of biomes, from temperate broadleaf and mixed forest in the south to boreal forest in the north. Red spruce and balsam fir dominate the north and high elevations, and sugar maple and beech are more common further south. The Appalachians, particularly the central and southern parts, are among the most biodiverse places in North America. Tourism is prominent, above all the Appalachian Trail, a hiking trail of 3,500 km from Mount Katahdin in Maine to Springer Mountain in Georgia.
appian-way: The Appian Way was the first long road built specifically to move troops outside the region of Rome. The Pontine Marshes, a malarial swamp between Rome and Capua, had defeated Roman supply in the First Samnite War of 343 to 341 BCE, and the Second Samnite War broke out in 327 BCE after Rome tried to plant colonies at Cales and Fregellae. In 312 BCE the censor Appius Claudius Caecus began public works without waiting for the Senate, among them the road, which crossed the marshes to the coast north-west of Naples and then turned north to Capua. It is credited with letting Rome concentrate and supply its forces; Etruria came to terms in 311 BCE and Samnium in 304 BCE.

The road began as a levelled dirt path with small stones and mortar, covered with gravel and topped with tightly fitting interlocking stones, cambered for drainage and flanked by ditches. The historian Procopius remarked that the stones seemed to have grown together. It is believed to be the first Roman road to use lime cement. From the Forum Romanum it left through the Porta Capena; across the marsh a stone causeway of about 31 kilometres needed constant repair, and in 162 BCE Marcus Cornelius Cathegus had a canal built beside it, which Romans preferred.

Rome to Capua was 132 Roman miles, and Capua to Brindisi 233 more. After the Battle of Sentinum in 295 BCE the road was extended past Capua to Beneventum, then toward Venusia and Tarentum, and it reached Brundisium in 264 BCE. Appius Claudius died in 273, but no one has displaced his name from it.

Supplied by the road, the Romans crushed King Pyrrhus of Epirus at the Battle of Beneventum in 275 BCE, and Tarentum fell in 272 BCE. In 71 BCE, after the defeat of the slave revolt led by Spartacus, 6,000 slaves were crucified along the 200 kilometres of the road from Rome to Capua. In 1943 the Allies landing at Anzio, meaning to advance along the line of the Via Appia to take Rome, were pinned down for four months and took Rome in May 1944.

The Roman section survives, lined with monuments of all periods, though the cement has eroded from the joints. Statius called it the queen of the long roads, and in July 2024 the Appian Way entered the UNESCO World Heritage List.
apuleius: Apuleius was born in Madauros, a colonia in Numidia on the North African coast bordering Gaetulia, and described himself as half-Numidian half-Gaetulian. Madauros lay well away from the coast of Roman influence, though it contains some pristine Roman ruins, and Augustine of Hippo later received his early education there. No ancient source gives his praenomen; late-medieval manuscripts began the tradition of calling him Lucius after the hero of his novel.

When their father, a municipal magistrate, died, Apuleius and his brother inherited nearly two million sesterces. He studied at Carthage, then Platonist philosophy at Athens, and then Latin rhetoric in Rome, most likely speaking in the law courts for a time. He also travelled in Asia Minor and Egypt, which furthered his knowledge of philosophy and religion but depleted his inheritance. He was an initiate in several Greco-Roman mysteries and a priest of Asclepius.

On a journey to Alexandria he fell ill at Oea, modern Tripoli, and was received into the house of Sicinius Pontianus, whom he had befriended in Athens. Pontianus's mother Pudentilla was a very rich widow, and with her son's consent Apuleius agreed to marry her. Her relatives were angry that her wealth would leave the family and impeached him for gaining her affections by charms and magic spells. The case was heard at Sabratha, about 158, before the proconsul Claudius Maximus. His defence survives as the Apologia. Of his later career little is known, but statues were erected in his honour by the senate of Carthage and by other senates, and he was responsible for gladiatorial shows and wild beast events in the province.

The date, place and circumstances of his death are unknown. There is no record of his activities after 170, which led some to think he died about 171, although other scholars believe he may have been alive in 180 or even 190.

The Metamorphoses, or Golden Ass, is the only Latin novel to survive in full. Its hero Lucius experiments with magic and is turned into an ass, and the frame story holds many digressions, the longest being the tale of Cupid and Psyche, a rare ancient literary fairy tale. It ends with Lucius, human again, initiated into the cult of Isis and then of Osiris.

His other surviving works include the Florida, twenty-three extracts from speeches and lectures; De Platone et dogmate eius, an outline of Plato's physics and ethics; De Deo Socratis, on daemons as intermediaries between gods and humans, which Augustine attacked in The City of God; and a probable Latin translation of De Mundo. De Deo Socratis holds the first recorded occurrence of the proverb that familiarity breeds contempt. Many other works, on subjects from agriculture to music, are lost.
apulia: Apulia, or Puglia, is one of the 20 regions of Italy, in the southern peninsular section of the country, bordering the Adriatic Sea to the east, the Strait of Otranto and Ionian Sea to the southeast and the Gulf of Taranto to the south. Its coastline is longer than that of any other mainland Italian region. In the north the Gargano promontory extends into the Adriatic like a spur, while in the south the Salento peninsula forms the heel of Italy's boot. Most of the region is flat, with only moderate hills.

Human settlement dates back at least 250,000 years, as the fossil remains of Altamura Man show. Around the start of the first millennium BCE the Iapygians settled the area with the tribes of the Daunians, Peucetians and Messapians, and Greek colonies, among them Taras (Taranto), were numerous in the south. Rome found its occupation in the third century BCE difficult because of the resistance of Tarentum and Brundisium, and in 216 BCE its army suffered its worst defeat at Cannae, against Hannibal. The Appian Way and the Via Traiana helped cities to prosper, and the region became the largest exporter of olive oil in the East.

After 476 the region saw unrest and Ostrogothic rule, then the Byzantine reconquest under Justinian I, ended in 554, and from 569 Lombard conquests. In the 9th century Saracens established the Emirate of Bari; they were driven out in the 870s and Byzantine rule returned. In 1043 the Norman William of Hauteville founded the county of Apulia, which merged in 1057 into the County of Apulia and Calabria under Robert Guiscard, and from 1130 it was part of the Kingdom of Sicily under Roger II.

Under Frederick II came a peak of prosperity and building, including Castel del Monte near Andria. From 1282 it was ruled by the Kingdom of Naples, later by the Aragonese, the Spanish and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, and it was annexed to the Kingdom of Italy after the Expedition of the Thousand.
Apulia has 3,865,277 inhabitants and its capital is Bari. Its economy moved from farming to services and tourism in the 1970s and 1980s. The region has two national parks, Alta Murgia and Gargano.
aq-qoyunlu: The Aq Qoyunlu were a Turkoman, culturally Persianate, Sunni Muslim tribal confederation founded in the Diyarbakır region by Qara Yuluk Uthman Beg. Byzantine chronicles first attest them in the district of Bayburt from at least the 1340s, under Tur Ali Beg, who attacked Trebizond without taking it. The leading tribe was the Bayandur, of the Oghuz Turks, and the rulers claimed descent from Bayindir Khan, a grandson of the semi-mythical Oghuz Khan. The name, meaning those with white sheep, is thought to come from a white sheep painted on their flags. In 1402 Timur granted them all of Diyar Bakr, and for long afterwards the rival Qara Qoyunlu confederation kept them from expanding.

The confederation reached its height under Uzun Hasan, who ruled from 1452 to 1478. He defeated the Qara Qoyunlu leader Jahan Shah in 1467 at the Battle of Chapakchur, and in 1469 defeated the Timurid ruler Abu Sa'id Mirza at the Battle of Qarabagh. He also took Baghdad and territories around the Persian Gulf, and made Tabriz his capital. Seeking allies against the Ottomans, he asked Venice for aid in 1464, but none came, and the Ottomans defeated him at the Battle of Otlukbeli in 1473 without destroying his state.

After his death his son Khalil held power for a few months before being defeated by his brother Ya'qub, who reigned from 1478 to 1490. Ya'qub put down seven pretenders in four years, and his neglect of popular religious practice alienated many Turkomans, who turned to the militant Safavid order. When Ya'qub's Shirvanshah vassals killed the Safavid leader Sheikh Haydar, pro-Safavid feeling grew. Civil war followed Ya'qub's death, and the state split among rival sultans. Ismail I, Haydar's son, defeated the Aq Qoyunlu in 1501 and conquered their lands in stages, taking Diyarbakır in 1507–1508 and Mesopotamia in 1508. The last sultan, Murad, was killed by Ismail's Qizilbash warriors.

At first the military reflected a loose political structure: a council of amirs and tribal chiefs, whose decision the sultan had to follow, and tribal levies who supported themselves from their pastures and booty. Uzun Hasan's armies grew to probably more than 100,000 men, built on a strong cavalry; the lack of firearms was their main weakness. After the conquest of Iran the rulers adopted Iranian administration and kept the existing bureaucracy, and Iranians held the four top civil posts. Uzun Hasan ruled in the manner of an Iranian king at Tabriz.

Ya'qub's court at Tabriz patronised Persian poets, among them Ahli Shirazi and Baba Fighani Shirazi, and Jami dedicated a poem to him. His workshop produced illustrated manuscripts, among them the Khamsa of Nizami of 1481. The Safavids were in a sense heirs of the Aq Qoyunlu: Ismail's mother was Uzun Hasan's daughter.
aquaculture: The Gunditjmara, an Aboriginal Australian people of south-western Victoria, may have raised short-finned eels as early as about 4,580 BCE. Evidence indicates that they developed about 100 square kilometres of volcanic floodplain near Lake Condah into a complex of channels and dams, and used woven traps to capture eels and preserve them to eat all year round. The Budj Bim Cultural Landscape there is a World Heritage Site and one of the oldest known aquaculture sites in the world. The anthropologist Peter Sutton disputes that these systems qualify as aquaculture, as there is no evidence that they involved the breeding, feeding, protecting or rearing of eels.

Aquaculture is the controlled cultivation of aquatic organisms such as fish, crustaceans, molluscs, algae and aquatic plants, in freshwater, brackish water or seawater. The Food and Agriculture Organization defines it as farming that implies some intervention in the rearing process, such as regular stocking, feeding and protection from predators, and individual or corporate ownership of the stock. It is contrasted with commercial fishing, which harvests wild fish.

It can be conducted in artificial facilities on land, such as tanks and ponds, in sheltered shallow waters near the shore, or in cages, racks or bags in open water. Mariculture is aquaculture in seawater and pisciculture is fish farming for food.

Fish farming is the most common form, and the most important farmed fish are carp, salmon, tilapia and catfish. Commercial shrimp farming began in the 1970s and grew steeply, with about 75% of farmed shrimp produced in Asia. Farmed shellfish include oysters, mussels and clams, which are filter feeders and are generally regarded as benign or even beneficial. Seaweeds dominate the production of farmed aquatic plants.

Harvests from wild fisheries stagnated and popular marine species were overexploited, which encouraged the domestication of further species. Some forms have environmental costs. About 20 percent of mangrove forests have been destroyed since 1980, partly because of shrimp farming, and 269,000 hectares of Indonesian mangroves were converted to shrimp farms over four decades.
aquifer: The word comes from the Latin prefix aqui-, a form of aqua, water, and the suffix -fer, bearing. An aquifer is an underground layer of permeable, porous or fractured rock, or of unconsolidated gravel, sand or silt, that holds water. Aquifers are sometimes described as underground rivers or lakes, but they are in fact porous rock saturated with water. They occur from near the surface to depths of more than 9,000 metres, and those nearer the surface are more likely to be replenished by local rainfall.

Aquifers are classified in several ways. A confined aquifer lies under an impermeable barrier, often clay, while an unconfined aquifer has none directly above it and its water level can rise with recharge. An aquitard is a bed of low permeability that restricts the flow of groundwater from one aquifer to another. Porous aquifers occur in sand and sandstone, karst aquifers develop in limestone as acidic water enlarges fissures, and a rock of low porosity can still serve if it is highly fractured. The study of water flow in aquifers is called hydrogeology.

Groundwater is drawn from aquifers through wells and used for drinking water, agriculture and industry. Many desert areas have limestone hills or mountains that can be exploited as groundwater resources: shallow aquifers are used in parts of the Atlas Mountains, the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges, and the Jebel Akhdar in Oman. Some aquifers hold fossil water from the last glaciation, as the Ogallala Aquifer of the central United States does, and where more water is taken out than is replenished the practical yield is exceeded.

Overdrafting can lower the water table, and along coasts such as those of Libya and Israel it has let sea water contaminate groundwater. Among the largest aquifers are the Great Artesian Basin of Australia, over 1.7 million square kilometres, and the Guarani Aquifer beneath Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay.

Hydrogeology has to establish how fast and in what direction groundwater travels. In porous aquifers water seeps slowly between sand grains, and a flow of 1 foot a day is a high rate. In karst aquifers dye traces in the Barton Springs Edwards aquifer measured flows of 0.5 to 7 miles a day, which makes them much more open to contamination. In 2013 large aquifers of low-salinity water were reported under the continental shelves of Australia, China, North America and South Africa, formed when sea levels were lower, before the end of the ice age 20,000 years ago.
aquileia: Aquileia lies at the head of the Adriatic at the edge of the lagoons, about 10 km from the sea, on the river Natiso, modern Natisone, whose course has changed somewhat since Roman times. The colony was founded south of the Julian Alps to protect the Veneti, faithful allies of Rome in the Second Punic War, and to check warlike peoples such as the Carni and the Histri. The site, at the end of the Baltic amber trade, had been commercially important since the thirteenth century BCE.

The colony was founded in 181 BCE by a triumvirate that led 3,000 families to settle it, most of them from Picenum, Samnium and Campania. Roads soon linked it to Bologna and, from 148 BCE, to Genua by the Via Postumia, and gold fields found near modern Klagenfurt in 130 BCE added to its importance. Wine, glassware, metalwork from Noricum and amber were traded. In 168 Marcus Aurelius made it the empire's principal fortress against the peoples of the north and east, and it soon had a population of 100,000. In 238 its restored walls held out for several months against Maximinus Thrax. After Diocletian emperors often resided in its palace, and its bishop became a metropolitan.

Alaric besieged it in 401, and in 452 Attila destroyed it so completely that its site was hard to recognise; the inhabitants fled to the lagoons, where they laid the foundations of Venice and Grado. It revived in diminished form until the Lombards destroyed it again in 590. The patriarch fled to Grado, and a rival line of patriarchs elected at Aquileia continued in schism until 699. In 787 Charlemagne named Paulinus II patriarch. In 1445 the patriarch Ludovico Trevisan accepted the loss of his estate for a Venetian salary of 5,000 ducats a year, and the diocese was suppressed in 1751.

Aquileia is a smaller town than the Roman colony. Sieges, earthquakes, floods and the pillaging of ancient buildings for materials mean that no Roman building stands above ground. Its ruins, including mosaics and an early Christian basilica, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Excavation has revealed the river port, the forum, baths, an amphitheatre and a circus. The cathedral, a basilica erected by Patriarch Poppo in 1031, was rebuilt in the Gothic style by Patriarch Marquard of Randeck between 1365 and 1381.
arab-byzantine-wars: The long Byzantine-Sasanian wars of the 6th and 7th centuries and recurring outbreaks of plague left both empires exhausted. The last of those wars ended with a Byzantine victory, when Emperor Heraclius regained all lost territory and restored the True Cross to Jerusalem in 629. Neither empire had time to recover before meeting the Arabs, newly united by Islam. The first skirmishes came under Muhammad, and the Battle of Mu'tah followed the murder of his envoy by the Ghassanids, a Byzantine vassal kingdom. Muhammad died in 632, and his successor Abu Bakr ended the Ridda Wars in control of the whole peninsula.

From 634 the Rashidun Caliphate attacked Syria and Palestine. Heraclius was ill and could not lead his army in person. The Rashidun army won near Ajnadayn in the summer of 634 and took Damascus under Khalid ibn al-Walid. Syria was captured in 639 and Egypt in 642, and the Exarchate of Africa fell gradually between 647 and 670. Arab fleets entered the Mediterranean from the 650s. The Umayyads, who succeeded the Rashidun in 661, besieged Constantinople in 674 to 678 and again in 717 to 718, and failed both times.

After the second siege the frontier settled along the Taurus Mountains, where raids and counter-raids became nearly ritualised and the border region was depopulated. The Abbasids, who overthrew the Umayyads in 750, were less expansionist, yet clashes continued almost every year until the mid-10th century. Abbasid vassals conquered Crete in 827 and took Sicily gradually from 831 to 878. In 863 the general Petronas won the Battle of Lalakaon, beginning a century of Byzantine offensives under the Macedonian dynasty, and Crete was reconquered in 961.

By the end of the 10th century the Fatimid Caliphate had replaced the Abbasids as the major Arab power in the Levant and halted further Byzantine advances. The Byzantines had lost much territory, and their focus shifted from the western reconquests of Justinian to defence against the Islamic armies in the east. The war strained relations between Rome and Byzantium, since the empire could no longer protect the papacy as it once had.

Walter Emil Kaegi notes that the Arabic sources contain obscurities and contradictions, and that Byzantine chronicles such as those of Theophanes and Nicephorus are terse and biased, so neither tradition can serve as the standard for the other.
arab-league: The Arab League, officially the League of Arab States, was formed following the adoption of the Alexandria Protocol in 1944. Its founding treaty, the Pact of the League of Arab States, was adopted in 1945 and stipulates that the League is composed of the independent Arab states that have signed it. Its first headquarters was the Boustan Palace in Cairo. Its aim, in the words of the charter, was to draw closer the relations between member states and co-ordinate collaboration between them, to safeguard their independence and sovereignty.

Each member state has one vote in the Council, and decisions are binding only on those states that voted for them. The Charter endorsed the principle of an Arab nation-state while respecting the sovereignty of each member. Mindful of earlier announcements in support of the Arabs of Palestine, the framers included Palestine from the start through an annex providing for an Arab delegate from Palestine until the country enjoyed actual independence.

The League's first major action was a joint intervention to keep Palestine from being divided into two states in keeping with the decision of the United Nations General Assembly. The Joint Defence and Economic Cooperation treaty of 13 April 1950 committed its signatories to coordinate military defence, and a common market was established in 1965. At the Cairo Summit of 1964 the League initiated the creation of an organisation representing the Palestinian people, and the Palestine Liberation Organization, founded on 2 June 1964, was shortly admitted to the League.

Egypt was suspended on 26 March 1979 because of its peace treaty with Israel, and the headquarters moved to Tunis. Egypt was readmitted in May 1989 and the headquarters returned to Cairo in September 1990. At the Beirut Summit of 28 March 2002 the League adopted the Arab Peace Initiative, a Saudi-inspired plan that offered full normalisation of relations with Israel in exchange for withdrawal from occupied territories.

Through bodies such as the Arab League Educational, Cultural and Scientific Organization, the League runs cultural, scientific, economic and social programmes, and it has served as a forum for settling disputes between states, as in limiting the 1958 Lebanon crisis. It has no military force of its own. Michael Barnett and Etel Solingen judge that it has achieved a relatively low level of cooperation, because its design reflects its leaders' concern for their own rule: they embraced the rhetoric of Arab unity but feared unity in practice. It now has 22 members, among them three non-Arab countries, Comoros, Djibouti and Somalia, and its official language is Literary Arabic.
arabia-petraea: Before 106 the area was ruled by the Nabataean Kingdom, whose last king, Rabbel II, died in early 105. A succession crisis followed, and Emperor Trajan refused to recognise any claimant. Instead he sent two legions: the Third Cyrenaica from Egypt advanced on Bostra from the south, and the Sixth Ferrata from Syria on Petra from the north. There may have been little resistance, since the former royal troops of Nabataea joined the Roman forces. The new province, Arabia Petraea, meaning Rocky Arabia, was the only province in the Near East that the Romans did not both gain and later lose during Trajan's reign. Petra was given the status of metropolis Arabica.

After the annexation Trajan built the Via Nova Traiana, about 430 km long, from the Syrian boundary to the Red Sea. It linked Bostra, Philadelphia, Petra and the route to Aila, now Aqaba, and eased administration, troop movement and taxation.

Under Septimius Severus the province was enlarged northward at the expense of Syria, with the region of Shahba, birthplace of the later emperor Philip the Arab. Around 300, under Diocletian's reforms, the Negev, Sinai and southern Transjordan passed to Palaestina. In the second half of the 4th century the southern part of Palaestina, with Petra as capital, became Palaestina Tertia Salutaris, which replaced the name Arabia Petraea. The territory was briefly lost to the Sasanian Empire in the war of 602 to 628 and then permanently to the Rashidun Caliphate.

Most of the province was desert, sparsely inhabited by nomadic Arab tribes, and its towns lay mainly in the north towards the Jordan and in the Hauran. The main cities were Petra, Bosra, Gerasa, Philippopolis and Philadelphia, now Amman, and the only major seaport was Ayla. Petra declined under Roman rule, partly because trade shifted to sea routes, and an earthquake in 363 damaged its water system, but papyri of the 530s to 590s found in a church show that it still flourished in the 6th century.

Greek civic life spread quickly. A new dating system, the Bostran era, began in 106, and the Babatha archive shows documents turning from Nabataean and Aramaic to Greek, so that a deed of 110 is in Greek. Bostra, built in local basalt, looks severe and unclassical, while Philippopolis was laid out on a Roman colonial plan.
arabian-peninsula: The Arabian Peninsula, or Arabia, covers about 3,237,500 square kilometres and is the world's largest peninsula. It is bounded by the Red Sea in the west, the Gulf of Aden and the Arabian Sea in the south, the Gulf of Oman and the Persian Gulf in the east, and Mesopotamia and the Levant in the north. Most of it is covered by the Arabian Desert, and mountains rise in the south-west, where Yemen receives more rain. Few permanent rivers exist, but where ancient aquifers surface oases form, and palm groves made the peninsula a great producer of dates.

A finger bone found at Al Wusta in the Nefud Desert, about 90,000 years old, is the oldest human fossil found outside Africa and the Levant. The written record is thought to begin in the early 1st millennium BCE. South Arabia saw the Kingdom of Saba, Awsan, Main and Himyar, central Arabia the Kingdom of Kinda, and eastern Arabia the Dilmun civilization. From 106 to 630 CE the north-west was under Roman control as Arabia Petraea, with Petra as its capital. Greco-Roman writers also spoke of Arabia Deserta for the centre and Arabia Felix for the south.

Muhammad was born in Mecca about 570, began preaching there in 610 and migrated to Medina in 622. After his death in 632 Abu Bakr became the first caliph and put down the Ridda wars, a rebellion of Arab tribes. Under the Rashidun and, from 661, the Umayyad caliphs, Arab armies conquered lands from the Iberian Peninsula to India, and the political focus of the Muslim world shifted away from Arabia, though Mecca and Medina remained its spiritual centres and pilgrimage destinations. The Ottomans never controlled central Arabia, the Najd.

The Al Saud began to emerge in 1744, when Muhammad bin Saud joined the religious leader Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, and the Emirate of Diriyah took Mecca in 1803. The Arab Revolt of 1916 to 1918, begun by Sherif Hussein ibn Ali, challenged Ottoman rule. Ibn Saud captured Riyadh in 1902 and by 1926 had subdued Al-Hasa, Jabal Shammar and the Hejaz. Vast oil reserves were discovered in the 1930s.

Nine countries lie wholly or partly on the peninsula: Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen, with the southern halves of Iraq and Jordan. Saudi Arabia covers the largest part. Mecca and Medina, with the Kaaba and the Prophet's Mosque, remain the principal destinations of the Hajj.
arabian-sea: The Arabian Sea is bounded on the west by the Arabian Peninsula, the Gulf of Aden and the Guardafui Channel, on the north by Iran and Pakistan, on the east by India, and on the southeast by the Laccadive Sea and the Maldives. Its area is about 3,862,000 square kilometres and its maximum depth 5,395 metres. The largest river flowing into it is the Indus. The Gulf of Aden connects it to the Red Sea through the strait of Bab-el-Mandeb, and the Gulf of Oman connects it to the Persian Gulf. The largest island is Socotra.

The sea has a monsoonal climate. Historically, trade across it was restricted by the monsoon winds and the currents they produce. Intense upwelling in the summer monsoon makes it one of the most productive marine regions in the world. Geologically, the sea descends from the Tethys Ocean, whose connection between the Atlantic and Indian Oceans closed in two steps, around 20 and 14 million years ago, a closure thought to have allowed the upwelling and the modern South Asian monsoon to be established.

The Arabian Sea has been a route of maritime trade since the development of early coastal sailing vessels in the northern Indian Ocean and southern Arabia in the 4th and 3rd millennia BCE. The straits of Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb served as gateways linking the polities of the eastern and western Old World from the first international trade networks of the 3rd millennium BCE. From the 2nd century BCE the sea and its surrounding lands formed the central nexus of the Maritime Silk Road.

The trade carried peoples, ideas, technologies, crops and diseases. Millet and sorghum, for instance, reached the Indus Valley Civilization through sea trade with East Africa. The maritime trade also helped Islam spread from the Arabian Peninsula across the Indian Ocean to East Africa, South Asia, Southeast Asia and the Malay Archipelago.

The countries with coastlines on the Arabian Sea are Yemen, Oman, Pakistan, Iran and India, together with the westernmost islands of the Maldives and Lakshadweep. Its ports include Mumbai, Karachi, Gwadar and Salalah. The island of Socotra is a UNESCO World Heritage Site because of its biodiversity.
arabic-language: Arabic is classified as a Central Semitic language of the Afroasiatic family. Arabia had a wide variety of Semitic languages in antiquity, among them Ancient South Arabian languages in the southwest, Dadanitic and Taymanitic in the oases of northern Hejaz and Hasaitic in the east. Safaitic and Hismaic, attested on the northwestern frontier, share important features with later forms of Arabic, and scholars theorise that they are early forms of it, to be counted as Old Arabic. Linguists generally believe that Old Arabic, a collection of related dialects, first emerged during the Iron Age.

Classical Arabic, the modern Arabic varieties and the Safaitic and Hismaic inscriptions share features found in no other Central Semitic language, evidence of descent from a hypothetical ancestor, Proto-Arabic. Because several Arabic varieties keep features that Classical Arabic lacks, the vernaculars cannot descend from Classical Arabic, which is a sister language rather than their direct ancestor.

Arabic usually means Standard Arabic, which Western linguists divide into Classical Arabic and Modern Standard Arabic. Classical Arabic is the language of the Quran, used from Pre-Islamic Arabia to the Abbasid Caliphate, and follows the norms set by classical grammarians such as Sibawayh and the vocabulary of classical dictionaries such as the Lisān al-ʻArab. Modern Standard Arabic largely follows its grammar and vocabulary but has taken new vocabulary for concepts of the industrial and post-industrial era. Alongside it stand regional vernacular dialects, usually acquired in families, which are not necessarily mutually intelligible. Educated Arabs speak both, a situation called diglossia.

Arabic has a root-and-pattern morphology. A root of usually three bare consonants is fitted into a pattern to form words: from k-t-b, meaning write, come katabtu, I wrote, kitābun, book, and kātibun, writer. It is written with the Arabic alphabet, an abjad that runs from right to left and derives from the Aramaic through Nabatean.

During the Middle Ages Arabic was a major vehicle of culture and learning, especially in science, mathematics and philosophy, and many European languages borrowed words from it. The influence is seen mainly in Spanish, and less in Portuguese, Catalan and Sicilian, owing to the long Arabic cultural and linguistic presence in southern Iberia in the Al-Andalus era. Maltese is a Semitic language that developed from a dialect of Arabic and is written in the Latin alphabet.

Persian, Turkish, Hindustani, Malay, Hausa and Swahili are among the languages most markedly influenced. The lexicographic tradition lasted about a millennium before the modern period: the Kitāb al-ʿAyn of the 8th century is considered the first lexicon to include all Arabic roots, and Ibn Manzur's Lisān al-ʿArab of 1290 gives 9,273 roots. Arabic is one of the official languages of the United Nations and the liturgical language of Islam.
arad-romania: Settlement on the northern bank of the Mureș began in the 5th millennium BCE. Roman troops conquered the Dacian settlement in what is now the Micălaca district between 101 and 102, and in the Second Dacian War Trajan took the land north of the Mureș. The name of the city comes from its first ispán, or count, Arad. The area became part of the Principality of Hungary at the end of the 9th century, and the town is first mentioned in the 11th century.
