The north-central high country belongs to the Colorado Plateau, with mountains, mesas, deep canyons and forests of pine, Douglas fir and spruce. The Mogollon Rim, an escarpment of about 609 metres, marks the plateau's south-western edge. Despite its dryness, 27 per cent of the state is forest, and it holds the world's largest stand of ponderosa pine.

For thousands of years before the modern era Arizona was home to Native American civilizations, among them the Hohokam, Mogollon and Ancestral Puebloan cultures, whose pueblos, cliff dwellings and rock paintings survive. The Spanish Franciscan Marcos de Niza made contact with native inhabitants, probably the Sobaipuri, in 1539, and the expedition of Coronado passed through in 1540–1542. The Jesuit Father Kino founded a chain of missions in the Pimería Alta in the 1690s, and Spain established presidios at Tubac in 1752 and Tucson in 1775.

The name probably derives from Arizonac, a Spanish rendering of the O'odham alĭ ṣonak, 'small spring', first applied to an area near a silver mining camp in Sonora; another suggested origin is the Basque haritz ona, 'the good oak'. After Mexican independence in 1821 the region became part of Alta California. Mexico ceded much of it to the United States in 1848 after the Mexican–American War, and the southern strip came with the Gadsden Purchase of 1853. Arizona was admitted on 14 February 1912 as the 48th state and the last of the contiguous states.

Phoenix is the capital and largest city; the original Capitol, with its copper dome, was dedicated in 1901 and is now a museum. The 2020 census counted 7,151,502 people, most of them living in the Phoenix and Tucson metropolitan areas. About a quarter of the state is Indian reservation land, home to 27 federally recognized tribes, including the Navajo Nation. Grand Canyon National Park is among four national parks in the state, which also has three public universities.
arjuna: In the Mahabharata, Arjuna is the third of the five Pandava brothers and half-divine by birth. King Pandu was cursed to die if he had sexual relations, so his wife Kunti used a mantra given to her by the sage Durvasa to invoke gods and bear children. Arjuna was her third son, conceived through the god Indra. He and his brothers grew up at Hastinapura with their cousins the Kauravas. The Brahmin warrior Drona taught them warfare. Arjuna alone agreed when Drona asked the princes to repay a favour in the future, and he became Drona's favourite pupil. The epic exists in many versions, and its oldest parts may date to near 400 BCE.

Arjuna wins Draupadi, princess of Panchala, at her svayamvara, or bridegroom choice, and there meets Krishna, his maternal cousin, who becomes his close friend and later his charioteer. During an exile for breaking an agreement about Draupadi he marries Ulupi, Chitrangada and Subhadra. With Krishna he helps the fire god Agni burn the Khandava forest, killing the creatures that flee it, and receives the bow Gandiva. After Yudhishthira loses everything at the rigged dice game, Karna calls Draupadi unchaste, and Arjuna vows to kill him. In the last year of the exile he lives disguised as Brihannala, teaching song and dance to Princess Uttara at King Virata's Matsya kingdom.

Before the Kurukshetra War, despair at seeing his kinsmen and teachers on the other side leads Arjuna to put down his weapons, and Krishna answers with the Bhagavad Gita. In the war Arjuna fells Bhishma and kills Karna.

After the war Arjuna follows the horse of Yudhishthira's Ashvamedha to Manipura, where his son Babhruvahana wounds him in battle, and Ulupi revives him. At the onset of the Kali Yuga the Pandavas leave the throne to Parikshit, Arjuna's grandson, and set out with Draupadi on a final journey to the Himalayas, where Arjuna dies. He is an epitome of heroism and devotion in the Hindu tradition. The Aṣṭādhyāyī, likely composed in the 5th or 6th century BCE, mentions his worship beside Vasudeva-Krishna. In Java and Bali he is the main character of several kakawin poems.
ark-of-the-covenant: In religious tradition the Ark of the Covenant, also called the Ark of the Testimony or the Ark of God, is a wooden chest decorated in solid gold, with an ornamental lid known as the Seat of Mercy. According to the Book of Exodus, God instructed Moses to build it during his 40-day stay on Mount Sinai, and Bezalel and Oholiab constructed it. The Book of Exodus and the First Book of Kings say it held the tablets of the Ten Commandments, and the Book of Numbers and the Epistle to the Hebrews add Aaron's rod and a pot of manna.

In the biblical account the Levites carried the Ark during the 40 years in the desert, and it stood in the Tabernacle when the Israelites camped. At the River Jordan it led the people, and the river is said to have run dry as the priests carrying it touched the water. Later the elders took it into battle against the Philistines, lost 30,000 men and saw it captured. After seven months the Philistines returned it. The narrative has King David bring it from Kiriath-Jearim toward Zion, and Solomon placed it in the Holy of Holies of his Temple.

Archaeologists have found strong cultic activity at Kiriath-Jearim in the 8th and 7th centuries BCE. Thomas Römer suggests that the Ark may not have gone to Jerusalem until the reign of Josiah, c. 640 to 609 BCE, while Yigal Levin finds no evidence that Kiriath-Jearim was ever a cult centre in the monarchical era.

No verified evidence shows where the Ark is. Jewish tradition says variously that it went to Babylon, that Josiah hid it, or, in Second Maccabees, that Jeremiah buried it in a cave until God gathers his people again. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church says it keeps the Ark in Axum, and the Lemba people say their ancestors carried it south. The Samaritans place it on Mount Gerizim.

Christians read it as a type of Christ and, in the Gospel of Luke, as a parallel to Mary. The Quran mentions it in Surah Al-Baqara 248, as a sign of Saul's kingship. It appears in Steven Spielberg's film Raiders of the Lost Ark of 1981.
arkansas: Arkansas is a landlocked state of the West South Central region. It can generally be split into two halves, the highlands of the north-west and the lowlands of the south-east. The highlands belong to the Southern Interior Highlands, which include the Ozark and Ouachita Mountains. The southern lowlands include the Gulf Coastal Plain and the Arkansas Delta, and the Mississippi River forms most of the eastern border. The name first applied to the Arkansas River. It comes from the French Arcansas, from the Algonquian akansa, the term for the Quapaw people, which is believed to mean south wind people.

Indigenous peoples lived in Arkansas for thousands of years, and the Caddo, Osage and Quapaw encountered the first European explorers. The first was the Spanish explorer Hernando de Soto in 1541, who crossed the Mississippi and marched across central Arkansas and the Ozark Mountains. He found nothing he considered of value and met native resistance throughout. Falling ill, he ordered his men to massacre the men of the nearby village of Anilco, whom he feared were plotting with the powerful polity of Quigualtam, and they were said to have killed women and children as well. He died in May 1542, probably near modern McArthur, and his men sank his body in the Mississippi River at night.

Arkansas was later part of French Louisiana and of the Louisiana Purchase. Its population grew from fewer than 15,000 in 1820 to 52,240 in 1835, and the territory was admitted as the 25th state on 15 June 1836. Much of the Delta was developed for cotton plantations, whose owners depended largely on the labour of enslaved African Americans. In 1861 Arkansas seceded and joined the Confederate States of America, and it returned to the Union in 1868.

After the war the state suffered economically from its overreliance on large-scale plantation agriculture, since cotton remained the leading crop while its market declined, and farmers and businessmen did not diversify. In the late 19th century the state passed Jim Crow laws to disenfranchise and segregate its African American population. In the civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s, Arkansas, and Little Rock in particular, was a major battleground in efforts to integrate schools. After the Second World War the economy began to diversify.

Little Rock, in the centre of the state, is the capital and most populous city. The 2020 census counted 3,011,524 residents. Among historic sites, Arkansas Post National Memorial, Fort Smith National Historic Site, Hot Springs National Park and Little Rock Central High School National Historic Site preserve parts of its past.
arkhangelsk: Arkhangelsk lies on both banks of the Northern Dvina River, near its mouth into the White Sea. The city spreads for over 40 km along the river banks and the numerous islands of its delta. The climate is subarctic, with long, very cold winters from November to March. The arms of the city show the Archangel Michael defeating the Devil; legend says that the victory took place near where the city stands, and gives the city its name.

The Vikings knew the area as Bjarmaland. Ohthere of Hålogaland told c. 890 of his travels in an area by a river and the White Sea, probably the place later known as Arkhangelsk. In the 12th century the Novgorodians established a monastery dedicated to the Archangel Michael in the estuary of the Northern Dvina. Norwegian and Russian interests rivalled in the north, and in 1419 the Norwegians plundered Russian settlements along the coast, among them the monastery. In 1478 Ivan III took the area for the Grand Duchy of Moscow.

In 1553 the English ship Edward Bonaventure, searching for the Northeast Passage to China, reached the mouth of the Dvina, and its captain Richard Chancellor agreed a trade with Ivan the Terrible. Dutch merchants came from the 1560s. In 1584 Ivan IV ordered the founding of New Kholmogory, later renamed after the monastery. Because Sweden largely controlled access to the Baltic, Arkhangelsk, although icebound in winter, was Muscovy's principal outlet for maritime trade, and the Pomors, its inhabitants, were among the first to explore trade routes to northern Siberia.

Peter the Great ordered a state shipyard in 1693 but, aware that ice limited the port for five months a year, founded Saint Petersburg in 1703. In 1722 he decreed that Arkhangelsk should take only goods for its own consumption, a decree that contributed to its deterioration until it was cancelled in 1762. The economy revived at the end of the 19th century, when the railway to Moscow was completed and timber became a major export. The city resisted Bolshevik rule from 1918 to 1920 as a stronghold of the White Army, and in World War II it was, with Murmansk, one of the two main destinations of the Arctic convoys. Surviving landmarks include the Merchant Yards (1668-1684) and the New Dvina Fortress (1701-1705).
arles: The Rhône forks into two branches just upstream of Arles, forming the Camargue delta. Because a large part of the Camargue, the largest wetlands in France, lies within the commune, Arles occupies 758.93 square kilometres and is the largest commune in metropolitan France by area, over seven times the size of Paris. Its population is 51,156. The climate is Mediterranean, with hot summers and a cold wind, the mistral, that can bring sudden frosts in winter.

The name Arelate is a form of a Gaulish word meaning by the marsh, or in front of the marsh. Ligurians lived in the area from about 800 BCE, and Celtic influences are also found. In the 6th century BCE Greek merchants from Massalia sailed up the Rhône and found a hill surrounded by marsh; excavations show Greek furniture in use, indicating a Greek trading base. The site was the first place to cross the Rhône from the sea, and lay on the main route from Italy to Spain.

The Romans took the town in 123 BCE and built a canal link to the Mediterranean in 104 BCE. Arles had to compete with Massalia further along the coast. The House of the Harpist, dating from 70-50 BCE and discovered recently, has yielded elaborate frescoes. In 2007 divers found a marble bust in the Rhône near Arles. Because archaeologists believed Julius Caesar had founded the colony Colonia Iulia Paterna Arelate Sextanorum in 46 BCE, they concluded preliminarily that the bust was a life portrait of Caesar, and in 2008 France's Minister of Culture reported it as the oldest known representation of him.

The Roman and Romanesque Monuments of Arles were listed as UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 1981. They include the Roman theatre, the amphitheatre, the Alyscamps necropolis, the Thermae of Constantine, the cryptoporticus, the obelisk and the Barbegal aqueduct and mill. The Church of St. Trophime, formerly a cathedral, is a major work of Romanesque architecture. Vincent van Gogh lived in Arles from 1888 to 1889 and produced over 300 paintings and drawings there.
arlon: Before the Roman conquest of Gaul, the area around Arlon belonged to the Treveri, a Celtic tribe. The local people adapted relatively easily to Roman culture, and the vicus of Orolaunum quickly became a commercial and administrative centre. The Germanic invasions of the 3rd century destroyed most of these gains despite the defensive walls built on the Knipchen hill.

In 1060 Waleran I of Limburg, Count of Arlon, built a castle on the Knipchen hill. When Duke Waleran III died in 1226, Arlon passed to his son Henry V the Fair, Count of Luxembourg, and became part of the county of Luxembourg. In 1558 French troops under Francis, Duke of Guise, destroyed nearly half the city, castle included. In the 17th century Capuchin friars built a convent on the castle's ruins, and a fire destroyed much of the city in 1785. On 9 June 1793 French Revolutionary troops defeated the Austrians outside it and took the city.

After the Treaty of London of 1839 the western part of the Duchy of Luxembourg, the province of Luxembourg with Arlon, went to the new Kingdom of Belgium. Arlon is the capital of that province and the smallest provincial capital in Belgium, with just over 28,000 people. On 26 August 1914, 121 inhabitants were executed on the orders of Colonel Richard Karl von Tessmar in the German invasion.

It holds one of the richest archaeological museums in Belgium, with Roman sculpture and Merovingian funerary art. A fragment of the Gallo-Roman wall of the 3rd century still stands, and the church of Saint Donat occupies the Knipchen hill. The carnival takes place at mid-Lent, and the Maitrank, white wine in which a local flower, Asperula odorata, has macerated, is the city's most popular drink.
armagh: Armagh, in Irish Ard Mhacha, meaning Macha's height, takes its name from the goddess Macha. Nearby Navan Fort was a pagan ritual or ceremonial site and, according to Irish mythology, one of the great royal sites of Gaelic Ireland and the capital of Ulster. It appears to have been largely abandoned after the 1st century. In the 3rd century a ditch and bank was dug around the top of Cathedral Hill, the heart of the present city, which suggests a pagan sanctuary that succeeded Navan.

By the 7th century Armagh was the site of the most important church, monastery and monastic school in the north of Ireland. The Book of Armagh was produced in the monastery in the early 9th century and contains some of the oldest surviving specimens of Old Irish. The Uí Néill High King Niall Caille was buried at Armagh in 846. The first Viking raids were recorded in 832, and the town suffered at least ten over the following century.

During the Tudor conquest of Ireland Armagh suffered greatly, because it lay between the English Pale and the O'Neill heartland of Tyrone. English troops occupied and fortified it in the 1560s, and Shane O'Neill then attacked and largely destroyed it. After the Battle of the Yellow Ford in 1598 the routed English army took refuge there before surrendering to Hugh O'Neill. By the end of the Nine Years' War Armagh lay in ruins.

Armagh has been an educational centre since the time of Saint Patrick. The Royal School was founded in 1608, the Armagh Observatory in 1790 and St Patrick's College in 1834. It was regarded as a city by 1226 as the seat of the Primate of All Ireland, lost the status in 1840 and regained it in 1994.

Armagh is a city and the county town of County Armagh, in Northern Ireland. It is the seat of both the Church of Ireland and the Roman Catholic Archbishops of Armagh, each Primate of All Ireland for their denomination. It has two cathedrals named after Saint Patrick, both on hills. The Church of Ireland cathedral dates back to around 445, and the Roman Catholic cathedral, with twin spires 64 metres high, was built in the latter half of the 19th century.
armenia: The modern Republic of Armenia is a landlocked country in the Armenian highlands of West Asia, in the South Caucasus. It borders Turkey to the west, Georgia to the north, Azerbaijan to the east, and Iran and the Azerbaijani exclave of Nakhchivan to the south. Its area is 29,743 square kilometres. The terrain is mostly mountainous, with fast-flowing rivers and few forests, and 85.9% of the country is mountain area.

Mount Aragats rises to 4,090 metres. Mount Ararat, at 5,137 metres, was historically part of Armenia and is now in Turkey, but is clearly visible from Armenia. Armenians regard it as a symbol of their land, and it appears on the national emblem.

Acheulean tools more than a million years old mark the first human traces, and thousands of artefacts about 325,000 years old were found at Nor Geghi 1. Early civilisation dates to about 4000 BCE. Excavations at the Areni-1 cave complex in 2010 and 2011 uncovered the world's earliest known leather shoe, skirt and wine-producing facility. Bronze Age cultures and states included the Trialeti-Vanadzor culture, Hayasa-Azzi and Mitanni, followed by the Nairi confederation and its successor Urartu. A cuneiform inscription indicates that Yerevan was founded in the summer of 782 BCE by King Argishti I.

The exonym Armenia appears as Armina in the Old Persian Behistun Inscription of 515 BCE. The Kingdom of Armenia reached its height under Tigranes the Great in the 1st century BCE and adopted Christianity as its official religion in 301 CE. The Bagratid Kingdom of Armenia, restored in the 9th century, fell in 1045, and Cilician Armenia lay on the Mediterranean coast between the 11th and 14th centuries. Up to 1.5 million Armenians were exterminated in the Armenian genocide during World War I.

Armenia is a representative parliamentary democratic republic. It followed a semi-presidential model until April 2018, and the National Assembly is a unicameral parliament of 105 members. The country is divided into ten provinces, with Yerevan having special status. Its population was 3,081,100 in 2025, down from a peak of 3.6 million in 1991. The diaspora is estimated at 8 million by some counts, far larger than the population in Armenia, with the largest communities in Russia, the United States and France.
armenians: The Armenians are an ethnic group indigenous to the Armenian highlands of West Asia, where their presence dates back some 4,000 years. According to legend the patriarch Hayk founded the nation by leading the Armenians to victory over Bel of Babylon. Their language is Indo-European, and its exact place in the family is debated. Until recently scholars thought it most closely related to Greek and Ancient Macedonian. The exonym Armenia is first attested around the 6th century BCE, when Darius I of Persia calls the land Armina in the Behistun Inscription of 517 BCE.

The first geographical entity called Armenia was the Satrapy of Armenia, set up in the late 6th century BCE under the Orontid dynasty within the Achaemenid Empire. The Orontids later ruled the independent Kingdom of Armenia, which reached its largest extent between 95 and 65 BCE under Tigran the Great of the Artaxiad dynasty, from the Caucasus to what is now central Turkey, Lebanon and northern Iran. In the early 4th century the kingdom became the first state to adopt Christianity as its state religion, a claim resting chiefly on the 5th-century account of Agathangelos, who describes the baptism of King Trdat III by Gregory the Illuminator.

In 885 the Armenians re-established a sovereign kingdom under Ashot I of the Bagratid dynasty. Many nobles and peasants fled the Byzantine occupation of 1045 and the Seljuk invasion of 1064 to Cilicia, where in 1080 they founded a principality and then a kingdom that had close ties with the Crusader States and succumbed to Mamluk invasions.

From the early 16th century Western and Eastern Armenia fell under Safavid rule, and after the Treaty of Zuhab Eastern Armenia was ruled by Safavid, Afsharid and Qajar Iran until the late 1820s, when the Treaty of Turkmenchay brought it into the Russian Empire, while the western part stayed Ottoman. The ethnic cleansing of Armenians in the last years of the Ottoman Empire is widely considered a genocide, with about 1.2 million victims, in waves from 1894 to 1896 and in 1915 and 1916.

Most Armenians belong to the Armenian Apostolic Church, a non-Chalcedonian church of Oriental Orthodoxy, called the world's oldest national church. Mesrop Mashtots invented the Armenian alphabet in 405. Armenian has Eastern and Western forms, which are mutually intelligible; Western Armenian is used mainly in the diaspora formed after the genocide. Small trading and religious communities have long existed abroad, among them an Armenian community in the Holy Land since the 4th century and the Armenian Quarter of the Old City of Jerusalem. Armenian architecture and miniature painting have dominated its art, and carpet weaving was historically a major occupation of women.
armillary-sphere: In China, Joseph Needham traced the earliest armillary sphere to the astronomers Shi Shen and Gan De in the 4th century BCE, who had a primitive single-ring instrument, but the sinologist Christopher Cullen rejects that dating and places the beginnings in the 1st century BCE. Under the Western Han, Geng Shouchang introduced the first permanently fixed equatorial ring in 52 BCE, and under the Eastern Han Fu An and Jia Kui added the ecliptic ring by 84 CE. Zhang Heng completed the sphere with horizon and meridian rings in 125 CE and operated it with an inflow water clock. Su Song's clock tower of 1094 was crowned by an armillary sphere.

The Greek astronomer Hipparchus credited Eratosthenes with the invention. Armillary spheres existed by the Hellenistic period and served as teaching tools in the 3rd century BCE, though the fully developed sphere of nine circles perhaps did not exist until the mid-2nd century CE.

An armillary sphere is a model of objects on the celestial sphere: a spherical framework of rings centred on Earth or the Sun, representing lines of the celestial coordinate system and features such as the ecliptic. It differs from a celestial globe, a smooth sphere meant mainly to map the constellations. The English name comes from the Latin armilla, 'circle' or 'bracelet'. In its simplest form it is a ring in the plane of the equator, crossed by a second ring in the plane of the meridian. With the Earth at the centre it is called Ptolemaic, and with the Sun at the centre, Copernican.

Islamic astronomers continued to build and improve armillary spheres, and the spherical astrolabe, a variant, was likely invented in the Middle East; the earliest description is by the Persian astronomer Nayrizi. In Korea, Chang Yŏngsil built one in 1433 for King Sejong. Before the European telescope of the 17th century, the armillary sphere was the prime instrument of astronomers for determining celestial positions. Renaissance scientists and public figures had themselves painted with a hand on one. It became a badge of Manuel I of Portugal and a symbol of Portugal and its overseas empire, and it appears on the national flag.
arminius: Arminius was born in 18 or 17 BCE in Germania, the son of the Cheruscan chief Segimerus, who was allied with Rome. The name Arminius is probably not his Germanic name, but one granted with Roman citizenship. He learned Latin and, with his younger brother Flavus, joined the Roman army, in which he served between 1 and 6 CE. He received a military education, Roman citizenship and the status of eques, which gave him knowledge of Roman politics and tactics that he later used against the Romans. He returned to northern Germania in 7 or 8 CE, where Rome had secured the lands east of the Rhine and was seeking to extend its hold to the Weser and Elbe under the governor Publius Quinctilius Varus.

Arminius plotted to unite the Germanic tribes against Rome, a hard task since they were strongly independent and many were enemies of each other. Between 6 and 9 CE the Romans moved eight of the eleven legions east of the Rhine to put down a revolt in the Balkans, leaving Varus with three. In autumn 9 CE Arminius brought Varus a false report of rebellion and persuaded him to divert his legions. In the Teutoburg Forest, near Kalkriese Hill about 20 kilometres north of present-day Osnabrück, the Cherusci and their allies ambushed and annihilated the army of over 20,000 men along a narrow forest road. Varus fell on his sword.

Between 14 and 16 Germanicus led punitive campaigns, fighting Arminius to a draw at Pontes Longi and, according to Tacitus, defeating him twice. Roman troops recovered two of the three lost legionary eagles, and Tiberius then fixed the frontier at the Rhine. In 15 Germanicus captured Arminius's wife Thusnelda while she was pregnant.

Arminius was murdered in 21 by opponents within his own tribe, who felt he was growing too powerful. Tacitus called him without doubt the liberator of Germania. Rome made no further concerted effort to hold Germania beyond the Rhine, and modern historians count his victory among the most decisive battles in history. The rediscovery of Tacitus made him a symbol of German national identity, and Martin Luther possibly first called him Hermann. Heinrich von Kleist wrote the play Die Hermannsschlacht in 1808, and the Hermannsdenkmal near Detmold, begun in 1838, was dedicated after the Franco-Prussian War.
armistice-of-11-november-1918: The position of the Central Powers had worsened rapidly since the Battle of Amiens in August 1918. After Bulgaria's resistance collapsed, an invasion of Germany from the south became possible, and the Allied blockade caused food shortages and disorder at home. On 29 September the Army Command told Wilhelm II the situation was hopeless, and Erich Ludendorff demanded a ceasefire. Prince Maximilian of Baden became chancellor on 3 October, and by 5 October Germany had asked Woodrow Wilson to negotiate on the basis of his Fourteen Points. The sailors' revolt at Wilhelmshaven on 29 to 30 October spread across Germany, and on 9 November Prince Max announced the Kaiser's abdication and handed power to Friedrich Ebert.

The German delegation, led by the civilian politician Matthias Erzberger, reached Ferdinand Foch's private train in the Forest of Compiègne on 8 November. The Germans were given 72 hours to agree, and there was little negotiation. Ebert told Erzberger to sign on 10 November. The armistice was agreed at 5:00 a.m. on 11 November and took effect at 11:00 a.m. Paris time.

Its 34 clauses ended hostilities on the Western Front and required German evacuation of France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Alsace-Lorraine within 15 days, and of the west bank of the Rhine, with bridgeheads at Mainz, Koblenz and Cologne. Germany had to surrender 5,000 artillery pieces, 1,700 aircraft and all its submarines, and the naval blockade continued. It was extended three times before the Treaty of Versailles took effect on 10 January 1920.

Fighting went on until 11 a.m., and 2,738 men died on the last day of the war. Reactions at the front were muted, with silence and emptiness after 52 months. The German High Command laid the blame on others, including the socialists in government, which unsettled the Weimar Republic and fed the stab-in-the-back myth. 11 November is commemorated as Armistice Day, Remembrance Day or Veterans Day.
armistice-of-mudros: In 1918 the Ottoman Empire advanced in the Caucasus after the Russian Caucasus Army fell apart, while in Syria British forces pushed the Ottomans steadily back, and Damascus fell in October. Enver Pasha, one of the most influential members of the government, hid information that made the position look weak and led most of the elite to believe the war was still winnable.

In September 1918 Allied forces under Louis Franchet d'Espèrey launched a sudden offensive on the Macedonian front, and Bulgaria sued for peace in the Armistice of Salonica. The Ottomans now faced defending Constantinople against an overland attack without Bulgarian help. Grand Vizier Talaat Pasha visited Berlin and Sofia, concluded the war could not be won and persuaded his colleagues to resign. The ministry stepped down on 13 October, and Ahmed Izzet Pasha, the new Grand Vizier, sent the captured British General Charles Townshend to the Allies to seek terms.

The British cabinet decided to negotiate alone, excluding the French, and chose an armistice rather than a peace treaty, which they thought would need the approval of all the Allies and be too slow. Talks began on Sunday 27 October on the battleship HMS Agamemnon. The Ottoman delegation was led by Minister of Marine Affairs Rauf Bey, and the British refused to admit the senior French naval officer. Admiral Somerset Arthur Gough-Calthorpe held 24 demands but could concede any except occupation of the Dardanelles forts and free passage through the Bosphorus.

Neither side knew the other was eager to settle, so the British draft was accepted largely unchanged. The Ottomans surrendered their garrisons outside Anatolia, granted the Allies the right to occupy forts on the Straits and any territory in case of disorder, demobilised the army, air force and navy, opened ports and railways, and withdrew to the pre-war borders in the Caucasus. It was signed on 30 October and took effect at noon the next day.

The French premier Georges Clemenceau disliked the British acting alone, but accepted the matter as closed after David Lloyd George pointed to the Salonica armistice, which the French had concluded themselves.

Italian and Greek incursions into Anatolia in the name of restoring order soon came close to partition, and the Treaty of Sèvres of 1920 divided the empire into zones of influence. Nationalist forces based in Ankara rejected it and took control of Anatolia by 1923. The Treaty of Lausanne, signed on 24 July 1923, superseded the armistice and set the borders of the Turkish state.
arnhem: Arnhem lies in the eastern Netherlands near the German border, on the Nederrijn and the Sint-Jansbeek. It is the capital of the province of Gelderland. The earliest human traces near it are two firestones about 70,000 years ago, and the first settlement dates from about 1500 BCE at the Hoogkamp. The town did not grow up on the bank of the Rhine but a little higher, along the Sint-Jansbeek, where the road from Nijmegen split towards Utrecht and Zutphen; seven streams supplied it with water, and it stood on the river itself only after the Rhine's flow was changed in 1530.

The place was first mentioned in 893 as Arneym or Arentheym. In 1233 Count Otto II of Guelders conferred city rights on the town, which had belonged to the abbey of Prüm, and fortified it. Arnhem joined the Hanseatic League in 1443 and was captured by Charles the Bold of Burgundy in 1473. Charles of Egmond, duke of Guelders, took it back in 1514, and in 1543 it fell to the emperor Charles V. As capital of the Kwartier van Veluwe it joined the Union of Utrecht in 1579 during the Eighty Years' War, and after Dutch and English troops captured it from the Spanish in 1585 it became part of the Republic of the Seven United Provinces.

The French occupied it from 1672 to 1674 and again from 1795 to 1813. In the early 19th century the old fortifications were almost entirely taken down, and only the Sabelspoort survives of the medieval walls. The town became a genteel resort known as the Little Hague of the East, because rich former planters from the Indies settled there.

In Operation Market Garden in September 1944 the British 1st Airborne Division under Major-General Roy Urquhart and the Polish 1st Independent Parachute Brigade were to secure the bridge at Arnhem. Landings began on 17 September, but the bulk of the force came down far from the bridge. Only the 2nd Parachute Battalion under Lieutenant Colonel John D. Frost reached it, and it could not secure both ends against the German 9th and 10th SS Panzer Divisions. The force at the bridge ran out of ammunition and was captured on 21 September, and the rest withdrew on 26 September.

A second battle in April 1945 liberated the city, and reconstruction lasted until 1969. The rebuilt bridge is named the John Frost Bridge, and the Arnhem Oosterbeek War Cemetery holds the graves of most of those killed in the landings.
arno: The Arno rises on Monte Falterona in the Casentino area of the Apennines and at first curves southward. Near Arezzo it turns west and runs through Florence, Empoli and Pisa to the sea at Marina di Pisa. It is the longest river of Tuscany and the most important river of central Italy after the Tiber.

Its tributaries include the Sieve (60 kilometres), the Bisenzio (49 kilometres), the Ombrone Pistoiese (47 kilometres), the Era, the Elsa, the Pesa and the Pescia. The drainage basin covers more than 8,200 square kilometres. It includes the Val di Chiana, a marshy plain that drained to the Tiber until it was drained in the 18th century. The mouth was once near Pisa but now lies several kilometres farther west.

The name comes from the Latin Arnus, which Pliny uses in his Natural History. The philologist Hans Krahe linked it to a paleo-European root derived from the Proto-Indo-European *er-, meaning to flow or move.

The river's flow is very irregular and is sometimes described as torrentlike, since it can pass from almost dry to near flood within a few days. Ferdinando Morozzi recorded that between 1177 and 1761 the Arno overflowed 54 times, more than half of them major or severe floods.

The flood of 4 November 1966 followed 338.7 millimetres of rain at Badia Agnano in 24 hours, with a flow of about 4,200 cubic metres per second. The embankment at Florence collapsed. Reports of the dead range from 35 to over 100, and millions of works of art and rare books were damaged or destroyed. An international relief effort followed, and new conservation techniques came out of the disaster, though hundreds of works still await restoration. Dams built upstream of Florence have since reduced the danger.

In Florence the Arno passes below the Ponte Vecchio and the Santa Trinita bridge, built by Bartolomeo Ammannati to a design inspired by Michelangelo. Before Pisa the Imperial Canal runs under the river through a tunnel at La Botte, draining the former Lago di Bientina, once the largest lake in Tuscany.

The water of the basin is used for drinking, irrigation and firefighting. Over 90 per cent of the fish species around Florence are non-native. The river god Arno, the personification of the river, is shown as a reclining, bearded figure holding an urn from which water flows, a Renaissance design that reused an ancient statue.
arnold-schoenberg: Arnold Schoenberg was born on 13 September 1874 in Vienna's Leopoldstadt, into a lower-middle-class Jewish family. His father Samuel, a shoe shopkeeper, came from Szécsény in Hungary, and his mother Pauline Nachod was from a Prague family. He began violin at eight and taught himself to write music by arranging and imitating what he played. Largely self-taught, he began studying counterpoint with Alexander von Zemlinsky about 1894. In 1898 he converted to Christianity, in keeping with the Jewish assimilation of the time, but his Jewish identity remained integral to him amid rising antisemitism. In 1901 he married Zemlinsky's sister Mathilde.

In his twenties Schoenberg supported himself by orchestrating operettas while composing his own music, among it the string sextet Verklärte Nacht (1899). In 1911 he moved to Berlin, where his paintings were shown beside those of Kandinsky and Marc in exhibitions of Der Blaue Reiter. In 1918 he founded the Society for Private Musical Performances in Vienna, which gave 353 performances before it went defunct amid the Austrian hyperinflation.

From 1925 he led the composition master class at the Prussian Academy of Arts in Berlin. When the Nazis took power in 1933 he was warned in France against returning to Germany and formally returned to Judaism at a Paris synagogue. He reached the United States on 31 October 1933 and adopted the spelling Schoenberg. He taught in Boston and then in Los Angeles, where he became visiting professor at the University of California, Los Angeles in 1935 and professor in 1936.

His music is traditionally divided into three periods. The first, 1894 to 1907, is Romantic, with traits of both Brahms and Wagner. The second, 1908 to 1922, experiments with extended tonality and the abandonment of key centres; his String Quartet No. 2 was the first piece with no stated key centre, and Pierrot lunaire (1912) belongs here. The third begins in 1923, when he began to use ordered tone rows, a method he described as composing with twelve tones related only to one another. Among his twelve-tone works are the Variations for Orchestra and the unfinished opera Moses und Aron.

The Nazis denounced his music as degenerate. After the war he memorialised the victims of the Holocaust in A Survivor from Warsaw (1947). His pupils included Alban Berg and Anton Webern, and his work influenced Milton Babbitt, Pierre Boulez and Theodor W. Adorno.
arnsberg: Arnsberg lies in the north-east of the Sauerland, in the valley of the Ruhr, which meanders around the south of the old town. The town is almost completely encircled by forest, and the nature park Arnsberger Wald lies to the north. It is in the Hochsauerland district of North Rhine-Westphalia and is linked by motorway and railway to Dortmund and the Ruhr region.

Arnsberg was first mentioned in 789 in the Carolingian records as belonging to the abbey of Werden. It was the seat of the Counts of Arnsberg from around 1070 and received city rights in 1238. In the 12th century it became the seat of Westphalian jurisdiction. In 1368 Gottfried IV, the last count, who had no heir, handed the city and county to the Electorate of Cologne, and it was incorporated into the Duchy of Westphalia, a possession of Cologne. Arnsberg Castle, whose remains can still be visited, was rebuilt by Johann Conrad Schlaun as a residence and hunting lodge for Elector Clemens August of Bavaria, and was destroyed in 1769 in the Seven Years' War.

In 1794, when the French attacked Cologne, part of the treasure of Cologne Cathedral and the relics of the Magi were brought to safety at Arnsberg. They were returned in 1804. In 1816 Arnsberg came under Prussian rule and was made a local administrative centre.

During the Second World War the town suffered widespread destruction and heavy loss of life when RAF Lancasters breached the dam of the Möhne Reservoir on the night of 16 to 17 May 1943 in Operation Chastise, which washed away the nearby Abbey Himmelpforten. Later British air raids aimed at the railway viaduct killed dozens of its citizens, and the target was finally destroyed on 19 March 1945 with a Grand Slam bomb.

The present city was formed in 1975 by merging twelve surrounding municipalities. Old Arnsberg and Neheim-Hüsten are the two main urban areas, and the other parts are mostly rural. The city is the seat of the Regierungsbezirk Arnsberg administration. Its arms show a white eagle, on blue since the 17th century in reference to the Bavarian blue of the House of Wittelsbach; the eagle was earlier on red, as introduced in 1278 for the counts of Arnsberg. Its population is mostly Roman Catholic, and it belongs to the Archdiocese of Paderborn.
arnstadt: Arnstadt lies on the river Gera in Thuringia, about 20 kilometres south of Erfurt, on the northern edge of the Thuringian Forest, which gives it the nickname Das Tor zum Thüringer Wald, the Gateway to the Thuringian Forest. It has a well-preserved historic centre with a partly preserved town wall and a population of about 27,000. Its notable buildings include the 13th-century Romanesque-Gothic Liebfrauenkirche, the former Franciscan church called the Oberkirche and the Bach Church.

A deed of gift issued on 1 May 704 by the Thuringian Duke Hedan II to the bishop Willibrord of Utrecht is the first written mention of Arnstadt, and the oldest documented reference to settlements in Thuringia. In 954 Emperor Otto I made peace there with his rebellious son Liudolf of Swabia. On 8 March 1198 the princes of the Holy Roman Empire gathered in Arnstadt and elected Philip of Swabia King of Germany. The town was first called a civitas in 1220, and a charter of 1266 made it a trade hub in timber, grain and wine.

The counts of Schwarzburg took possession between 1302 and 1306, and Erfurt's attempts to seize the town in 1342 and 1345 failed because of its strong fortifications. In the German Peasants' War 95 ringleaders were beheaded in the marketplace in 1525. The Reformation was introduced in 1531, and the count's residence, Neideck Castle, was begun in 1553.

Johann Sebastian Bach was appointed organist of the New Church in 1703, at the age of eighteen, in his first post. The organ, newly built by Johann Friedrich Wender, was a modern instrument with well-tempered tuning. His time in Arnstadt ended in 1707, and the church is now called the Bach Church. The town claims the Bratwurst, citing a reference of 1404, and is a manufacturing centre with glassworks and foundries. Its old town is closed to traffic.
arnulf-of-carinthia: Arnulf was the son of Carloman of Bavaria and Liutswind. West Frankish writers call him illegitimate, but it is possible that Carloman later married Arnulf's mother, which would have legitimised him. His father gave him the Duchy of Carinthia, and he spent his childhood at Moosburg in Carinthia, which was close to the Carolingian palace at Karnburg. After a stroke incapacitated Carloman in 879, Arnulf was confirmed in Carinthia. In 882 he supported Engelschalk II of Pannonia in the Wilhelminer War, which ruined his relationship with his uncle, Emperor Charles the Fat, and set him at war with Svatopluk of Moravia.

In November 887 a diet at Tribur met, and Arnulf, supported by nobles from the eastern parts of the empire, deposed the ailing Charles the Fat and was proclaimed king. Charles died at the start of 888. Regions of West Francia, Burgundy and Italy elected their own rulers, though Odo of Paris formally accepted Arnulf's suzerainty. In 891 Vikings crushed an East Frankish army at Maastricht, but in September Arnulf repelled them, and the Annales Fuldenses report that the dead Northmen blocked the river. At the Diet of Worms in May 895 he crowned his illegitimate son Zwentibold king of Lotharingia.

Arnulf failed to conquer Great Moravia in 892, 893 and 899, but Bohemia broke away from Moravia in 895 and became his vassal. In 894, at the request of Pope Formosus, he invaded Italy and took Pavia. He returned in 895 and took Rome by force on 21 February 896, and Formosus crowned him emperor on 22 February. A stroke then forced him to return to Bavaria, and he kept power in Italy only while he was there.

After the stroke Arnulf also suffered from an infestation of lice on his eyelid, which prevented him from dealing with his problems. Italy was lost, raiders from Moravia and the Magyars harassed his lands, and Lotharingia revolted against Zwentibold. He died at Regensburg on 8 December 899 and is entombed in St. Emmeram's Basilica. His only legitimate son, Louis the Child, succeeded him, and when Louis died in 911 the East Frankish branch of the Carolingian dynasty ceased to exist. In his last year Arnulf had sought help from the Magyars against Moravia, and they were then settled in the Carpathian Basin. Zwentibold ruled Lotharingia until his murder in 900.
arpad: Árpád was the son of Álmos, whom all Hungarian chronicles name as the first head of the confederation of the Magyar tribes. His mother's name and family are unknown. The historian Gyula Kristó holds that he was born around 845, and his name derives from the Hungarian word for barley, árpa. Most details of his life are debated, because the sources contradict one another. He may have been the sacred ruler, the kende, or the military leader, the gyula. The Byzantine emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus says the Hungarians had never had another prince before him, and that he was made prince by being lifted on a shield.

The earliest reliable source says that the Byzantine emperor Leo VI sent his envoy Nicetas Sclerus to the Hungarians in 894 or 895 to incite them against Bulgaria. Sclerus met their two leaders, Árpád and Kurszán, on the Lower Danube, and a Hungarian army crossed the river on Byzantine ships and defeated the Bulgarians. The Bulgarians then hired the Pechenegs, and in 895 or 896 the two attacked Hungarian lands in the western Pontic steppes. The destruction of their dwellings forced the Hungarians to cross the Carpathian Mountains towards the Pannonian Plain.

Historians disagree about Árpád's position. Sources written in East Francia do not know his name and mention only Kurszán, so Kristó and others think Kurszán commanded the forces as gyula while Árpád was the sacred kende. Chronicles written centuries later, such as the Gesta Hungarorum, stress Árpád's preeminent part in the conquest of the Carpathian Basin.

The date of his death is debated, and the Gesta Hungarorum gives 907. Constantine Porphyrogenitus names four sons, Tarkatzous, Ielech, Ioutotzas and Zaltas. Until the male line of his dynasty died out in 1301, Hungary was ruled by a single line of princes, all descended from Árpád. Hungarians call him honalapító, the founder of our homeland.
arpad-goncz: Árpád Göncz was born on 10 February 1922 in Budapest into an upper-middle-class family of noble origin. His father, Lajos Göncz, worked as a post officer, and his mother, Ilona Haimann, was born in Transylvania. After the Soviet occupation of Hungary he joined the anti-communist Independent Smallholders' Party, which won the November 1945 election but had to accept a coalition in which the Communists kept the Interior Ministry and the police. He worked as personal assistant to the party's general secretary, Béla Kovács. After 1949, with the party absorbed into a communist-led front, he worked as a manual labourer and later as an agronomist.

During the revolution of 1956 Göncz was present at the demonstration of 23 October. He was arrested on 28 May 1957 with István Bibó, and on 2 August 1958 he was secretly tried and sentenced to life imprisonment, shortly after the execution of Imre Nagy. He was held in Budapest and then at Vác, where he learned to read and write English and translated John Galsworthy's The Forsyte Saga. Released in 1963, he made his living as a translator of more than a hundred literary works. His best-known translation is J. R. R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings, published in Hungary in 1981; Dezső Tandori translated its poems.

In 1988 Göncz co-founded the Historical Justice Committee, which demanded a proper reburial for Imre Nagy. He helped organise the reburial on 16 June 1989 and opened the ceremony. He was also a founding member of the Alliance of Free Democrats.

Göncz became Speaker of the National Assembly, the de facto head of state, and on 4 August 1990 the Assembly elected him president by 295 votes to 13. He was Hungary's first freely elected head of state, and the first in 42 years who was not a communist or fellow traveller. In his inaugural speech he said he would serve those who lacked the means to protect themselves. He served until 4 August 2000, when Ferenc Mádl succeeded him. He attended the signing of Hungary's accession to the European Union in Athens in April 2003 and died in Budapest on 6 October 2015, aged 93.
arpanet: Traditional telephone networks used circuit switching, in which each call is allocated a dedicated end-to-end connection. In the early 1960s Paul Baran at the RAND Corporation challenged this model, researching systems that could keep operating during partial destruction, but the telecommunication establishment rejected his work. Donald Davies at the National Physical Laboratory in the United Kingdom independently arrived at a similar concept in 1965.

In February 1966 Bob Taylor lobbied the director of the Advanced Research Projects Agency, Charles M. Herzfeld, to fund a network project, and Herzfeld redirected one million dollars from a ballistic missile defense program. Taylor hired Larry Roberts as program manager in January 1967. After an April 1967 design session, Wesley Clark proposed using minicomputers as interfaces, which Roberts named Interface Message Processors. In 1969 the contract to build them went to Bolt Beranek & Newman.

The initial configuration linked UCLA, the Augmentation Research Center at Stanford Research Institute, the University of California, Santa Barbara, and the University of Utah. The nodes were connected electronically in 1969, but applications became possible only with the Network Control Program, implemented in 1970 under the leadership of Steve Crocker, then a graduate student at UCLA. The network was declared operational in 1971, and by 1981 it numbered 213 host computers.

In 1971 Ray Tomlinson of BBN sent the first network email, and a study in 1973 found that three-quarters of the traffic consisted of email. The network was a research project, and because of its government funding personal and commercial use was discouraged or prohibited.

Bob Kahn and Vint Cerf formulated the Transmission Control Program for internetworking, which joined separate networks into a network of networks. TCP/IP became the standard for the ARPANET on 1 January 1983, after the Department of Defense had made it the standard for all military computer networking. The National Science Foundation funded the Computer Science Network in 1981 and NSFNET in 1986.

The ARPANET was formally decommissioned on 28 February 1990. Its packet switching, decentralised design and protocols laid the foundation of the Internet. Charles Herzfeld said the network was not begun to build a command system that would survive a nuclear attack, as many later claimed, but out of frustration that researchers were geographically separated from the few powerful computers.
arquebus: The word comes from the Dutch haakbus, hook gun, and was applied to many kinds of firearm. It first meant a handgun with a hook-like lug under the barrel, used to steady it against battlements. In their earliest forms these were defensive weapons mounted on German city walls in the early 15th century. The first certain use of the term dates from 1364, when Bernabò Visconti, lord of Milan, recruited 70 archibuxoli, though these were almost certainly hand cannon.

A shoulder stock was added in Europe around 1470, and the matchlock mechanism appeared a little before 1475, making the arquebus the first firearm with a trigger. The dating is disputed: some scholars have proposed that the matchlock was invented in Turkey by 1465, while others find the evidence for a European origin overwhelming.

In the matchlock, a length of smouldering rope soaked in saltpetre, the match, was held in a clamp. Squeezing the trigger lowered it into a priming pan, and the flash passed through the touch hole to ignite the powder in the barrel. A heavy version, later called the musket, appeared around 1521 to pierce plate armour. In the later 16th century the standardised caliver allowed faster loading, since bullets fitted its bore. The matchlock arquebus is seen as the successor to the hand cannon and the forerunner of the flintlock musket.

The Ottomans used arquebuses in the 1440s, and arquebusiers fought at the second battle of Kosovo in 1448. In Europe the Black Army of Hungary under Matthias Corvinus used them in unusual numbers, one infantryman in four, though by about 1500 only some 10 per cent of Western European infantry carried firearms. At Cerignola in 1503 they played a decisive role.

The Mamluks scorned gunpowder weapons, and in 1514 an Ottoman army of 12,000 arquebusiers devastated a much larger Mamluk army. The arquebus was cheap, since a helmet, breastplate and pike cost about three and a quarter ducats and an arquebus a little over one, and an arquebusier could be trained in two weeks.

It reached India by 1500, Southeast Asia by 1540 and China between 1523 and 1548. Portuguese traders introduced it to Japan in 1543 on Tanegashima, and within ten years upwards of three hundred thousand were reported made there. Arquebusiers needed protection while reloading, so pikemen, archers, artillery or fortified wagons were paired with them. At Nieuwpoort in 1600 Maurice of Nassau used the countermarch volley technique.
arras: Arras stands in northern France at the confluence of the rivers Scarpe and Crinchon, on a large chalk plateau, 182 kilometres north of Paris. Its chalk was quarried to build the most prestigious buildings and houses, so that residents once nicknamed it La ville blanche, the White Town, while its clay was used for bricks. The Crinchon flows through the city underground, and the Scarpe, two-thirds of it turned into canals, runs on through Douai to join the Scheldt.

Stone tools of the Mousterian culture mark prehistoric settlement in the Scarpe basin. The town was founded on the hill of Baudimont by the Belgic tribe of the Atrebates, who named it Nemetocenna after a nemeton that probably stood there. The Romans renamed it Nemetacum or Atrebatum and made it an important garrison town. In the 4th century it was known for its arts and crafts and its textile trade. Germanic invaders took and destroyed it in 406 or 407, and in 428 the Salian Franks under Clodion took control of the region.

After Clovis I became a Catholic, a diocese was created at Arras in 499 and given to Saint Vaast, who established an episcopal see and a monastic community. It was suppressed in 580 to found the diocese of Cambrai, from which Arras re-emerged five centuries later. By 843 Arras was the seat of the County of Artois, which joined the royal domain in 1191. Arras was once part of the Spanish Netherlands, controlled by Spain from 1556 to 1714; Louis XIII conquered it in 1640, and it officially became part of France in 1659.

Arras is the prefecture of the Pas-de-Calais department, and 42,621 residents were counted in 2022. The city centre is marked by two squares, La Grand'Place and La Place des Héros, surrounded by 155 Flemish-Baroque townhouses built in the 17th and 18th centuries, most of which were so badly damaged in 1918 that they had to be restored. The town hall and its 75-metre belfry date from the early 16th century and were rebuilt after the First World War; the belfry has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005. Beneath the city lies the Boves, tunnels 10 metres down that sheltered residents in both world wars. Arras was a centre of trouvère poetry, and Maximilien de Robespierre was born there.
arrian: Arrian was born in Nicomedia, the provincial capital of Bithynia, between about 85 and 90 CE. His full Roman name, Lucius Flavius Arrianus, shows that he was a Roman citizen, and his family belonged to the Greek provincial aristocracy, with citizenship probably going back several generations to the time of the Roman conquest. While in Epirus, probably at Nicopolis, he attended the lectures of Epictetus and became his pupil. In Athens he came to be known as the young Xenophon, because his relationship to Epictetus resembled Xenophon's to Socrates.

About 126 he was a friend of the emperor Hadrian, who appointed him to the Senate. He became consul suffectus about 130 and in 132, though one scholar gives 131, Hadrian made him governor of Cappadocia, a post he held for six years. According to Cassius Dio, after the Bar Kokhba revolt was suppressed in 135, King Pharasmanes II of Iberia caused the Alani to invade neighbouring lands, including Cappadocia, where Arrian's legions halted them. Dio adds that the Alani were also persuaded by gifts from Vologaesus and stood in dread of Arrian. Lucian called him a Roman of the first rank with a life-long attachment to learning, and Arrian himself used the title of second Xenophon.

Eight of his works survive; only the Anabasis and the Indica are wholly intact. The Anabasis of Alexander, in seven books, is considered the best source on the campaigns of Alexander the Great, modelled on Xenophon's account of the march of Cyrus. Scholars have generally preferred Arrian to other surviving primary sources, though modern study of his method has qualified this. The Indica draws on Megasthenes for India and on the journal of Nearchus for the voyage in the Persian Gulf.

He recorded the teaching of Epictetus in the Discourses, which he says he published because his notes were being circulated without authority, and in the Enchiridion, a short handbook of Epictetus's principles. Other works include a Periplus of the Euxine Sea addressed to Hadrian, the Techne Taktike on cavalry and tactics (136 or 137), and a treatise on hunting with hounds meant as an addition to Xenophon. His Parthica, on Trajan's Parthian war, his history of Alexander's successors and several biographies are lost or survive in fragments. Pliny the Younger addressed seven letters to him.
arsaces-i: Literary sources on Arsaces are very scarce and come from contradictory Greek and Roman accounts written centuries after his death, and modern scholars once doubted that he existed until studies and archaeological finds in the 1960s confirmed him. The most accepted view, from the geographer Strabo, is that he was a Scythian chieftain who led the Parni, one of the three tribes of the Dahae confederacy of Central Asia. Ammianus Marcellinus calls him a bandit of low birth, and some modern historians argue that he was a native Persian. The Parni had moved into Parthia, then under Seleucid rule, and by the middle of the 3rd century BCE they had adopted the Parthian language and Zoroastrianism. Arsaces himself was probably born and raised in Parthia.

About 250 BCE Arsaces and his followers seized Astauene, and probably about 247 BCE he was crowned at Asaak, a city he had founded, which became the Arsacid royal necropolis. Andragoras, governor of the Seleucid province of Parthia, had declared his independence from Seleucus II Callinicus, and the Parni took the northern region from him and then the rest of Parthia, killing him. They also conquered Hyrcania. When Seleucus II led an expedition against him in 228 BCE, Arsaces made peace with the Greco-Bactrian ruler Diodotus II to avoid a war on two fronts, and withdrew to Central Asia among the Apasiacae. Seleucus II had to leave because of trouble elsewhere in his empire, and Arsaces regained his territory.

According to Justin, he 'settled the Parthian government, levied soldiers, built fortresses, and strengthened his towns'. He founded Dara and Nisa, which served as the Arsacid royal residence until the 1st century BCE. His coins, minted at Nisa, show a seated archer in Iranian dress in place of the Seleucid Apollo, and they bear the title kārny, once held by prominent Achaemenid military leaders, rather than the royal title basileus.

Arsaces died in 217 BCE and was succeeded by his son Arsaces II. Earlier scholars, following Jean Foy-Vaillant in 1725, held that his brother Tiridates also ruled, but numismatic data, a study by Józef Wolski and the discovery at Nisa of an ostracon bearing the name of Arsaces led to the conclusion that Tiridates is fictional. An everlasting fire in his honour was still guarded at Asaak more than two centuries after his death. His name became a royal honorific used by all the Arsacid kings, and his dynasty ruled for four and a half centuries until the Sasanian Empire overthrew it in 224 CE.
art-nouveau: The new style had its roots in Britain, in the floral designs of William Morris and the Arts and Crafts movement, which called for better treatment of the decorative arts and took inspiration from medieval craftsmanship and nature. Early prototypes include the Red House, with interiors by Morris and architecture by Philip Webb (1859), and Arthur Mackmurdo's chair and book cover of 1883.

The term Art Nouveau was first used in the 1880s in the Belgian journal L'Art Moderne to describe Les Vingt, twenty painters and sculptors seeking reform. The Franco-German dealer Siegfried Bing popularised it by opening the Maison de l'Art Nouveau in Paris in 1895, though he wrote in 1902 that it had been merely the name of a house meant as a rallying point for young artists.

Art Nouveau used the sinuous curves of plants and flowers, asymmetry and whiplash lines, and modern materials such as iron, glass, ceramics and later concrete. Early Belgian and French work took forms from lilies, vines and flower stems, and borrowed butterfly and dragonfly patterns from Japanese art. One aim was to break down the distinction between fine arts and applied arts.

The first Art Nouveau town houses, by Paul Hankar and Victor Horta, were built almost simultaneously in Brussels in 1892 and 1893, and Horta's innovation lay in the interior, where iron and glass opened up space and let in light.

The style took local forms. In Barcelona Antoni Gaudí's Modernisme used organic forms in the Palau Güell. The Vienna Secession was founded in April 1897 by Gustav Klimt, Koloman Moser, Josef Hoffmann and others. German Jugendstil took its name from the Munich journal Jugend, founded in 1896. In the United States the firm of Louis Comfort Tiffany played the central role.

The Paris Exposition Universelle of 1900 marked the high point of the style, attracting nearly fifty million visitors between April and November. By 1914 and the beginning of the First World War Art Nouveau was largely exhausted, and in the 1920s Art Deco and then modernism replaced it as the dominant style. It began to receive more positive attention from critics in the late 1960s, and a major exhibition of Hector Guimard's work was held at the Museum of Modern Art in 1970.
arta-greece: The first settlement in the area dates to the 9th century BCE. Ambracia was founded as a colony of Corinth in the 7th century BCE. In 294 BCE it was given to Pyrrhus, king of the Molossians and of Epirus, who made it his capital and a base for attacking the Romans, and adorned it with a palace, temples and theatres. In 146 BCE it became part of the Roman Republic. Arta is first attested under that name in 1082, when the Normans under Bohemond besieged it. In the Komnenian period it flourished as a commercial centre with links to Venice, and by 1157 it was a bishopric.

After the fall of Constantinople to the Fourth Crusade, the Partitio Romaniae of 1204 assigned the city to Venice, but in 1205 Michael I Komnenos Doukas came to Arta and founded the principality known as the Despotate of Epirus. The city remained its capital for most of its history, and it saw much building: the Church of the Parigoritissa and the Church of the Kato Panagia, and fortifications after 1227. Its exports to Venice and Ragusa included dried meat, lard, ham, furs and indigo.

Later the city changed hands often. Troops of the Empire of Nicaea took it after the Battle of Pelagonia in 1259, but John I Doukas soon recovered it. Andronikos II Palaiologos attacked it unsuccessfully in 1292, and the Angevins besieged it in 1303. Epirus passed to the Orsini family in 1318 and to Andronikos III Palaiologos in 1335. Arta fell to the Serbian king Stefan Dušan in 1347, was held by Albanian rulers from about 1367, and was captured by Carlo I Tocco in 1416. In 1449 it fell to the Ottomans, who called it Narda.

Arta lies on the Arachthos River, on the site of ancient Ambracia, whose remains include walls, the ruins of a temple of Apollo and a small theatre. The Castle of Arta was built by Michael I Komnenos Doukas in the early 13th century, though its present form is largely post-Byzantine. The palace of the Despots has vanished completely, but many churches survive, among them the cathedral Church of the Paregoretissa, built about 1290 by Nikephoros I Komnenos Doukas and his wife Anna Palaiologina Kantakouzene, and the Monastery of Saint Theodora, which holds the tomb of the city's patron, Theodora of Arta. The city was annexed to the Greek Kingdom in 1881.
artaxerxes-i: Artaxerxes I was the fifth King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire, ruling from August 465 to December 424 BCE. He was the third son of Xerxes I. Greek sources surname him Long-handed, allegedly because his right hand was longer than his left. He came to the throne after Xerxes was murdered in 465 BCE by Artabanus, commander of the royal bodyguard, with the help of a eunuch, Aspamitres. Greek writers disagree on details, but after Artaxerxes discovered the murder he killed Artabanus and his sons.

From 460 to 454 BCE he faced a revolt in Egypt led by Inaros II, who with Athenian help defeated the Persian army of the satrap Achaemenes. Megabyzus defeated the Athenians in 454 BCE after a two-year siege, and Inaros was captured and taken to Susa.

After the Persian defeat at the Battle of the Eurymedon, around 469 BCE, fighting stopped. Artaxerxes adopted a strategy of weakening Athens by funding its enemies in Greece. Fighting resumed in 450 BCE at the Battle of Cyprus, and when Cimon achieved little, hostilities ceased. Later sources say that the Peace of Callias was agreed among Athens, Argos and Persia in 449 BCE, but the existence of a formal treaty is disputed.

Artaxerxes gave asylum to Themistocles, the victor of Salamis over his father, after his ostracism from Athens, and gave him Magnesia, Myus and Lampsacus. Themistocles learned Persian customs and language.

Josephus and several ancient traditions identify him as the Ahasuerus of the Book of Esther. In Ezra 7 a king Artaxerxes commissions the scribe Ezra to take charge of the religious and civil affairs of the Jews. The text does not say whether Artaxerxes I or Artaxerxes II is meant; most scholars hold that Ezra lived under Artaxerxes I. In his twentieth year Nehemiah, his cup-bearer, told him of the plight of Jerusalem, and the king sent him with letters of safe passage to rebuild the city walls.
artaxerxes-iii: Artaxerxes III, whose personal name was Ochus, was the legitimate son of Artaxerxes II and his wife Stateira. Before he became king he was a satrap and commander of his father's army. The Roman writer Justin tells how his eldest brother Darius, the heir, was executed for plotting against their father, and how Ochus, with the support of some eunuchs, drove another brother, Ariaspes, to suicide and had the favoured illegitimate son Arsames killed. Ochus was then appointed crown prince. After taking the throne he murdered much of the royal family to secure his position.

On his accession he ordered the satraps of western Anatolia to disband their mercenary forces, to consolidate royal power. In 356 BCE he tried to dismiss Artabazus II from his satrapy, and Artabazus revolted, defeated royal satraps with Athenian and Theban help, and fled to Macedonia in 354 BCE. About 351 BCE Artaxerxes invaded Egypt, but Nectanebo II, supported by Greek mercenaries, defeated him, and Phoenicia, Anatolia and Cyprus then declared independence. Idrieus of Caria reduced Cyprus, and Artaxerxes led a large army against Sidon, whose king Tennes tried to buy a pardon by betraying 100 citizens. The Persian king had them killed and then 500 more. Sidon was burnt and forty thousand people died.

After years of preparation Artaxerxes invaded Egypt again, led in person, with Greek mercenaries under Mentor of Rhodes. He created three divisions of shock troops, Pelusium and Bubastis surrendered, and Nectanebo abandoned the country. Egypt returned to Persian rule after about six decades. The king had city walls destroyed, looted temples and levied high taxes, and the native religion was persecuted. He also supported the city of Perinthus against the siege of Philip II of Macedon.

In late August or September 338 BCE the court eunuch Bagoas had Artaxerxes poisoned through his physician. Bagoas had most of the king's sons murdered and put the young Arses on the throne as Artaxerxes IV. His death proved a problem for Persia and may have weakened the country, which Alexander the Great later conquered. Artaxerxes had begun a building programme at Persepolis, with a new palace and the Unfinished Gate, and his tomb was cut into the mountain behind the platform, next to his father's. Silver coins issued while he was in Egypt carry an inscription in an Egyptian script reading Artaxerxes Pharaoh.
artemis: In ancient Greek religion Artemis was the goddess of hunting, the wilderness, wild animals, transitions, nature, vegetation, childbirth, care of children and chastity. She was thought of as an unmarried maiden and as one of the three major virgin goddesses, alongside Athena and Hestia. She protected children, especially girls, and animal cubs, and was worshipped and feared as a goddess of childbirth and midwifery along with Eileithyia and Hera. She was believed to grant health or to send illness and death to women and children.

Classically she is a young huntress in a short skirt and hunting boots, with a quiver and a golden or silver bow, often roaming the mountains with a retinue of nymphs. Homer calls her Potnia Theron, mistress of animals, a title linked with images of a woman between two animals that go back to the Bronze Age. The deer was sacred to her, and the etymology of her name is uncertain.

Artemis was worshipped throughout ancient Greece with many local variations. Her best-known cults were on Delos, in Attica at Brauron and Mounikhia, and in Sparta, where the Spartans sacrificed to her before a campaign. The cult at Ephesus, where she was worshipped chiefly as a mother goddess like the Phrygian Cybele, eventually surpassed the others in fame. At Patras the Laphria festival centred on an annual bonfire into which domestic and wild animals were thrown alive.

Common practices included animal sacrifice, hymns, dances and processions, and votive offerings of jewellery, clothing or pottery. Her temples often stood outside city limits or between land and water. Her virginity may relate to her role as huntress, since hunters traditionally abstained from sex before a hunt.

Myths tell how the hunter Actaeon was turned into a stag and killed by dogs, in some versions for seeing Artemis bathing, and how she demanded the sacrifice of Iphigenia after Agamemnon killed her sacred deer. In the Trojan War she took the side of the Trojans. The Romans identified her with Diana and with the moon goddess Selene, although no record has been found of the Greeks calling Artemis a lunar deity. Her name survives in the genus Artemia, the brine shrimp.
arthashastra: The Sanskrit title can be rendered as a treatise on political science, economic science or simply statecraft, since the word artha has a broad range of meanings. Artha, prosperity or material security, is one of the four aims of human life in Hinduism, beside dharma, kama and moksha. The text names two compilers, Kautilya (or Kautalya) and Vishnugupta, and a later interpolation and the traditions of the Gupta era and the Middle Ages identified Kautilya with Chanakya. Scholarship has questioned that identification, and the main studies since 1965 reject it.

Patrick Olivelle and McClish hold that the work grew in layers: earlier arthashastras dating from the 2nd century BCE to the 1st century CE were compiled in the 1st century CE, and a major redaction followed in the 2nd or 3rd century CE. Stylistic differences point to several hands, and some details fit the first centuries CE better than the Mauryan age.

The surviving text has 15 books, 150 chapters and 180 topics. It covers the training of a king, the work of the superintendents who ran mines, workshops, customs, agriculture and shipping, civil and criminal law, spying, diplomacy and war. It also deals with ministers, marriage and the remarriage of women, forests and wildlife, and taxation. The economy it describes is mixed: mines were owned by the state but leased to private parties, and private enterprise was taxed and regulated.

The ideal ruler is the sage king, who masters lust, anger, greed, conceit, arrogance and foolhardiness. On war, the text advises that where progress is equal, peace is to be preferred, since war brings losses, expense and absence from home. Books on foreign policy set out the sixfold strategy and the theory of the circle of states, and the text recommends a network of trained spies, including the use of women to sow quarrels among the chiefs of an enemy council.

The work was influential until the 12th century, when it disappeared from view. R. Shamasastry rediscovered a manuscript in 1905, published the Sanskrit text in 1909 and the first English translation in 1915. Verses of the work have also been found on fragments from Buddhist monasteries in north-west China, Afghanistan and north-west Pakistan, among them the Spitzer Manuscript, of about 200 CE.

In 1919 Max Weber wrote that Machiavelli's The Prince was harmless beside it. Later readers disagree about its character: Roger Boesche compared its state to a welfare-minded surveillance state, while Thomas Trautmann stresses that it recognises private property and land sales, though under rules of first refusal that do not make a free market.
arthur-conan-doyle: Arthur Ignatius Conan Doyle was born on 22 May 1859 at 11 Picardy Place, Edinburgh. His father, Charles Altamont Doyle, was born in England of Irish Catholic descent, and his mother, Mary, née Foley, was Irish Catholic. In 1864 the family was scattered because of Charles's growing alcoholism, and it came together again in 1867. His father died in 1893 in the Crichton Royal, Dumfries, after many years of psychiatric illness.

From 1876 to 1881 Doyle studied medicine at the University of Edinburgh Medical School and began writing short stories as a student. His first published piece, "The Mystery of Sasassa Valley", appeared in Chambers's Edinburgh Journal on 6 September 1879.

Doyle served as a doctor and surgeon on two sea voyages and then ran an unsuccessful medical practice in Portsmouth. His first Sherlock Holmes work, A Study in Scarlet, was written in three weeks and accepted by Ward Lock & Co on 20 November 1886 for £25. From "A Scandal in Bohemia" (1891) the Holmes stories appeared monthly in The Strand Magazine. Ambivalent about the character, he had Holmes killed in "The Final Problem" (1893), but public outcry brought him back in The Hound of the Baskervilles (1901), and he wrote Holmes stories until 1927. He also wrote The Lost World (1912), featuring Professor Challenger.

In 1900 he served as a volunteer physician at Bloemfontein during the Second Boer War and wrote a widely translated pamphlet defending the United Kingdom's role in it. He believed it earned him his knighthood from King Edward VII in 1902. He twice stood unsuccessfully for Parliament, in 1900 and 1906.

Doyle personally investigated two closed cases. The first, in 1906, concerned George Edalji, a lawyer of mixed British and Indian descent accused of threatening letters and animal mutilations at Great Wyrley; Edalji was exonerated, and the case partly led to the establishment of the Court of Criminal Appeal in 1907. Raised a Catholic, Doyle became agnostic as a young adult and later a spiritualist. His public support for the Cottingley Fairies, later confirmed as a hoax, led to a falling-out with the magician Harry Houdini. He died of a heart attack at Windlesham Manor, Crowborough, on 7 July 1930, aged 71.
arthur-evans: Arthur Evans was born on 8 July 1851 at Nash Mills, Hemel Hempstead, the first child of John Evans and Harriet Ann Dickinson. His father worked in the paper mill owned by the family of Harriet's father, John Dickinson, and profits from the mill later helped fund Evans's excavations at Knossos and his publications. He entered Harrow School in 1865 and matriculated at Brasenose College, Oxford, on 9 June 1870, where he read Modern History. His sight was blurry beyond a close distance, and he carried a cane he called Prodger to explore his surroundings.

Evans returned to Oxford with his wife Margaret in January 1883 and became Keeper of the Ashmolean Museum, then in a chaotic state of transition. He led the excavation of an Iron Age cemetery at Aylesford in Kent, published in 1890, and concluded that its culture was closely related to the continental Belgae, which remains the modern view. In 1898 he reported for the Manchester Guardian on the violence against Crete's Muslim minority and condemned religiously motivated violence from both sides.

The first excavation at Knossos was begun in 1877 by Minos Kalokairinos, until the Ottoman authorities stopped it. Evans bought the land with private funds and began work in March 1900, with Duncan Mackenzie and the architect Fyfe and 32 diggers. Within months they uncovered a large part of what he called the Palace of Minos, an intricate set of over 1,000 interlocking rooms that included workshops and wine presses and served as a storage, religious and administrative centre. He resigned as Keeper in 1908, became president of the Society of Antiquaries in 1914, and was knighted in 1911.

From what he found at Knossos and across the eastern Mediterranean, Evans concluded that he must distinguish the Minoan civilisation from Mycenaean Greece. He found about 3,000 clay tablets, which he transcribed and published in Scripta Minoa; some are now missing, so his transcriptions are the only record of their marks. He saw that the scripts were two separate systems, which he named Linear A and Linear B, with A the earlier, and he also defined an earlier pictographic writing. Linear B proved to be Greek, and Linear A has not been convincingly deciphered. His classifications and transcriptions have been of great value to scholars of Mycenaean Greece.

He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society and a founding Fellow of the British Academy in 1901. He lived at Youlbury from 1894 until his death in 1941 and left part of his estate to the Boy Scouts.
arthur-seyss-inquart: Seyss-Inquart was born on 22 July 1892 in Stannern, a German-speaking village near Iglau in Moravia, an area that formed a German linguistic island in a Czech-speaking region. His father, a school principal, was Czech and had changed his surname from Zajtich; his mother was German. The family moved to Vienna in 1907, and he studied law at the University of Vienna. In August 1914 he enlisted with the Tyrolean Kaiserjäger and served in Russia, Romania and Italy, and he was decorated for bravery several times. After the war he set up a law practice in 1921, and in 1933 he was invited to join the cabinet of Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss.

Under Kurt Schuschnigg he became a State Councillor in 1937. He was not at first a member of the Austrian National Socialist party, but by 1938 he had become a respectable frontman for it. In February 1938 Schuschnigg made him Minister of the Interior after Hitler threatened military action.
