On 11 March Schuschnigg resigned in the face of a German invasion, and President Wilhelm Miklas reluctantly appointed Seyss-Inquart chancellor. German troops crossed the border the next day at his telegraphed invitation, a telegram drafted beforehand. Hitler chose full Anschluss over a puppet state; Seyss-Inquart drafted the act making Austria the province of Ostmark, joined the Nazi Party on 13 March and became its governor.

After the invasion of Poland he was deputy to Hans Frank in the General Government until 18 May 1940. After the Dutch capitulation on 15 May 1940 he became Reichskommissar for the occupied Netherlands, answering directly to Hitler. He authorized about 800 executions, some reports putting the total above 1,500, and imposed a collective fine of 18 million guilders after the strikes of May 1943. Around 530,000 Dutch civilians were forced to work for the Germans. Of about 140,000 registered Jews, only 30,000 survived the war.

He was arrested on 5 May 1945 on the Elbe Bridge in Hamburg. At the Nuremberg trials he faced four charges and was acquitted of conspiracy but convicted on the others and sentenced to death by hanging; the judgment stressed his reign of terror in the Netherlands. He denied knowledge of the shooting of hostages and said his conscience was untroubled. He was hanged on 16 October 1946.
arthur-wellesley-1st-duke-of-wellington: Arthur Wellesley was born into an Anglo-Irish family of the Protestant Ascendancy, as the Hon. Arthur Wesley, the sixth of nine children of Garret Wesley, 1st Earl of Mornington, and Anne, Countess of Mornington. The exact date and place of his birth are not known; biographers mostly follow newspaper evidence that he was born on 1 May 1769, the day before his baptism at St. Peter's Church in Dublin.

The family was short of money, and on his mother's advice his brother Richard asked the Duke of Rutland, then Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, to consider Arthur for an army commission. He was gazetted ensign in the 73rd Regiment of Foot on 7 March 1787 and became aide-de-camp to successive lords lieutenant, in a post whose duties were mainly social. In 1798 he changed the spelling of his surname to Wellesley.

He reached Calcutta in February 1797, and his brother Richard, Lord Mornington, soon became Governor-General of India. In the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War against Tipu Sultan he ended the conflict with a victory at Seringapatam in 1799 and was appointed governor of Seringapatam and Mysore. As a major general he won a decisive victory over the Maratha Confederacy at the Battle of Assaye in 1803. In the Peninsular War he left Cork on 12 July 1808 and defeated the French at Roliça and Vimeiro. Recalled to face a Court of Enquiry after the Convention of Sintra, which he had not signed, he was cleared. He was promoted field marshal after the victory at Vitoria in 1813.

After Napoleon's first exile in 1814 he served as ambassador to France and was made Duke of Wellington. When Napoleon escaped from Elba on 26 February 1815, Wellington took command of a British-German and Dutch army in the Netherlands beside Blücher's Prussians. After Ligny and Quatre Bras he withdrew to a ridge south of Waterloo, where on 18 June he met Napoleon for the first time. He was prime minister from 1828 to 1830 and for under a month in 1834, oversaw the Roman Catholic Relief Act 1829 and strongly opposed the Reform Act 1832.

Wellington died at Walmer Castle in Kent on 14 September 1852, aged 83, of the after-effects of a stroke. He was given a state funeral in London on 18 November 1852, one of a small number of British subjects so honoured. The nickname Iron Duke relates to his political career, and its use is often disparaging; it may date from the iron shutters fitted at Apsley House in 1832 against rioters. Napoleon called him a Sepoy General, while Tsar Alexander I called him the conqueror of the world's conqueror.
artificial-cardiac-pacemaker: In 1889 John Alexander MacWilliam reported in the British Medical Journal that an electrical impulse applied to a human heart in asystole caused a ventricular contraction, and that a rhythm of 60 to 70 beats a minute could be evoked by impulses at the same spacing. In 1950 the Canadian engineer John Hopps designed and built the first external pacemaker, working from observations by the surgeons Wilfred Gordon Bigelow and John Callaghan at Toronto General Hospital. It used vacuum tubes and mains power, was crude and painful in use, and carried a risk of electrocuting the patient. Paul Zoll and others made smaller devices from 1952, powered by a large rechargeable battery.

In 1958 the engineer Earl Bakken of Minneapolis made the first wearable external pacemaker, a transistorised device in a small plastic box, for a patient of C. Walton Lillehei. In 1959 Seymour Furman and John Schwedel first demonstrated temporary transvenous pacing, inserting the electrode through a vein of the arm.

A pacemaker keeps an even heart rate when the heart's natural pacemaker gives an inadequate or irregular beat or when its electrical conduction system is blocked. A permanent pacemaker is implanted under the skin below the collarbone, with one or more electrode leads passed along a vein into the chambers of the heart under X-ray guidance. Most modern devices are pacing on demand: they sense the heart's own rhythm and stimulate it only if no beat comes within a set interval, most commonly one second. They are programmable from outside the body. Biventricular pacemakers pace both sides of the heart in heart failure, and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators combine pacing with defibrillation.

The first implantable devices suffered from the short life of the available mercury batteries. In the late 1960s several companies, among them ARCO in the United States, developed isotope-powered pacemakers, and in early 1969 researchers at the National Heart Institute tested a nuclear-powered one that used heat from plutonium-238 in a titanium case. The lithium iodide cell developed in 1971 by Wilson Greatbatch overtook them, and lithium cells became the standard. In 1982 Anthony Rickards of the National Heart Hospital in London invented the first rate-responsive, or dynamic, pacemaker. In 2013 several firms announced capsule-sized leadless pacemakers, inserted through a catheter in the leg.
arturo-toscanini: Arturo Toscanini was born in Parma, in Emilia-Romagna, the son of a tailor. He won a scholarship to the Parma Conservatory, where he studied the cello. Living conditions there were harsh and strict, and the menu consisted almost entirely of fish; in his later years he steadfastly refused to eat anything that came from the sea.

Toscanini's reputation as an operatic conductor of unusual authority and skill gradually supplanted his cello career. He was entrusted with the world premieres of Puccini's La bohème and Leoncavallo's Pagliacci. By 1898 he was principal conductor at La Scala, where he remained until 1908, returning as music director from 1921 to 1929. In December 1920 he brought the La Scala Orchestra to the United States and made his first recordings, for the Victor Talking Machine Company.

He had become disillusioned with Fascism before the March on Rome of October 1922 and repeatedly defied Mussolini, refusing to display his photograph or conduct the Fascist anthem Giovinezza at La Scala. In 1936 he resigned from the New York Philharmonic, and David Sarnoff, president of the Radio Corporation of America, proposed a radio orchestra for him. He conducted his first broadcast concert with the NBC Symphony Orchestra on 25 December 1937 in Studio 8-H at Rockefeller Center. Between 1948 and 1952 he conducted ten concerts telecast on NBC.

Toscanini conducted the world premieres of Pagliacci, La bohème, La fanciulla del West and Turandot, which have become part of the standard operatic repertoire, and the world premiere of Samuel Barber's Adagio for Strings. He was especially known for his performances of Beethoven, Brahms, Wagner, Richard Strauss, Debussy, Rossini, Verdi, Boito and Puccini.

At La Scala he pushed through reforms in the performance of opera, insisting on dimming the house lights during performances. His biographer Harvey Sachs wrote that he believed a performance could not succeed artistically unless unity of intention was first established among singers, orchestra, chorus, staging, sets and costumes. He disliked recording, especially the acoustic method, and began recording regularly only in 1938, at the age of seventy. He appeared three times on the cover of Time magazine, in 1926, 1934 and 1948.
artvin: Artvin stands on a hill overlooking the Çoruh River near the Deriner Dam, about 30 kilometres inland from the Black Sea. Above the town is a fortress that once lay within the medieval Georgian district of Nigali, with a single circuit wall around the summit, several rooms and a large donjon at the west.

Artifacts from the Bronze Age and earlier have been found. The area was part of Colchis and of Greater Armenia, and was invaded first by Scythians and then by Muslim armies led by Habib, son of Caliph Uthman, who held it from 853 CE until the Byzantines conquered it in 1023. The Principalities of Tao-Klarjeti arose in the 7th and 8th centuries and made the region one of the most important religious centres of Georgia. The Seljuk Turks conquered it in 1064, and the Safavids took it in 1502.

The Ottomans under Mehmed II defeated the Empire of Trebizond and brought the eastern Black Sea coast and its mountain hinterland under their control, and on 13 July 1551 their hold on Artvin was secure. After about 250 years the area was ceded to Russia following the war of 1828 to 1829, recovered, and ceded again after the Russo-Turkish War of 1877 to 1878. Much of the largely Muslim Georgian population moved west. British troops arrived in 1918, followed by the Democratic Republic of Georgia, and the Treaty of Kars in 1921 ceded Artvin to Turkey.

Artvin is the seat of Artvin Province and Artvin District, with 25,841 people in 2021, and the home of Artvin Çoruh University. The castle, also called Livane, was built in 937, and Ottoman buildings include the Salih Bey mosque of 1792 and the fountain of Çelebi Efendi of 1783. The Camili (Macahel) area is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve. Artvin is also a former Armenian Catholic see, established in 1850 and listed as a titular see since 1972.
arunachal-pradesh: Arunachal Pradesh, meaning Land of the Dawn-Lit Mountains, has an area of 83,743 km2. It shares borders with Bhutan in the west and Myanmar in the east, and a 1,129 km border with China's Tibet Autonomous Region in the north at the McMahon Line. Its highest peak is Kangto, at 7,060 metres. Historical Indian texts describe its mountains, the Aruna Mountains, as the place where the sun rises. The state has among the highest diversity of mammals and birds in India.

Little is known of the ancient history of the region apart from the northwest, which came under the Monpa kingdom of Monyul, under Tibetan influence, between 500 BCE and 600 CE. In the 17th century the 5th Dalai Lama, Ngawang Lobsang Gyatso, who gained political supremacy over Tibet in 1642, imposed a tax called Khrey over Monyul and ordered fortresses called Dzong built in the Monpa area as centres of administration and tax collection. The tax was carried to Tawang Monastery and then to Lhasa.

After the annexation of Assam following the First Anglo-Burmese War, the British inherited the Ahom Kingdom's system of payments to the frontier tribes, known as posa, and set out to curb headhunting, civil wars and slavery. In the 19th century there was no urgency to demarcate the border. After independence in 1947, the People's Republic of China maintained that the McMahon Line was not valid. The North-East Frontier Agency was renamed Arunachal Pradesh on 20 January 1972 and became a union territory, and on 20 February 1987 it became a state.

Itanagar is the capital and largest town. The 2011 census counted 1,383,727 people, at 17 per square kilometre the least densely populated state of India. About 23 major tribes and 100 sub-tribes live there, among them the Nyishi, the largest group, and the Adi, Apatani, Galo, Tagin, Singpho and Nocte. China claims nearly four-fifths of the state as Southern Tibet.
arusha: Arusha stands at an elevation of 1,400 metres on the southern slopes of Mount Meru, on the eastern edge of the eastern branch of the Great Rift Valley. The height keeps temperatures relatively low, typically between 10 and 30 °C, and the region has two rainy seasons, the long masika rains from March to May and the shorter vuli rains in November and December. It lies close to the Serengeti National Park, the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, Olduvai Gorge and Mount Kilimanjaro.

The site was first settled in the 1830s by the agro-pastoral Arusha Maasai from the Arusha Chini community, south of Mount Kilimanjaro. They traded grain, honey, beer and tobacco with the pastoral Kisongo Maasai for livestock, milk, meat and skins, and demand grew in the 1860s when the Pangani Valley trade route was extended through Arusha to western Kenya. The Germans conquered it in 1896 and built a military fort in 1900, forcing many Africans from their land to dig lime or carry stones for it. The British took the town in 1916. The railway reached it from Moshi in 1928-29.

The United Kingdom signed the documents ceding independence to Tanganyika at Arusha in 1961, and the Arusha Declaration was signed there in 1967. The Arusha Accords, between factions in the Rwandan civil war, were signed on 4 August 1993. The United Nations Security Council decided on 8 November 1994 that the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda would sit in the city; it indicted 93 individuals and sentenced 62. Arusha received city status in 2012.

Arusha is the capital of the Arusha Region and the headquarters of the East African Community. It hosts the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights and a branch of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals. The National Natural History Museum occupies the former German administrative outpost and holds models of Australopithecus.
aryabhata: In the Aryabhatiya Aryabhata says that he was 23 years old in the year 3600 of the Kali Yuga, which corresponds to 499 CE and implies a birth in 476 CE. He called himself a native of Kusumapura or Pataliputra, near present-day Patna in Bihar. His name is properly spelled Aryabhata, not Aryabhatta: every astronomical text spells it so, including Brahmagupta's references to him by name in more than a hundred places. His disciple Bhaskara I calls him āśmakīya, one belonging to the Aśmaka country, and some have argued for a Kerala origin.

He probably went to Kusumapura for advanced studies and lived there. A verse mentions him as head of an institution there, and it has been speculated that he headed the university of Nalanda, a link he never claimed himself. He is also reputed to have set up an observatory at the Sun temple in Taregana, Bihar.

He wrote several treatises, but only the Aryabhatiya survives. It has 108 verses and 13 introductory verses in four chapters, written in the terse style of sutra literature, so that commentators such as Bhaskara I and Nilakantha Somayaji (1465) explained its meaning. Its mathematics covers arithmetic, algebra, plane and spherical trigonometry, continued fractions, quadratic equations and a table of sines. The Arya-siddhanta, now lost, is known through Varahamihira, Brahmagupta and Bhaskara I.

He gave an approximation of π, 62,832 for a circle of diameter 20,000, accurate to two parts in a million. His kuṭṭaka method solved first-order indeterminate equations. In astronomy he stated that the Earth is round and rotates daily on its axis, so that the stars' apparent westward motion is relative, comparing it to a man in a boat who sees the shore moving backward. His model of the Solar System was geocentric, with epicycles. He explained eclipses by shadows, not by Rahu and Ketu, and calculated the sidereal rotation as 23 hours, 56 minutes and 4.1 seconds.

His work shaped Indian astronomy and, through an Arabic translation of about 820 CE, influenced the Islamic world. Al-Khwarizmi cites it, and the term sine descends from his jya. His calendar calculations are still used for the Panchangam.
asaf-ud-daula: Born on 23 September 1748, Asaf-ud-Daula was the son of Shuja-ud-Daula and of Umat-ul-Zohra, better known as Bahu Begum. He became nawab at the age of 26 on his father's death in January 1775, with the aid of the British East India Company. His younger brother Saadat Ali led a mutiny in the army, which the British Colonel John Parker defeated decisively. Asaf's first chief minister, Mukhtar-ud-Daula, was assassinated in the revolt. His position as Nawab wazir was ratified by the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II.

After the revolt he restructured the government, appointing nobles favourable to him and British officers to his army. Hasan Riza Khan became chief minister, ably assisted by Haydar Beg Khan, and Tikayt Ray finance minister. His mother remained a challenge to his rule: she controlled much of the treasury, held her own jagirs and armed forces, and at one point sought the Company's help in appointing ministers opposed to him.

Shuja-ud-Daula had left two million pounds sterling in the vaults of the zenana, which his widow and his mother claimed under a will that was never produced. When Warren Hastings pressed the nawab for the debt due to the Company, Asaf obtained from his mother a loan of 26 lakh rupees against a jagir of four times the value, and later 30 lakh more in return for a full acquittal and the Company's recognition of her jagirs for life. The jagirs were afterwards confiscated on the ground of her complicity in the rising of Chait Singh.

The Bara Imambara, or Asafi Imambara, was begun as a charitable project to give employment in the famine of 1784, in which even nobles were reduced to penury. It is said that over 20,000 people worked on it, and that nobles were paid to pull down part of the work in secret at night so that their dignity was kept. The Rumi Darwaza, sixty feet tall, was modelled in 1784 on the Sublime Porte in Istanbul.

He died in Lucknow on 21 September 1797 and is buried at the Bara Imambara. A saying still known in the city records his generosity: to whom even God does not give, Asaf-ud-Daula gives. The painter Johann Zoffany portrayed him several times, and the Urdu poet Mir Taqi Mir was at his court.
aschaffenburg: Aschaffenburg stands on both sides of the Main in north-west Bavaria, bordering Hesse, about 41 kilometres south-east of Frankfurt. The smaller Aschaff flows into the Main there and gave the town its name, originally "castle at the ash tree river". The Spessart hills separate it from the rest of Lower Franconia, so its inhabitants speak a local form of Rhine Franconian, not Bavarian or East Franconian.

The earliest settlement remains date from the Stone Age; the place was originally a settlement of the Alamanni, and Roman legions were stationed there. The Franks conquered the area around 550. A Benedictine monastery of St Michael, reportedly founded by Saint Boniface in the 8th century, became the collegiate church of St Peter and Alexander in 957. King Louis the Younger married Liutgard of Saxony there in 869. Archbishop Willigis, who reportedly built a stone bridge over the Main in 989, made it his second residence, and from 982 it belonged to the Archbishopric of Mainz for more than 800 years. A synod met there in 1292, and an imperial diet of 1447 approved a concordat sometimes called the Aschaffenburg Concordat.

The late-Gothic castle was destroyed in 1552 and replaced in 1605 to 1614 by the Renaissance Schloss Johannisburg. The town suffered greatly in the Thirty Years' War, being held in turn by the various belligerents. In 1803 it was made over to Archbishop Karl Theodor von Dalberg as the Principality of Aschaffenburg, which joined the Grand Duchy of Frankfurt in 1810, and in 1814 a treaty transferred it to Bavaria. From 1840 to 1848 King Ludwig I had the Pompejanum built, a Roman villa modelled on the house of Castor and Pollux at Pompeii. Allied bombing heavily damaged the town in the Second World War, and the Battle of Aschaffenburg from 28 March to 3 April 1945 destroyed much more.

The Schloss Johannisburg, completely restored after the war, holds a library with incunabula and a collection of engravings and paintings. The collegiate church of St Peter and Alexander dates mainly from the early twelfth century and preserves monuments by the Vischers and a painting by Matthias Grünewald. Across the river are the Park and Schloss Schönbusch. The town is the seat of a district but not part of it.
aschersleben: Aschersleben lies in the Salzlandkreis district of Saxony-Anhalt, near the confluence of the rivers Eine and Wipper, about 22 kilometres east of Quedlinburg and 45 kilometres north-west of Halle (Saale). Its municipality includes a number of villages incorporated between 2008 and 2010.

Aschersleben was first mentioned in 753, which makes it the oldest town of Saxony-Anhalt. The Latin name of its castle, Ascharia, gave the House of Ascania its name. The town obtained municipal status in 1266 and the right to build a city wall with defence towers in 1322. From 1252 to 1315 it was the capital of Anhalt-Aschersleben, after which it passed to the Bishopric of Halberstadt. In 1426 it joined the Hanseatic League, and the cultivation and trade of hops, for which a market place was laid out, brought an economic boom. After the Peace of Westphalia of 1648 it became part of the Principality of Halberstadt, and in 1815 it became part of the Prussian Province of Saxony.

In the 1930s a Junkers factory for aircraft fuselages was built there; the first fuselages were made in May 1935, and the works covered 564,000 square metres and employed about 6,000 people. From July 1944 about 950 prisoners from a subcamp of the Buchenwald concentration camp were forced to work there. The town was bombed from 1942 to 1945, and about 20 per cent of it was destroyed in nine raids, most heavily on 31 March 1945. U.S. forces occupied it on 17 April 1945, and it was handed to British forces on 23 May and to the Soviets on 1 July. It was part of East Germany until 1990, when it became part of Saxony-Anhalt.

Aschersleben is one of few German towns that keep large parts of their medieval city wall: 1.8 kilometres of an original 2.2, with 15 of 51 towers and bastions still standing, among them the Johannistorturm of 1380. The historic centre combines Romanesque (the Grauer Hof, of the 12th century, considered the oldest house in town), Gothic (the Protestant church of St. Stephani, of the 14th century), Renaissance (the town hall, built from 1517, and the Krukmannsches Haus of 1572) and Baroque buildings. A bronze statue of the polymath Adam Olearius (1599–1671), who designed the Globe of Gottorf, stands on a fragment of the city wall beside the Johannis gate tower.
asclepius: Asclepius is the son of Apollo and, in the earliest accounts, a mortal woman, Koronis, a princess of Tricca in Thessaly. When she slept with a mortal named Ischys, Apollo learned of it by his prophetic powers and killed Ischys, and Artemis killed Koronis, who was laid on a funeral pyre. Apollo rescued the child by cutting him from her womb.
Other traditions differ: a Phoenician tradition has him born of Apollo without any woman, and in a version set at Epidaurus Koronis exposed him on Mount Tittheion, where a goat gave him milk.

He was educated by the centaur Chiron. In one story a snake licked his ears clean and taught him secret knowledge; to the Greeks snakes were sacred beings of wisdom, healing and resurrection, and the rod wreathed with a snake became his emblem.

Asclepius is a hero and god of medicine in Greek religion, representing the healing aspect of the medical arts. He shared with Apollo the epithet Paean, "the Healer". He married Epione, and their daughters Iaso, Panacea, Hygieia, Aceso and Aegle personify aspects of health and healing. He was associated with the Roman and Etruscan god Vediovis and the Egyptian Imhotep. In myth he began to bring the dead back to life, and Zeus killed him with a thunderbolt, because Hades complained or because Zeus feared he would teach resurrection to other humans. At Apollo's request he was made immortal as a star, the constellation Ophiuchus.

From the fifth century BCE the cult grew very popular and pilgrims flocked to the healing temples, the Asclepieia. Strabo called the one at Trikala the most ancient. Others stood at Epidaurus, in the fourth century BCE, on the island of Kos, where Hippocrates may have begun his career, and at Pergamum. Ritual purification was followed by offerings, and the supplicant then spent the night in the holiest part, the abaton. Any dreams were reported to a priest, who prescribed a therapy by interpreting them.

Some temples used sacred dogs to lick the wounds of petitioners, and non-venomous snakes, now called Aesculapian snakes, moved freely in the dormitories where the sick slept. The original Hippocratic Oath begins with an invocation of Apollo the Physician and of Asclepius.
ascoli-piceno: Ascoli Piceno lies at the confluence of the River Tronto and the small River Castellano and is surrounded on three sides by mountains. The Sibillini National Park borders it on the northwest and the Monti della Laga National Park on the south. National Road 4, the Salaria, links it with Rome, following the Roman Via Salaria, the salt road that connected Latium with the salt-producing areas of the Adriatic coast.

Asculum in ancient Picenum was founded by the Italic Piceni and was originally a Sabine city. After its defeat by the Romans in 268 BCE it became a civitas foederata with nominal independence. One account describes its people as warlike and bearing a generations-old grudge against Rome for encroaching on their northern territories. Its siege in 89 BCE, after the Battle of Asculum, involved at least four Roman legions with Gallic and Spanish auxiliaries, as sling bullets found in the city show. It then became a municipium, and under the triumvirs or Augustus a colonia.

In the Middle Ages the Ostrogoths and then the Lombards of King Faroald ravaged it in 578. It was part of the Lombard Duchy of Spoleto from 593 to 789 and then ruled by vicars of the Franks, but the bishops gained the most influence. A free republican commune was established in 1189, but internal strife opened the way to outside rulers such as the condottiero Galeotto I Malatesta and Francesco Sforza, who was ousted in 1482. Ascoli then submitted again to papal suzerainty, and in 1860 it was annexed to the Kingdom of Italy.

Many buildings of the historic centre are of local travertine. Tradition holds that the city had some two hundred towers in the Middle Ages, and about fifty can still be seen. The Cathedral of Sant'Emidio houses an altarpiece by Carlo Crivelli. Roman remains include the Porta Gemina of the 1st century BCE, through which the Via Salaria entered the city, and the Ponte di Cecco over the Castellano. On the first Sunday in August a parade of more than 1,500 people in Renaissance costume honours Saint Emidio, protector of the city, and is followed by the Quintana, a tournament among knights of the six neighbourhoods.
ashanti-empire: The Asante Empire, Asanteman, also called the Ashanti Empire, was an Akan state in what is now Ghana. The name Asante means because of war, from the Twi ɔsa, war, and nti, because of, and comes from the state's origin as a kingdom created to fight Denkyira; Ashanti is the British transcription. The ancestors of the Asante moved north from Amansie, remembered by the Akan as their early homeland, to the Kumasi area as the Akan heartland broke up in disputes over succession and trade. Denkyira, which controlled much of the region's gold, made Oti Akenten, ruler of Kwaman, pay annual tribute and send a royal relative to its court, and he sent his nephew Osei Tutu.

Around 1680 leadership of the Asante union passed to Obiri Yeboa, whose death in battle with the Dormaa led to the rise of Osei Tutu. When the Denkyirahene Ntim Gyakari demanded heavy tribute and the Asante refused, war broke out around 1698. In tradition the Golden Stool, Sika dwa, became the central symbol of unity under Osei Tutu, with his adviser Okomfo Anokye.

After the Asante conquered Denkyira in 1701 they were the dominant inland power, with access to the coast and its trade with Europeans, and inland trade shifted toward Kumasi. The economy rested on gold and agricultural exports, slave trading, crafts and trade with markets further north. Osei Tutu was killed in 1717 in a war with Akyem, and the Aowin sacked Kumasi. In 1721 and 1722 the Asante defeated Aowin and Nzima, and Aowin prisoners were sold as slaves at Elmina, Cape Coast and Anomabo. By 1816, under Osei Bonsu, the Asante had absorbed the Fante Confederacy.

The Asante held their own against the British in the first two of the five Anglo-Ashanti Wars, killing General Sir Charles MacCarthy in 1824, but the British later burnt Kumasi. In the War of the Golden Stool, from March to September 1900, the court members not exiled, led by Yaa Asantewaa, Queen-Mother of Ejisu, attacked the British Residents at Kumasi Fort. The British won and exiled her and others to the Seychelles, where King Prempeh I already was.

The Asante state was centralised. The family, under its Abusua Panyin, was the basic political unit, and villages under an Odikro were grouped into divisions under an Ohene, which formed states under an Omanhene, and all the states formed the empire under the Asantehene. The Asante Kingdom survives today as a constitutionally protected traditional state within Ghana.
ashgabat: Ashgabat lies on a highly seismically active oasis plain between the foothills of the Köpetdag mountains to the south and the Karakum Desert to the north, about 50 kilometres from the border with Iran. Most of the city stands between 200 and 255 metres above sea level. The climate is cold arid, bordering on semi-arid, with very hot, dry summers and cool, short winters, and the Soviet-era Karakum Canal runs through the city, carrying water from the Amu Darya.

The city grew on the ruins of Konjikala, a Silk Road city first mentioned as a wine-producing village in the 1st or 2nd century BCE and levelled by an earthquake in the 1st century BCE. Konjikala was rebuilt because of its favourable position on the Silk Road and flourished until the Mongols destroyed it in the 13th century. It then survived as a small village until the Russians took over in the 19th century.

Russian military engineers founded the city on 18 January 1881 as a fortified garrison on the western edge of the Turkmen village of Askhabad. Sixty-seven Turkmen families were compensated for the land taken. Until then buildings other than yurts were adobe and limited to one storey because of the earthquake risk, and in 1900 only the municipal museum had two.

Soviet rule was established in December 1917, but in July 1918 a coalition of Mensheviks, Social Revolutionaries and former Tsarist officers revolted and set up the Ashkhabad Executive Committee. After the British withdrew in April 1919 the Tashkent Soviet resumed control. From 1919 to 1927 the city was named Poltoratsk after the local revolutionary Pavel Poltoratskiy, and in 1924 it became capital of the Turkmen Soviet Socialist Republic. Much of it was destroyed by the earthquake of 1948.

Ashgabat is the capital and largest city of Turkmenistan, with about one million inhabitants, and is a multiethnic city with ethnic Turkmen as the majority. It stands apart from Ahal Province, which surrounds it. After the earthquake it was extensively rebuilt, and since independence its monumental buildings have been sheathed in white marble. It has been spelled Ashkhabad in English, from the Russian form, and in 2021 marked 140 years of its written history.
ashkelon: The name Ashkelon is probably Western Semitic and may be connected with the root š-q-l, "to weigh", perhaps pointing to the importance of the place as a centre of trade. It appears in the Egyptian execration texts in a form that suggests the earliest pronunciation was ʾaθqalānu. The ancient site, now called Tel Ashkelon, was the oldest and largest seaport in Canaan. It belonged to Philistia, the pentapolis of the Philistines, north of Gaza City and south of Jaffa.

Ascalon was an important city under Roman, Byzantine and early Muslim rule, and again in the time of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, because it lay near the coast and between the Crusader states and Egypt. The Battle of Ascalon was the last action of the First Crusade. After Baybars ordered the fortifications and harbour destroyed in 1270, the inhabitants moved to Majdal ʿAsqalān, which he established as a substitute 3 kilometres inland, with a congregational mosque, a marketplace and religious shrines.

Ottoman records of 1596 show Majdal as a large village of 559 Muslim households, the seventh most populous place in Palestine, helped by its position on the Cairo to Damascus road. In the late Ottoman and Mandatory periods it became the main weaving centre of the Gaza District. It had about 500 looms in 1909 and about 2,000 by the 1940s, often set up in private rooms, and made striped fabrics for abaya coats and regional dresses. In 1945 its population was 9,910, of whom 9,820 were Muslims.

Egyptian forces occupied Majdal early in the 1948 war, and Israeli forces captured it in early November 1948. All but about 1,000 residents had left by then. The remaining Palestinians were confined to a fenced area and deported in stages from 17 August 1950; Israeli records give 2,333 sent to the Gaza Strip, 60 to Jordan and 302 to other towns in Israel. Jewish immigrants and demobilised soldiers settled from July 1949. The town was renamed several times, the Afridar neighbourhood for South African immigrants was incorporated in 1953, and the name Ashkelon was adopted that year.

The ancient site is administered as Ashkelon National Park, where the city walls, Canaanite earth ramparts and Roman, Byzantine and Crusader ruins can be seen. The largest dog cemetery of the ancient world was found there. Majdal's Great Mosque, founded in 1300, now houses a museum. Ashkelon is the third largest city in Israel's Southern District.
ashkenazi-jews: Ashkenazi Jews are an ethnic subdivision of the Jewish diaspora. They emerged from Jewish communities that consolidated during the 10th century in the Rhineland and northern France, having migrated there from centres such as the Italian Peninsula and the Southern Levant. How the Ashkenazim came to exist as a distinct community is unknown and has given rise to several theories. The name derives from the biblical figure Ashkenaz, a son of Gomer in the Table of Nations; the biblical name is usually derived from the Assyrian Aškūza, a people identified with the Scythians.

After numerous massacres of Jews during the Crusades, the Ashkenazim began a gradual eastward migration, driven by mounting restrictions in the Holy Roman Empire and the favourable policies of Casimir III the Great of Poland and others. Expulsions from England in 1290, France in 1394 and parts of Germany in the 15th century pushed it further. In Poland, Jews received special protection from the Statute of Kalisz of 1264.

The migration increased after the persecution of Jews during the Black Death, and by the 16th century the bulk of Ashkenazi Jews lived in the Kingdom of Poland. By the 15th century the Ashkenazi communities of Poland were the largest in the Diaspora, and the area remained the main centre of Ashkenazi Jewry until the Holocaust.

From the late 18th century the communities were transformed by the Haskalah, or Jewish Enlightenment, and the struggle for emancipation. Maskilim advocated national languages in place of Yiddish and the revival of Hebrew. In the 19th century millions emigrated from Europe, to Ottoman Palestine and to the United States. Of about 8.8 million Jews in Europe at the start of the Second World War, mostly Ashkenazi, about 6 million were murdered in the Holocaust, including 3 million of 3.3 million Polish Jews.

The Ashkenazim adapted their traditions to Europe. They follow the German rite in the synagogue and until the Holocaust mostly spoke Yiddish, an offshoot of Middle High German written in the Hebrew script, with Hebrew, Aramaic and Slavic influence; it was spoken by over 11 million people before the Holocaust. Because Germany lay far from the Jewish religious authorities of Baghdad and Islamic Spain, Ashkenaz developed a minhag of its own. Joseph Karo's Shulchan Aruch of 1563, with the notes of Moses Isserles, became the normative code of law for Ashkenazic Jews.
ashoka: Information about Ashoka comes from his own inscriptions, other inscriptions that mention him, and ancient literature, especially Buddhist texts, which often contradict one another. His inscriptions concern mainly dhamma, and the American scholar John S. Strong suggests they are sometimes best thought of as the propaganda of a politician presenting a favourable image of himself. The Buddhist legends were composed long after his time and call for caution.

His inscriptions do not name his ancestors. The Puranas and the Mahavamsa state that his father was the Maurya emperor Bindusara and his grandfather Chandragupta, founder of the empire. His inscriptions mention rulers such as Antiochus II Theos and Ptolemy II Philadelphus, which places him in the 3rd century BCE. According to the Mahavamsa he was viceroy at Ujjain, which his own rock edict supports by mentioning a prince viceroy there.

Ashoka became emperor of Magadha around 268 BCE, with his capital at Pataliputra. His inscriptions show an empire covering almost the whole subcontinent except the far south, and reaching into Afghanistan. In Major Rock Edict 13 he states that he conquered Kalinga eight years after his accession; 100,000 men and animals were killed, many times that number perished, and 150,000 were carried away. He writes that remorse over this suffering led him to devote himself to dharma.

His edicts urge righteous conduct and respect for all sects, and mention medical facilities for people and animals, wells and roadside trees. Minor Rock Edict 1 shows him as a lay follower of Buddhism, though the inscriptions do not mention doctrines such as the Four Noble Truths. Buddhist legends credit him with 84,000 stupas, patronage of the Third Buddhist council and missions to Sri Lanka led by his son Mahinda, and the Ashokavadana also describes acts of violence after his conversion.

His last dated inscription is from his 26th regnal year, and the only source for his later years is Buddhist legend. According to the Sri Lankan tradition he died in his 37th regnal year, which suggests about 232 BCE. Twenty of his pillars survive. The Lion Capital of Ashoka was adapted for the State Emblem of India, and the Ashoka Chakra stands at the centre of its flag. His existence as a historical emperor had almost been forgotten until the decipherment of Brahmi in the 19th century.
ashura: Ashura is an Aramaic word meaning tenth, and shares its root with the Hebrew asor. According to the traditions, fasting on Ashura was a Jewish practice that Muhammad adopted after his arrival in Medina in 622, and the hadith literature derives the observance from Yom Kippur. In a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, Muhammad finds the Jews of Medina fasting on the tenth of Muharram and says that Muslims have more right to observe the fast. The fast ceased to be obligatory after about a year, when relations with the Jews of Medina deteriorated, a change often associated with verses of the Quran that make Ramadan the main month of fasting. Other Sunni traditions describe fasting on Ashura as a pre-Islamic practice of the Quraysh.

For Shia Muslims, Ashura commemorates the death of Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of Muhammad and third imam, killed with most of his male relatives and his small retinue on 10 Muharram 61 AH (10 October 680) at the Battle of Karbala against the army of the Umayyad caliph Yazid ibn Mu'awiya. They had been surrounded for some days and deprived of the water of the nearby Euphrates. The women and children were taken prisoner and marched to Damascus. In Shia belief Karbala symbolises the struggle between good and evil, and mourning for Husayn is an act of protest against oppression and an act of worship.

Sunni Muslims also regard the killing of Husayn as a tragic event, but the ninth and tenth of Muharram are days of voluntary fasting, strongly encouraged by jurists. Ashura is also associated with the parting of the Red Sea by Moses and Noah's disembarking from the Ark.

Shia Muslims commemorate Karbala through the months of Muharram and Safar, most of all in the first ten days of Muharram. Gatherings called majalis centre on the narration of the Karbala story and the recitation of elegies, intended to move the audience to tears. Processions march in major Shia cities, carrying objects such as the alam, the ensign of Husayn. Mild self-flagellation, striking the face and chest, is common, while extreme forms with knives or chains have been condemned by many clerics. Ta'ziyeh, a dramatic reenactment of the martyrdom, is performed in Iran and elsewhere.

Sunni festivities on the day were established by the time of the jurist Ibn Taymiyya, who died in 1328, and may have grown up in response to Shia mourning: the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan made Ashura a festive public holiday to counter the commemoration of Husayn. In the Maghreb the day is marked by fasting, almsgiving, special dishes, bonfires and carnivals.
ashurbanipal: Ashurbanipal was born c. 685 BCE, probably the fourth eldest son of King Esarhaddon. After the unexpected death of the first crown prince, Sin-nadin-apli, in 674, Esarhaddon named Ashurbanipal heir to Assyria and his elder son Shamash-shum-ukin king of Babylon, the two to rule as equal brothers. Ashurbanipal trained in hunting, riding, scholarship, archery and chariotry, and with his father often ill he managed the empire's intelligence network.

Ashurbanipal succeeded in 669 BCE. His early years went on rebellions in Egypt, which Esarhaddon had conquered. His largest campaigns were against Elam, defeated in 665, 653 and 647 to 646, and against Shamash-shum-ukin, who rebelled in 652 with a coalition of Assyria's enemies and died during the siege of Babylon in 648. His sack of Babylon weakened the empire and fed anti-Assyrian feeling in the south, perhaps contributing to the rise of the Neo-Babylonian Empire five years after his death. His destruction of Elam has been described as a genocide, and he boasted of massacres of rebellious civilians.

Little is known of his late reign, since the eponym canon ends in 649. He promoted eunuchs over the nobility. Whether his policies caused the fall of Assyria some two decades after his death is disputed among Assyriologists.

Ashurbanipal read Akkadian and Sumerian from his youth. He had scribes collect and copy texts from temple libraries across the empire for the Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, which perhaps held over 100,000 texts, including omens, dictionaries, rituals and prayers. Around 30,000 survived the destruction of Nineveh in 612 BCE. Hormuzd Rassam found the North Palace in December 1853. Greek and Roman writers remembered a distorted figure, Sardanapalus, an effeminate, decadent last king of Assyria.
ashvaghosha: Aśvaghoṣa is said to have been born at Saketa, today Ayodhya. His original name is unknown, and Aśvaghoṣa, meaning Horse-Cry, is a later nickname. According to his traditional biography, translated into Chinese by Kumārajīva, he began as a wandering ascetic who defeated all comers in debate. Challenged by the monk Pārśva, he lost, became Pārśva's disciple and was fully ordained as a bhikṣu. The same biography says that a Kuṣāna king besieged the central kingdom and took Aśvaghoṣa as part of the tribute. There he preached to seven horses that had been starved, and they listened in tears, so that he received his name. Other sources say all the horses of the country cried out at his birth.

His school is uncertain. He seems not to belong to the Mahayana period and may have been ordained in a Mahasanghika subsect, though research on the Saundarananda, which may draw on the Yogacarabhumi, raises the possibility of a link to the Yogacara or Sautrantika schools.

Much Buddhist literature before him was composed in Pāli and Prakrit, but Aśvaghoṣa wrote in classical Sanskrit. He is believed to have been the first Sanskrit dramatist and is considered the leading Indian poet before Kālidāsa. His Buddhacarita, or Acts of the Buddha, is an epic life of the Buddha. The monk I-tsing (Yijing) reported that it was read in all the five parts of India and in the countries of the South Sea, because it set out the doctrine in compact form. The Saundarananda, a kāvya poem, tells of the conversion of the Buddha's half-brother Nanda: the first half describes Nanda's life and the second sets out Buddhist doctrine and ascetic practice.

A fragment of his play, the Śāriputraprakaraṇa, survives in Sanskrit. Other works are attributed to him with doubtful authority. The Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana, once ascribed to him, is agreed by modern scholars to have been composed in China. The Vajrasuchi, a poem critical of class and inequity under Vedic religion, was first translated by Brian Houghton Hodgson in 1835.
asia: Asia holds roughly 60% of the world's population. It shares the landmass of Eurasia with Europe, and its border with Europe is a historical and cultural construct, as there is no clear physical separation between them. Greek geographers such as Anaximander and Hecataeus used a threefold division of the Old World from the 6th century BCE, and the Ural River prevailed as the boundary in the mid-19th century. The boundary with Africa is the Suez Canal, the Gulf of Suez, the Red Sea and the Bab-el-Mandeb. Asia has the longest coastline of any continent, at 62,800 kilometres.

Researchers believe modern humans migrated to South Asia along the Indian Ocean about 60,000 years ago, and that they interbred with Denisovans in Southeast Asia. The history of Asia can be seen as the distinct histories of several peripheral coastal regions, East Asia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Central Asia and West Asia.

The coastal periphery was home to some of the world's earliest known civilisations, each developing around fertile river valleys: those of Mesopotamia, the Indus Valley and the Yellow River shared many similarities and may have exchanged technologies and ideas such as mathematics and the wheel, while writing seems to have developed independently in each area.

Evidence of farming in West Asia dates back to around 9000 BCE. China and India traded places as the largest economies in the world from 1 to 1800 CE, and the Silk Road became the main east–west trading route in the Asian hinterlands, while the Straits of Malacca stood as a major sea route. Asia was the birthplace of most of the world's mainstream religions, including Islam, Judaism, Christianity, Hinduism and Buddhism.

Asia is subdivided into 49 countries, five of them transcontinental (Georgia, Azerbaijan, Russia, Kazakhstan and Turkey). The United Nations Statistics Division divides it into North Asia, Central Asia, West Asia, South Asia, East Asia and Southeast Asia, solely for statistical reasons. It has no single culture: various independent cultures coexist, and it varies greatly in ethnic groups, environments, economies and government systems. Asia is home to several language families, and more than 700 languages are spoken in Indonesia, over 400 in India and more than 100 in the Philippines.
asia-pacific-economic-cooperation: The inspiration for APEC came from the post-ministerial conferences of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, launched in the mid-1980s, which showed the value of regular meetings between developed and developing economies. These led the Australian prime minister Bob Hawke to believe in the need for region-wide economic co-operation, and in January 1989 he called for more effective co-operation across the Pacific Rim. The first meeting took place in Canberra in November 1989, chaired by the Australian foreign affairs minister Gareth Evans and attended by ministers from twelve countries.

The organisation was at first an Australian initiative intended to secure greater Japanese engagement in the region. Its early years saw tension between members favouring a structured trade agreement and those, like the United States, who preferred a looser, consultative approach.

The first four annual meetings were attended by ministers. From 1993 they became Economic Leaders' Meetings, attended by heads of government from every member except Taiwan, which sends a ministerial-level official. In 1994 at Bogor the leaders adopted the Bogor Goals, aiming at free and open trade and investment by 2010 for industrialised economies and by 2020 for developing ones. In 1995 an Osaka meeting agreed to set up the APEC Business Advisory Council from 1996.

At Vancouver in 1997, Royal Canadian Mounted Police officers used pepper spray on protesters who objected to the presence of leaders such as Indonesia's president Suharto. At Shanghai in 2001 the leaders endorsed the Shanghai Accord, committing members to reduce trade transaction costs by five percent over five years. APEC began discussing a Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific in 2006, an idea traced to a proposal by the Japanese economist Kiyoshi Kojima in 1966.

APEC calls its members economies rather than countries, because the criterion for membership is being an independent economic entity rather than a sovereign state. Its 21 members include Taiwan, participating as Chinese Taipei, alongside the People's Republic of China, and Hong Kong. It has three official observers: the ASEAN Secretariat, the Pacific Economic Cooperation Council and the Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat. The Secretariat is based in Singapore, and the meeting rotates annually among members. In 1993 the United States president Bill Clinton insisted on informal attire and gave the leaders leather bomber jackets, which began the tradition of leaders dressing in the host's national costume for the group photograph.
asia-roman-province: Asia was a Roman province covering most of western Asia Minor. After the Romans crushed Antiochus III at Magnesia in 190 BCE, the Treaty of Apamea in 188 BCE gave most of the territory to the Attalid dynasty of Pergamum. King Attalus III, a close ally of Rome without a legitimate heir, bequeathed his kingdom to Rome. On his death in 133 BCE the pretender Eumenes III rebelled, and the consul Marcus Perperna defeated him. Manius Aquillius then formally established the province. It first took in Mysia, the Troad, Aeolis, Lydia, Ionia and Caria, and the Aegean islands except Crete.

A law of Gaius Gracchus in 123 BCE gave members of the equestrian order the right to collect taxes in Asia. Communities that could not pay borrowed from Roman lenders at exorbitant rates and often lost their land. By 88 BCE Mithridates VI of Pontus had conquered virtually all of Asia and ordered the slaughter of all Romans and Italians in the province, with estimates of the dead from 80,000 to 150,000. Sulla defeated him and in 85 BCE reorganized the province into eleven assize districts, among them Ephesus, Pergamum and Smyrna, which competed for dominance.

Under Augustus it became a proconsular province and the most prestigious senatorial one. It was a system of hundreds of largely self-governing Greek cities that competed for status through festival games, cults and oratory, and it had no full legions. In the 3rd century the Antonine plague and the Gothic invasions of the 250s and 260s brought decline. Diocletian divided the province into seven in the 4th century, and after the great plague of 543 many interior cities shrank to villages.
asir: Asir lies on a high plateau that receives more rain than the rest of Saudi Arabia and holds the country's highest peaks, rising to almost 3,200 metres at Jabal Soudah near Abha. Average annual rainfall in the highlands probably ranges from 300 to 500 millimetres, falling in two seasons, chiefly in March and April. Daily temperature ranges are very large, with frosty mornings and afternoons often above 30 °C, and there is more natural vegetation than elsewhere in the country, including dense coniferous forest in sheltered areas. Farmers chiefly grow wheat and fruit, and historically the region produced coffee, barley, senna and frankincense.

The origin of the name is debated. Al-Masudi suggested that the region was first known as the Land of Azd; another view derives it from the Arabic ʿUsrah, hardship, for the rugged terrain; and Fuad Hamza links it to the prominence of the tribe of Banu Asir.

In 25 BCE the Roman commander Aelius Gallus marched south from Egypt on an expedition of some 1,300 miles to seize the overland trade routes towards Hadhramaut, hoping to capture Marib, capital of Saba, and the incense trade. The expedition was a disaster, and little information about Asir came of it.

After the Ottomans destroyed the First Saudi state in 1818, the Asiris went on fighting the forces of Ottoman Egypt. When the Ottomans withdrew in 1840, the dynasty of Al-Ayedh took control of the highlands. The Ottomans occupied them again after defeating and executing the Al-Ayedh leader in 1872 and set up a sub-governorate at Abha.

About 1906 Muhammad ibn Ali al-Idrisi began to establish control; he allied secretly with Great Britain in 1915, and after the First World War he ruled the Emirate of Asir, an internationally recognised state, until his death in 1920. Ibn Saud then began to annex the region, took Abha in 1920 and incorporated the rest by 1923. The Treaty of Taif of 1934 settled the claim of the Zaydi Imam of Yemen, and in 1935 Asir was made a separate governorate.

Asir is a province of Saudi Arabia of 76,693 square kilometres, with its seat at Abha. It borders the provinces of Mecca, Al-Baha, Riyadh, Najran and Jazan, and Yemen to the south. It has 17 governorates, and Khamis Mushait is its largest city. Asir National Park, established in 1981, extends from the Red Sea coast through the western foothills to the escarpment. King Khalid University, founded in 1998, has its main campus in Abha.
asmara: Asmara stands at 2,325 metres on a rocky highland plateau, at the tip of an escarpment that forms the north-western edge of the Eritrean Highlands. The plateau separates the western lowlands from the eastern coastal plains, and the fertile land to the south is among the best farmland of the region. The climate is mild for the latitude, with most rain falling in July and August and frost extremely rare.

According to Tigrinya oral tradition, four clans lived on the Kebessa Plateau, named Gheza Gurtom, Gheza Shelele, Gheza Serenser and Gheza Asmae. Clans from the lowlands attacked their villages often, until the women of each clan decided that the four must unite for peace. The name Arbate Asmera means in Tigrinya that the four, feminine plural, made them unite. The first written mention is in a Latin itinerary from the reign of Emperor Dawit I (1382–1411). In the late 19th century the town was for a time the capital of Bahr Negash Gerada Zeray, and it then passed between several regional chiefs, the last of them Ras Alula.

Italian forces occupied the town in 1889, in coordination with local chiefs, and Governor Ferdinando Martini made it the capital of Italian Eritrea in 1897. The Eritrean Railway to the coast ran through Ghinda under the direction of Carlo Cavanna. By the 1939 census Asmara had 98,000 inhabitants, 53,000 of them Italian, out of 75,000 Italians in all Eritrea. Most of central Asmara was built between 1935 and 1941, a period when Benito Mussolini planned a second Roman Empire in Africa, and by the late 1930s it was called Piccola Roma, or Little Rome.

In 1952 the United Nations resolved to federate the former colony under Ethiopian rule, and the capital moved to Addis Ababa. In 1961 Emperor Haile Selassie I ended the federal arrangement and made the territory a province of Ethiopia, and the Eritrean War of Independence began. The city was home to the United States Army's Kagnew Station from 1943 to 1977. Asmara was left relatively undamaged in the war, which ended in 1991 with Eritrean independence, and it again became the capital.

Asmara is known for its early 20th-century buildings, among them the Art Deco Cinema Impero, which opened in 1937, the futurist Fiat Tagliero Building, the Cubist Africa Pension and the neo-Romanesque Church of Our Lady of the Rosary. In July 2017 UNESCO listed the city as a World Heritage Site, the first modernist city listed in its entirety. It is the see of the archbishop of the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church, which became autocephalous in 1993.
asparuh-of-bulgaria: Asparuh, also called Ispor or, rarely, Isperih, was a Bulgar khan of the second half of the 7th century. The Nominalia of the Bulgarian Khans says that he belonged to the Dulo clan. According to Byzantine sources he was a younger son of Kubrat, who had founded a spacious state, Great Bulgaria, in the steppes of modern Ukraine. Kubrat probably died in 665. The state broke up under Khazar attack in 668, and Asparuh and his brothers parted ways, each leading his people to seek a safer home.

Asparuh was followed by 30,000 to 50,000 Bulgars. He reached the Danube, and while the Arab caliph Muawiyah I besieged Constantinople, from 674 to 678, he and his people settled in the Danube Delta. In 680 the Byzantine emperor Constantine IV marched against the Bulgars and their Slav allies and drove them into a fortified encampment. The emperor then left the army to seek treatment for his ailments, and rumours that he had fled demoralised his troops. Some deserted, and the Bulgars broke through the blockade and routed their enemy at the Battle of Ongala in 680.

The victory led to the Bulgar conquest of Moesia and to some form of alliance with local Slavic groups. When Asparuh began raiding across the mountains into Byzantine Thrace in 681, Constantine IV made a treaty under which the empire paid the Bulgars an annual tribute. These events are seen in retrospect as the founding of the Bulgarian state and its recognition by the Byzantine Empire. Later tradition credits Asparuh with building Pliska and Drăstăr.

The length and dates of his reign are uncertain, and modern chronologies differ. A late tradition says he died fighting the Khazars on the Danube, and one theory, advanced by the historian Vaklinov, places his grave near Voznesenka on the Dnieper in Ukraine. Bulgarian historians have stressed that his state had a capital and a state tradition that could later be viewed as national, although in its first century or two it was plainly multi-tribal and hegemonic. The town of Isperikh bears his name.
assam: Assam lies south of the Eastern Himalayas along the Brahmaputra and Barak River valleys. The Brahmaputra, the lifeline of Assam, is an antecedent river older than the Himalayas, forming a flood plain 80 to 100 kilometres wide and about 1,000 kilometres long. The first dated mention of the region comes from the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea in the 1st century. Until the 12th century the region east of the Karatoya River was called Kamarupa. The name Assam, first used by the British in the Treaty of Yandabo in 1826, is associated with the Ahom people, originally called Shyam (Shan).

A rock-cut stupa at Sri Surya Pahar has been dated to 200 BCE. The region was a frontier of the Gupta Empire in the fourth century and was ruled by the Varmanas (c. 350 to 650), the Mlechchhas (c. 655 to 900) and the Kamarupa-Palas (c. 900 to 1100). After Kamarupa declined, authority was divided among the Kamata, Chutia and Kachari kingdoms, the Baro-Bhuyans and the Ahom kingdom of Upper Assam, with interventions from the Bengal Sultanate and later the Mughal Empire.

The Ahom kingdom, established in the 13th century, ruled until the early 19th century. The Moamoria rebellion (1769 to 1805) severely weakened it, and a rivalry between the Prime Minister Purnananda Burhagohain and the Ahom Viceroy of Western Assam, Badan Chandra Borphukan, led Borphukan to invite the Burmese. Three successive Burmese invasions followed, and King Chandrakanta Singha was defeated. The British then established tea estates, the region became part of the Bengal Presidency, and the Assam Province was created in 1912. Assam became a state of India on 26 January 1950.

Dispur is the capital of Assam, and Guwahati is the largest city. Assamese and Bodo are official languages. Assam is known for its tea and silk, and the Kaziranga and Manas National Parks are World Heritage Sites; more than half of the surviving wild population of the one-horned Indian rhinoceros lives in the state.
assassination-of-archduke-franz-ferdinan: Under the Treaty of Berlin of 1878, Austria-Hungary received the mandate to occupy and administer the Ottoman Vilayet of Bosnia, and it formally annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1908. The assassins were members of a revolutionary movement later known as Young Bosnia, whose political aim was to free Bosnia and Herzegovina of Austro-Hungarian rule and establish a common South Slav state. All six were Austro-Hungarian citizens, and none came from Serbia.

In spring 1914 Gavrilo Princip, then in Belgrade, was shown a newspaper cutting announcing the archduke's visit to Bosnia in June. He asked Trifko Grabež to join the plot and wrote to Danilo Ilić in Sarajevo to recruit others. The conspirators were helped by the Black Hand, a Serbian secret nationalist group, and Major Vojislav Tankosić supplied bombs and pistols and trained them.

On the morning of Sunday 28 June 1914 Ilić posted six assassins along the motorcade route. Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, rode in the third car, an open sports car, with Governor Oskar Potiorek. Two assassins failed to act, and Nedeljko Čabrinović threw a bomb. At the Town Hall the archduke interrupted the mayor's welcome to protest that he had come on a visit and was greeted with bombs.

Princip had moved to a position near the Latin Bridge. When the motorcade took a wrong turn and the driver stalled the car close to him, Princip stepped up to the footboard and shot the archduke and the duchess at point-blank range. He tried to shoot himself but was seized at once. At his sentencing he said that his intention had been to kill Potiorek, rather than Sophie.

Twenty-five people were indicted in the Sarajevo trial of October 1914. Five of the six assassins were under 20, and Princip, too young to be executed, was sentenced to 20 years in jail. Five of the older prisoners were sentenced to be hanged. Black Hand members were tried in Salonika in 1917 on charges later widely regarded as fabricated, and three of their leaders were executed.

The assassination precipitated the July Crisis, which led Austria-Hungary to declare war on Serbia and began the First World War. At first there was much sympathy across Europe for the Austrian position. Princip's legacy was re-evaluated after the breakup of Yugoslavia, and opinion of him in the successor states is largely divided along ethnic lines.
assia-djebar: Fatima-Zohra Imalayen was born on 30 June 1936 in Cherchell, a small seaport near Algiers, to Tahar Imalhayène and Bahia Sahraoui, a family of Chenoua Berber origin. Her father taught French at the primary school in Mouzaïaville that she attended. She later went to a Quranic private boarding school in Blida, where she was one of only two girls, and studied at the Collège de Blida, where she was the only Muslim in her class. In 1955 she entered the École normale supérieure de jeunes filles, the first Algerian and Muslim woman educated at France's most elite schools. Her studies were interrupted by the Algerian War, and she continued them in Tunis.

In 1957 she chose the pen name Assia Djebar for her first novel, La Soif. Les Impatients followed in 1958. She taught at the University of Rabat from 1959 to 1962 and then at the University of Algiers, where she became head of the French section. She returned to Algeria in 1962 and published Les Enfants du Nouveau Monde; Les Alouettes naïves came in 1967. She lived in Paris from 1965 to 1974 and married the Algerian poet Malek Alloula in 1980. From 1997 to 2001 she directed the Center of French and Francophone Studies at Louisiana State University. She also made films, among them La Nouba des femmes du Mont Chenoua in 1977 and La Zerda ou les chants de l'oubli in 1979.

Most of Djebar's works deal with obstacles faced by women, and she is noted for a feminist stance. One critic describes her novels as focused on creating a genealogy of Algerian women, with a politics both anti-patriarchal and anti-colonial. In L'Amour, la fantasia of 1985, translated as Fantasia: An Algerian Cavalcade, she repeatedly states her ambivalence about language and about her identity as a Western-educated, Algerian, feminist, Muslim intellectual. She won the Neustadt International Prize for Literature in 1996 and the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade in 2000.
On 16 June 2005 she was elected to the Académie française, the first writer from the Maghreb to be so honoured and the fifth woman to join. She died in Paris in February 2015, aged 78.
assisi: Assisi is a town and comune of Italy in the Province of Perugia, in Umbria, on the western flank of Monte Subasio. The Romans built the municipium Asisium on a series of terraces on the mountain. Roman remains include city walls, the forum, now the Piazza del Comune, a theatre, an amphitheatre of the early 1st century CE and the Temple of Minerva, now the church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva. A Roman villa with frescoes and mosaics was discovered in 1997.

The earliest attested people of Assisi were the Umbri. The Romans took control of central Italy after the Battle of Sentinum in 295 BCE. The poet Propertius, born about 50-45 BCE, is generally regarded as a native. According to tradition Assisi was converted to Christianity in 238 by Bishop Rufino, who was martyred at Costano. The Ostrogoths of King Totila destroyed most of the town in 545, after which it came under the Lombard and then Frankish Duchy of Spoleto.

In the 11th century it became an independent Ghibelline commune, in constant struggle with Guelph Perugia. In a battle at Collestrada, Giovanni di Bernardone, better known as Saint Francis, was taken prisoner, which set in motion the events that led him to live as a beggar and found the Order of Friars Minor in the town in 1208. Clare of Assisi, with Francis, founded the Order of Poor Ladies. In the 13th century the city grew beyond its Roman walls and was under papal jurisdiction. It later fell to Perugia and a series of despots, and declined deeply with the Black Death of 1348. Two earthquakes in September 1997 damaged many historical sites.

UNESCO designated the Franciscan structures of Assisi a World Heritage Site in 2000. They include the Basilica of San Francesco, built between 1228 and 1253 after Francis's canonisation, whose lower church has frescoes by Cimabue and Giotto; the Basilica of Santa Chiara, begun in 1257, with the tomb of Saint Clare; the Church of San Damiano, given to Clare as the first home of the Poor Clares; and the Porziuncola, a chapel restored by Francis, inside Santa Maria degli Angeli.
association-of-southeast-asian-nations: The predecessor of ASEAN was the Association of Southeast Asia, formed on 31 July 1961 and made up of Thailand, the Philippines and Malaya. ASEAN itself was created on 8 August 1967, when the foreign ministers of Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand signed the ASEAN Declaration at Saranrom Palace in Bangkok. The Declaration aims to accelerate economic, social and cultural development, to promote regional peace and to maintain close cooperation with existing international organisations. Originally the association was founded to contain communism, but it gradually reoriented itself to economic development and to preventing foreign interference in Southeast Asia as a whole.

Brunei became the sixth member on 7 January 1984 and Vietnam the seventh on 28 July 1995, after the end of the Cold War. Laos and Myanmar joined on 23 July 1997. A Cambodian coup in 1997 and internal instability delayed Cambodia's admission until 30 April 1999. Timor-Leste joined on 26 October 2025 as the eleventh member. The first summit of heads of government was held in Bali in 1976, and the ASEAN Free Trade Area was signed in Singapore on 28 January 1992. A charter, signed in November 2007 and launched in Jakarta on 15 December 2008, formally established ASEAN as a legal entity.

ASEAN is an intergovernmental forum of all 11 states in Southeast Asia, with its headquarters in Jakarta. It operates on the principle of consensus and respect for national sovereignty, so that it cannot force a member state to change its domestic laws. The ASEAN Way, as scholars describe it, is an informal and personal working style that relies on compromise, consensus and consultation, and on quiet diplomacy that spares members public embarrassment. Every two years ASEAN organises the SEA Games, a sporting event meant to promote cultural exchange among its members.
assur: The remains of Assur lie on the western bank of the Tigris, north of its confluence with the Little Zab, in what is now the al-Shirqat District of the Saladin Governorate in Iraq. The city lies on a south-facing mountain spur with a triangular layout. Its higher northern area held the public buildings, including the palace and the temples of Ashur, Anu, Adad, Sin, Shamash and Ishtar.

Occupation lasted about 3,000 years, from the Early Dynastic Period to the mid-3rd century CE. In the Ur III period, about 2112 to 2004 BCE, it was governed from Ur. In the Old Assyrian period it was a hub of the karum trading network that reached through Mesopotamia, Syria and Anatolia, and a city assembly with legislative and judicial power ruled it. Shamshi-Adad I conquered it and made it his religious capital, and Hammurabi of Babylon took it around 1756 BCE. Ashur-uballit I later founded the Middle Assyrian Empire, and Tukulti-Ninurta I built a new temple to Ishtar there.

In the Neo-Assyrian Empire the royal residence moved elsewhere: Ashurnasirpal II made Kalhu the capital, Sargon II built Dur-Sharrukin, and Sennacherib chose Nineveh. Assur stayed the religious centre because of the temple of the national god Ashur, and many kings were buried beneath the Old Palace. It was sacked in the decisive battle of Assur against Median and Babylonian armies. It revived under the Parthian Empire, and Ardashir I of the Sasanian Empire sacked it about 257 CE, after which it was sparsely populated.

German archaeologists began regular exploration in 1898 and, between 1903 and 1914, under Robert Koldewey and later Walter Andrae, uncovered the temples, the ziggurat and the Old Palace, along with more than 16,000 cuneiform tablets now in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin. Assur is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, placed on the list of sites in danger in 2003 because of a proposed dam that would flood part of it.
assyrian-empire: Agricultural villages existed in the region by about 6300 BCE, and the earliest archaeological evidence from Assur dates to about 2600 BCE. The city was probably not independent until the collapse of the Third Dynasty of Ur, when a line of kings beginning with Puzur-Ashur I began to rule it. In the Old Assyrian period it was a city-state named for its god Ashur, governed in many respects as an oligarchy: the kings were stewards of Ashur and presided over a city assembly, probably of powerful merchant families.

Assyria rose as a territorial state under Ashur-uballit I in the early fourteenth century BCE. He was the first native ruler to claim the title of king, and soon claimed the dignity of a great king equal to the Egyptian pharaohs and Hittite kings. Its rise was linked to the decline of its former suzerain, the Mitanni kingdom. In the Neo-Assyrian period the army was the strongest in the world and the empire the largest yet assembled, from parts of Iran to Egypt.

In the late seventh century BCE, weakened by civil war, it fell to a coalition of Babylonians and its former vassals, the Medes and Scythians. The capitals Assur, Nimrud and Nineveh were nearly abandoned, and the region stayed sparsely populated.

At the top of society stood long-established families called houses, whose members held the most important offices, among them the vizier. Territory was divided into provinces, each under a governor responsible for order, public safety and the economy. The army was mostly levies called up for campaigns, with a small standing unit, the king's unit, in the Neo-Assyrian period. Assur remained the ceremonial centre even when the king ruled from elsewhere, since the king was Ashur's representative on earth.

Assyria's success is attributed not only to its warrior-kings but to its ability to govern conquered lands efficiently, and later empires continued to use its methods of warfare and administration. Assyrian culture endured after the fall, and several Assyrian kingdoms emerged under Parthian rule. The Assyrian people, among the first to accept Christianity, developed the East Syriac rite and live today in their ancient heartland and in the diaspora.
astana: Astana lies in central Kazakhstan, on the Ishim River, in a very flat, semi-arid steppe region at an elevation of 347 metres. The city covers 722 square kilometres, with the older boroughs north of the river and the newer ones south of it. It is almost 1,000 kilometres from Almaty, the former capital, and the nearest big cities are Karaganda, 200 kilometres away, and Omsk in Russia, 450 kilometres away.

Many centuries ago the settlement of Bozok stood on the territory of modern Astana, a military fortress on the steppe section of the Silk Road and a large settlement of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries. The settlement of Akmoly was established on the Ishim on 18 June 1830 by Fyodor Shubin as the seat of an okrug. In 1832 it was granted town status and named Akmolinsk. In 1838, at the height of the liberation movement headed by Kenesary Khan, the Akmolinsk Fortress was burned; it was rebuilt after the movement was repressed. On 16 July 1863 Akmolinsk was declared an uyezd town.

Under Nikita Khrushchev the town was renamed Tselinograd, Russian for City of Virgin Lands. In 1989 it had a population of 281,000, of whom about 54.1 per cent were Russian and 17.7 per cent Kazakh. After Kazakhstan's independence the name was changed in 1991 to Akmola.

In December 1997 the city replaced Almaty as the capital of Kazakhstan, and in May 1998 it was renamed Astana, which means capital city in Kazakh. The decision to make it a modern, planned city was guided by Kisho Kurokawa, and its population more than doubled in the first decade as capital, passing 600,000 by 2007.

Astana is the capital of Kazakhstan and the seat of its government. Its landmarks include Akorda, the residence of the president, the Baiterek tower, 105 metres tall and built in 1996 to mark the transfer of the capital from Almaty, and the Astana Grand Mosque, the largest mosque in Central Asia, completed in 2022. The city hosted Expo 2017, the first world's fair held in Central Asia.
astarte: Astarte is the Hellenized form of the Ancient Near Eastern goddess ʿAṯtart, the Northwest Semitic counterpart of the East Semitic goddess Ishtar. Her name is first recorded at Ebla in the 3rd millennium BCE, in the forms Aštarta and Ištarta. Her main cult centre was Mari, and she was originally associated with Amorite cities such as Ugarit, Emar, Mari and Ebla. The meaning of her name remains unclear. She was worshipped from the Bronze Age through classical antiquity.

At Ugarit ʿAṯtartu had no astral aspect and played a minor role in myth, but she is often named in ritual and administrative texts, which suggests importance for the institution of kingship. She was regularly paired with the goddess Anat, with whom she shared beauty and a love of war, and the two are described hunting together. In the Baʿal Epic she is an ally of Baal against the sea god Yam.

Across cultures Astarte was linked with war, sexuality, royal power, beauty and healing, and at Ugarit and Emar with hunting. Her symbol was the lion, and she was associated with the horse and so with chariots, and perhaps the dove. The only images identified with certainty as Astarte show her as a combatant on horseback or in a chariot. In New Kingdom Egypt she was known as a West Semitic war goddess, with a cult attested from the reign of Amenhotep II in the 15th century BCE, and was sometimes paired with the god Resheph.

In the Iron Age the Canaanites worshipped her as ʿAštart. In Phoenicia in the 1st millennium BCE she overshadowed the other Semitic goddesses and became the main personification of a less warlike and more sensual vitality. As a fertility goddess she promoted love and presided over the reproduction of cattle and family growth, and was the consort of Hadad or Baal.

Her cult spread to Cyprus, where she may have merged with an ancient Cypriot goddess who may in turn have been adopted into the Greek pantheon to form Aphrodite. Phoenicians introduced her cult in their colonies on the Iberian Peninsula. At Memphis a temple of the goddess stood within the temple of Ptah, and from at least the 6th century BCE she was identified with Isis. Lucian of Samosata wrote that the temple of Astarte in the territory of Sidon was sacred to Europa, and Plutarch names her as the queen of Byblos in the story of Osiris.

The Masoretic vocalisation of her name in the Hebrew text, ʿAštōret, is thought by most scholars to put the vowels of the Hebrew word for shame on her consonants. In later kabbalistic and occult texts the name Astaroth was given to a male demon bearing little resemblance to the ancient goddess.
astrakhan: Astrakhan lies on two banks of the Volga, in the upper part of the Volga Delta, on eleven islands of the Caspian Depression, about 100 kilometres from the Caspian Sea. At 28 metres below sea level it is the lowest city in Russia. The delta is rich in sturgeon. The name began as the Russian form of Hajji Tarkhan, from hajji, the title of a Muslim who has made the pilgrimage to Mecca, and tarkhan, a term in the Mongol states for a man not subject to taxation. A Tatar legend, first recorded by Ibn Battuta, says the settlement was founded by a Turkic pilgrim whose piety earned the future city exemption from taxation.

Travellers first mention the town in the early 13th century as Xacitarxan. Timur burned it to the ground in 1395 in his war with the Golden Horde, and from 1459 to 1556 it was the capital of the Astrakhan Khanate of the Astrakhan Tatars. Ivan the Terrible conquered the khanate in 1556 and had a kremlin built on a steep hill overlooking the Volga in 1558, traditionally taken as the foundation of the modern city. The Ottomans besieged it in 1569 and retreated, and a year later the sultan renounced his claims, opening the whole Volga to Russian traffic. In the 17th century merchants from Armenia, Safavid Persia, Mughal India and the Khivan Khanate settled there.
