He attended schools in Valparaíso and Quillota and entered the Military School in Santiago in 1931. His records show an average student, and in 1935 he graduated as a second lieutenant in the infantry. After postings to regiments in Concepción, Valparaíso and Iquique, he entered the Chilean War Academy, and he later wrote two books on military subjects, Geopolítica (1968) and Campaña de Tarapacá (1972).

He became General Chief of Staff in early 1972 and was appointed commander-in-chief of the army by President Salvador Allende on 23 August 1973. On 11 September 1973 the combined armed forces, including the Navy, Air Force and Carabineros, overthrew Allende's government, and the presidential palace, La Moneda, was shelled. A junta of four commanders was established; it suspended the Constitution and Congress, imposed censorship and a curfew, and banned the parties of Allende's coalition and then all others. Historians differ on the part played by the United States, which tacitly supported the junta after the coup; some authors describe a covert campaign against Allende, while Sebastián Hurtado finds no documentary evidence of an active American role in the coup itself.

Pinochet was proclaimed Supreme Chief of the Nation on 17 June 1974 and officially titled President of the Republic on 17 December 1974. General Gustavo Leigh of the Air Force, who opposed him, was forced into retirement in 1978. The regime persecuted leftists and critics through executions, forced disappearances, internment and torture; a government commission report that took testimony from more than 30,000 people recorded at least 3,197 killed and about 29,000 tortured. Economists known as the Chicago Boys guided a programme of market liberalisation. A plebiscite in 1980 approved a new constitution, and on 5 October 1988 voters rejected a further presidential term, which led to elections.

Pinochet stepped down in 1990 but remained commander-in-chief of the army until 10 March 1998, when he became a senator for life. He was arrested in London in October 1998 on an international warrant, the first time a former head of government was arrested on the principle of universal jurisdiction, and was released on medical grounds by the Home Secretary Jack Straw in March 2000. Back in Chile, he faced about 300 criminal charges when he died of heart failure at the Military Hospital in Santiago on 10 December 2006, without having been convicted. A United States Senate investigation in 2004 found a network of accounts at Riggs Bank that he and his associates used to move money.
augustus-ii-the-strong: Augustus was born in Dresden on 12 May 1670, the younger son of John George III, Elector of Saxony, and Princess Anna Sophie of Denmark. As the second son he had no expectation of inheriting the electorate, which passed to his older brother John George IV when their father died on 12 September 1691. Augustus was well educated and toured France and Italy from 1687 to 1689; the court at Versailles impressed him deeply. He married Christiane Eberhardine of Brandenburg-Bayreuth on 20 January 1693, and their son, the future Augustus III, was born in 1696. John George IV died of smallpox on 27 April 1694, and Augustus became Elector of Saxony.

To be eligible for election to the Polish throne in 1697, Augustus converted to Roman Catholicism. The step shocked Protestant Europe, since Saxony had been a stronghold of German Protestantism, and he guaranteed its religious status quo. He won the election with the backing of Russia and Austria, although another candidate, François Louis, Prince of Conti, had received more votes. Contemporaries mocked the costly bribery of the Polish nobility as his Polish adventure.

He joined Frederick IV of Denmark and Peter I of Russia against Charles XII of Sweden in the Great Northern War. Charles defeated his armies at Riga in 1701 and at Kliszów in 1702, captured Warsaw, and in 1704 had Stanisław Leszczyński installed as king. After the Battle of Fraustadt on 1 September 1706 Charles invaded Saxony, and by the Treaty of Altranstädt in October 1706 Augustus gave up the Polish throne. Peter's victory at Poltava in 1709 allowed Augustus to return under Russian auspices. His attempts to build an absolute monarchy met resistance from the nobility, and in 1717 Peter forced him and the nobles to accept the Silent Sejm, an accommodation favourable to Russia.

Augustus died at Warsaw in 1733. His body was buried in Wawel Cathedral in Kraków, while his heart rests in Dresden Cathedral. He had not made the Polish throne hereditary, but his son Augustus III succeeded him, installed by the Imperial Russian Army during the War of the Polish Succession.

He is best remembered as a patron of the arts. In Dresden he began the Zwinger and built Pillnitz Castle, and he opened the Green Vault in 1723. In Warsaw he expanded the Saxon Palace and its Saxon Garden. He sponsored the alchemist Johann Friedrich Böttger, whose work led to the Meissen porcelain manufactory, founded in 1709, and in 1705 he founded the Order of the White Eagle. Contemporary sources claimed he fathered between 360 and 380 children; the number cannot be verified and is probably greatly exaggerated.
augustus-iii: Augustus was born on 17 October 1696 in Dresden, the only legitimate son of Augustus II the Strong. His mother, Christiane Eberhardine of Brandenburg-Bayreuth, remained a fervent Protestant and never set foot in Catholic Poland, which the Polish nobility took as a provocation. He was groomed from youth to succeed as king and studied Polish, German, French and Latin. Raised at first as a Lutheran by his grandmother, he was taken by his father on a tour of Catholic countries and converted to Catholicism in November 1712 in Italy. On 20 August 1719 he married Maria Josepha of Austria, daughter of Emperor Joseph I, and the wedding in Dresden was one of the most splendid of the Baroque era.

Augustus II died on 1 February 1733, and Augustus inherited the Saxon electorate without difficulty. His election to the Polish throne was harder. By the Löwenwolde Treaty with Austria and Russia, Russia would supply troops to ensure his election and he would recognise Anna as Empress and give up Polish claims to Livonia and Courland, while renouncing any claim to the Austrian succession. Stanisław Leszczyński was chosen at the election sejm with 12,000 votes to 3,000 for Augustus, but 30,000 Russian troops had entered Poland. The War of the Polish Succession followed, and Stanisław fled in 1734. The Pacification Sejm of 1736 confirmed Augustus.

He spent less than three years of his thirty-year reign in Poland, preferring hunting, opera and collecting art. The feuding of the Czartoryski and Potocki families paralysed the Sejm through the liberum veto. His adviser Heinrich von Brühl ran Saxony and in effect Poland, leaving Polish politics to the great magnates. Saxony joined Austria in the War of the Austrian Succession and again in the Seven Years' War, when Prussia invaded in 1756 and drained it. Under the Treaty of Hubertusburg of 1763 Saxony renounced its claim to Silesia.

Augustus died of a stroke in Dresden on 5 October 1763 and was buried at Dresden Cathedral, one of the few Polish monarchs buried outside Poland. His son Frederick Christian succeeded as elector and died two and a half months later. In 1764 Stanisław August Poniatowski was elected king with Russian support. Augustus was a patron of the arts. He enlarged the Dresden art gallery and founded the opera house in Warsaw in 1748, and Johann Sebastian Bach dedicated the Kyrie and Gloria of his Mass in B minor to him. Critics in Poland have long judged him lazy, though a historian found in the Dresden archives a description of him as honest and affectionate.
auld-lang-syne: The text is a Scots poem written by Robert Burns in 1788 on the basis of an older Scottish folk song. Burns sent it to the Scots Musical Museum with the remark that it was an old song, of the olden times, which had never been in print nor even in manuscript until he took it down from an old man.

Some of the words were indeed collected rather than composed. A ballad, Old Long Syne, printed by James Watson in 1711, resembles the first verse and chorus closely and almost certainly derives from the same old song, so it is a fair supposition that the rest of the poem is Burns's own. The phrase auld lang syne also occurs in poems by Robert Ayton, Allan Ramsay and James Watson, and in older folk songs. The Scots title may be rendered as old long since, or less literally as days gone by.

The song opens by asking whether old times should be forgotten, which is generally read as a call to remember long-standing friendships. In George Thomson's Select Songs of Scotland of 1799 the second verse, about greeting and toasting, was moved to its present place at the end. The song originally had another melody, traced to about 1700 and judged mediocre by Burns. The first documented use of the tune now standard was in 1799, in Thomson's second volume. It is a pentatonic Scots folk melody, probably once a sprightly dance at a much quicker tempo, and there is some doubt that Burns intended it.

The composer William Shield seems to quote it in the overture to his opera Rosina of 1782, but both may have taken it from a common source, possibly a strathspey. In 1792 Joseph Haydn arranged it for George Thomson, and Beethoven later made an arrangement too.

Singing the song on Hogmanay, or New Year's Eve, quickly became a Scots custom that spread to other parts of the British Isles, and emigrants took it round the world. At Hogmanay in Scotland everyone joins hands in a circle and crosses arms at the last verse, while the tradition of singing it when parting with hands crossed arose in the mid-19th century among Freemasons and other fraternal organisations. It is also used at funerals, graduations, the closing of Scout jamborees and Burns suppers.

The melody has carried other words. In France the Jesuit Jacques Sevin translated the song in 1920 as Ce n'est qu'un au revoir. In Japan the tune serves for Hotaru no Hikari, played at school graduations. It was the tune of the Korean exile government's anthem from 1919 to 1945, and of the anthem of the Maldives until 1972. The first recording was made on a wax cylinder in 1898.
aung-san: Aung San was born on 13 February 1915 in Natmauk, Magway District, the youngest of nine children of a middle-class family. His father, U Phar, was a lawyer who went into business instead. He entered Rangoon University in 1933 and became a student leader, elected to the executive committee of the Rangoon University Students' Union and editor of its magazine Oway. In February 1936 he and U Nu were expelled for refusing to name the author of an article criticizing a senior university official, which led to the Second University Students' Strike, after which both were reinstated.

In October 1938 he left his law classes for national politics and became a Thakin by joining the Dobama Asiayone, acting as its general secretary until August 1940. He helped organise the countrywide strikes known as the ME 1300 Revolution. With the outbreak of war he helped found the Freedom Bloc under Dr. Ba Maw. In 1940 he met Nehru, Gandhi and Subhas Chandra Bose at the Indian National Congress assembly in Ramgarh, and then spent the rest of the year in Tokyo.

On 28 December 1941 he and the Thirty Comrades inaugurated the Burma Independence Army in Bangkok, with about 3,500 volunteers. It entered Burma behind the Japanese Fifteenth Army, and its arrival in many areas was followed by communal violence, especially against Karen people, until the Japanese Army intervened. Aung San served as minister of war under Ba Maw in the Japan-backed State of Burma, then switched sides and merged his forces with the Allies. In London he signed an agreement with Clement Attlee on 27 January 1947 on the terms of independence; U Saw and Thakin Ba Sein refused to sign it, and Karen and Shan leaders warned they would not consider it binding on their communities.

At 10:37 on 19 July 1947 a jeep carrying gunmen in military fatigues drove into the courtyard of the Secretariat Building, where Aung San was meeting his cabinet. The gunmen shot the guard, burst into the chamber and shot Aung San in the chest. Four other council members died at once and three more were mortally wounded. U Saw, the last pre-war prime minister, was arrested the same day and later hanged, but other claims of responsibility have been made, including that a rogue faction in British intelligence was involved. Aung San is considered the founder of modern Myanmar and of the Tatmadaw, and is called the Father of the Nation.
aurangabad: Aurangabad stands on hilly upland in the Deccan Traps, surrounded by the Ajanta mountain range, and is the largest city of the Marathwada region of Maharashtra. Paithan, the capital of the Satavahana dynasty from the 1st century BCE to the 2nd century CE, and Devagiri, the capital of the Yadava dynasty from the 9th to the 14th century, lay within the bounds of the modern district. In 1327 Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq moved the capital of the Delhi Sultanate from Delhi to Daulatabad, ordering a mass relocation of Delhi's population, and reversed the decision in 1334.

Malik Ambar, an Ethiopian military leader brought to India as a slave who rose to be prime minister of the Ahmadnagar Sultanate, died in 1626. His son Fateh Khan renamed the city Fatehnagar, and with the capture of Devagiri Fort it passed to the Mughals. In 1653 Aurangzeb, then viceroy of the Deccan, made it his capital and renamed it Aurangabad. In 1681, as emperor, he moved his court there to conduct his Deccan campaigns. A city wall was built about 1683 in response to Maratha raids.

Although Aurangzeb did not reside there after 1684, the city stayed the main military outpost of the Mughal Deccan and a centre of trade, of embroidered silks and of Persian and Urdu literature, with an estimated 200,000 people.

The transfer of the Nizam's capital to Hyderabad in 1763 brought economic decline, and by the beginning of the nineteenth century the city was underpopulated and its buildings in decay, though it stayed the second city of the Nizam's dominions. The British set up a cantonment outside it in 1816, and its first cotton mill opened in 1889. In 1960 Aurangabad and the Marathwada region became part of Maharashtra.

The city is called the City of Gates for the 52 gates built in the Mughal era, some of which still stand. Bibi Ka Maqbara, the mausoleum of Aurangzeb's wife Dilras Banu Begum, imitates the Taj Mahal. The Panchakki is a seventeenth-century watermill fed by an underground channel more than 8 km long. The Ajanta and Ellora caves on the outskirts have been World Heritage Sites since 1983. Marathi is the official language, followed in use by Urdu and Hindi.
aurangzeb: Aurangzeb, known as Alamgir I, was born at Dahod on 3 November 1618, the sixth child of Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal. In 1626, after an unsuccessful rebellion by his father, the eight-year-old and his brother Dara Shikoh were sent to the Mughal court at Lahore as hostages of their grandfather Jahangir and his wife Nur Jahan, and were reunited with Shah Jahan at Agra in 1628. He became viceroy of the Deccan in 1636, when he brought the Nizam Shahi dynasty to an end, and governor of Gujarat in 1645. His efforts in 1649 and 1652 to dislodge the Safavids from Kandahar ended in failure.

There was no Mughal tradition of primogeniture; it was customary for sons to overthrow their father and brothers to fight to the death. In September 1657 Shah Jahan nominated Dara Shikoh as his successor. Aurangzeb proclaimed himself emperor in February 1658, defeated Dara at the Battle of Dharmat in April and at Samugarh in May, and later imprisoned his father in the Agra Fort.

In 1679 he reimposed the jizya on non-Muslim subjects, abated for a hundred years, which many Hindu rulers and court officials criticised. An orthodox Muslim, he patronised Arabic calligraphy and made the Fatawa-i Alamgiri the principal regulating body of the empire. According to Sikh accounts, the Guru Tegh Bahadur was arrested on his orders and beheaded in Delhi in 1675 after refusing to convert. The Maratha king Sambhaji was captured and executed. By 1689 the conquest of Golconda had expanded the empire to 4 million square kilometres.

Aurangzeb died on 3 March 1707. The highpoint of imperial centralisation under him coincided with the start of the imperial downfall, in the words of the historian Jos Gommans, and his constant warfare, especially with the Marathas, drove the empire to the brink of bankruptcy.

His emperorship has a complicated legacy. Critics, citing his actions against non-Muslims and his conservative view of Islam, argue that he abandoned the pluralism and tolerance of earlier Mughal emperors. Others reject this, arguing that he opposed bigotry against Hindus, Sikhs and Shia Muslims and employed more Hindus in his bureaucracy than his predecessors.
aurel-stein: Marc Aurel Stein was born on 26 November 1862 in Budapest to Náthán Stein and Anna Hirschler, a Jewish couple. His parents and sister kept their faith, but Stein and his brother Ernst Eduard were baptised as Lutherans. The family spoke German and Hungarian at home. He studied at the universities of Vienna, Leipzig and Tübingen, graduating in Sanskrit and Persian, and took his doctorate at Tübingen in 1883. In 1884 he went to England to study oriental languages and archaeology, and in 1887 to India, where he became Registrar of the University of the Punjab and then, from 1888 to 1899, Principal of the Oriental College at Lahore.

Influenced by Sven Hedin's Through Asia, Stein sought the help of the Indologist Rudolf Hoernle in June 1898 to find and study Central Asian antiquities. With Hoernle's lobbying, the governments of Punjab and India approved his proposal, and he received funds for his first expedition in January 1899. He became a British citizen in 1904. He made four major expeditions, in 1900 to 1901, 1906 to 1908, 1913 to 1916 and 1930. On the first he uncovered relics at the oasis of Dandan Oilik in the Taklamakan Desert, and on the third he excavated at Khara-Khoto. In 1901 he exposed the forgeries of Islam Akhun. On the second expedition he lost several toes to frostbite in the Kunlun Mountains.

His most significant find came in 1907 at the Mogao Caves near Dunhuang, where he found a printed copy of the Diamond Sutra dated 868 and some 40,000 other scrolls. He gained the confidence of the Taoist caretaker, whom he also paid, and took away 24 cases of manuscripts and 4 of paintings and textiles. He was knighted, but Chinese nationalists called him a burglar and staged protests. His fourth expedition ended in failure.

Stein was also an ethnographer, geographer, linguist and surveyor. He translated Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī, a chronicle of the kings of Kashmir, which was published in 1900, and wrote up his journeys in Ancient Khotan, Serindia and Innermost Asia. He found manuscripts in the Tocharian languages at Miran and recorded many sites in Iran and Balochistan. Between 1940 and 1943 he surveyed the Ghaggar-Hakra River and identified about 100 prehistoric and historical sites. His collections are divided among the British Museum, the British Library, the Srinagar Museum and the National Museum in New Delhi.

He received the Royal Geographical Society's Founder's Medal in 1909 and was made a Knight Commander of the Order of the Indian Empire in 1912. He never married, and was always accompanied by a dog named Dash, of which there were seven. He died in Kabul on 26 October 1943 and is buried in the Sherpur Cantonment there.
aurich: Aurich is a town in the East Frisian region of Lower Saxony and the capital of the district of Aurich. After Emden it is the second largest town in East Frisia by population, and after Wittmund by area. The origin of its name is uncertain: it may refer to a person, the East Frisian first name Affo, and his property, or to waterworks on the fertile, water-rich lowland of the Aa river, on which the town stands. Medieval spellings include Aurichove, Auwerck and Aurickeshove.

The settlement of Aurechove is mentioned in the Frisian document known as the Brokmerbrief in 1276. In 1517 Count Edzard of the House of Cirksena began rebuilding the town after an attack. In 1539 the land authorities were brought together in Aurich, making it the capital of the county, and it stayed the seat of the authorities of East Frisia when the region was inherited by the Kingdom of Prussia in 1744.

After the Prussian defeat at the Battle of Jena in 1807, Aurich became part of the Kingdom of Holland in 1808. When France annexed Holland in 1810 the town became capital of the department of Ems-Oriental in the First French Empire. After Napoleon's defeat it passed to the Kingdom of Hanover in 1815, and Prussia annexed it in 1866, making it part of the Province of Hanover. From 21 October to 23 December 1944 a subcamp of the Neuengamme concentration camp was run there. After the Second World War Aurich became part of the new state of Lower Saxony.

Aurich is twinned with Appingedam in the Netherlands. Among those born there are the East Frisian counts Johan II and Enno III, the jurist Rudolf von Jhering, the pathologist Friedrich Theodor von Frerichs, the writer and jurist Karl Heinrich Ulrichs and the philosopher Rudolf Eucken, winner of the 1908 Nobel Prize for Literature.
auschwitz-concentration-camp: Auschwitz, also known as Oświęcim, was a complex of over 40 concentration and extermination camps run by Nazi Germany in occupied Poland, in a portion annexed into Germany in 1939. It had three main parts: Auschwitz I, the main camp and administrative headquarters; Auschwitz II-Birkenau, a concentration and extermination camp with gas chambers; and Auschwitz III-Monowitz, a labour camp for the chemical conglomerate IG Farben, with dozens of subcamps. Auschwitz I stood fifty kilometres south-west of Kraków on the site of a former First World War camp for transient workers and later a Polish army barracks.

After Germany invaded Poland in September 1939, the SS converted the barracks into a prisoner-of-war camp, and Heinrich Himmler ordered on 27 April 1940 that the camp be established. Rudolf Höss was its first commandant. The first transport of political detainees consisted almost entirely of Poles, who made up the majority of inmates for the first two years. Prisoners were beaten, tortured and executed for the most trivial reasons. The first gassings, of Soviet and Polish prisoners, took place in block 11 of Auschwitz I around August 1941, and construction of Birkenau began in October 1941.

From 1942 until late 1944 freight trains brought Jews from all over German-occupied Europe to the gas chambers of Birkenau. Of 1.3 million people sent to the camp, 1.1 million were murdered, among them 960,000 Jews, 74,000 non-Jewish Poles, 21,000 Romani and 15,000 Soviet prisoners of war. Those not gassed died of starvation, exhaustion, disease, executions and beatings, and some were killed in medical experiments. Prisoners were tattooed with a serial number, a practice unique to Auschwitz, and sorted by coloured triangles, with Jews at the bottom of a racial hierarchy.

At least 802 prisoners tried to escape, 144 of them successfully. On 7 October 1944 two Sonderkommando units, prisoners forced to work at the gas chambers, launched an unsuccessful uprising. As the Red Army approached in January 1945, the SS sent most of the prisoners west on a death march to camps in Germany and Austria. Soviet troops liberated the camp on 27 January 1945.

Only 789 SS personnel, no more than 15 percent, ever stood trial, and several were executed, including Höss. Survivors such as Primo Levi, Viktor Frankl, Elie Wiesel and Edith Eger wrote of their experiences, and the camp became a dominant symbol of the Holocaust. Poland founded the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum on the site of Auschwitz I and II in 1947, and UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site in 1979. The date of the liberation has been commemorated since 2005 as International Holocaust Remembrance Day.
ausonius: Decimus Magnus Ausonius was born about 310 in Burdigala, the son of Julius Ausonius, a physician of Greek ancestry, and Aemilia Aeonia, from established land-owning Gallo-Roman families of south-western Gaul. His aunt and grandmother raised him strictly. He was educated at Bordeaux and at Toulouse, where his maternal uncle Aemilius Magnus Arborius was a professor. He did well in grammar and rhetoric but said that his Greek was unsatisfactory. After training for a time as an advocate he preferred teaching, and in 334 he became a grammaticus at a school of rhetoric in Bordeaux, and afterwards a professor. His best-known pupil was the poet Paulinus, who later became Bishop of Nola.

After thirty years of teaching, Ausonius was summoned by Emperor Valentinian I to teach his son Gratian, and accompanied them on the German campaigns of 368 and 369. Valentinian gave him the rank of quaestor, and at court in 369 he met Quintus Aurelius Symmachus. When Gratian became emperor in 375 he heaped honours on Ausonius and his family: Ausonius became Praetorian Prefect of Gaul, his father, nearly ninety, was given the rank of prefect of Illyricum, and in 376 his son Hesperius was made proconsul of Africa. In 379 Ausonius was awarded the consulate, the highest Roman honour.

In 383 the army of Britain under Magnus Maximus revolted and assassinated Gratian at Lyons. Ausonius retired to his estates near Bordeaux, which he called the nest of his old age, and spent the rest of his life composing poetry and writing to eminent contemporaries, many of them former pupils. He appears to have been a late convert to Christianity. He died about 395.

His best-known poems are the Mosella, a description of the River Moselle, and the Ephemeris, an account of a typical day, of which only the beginning and end survive. The Parentalia commemorates dead relatives, and the Commemoratio professorum Burdigalensium treats the teachers of Bordeaux he had known. He also wrote epigrams, verse letters and a cento wedding poem built from lines of Vergil. His contemporaries admired him, but later critics rank him below the finest Latin authors. Edward Gibbon wrote that his poetical fame condemns the taste of his age. His references to winemaking are cited as early evidence of large-scale viticulture around Bordeaux, and the Mosella mentions a water-driven saw cutting marble.
austin-texas: Austin lies in Central Texas on the Colorado River, within the greater Texas Hill Country. It is 146 miles (230 km) northwest of Houston, 182 miles (290 km) south of Dallas and 74 miles (120 km) northeast of San Antonio, and it is the southernmost state capital of the contiguous United States. The river is dammed into Lady Bird Lake, formerly Town Lake, and the city has Barton Springs and Barton Creek. Its climate is humid subtropical, in a narrow transitional zone between the dry deserts of the American Southwest and the more humid Southeast. Its skyline was long modest, dominated by the Texas State Capitol.

The area has been inhabited since at least 9200 BCE. The earliest known inhabitants lived in the late Pleistocene and are linked to the Clovis culture, on the evidence of the Gault Site, midway between Georgetown and Fort Hood. Excavations at the French Legation in downtown Austin revealed a site used in the Archaic period about 5,000 years ago. The city was incorporated on 27 December 1839. Since the late 19th century it has been called the City of the Violet Crown, for the colourful glow of light across the hills just after sunset.

The city's economy long rested on government and education. Its technology industry has roots in the 1960s, when the defence electronics contractor Tracor began operations there in 1962 and IBM opened a plant for its Selectric typewriters in 1967. Texas Instruments arrived two years later, and Motorola started semiconductor manufacturing in 1974. In the 1990s the city took the nickname Silicon Hills, and it was strongly affected by the dot-com boom of the late 1990s and the bust that followed.

Austin is the capital of Texas and the county seat of Travis County, and the home of the University of Texas at Austin, one of the largest universities in the United States. It is governed by a city council and a hired city manager. Its official slogan is The Live Music Capital of the World, and the annual South by Southwest festival of film, interactive media and music takes place there. Its landmarks include the Texas State Capitol and the Bob Bullock Texas State History Museum.
austral-islands: The Austral Islands, called Tuha'a Pae in Tahitian, are the southernmost group of French Polynesia and consist of two separate chains. In the north-west are the Tupua'i Islands: Maria, Rimatara, Rurutu, Tupua'i (Tubuai) itself and Raivavae. In the south-east are the Bass Islands, made up of Rapa Iti and the small rocks of Marotiri. They are the product of a hot spot beneath the Macdonald seamount, so the islands are oldest in the north-west and youngest in the south-east. Maria is an atoll and Marotiri a group of rugged volcanic rocks, and neither is suited to lasting habitation.

Little is known of the early past, since only a few excavations have been made. Scholars suspect that the islands were settled relatively late, possibly from the Society Islands, Mangareva or the Cook Islands. Excavations at Atiahara on Tubuai point to settlement at the beginning of the second millennium CE and show a stratified society with separate dwellings for aristocrats, priests, artisans and warriors. Increasing warfare drove people from the beaches into fortified hill settlements, 15 of which are recorded on Rapa.

James Cook sighted Rurutu in 1769 and Tubuai in 1777 but did not land. In 1789 the mutineers of HMS Bounty tried to settle on Tubuai; clashes in which 66 islanders were killed ended the attempt after three months. In 1819 King Pomaré II of Tahiti brought missionaries of the London Missionary Society to the islands and mediated an end to a tribal war. Christianity spread peacefully and ended the wars, but broke the near-absolute power of the chiefs, and the islands stayed under Tahitian influence.

France declared a protectorate over Tubuai in 1874 and Raivavae in 1876, and annexed the islands as a colony in 1880 after the end of the Pomaré dynasty. Rurutu and Rimatara stayed independent kingdoms until they accepted French suzerainty in March 1889, and their annexation followed later.

The islands form an administrative subdivision of French Polynesia, with Tupua'i as its capital, and their people live mostly in small villages, from subsistence farming and fishing. French is the official language, and the Austral language and Rapa are also spoken. The islands are known for a rich tradition of carving: the sculpture of the god A'a from Rurutu is in the British Museum, and the large vertical drums called pahu are another distinctive work.
australia: Australia comprises the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania and numerous smaller islands. It has a land area of 7,688,287 square kilometres, the sixth largest in the world, and the mainland is the world's smallest continent. About 70% of the landmass is arid or semi-arid, and the mainland is relatively flat. The Great Dividing Range runs along most of the east, and Mount Kosciuszko, at 2,228 metres, is the highest mountain on the mainland. The Murray-Darling is the major river system. The Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef, lies off the north-east coast and extends for more than 2,300 kilometres.

Human habitation is estimated to have begun 50,000 to 65,000 years ago, with migration from what is now Southeast Asia. Aboriginal Australian culture is one of the oldest continuous cultures on Earth. At first European contact Aboriginal Australians belonged to a wide range of societies across at least 250 language groups, and estimates of their population before British settlement range from 300,000 to 3 million. Torres Strait Islander people first settled their islands at least 2,500 years ago and are culturally and linguistically distinct from mainland peoples. Trade had been established by the mid-18th century between Aboriginal groups in the north and Makassan trepangers visiting from present-day Indonesia.

In 1606 the crew of the Dutch ship Duyfken, captained by Willem Janszoon, made the first documented European landing. Abel Tasman's voyage of 1642 was the first known European expedition to reach Van Diemen's Land, and the Dutch named the continent New Holland. British colonisation began in 1788 with the penal colony of New South Wales. Governor Lachlan Macquarie recommended the name Australia in December 1817. By 1890 each of six self-governing colonies had gained responsible government, and they federated in 1901 as the Commonwealth of Australia. The Australia Act 1986 completed the process of increasing autonomy from the United Kingdom.

Australia has a population of 27,801,023, heavily concentrated on the east coast and highly urbanised, with Canberra as capital and Sydney and Melbourne as the most populous cities. It is a constitutional monarchy, a parliamentary democracy and a federation of six states and ten territories, with a constitution mostly unchanged since 1901. The white Australia policy, strengthened after Federation, ended in 1973, and immigrants now account for 30% of the population. Indigenous art includes more than 100,000 Aboriginal rock art sites.
australian-labor-party: The party descends from the labour parties founded in the Australian colonies in the 1890s, before federation. Labor tradition ascribes the founding of Queensland Labour to a meeting of striking pastoral workers under a ghost gum known as the Tree of Knowledge at Barcaldine, Queensland, and the 1891 shearers' strike is credited as one of the factors in the party's formation. Labour sat as a parliamentary party from 1891 in New South Wales and South Australia and from 1893 in Queensland. The spelling of the name was not fixed at first, and only in 1918 did the federal party resolve that state branches should all adopt Australian Labor Party.

In the first federal election, in 1901, the state Labour parties won 15 of the 75 seats in the House of Representatives and held the balance of power. Under Chris Watson, Labour doubled its vote in 1903. In April 1904 Watson and Alfred Deakin fell out over the Conciliation and Arbitration bill, Deakin resigned, and Watson became prime minister, aged 37. His minority government lasted only four months, but it is considered the world's first national labour government. At the 1910 federal election Labor became the first party in Australia to win a majority in either house of parliament.

John Curtin became prime minister in October 1941 when two independents crossed the floor, and led Australia through the Pacific War. In December 1941 he declared that Australia looked to America, which helped to establish the alliance later formalised as ANZUS. Curtin died in office shortly before the war ended, and Ben Chifley succeeded him and won the 1946 election.

Labor is often called the party of the unions because trade unions founded it, and most Australian unions are affiliated. Affiliated unions hold half the delegate places at state and national conferences, and rank-and-file members hold the other half. Its constitution has stated since 1921 a socialist objective, the democratic socialisation of industry, later qualified by support for a competitive private sector. The Chifley government's failure to nationalise the private banks in the 1940s was the last attempt at such socialisation.
austria: Austria is a landlocked country in Central Europe, lying in the Eastern Alps, and occupies 83,879 square kilometres. Only about a quarter of its area can be considered low-lying, and only 32% of the country lies below 500 metres. The Eastern Alps make up 62% of the total area, and the Alps of the west give way to lowlands and plains in the east. The Austrian granite plateau, part of the Bohemian Mass, accounts for 10%, and forest covers about 47% of the land. It is a federation of nine states, of which Vienna is the most populous.

By the 6th century BCE the region was settled by Celtic tribes and served as the core of the Hallstatt culture; the city of Hallstatt has the oldest archaeological evidence of the Celts in Europe. The Celtic Kingdom of Noricum was conquered by the Roman Empire in 16 BCE and lasted as a province until 476, while eastern parts fell in Pannonia and the west in Raetia.

Carnuntum, an army camp turned capital, was home to 50,000 people for nearly 400 years. After the fall of the Roman Empire, Odoacer conquered most of the area in 487, the Ostrogoths followed by 493, and the Alemanni, Baiuvarii, Slavs and Avars after them. Charlemagne defeated the Avars in the late eighth century and set up frontier marches.

In 976 Emperor Otto II appointed Leopold I of the House of Babenberg as margrave of the marchia Orientalis. The name Austria first appears in writing in 996, as Ostarrîchi. The Privilegium Minus made Austria a duchy in 1156, and the Babenbergs acquired Styria in 1192; the line ended with Frederick II in 1246. Ottokar II of Bohemia then took control of the duchies until Rudolph I of Germany defeated him at Dürnkrut in 1278. From then until the First World War, Austria's history was largely that of the Habsburgs, and it became an archduchy in 1453.

Austria had established its own empire two years before the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806, and Austria-Hungary followed in 1867. The empire's defeat in the First World War led to the Republic of German-Austria in 1918 and the First Austrian Republic in 1919. An Austrofascist dictatorship under Engelbert Dollfuss formed in 1934, and Nazi Germany annexed the country a year before the Second World War.

After liberation in 1945 and a decade of Allied occupation, Austria regained its sovereignty and declared perpetual neutrality in 1955. It joined the European Union in 1995 and adopted the euro in 1999; its population was estimated at 9,220,882 in April 2026, and Vienna exceeds 2 million.
austrian-empire: The Habsburgs began as relatively minor nobles in what is now Switzerland and expanded their influence across Central Europe through dynastic marriages, summed up in the phrase Bella gerunt alii, tu felix Austria nube, meaning let others wage war; you, happy Austria, marry. By the 16th century they controlled the Austrian hereditary lands, Bohemia and Hungary as a loose composite monarchy, each region keeping its own laws, elites and traditions. They defended Catholicism during the Reformation and faced persistent Ottoman pressure in Hungary and the Balkans, which pushed the monarchy towards centralisation and military reform.

The Imperial Recess of 24 March 1803 cut the number of ecclesiastical states of the Holy Roman Empire from 81 to 3 and the free imperial cities from 51 to 6. Foreseeing the end of that empire, or Napoleon's accession as its emperor, Francis II created the title Emperor of Austria for himself and his successors, becoming Francis I of Austria. He held both titles until he abdicated the Holy Roman throne in 1806. The new Kaiserthum was legally a single state, though the status of its component lands at first stayed much as before. Hungary kept its own King and Diet and was described in its constitution of 1790 as a Regnum Independens.

The Napoleonic Wars dominated foreign policy from 1804 to 1815. After the defeat at the Battle of Austerlitz, the Treaty of Pressburg gave time to rebuild, and Archduke Charles reformed the army. On 9 April 1809 an Austrian force of 170,000 men attacked Bavaria. Austria and its allies emerged victorious, and the Congress of Vienna reaffirmed the empire as a great power. After the Austro-Prussian War of 1866, the Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867 joined the Kingdom of Hungary and the Empire of Austria to form Austria-Hungary.

After 1815 the empire's crown lands included the Archduchy of Austria, the Kingdom of Bohemia, the Margraviate of Moravia, the Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria, the Kingdom of Dalmatia, the Kingdom of Hungary with Croatia and Slavonia, the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia and the Grand Principality of Transylvania. Lombardy-Venetia was lost in 1859 and 1866. German was the main language of higher education.

The population was multinational, with Germans, Hungarians, Slavs, Italians and Romanians. Dr. Becher's statistics give 36,950,401 in 1840. During the Revolutions of 1848 the Croats, Serbs and Romanians of the Kingdom of Hungary supported the monarchy when Hungary revolted.
austrian-peoples-party: The party is an unofficial successor of the Christian Social Party, a staunchly conservative movement founded in 1893 by Karl Lueger, the mayor of Vienna. Most of the founding members of the new party had belonged to the Fatherland Front, led by Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss, himself a member of the Christian Social Party before the Anschluss. Some in the party still honour Dollfuss for resisting Adolf Hitler, but the regime he built was authoritarian and has been called Austrofascism. The ÖVP was established immediately after Austria's independence was restored in 1945.

In the first postwar election, in 1945, the ÖVP won almost half the vote and an absolute majority in the legislature. Memories of the hyper-partisanship of the First Republic led it to keep the grand coalition with the Communist Party of Austria and the Social Democratic Party of Austria that had governed since early 1945. It remained the senior partner in coalition with the Social Democratic Party of Austria until 1966 and governed alone from 1966 to 1970. It returned to government in 1986, and has not been wholly out of power since 1945, owing to a long tradition that all major interest groups were to be consulted on policy.

After the 1999 election the party formed a coalition with the Freedom Party of Austria under Jörg Haider, and Wolfgang Schüssel became Chancellor, the first from the ÖVP since 1970. This caused widespread outrage in Europe, and the European Union imposed informal diplomatic sanctions on Austria, the first it had imposed on a member state; they were dropped a few months later after a fact-finding mission by three former European prime ministers, the so-called three wise men. In the 2002 election the ÖVP won 42.27% of the vote. In 2006 it became the junior partner in a grand coalition under Alfred Gusenbauer.

The party is described as Christian democratic, conservative and liberal-conservative, a catch-all party of the centre-right. For most of its existence it defined itself as Catholic and anti-socialist, holding to subsidiarity as set out in the encyclical Quadragesimo anno and to decentralisation. In the first postwar election it presented itself as the Austrian Party and the Party of the centre, and its economic policy generally upheld a social market economy. Its strongholds have long been the rural states of Lower Austria, Upper Austria, Salzburg, Styria, Tyrol and Vorarlberg, while it is less popular in Vienna, Burgenland and Carinthia. With the Social Democratic Party of Austria it has been one of Austria's two traditional major parties.
austro-hungarian-empire: Austria-Hungary was the last phase in the constitutional evolution of the Habsburg monarchy. After the Battle of Mohács in 1526 the Habsburgs assumed the Hungarian throne, and by the Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718 all the former Hungarian territories had passed from the Ottomans to them. Hungary rebelled against Habsburg rule in Rákóczi's War of Independence of 1703 to 1711 and in the Hungarian Revolution of 1848 to 1849, which the Austrian army crushed with Russian help, replacing Hungarian autonomy with absolutist rule from Vienna. After the Austro-Prussian War, which the Peace of Prague of 1866 settled in favour of a Lesser German solution, the Compromise of 1867 created the dual monarchy.

The state was a real union between Cisleithania, the western and northern lands of the former Austrian Empire, and Transleithania, the Kingdom of Hungary. The two halves were co-equal and shared one monarch, titled Emperor of Austria and Apostolic King of Hungary. They conducted a common diplomatic, defence and monetary policy through common ministries of foreign affairs and defence and a finance ministry that paid for them. Croatia-Slavonia was an autonomous region under the Hungarian crown, with its own settlement of 1868.

The economy, largely rural, slowly modernised after 1867. Railways opened remote areas, and by 1913 the combined track length reached 43,280 kilometres. The Austro-Hungarian Bank was established in 1878 with offices in Vienna and Budapest. Vienna was a centre of European modernism, home to the Vienna Secession and to composers such as Gustav Mahler and Arnold Schoenberg.

Austria-Hungary took over Bosnia and Herzegovina under joint rule in 1878 and annexed it in October 1908, provoking the Bosnian crisis. The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 was followed by anti-Serb riots, and the authorities in Bosnia imprisoned or deported about 5,500 prominent Serbs, of whom 700 to 2,200 died in prison. The empire declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914 and fought as one of the Central Powers.

By 1918 the economy had deteriorated and support for the war had gone. Strikes and army uprisings became common, and nationalist movements, encouraged by the Allies, demanded separation. The armistice of Villa Giusti was signed on 3 November 1918, when the state had already effectively dissolved. Hungary and Austria were treated as its successors, and Czechoslovakia, Poland and Yugoslavia were recognised as independent.
austro-prussian-war: After 1815 the German states were organised in the German Confederation under Austrian leadership, but Prussia had been contesting Austria's supremacy since at least 1850. At the time of the war there was no strong national consciousness in Germany, and religion divided the southern Catholic and northern Protestant states. The immediate dispute concerned Schleswig-Holstein, which Prussia and Austria had conquered from Denmark and agreed to occupy jointly at the end of the Second Schleswig War in 1864.

On 8 April 1866 Bismarck made an alliance with Italy, which committed it to war if Prussia fought Austria within three months. Austria mobilised its Southern Army on the Italian border on 21 April, and Prussia's general mobilisation orders were signed in steps in May. Historians differ on whether Bismarck sought the war; he himself later maintained that he had orchestrated it.

Most of the southern German states, including Bavaria and Württemberg, sided with Austria, as did Hanover and Hesse-Kassel. Most northern states joined Prussia, and Italy fought alongside it. Napoleon III of France kept his army unmobilised. The Prussian army used railways to concentrate troops and the Dreyse breech-loading needle gun, which could be loaded while the soldier lay under cover, whereas Austrian muzzle-loading rifles were loaded slowly and generally standing.

On 24 June the Austrians defeated the Italian army at the Battle of Custoza. On 27 June Hanover's army defeated Prussia's at the Battle of Langensalza, though Hanover surrendered two days later. On 3 July the Prussians won an overwhelming victory over the Austrians at the Battle of Königgrätz. On 20 July the Austrian fleet decisively defeated the Italian fleet at the Battle of Lissa.

The Peace of Prague on 23 August 1866 dissolved the German Confederation, brought Prussian annexation of four of Austria's former allies and permanently excluded Austria from German affairs. Austria ceded Venetia to Italy by the Treaty of Vienna, later confirmed by plebiscite. Prussia annexed Schleswig-Holstein, Hanover, Nassau, Hesse-Kassel and Frankfurt, and formed the North German Confederation, finalised the next year, which incorporated the German states north of the Main River. Bavaria lost some small possessions and became a permanent ally against France.
autun: Augustodunum was founded during the reign of Augustus as the tribal capital of the Aedui, Continental Celts who had been allies and brothers of Rome since before Julius Caesar's Gallic Wars. It replaced the original oppidum of Bibracte, about 25 kilometres away. In Roman times it may have held between 30,000 and 100,000 people. In 356 a force of Alemanni besieged Autun, whose walls were in disrepair, and the arrival of Emperor Julian saved it. In late antiquity it became known for its schools of rhetoric.

In 532 the Merovingian kings Childebert I and Chlothar I defeated the Burgundians under King Godomar at the Battle of Autun and took over Burgundy. In 880 Count Richard of Autun was made the first Duke of Burgundy. In 1788 Charles Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord became bishop of Autun. Giuseppe Garibaldi chose the city as headquarters for the Army of the Vosges in 1870.

Autun is a subprefecture of the Saône-et-Loire department, on the Arroux river, with a population of about 13,000. Two Roman gates, the Porte Saint-André and the Porte d'Arroux, and parts of the wall survive. The Roman theatre, one of the largest in the western empire, held 17,000 people.

Autun Cathedral, also called Saint Lazare, dates from the early 12th century and is a major example of Romanesque architecture. It was built as a pilgrimage church for the relic of Saint Lazarus, and bishop Étienne de Bâgé probably built it in response to Ste. Madeleine at nearby Vézelay. Its sculpture, notably the Last Judgment on the west tympanum, is traditionally attributed to Gislebertus, whose name appears there, though it is uncertain whether that is the sculptor's name or a patron's. Oil shale was first mined commercially near Autun in 1837.
auxerre: Auxerre is the capital, or prefecture, of the Yonne department and the fourth-largest city in the historical region of Burgundy, southeast of Paris. It lies on the river Yonne and the Canal du Nivernais, about 150 km southeast of Paris and 120 km northwest of Dijon. It is a commercial and industrial centre, with food production and woodworking among its industries, and neighbouring areas produce Burgundy wines, including Chablis. In 1995 it was named a Town of Art and History.

Auxerre was a flourishing Gallo-Roman centre, called Autissiodorum, through which passed the Via Agrippa of the 1st century CE, which crossed the Yonne here. In the third century it became the seat of a bishop and a provincial capital of the Roman Empire, and in the 5th century it received a cathedral. In the late 11th and early 12th century the existing communities were enclosed within a new line of walls built by the feudal counts of Auxerre.

From the twelfth century bourgeois activities accompanied the cultivation of land and vines, and Auxerre developed into a commune; its Hôtel de Ville was completed, in its original form, in 1452. The Burgundian city, which became part of France under King Louis XI, suffered during the Hundred Years' War and the Wars of Religion, and in 1567 the Huguenots captured it and damaged many Catholic buildings. The medieval ramparts were demolished in the 18th century.

The Cathedral of St Étienne, built from the 11th to the 16th centuries in the Gothic style, has three doorways with bas-reliefs, and its 11th-century crypt houses the remains of the former Romanesque cathedral. The Abbey of Saint-Germain, existing from the 6th century, has in its crypt some of the oldest mural paintings in France and the tomb of the bishops of Auxerre. Germanus of Auxerre, bishop and missionary to Britain, who lived from about 378 to about 442 to 448, is among its notable figures, as is the mathematician Jean Baptiste Joseph Fourier, born in Auxerre in 1768.
avalokitesvara: The name combines ava, down, lokita, looked, and īśvara, lord, and so means the lord who gazed down at the world. The usual Chinese name Guanyin, perceiving sound, comes from the form Avalokitasvara, which is now understood to be the original and appears in Sanskrit fragments from the fifth century. The reading of the name as an īśvara shows Hindu influence, but the mainstream of his devotees kept the Buddhist rejection of any creator god.

Scholars have not agreed on the origin of his veneration. Some suggest Mahayana absorbed Shiva or Vishnu. The scholar Shu Hikosaka proposes that Mount Potalaka, his home in the Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra, is Mount Potigai on the Tamil Nadu and Kerala border. Around 400 CE the monk Faxian saw offerings made to him at Mathura.

In East Asia a female form, the White-Robed Avalokiteśvara, is worshipped as a divine mother. He is counted among the Four Great Bodhisattvas, with Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra and Kṣitigarbha, and assists Amitabha Buddha. A popular story tells that he vowed to rest only when all beings were freed from saṃsāra. His head split into eleven pieces from the effort of grasping their needs, and Amitābha gave him eleven heads; his arms shattered as he reached out, and Amitābha gave him a thousand arms. This Thousand-armed form is among his most popular in China, Japan and Korea. Tibetan tradition has the goddess Tara arise from one of his tears.

In Tibetan Buddhism the central mantra is Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ. Reciting it on prayer beads is the most popular religious practice, and prayer wheels carry repetitions of it. Its link with him is first documented in the Kāraṇḍavyūhasūtra, dated to around the late 4th to early 5th century. In East Asia the 82-syllable Nīlakaṇṭha Dhāraṇī, the Great Compassion Mantra, is very popular.

In Sri Lanka, where he is called Nātha, the Buddhism is almost exclusively Theravada, yet he is the one Mahayana deity to enter the worship of ordinary Buddhists. Many there believe Nātha to be the Buddha yet to come, Maitreya, though the iconography, with an image of Amitābha on the crown, points to Avalokiteśvara. In Myanmar he is Lokanat and in Thailand Lokesvara.
avarua: Avarua is a district and township in the north of Rarotonga, the largest island of the Cook Islands, and one of the island's five districts. The name means two harbours in Māori. The township is built around two harbours, Avatiu Harbour, where the main port is, and Avarua Harbour at Takuvaine, which used to be the main port and is now a small fishing port. The district is divided into 19 tapere, traditional sub-districts. The township is the central business district of Rarotonga and the location of government offices.

The Cook Islands were inhabited largely by indigenous Māori people until the late 19th century. Avarua was not the main centre of Rarotonga until missionaries of the London Missionary Society arrived in 1823 and set up their national headquarters there. Trading ships also based themselves there, and from the middle of the 19th century it was the religious and commercial centre of the Cook Islands. The islands became a British protectorate in 1888, and after the first British resident was appointed Avarua became the administrative and educational centre. The Cook Islands became part of New Zealand in 1901, and a Resident Commissioner governed until 1946, after which they began a transition to self-governance. In 1965 they achieved self-government in free association with New Zealand.

Avarua is the capital of the Cook Islands and an important commercial centre. Rarotonga International Airport and Avatiu Port, the main commercial harbour, are there. The township hosts the Sir Geoffrey Henry National Culture Centre, which includes the National Library and the Cook Islands National Museum. The coastal ring road Ara Tapu encircles the island, and the inner road Ara Metua, built in the 11th century, skirts the interior.
aventine-hill: The Aventine is the southernmost of the seven hills on which ancient Rome was built and belongs to Ripa, the modern twelfth rione of the city. It has two distinct heights, a greater one to the northwest, Aventinus Major, and a lesser one to the southeast, Aventinus Minor, divided by a steep cleft that carried an ancient road. Most Roman sources trace the hill's name to a king named Aventinus, a figure of tradition. In the founding myth, Remus takes his auspices on the Aventine and Romulus on the Palatine.

According to Roman tradition the Aventine lay outside the original city and its sacred boundary, the pomerium. Livy reports that Ancus Marcius, the fourth king, settled the Latins of Politorium there, and Strabo credits him with a wall to include the hill, while others credit Servius Tullius. It served as a staging post for foreign peoples and cults entering Rome. Servius Tullius built a temple of Diana there for the Latin League, and around 493 BCE the Senate provided a temple for Ceres, Liber and Libera, patron deities of the plebs, after one of the first plebeian secessions. Around 456 BCE a Lex Icilia gave the plebs property rights there.

In 392 BCE Camillus established a temple of Juno Regina, and later cults arrived, among them Summanus, Vortumnus and Minerva. In the imperial era the hill became an aristocratic quarter, with the private houses of Trajan and Hadrian before they became emperors and the Baths of Decius, built in 252. Its character probably led to its total destruction in the sack of Rome by Alaric I in 410.

The Aventine is now an elegant residential district with palaces, churches and gardens, among them the basilica of Santa Sabina and the Rome Rose Garden. In the Fascist period, many opposition deputies withdrew there after the murder of Giacomo Matteotti, an episode known as the Aventine Secession, which ended their presence in Parliament.
averroes: Averroes was born in Córdoba on 14 April 1126. His full name was Abu l-Walid Muhammad ibn Ahmad Ibn Rushd, and the nickname al-Hafid, the Grandson, is sometimes added to distinguish him from his grandfather, a noted judge and jurist. His family was well known for public service in legal and religious fields: his grandfather was chief judge of Córdoba and imam of its Great Mosque under the Almoravids, and his father was also chief judge until the Almohads replaced the Almoravids in 1146. By 1153 Averroes was in Marrakesh, the Almohad capital, making astronomical observations and supporting the building of new colleges, and he probably met the philosopher Ibn Tufayl there.

He wrote more than 100 books and treatises on philosophy, medicine, law, theology and linguistics. His commentaries on Aristotle fall into short, middle and long forms; the middle ones were probably written in response to the caliph Abu Yaqub Yusuf's complaints that Aristotle was hard to follow. He tried to return to what he considered the original Aristotle and rejected the Neoplatonist tendencies of al-Farabi and Avicenna.

In 1178 his Decisive Treatise argued that Islam and philosophy are compatible, and his Incoherence of the Incoherence of 1180 answered al-Ghazali's attack on the philosophers. As a Maliki judge he wrote the Bidayat al-Mujtahid, explaining why the schools of Islamic law differ. His General Principles of Medicine, known in Latin as the Colliget, was written around 1162. He might have been the first to see that the retina senses light, although scholars dispute what he meant.

Averroes's works survive chiefly in Hebrew and Latin translations; only a tiny handful of Arabic manuscripts of his long commentaries remain, and his legacy in the Islamic world was modest. In western Europe his commentaries entered in the thirteenth century and led him to be called simply the Commentator. His thesis that all humans share one intellect became the best-known and most controversial doctrine of Averroism, and his works were condemned by the Catholic Church in 1270 and 1277. Latin Averroism nonetheless attracted followers up to the sixteenth century.
aveyron: Aveyron, named after the river Aveyron, is a department in the Occitania region of southern France, and its prefecture is Rodez. It lies at the centre of a triangle formed by Toulouse, Clermont-Ferrand and Montpellier, in the south of the Massif Central, and approximately follows the outline of the former province of Rouergue. With an area of 8,735 square kilometres it is the fifth largest department in metropolitan France, yet largely rural, with 279,609 inhabitants in 2023. It consists of an ancient high rocky plateau, in which the Truyère, Lot, Aveyron and Tarn rivers have carved deep gorges. Its highest point is the Signal de Mailhebiau, at 1,469 m on the Plateau of Aubrac.

The earliest known inhabitants were the Rutenii tribe, though the area was inhabited before them, and the inhabitants of Rodez are still called Ruthénois after them. The department has many prehistoric monuments, including over a thousand dolmens, the most of any department in France. Until the 1790s the territory formed a province known as Rouergue. Aveyron is one of the original 83 departments created on 4 March 1790.

In 1797 Victor of Aveyron, a feral child, was found wandering the woods in the area, and his story is told in the film The Wild Child. In 1817 a local prosecutor, Antoine Bernardin Fualdès, was assassinated, and the sordid circumstances, in which his body was found floating in the river Aveyron, made the matter a cause célèbre. Recent studies indicate that he died at the initiative of a royalist organisation known as the Chevaliers de la Foi.

The regional dialect is Rouergat, a form of Languedoc Occitan. Several associations have asked the state for an ambitious language policy because of the risk of its disappearance. The department is known for Roquefort cheese, from the village of that name, and the couteau de Laguiole. Among its monuments are the medieval castle ruin of Najac and the abbeys of Conques, Sylvanès, Bonneval and Loc-Dieu. At Millau the Millau viaduct was opened in December 2004. Ten of its villages belong to the association Les Plus Beaux Villages de France, founded in 1901.
avicenna: Avicenna was born around 980 in the village of Afshana in Transoxiana, to a Persian family. The village was near the Samanid capital of Bukhara, his mother's hometown. His father Abd Allah, a native of Balkh, was a Samanid official who had governed a village of the royal estate of Harmaytan during the reign of Nuh II. The family soon settled in Bukhara, a centre of learning, where Avicenna was educated, seemingly at first by his father. Under the Samanids Bukhara rivalled Baghdad as a cultural capital, and he had access to the great libraries of Balkh, Khwarazm, Gorgan, Rey, Isfahan and Hamadan.

At 17 Avicenna was made a physician of Nuh II. When he was at least 21 his father died, and he was given an administrative post, possibly succeeding his father as governor of Harmaytan. He later moved to Gurganj, the capital of Khwarazm, which he reports he did out of necessity, and served the Ma'munid ruler Abu al-Hasan Ali, who ruled from 997 to 1009.

He may have left in 999, when the Samanid Empire fell after the Kara-Khanid Khanate captured Bukhara and imprisoned the emir Abd al-Malik II; his close ties to the Samanids may have left him in an unfavourable position. While imprisoned in the castle of Fardajan near Hamadhan, he wrote the thought experiment known as the floating man.

Of about 450 works he is believed to have written, around 240 survive, including 150 on philosophy and 40 on medicine. He wrote mostly in Arabic and some in Early New Persian, notably the Danishnama. The Canon of Medicine, in five books, postulated that invisible tainted organisms were associated with disease and recommended isolating the ill. It served as a standard medical textbook in the Islamic world and Europe up to the 18th century. The Book of Healing, begun in 1014 and completed around 1020, treats logic, natural sciences, mathematics and metaphysics, not medicine.

His philosophy belongs to the Peripatetic school derived from Aristotle, though his commentaries often criticised Aristotle. In the floating man, a person suspended in the air and cut off from all sensation would still be self-aware, which he took to show that the soul is an immaterial substance. The historian of philosophy Peter Adamson calls his Proof of the Truthful, which identifies an entity that cannot not exist with God, one of the most influential medieval arguments for God's existence.
avignon: Avignon lies on the left bank of the Rhône, a few kilometres above its confluence with the Durance, about 580 km south-east of Paris, 229 km south of Lyon and 85 km north-north-west of Marseille. The river passes the western edge of the city in two branches, the Petit Rhône and the Grand Rhône, separated by the Île de la Barthelasse. The region is rich in limestone, and the present city walls, 4,330 metres long, were built of the soft limestone called mollasse burdigalienne. The climate is mediterranean, though sheltered inland, and the city is often windy, the strongest wind being the mistral. A medieval Latin proverb called it windy Avignon, pest-ridden when there is no wind and wind-pestered when there is.

The earliest forms of the name were reported by Greek writers, among them Strabo and Ptolemy. The Roman name Avennio Cavarum, in Mela and Pliny, shows that Avignon was one of the three cities of the Celtic-Ligurian tribe of the Cavares, with Cavaillon and Orange. Between 1309 and 1377, during the Avignon Papacy, seven successive popes resided in the city. In 1348 Pope Clement VI bought the town from Joanna I of Naples. Papal control persisted until 1791, when it became part of France during the French Revolution, which is why Avignon is also known as La Cité des Papes. Pope Gregory XI, born around 1329 and dead in 1378, was the seventh and last of the Avignon popes.

The medieval University of Avignon grew out of the schools already in the city and was formally constituted in 1303 by Boniface VIII in a papal bull. Boniface VIII and King Charles II of Naples were its first great protectors and benefactors. Its law department, covering both civil and ecclesiastical law, was the most important throughout the university's existence. Avignon absorbed Montfavet between 1790 and 1794, ceded Morières-lès-Avignon in 1870 and ceded Le Pontet in 1925.

Avignon is the prefecture of the Vaucluse department in the region of Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur, with 92,188 inhabitants in 2023. About 16,000 live in the ancient centre enclosed by the medieval walls, one of the few in France to have preserved its mediaeval city walls. The centre includes the Palais des Papes, Avignon Cathedral and the Pont d'Avignon, and was listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 1995. The Festival d'Avignon, founded in 1947, brings theatre, dance, music and cinema to the town's historic monuments each summer. The song Sur le Pont d'Avignon dates from the mid-19th century, when Adolphe Adam included it in an opéra comique first performed in Paris in 1853.
avila: Ávila lies in the centre of the Iberian Peninsula, north of the Sistema Central, on the right bank of the Adaja, a tributary of the Duero. At 1,132 metres above sea level it is the highest provincial capital in Spain. It is built on the flat summit of a rocky hill that stands above a brown, arid, treeless table-land strewn with grey boulders. Annual precipitation is 416 mm, and the Adaja is dry for several months of the year, so the town has historically had water supply problems.

In pre-Roman times, in the 5th century BCE, Ávila was inhabited by the Vettones, who called it Obila, meaning high mountain, and built one of their strongest fortresses there. Bronze Age stone statues of boars, known as verracos, stand nearby. The Roman town, called Abila or Abela, kept a rectangular plan with two main streets crossing at a forum. By tradition Secundus brought the Gospel to Ávila in the 1st century and became its first bishop.

After the fall of the Western Roman Empire Ávila became a stronghold of the Visigoths. The Moors conquered it, and as northern Christian kingdoms repeatedly attacked it, it became a virtually uninhabited no man's land. It was repopulated about 1088 after Raymond of Burgundy, son-in-law of Alfonso VI of León and Castile, definitively reconquered the area. Tradition holds that he employed two foreigners, Casandro Romano and Florin de Pontuenga, to build the walls that still stand. Ávila had a Jewish community, documented from 1144, which ceased to exist after the expulsion of 1492.

During the Revolt of the Comuneros the Santa Junta first met there on 1 August 1520, and in the summer it drafted in the cathedral the Proyecto de Ley Perpetua, a proto-constitutional draft that never came into force. A long decline from the 17th century reduced the population to just 4,000.

Ávila is the capital of the Province of Ávila in Castile and León, sometimes called the City of Stones and Saints. Its Old Town and the churches outside the walls became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985. The walls, begun in 1090 and built between the 11th and 14th centuries, enclose 31 hectares with a perimeter of 2,516 metres, 88 towers and nine gates. Saint Teresa, the town's best-known resident and the first female Doctor of the Church, founded the Convent of Saint Joseph, the first of the Discalced Carmelite nuns, in 1562.
avitus: Eparchius Avitus was born at Avernia, the present Clermont-Ferrand, into a family of the Gallo-Roman nobility. His daughter Papianilla married the writer Sidonius Apollinaris, whose letters and panegyrics are an important source for his life. Avitus came to know the Gothic court: around 439 he met the future Theodoric II, whom he inspired to study the Latin poets. He served under the general Aetius against the Burgundians and defeated Hunnic raiders near Avernia in 437, and in 439 he became praetorian prefect of Gaul. In 451, when Attila invaded, he persuaded Theodoric to ally with Rome.

In 455 Emperor Petronius Maximus sent Avitus as an envoy to Theodoric II at Toulouse. While he was there news arrived that Maximus was dead and that Rome had been sacked by the Vandals under Gaiseric. Theodoric proclaimed Avitus emperor, and on 9 July the Gallic chiefs at Viernum did the same; about 5 August the Senate recognised him. He entered Rome on 21 September. He brought several Gallic senators into the administration, a policy opposed by the Roman aristocracy and people, and on 1 January 456 he took the consulate alone, which the Eastern court refused to recognise.

At his request Theodoric invaded Hispania, and on 5 October 456 the Visigoths defeated the Suebi on the Órbigo, but this left them unable to help him at home. Rome suffered from food shortages, and the treasury was so empty that Avitus melted down bronze statues to pay the Gothic guard he had been forced to disband. The generals Ricimer and Majorian rebelled, and the Senate deposed him. He fought them near Piacenza on 17 or 18 October 456, fled, and was spared on condition that he became Bishop of Piacenza.

The manner and date of Avitus's death are uncertain. Gregory of Tours says he died while travelling to Gaul to bring gifts to the basilica of Saint Julian; other sources have him strangled or starved on his successor's orders. He died in 457 or late in 456 and was buried at Brioude beside the tomb of Saint Julian.
avranches: Avranches is a subprefecture of the Manche department, at the southern end of the Cotentin Peninsula, where the E40 road links Saint-Lô with Brittany. The town was founded on high ground overlooking the dunes and coastal marshes of the bay between the Cotentin and Brittany, and from it Mont Saint-Michel can be seen. The mount was founded by Saint Aubert, Bishop of Avranches, in the 8th century. The inhabitants are called Avranchinais.

By the end of the Roman period the settlement of Ingena, capital of the Abrincatui, had taken the name of the tribe, which became Avranches. In 511 it became the seat of a diocese, suppressed in 1790, and later of a major Romanesque cathedral dedicated to Saint Andrew, dismantled during the Revolution. Around the turn of the 10th century the Avranchin was briefly held by Alan I of the Kingdom of Brittany, and in 933 Avranches and its territory were ceded to the Normans. Hugh d'Avranches, 1st Earl of Chester, a magnate under William the Conqueror, was the son of Richard le Goz, Vicomte d'Avranches.

A council was held at Avranches on 27 and 28 September 1172 after the murder of Thomas Becket. Henry II of England did penance there on 21 May 1172, swore fidelity to Pope Alexander III in the person of the papal legate and was absolved, reaching the Compromise of Avranches with the Church. The town was damaged in the Hundred Years' War and the Wars of Religion. On 8 August 1444 Henry VI of England made Álvaro Vaz de Almada the 1st Count of Avranches.

The town lost influence after the French Revolution, when the diocese was abolished and schools were closed, and it was occupied and raided by republican troops and by Chouans. The diocese was restored in 1802 as part of the Diocese of Coutances. Many English families settled there after the Treaty of Paris of 1814. The liberation of Avranches, led by General George S. Patton, began on 31 July 1944 and is regarded as the start of Operation Cobra, called La Percée d'Avranches in French.

Le Scriptorial museum houses the manuscripts of Mont Saint-Michel, deposited in the municipal archives during the Revolution, one of the largest collections of medieval illuminated manuscripts in France outside national and university libraries. A grassed terrace, La Plate-Forme, overlooking the bay, marks the site of the destroyed cathedral where Henry II did penance. The Gothic Revival church of Notre Dame des Champs was built in the 19th century, and the Basilica of Saint Gervasius and Protasius holds a treasury with the purported skull of Saint Aubert, probably a prehistoric trepanned skull. Botanical gardens were founded in the late 18th century in the grounds of a Franciscan convent.
avvakum: Avvakum Petrov was born about 1620 in Grigorovo, in what is now the Nizhny Novgorod region, to a priest named Pyotr and a nun, Maria. By his own account he became a deacon at twenty-one and an archpriest at Yurevyets at twenty-eight. In the late 1640s he and the future Patriarch Nikon belonged to the Zealots of Piety, a circle that aimed to purify religious life. When Nikon became patriarch in 1652, he began reforms intended mainly to bring Russian liturgy into line with other Eastern Orthodox churches, including changing the sign of the cross from two fingers to three. Avvakum rejected them as a corruption of the Russian Church.

For his opposition Avvakum was repeatedly imprisoned and exiled. In 1653 he and his family were sent to Tobolsk in Siberia, and later he went with Afanasy Pashkov's expedition to Dauria on the Chinese border, in which two of his sons died. Allowed to return to Moscow in 1664, after Nikon was no longer patriarch, he was exiled again, to Mezen. The Great Moscow Synod of 1666–1667 anathematised all who refused the changes, and Avvakum and his fellow Old Believers Lazar, Fyodor and Epifany were banished to Pustozersk, above the Arctic Circle. From 1670 they were condemned to a life on bread and water in a dugout. On 14 April 1682 they were burned alive in a log house.

During his imprisonment Avvakum wrote his autobiography, The Life Written by Himself. The first version was drafted in 1669–1672, with three more redactions to 1675. He called it a zhitie, a hagiography, and it tells of his struggle against the reforms, his sufferings in Siberia, his exorcisms and his love of nature. It circulated in manuscript for nearly two centuries before it was first printed in 1861. Viktor Vinogradov observed that it combines high literary language with vernacular, colloquialisms and profanity. Scholars such as Alan Wood regard it as a prototype of Siberian prison literature. Groups rejecting the liturgical changes survived his death and came to be called the Old Believers.
awash-river: The Awash is about 1,200 kilometres long and runs entirely within Ethiopia. It rises at an elevation of about 3,000 metres in the central highlands, west of Addis Ababa, then enters the floor of the Great Rift Valley, loops around Mount Zuqualla, passes the city of Adama and the Awash National Park, and is joined by its chief tributary, the Germama or Kasam. It ends in a chain of linked lakes that begins with Lake Gargori and finishes at Lake Abbe, on the border with Djibouti, at about 250 metres. It is the principal stream of a basin with no outlet to the sea, which covers about a tenth of Ethiopia.

The Awash Valley, and above all the Middle Awash, has a very high density of fossil hominins, dating from roughly 5.6 to 2.5 million years ago. They include many Australopithecines, among them Lucy, together with Ardipithecus and Homo erectus. The lower valley was inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 1980 for its palaeontological and anthropological importance.

In the 16th century the river was called the great Dir river and lay in the country of the Muslims. The valley from about 9° N downstream is the traditional home of the Afar people and the Issa Somali clan, and it has been counted as part of the historic regions of Fatagar, Ifat and Shewa. The first European to follow the river to its end, in the oasis of Aussa and Lake Abbe, was Wilfred Thesiger in 1933 and 1934.

The Koka Dam, completed across the river in 1960 about 75 kilometres from Addis Ababa, provides hydroelectric power and created Lake Gelila, also called the Koka Reservoir, which covers about 180 square kilometres. The river and its tributaries supply water to Addis Ababa and other towns and to irrigated farmland, including sugar-cane plantations. The lower valley is one of the last refuges of the African wild ass.
axis-powers: The Italian prime minister Benito Mussolini first applied the word axis to the Italo-German relationship in September 1923, writing that the axis of European history was passing through Berlin; he was then seeking an alliance with the Weimar Republic against Yugoslavia and France. After negotiations between Galeazzo Ciano and Ulrich von Hassell, Ciano and Konstantin von Neurath signed a Nine-Point Protocol in 1936, and on 1 November Mussolini announced a Rome-Berlin axis.

The Anti-Comintern Pact, an anti-communist treaty between Germany and Japan, was ratified in November 1936. Italy joined it in 1937, followed by Hungary and Spain in 1939. The Rome-Berlin Axis became a military alliance under the Pact of Steel, and the Tripartite Pact of 1940 formally integrated the military aims of Germany, Italy and Japan.

Six other countries signed the Tripartite Pact. Hungary was the first, on 20 November 1940, under Regent Miklós Horthy. Slovakia, Bulgaria, the Independent State of Croatia and Romania also took part in Axis military operations, while Yugoslavia's signatory government was overthrown in a coup days after it signed, and the membership was reversed. Japan set up puppet governments in occupied China, merged on 29 March 1940 into the Reorganized National Government at Nanjing under Wang Jingwei, which had no real power. A State of Burma was formed on 1 August 1943 under Ba Maw.

When Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, the Tripartite Pact required Germany and Italy to help only if Japan were attacked, yet Hitler ordered the Reichstag to declare war on the United States, and Italy also declared war.
